(2) Off-hours activity -- service account active at 2AM when scheduled tasks don't run at that time; compare against known-good baseline. (3) Unusual network connections -- service account's process making outbound connections to unknown external IPs. (4) New SPNs added -- Kerberoasting generates new TGS tickets; monitor EventCode=4769 for service accounts with encryption type 0x17 (RC4). (5) Password spray signals -- EventCode=4771 (Kerberos pre-auth failure) spike against service account. INVESTIGATION: (6) Timeline reconstruction -- pull all authentication events for the account from SIEM; map: when first seen, what systems accessed, what actions taken. (7) Process lineage -- on compromised host, trace what process used the service account credentials; parent-child process chain leads to initial compromise vector. (8) Lateral movement -- what other systems did the attacker access with this account? Pivot to those systems' logs. (9) Privilege assessment -- what can this service account do? Map permissions (AD group memberships, ACLs on file shares, SQL server permissions, cloud IAM); understand attacker's potential access. (10) Data access -- did attacker access sensitive data? Check file share audit logs (EventCode=5145), database audit logs, SharePoint access logs. REMEDIATION: Immediately reset service account password; rotate all credentials the account had access to (API keys in config files, vault secrets); review and trim permissions; implement LAPS-equivalent for service accounts; consider gMSA (auto-rotating password).
What is endpoint detection and response (EDR)?

EDR (Endpoint Detection and Response): security technology that continuously monitors endpoint devices (laptops, servers) to detect, investigate, and respond to threats. Core capabilities: real-time monitoring of: process creation, network connections, file system changes, registry modifications, memory operations, parent-child process relationships; behavioural detection (not just signature-based); threat hunting query interface; automated response (isolate host, kill process, quarantine file); forensic data collection. How it differs from antivirus: traditional AV: signature-based (known malware hashes and patterns); reactive; limited visibility; EDR: behavioural analysis; detects novel threats; full telemetry; enables investigation of how attacker moved through system; records everything for retrospective analysis. Detection approaches: YARA rules (file pattern matching); behavioural heuristics (process injection pattern, credential dumping behaviour, lateral movement); machine learning anomaly detection; threat intelligence integration (known bad hashes, IPs, domains). Response capabilities: network isolation (cut off compromised endpoint from network while maintaining management channel); process kill (terminate malicious process); file quarantine (move to isolated location); rollback (some EDRs can undo file changes made by ransomware); remote shell for IR team. Leading vendors: CrowdStrike Falcon (agent lightweight; cloud-native analysis; Threat Graph database); SentinelOne (autonomous AI response; Storyline AI for attack reconstruction); Microsoft Defender for Endpoint (built-in Windows; tight Azure integration; good value); Carbon Black (VMware; strong threat hunting); Palo Alto Cortex XDR. XDR (Extended Detection and Response): evolution of EDR; integrates endpoint, network, cloud, email telemetry; single pane of glass; correlates across all sources; Palo Alto Cortex XDR, CrowdStrike XDR, Microsoft Defender XDR. Evasion techniques attackers use: direct syscalls (bypass user-mode hooks); process injection into trusted processes; disabling EDR (requires admin or kernel exploit to unload driver); BYOVD (bring your own vulnerable driver -- exploit legitimate signed driver to gain kernel access and disable EDR sensor).
What is vulnerability disclosure and how does responsible disclosure work?

Vulnerability disclosure: process of reporting security vulnerabilities found in software, hardware, or services to those who can fix them. Types: Full disclosure: publish all vulnerability details immediately without notifying vendor; vendor has no time to patch; defenders can protect by awareness but attackers can exploit before patches; controversial; used historically when vendors ignored researchers (Bugtraq mailing list). Responsible/Coordinated disclosure: researcher notifies vendor privately; vendor given time to patch (typically 90 days); after patch released (or deadline passes): researcher publishes details publicly; standard today; balances vendor time to fix with researcher right to publish. 90-day disclosure deadline: Google Project Zero (P0) standardised 90-day deadline; after 90 days: publish regardless of patch status (with 7-day extension if patch imminent); forces vendors to prioritise security patches; some vendors (Apple, Microsoft) occasionally miss deadline. CVE process: security researcher or vendor submits to CVE Numbering Authority (CNA) -- organisations authorised to assign CVEs (100+ CNAs include major vendors, GitHub Security Lab, CERT/CC); CVE assigned identifier (CVE-2024-1234); published to NVD (National Vulnerability Database) with CVSS score. Bug bounty earnings: high-end researchers (full-time): $500K+ annually; top finds: $2M (Apple iBoot 4-chain RCE); $1M+ (Exodus Intelligence pays for zero-days).
What is network segmentation and microsegmentation?

Network segmentation: dividing network into segments (subnetworks) to limit lateral movement and contain breaches. Traditional segmentation: VLAN (Virtual LAN): logical separation at Layer 2; different VLANs cannot communicate without routing through firewall; separate VLANs for: servers, workstations, printers, guest Wi-Fi, IoT devices, DMZ (externally accessible servers), OT/ICS; firewall rules between VLANs enforce what traffic is permitted. DMZ (Demilitarised Zone): separate network segment hosting internet-facing servers (web, email, DNS); inbound from internet to DMZ allowed for specific services; DMZ to internal network strictly controlled; outbound from internal to DMZ allowed; prevents direct internet-to-internal connection. Network Access Control (NAC): policy-based control of device access to network; checks device posture (domain-joined, AV running, patches current) before granting network access; quarantine non-compliant devices to remediation VLAN; Cisco ISE, Aruba ClearPass, Forescout NAC solutions. Microsegmentation: granular segmentation at individual workload or application level; goes beyond VLAN-level segmentation; implemented via: software-defined networking (SDN); host-based firewalling (every server has per-process firewall rules); cloud security groups (AWS: security group per EC2 instance; only required ports between specific security groups); Kubernetes NetworkPolicy (pod-to-pod traffic control); service mesh (Istio, Linkerd: mutual TLS between microservices; policy at API call level). Zero Trust and microsegmentation: microsegmentation key component of Zero Trust; assumes breach; if attacker compromises one workload: cannot reach others due to explicit-deny rules; limits blast radius. Benefits: contains breach to single segment; reduces attacker lateral movement; compliance (PCI DSS: cardholder data environment separated from other networks); reduces attack surface. Implementation challenges: requires comprehensive understanding of all network flows; initial mapping of legitimate traffic is complex; legacy applications with hard-coded IP addresses; performance impact of inspection at every segment boundary.
What are common web API vulnerabilities beyond OWASP Top 10?

API-specific vulnerabilities extending beyond classic OWASP Top 10: Mass assignment: REST APIs auto-bind request JSON to object properties; attacker sends extra fields (isAdmin:true, role:admin, balance:1000000) not in UI form; API framework assigns all fields including privileged ones without explicit filtering; defence: explicit DTO (Data Transfer Object) with only allowed fields; allowlist approach in serialisation. GraphQL vulnerabilities: introspection query discloses entire API schema (fields, types, mutations); no introspection in production: disable or limit to authenticated users; deeply nested queries (N+1 problem): recursive query nesting causes exponential database queries = DoS; query depth limiting and complexity analysis; batching attacks: send hundreds of mutations in single request bypassing rate limiting (batch multiple login attempts = brute force bypass). Server-side parameter pollution (SSPP): inject additional parameters into server-side requests: GET /api/user?id=123 -> server calls backend: GET /backend/user?id=123; inject: id=123&admin=true -> GET /backend/user?id=123&admin=true; if backend trusts these parameters: privilege escalation. HTTP verb tampering: some APIs restrict POST but allow PUT or PATCH to same endpoint without auth check; test all HTTP methods against all endpoints. API versioning: v1 API deprecated but not removed; security controls only added to v2; access v1 endpoints to bypass security; test /api/v1/, /api/v2/, /api/beta/, /api/test/. JWT kid SQL injection: kid (key ID) parameter used in database lookup without sanitisation; SQL injection in JWT kid to bypass signature verification. Webhook vulnerabilities: attacker-controlled URLs in webhook configuration (SSRF); unvalidated webhook delivery (anyone can trigger your webhook endpoint if URL guessable); missing signature verification on incoming webhooks. API documentation as attack surface: public Swagger/OpenAPI docs reveal all endpoints, parameters, authentication requirements; developer test endpoints left in production; postman collections accidentally committed to GitHub revealing internal API details.
How do you exploit prototype pollution vulnerabilities?

Prototype pollution: JavaScript vulnerability where attacker can modify base Object prototype; all JavaScript objects inherit from Object.prototype; modifying it affects all objects in application. JavaScript prototype chain: every object inherits from Object.prototype; property lookup traverses prototype chain; if obj.x not found: check obj.__proto__.x (Object.prototype.x); if attacker sets Object.prototype.isAdmin = true: all objects gain isAdmin property. How it works: vulnerable code merges user-controlled keys into objects without sanitisation: function merge(target, source) { for (let key in source) { target[key] = source[key]; } }; attacker provides {__proto__: {isAdmin: true}} as source; merge loop processes __proto__ key; sets target.__proto__.isAdmin = true -- pollutes Object prototype; all objects now have isAdmin:true. Client-side prototype pollution: in browser JavaScript; attacker controls JSON parsed and merged; can override security checks: if (user.isAdmin) grantAccess(); is bypassed if isAdmin polluted onto Object.prototype. Server-side prototype pollution (Node.js): more dangerous; can lead to RCE; lodash merge, deep-merge, and similar utilities historically vulnerable; CVEs in lodash, qs, jquery (now patched); hoek (Hapi.js utility) had prototype pollution. From pollution to RCE in Node.js: pollute properties used in shell execution: if spawn uses options.shell = false; polluting shell to true via prototype: spawn({shell: true}) = shell injection; Nodemailer SSRP: pollute outputEncoding used in child_process.spawn options. Finding: use vulnerability scanners (snyk); manual: submit {__proto__: {polluted: true}} in JSON bodies; check if all subsequent objects have polluted:true; client-side: check URL parameters merged into objects. Tools: ppmap (prototype pollution scanner); Burp Suite extension for prototype pollution. Fixes: Object.create(null) for dictionaries (no prototype chain); use Map instead of Object; validate/sanitise keys before merging (block __proto__, constructor, prototype keys); use safe merge libraries (like lodash 4.17.21+); freeze Object.prototype: Object.freeze(Object.prototype).
What is serialisation and deserialisation vulnerabilities?

Deserialisation vulnerabilities: insecure deserialisation of attacker-controlled data; can lead to RCE, privilege escalation, or DoS; OWASP Top 10 A08 (2021). How it works: serialisation converts object to storable/transmissible format (JSON, XML, YAML, Java serialised bytes, Python pickle, PHP serialised strings); deserialisation reconstructs object from data; if attacker controls serialised data: can modify object properties, invoke methods during deserialisation, trigger gadget chains leading to code execution. Java deserialisation: Java ObjectInputStream.readObject() is dangerous entry point; gadget chains: reuse existing classes (in classpath) to achieve RCE without custom code; ysoserial tool generates payloads for common gadget chains (CommonsCollections, Spring, JDK); vulnerable formats: Java serialised objects (magic bytes AC ED 00 05 in base64: rO0AB...); affected: JBoss, WebLogic, Jenkins, WebSphere historically. Python pickle: pickle.loads() executes arbitrary Python code; pickle.loads(attacker_data) = instant RCE; never unpickle untrusted data; example payload: class Exploit(object): def __reduce__(self): return (os.system, (id,)). PHP serialisation: unserialize() with magic methods (__wakeup, __destruct, __toString); PHP object injection: inject serialised object with malicious magic method calls; Joomla, WordPress plugins historically vulnerable; POP (Property Oriented Programming) chains similar to Java gadget chains. JSON/YAML: JSON itself safe (no code execution); but type confusion: JSON input mapped to class with dangerous properties; YAML: yaml.load() without Loader in Python = arbitrary Python execution; yaml.safe_load() required; Ruby YAML/Marshal. Detection: intercept serialised data in transit; identify format (Java: AC ED, PHP: O:, Python: base64 of pickle); replace with generated payload; test for RCE via DNS callback to Burp Collaborator. Mitigation: avoid deserialisation of untrusted data; use safer formats (JSON) where possible; Java: use ObjectInputFilter to whitelist allowed classes (Java 9+); sign and verify serialised data before deserialisation; monitor for deserialisation class loading anomalies.
What is SSRF (Server-Side Request Forgery) and how do you exploit it?

SSRF: attacker tricks server into making HTTP request to attacker-specified URL; server makes requests using its own credentials and network access; attacker uses server as proxy. Basic SSRF: web application fetches URL based on user input: http://target.com/fetch?url=USER_INPUT; change to: ?url=http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/ (AWS metadata); server fetches and returns cloud metadata (AWS credentials). Impact varies by context: cloud metadata (AWS IMDSv1): ?url=http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/ROLE = AWS access keys; internal services: ?url=http://192.168.1.1/admin (access admin interface not internet-accessible); port scanning: ?url=http://192.168.1.1:22 (different responses for open vs closed ports reveal internal network topology); local file: ?url=file:///etc/passwd (if file:// URI supported); blind SSRF: no response but server makes request -- use Burp Collaborator for DNS/HTTP callbacks. Bypassing SSRF filters: whitelist bypass: developer blocks 169.254.169.254; bypass: octal IP: http://0251.0376.0251.0376 (169.254.169.254 in octal); hex: http://0xa9fea9fe; decimal: http://2852039166; IPv6: http://[::ffff:169.254.169.254]; DNS rebinding: evil.com initially resolves to benign IP (passes filter), rebinds to 169.254.169.254 (real request hits metadata); URL redirection: ?url=http://redirect.attacker.com/metadata (server follows redirect to 169.254.169.254); alternative URL schemes: gopher:// (sends arbitrary TCP data -- pivot to Redis, Memcached; gopher://redis:6379/_SET key malicious_value). SSRF to RCE: reach internal Jenkins with SSRF; trigger Groovy script execution; reach Kubernetes API; reach Redis; SSRF + deserialization; SSRF to cloud metadata = credential theft = full cloud compromise. Real examples: Capital One breach (2019) via SSRF + excessive IAM permissions; GitLab SSRF vulnerabilities; multiple SSRF via PDF generators, image processors, URL previews. Detection: all HTTP requests made by server: are source URLs user-controllable? Does server return response body? Does server follow redirects? Headers: X-Forwarded-For might reach internal services; blind SSRF: DNS resolution still occurs even if HTTP response not returned. Mitigation: allowlist of permitted domains/IPs; block private IP ranges (RFC1918) and link-local; use IMDSv2 (requires PUT pre-flight token -- blocks SSRF without session token); disable file:// and gopher:// URI schemes; no redirect following on user-supplied URLs.
How do web application firewalls work and what are their limitations?

WAF (Web Application Firewall): security appliance or service that inspects HTTP/HTTPS traffic and blocks malicious requests before they reach web application. How WAFs work: pattern matching: inspect request (URL, headers, body, cookies) for known attack signatures (SQLi patterns: UNION SELECT; XSS patterns: <script>; LFI:../etc/passwd); OWASP Core Rule Set (CRS): open-source rule set for ModSecurity WAF; regularly updated with signatures for known attacks; rate limiting: block IPs making too many requests per second; GeoIP blocking: block requests from specific countries or Tor exit nodes; bot detection: challenge suspicious visitors with CAPTCHA or JavaScript challenges; identify headless browsers, known bot user-agents; anomaly scoring: each matched rule adds score; total score above threshold = block; avoids single-rule false positives. Deployment modes: inline (active blocking): WAF between internet and web app; inspects and blocks in real-time; adds latency; network WAF (hardware appliance), cloud WAF (Cloudflare, AWS WAF, Akamai Kona); reverse proxy WAF (NGINX + ModSecurity, HAProxy). Detection-only mode: log and alert without blocking; safe for initial deployment; tune rules before enabling blocking. Limitations: cannot inspect encrypted traffic without TLS termination at WAF; false positives: legitimate requests blocked (developer submitting code snippet blocked for injection patterns); false negatives: novel attacks not matching signatures pass through; complex obfuscated payloads bypass regex-based signatures (URL encoding, Unicode, HTTP parameter pollution); application-level logic flaws bypass WAF (IDOR, mass assignment, business logic -- no malicious pattern to detect); WAF is not substitute for secure coding; performance overhead (latency, throughput); maintenance burden (tuning rules to reduce false positives); attackers specifically target WAF bypass techniques for known WAF products (ModSecurity CRS bypass techniques published openly); real-time threat intelligence integration required to stay current.
What are container escape techniques?

Container escape: breakout from Docker/container isolation to host OS or other containers. Privileged container escape: docker run --privileged gives all capabilities and host device access; fdisk -l shows host disks; mount /dev/sda1 /mnt; access entire host filesystem; install cron backdoor; escape complete; check privilege: cat /proc/self/status | grep CapEff (EffCap = 0000003fffffffff means all capabilities = privileged). Volume mount escape: if host directory mounted into container with -v /:/host: chroot /host /bin/bash = host root shell; or -v /etc:/host-etc: overwrite /host-etc/crontab. Docker socket mount escape: if Docker socket mounted: -v /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock; docker.sock access = control Docker daemon on host; create new privileged container: docker run -v /:/mnt --privileged --rm ubuntu chroot /mnt bash; read entire host from within new container. Capability exploitation: CAP_SYS_ADMIN: mount filesystems, load kernel modules; CAP_NET_ADMIN: configure network, sniff traffic; CAP_SYS_PTRACE: ptrace host processes (if PID namespace shared); individual dangerous capabilities can enable escape without full --privileged. Kernel exploit: container shares host kernel; kernel vulnerability exploitable from within container to gain root on host; affects all containers on host; Dirty COW (CVE-2016-5195) exploitable from container. cgroup escape (CVE-2022-0492): unpriv cgroup mount + cgroup release_agent escape technique; write to release_agent file triggers host command; complex conditions required. runc vulnerability (CVE-2019-5736): overwrite runc binary from within container via /proc/self/exe; any docker exec or docker run triggers overwritten binary on host. Mitigation: read-only root filesystem (--read-only); drop all capabilities, add only needed (--cap-drop ALL --cap-add NET_BIND_SERVICE); no privileged containers in production; seccomp profiles (restrict system calls); AppArmor/SELinux MAC policies for containers; rootless Docker (containers run as non-root user on host); Kata Containers (lightweight VM isolation instead of shared kernel); gVisor (sandboxed kernel).
What is the OWASP API Security Top 10?

OWASP API Security Top 10 (2023): framework specifically for API vulnerabilities, distinct from standard OWASP Top 10. API1:2023 Broken Object Level Authorisation (BOLA/IDOR): most common; user A accesses user B resources by changing object ID; test by swapping IDs between accounts. API2:2023 Broken Authentication: weak authentication mechanisms; missing token expiry; JWT algorithm none; weak API keys (sequential, short); missing rate limiting on auth endpoints. API3:2023 Broken Object Property Level Authorisation: combine mass assignment + excessive data exposure; API returns full database object exposing sensitive fields (hashed password, internal IDs, admin flags); attacker also able to write admin-only fields via mass assignment; check what extra fields can be written and what extra fields are returned. API4:2023 Unrestricted Resource Consumption: no rate limiting on resource-intensive operations; bulk actions consume backend resources; SMS sending APIs without limits (expensive); large file upload without quota; GraphQL N+1 without query complexity limits; financial cost to provider + DoS. API5:2023 Broken Function Level Authorisation (BFLA): unauthorised access to administrative functions; regular user calls admin-only endpoints; GET /api/users works for regular user but POST /api/admin/users should not; missing authorisation checks on administrative operations. API6:2023 Unrestricted Access to Sensitive Business Flows: legitimate endpoint abused for malicious business purpose; buy unlimited items at discount; create unlimited accounts; enumerate valid users via account existence check; automated attacks on business logic without technical vulnerability. API7:2023 Server Side Request Forgery: API fetches URLs on behalf of user; SSRF via API parameter; webhook URL, image URL, external content fetch parameters. API8:2023 Security Misconfiguration: missing security headers; verbose error messages; unnecessary HTTP methods enabled; default credentials; unpatched API frameworks; CORS misconfiguration. API9:2023 Improper Inventory Management: outdated API versions (/api/v1/) not decommissioned; development/debug endpoints in production; shadow APIs not in documentation; test environments with weaker security. API10:2023 Unsafe Consumption of APIs: third-party API data processed without validation; SQL injection via data from trusted third-party API; SSRF via webhook from external service; trust but verify all inputs even from trusted APIs.
What is secrets management and how do you implement it?

Secrets management: secure storage, access control, rotation, and auditing of credentials, API keys, tokens, and other sensitive values used by applications and humans. Problem: hardcoded secrets in source code (committed to Git); secrets in configuration files (deployed with app); secrets in environment variables (visible in ps aux, /proc, crash dumps); secrets in logs (accidentally logged); secrets shared via email/Slack (not revoked, no audit trail). Solutions: HashiCorp Vault: dedicated secrets management; dynamic secrets (generates temporary database credentials per request; credentials expire automatically; no long-lived credentials); policies control who/what can access which secrets; detailed audit log of every secret access; AppRole authentication for machines; Kubernetes integration (Vault agent sideinjector); transit secrets engine (encryption as a service); HSM integration for root key protection. Cloud-native: AWS Secrets Manager: stores credentials, rotates automatically (Lambda function for RDS, Redshift, DocumentDB); integrates with IAM for access control; automatic rotation. Azure Key Vault: stores keys, secrets, certificates; RBAC integration; HSM-backed premium tier; managed identities for VMs (no credential needed). GCP Secret Manager: similar capabilities; IAM integration; Workload Identity Federation (no service account key). Kubernetes secrets: base64-encoded (NOT encrypted by default); encrypt at rest with KMS (cloud-managed or Vault KMS plugin); use external-secrets-operator to sync from Vault/AWS SM into Kubernetes secrets; seal with Sealed Secrets (asymmetric encryption -- only cluster can decrypt). Best practices: least privilege: applications access only secrets they need; short TTL: credentials expire frequently; automatic rotation: no manual password changes; audit logging: who accessed what secret when; emergency rotation: immediately revoke on suspected compromise; no local caching without encryption; separate secrets per environment (dev/staging/prod never share secrets).
How do you test for business logic vulnerabilities?

Business logic vulnerabilities: flaws in application's intended functionality rather than implementation bugs; cannot be detected by automated scanners because they require understanding of business rules. Types: (1) Price manipulation: change product price in request body; checkout with negative quantity (credit); apply discount code multiple times; price in hidden form field or cookie; test: intercept checkout request, modify price to 0.01 or negative. (2) Workflow bypass: skip required steps in multi-step process; jump directly to final step (step 4 of 4 without completing 1-3); direct API call to complete-purchase without add-to-cart and payment-entry steps. (3) Privilege escalation via account modification: change account type in profile update request (type=admin); IDOR on profile endpoint to modify another user's type. (4) Race conditions: two simultaneous requests each independently pass single-use check (see race condition section); coupon codes, gift cards, limited inventory. (5) Quantity manipulation: negative quantities for credit; decimal quantities (order 0.5 items); integer overflow (max int + 1 wraps to negative). (6) Transfer manipulation: transfer more than balance; transfer to self; currency/unit confusion (cents vs dollars). (7) Account takeover via logic: password reset with predictable token; reuse expired reset token; use reset token for wrong account (change email in URL). (8) State confusion: cancel already-shipped order; submit already-processed refund; revert confirmed transaction. Testing methodology: map all business workflows; identify assumptions the application makes; test what happens when you violate each assumption; pay special attention to: ordering of steps; uniqueness checks; state transitions; privilege changes; numeric values; time-based logic. Tools: Burp Suite for intercepting and modifying all requests; manual testing with multiple accounts; automation with specific scripts for race conditions (Turbo Intruder). Documentation: document business rules understood from functionality; document which rules are enforced vs assumed; findings should reference the business impact not just technical description.
What is exploit development and how does it work?

Exploit development: process of creating reliable code that takes advantage of a vulnerability to achieve attacker goal (code execution, privilege escalation). Stages: (1) Vulnerability research: identify vulnerable code (source code review, fuzzing, binary analysis); understand vulnerability class (buffer overflow, use-after-free, format string). (2) Proof of concept (PoC): demonstrate crash; send input that triggers vulnerability reliably. (3) Controlling execution: for buffer overflow: overwrite return address (EIP/RIP) with attacker-controlled value; determine offset to return address (cyclic pattern: msf-pattern_create; find offset: msf-pattern_offset). (4) Finding jump point: for classic stack overflow: find JMP ESP instruction in binary or loaded DLL (not ASLR-randomised); use mona.py in Immunity Debugger or pwntools). (5) Shellcode: position-independent code to execute (reverse shell, add user); avoid bad characters (null bytes, newlines); generate with msfvenom or write custom; test shellcode standalone. (6) Bypass mitigations: ASLR (Address Space Layout Randomisation): randomises memory layout; bypass: information leak to get base address; return-oriented programming (ROP -- use existing code gadgets at known offsets); ASLR+NX bypass with ROP chain. NX/DEP (No-Execute/Data Execution Prevention): stack and heap not executable; bypass: ROP chains (reuse existing code); ret2libc (return to libc system() function). Stack Canaries: random value on stack; detected if overwritten; bypass: leak canary value (format string vulnerability), brute force (32-bit), partial overwrite. RELRO: read-only relocation; full RELRO makes GOT read-only; prevents GOT overwrite. (7) Reliability: test on multiple targets; handle different patch levels; adjust for different OS versions. Tools: pwntools (Python exploit framework: cyclic, p32/p64, remote, process, ELF, ROP); GDB + pwndbg/PEDA (debugging); Ghidra, IDA Pro, Binary Ninja (reverse engineering); ROPgadget, ropper (ROP chain construction); Immunity Debugger + mona.py (Windows exploitation).
What is binary reverse engineering?

Binary reverse engineering: analysing compiled executable to understand its functionality without source code. Use cases: malware analysis; vulnerability research; interoperability (reverse proprietary protocol); CTF challenges; software piracy (license bypass -- legal issues); anti-cheat analysis. Tools: Static analysis (without running): Ghidra (NSA open-source; decompiler; disassembler; scripting; excellent free option); IDA Pro (industry standard; expensive; best decompiler with Hex-Rays plugin; IDAPython scripting); Binary Ninja (commercial; good API; team collaboration); Radare2 (open-source; steep learning curve; r2pipe Python API); objdump, strings, file (Linux built-in basics). Dynamic analysis (running with debugger): GDB (Linux; pwndbg or PEDA plugin for better UI); x64dbg / OllyDbg (Windows); WinDbg (Windows kernel debugging); Frida (dynamic instrumentation: inject JavaScript into running process; hook functions; modify behaviour; excellent for mobile app analysis). Disassembly vs decompilation: disassembly: convert machine code to assembly instructions (one-to-one); accurate but verbose and architecture-specific; decompilation: convert to pseudo-C code; less accurate (heuristics); much more readable; Ghidra and IDA decompilers both excellent. Key concepts: calling conventions (x86: cdecl arguments right-to-left on stack; x64 Windows: RCX, RDX, R8, R9; Linux: RDI, RSI, RDX, RCX, R8, R9); function prologue/epilogue; identifying data structures; recognising library functions; following control flow (conditionals, loops, function calls). Obfuscation challenges: packing (compress/encrypt binary; only unpacks in memory; dump from memory after unpack); anti-debugging (IsDebuggerPresent; timing checks; INT3 traps); virtualisation (custom VM -- opaque bytecode; very expensive to reverse; used by some malware and commercial packers). CTF techniques: use file command to identify binary type; strings to find interesting strings; ltrace/strace to trace library/system calls; GDB with break at main; step through logic; common patterns: XOR obfuscation, custom encoding, anti-reversing tricks.
What is the cyber kill chain and how is it used?

Cyber Kill Chain: threat intelligence framework developed by Lockheed Martin (2011); describes phases of a cyberattack; modelled after military kill chain concept. Seven phases: (1) Reconnaissance: attacker gathers information about target; OSINT (LinkedIn, Shodan, DNS enumeration, Google dorking); active scanning; email harvesting; objective: find attack vectors (exposed services, employee names, email format). (2) Weaponisation: create attack tool combining exploit + payload; develop or purchase malware; embed in phishing document; create exploit for discovered vulnerability; no interaction with target in this phase. (3) Delivery: transmit weapon to target; phishing email (most common); watering hole attack (compromise website target visits); USB drop; drive-by download; supply chain compromise. (4) Exploitation: exploit vulnerability to execute code; click on malicious link/attachment triggers exploit; Java applet, Office macro, browser exploit; vulnerability in public-facing server exploited. (5) Installation: install persistent access; malware drops backdoor, RAT, webshell; registry persistence, scheduled tasks, service installation; objective: survive reboots. (6) Command and Control (C2): establish communication channel between malware and attacker; HTTP/HTTPS beacons, DNS C2, social media C2; attacker issues commands to compromised system. (7) Actions on Objectives: attacker achieves goal; data exfiltration; ransomware deployment; lateral movement to other targets; credential theft; sabotage. Using Kill Chain defensively: identify which controls prevent which phases; if attacker reaches phase 6 without detection: hunting exercise to find C2; focus controls on early phases (detection at Delivery prevents Installation); kill chain analysis of past incidents; Intel-driven defence: if attacker in reconnaissance phase (detected Shodan scans): proactively harden before delivery. Limitations of Kill Chain: designed for external perimeter-based attacks; does not well model insider threats; less applicable for cloud-native attacks; MITRE ATT&CK more detailed alternative (188 techniques vs 7 phases).
What is threat modelling and how do you perform it?

Threat modelling: structured process for identifying security threats to a system and designing mitigations; done during design phase (less expensive to fix than post-development). Methodologies: STRIDE (Microsoft): categorise threats by type: Spoofing identity, Tampering with data, Repudiation (denying action), Information disclosure, Denial of Service, Elevation of privilege; applied to each component and data flow in system. PASTA (Process for Attack Simulation and Threat Analysis): 7-stage process; business objective-focused; risk-centric; used in enterprise. LINDDUN: privacy-focused threat modelling; Linkability, Identifiability, Non-repudiation, Detectability, Disclosure, Unawareness, Non-compliance. Attack trees: hierarchical representation of how goal achieved; root node = attacker goal (steal user passwords); child nodes = methods; leaf nodes = specific attacks; probability and cost assigned. MITRE ATT&CK-based: use threat actor profiles (known TTPs) to model realistic threats for your industry; more realistic than abstract threat enumeration. Process: (1) Decompose the application: create data flow diagrams (DFD); identify components (web server, database, API, auth service); identify data flows; identify trust boundaries (where data crosses security boundary). (2) Determine threats: for each component and flow: apply STRIDE; or brainstorm threats using MITRE ATT&CK. (3) Determine countermeasures: for each threat: identify mitigation; determine if already implemented or needs implementation; priority based on risk (likelihood x impact). (4) Rank and prioritise: DREAD (Damage, Reproducibility, Exploitability, Affected users, Discoverability) scoring; or CVSS for individual threats. Tools: OWASP Threat Dragon (free, open-source, diagram-based); Microsoft Threat Modeling Tool (STRIDE-focused; integrates with Azure); IriusRisk (commercial, code-integrated); Tutamantic; draw.io for DFDs. When: design phase (architecting new feature); API design review; infrastructure changes; acquisition due diligence; annually for critical systems.
How do you secure microservices architecture?

Microservices security: unique challenges compared to monolithic applications; distributed, multiple communication channels, complex identity. Service-to-service authentication: mutual TLS (mTLS): each service has certificate; authenticate bidirectionally; service mesh (Istio, Linkerd) automates mTLS between services; sidecars handle TLS without application code changes. JWT tokens: service A calls service B with JWT signed by trusted identity provider; service B validates JWT signature and claims; short-lived tokens (15 minute TTL) with automatic refresh. API Gateway: single entry point for external requests; handles authentication (OAuth, API keys, JWT) centrally; rate limiting, DDoS protection, SSL termination; WAF at gateway; eliminates need for each microservice to implement auth; Kong, AWS API Gateway, Azure API Management, NGINX. Authorisation: OAuth 2.0 scopes for service-level permissions; OPA (Open Policy Agent): policy engine for fine-grained authorisation decisions across services; each service checks OPA for authorisation decision using centralised policies. Secrets: no hardcoded secrets; each service has unique credentials with least privilege (database user for service A cannot access service B database); Vault or cloud KMS for secrets delivery; Kubernetes secrets encrypted at rest. Network policies: Kubernetes NetworkPolicy restricts pod-to-pod communication; explicitly allow only required paths; deny-all default with explicit allows; service mesh policies layer additional controls. Container security: minimal base images (distroless or Alpine); non-root user; read-only filesystem; resource limits (CPU, memory -- prevent DoS within cluster); Pod Security Standards (restricted profile). Logging and tracing: distributed tracing (OpenTelemetry, Jaeger, Zipkin): track request across multiple services; security events correlated across services; correlation IDs in all logs; centralised log aggregation. Vulnerability management: scan container images in CI/CD (Trivy, Snyk); patch base images regularly; dependency scanning for each service; service mesh telemetry for anomaly detection.
What is mobile application security testing?

Mobile app security testing methodology: covers iOS and Android application analysis. Static analysis (Android): decompile APK: apktool d app.apk (decode resources and smali code); jadx app.apk (decompile to Java); extract APK: mv app.apk app.zip; unzip. Look for: hardcoded secrets (API keys, passwords, private keys in code, assets, strings.xml); custom permissions (AndroidManifest.xml -- exported activities without permission requirements = security bypass); backup allowed (allowBackup=true: backup extracts private data); debuggable=true in production; network security config (cleartext traffic allowed to specific domains?); deep link handlers (handle URLs without proper validation?). Static analysis (iOS): download IPA; unzip; Mach-O binary analysis with class-dump (extract Objective-C headers), otool, nm; plist files (Info.plist reveals URL schemes, permissions, ATS exceptions); strings analysis for hardcoded secrets; Frida Gadget injection for dynamic analysis without jailbreak. Dynamic analysis (Android): install on emulator or rooted device; Burp Suite proxy (configure device to trust Burp CA; Android 7+ restricts user CAs for apps using network_security_config: use MagiskTrust module or patch app with apktool); Android Studio emulator for ADB access; adb shell; MonkeyRunner for automated UI testing. Dynamic analysis (iOS): jailbroken iPhone (Checkra1n, Unc0ver) or Corellium (cloud iOS virtualisation); Frida for runtime manipulation; Objection (Frida-based mobile security testing framework): objection -g BUNDLE_ID explore; SSL pinning bypass: objection run ios sslpinning disable; android sslpinning disable. Key tests: insecure data storage (SharedPreferences, SQLite databases, logs, clipboard without sensitivity); Frida script reads SharedPreferences; traffic interception (bypass SSL pinning); client-side authentication bypass; reverse engineering protection (code obfuscation, root/jailbreak detection); deep link injection; Intent hijacking; WebView vulnerabilities (JavaScript enabled with file:// access). Tools: MobSF (Mobile Security Framework: automated static and dynamic analysis); Burp Suite; Frida; Objection; apktool; jadx; drozer (Android attack framework); adb (Android Debug Bridge).
What are OAuth 2.0 PKCE and why is it important?

PKCE (Proof Key for Code Exchange, RFC 7636): OAuth 2.0 extension preventing authorisation code interception attacks; required for public clients (mobile apps, SPAs) that cannot securely store client_secret. Problem without PKCE: mobile app initiates OAuth with code request; redirect_uri is app custom scheme (myapp://callback); authorisation code returned in redirect; malicious app on same device can register same custom URL scheme; intercepts authorisation code; exchanges code for tokens at token endpoint; steals user session. PKCE flow: (1) App generates code_verifier: cryptographically random 43-128 character string. (2) App generates code_challenge = BASE64URL(SHA256(code_verifier)). (3) Authorisation request includes: code_challenge=HASH, code_challenge_method=S256. (4) Auth server stores code_challenge alongside authorisation code. (5) App receives authorisation code; sends code + code_verifier to token endpoint. (6) Auth server: hash code_verifier; compare to stored code_challenge; only issue tokens if match. (7) Malicious app that intercepted code cannot exchange it (does not know code_verifier that matches stored code_challenge). Why effective: code_verifier generated per-session; never sent to authorisation endpoint (sent only to token endpoint with TLS); malicious app that only intercepted redirect (authorisation code) cannot derive code_verifier from code_challenge (SHA256 is one-way). PKCE for confidential clients: even server-side apps (with client_secret) should use PKCE; defence in depth against code interception; OAuth 2.1 will mandate PKCE for all clients. Implementation: most OAuth SDKs handle PKCE automatically; PKCE requires state parameter for CSRF protection; security issue if server accepts PKCE without requiring code_verifier at token exchange (allows downgrade attack -- submit code without verifier; server should reject). OpenID Connect: PKCE supported in all OIDC flows; nonce parameter also required for replay protection in ID token.
What is an intrusion detection system (IDS) and how does it work?

IDS (Intrusion Detection System): monitors network or host activity for malicious patterns; alerts on detected threats; passive (detection only, not blocking). Types: NIDS (Network IDS): monitors network traffic; deployed at network tap or span port; analyses packets; example: Snort, Suricata, Zeek (Bro). HIDS (Host IDS): monitors single host; system calls, file integrity, log analysis; example: OSSEC, Wazuh, Samhain. Detection methods: Signature-based: compares traffic against database of known attack signatures; high accuracy for known attacks; zero false positives for matched signatures; misses zero-day and novel attacks (signature not yet written); must update signatures regularly. Anomaly-based (behavioural): establishes baseline of normal activity; alerts on deviations; detects novel attacks; high false positive rate (normal variation triggers alerts); machine learning can reduce false positives; example: normal SSH login volume = 10/hour; 1000/hour = alert. Stateful protocol analysis: understands expected protocol behaviour; alerts on protocol violations; HTTP request with method not in RFC; DNS response before query. Zeek (formerly Bro): network analysis framework; logs all network activity in structured logs (conn.log, http.log, dns.log, ssl.log, files.log, x509.log); generates events for scripts to analyse; not traditional signature-based; flexible scripting in Zeek language; used for threat hunting and security analytics. Snort/Suricata: signature-based NIDS; Snort rules: alert tcp any any -> 192.168.1.0/24 80 (msg:HTTP attack; content:UNION SELECT; sid:1000001;); Suricata: multi-threaded (faster); compatible with Snort rules; adds protocol parsers; Emerging Threats Pro (commercial) and Emerging Threats (free) rule sets. IDS vs IPS: IDS: passive; detects and alerts; IPS (Intrusion Prevention System): inline; can block detected attacks; adds latency; same technology deployed differently.
How does AES encryption work?

AES (Advanced Encryption Standard): symmetric block cipher; encrypts 128-bit blocks; key sizes: 128, 192, 256 bits; NIST standard since 2001; successor to DES; used in TLS, disk encryption, VPN, file encryption. Structure: substitution-permutation network (not Feistel like DES); operates on 4x4 byte state matrix; rounds: AES-128 = 10 rounds, AES-192 = 12 rounds, AES-256 = 14 rounds. Each round (except last): SubBytes: non-linear byte substitution using S-box (substitution box); provides confusion; same substitution for each byte regardless of position; S-box based on multiplicative inverse in GF(2^8). ShiftRows: cyclically shift rows of state by 0, 1, 2, 3 bytes; provides diffusion across columns. MixColumns: multiply each column by fixed polynomial in GF(2^8); each output byte depends on all 4 input bytes in column; further diffusion. AddRoundKey: XOR state with round key (derived from key schedule from original key). Operation modes (critical for security): ECB (Electronic Codebook): each block encrypted independently with same key; INSECURE; identical plaintext blocks = identical ciphertext (famous ECB penguin image demo); never use for more than one block. CBC (Cipher Block Chaining): XOR each plaintext block with previous ciphertext before encryption; IV (Initialisation Vector) for first block; sequential; padding oracle attacks (POODLE); slower. CTR (Counter Mode): turns AES into stream cipher; XOR keystream (AES(IV+counter)) with plaintext; parallelisable; no padding needed; reuse of IV = catastrophic (XOR same keystream = attacker can XOR two ciphertexts to get XOR of plaintexts). GCM (Galois/Counter Mode): CTR mode + authentication tag (GHASH); authenticated encryption; provides confidentiality AND integrity; detects tampering; recommended for most use cases; nonce (IV) must never reuse (reuse breaks both confidentiality and authentication). AES security: no practical attack faster than brute force for properly implemented AES; 128-bit key = 2^128 combinations (computationally infeasible); quantum computers: Grover algorithm reduces to 2^64 effective security (AES-256 remains safe against quantum).
How does RSA encryption work and what are common RSA attacks?

RSA: asymmetric (public-key) cryptosystem; basis of TLS, SSH, code signing, PKI; invented 1977 by Rivest, Shamir, Adleman. Key generation: choose two large prime numbers p and q; n = p * q (modulus; 2048-4096 bit RSA uses 1024-2048 bit primes); phi(n) = (p-1)(q-1); choose e (public exponent; typically 65537 = 0x10001; prime, small, coprime to phi(n)); d = modular inverse of e mod phi(n) (private exponent); public key: (n, e); private key: (n, d). Encryption: C = M^e mod n (M = message as integer, C = ciphertext); Decryption: M = C^d mod n. Security: based on difficulty of factoring large n into p and q; if n factored: attacker computes phi(n) and derives d; RSA-2048 considered safe against classical computers; estimated 300,000 qubits (logical) for Shor algorithm to factor 2048-bit RSA -- quantum threat real but distant. Common attacks: Small exponent (e=3 with no padding): if same message sent to 3 servers with e=3 and different n: CRT (Chinese Remainder Theorem) recovers M (Hastad broadcast attack); small m^3 < n: take cube root directly. Common modulus: if two messages encrypted with same n but different e: can recover plaintext if gcd(e1,e2)=1 via extended Euclidean. Timing attacks: RSA decryption time varies based on private key bits (square and multiply algorithm); statistical timing measurements reveal bits of d; Montgomery multiplication with blinding mitigates. PKCS#1 v1.5 padding oracle: Bleichenbacher attack (1998); Oracle tells whether decrypted ciphertext has valid PKCS#1 v1.5 padding; adaptive chosen ciphertext attack recovers plaintext in 2^20 queries; DROWN attack exploits this in SSLv2. Fix: OAEP (Optimal Asymmetric Encryption Padding) for encryption; PSS (Probabilistic Signature Scheme) for signing; constant-time implementation; RSA used only for key exchange not bulk encryption (too slow); modern TLS: ECDHE for key exchange (Perfect Forward Secrecy); RSA only for certificate signature verification.
What is cryptographic hashing and what are common hash attacks?

Cryptographic hash functions: one-way functions producing fixed-length output (digest) from arbitrary input; deterministic; avalanche effect (small input change = dramatically different output). Properties: preimage resistance: given h, computationally infeasible to find M where H(M) = h; second preimage resistance: given M1, computationally infeasible to find M2 where H(M1) = H(M2); collision resistance: computationally infeasible to find any M1 != M2 where H(M1) = H(M2). Common algorithms: MD5: 128-bit output; BROKEN (collisions found 1996; practical collision attack 2004); still used for non-security checksums (file integrity); do not use for security. SHA-1: 160-bit output; BROKEN (theoretical collision 2005; practical chosen-prefix collision SHAttered 2017 by Google; 6500 GPU years); deprecated by CA/Browser Forum 2017; Certificates must use SHA-256+. SHA-2 family: SHA-256 (256-bit), SHA-384, SHA-512; currently secure; NIST standard; used in TLS 1.3, Bitcoin, most certificates. SHA-3 (Keccak): different design (sponge construction); NIST standard 2015; alternative to SHA-2; not SHA-2 vulnerability hedge but different attack surface. BLAKE2/BLAKE3: fast, secure; used in password hashing contexts; Argon2 uses Blake2. Password hashing (different from cryptographic hashing): MD5, SHA1, SHA256 too fast for passwords (billions per second on GPU = fast cracking); use slow algorithms: bcrypt: cost factor adjusts iterations; 10-12 common; ~100-1000 hashes/second with GPU. argon2id: memory-hard; time and memory configurable; NIST and OWASP recommended; scrypt: memory-hard; Litecoin uses for PoW. Hash attacks: rainbow tables: precomputed hash-to-plaintext lookup; defeated by salting (unique random value per hash, stored alongside); modern password databases all use salt. Length extension attack: SHA-256 is vulnerable (Merkle-Damgard construction); given H(secret || message), attacker can compute H(secret || message || attacker_data) without knowing secret; use HMAC or SHA-3 to mitigate. Birthday paradox: collision probability 50% after 2^(n/2) inputs; SHA-256 collision requires 2^128 operations (safe); MD5 requires 2^64 (practical).
What is penetration testing methodology and reporting?

Penetration testing methodology: structured approach ensuring comprehensive, repeatable, and defensible assessments. Methodologies: PTES (Penetration Testing Execution Standard): phases: Pre-engagement, Intelligence Gathering, Threat Modelling, Vulnerability Analysis, Exploitation, Post-Exploitation, Reporting. OWASP Testing Guide: comprehensive web application testing framework; 100+ test cases for each vulnerability category. NIST SP 800-115: Technical Guide to Information Security Testing; government standard. Phases: (1) Pre-engagement: scope definition (IP ranges, domains, applications, out-of-scope); rules of engagement (testing hours, emergency contacts, allowed techniques); authorisation documentation (signed statement of work or written permission); emergency contacts (when to stop testing); legal review. (2) Reconnaissance: passive (OSINT: WHOIS, DNS, search engines, LinkedIn, Shodan) and active (port scanning, service enumeration, web crawling). (3) Vulnerability identification: automated scanning (Nessus, OpenVAS); manual testing (Burp Suite, custom scripts); OSINT on discovered software versions for known CVEs. (4) Exploitation: attempt to exploit discovered vulnerabilities; prove exploitability (actual PoC, not just theoretical); chain vulnerabilities for greater impact; document evidence (screenshots, command output, timestamps). (5) Post-exploitation: demonstrate business impact (access sensitive data, pivot to other systems, establish persistence -- only if in scope); avoid causing damage. (6) Reporting: findings document; executive summary (non-technical, business risk, strategic recommendations); technical findings (vulnerability details, reproduction steps, evidence, CVSS score, remediation guidance); appendices (raw output, tool lists, methodology). Report quality: unambiguous reproduction steps; test in lab to verify steps before submitting; business risk for each finding (not just CVE score); prioritised remediation with quick wins and longer-term fixes; executive summary readable in 10 minutes without technical background.
What is the difference between black-box, grey-box, and white-box testing?

Black-box: tester has no prior knowledge of system internals; simulates external attacker; tests from user perspective only; finds externally discoverable vulnerabilities; slower; realistic attacker simulation; misses issues only visible with code access. Grey-box: partial knowledge (architecture diagrams, limited credentials, API documentation); balances realism with efficiency; faster than black-box; finds more issues than pure black-box; most common for web application testing. White-box: full knowledge (source code, architecture, credentials, network diagrams); most comprehensive; finds issues missed in black/grey-box (insecure crypto in code, business logic in code, hardcoded secrets); slowest; code review included; also called crystal-box or glass-box. When to use each: external penetration test simulating real attacker: black-box; time-efficient internal assessment: grey-box; secure SDLC pre-deployment review: white-box; compliance-driven code review: white-box; red team engagement: black-box or grey-box depending on scenario.
What is malware analysis and what are the phases?

Malware analysis: studying malicious software to understand its functionality, origin, and impact. Safety: ALWAYS analyse in isolated VM (VMware or VirtualBox with snapshots; no host-to-VM shared folders; no network or NAT to isolated/dummy network; no copy-paste clipboard sharing); use FlareVM (Windows-based malware analysis distro) or Remnux (Linux). Phases: (1) Static analysis (basic): extract file metadata: file, strings, MD5/SHA256 hash; check hash on VirusTotal; PE header analysis (pefile library or PEiD): import table (which DLLs and functions imported -- reveals capabilities: ws2_32.dll = network; crypt32.dll = crypto; advapi32 registry = persistence); sections (unusual section names, high entropy sections = packed/encrypted code). (2) Dynamic analysis: run in sandbox; Cuckoo Sandbox or ANY.RUN or Hybrid Analysis online; observe: processes created, network connections, files created/modified, registry changes, loaded DLLs; ProcMon, Process Hacker, Wireshark during execution. (3) Static analysis (advanced): disassembly and decompilation in IDA Pro or Ghidra; reverse engineer algorithms; identify obfuscation (XOR encryption keys; base64 decoded strings); extract IoCs (hardcoded C2 domains, IPs, file paths, registry keys). (4) Code analysis: identify C2 protocol; persistence mechanism; evasion techniques (anti-debug, anti-VM, anti-sandbox checks: CPUID, timing, mouse movement); decrypt strings; extract config (C2 address, sleep time, encryption key). Tools: FLOSS (FireEye: automated obfuscated string extraction); YARA (write signatures from analysis); yarGen (auto-generate YARA from unique strings).
What is network traffic analysis?

Network traffic analysis (NTA): monitoring and analysing network communications to detect threats, anomalies, and policy violations. Approaches: Full packet capture (PCAP): capture all packets including payload; Wireshark, tcpdump; high storage requirements; maximum visibility; decrypt TLS with session keys. NetFlow/IPFIX: metadata only (source IP, destination IP, port, protocol, bytes, duration); no payload; lower storage (100x less than PCAP); sufficient for many detections; supported by all routers and switches. DNS logs: every DNS query reveals what hosts are communicating with; high value for threat detection; Zeek dns.log. Threat detection via NTA: lateral movement: unusual SMB (port 445) or WMI (135/EPM) between workstations; beaconing: regular interval connections to external IP (consistent timing, specific interval = C2 beacon); data exfiltration: large outbound transfers at unusual times; DNS tunneling: high volume of long subdomain queries to single domain; brute force: many connections to port 22, 3389, 445 with connection failures; port scanning: one source IP connecting to many destination ports; malware propagation: infection spreading (high SYN rate to internal IPs = worm). Tools: Zeek (Bro): generates structured logs from packets; rich protocol parsers; scriptable; produces conn.log, http.log, dns.log, ssl.log, files.log; essential for security analytics. Suricata: IDS signatures on live traffic or PCAP. RITA (Real Intelligence Threat Analytics): analyses Zeek logs; specifically detects beaconing (statistical analysis of connection intervals), long connections, DNS tunneling. Arkime (formerly Moloch): full packet capture and search; web UI; PCAP indexed and searchable. NetworkMiner: Windows-based; passive network sniffer; extracts files, credentials, hosts from PCAP.
What is a honeypot and how does it work?

Honeypot: decoy system or resource designed to attract attackers; generates alerts when accessed (only attackers interact; no legitimate use); valuable threat intelligence and early warning. Types: Low-interaction: simulates limited services; limited functionality; records connections; examples: OpenSSH server that logs logins but does not allow real login; Honeyd simulates many hosts; lower risk of attacker using as pivot. High-interaction: real operating system and services; full interaction; maximum intelligence gathered (attacker TTPs, tools, targets); higher risk (attacker may use to attack others); requires containment (network isolation). HoneyTokens: fake credentials, files, or records embedded in real environment; access triggers alert; examples: canarytoken (Canary Tokens: fake AWS credentials in fake configuration file; used anywhere = DNS lookup to token server = alert), fake Active Directory service account with no real access (any login attempt = alert; rarely false positive), fake database records (if queried by application = data breach indicator), fake user in LDAP directory. HoneyFiles: files with audit SACL (Security Access Control List); any read triggers Windows Event 4663; placed in sensitive directories; ransomware will encrypt them early = ransomware alert before extensive damage. Production vs Research: production honeypots protect real networks; deployed inside corporate network alongside real servers; research honeypots gather threat intelligence; isolated; publicly accessible; study attack techniques. Deployment: isolated VLAN with internet access but no internal network access; all outbound connections monitored; containment prevents pivot. Examples: SSH honeypots: Cowrie (logs all commands, file downloads, credentials attempted); telnet honeypots; web application honeypots (Glastopf); database honeypots (fake MySQL listening on 3306); ICS honeypots (Conpot simulates PLCs). Value: detect scanners and opportunistic attackers; get early warning of targeted attacks; gather malware samples; study attacker techniques.
What is the NIST Cybersecurity Framework?

NIST CSF (Cybersecurity Framework): voluntary framework for managing cybersecurity risk; developed with industry in 2014; widely adopted by US government and private sector; version 2.0 released 2024. Core functions (CSF 1.1): IDENTIFY: understand organisation assets, risks, and governance; asset management, business environment, governance, risk assessment, risk management strategy. PROTECT: implement safeguards; access control, awareness and training, data security, information protection, maintenance, protective technology. DETECT: identify cybersecurity events; anomalies and events, continuous monitoring, detection processes. RESPOND: take action on detected events; response planning, communications, analysis, mitigation, improvements. RECOVER: restore capabilities; recovery planning, improvements, communications. CSF 2.0 adds GOVERN function: establish organisational cybersecurity risk management strategy, expectations, and policy; overarches all other functions. Implementation tiers: Tier 1 Partial: ad hoc, reactive; no formal risk management process. Tier 2 Risk Informed: risk management practices approved by management; not organisation-wide. Tier 3 Repeatable: formal policies in place; organisation-wide processes. Tier 4 Adaptive: continuous improvement; advanced threat awareness. Profiles: Current Profile (as-is state) vs Target Profile (desired state); gap analysis identifies improvement priorities. Use cases: structure cybersecurity program; communicate risk to executives; align with other frameworks (ISO 27001, CIS Controls, COBIT); vendor risk assessment; regulatory compliance basis (DoD CMMC, HIPAA, PCI DSS all map to CSF). Adoption: executive order 13800 (May 2017) required federal agencies to use CSF; 30% of US organisations use CSF; internationally recognised though not mandatory.
What is the CIS Critical Security Controls?

CIS Controls (Center for Internet Security Critical Security Controls): prioritised set of defensive actions to prevent most common cyber attacks; originally developed from NSA analysis of most effective attack prevention measures; version 8 released 2021. Three implementation groups: IG1 (Essential Cyber Hygiene): minimum standard for all organisations; 56 safeguards; for small organisations with limited IT resources; prevents most common attacks. IG2 (next priority): 74 additional safeguards; for organisations with dedicated IT staff; handles more sophisticated attacks. IG3 (comprehensive): all 153 safeguards; large enterprise; sophisticated adversaries; mature security programme. 18 Controls: CIS 1: Inventory and Control of Enterprise Assets; CIS 2: Inventory and Control of Software Assets; CIS 3: Data Protection; CIS 4: Secure Configuration of Enterprise Assets and Software; CIS 5: Account Management; CIS 6: Access Control Management; CIS 7: Continuous Vulnerability Management; CIS 8: Audit Log Management; CIS 9: Email and Web Browser Protections; CIS 10: Malware Defenses; CIS 11: Data Recovery; CIS 12: Network Infrastructure Management; CIS 13: Network Monitoring and Defense; CIS 14: Security Awareness and Skills Training; CIS 15: Service Provider Management; CIS 16: Application Software Security; CIS 17: Incident Response Management; CIS 18: Penetration Testing. Why effective: based on actual attack data; prioritised by impact; actionable (specific technical safeguards not vague guidelines); mapped to MITRE ATT&CK, NIST CSF, ISO 27001; CIS Benchmarks (hardening guides for OS, cloud, network devices) complement Controls. Comparison to NIST CSF: NIST CSF = risk management framework (what to do); CIS Controls = prescriptive technical controls (how to do it); complementary; CIS Controls mapped to CSF functions; organisations use CSF for strategy, CIS Controls for implementation.
What is ISO 27001 and how does certification work?

ISO 27001: international standard for Information Security Management Systems (ISMS); published by ISO (International Organisation for Standardisation) and IEC; latest version: ISO 27001:2022; globally recognised; provides framework for managing information security risks. ISMS: systematic approach to managing sensitive company information; includes people, processes, and IT systems; risk-based approach rather than prescriptive technical controls. Structure: 93 controls organised in 4 themes (2022 update from 14 domains): Organisational controls (37); People controls (8); Physical controls (14); Technological controls (34). Annex A: normative reference listing all 93 controls; organisations select controls based on risk assessment; Statement of Applicability (SoA) documents which controls implemented and justification for exclusions. Key requirements: context (understand organisation and interested parties); leadership (management commitment; ISMS scope; information security policy); planning (risk assessment and treatment; objectives); support (resources; competence; awareness; communication; documented information); operation (risk treatment plan; controls implementation); performance evaluation (monitoring; internal audit; management review); improvement (nonconformity; corrective action; continual improvement). Certification process: (1) Gap analysis against ISO 27001 requirements; (2) Implement ISMS controls; (3) Stage 1 audit: documentation review by accredited certification body; (4) Stage 2 audit: on-site assessment of implementation; (5) Certificate issued (3-year validity); (6) Surveillance audits annually; (7) Recertification audit every 3 years. Accreditation bodies: UKAS (UK), DAkkS (Germany), ANAB (USA); certification bodies: BSI, Bureau Veritas, Intertek, LRQA, SGS. Benefits: customer trust; regulatory compliance basis (GDPR alignment); contractual requirement from enterprise customers; structured risk management; competitive advantage in B2B.
What is PCI DSS and who needs to comply?

PCI DSS (Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard): information security standard for organisations handling credit card data; developed by PCI Security Standards Council (Visa, Mastercard, Amex, Discover, JCB); version 4.0 released March 2022; non-compliance = fines, increased transaction fees, card brand termination. Who must comply: any organisation that stores, processes, or transmits cardholder data (CHD); CHD: primary account number (PAN), cardholder name, expiry date, service code; sensitive authentication data (SAD): full track data, CVV/CVC, PINs. Merchant levels based on transaction volume: Level 1 (>6M transactions/year): annual Report on Compliance (ROC) by Qualified Security Assessor (QSA); quarterly network scans. Level 2 (1-6M): annual Self-Assessment Questionnaire (SAQ); quarterly scans. Levels 3 and 4 (smaller merchants): SAQ; quarterly scans. 12 Requirements (v3.2.1): Build and maintain secure network (firewalls; no vendor defaults); Protect cardholder data (encryption; key management); Vulnerability management (antivirus; patch management); Strong access control (need-to-know; unique IDs; no sharing credentials; physical access control); Monitor and test (logging; intrusion detection; pen testing); Maintain information security policy. Key v4.0 changes: customised approach (alternative to prescriptive controls if equivalent security demonstrated); targeted risk analysis (assess individual controls based on risk); MFA required for all CDE access (not just remote); password complexity increased (12+ characters); automated threat detection for payment pages; software security requirements updated. Scope reduction: isolate cardholder data environment (CDE); reduce scope by minimising where CHD exists; tokenisation (replace PAN with token in non-CDE systems); P2PE (point-to-point encryption): CHD encrypted from point of interaction to processor; scope dramatically reduced. Penetration testing requirement: PCI DSS 11.4: annual penetration test on CDE; after significant infrastructure changes; segmentation pen test verifying CDE isolation.
What is GDPR and what are the security implications?

GDPR (General Data Protection Regulation): EU regulation (2018) governing personal data of EU residents; extraterritorial scope (any organisation handling EU resident data regardless of location); significant security implications and breach notification requirements. Security-relevant requirements: Article 25 Data Protection by Design and Default: integrate data protection from system design; privacy-preserving architecture; minimum necessary data collection; default privacy settings most protective. Article 32 Security of Processing: implement appropriate technical and organisational measures; risk-appropriate security; encryption, pseudonymisation; confidentiality, integrity, availability, resilience; regular testing (penetration testing, vulnerability scanning); business continuity and recovery. Article 33 Breach Notification to Supervisory Authority: notify within 72 hours of becoming aware of personal data breach; if notification delayed beyond 72h: reason required; notification includes: nature of breach, categories and approximate number of data subjects affected, likely consequences, measures taken/proposed. Article 34 Communication to Data Subjects: if breach likely to result in high risk to individuals: must notify affected individuals without undue delay; exemptions: encrypted data (key not compromised); subsequent measures ensure high risk no longer likely. Fines: tier 1 (less severe): up to 10M EUR or 2% global annual turnover (whichever higher); tier 2 (more severe, including Article 32 security failures): up to 20M EUR or 4% global annual turnover. Notable fines: British Airways (2020, data breach): initially 183M GBP reduced to 20M GBP; Marriott (data breach): initially 99M GBP reduced to 18.4M GBP; Meta (2023): 1.2B EUR for data transfers to US; DPDP (India) and various national laws follow GDPR model globally. Practical security implications: encryption at rest and transit required; access control logs required; DPA (Data Protection Authority) may audit security measures; DPIA (Data Protection Impact Assessment) required for high-risk processing; Article 17 right to erasure requires data deletion capability (impacts backup strategy and database design).
What are cloud security best practices for AWS?

AWS security best practices across key domains: Identity: root account: MFA required; no programmatic access; used only for initial setup; create admin IAM user instead; IAM policies: least privilege; explicit deny for sensitive actions; avoid wildcard (*) actions and resources; use IAM roles for EC2/Lambda (no access keys in code); rotate access keys every 90 days; CloudTrail records all API calls for accountability. Network: VPC (Virtual Private Cloud): private subnets for databases and backend services; public subnets only for load balancers; NACLs and Security Groups in layers (Security Groups: instance-level; NACLs: subnet-level); Security Group rules: specific IPs not 0.0.0.0/0; no 0.0.0.0/0 for port 22 or 3389; VPC endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB (traffic stays on AWS network; no internet); AWS WAF on CloudFront and ALB. Compute: EC2: Systems Manager Session Manager instead of SSH/RDP (no port 22/3389 exposed; no bastion host required); IMDSv2 mandatory (prevents SSRF to metadata); latest AMI with patches; patch management via Systems Manager Patch Manager. Storage: S3: Block Public Access (account level AND bucket level); bucket policies requiring HTTPS (aws:SecureTransport); versioning for accidental deletion; S3 Object Lock for ransomware protection (WORM); S3 server-side encryption (SSE-S3 or SSE-KMS); access logging; Macie for sensitive data discovery. Logging and monitoring: CloudTrail: enable in all regions; CloudWatch Logs for application logging; GuardDuty: threat detection service analysing CloudTrail, VPC Flow Logs, DNS logs; findings for: unusual API calls, crypto mining, C2 communication, credential compromise; Security Hub: aggregate findings from GuardDuty, Inspector, Macie, Trusted Advisor; AWS Config: compliance checking (is MFA enabled? Are S3 buckets public? Are Security Groups too permissive?); EventBridge + Lambda for automated remediation. Encryption: KMS CMK for all encryption; CloudHSM for highest security requirements; Secrets Manager for database credentials with auto-rotation.
What is DevSecOps and how do you implement it?

DevSecOps: integrating security into DevOps practices; security as code; shift-left security (find issues earlier in SDLC when cheaper to fix); everyone responsible for security (not just security team). Why shift left: security bug found in design: costs 1x to fix; in development: 10x; in testing: 100x; in production: 1000x (cost of breach, remediation, regulatory fine, reputation). DevSecOps pipeline integration: Pre-commit hooks: detect-secrets (block committing API keys, passwords); gitleaks; talisman; run fast security checks before commit accepted. Code (SAST -- Static Application Security Testing): Semgrep (fast, accurate, open-source); CodeQL (GitHub; complex data flow analysis); SonarQube (comprehensive; technical debt tracking); Checkmarx, Veracode (commercial); scan for: SQL injection patterns, insecure crypto, hardcoded credentials, XSS. Build (SCA -- Software Composition Analysis): Snyk (open source, container, IaC scanning; most popular); Dependabot (GitHub native; auto-PRs for vulnerable dependencies); OWASP Dependency-Check (free); Black Duck (commercial); scan all dependencies for known CVEs; SBOM generation. Test (DAST -- Dynamic Application Security Testing): OWASP ZAP in CI/CD (docker run zaproxy/zap-stable zap-baseline.py); Nuclei (fast template-based scanner); DAST runs against deployed test environment; blocks deployment if Critical/High findings. Container security: Trivy (fast, comprehensive; scans images in seconds); Snyk Container; Grype; integrate in CI/CD before push to registry. Infrastructure as Code security: Checkov (Terraform, CloudFormation, Kubernetes YAML); tfsec (Terraform); kube-score (Kubernetes). Deployment: immutable infrastructure (no manual changes; rebuild from IaC; eliminates configuration drift); feature flags (disable vulnerable features without redeployment). Production: runtime security (Falco for container/Kubernetes runtime threat detection); continuous vulnerability management; DAST against production periodically; bug bounty program. Culture: security champions in development teams; security training for developers; blameless postmortems; security as enabler not gatekeeper.
What is log management and SIEM tuning?

Log management and SIEM tuning: critical for effective security monitoring; balance between detection coverage and alert fatigue. Log sources priority: Tier 1 (critical): authentication logs (AD/Okta/Azure AD); endpoint security (EDR alerts); firewall/proxy; DNS; email gateway; privileged access (PAM). Tier 2 (important): application logs; VPN; network flow; cloud API logs (CloudTrail). Tier 3 (supplementary): physical access; application debug logs (very noisy). Log volume estimation: Windows Event Log on DC: 500-5000 events/minute; firewall: 10,000-100,000 events/minute; proxy: 50,000+ events/minute; size all storage appropriately; retention: security events: 1 year minimum (PCI DSS 3.2.1: 1 year; GDPR: as long as needed; some regulations 7 years). SIEM tuning process: start with high-fidelity alerts only; enable rules one at a time; measure: how many alerts per day? False positive rate? Analyst capacity (average 15-20 alerts per analyst per day); tune aggressive rules: add exceptions for known-good (backup servers triggering port scan rules; vulnerability scanner IP excluded from brute force rules); add context (asset criticality, user role, location). Alert quality metrics: precision = true positives / (true positives + false positives); recall = true positives / (true positives + false negatives); acceptable: precision > 60% for alerts requiring investigation; precision > 90% for auto-blocking rules. Common false positives to tune: vulnerability scanner triggering web attack rules (whitelist scanner IP); backup jobs triggering large file transfer rules (exclude backup server); HR system triggering account creation rules (exclude HR system account); pen test triggering everything (track pen test windows and exclude or expect). Correlation rules: start with MITRE ATT&CK technique detections; build from simple to complex; example: T1003 credential dumping: lsass.exe access by non-system process; tune: exclude Defender, Sophos processes; alert on truly unexpected processes. Use case library: Splunk Security Essentials; Microsoft Sentinel Fusion; Elastic SIEM detection rules; Sigma rules (open-source community-maintained detection rules convertible to any SIEM query language).
How do you perform password auditing in Active Directory?

AD password auditing: assess password quality and identify weak or compromised credentials. Extract hashes (requires Domain Admin or DCSync rights): Impacket secretsdump.py: secretsdump.py domain/admin:pass@DC01 (dumps NTDS.dit via DCSync); or offline: ntdsutil snapshot to extract NTDS.dit + SYSTEM registry hive; secretsdump.py -ntds ntds.dit -system SYSTEM LOCAL. Hash format: username:RID:LM_HASH:NT_HASH::: (NT hash is what gets cracked). Cracking with Hashcat: hashcat -m 1000 ntds.txt rockyou.txt (mode 1000 = NTLM); rules: hashcat -m 1000 ntds.txt rockyou.txt -r rules/best64.rule; combination: hashcat -m 1000 ntds.txt -a 1 wordlist1.txt wordlist2.txt; mask attack (pattern-based): hashcat -m 1000 ntds.txt -a 3 Company?d?d?d?d (Company + 4 digits = common corporate pattern); incremental: -a 3 ?a?a?a?a?a?a?a?a (all 8-char combinations -- very slow). Credential hygiene analysis: DSInternals PowerShell module: Get-ADReplAccount (enumerate accounts); Test-PasswordQuality: Find-WeakPasswordList, Find-DuplicatePasswordGroups (multiple accounts with same password), Find-EmptyPasswordAccounts, Find-SmartCardBypassAccounts; compare against HaveIBeenPwned breach corpus (100B+ leaked passwords); export NT hashes; compare to NTLM hashes from HIBP. NTLM hash comparison: not sending passwords to HIBP; HIBP has NTLM hash format too; download HIBP password list NTLM version; sort; compare with fgrep or PowerShell; identify breached passwords even if complex. Reporting: percentage cracked; common password patterns found; accounts using breached passwords; accounts with same password as another account; accounts with passwords matching username; accounts not changed > 1 year; service account password age. Tooling alternatives: Netwrix Password Policy Enforcer; Specops Password Auditor (free version audits against HIBP); Purple Knight (free AD security assessment including password findings).
What is web cache poisoning?

Web cache poisoning: attacker manipulates HTTP cache to store malicious response that gets served to other users. How caches work: CDNs and reverse proxies (Varnish, Nginx) cache responses; cache key = request attributes that determine uniqueness (typically URL + Host header); cached response served to all users with matching cache key. Cache poisoning: if cache includes request data not in cache key in response: attacker sends request with malicious header value; response includes attacker header value (reflected); response cached because only URL and Host in cache key; other users requesting same URL get cached malicious response.
