Microsoft Defender Antivirus (MDAV): traditional AV engine; signature-based + behaviour-based; cloud-delivered protection (real-time reputation queries); AMSI (Antimalware Scan Interface): PowerShell, VBScript, JScript pass code to MDAV before execution; catch fileless malware in memory. Microsoft Defender for Endpoint (MDE, formerly ATP): EDR solution; automatically collects telemetry; cross-machine correlation; attack surface reduction (ASR) rules: block specific attack techniques (block Office macros from spawning processes, block JS/VBScript execution, credential theft from LSASS protection); Exploit Guard: network protection (block connections to known malicious domains), controlled folder access (ransomware protection), attack surface reduction, exploit protection (ASLR, DEP, CFG enforcement). Threat and Vulnerability Management (TVM): continuous vulnerability assessment within MDE (no separate scanner); risk-based prioritisation; integrated remediation workflow. Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR): timeline: process, file, network, registry events for each device; advanced hunting: KQL queries over 30 days of endpoint data; custom detections: alert when specific behaviour observed. Microsoft Defender for Identity (MDI, formerly ATA): analyses AD authentication traffic; detects: lateral movement (pass the hash, pass the ticket), privilege escalation (golden ticket, DCSync), reconnaissance (LDAP queries, BloodHound-like enumeration); deployed as sensor on DC or standalone. Microsoft Defender for Office 365 (MDO): phishing protection; safe links (rewrite URLs, check at click time); safe attachments (sandbox execute attachments before delivery); spoof intelligence; anti-phishing ML. Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps (MCAS): CASB solution; monitor cloud app usage; shadow IT discovery; DLP in cloud apps; conditional access. Integration: all report to Microsoft 365 Defender portal (now Microsoft Defender XDR); unified incident correlation across identity, endpoint, email, cloud apps; Sentinel integration for SIEM; automated investigation and response (AIR); Microsoft Security Copilot (AI-assisted investigation). Deployment: MDE deployed via Intune (MDM), SCCM (ConfigMgr), or GPO; onboard all Windows 10/11 endpoints; MDE available on Linux, macOS, iOS, Android (limited EDR on mobile).
How do you perform application security threat hunting?

Application security threat hunting: proactively search for threats that evaded automated detection; hypothesis-driven investigation of application logs. Difference from incident response: IR: react to alert; hunting: proactive, no trigger required; assume compromise; look for evidence of attacker living in application. Hypotheses: hypothesis 1: attacker performed SQL injection reconnaissance; look for: SQL syntax in application logs (SELECT, UNION, FROM, information_schema, -- comment), repeated 500 errors or DB exceptions from same IP, sequential parameter manipulation in URL logs; hypothesis 2: attacker is testing authentication bypass; look for: login attempts with special characters (or 1=1, admin--,), sequential username enumeration (same IP trying many usernames), login success after many failures (credential stuffing success), logins from TOR exit nodes or suspicious IPs; hypothesis 3: attacker accessed other user data (IDOR); look for: same session accessing many different user resource IDs in short window, resource IDs accessed sequentially (1000, 1001, 1002...), API endpoints returning resources belonging to different users than authenticated user; hypothesis 4: attacker uploaded web shell; look for: file upload endpoints receiving non-image files, HTTP requests to uploaded file URLs with suspicious parameters (cmd=, exec=), unusual user agents making requests to uploaded file paths, file with.php/.asp extension served from upload directory. Data sources for application threat hunting: WAF logs (Cloudflare, AWS WAF): attack payloads logged even when blocked; CDN access logs; application server logs (Apache/Nginx: request URI, response code, bytes, referrer, user agent); application event logs (auth events, API calls, errors); database query logs (slow query log -- may catch blind SQLi time delays). Hunting workflow: develop hypothesis; identify data source; write query to test hypothesis; triage results (expected vs anomalous); confirm true positive; scope and escalate. Tools: Elastic/Kibana: KQL queries over log data; Splunk SPL; AWS Athena: SQL over CloudWatch Logs or S3 access logs; SIEM custom queries; Jupyter notebook for statistical analysis.
What is security by design?

Security by design: integrate security into architecture and development process from the start; not added as afterthought. Principles: least privilege: give every component and user exactly the permissions needed, nothing more; service account needs read access to one table: grant only that; fail securely: when component fails, default to deny access (not permit); authentication failure: deny access, not grant guest access; open design: security should not rely on secrecy of design (only on secrecy of keys); Kerckhoffs principle -- algorithm public, key private; defence in depth: multiple independent controls; compromise of one does not defeat all; separation of privilege: require multiple conditions to authorise high-impact actions (MFA = two separate factors required); do not trust services: validate all data received from external systems (APIs, databases, microservices); economy of mechanism: keep security design simple; complexity hides flaws; complete mediation: check access every time, not just at first access (re-validate on each request, not just session start); weakest link: system security limited by weakest component; identify and strengthen; secure defaults: default configuration is secure; users must consciously weaken (opt-out of security); psychological acceptability: security controls must not make product too inconvenient to use; users work around usability barriers. Implementation patterns: trust boundaries in architecture: diagram where trust changes; validate at each crossing; data classification: classify all data; apply controls proportional to sensitivity; threat modelling (see threat modelling entry): structured identification of threats in design; secure coding standards: language-specific secure coding guidelines; input validation, output encoding, crypto usage; privacy by design: GDPR Article 25: collect minimum data; anonymise or pseudonymise; retention limits; consent management; security requirements: security requirements alongside functional requirements; written before development; verified in testing; attack surface minimisation: expose minimum functionality; every feature is potential attack vector; disable unused features; remove default accounts, sample applications, demo functionality before production.
What is penetration testing report writing?

Penetration testing report: document findings, demonstrate risk, and guide remediation. Report structure: executive summary: 1-2 pages; non-technical; business language; key risk statement; overall risk rating; critical findings summary; remediation priorities; business impact narrative; scope and methodology: what was tested; testing type (black box/grey box/white box); timeframe; tools and techniques used; limitations (time constraints, areas not accessible); assumptions; risk rating methodology: how risks are rated (CVSS, likelihood x impact matrix, custom); rating definitions (Critical = remote code execution, data breach; High = privilege escalation, sensitive data access; Medium = authentication weakness; Low = information disclosure; Informational = best practice); findings: one entry per vulnerability; format: title (descriptive: SQL Injection in Login Form -- Authentication Bypass), severity (Critical/High/Medium/Low/Informational), CVSS score (3.0 or 3.1), CVE (if applicable), description (what is the vulnerability; technical explanation), proof of concept (step-by-step reproduction; screenshots; HTTP request/response), evidence (attacker can see...; payload:...; response showing...), impact (what could attacker achieve with this vulnerability; business consequence), remediation (specific actionable fix; code example if applicable; not generic use parameterised queries but location and specific fix), references (OWASP, CWE, CVE); attack chain (optional but valuable): narrative of how multiple findings combine to achieve critical impact; step-by-step from initial access to domain admin or data exfiltration; demonstrates real-world attacker path; remediation summary: table of all findings; sorted by severity; remediation timeline recommendation; retesting recommendation. Tone: factual, not alarmist; objective descriptions of technical facts; avoid sensational language; constructive remediation guidance. Sensitive data handling: handle discovered credentials, PII with care; do not include full plaintext credentials in report (last 4 chars only); encrypt report in transit and at rest (password-protected PDF or encrypted ZIP); confidentiality notice and distribution restrictions. Retesting: offer retesting of critical and high findings after remediation; verify fixes effective; document in addendum to original report.
What is a purple team exercise?

Purple team: collaboration between red team (attackers) and blue team (defenders); improve detection and response together; bridge gap between offensive and defensive security. Why purple team: traditional red team: blue team sees only final findings (compromised X, Y, Z); does not know WHICH techniques blue team detected or missed; purple team: real-time collaboration; test each technique; see exactly what was detected; tune detection immediately. Exercise format: structured sessions: half-day to full-day workshop; conference room or virtual; both teams present; atomic testing: one technique at a time; red team: execute specific ATT&CK technique against live environment; blue team: check if SIEM/EDR alerted within agreed time (5-10 minutes); record: detected or not detected; if not detected: blue team analyses data sources; identify: should this data exist? (is telemetry collected?); if data exists: why no alert? (tuning needed); if data does not exist: what data source should be enabled? Four outcomes per technique: detected and alerted (correct detection); detected in data but no alert (tuning gap -- add detection rule); data exists but no detection logic (coverage gap -- write new rule); no data (collection gap -- enable data source). MITRE ATT&CK navigation: use ATT&CK Navigator to track tested techniques; colour: green = detected, yellow = partial, red = not detected; show coverage heat map; prioritise red areas for next purple team session. Outputs: detection coverage map (ATT&CK Navigator export); detection rules created or tuned; data source gaps identified; data source enablement plan; updated runbooks for detected techniques; purple team report: techniques tested, detection rate, improvements made. Tools for atomic testing: Atomic Red Team (Red Canary): open-source library of atomic tests mapped to ATT&CK; one-liner per technique: Invoke-AtomicTest T1003.001 (LSASS dump); CALDERA (MITRE): automated adversary emulation; Prelude Operator; Vectr: track purple team exercises; C2 frameworks for more realistic simulation (Cobalt Strike, Havoc). Frequency: quarterly full-day purple team sessions; continuous via BAS (Breach and Attack Simulation) tools between sessions; post-incident: test detection for observed attacker techniques.
What is the principle of least privilege in practice?

Least privilege: grant minimum access needed for function; no more permissions than required; applied to users, service accounts, applications, network traffic, and processes. User account privilege: avoid giving admin accounts to regular users; standard user account for daily work (email, browser, productivity); separate admin account for administrative tasks only; admin account not used for email or web browsing (reduces exposure of high-privilege credentials); time-limited privilege elevation (JIT access): request elevated access for specific task with justification; access granted for limited time (1-4 hours); automatically expires; Sailpoint, CyberArk, BeyondTrust, Microsoft PIM (Privileged Identity Management). Service accounts: every service runs as dedicated service account; account permissions: exactly what service needs (read from this DB table, write to this S3 bucket); no shared service accounts; unique password per service account; gMSA (Group Managed Service Account) in Windows: AD manages 240-char password; no human knows it; automated rotation. Database accounts: application DB user: SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE on required tables only; no CREATE TABLE, DROP TABLE, GRANT; reporting user: SELECT only; migration user: schema change permissions (used only for deployments, then revoked). Network least privilege: firewall allow only required ports and protocols between specific hosts; not any to any; workstations cannot initiate connections to servers except specific required services; servers cannot initiate connections to other servers except specific required flows; ZTNA for application access (application-level not network-level). Cloud IAM: IAM policies: specify exact actions, resources, conditions (time, IP, MFA required); not administrator access when read access sufficient; resource-based policies: restrict who can assume IAM role; SCP (Service Control Policy) in AWS Organizations: guardrail; even if IAM policy grants admin, SCP limits what is actually allowed; no root access keys. Implementation: start with current state audit (what permissions do users and service accounts currently have?); identify over-privilege; remediate (remove unneeded permissions -- may break things: test in staging first); privilege access review: quarterly review of all privileged accounts; access certifications (manager confirms each report still needs their access).
What is the Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS)?

CVSS (Common Vulnerability Scoring System): standardised framework for rating severity of security vulnerabilities; 0.0-10.0 scale; current version 3.1 (v4.0 published 2023). Base Score metrics: Attack Vector (AV): Network (N, 0.85), Adjacent (A, 0.62), Local (L, 0.55), Physical (P, 0.2); how attacker reaches vulnerable component. Attack Complexity (AC): Low (L, 0.77) -- no special conditions, High (H, 0.44) -- specific conditions required. Privileges Required (PR): None (N, 0.85), Low (L, 0.62), High (H, 0.27). User Interaction (UI): None (N, 0.85), Required (R, 0.62). Scope (S): Unchanged (U) vs Changed (C) -- does vulnerability impact component beyond vulnerable component. Confidentiality/Integrity/Availability Impact: None (N, 0.0), Low (L, 0.22), High (H, 0.56). Score ranges: 0.0 = None; 0.1-3.9 = Low; 4.0-6.9 = Medium; 7.0-8.9 = High; 9.0-10.0 = Critical. Example: Log4Shell (CVE-2021-44228): AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:H = 10.0 Critical (remote, no complexity, no privileges, no interaction, changed scope, full CIA impact). Temporal Score: adjusts base score based on: Exploit Code Maturity (proof of concept vs weaponised), Remediation Level (official fix vs workaround vs unavailable), Report Confidence (confirmed vs reasonable). Environmental Score: adjust for specific environment: asset importance, security controls in place; organisation-specific score. CVSS limitations: score does not reflect exploitability in wild (high CVE may have no public exploit); does not reflect attacker motivation or target value; same score for very different vulnerabilities; EPSS (Exploit Prediction Scoring System): probability score 0-1 that vulnerability will be exploited in wild within 30 days; based on ML from actual exploitation data; better for prioritisation than CVSS alone; VPR (Vulnerability Priority Rating, Tenable proprietary): combines CVSS + EPSS + threat intelligence + asset criticality; recommended: use CVSS for initial triage; combine with EPSS and exploit availability for prioritisation; CISA KEV catalog as highest priority filter (known exploited = patch now regardless of CVSS).
What is network access control (NAC)?

NAC (Network Access Control): enforce security policy before granting network access; check device health and identity before allowing onto corporate network. Purpose: prevent unhealthy or unmanaged devices from joining network; enforce: patch level compliance, AV presence and updated signatures, disk encryption enabled, management agent installed, domain membership; authenticate device and user before network access; provide appropriate network segment based on compliance status. How it works: device connects to network switch or wireless AP; NAC solution intercepts (802.1X EAP); authenticates device certificate and user credentials; checks device health (posture assessment); makes access decision: compliant: full network access (production VLAN); non-compliant: quarantine VLAN (limited -- only update servers and remediation resources); unknown/unmanaged: guest VLAN or no access; posture check methods: agent-based (agent installed on endpoint collects detailed health data); agentless (scan from network; less detailed; no MAC bypass). IEEE 802.1X: standard authentication for wired and wireless; Supplicant (device), Authenticator (switch/AP), Authentication Server (RADIUS); EAP methods: EAP-TLS (certificate -- strongest), PEAP-MSCHAPv2 (username/password in TLS tunnel), EAP-FAST, EAP-TTLS; RADIUS (Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service): receives 802.1X request; validates credentials against AD via LDAP/Kerberos; returns Access-Accept or Access-Reject with VLAN assignment. Products: Cisco ISE (Identity Services Engine): most enterprise-grade; comprehensive posture, device profiling, guest management; FortiNAC; Aruba ClearPass; PacketFence (open-source). Use cases: BYOD management: personal devices on guest VLAN; corporate devices on production VLAN; IoT devices: profile and segment (fingerprint by MAC OUI, DHCP, HTTP user-agent); medical devices, IP cameras, printers in dedicated VLANs; guest network: captive portal authentication; time-limited access; contractor access: limited to specific resources. Challenges: complex deployment; 802.1X on all switches and APs required; exceptions management; impact on operations during rollout (broken network access for non-compliant devices); MAC address spoofing can bypass some NAC.
What is red team OPSEC?

Red team OPSEC (Operational Security): techniques red team uses to avoid detection during engagement; simulate realistic advanced persistent threat. Why OPSEC matters: red team detected too early = unrealistic; real APT spends weeks or months undetected; red team should test if blue team can detect sophisticated attacker; if red team triggers alerts on first day: test incomplete. Infrastructure OPSEC: attribution separation: use infrastructure not connected to red team firm or client; separate hosting providers for each engagement; aged domains (registered 1-2 years before engagement; categorised as business; not flagged as new domain); domain categorisation: test domain category via Bluecoat Site Review, McAfee SmartFilter before use; categorise as technology/business; traffic blending: malleable C2 profiles that mimic legitimate software (Office365, Slack, CDN traffic); CDN fronting (legitimate CDN forwards traffic to C2; IP logs show CDN not attacker); HTTPS (encrypted, appears as normal web traffic); multiple redirectors (chain of servers between victim and team server; add layers; each compromised separately). Operational OPSEC: avoid noisy tools: nmap with default settings creates obvious patterns; slow scan -T1 or -T2; avoid well-known offensive tool signatures: custom implants or heavily modified public tools; don not use default Cobalt Strike settings (JA3 fingerprint known); change default port, certificate, sleep intervals; timing: avoid obvious offensive activity patterns (all activity 9 AM - 5 PM in single timezone); spread activity across time zones; avoid off-hours that look suspicious (3 AM mass file deletion = obvious); stealth techniques: Living Off The Land (LOLBins): use Windows built-in tools (certutil, mshta, regsvr32, rundll32, wmic); no foreign binaries; process injection: inject into legitimate processes (svchost.exe, explorer.exe); looks like legitimate process; avoid writing to disk: in-memory only payloads; fileless persistence (WMI subscriptions, registry -- no dropped binaries). Logging awareness: know which events leave forensic traces; avoid generating Event ID 4769 RC4 tickets if blue team hunting Kerberoasting; use OPSEC-safe modules (Rubeus /opsec flag for safer Kerberoasting); clean artefacts: delete tools and logs after use.
What is the software development lifecycle (SDLC) and where does security fit?

SDLC security integration: incorporate security activities at each phase of software development; shift left. SDLC phases and security activities: Requirements phase: define security requirements alongside functional requirements; include: authentication requirements, authorisation model, data classification, compliance requirements (PCI DSS, HIPAA applicable to product?), encryption requirements; security misuse cases: how could this feature be misused? Define abuse scenarios; regulatory: GDPR data minimisation, consent management, retention limits. Design phase: threat modelling (STRIDE, PASTA): identify threats before a line of code written; architectural review: security architect reviews design; check: trust boundaries, data flow, encryption in transit and at rest, authentication and authorisation design, API security design, third-party component selection; security design patterns: fail-secure, least privilege, complete mediation, defence in depth applied to architecture. Development phase: secure coding standards: language-specific guides; OWASP Secure Coding Practices; SAST in IDE (SonarLint, Semgrep): real-time feedback as developer types; dependency management: SCA tool (Snyk) in IDE alerts on vulnerable library added; peer code review with security checklist; security unit tests: test authentication bypass, SQL injection prevention, access control; pre-commit hooks: secret scanning (GitGuardian, TruffleHog pre-commit). Testing phase: SAST in CI/CD: fail PR on new critical findings; DAST against staging: OWASP ZAP baseline scan; container image scanning: Trivy in CI; IaC scanning: Checkov; penetration testing (if major feature or product release): professional third-party test; API security testing. Deployment phase: security review of configuration (no debug mode, secure headers configured); secrets management: no secrets in environment variables (use secrets manager); production hardening; WAF configuration. Operations phase: vulnerability management: patch CVEs in dependencies and OS; SIEM monitoring of application; bug bounty programme (external researchers find vulnerabilities); security retrospectives: lessons learned from incidents and pen test findings; continuous improvement. Governance: security requirements in definition of done (DoD): no High+ open findings to deploy; security training for all developers annually; security champion: security-aware developer in each team; security leads code review of critical components.
What are common API vulnerabilities and how do you prevent them?

API vulnerabilities: web APIs have same web vulnerabilities plus API-specific issues. Broken Object Level Authorisation (BOLA/IDOR): GET /api/orders/12345 returns order 12345 regardless of who is authenticated; fix: check if authenticated user owns resource 12345 before returning; every object access must check ownership or explicit share permission. Broken Authentication: no authentication; API keys in URL (logged by server, proxy, browser history); weak tokens (predictable, short, no expiry); no MFA for sensitive operations; fix: strong token-based authentication (JWT RS256, OAuth 2.0); tokens in Authorization header only; rotate and expire tokens; MFA for admin APIs. Excessive Data Exposure: API returns full object with all fields; client filters to show only some; attacker calls API directly; sees all fields including sensitive (SSN, password_hash, internal_id, private_notes); fix: return only needed fields; field-level authorisation; Mass Assignment: API accepts all user-provided fields in JSON; UPDATE user accepts role field (not intended); user submits {name: Alice, role: admin}; role updated to admin; fix: explicitly allowlist accepted fields; do not bind request body directly to database model. Security Misconfiguration: CORS wildcard on authenticated API (Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *); stack traces in errors; HTTP instead of HTTPS; unused HTTP methods enabled; debug endpoints in production; fix: strict CORS; handle errors generically; HTTPS only; disable unused methods; audit all endpoints. Lack of Rate Limiting: no throttling on login endpoint (brute force); no limit on password reset (spam); no limit on expensive operations (search, export); fix: rate limit per endpoint, per user, per IP; exponential backoff for auth failures; Improper Inventory Management: shadow APIs (old versions still running); test endpoints in production (/api/test, /api/debug); internal APIs exposed externally; fix: API gateway; version management; decommission old versions; disable test endpoints before production. Business Logic Flaws: can order negative quantity (receive refund without item); can apply coupon infinitely; can reference other users resources through relation; fix: server-side validation of all business rules; test edge cases; abuse case coverage in test suite. Tools: 42Crunch (API security audit against OpenAPI spec); Postman; OWASP ZAP API scan; Burp Suite; Noname Security (runtime API security).
What is malware command and control (C2) and how does it work?

C2 (Command and Control): infrastructure attacker uses to communicate with malware implanted on victim systems; issue commands, receive data, maintain persistence. C2 architecture: attacker operators connect to team server; team server manages multiple beacons; beacons on victim machines beacon to team server; communication channel: HTTP/HTTPS, DNS, ICMP, custom protocols; callback interval: beacon periodically checks in (every 1-60 minutes) plus jitter (random variation: 50 second interval +/- 10 seconds randomises timing to evade correlation). HTTP/HTTPS C2: most common; blends with web traffic; malware sends HTTP GET or POST to attacker domain; response contains encoded commands; Cobalt Strike HTTP beacon: HTTP GET to check for tasks; HTTP POST to send results; malleable profile changes: URI path, User-Agent, headers; HTTPS: encrypted by TLS; deep packet inspection cannot read content; C2 domain fronting: route C2 through legitimate CDN (Cloudflare, AWS CloudFront, Azure CDN); CDN forwards to real C2; network logs show CDN IP not attacker IP; increasingly mitigated by CDN providers restricting fronting. DNS C2: encode commands/data in DNS queries: data.chunk1of3.attacker.com; use TXT record responses for commands; slow but stealthy; passes through most firewalls (DNS allowed outbound); detection: large number of queries to single domain; high entropy subdomains; long subdomain labels; tools: iodine (DNS tunneling); dnscat2. Domain Generation Algorithm (DGA): malware generates list of domains using pseudorandom algorithm seeded with date; registers one from list as active C2 each day; defenders cannot block all generated domains (thousands); both attacker and malware synchronise on same algorithm; detection: DGA domains have high entropy, unusual character distribution; ML classifiers detect DGA. Peer-to-peer C2: no central server; beacons communicate with each other; resilient to takedown of single server; harder to track (no single C2 IP); Emotet, TrickBot used P2P C2. Detection: beaconing pattern (regular interval connections, even with jitter, statistically detectable); new domain (recently registered, low reputation, never seen in environment before); network flow analysis: same destination IP at regular intervals; RITA (Real Intelligence Threat Analytics): open-source beaconing detection; commercial: ExtraHop, Darktrace, Vectra AI.
How do you implement secure session management?

Secure session management: protect authenticated sessions from theft, fixation, and hijacking. Session token generation: cryptographically random: use CSPRNG (os.urandom in Python, SecureRandom in Java, crypto.randomBytes in Node.js); minimum 128-bit entropy (32 hex chars or 44 base64url chars); never generate sequentially or predictably (timestamp, user ID, incrementing counter). Session storage: server-side sessions (reference tokens): token stored in cookie; session data stored server-side (Redis, database, memory); token is meaningless identifier; preferred for sensitive applications; client-side tokens (JWTs): all session data in token; signed (not encrypted by default); server stateless; validate signature on every request; never store sensitive data in JWT payload (visible to client). Cookie attributes: Secure: only sent over HTTPS; HttpOnly: not accessible by JavaScript; prevents XSS-based session theft; SameSite: Strict or Lax: prevents CSRF; SameSite=Strict: cookie not sent with any cross-site request; SameSite=Lax: cookie sent with top-level navigation GET but not other cross-site requests; Path and Domain: restrict cookie to specific path and domain; avoid setting Domain to parent domain unless needed. Session lifecycle: creation: generate new session ID on login; invalidate any pre-existing session ID (session fixation prevention); expiry: absolute expiry: session invalid after fixed time regardless of activity (24 hours for standard; 15 minutes for financial); relative/idle expiry: session invalid after N minutes of inactivity; shorter for sensitive applications; logout: invalidate server-side session (delete from Redis/database); clear client-side cookie (set to empty string with past expiry); for JWTs: add to token blocklist or use short expiry + refresh token; re-authentication: sensitive operations (password change, payment, privilege actions) require re-authentication or step-up MFA even within active session. Session fixation prevention: generate new session ID after authentication (PHP: session_regenerate_id(true); Java Spring: SessionManagementConfigurer.sessionFixation().changeSessionId()); never honour session ID from URL parameter or accept externally provided session ID. Concurrent session control: limit active sessions per user (optional); alert on concurrent sessions from different countries; provide session management UI (users see active sessions, revoke old devices).
What is security incident detection using SIEM alerts?

SIEM alert-based detection: translate threat intelligence and hypotheses into automated detection rules; identify security incidents from log correlation. Alert creation workflow: define threat scenario (hypothesis: user account compromised via credential stuffing); identify data sources (authentication logs from AD, VPN, web apps); translate to rule: multiple failed logins from different IPs for same account (password spray) followed by success (credential stuffing success); test on historical data (tune to reduce false positives); deploy to production; alert on match. Rule types in practice: threshold: count events exceeding threshold in time window; events: failed login count > 10 for same account in 5 minutes; correlation: sequence of events from different sources; event A then event B within window; example: recon scan from IP then exploit attempt from same IP within 1 hour; aggregation: group similar events; aggregate all DDoS indicators; alert if DDoS traffic exceeds threshold; statistical baseline deviation: current value vs rolling average baseline; today download volume vs 30-day average; alert on 3x deviation. Alert fields: rule name (descriptive: Windows -- Multiple Failed Logon Attempts); severity (map to P1-P4); MITRE ATT&CK technique (T1110.001 -- Password Spraying); data source; triggered logic (threshold: 5 failures from single source IP in 60 seconds); recommended action (SOC analyst triage: check if legitimate testing, validate IP reputation, correlate with other events); false positive rate (expected: low -- few legitimate sources would trigger 5+ failures); assigned team. Alert tuning lifecycle: deploy alert; monitor for 2 weeks; review every triggered alert (TP or FP?); for each FP: add exception (known vulnerability scanner IP, known test account, legitimate service); if >20% FP rate: adjust threshold or add filter; aim for >80% precision; alert fatigue: SOC analysts stop responding if too many FPs; quality over quantity; 50 high-quality alerts reviewed daily better than 500 low-quality. SOC workflow: alert fires; L1 analyst triages (is this real?); if confirmed suspicious: escalate to L2; L2 investigates (full scope, log deep-dive); if confirmed incident: escalate to IR; IR team executes playbook.
What is a cybersecurity framework and how do you select one?

Cybersecurity framework: structured approach to managing cybersecurity risk; common language for programmes; baseline for assessment. NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) 2.0: most widely adopted globally; six core functions: GOVERN (new in 2.0): organisational context, risk strategy, supply chain; IDENTIFY: asset management, risk assessment, vulnerabilities; PROTECT: access control, data security, platform security, technology resilience; DETECT: continuous monitoring, adverse event analysis; RESPOND: incident management, incident analysis, incident communication, mitigation; RECOVER: recovery plan execution, communication, restoration; each function has categories and subcategories; implementation tiers: 1 (Partial) to 4 (Adaptive); profiles: current state vs target state; gap analysis drives roadmap. ISO 27001/27002: international standard; 93 controls in Annex A (2022 edition); 11 themes: organisational, people, physical, technological; risk-based; certifiable (external audit); globally recognised; resource intensive to implement; appropriate for organisations requiring certification for customer trust or regulatory compliance. CIS Controls v8: 18 control groups; 153 safeguards; implementation groups: IG1 (basic hygiene), IG2 (mid-size org), IG3 (large org); practical and technical; prescriptive; good starting point for smaller organisations; mappable to NIST CSF and ISO 27001. PCI DSS 4.0: payment card industry standard; 12 requirements; mandatory for cardholder data environments; very prescriptive; compliance validated by QSA (Qualified Security Assessor). HIPAA Security Rule: US healthcare; administrative, physical, technical safeguards for ePHI; required vs addressable safeguards; not prescriptive (reasonable and appropriate). Framework selection: if no existing framework: NIST CSF or CIS Controls (start with CIS IG1 for small org); regulated industry: align with sector-specific framework (HIPAA, PCI DSS, NERC CIP for energy, ICS-62443 for OT/ICS); global customer base: ISO 27001 for internationally recognised certification; multiple frameworks: map controls (CIS maps to NIST CSF; ISO maps to NIST CSF); manage one programme that satisfies multiple; assess current vs target state; prioritise gaps by risk; build roadmap.
What are the main techniques for network evasion during penetration testing?

Network evasion: avoid detection by IDS, IPS, WAF, and monitoring tools during penetration testing. Packet level: fragmentation: split malicious payload across multiple IP fragments; IDS may not reassemble before checking signature; most modern IDS do reassemble but some miss; slow scan timing: -T1 or -T2 in Nmap; sends packets slowly; avoids rate-based detection; looks less like automated scan; decoy scanning: Nmap -D RND:10 TARGET (send scans from 10 random decoy IPs mixed with real IP); IDS sees many source IPs; harder to identify real attacker; source port manipulation: nmap --source-port 53 (appear to come from DNS); firewall may allow traffic from port 53; some older firewall ACLs allow established connections from port 53. Application layer evasion: encoding: URL encoding, double URL encoding, Unicode encoding of attack payloads; bypass signature-based WAF detection; case variation in protocol keywords (GET vs gEt); HTTPS: encrypted traffic cannot be inspected without SSL interception; protocol anomalies: HTTP/1.0 vs 1.1 differences; unusual HTTP methods; chunked transfer encoding; whitespace manipulation in headers; custom user agents: avoid known scanner UAs (Nmap, Nikto, sqlmap); use browser-like UA; or mimic specific applications. IPv6: many IDS/IPS rules written for IPv4; IPv6 traffic may bypass detection; dual-stack hosts reachable via IPv6 if IPv4 detection blocks IPv4. Application payload obfuscation: SQL injection: comment injection (UN/**/ION), case variation (uNiOn), encoding (CHAR() instead of string literals), double-encode characters; XSS: JSFuck (JavaScript using only []()!+), HTML entities, non-standard event handlers; shellcode encoding: Metasploit encoders (shikata_ga_nai -- polymorphic XOR/feedback encoder); but many AV detect even encoded shellcode now. Timing attacks: slow operations: Slowloris, RUDY (slow HTTP POST); avoids volume-based detection; slow scan with long sleep between requests. Operational considerations: evasion is NOT about breaking security controls in production (avoid causing system instability); goal: demonstrate that detection may miss sophisticated attacker; document evasion techniques used in report; recommend improvements (SSL inspection, better IDS rules, network segmentation that makes evasion harder).
What is security automation and orchestration?

Security automation: automate repetitive security tasks; reduce analyst workload; improve consistency and speed. Why automate: SOC analysts spend 40-60% of time on repetitive tasks (alert triage, indicator lookup, ticket creation); automation handles routine; analysts focus on complex decisions; consistency: automated playbook handles same alert identically every time; speed: MTTR reduced; automation acts in seconds vs human minutes or hours. What to automate: alert enrichment: every alert automatically enriched before analyst sees it; lookup source IP in threat intel (VirusTotal, Shodan, ThreatFeed); lookup user in AD (get manager, department, recent logon locations); lookup asset criticality from CMDB; add risk score; present enriched alert to analyst: one click shows all context instead of manual lookup; indicator lookups: IOC matched against threat intel feeds automatically; false positive filtering: known-good IPs or services filtered before analyst queue; repetitive response actions: auto-isolate endpoint when EDR detects ransomware behaviour; auto-disable account when impossible travel detected (confirm with user via SMS first); auto-block IP when multiple sources flag as malicious; auto-delete phishing email from all mailboxes when confirmed by security. SOAR platform: Splunk SOAR (Phantom): 3000+ actions across security tools; visual playbook builder; conditional logic; human approval steps; community app exchange; Palo Alto XSOAR: Cortex XDR integration; marketplace of integrations; FortiSOAR; IBM Security SOAR; Microsoft Sentinel: native SOAR capability via Logic Apps; Tines: simpler no-code SOAR; good for teams without dedicated SOAR admin; D3 SMART SOAR. Playbook design: identify high-volume repetitive alert type; map current manual workflow; convert to automated playbook; identify: automatic steps (no human needed -- IP lookup, ticket create), human-in-loop steps (approve action with business impact -- block critical supplier IP, disable VP account); test in lower environment; monitor false action rate after deployment. Metrics: playbook automation rate (% of alert workflow automated); MTTR improvement (before vs after automation); analyst capacity (how many additional alerts handled per analyst per day); false automation rate (automation took wrong action -- track and reduce).
What is cloud-native application protection (CNAPP)?

CNAPP (Cloud Native Application Protection Platform): unified platform combining multiple cloud security capabilities; converges CSPM, CWPP, CIEM, container security, IaC scanning, and more. Why CNAPP: previously separate tools for each cloud security domain; siloed: CSPM found public S3 bucket; CWPP found vulnerable library in running container; CIEM found overprivileged role; no correlation between findings; CNAPP: connect dots; show: EC2 with critical CVE + has internet exposure + has overprivileged IAM role = critical attack path. Core capabilities integrated in CNAPP: CSPM (Cloud Security Posture Management): configuration compliance, misconfiguration detection; CWPP (Cloud Workload Protection Platform): vulnerability scanning, runtime protection for VMs, containers, serverless; CIEM (Cloud Infrastructure Entitlement Management): identity and permission analysis, privilege escalation path detection; Container and Kubernetes security: image scanning, registry scanning, Kubernetes admission control, runtime container protection; IaC Security: scan Terraform, CloudFormation before deployment; vulnerability management: CVE identification across workloads; network exposure analysis: which resources are internet-reachable? Attack path analysis: connect all findings; show: if attacker exploits vulnerability in internet-facing EC2 with overprivileged role: impact is access to all S3 buckets including production data store; risk-based prioritisation: 1000 vulnerabilities; CNAPP shows which 10 are in critical attack paths; fix those first. Products: Wiz: market leader; agentless (read-only cloud API + out-of-band scanning); fastest deployment; graph-based attack path analysis; supports AWS, Azure, GCP, OCI, Alibaba; Prisma Cloud (Palo Alto): comprehensive; agent + agentless; strong runtime protection; Lacework: anomaly detection; good for multi-cloud; Orca Security: agentless; SideScanning technology; Aqua Security: container-focused; strong Kubernetes; Sysdig: Falco-based; strong runtime; Trend Cloud One. Deployment: agentless CNAPP (Wiz, Orca): read-only cloud API access; no performance impact; no agent installation; broader coverage; limited runtime visibility; agent-based (Prisma Cloud Defender): full runtime protection; performance overhead; deployment complexity; hybrid: agentless for breadth + agent for critical workloads requiring runtime.
How do you detect network reconnaissance?

Network reconnaissance detection: identify attacker probing activity before exploitation. Types of reconnaissance and detection: Port scanning: nmap, masscan, ZMap, Shodan-like scanning; produces: many TCP SYN packets to multiple ports from single source; many closed port responses; detection: threshold alert on failed connection rate from single IP (> 100 failed TCP connections in 60 seconds from same source); IDS signature: NMAP OS detection probes (unusual packet combinations); Zeek: notice in scan.log. Ping sweep / host discovery: ICMP echo request to many IPs; ARP requests (broadcast); detection: many ICMP packets from single source; new ARP requests for IP range; internal: arp-scan patterns; threshold: >50 ICMP requests from single internal host in 60 seconds. Service enumeration: banner grabbing (connect, read banner, disconnect); NULL scans, FIN scans, XMAS scans (stealth scan types with unusual TCP flags); detection: IDS rules for FIN/NULL/XMAS scans (unusual TCP flag combinations); connection with immediate RST after banner read. Web application reconnaissance: directory scanning (gobuster, dirbuster, ffuf): many 404 responses from single IP; sequential path testing; detection: WAF logs; alert on > 50 4XX responses per minute from same IP; 403/401 spike. DNS reconnaissance: zone transfer attempt (AXFR): mostly blocked but attempted; many DNS queries for subdomains (brute force); detection: Zeek dns.log: AXFR requests; high rate of NX (non-existent domain) responses from DNS. Vulnerability scanning: Nessus, OpenVAS signatures well-known; detection: IDS signatures for scanner UAs; characteristic probe patterns; many vulnerabilities probed sequentially. LDAP/SMB enumeration: many LDAP queries for user enumeration; SMB null session (attempt to list shares without credentials); detection: Event 4776 NTLM auth failures; LDAP anomaly (many queries from single IP); high rate of SMB session setup failures. Context: internal scanning from workstation = unusual (workstation should not scan entire network); flag immediately; external scanning from internet = normal background noise (Shodan, Censys scan everything continuously); focus on targeted scanning of your specific IPs from single source; correlation: scan followed by exploitation attempt = high confidence attack; alert chain these events.
What is memory forensics and how do you analyse volatile memory?

Memory forensics: capture and analyse computer RAM; find artefacts not present on disk; detect fileless malware, running processes, encryption keys, credentials, network connections. Why memory forensics: fileless malware lives only in memory (no disk artefact); encryption keys in memory at runtime (not stored on disk); process injection hides processes from disk; live network connections; decrypted data in memory. Memory acquisition: live system: winpmem (Windows, open-source); DumpIt; Magnet RAM Capture; FTK Imager (live acquisition); LiME (Linux Memory Extractor): loadable kernel module; acquire from running Linux; Volatility-compatible format: raw, LiME, EWF; crashed system: crash dump (Windows: MEMORY.DMP); hibernation file (hiberfil.sys): compressed memory snapshot; virtual machine: suspend VM and copy VMEM file + VMSS file. Volatility framework: most widely used memory forensics tool; Python-based; supports Windows, Linux, macOS memory images; version 2.6 (Volatility 2, older but widely used) and Volatility 3 (newer API). Core Volatility plugins: imageinfo / windows.info: identify OS version, architecture; pslist: list running processes from EPROCESS linked list; pstree: show process parent-child relationships; psscan: find hidden processes by scanning memory (rootkits hide from pslist by removing from list but psscan finds by structure signature); cmdline: command line arguments for each process; network: connections established at time of capture; dlllist: DLLs loaded by each process; handles: open handles per process (files, registry keys, sockets); malfind: find memory regions with executable permissions injected into non-image-backed memory (process injection); memdump: dump process memory for further analysis; hashdump: extract NTLM hashes from LSASS process memory; strings: find strings in specific process or entire image; hivelist/printkey: Windows registry hives in memory; filescan: find FILE_OBJECT structures (find deleted or hidden files). Analysis workflow: dump all process command lines (pslist + cmdline); identify suspicious processes: no icon process in unusual path, svchost without parent services.exe, powershell spawned from Word; malfind: find injected memory regions; dump suspicious process memory; run YARA against dump; extract network connections; correlate with network logs; extract LSASS memory region; hashdump for credential exposure; find encryption keys (AES key schedule signature in memory).
What is the role of threat hunting in a SOC?

Threat hunting: proactive search for threats that evaded automated detection; assumes compromise and looks for evidence; hypothesis-driven investigation. Why hunting: MTTD (Mean Time to Detect) industry average: 21-200+ days; attackers dwell in network during this time; automated detection finds known threats; hunting finds unknown or sophisticated threats that evade signatures and rules. Hunting vs incident response: IR: reactive (alert fired, investigate); hunting: proactive (no alert, search for threat); hunting discovers threats that trigger IR. Types of hunts: structured: based on known threat actor TTP; hunt for specific technique in your environment; example: Cobalt Strike beacon hunting (look for beaconing patterns, JA3 fingerprints, sleep+jitter pattern); unstructured: anomaly-based; identify statistical outliers in data; example: identify processes making unusual external connections; situational: triggered by external intelligence (CISA advisory about threat actor targeting your sector); hunt for their specific techniques immediately. Hunting process: (1) Develop hypothesis: based on threat intel, TTP knowledge, intuition; example: Attacker has persistent foothold via scheduled task; (2) Determine data source: which logs would contain evidence? Windows event logs (4698 scheduled task creation), Sysmon event 1 (process creation from scheduled task), endpoint telemetry; (3) Write query: SIEM or endpoint data lake query; filter for scheduled tasks created by unusual parents, with unusual names, or running unusual commands; (4) Triage results: expected (backup software, antivirus) vs unexpected; investigate suspicious hits; (5) If found: escalate to IR; if not found: document hypothesis as hunted and cleared; (6) Improve detections: convert successful hunt into automated detection rule (do not hunt the same thing manually every time). Skills needed: attacker TTPs knowledge (ATT&CK framework); data analysis (SQL/SPL/KQL query writing); pattern recognition; understanding of normal baseline; tools: EDR telemetry (CrowdStrike, SentinelOne, Defender for Endpoint); SIEM; endpoint data lake (Elastic, Splunk, Microsoft 365 Defender Advanced Hunting -- KQL); packet capture (Zeek logs, PCAP). Metrics: hunts per quarter; findings per hunt (% of hunts that discover real threat); dwell time reduction (hunting discovers threats earlier than automated detection); MTTD improvement attributable to hunting programme.
What is cyber threat intelligence lifecycle?

CTI (Cyber Threat Intelligence) lifecycle: process to produce actionable intelligence from raw data; six phases. Planning and direction: define intelligence requirements; what questions does the organisation need answered? (What threat actors target us? What TTPs does ransomware targeting our sector use? Are our credentials in breach databases?); types of intelligence needed: strategic (executive decision making), operational (SOC priorities), tactical (detection rules). Collection: gather raw data from multiple sources; open source (OSINT): threat feeds, Twitter/X security researchers, government advisories (CISA, NCSC), Shodan, VirusTotal, Darknet monitoring, security vendor reports; commercial: Recorded Future, Mandiant, Crowdstrike Intelligence, Anomali ThreatStream, Flashpoint; technical: malware sandboxes (ANY.RUN, Hybrid Analysis), honeynet logs, endpoint telemetry, network captures; human: ISACs (Information Sharing and Analysis Centers), vendor relationships, law enforcement partnerships. Processing: normalise raw data to common format; STIX 2.1 (Structured Threat Information eXpression): standard format for threat intel objects: indicator (IoC: IP, domain, hash), threat-actor, campaign, course-of-action, vulnerability, malware; TAXII (Trusted Automated eXchange of Intelligence Information): protocol for sharing STIX over HTTPS; deduplicate IoCs from multiple sources; enrich (add geolocation, WHOIS, historical data); expire time-limited IoCs (IP address ownership changes; 30-90 day expiry for most IoCs). Analysis: interpret data in context; create finished intelligence; assess confidence level (confirmed vs suspected); attribute to threat actor (with appropriate caveats); identify patterns and trends; analytical techniques: structured analytic techniques (ACH -- Analysis of Competing Hypotheses); diamond model (four points: adversary, capability, infrastructure, victim); kill chain mapping; ATT&CK TTP mapping. Dissemination: share intelligence with right audience in right format; strategic: board briefing (high-level risk); operational: SOC advisory (new campaign targeting sector); tactical: SIEM IoC feed (automated push to detection system). Feedback: consumers provide feedback; did intelligence lead to detection? Was attribution correct? Refine requirements; close loop; improve future cycles.
What are common Windows persistence mechanisms?

Windows persistence: maintain access after reboot, credential change, or other disruption. Registry run keys: HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run: executes for current user at logon; HKLM\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run: executes for all users at logon (requires admin); HKLM\Software\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Image File Execution Options\sethc.exe (debugger key): replace sethc.exe (Sticky Keys) with cmd.exe: trigger by pressing Shift 5 times at lock screen; runs as SYSTEM; similar: utilman.exe, narrator.exe, magnify.exe; detection: Autoruns.exe (Sysinternals): shows all auto-start locations; reg query HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run. Scheduled tasks: schtasks /create /tn TaskName /tr C:\backdoor.exe /sc daily; encoded base64 commands in task actions; task XML with obfuscated content; detection: schtasks /query /fo LIST /v; Event ID 4698/4702 (scheduled task created/modified); Autoruns shows scheduled tasks. Services: sc create name binpath= C:\backdoor.exe start= auto; detection: Event 7045 (new service installed); sc query; Autoruns services tab. DLL hijacking persistence: DLL search order: application directory, System32, current directory, PATH; place malicious DLL in application directory; loaded every time application runs; AppInit_DLLs: HKLM\Software\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Windows\AppInit_DLLs: loaded by every process that calls user32.dll; powerful but detected by most EDR. COM object hijacking: HKCU\Software\Classes\CLSID registry: user-writable; override COM object path; application loads user COM instead of system COM; no admin required; detection: Sysmon registry events. Boot and pre-OS: bootkit (boot sector persistence): MBR or VBR infection; UEFI rootkit: firmware-level (CosmicStrand, LoJax); survives OS reinstall; requires firmware flash; detection requires hardware attestation. WMI event subscriptions: permanent subscriptions survive reboot; see WMI section; detection: Event 5861; wmic /namespace:\\root\subscription path CommandLineEventConsumer get. Shortcut (LNK) hijacking: replace legitimate shortcut with one pointing to malicious + legitimate binary; user launches shortcut: executes both. Scheduled task via COM (DCOM): some schedulers accessible via COM without creating visible task; advanced technique. BITS (Background Intelligent Transfer Service): bitsadmin /addfile /setnotifycmdline: runs command when download completes; persistent across reboots; detection: bitsadmin /list /verbose; Windows Autoruns.
What is the NIST SP 800-53 security control framework?

NIST SP 800-53: Recommended Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations; most comprehensive US federal security control catalogue; Revision 5 (current, 2020). Scope: applicable to all federal information systems (mandatory for US federal agencies via FISMA -- Federal Information Security Modernization Act); widely adopted by private sector; used for FedRAMP (cloud service authorisation for federal); referenced by NIST CSF. Structure: 20 control families (each designated by two-letter ID): AC (Access Control): 25 controls; least privilege, session management, remote access; AT (Awareness and Training): security awareness, role-based training; AU (Audit and Accountability): logging, audit record review, protection; CA (Assessment, Authorization, Monitoring): assessments, authorisation, continuous monitoring; CM (Configuration Management): baseline, change control, software usage; CP (Contingency Planning): backup, disaster recovery, testing; IA (Identification and Authentication): MFA, password management, device authentication; IR (Incident Response): IR policy, training, testing, handling; MA (Maintenance): system maintenance, maintenance tools; MP (Media Protection): media access, media storage; PE (Physical and Environmental Protection): physical access, power, environmental controls; PL (Planning): security plans; PM (Program Management): programme-level controls; PS (Personnel Security): security screening, termination; RA (Risk Assessment): risk assessment process, vulnerability scanning; SA (System and Acquisition Services): supply chain, development practices; SC (System and Communications Protection): network isolation, encryption, boundary protection; SI (System and Information Integrity): malware protection, security alerts, error handling; SR (Supply Chain Risk Management): new in Rev 5; supplier assessment, traceability. Control baselines: low-impact, moderate-impact, high-impact systems; more controls required for higher impact; FISMA categorisation determines baseline. FedRAMP uses NIST 800-53 Rev 5 with additional requirements; cloud vendors seeking FedRAMP authorisation implement all moderate or high baseline controls. Comparison: NIST CSF = what to do (functions and categories); NIST 800-53 = how to do it (specific technical and procedural controls); 800-53 maps to CSF; implementing 800-53 satisfies CSF; 800-53 more prescriptive and comprehensive than ISO 27001 controls.
How do you detect lateral movement using Windows event logs?

Lateral movement detection via Windows event logs: identify attacker traversal between systems using authentication and process creation logs. Key event IDs for lateral movement: Event 4624 (Logon Success) on target host: Logon Type 3 (Network): remote file access, SMB, PsExec, WMI (most lateral movement is type 3); Logon Type 10 (Remote Interactive): RDP connection; Logon Type 2 (Interactive): local or physical logon; filter: type 3 from unusual sources (workstation to workstation rather than expected server sources). Event 4648 (Logon with Explicit Credentials): process explicitly provides credentials (RunAs, PsExec -u, Mimikatz pass-the-hash); high-value alert when seen outside expected admin activities. Event 4672 (Special Privileges Assigned to New Logon): admin-level privileges at logon; correlate with 4624 to identify privileged network logon. Event 4769 (Kerberos Service Ticket Request) on DC: Ticket Encryption Type = 0x17 (RC4) from service account SPN = Kerberoasting; unusual SPNs requested; high volume TGS requests for many services from single source = BloodHound-style enumeration. Event 7045 (New Service Installed) on target: PsExec installs PSEXESVC service; unusual service name pattern. Event 4688 (Process Creation with CommandLine): requires audit process creation + include command line auditing enabled; on target: cmd.exe or powershell.exe spawned by unusual parent process (wmic.exe, mshta.exe, services.exe after 7045). Correlation rules for lateral movement: same account authenticates to multiple hosts within short time window (>5 hosts in 10 minutes = suspicious); account authenticates to host it has never accessed before (first-time host access); workstation-to-workstation network logon (type 3 from WORKSTATION$ to WORKSTATION$); privileged account (domain admin) authenticating to workstation directly (should use jump server); admin service installation followed immediately by process execution. Baselines: establish normal logon patterns per account; first-seen analysis (new source IP, new target host, new account-to-host pair); alerting on deviations from baseline reduces false positives. Honeytoken accounts: create fake AD accounts with no legitimate use; any logon event for these accounts = attacker testing stolen credentials; zero false positives; immediate high-confidence alert.
What are best practices for securing cloud storage?

Cloud storage security: S3 (AWS), Blob Storage (Azure), GCS (Google Cloud), and similar services; high-risk if misconfigured. Access control -- block public access: AWS: Block Public Access at account level (4 settings all enabled): BlockPublicAcls, IgnorePublicAcls, BlockPublicPolicy, RestrictPublicBuckets; Azure: disable public access on Storage Account; GCS: set allUsers not to have storage.objects.get; default: deny all public access; explicitly grant only when needed (CDN serving public content). Bucket policies and IAM: bucket policy: allowlist IAM principals who can access; deny explicit for unknown principals; IAM role permissions: only needed services have access to specific bucket and only required actions (s3:GetObject vs s3:*); cross-account access: explicit trust relationship required; no public access or AllAccount wildcards. Encryption: S3 server-side encryption: SSE-S3 (AWS manages keys, AES-256), SSE-KMS (customer manages via KMS -- key policy controls access; rotation enabled; audit via CloudTrail), SSE-C (customer provides key per request; rarely used); default encryption: enforce via bucket policy: Deny PutObject if s3:x-amz-server-side-encryption is not aws:kms; client-side encryption: encrypt before upload (E2E); only decryptable by holder of key; Azure: Storage Service Encryption with CMK (Customer Managed Key) via Azure Key Vault; GCS: CMEK via Cloud KMS. Object versioning and deletion protection: enable versioning: deleted objects become delete markers; recoverable; object lock / immutability: WORM (Write Once Read Many): compliance mode (no delete even by admin during retention period); governance mode (authorised users can unlock); protect backups from ransomware; use S3 Object Lock for backup buckets. Access logging: S3 server access logging: log all requests to access log bucket; who accessed what when; CloudTrail data events: API-level logging for GetObject, PutObject, DeleteObject; more detailed; correlate with IAM identity. Monitoring: AWS GuardDuty: detect unusual access patterns (access from unfamiliar IPs, access from Tor, exfiltration volume anomalies); AWS Macie: sensitive data discovery in S3; alert on PII in unsecured bucket; regular access review: audit bucket policies and IAM permissions quarterly.
What is CVSS environmental scoring?

CVSS Environmental Score: customise base score for specific organisation; reflect how security controls and asset importance change risk in your environment. Why environmental score: CVE-2021-44228 (Log4Shell): CVSS Base Score 10.0 for any system; but: your organisation runs Log4j only in one internal batch processing system, isolated from internet, no sensitive data; Environmental Score: much lower; allows proper prioritisation vs a public-facing customer service application running Log4j directly accessible from internet. Environmental metrics: Modified Attack Vector: does your network architecture change effective attack vector? If internet-facing system (network AV) is in DMZ with firewall to internet: modified AV might be Network still; if exploitable only from internal (perimeter blocks all access): modified AV = Network (unchanged) but contextually harder to reach; Modified Attack Complexity: do your controls add complexity? WAF requiring HTTPS mutual auth makes exploitation harder; Modified Privileges Required: additional controls reduce privilege requirements for attacker? Modified User Interaction: additional security training makes phishing-based vulnerabilities harder to exploit (marginal impact); Modified Impact: CIA Confidentiality Impact: if encrypted data at rest: confidentiality impact reduced even if attacker reads encrypted files; Asset criticality modifier (not CVSS but many tools): if affected system is critical (tier 1 production): multiply risk; if test system with no production access: reduce. Implementation: Tenable / Qualys allow setting environmental scores in vulnerability management platform; set per asset criticality (business critical, important, standard); set control adjustments (WAF present, network isolation, encryption at rest); scanner calculates adjusted priority for each vulnerability on each asset; CVSS Environmental Score calculation: ModifiedImpact and ModifiedExploitability sub-scores replace base sub-scores; Environmental Score = Roundup(Roundup(min(ModifiedImpactSubScore + ModifiedExploitabilitySubScore, 10)) * ExploitCodeMaturity * RemediationLevel * ReportConfidence). Practical recommendation: always document why environmental adjustments made; management should approve adjustments to high-severity findings; use VPR (Tenable) or similar combined score for operational prioritisation; environmental score should guide SLA determination for patch application.
What is a firmware attack and how do attackers target UEFI?

Firmware attacks: compromise firmware (UEFI, BIOS, storage controller, NIC firmware, baseboard management controller); most persistent attack; survives OS reinstall, hard drive replacement, even some motherboard replacements. UEFI (Unified Extensible Firmware Interface): replacement for BIOS; initialises hardware before OS boots; responsible for Secure Boot; UEFI attacks most impactful because: UEFI loads before OS and security software; AV cannot scan it; persists across OS reinstalls; UEFI Secure Boot is supposed to prevent unsigned code from running. Notable UEFI threats: LoJax (2018, APT28): first in-wild UEFI rootkit; modified SPI flash (persistent UEFI module); implanted agent survived OS reinstall; CosmicStrand (2022): sophisticated UEFI bootkit; discovered by Kaspersky; linked to China-based threat actors; MosaicRegressor (2020): linked to North Korea; UEFI rootkit delivered via compromised supply chain; MoonBounce (2022): Kaspersky; implanted in CORE_DXE firmware volume; persisted across hard drive swaps. Attack vectors: compromised UEFI update mechanism: attacker with OS admin access calls vendor UEFI update tool with malicious firmware image; infected SPI flash: attacker with physical access uses hardware flasher; supply chain: malicious firmware pre-installed before delivery (Nation-state and hardware supply chain attacks); BIOS/UEFI vulnerabilities: code execution vulnerabilities in UEFI modules; CVE-2020-10713 (BootHole) -- GRUB2 bootloader vulnerability bypassing Secure Boot; LogoFAIL (2023): vulnerabilities in UEFI image parsers allow code execution during logo display. Detection: Intel Boot Guard: hardware-based protection; cryptographic verification of firmware; prevents modification even with privileged OS access; CHIPSEC: Intel tool for hardware security assessment; scan UEFI configuration and flash for anomalies; Measured Boot + TPM: each boot component measured into TPM PCRs; remote attestation verifies chain; EDR: UEFI firmware scanning (Kaspersky, ESET detect known UEFI malware); anti-evil-maid: verify boot process integrity. Prevention: Secure Boot: verify boot loader and kernel signatures; vendor UEFI signing; HP Sure Start, Dell SafeBIOS, Lenovo ThinkShield: hardware-based UEFI protection; vendor firmware updates: sign and verify; physical security: prevent physical access to flash SPI; supply chain verification.
What is certificate pinning and when should you use it?

Certificate pinning: hardcode expected certificate or public key in application; verify actual certificate at runtime; prevent MITM even with valid CA-signed certificate. Types: Certificate pinning: pin specific certificate (Subject, Serial, or full DER encoding); problem: certificate expires and rotates; must update application with new cert; Public key pinning: pin certificate public key (SPKI hash); key can be retained across certificate renewals (same key, new certificate); more resilient; CA pinning: pin specific CA public key; any certificate from that CA accepted; easier key rotation; less specific. HTTP Public Key Pinning (HPKP): deprecated browser header; pinned CA public key hash in HTTP header; browser rejected different cert for 60 days; many sites accidentally broke; browser removed support 2019. How pinning works in mobile apps: developer embeds expected SPKI hash (SHA-256 of SubjectPublicKeyInfo) in app binary; at TLS connection: extract server certificate SPKI; compute SHA-256; compare to embedded hash; if mismatch: abort connection; prevents: MITM even with corporate SSL inspection proxy, MITM with forged CA-signed certificate, rogue CA issuing valid cert for your domain. Bypassing pinning: Frida: hook SSL verification function; return success regardless of cert; objection: ios sslpinning disable / android sslpinning disable; Apk-MITM: patch APK to remove pinning; justTrustMe (Xposed): modify Android SSL functions; network_security_config.xml bypass (Android); detection resistant pinning: detect Frida/Xposed/Substrate; check for debugger; integrity check of pinning code; multi-layer pinning (OkHttp + native layer + JNI). When to use: high-security applications: banking, password managers, military, healthcare; where MITM against the specific app is a relevant threat; apps handling highly sensitive data; when NOT to use: general consumer apps (breaks corporate SSL inspection proxy; users on restrictive networks fail); if frequent cert rotation needed without app update; if strong CA ecosystem sufficient. Best practices: pin 2+ public keys (primary + backup pin); backup pin allows key rotation without breaking app; document rotation procedure; test rotation before production.
What is a business logic vulnerability?

Business logic vulnerability: flaw in application workflow, assumptions, or process; not technical injection but abuse of intended functionality in unintended ways; automation misses these; require understanding of business context. Types: insufficient process validation: skip required workflow steps; multi-step checkout: select item, add to cart, enter payment; skip to order confirmation step without payment; insecure direct object reference in workflow: view order status of another user (IDOR); change order quantity to negative (refund without return); price manipulation: change item price in request (if price comes from client); apply discount code multiple times (no validation of previous use); integer overflow in quantity: quantity 2147483647 + 1 wraps to negative; order negative quantity; get credit. Account and authentication logic: password reset: generate reset token; attacker requests token for victim account (just needs to know email); token sent to attacker-controlled email (email typo, email change during reset); race conditions: concurrent discount code use; concurrent vote; concurrent balance modification. Workflow bypass: step-by-step registration process; skip security check step; hit payment endpoint directly without completing KYC (Know Your Customer) step; email verification: can you use account before email verified? If yes: attacker creates account with victim email, victim never gets access. Trust boundary confusion: internal-only API endpoint accessible externally; API gateway supposed to validate business rules; backend skips validation (trusts gateway); direct backend call bypasses rules. Function chaining: each function individually secure; combination insecure; password reset sends email to registered address; email change requires password; password reset + email change: change email during reset flow; reset token goes to new email. Testing approach: map all application workflows (user journeys); identify business rules (each item can be purchased once, discount valid once per user, etc.); attempt to violate each rule: submit requests out of order, repeat steps meant to be single-use, change numeric values to negative, change prices, skip required steps; think like a fraudster not just a hacker; negative testing critical (what happens with edge cases?). Prevention: server-side business rule validation at every step; stateful workflow tracking server-side; validate all client-supplied values server-side (price, quantity, discount code, step completion status).
How do you perform wireless network exploitation?

Wireless network exploitation: after wireless assessment identifies vulnerabilities, exploit them to gain network access. WPA2 Personal crack: capture WPA2 4-way handshake (airodump-ng + aireplay-ng deauth); convert: cap2hccapx or hcxpcapngtool (convert to hashcat format); crack with hashcat: hashcat -m 22000 handshake.hc22000 /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt --rules-file best64.rule; PMKID attack (no client needed): hcxdumptool --enable_status=3 -o capture.pcapng -i wlan0mon; hcxpcapngtool -o hash.hc22000 capture.pcapng; hashcat -m 22000. WPS attack: WPS (Wi-Fi Protected Setup) PIN: 8-digit PIN split into two 4-digit halves; each verified separately; max 11000 attempts; Reaver: reaver -i wlan0mon -b BSSID -vv; Pixie Dust attack (offline WPS attack): some routers use weak E-S1 and E-S2 nonces; pixiewps recovers PIN offline in seconds; --pixie-dust flag in Reaver. Evil twin / KARMA attack: hostapd-wpe: rogue AP for capturing Enterprise (WPA2-Enterprise) credentials; captures MSCHAPv2 challenge/response; crack with asleap: asleap -C challenge -R response -W wordlist; KARMA attack: respond to any SSID probe request from client; client connects to malicious AP matching remembered network name; automate with wifi-pumpkin3 or bettercap. Deauthentication: aireplay-ng -0 10 -a BSSID -c CLIENT wlan0mon (send 10 deauth frames to specific client); forces client to reconnect; capture handshake; or: keep deauthing to maintain DoS; 802.11w Management Frame Protection prevents deauth spoofing (not widely enforced on older hardware). LEAP exploitation: Lightweight EAP: older enterprise protocol; username transmitted plaintext; MSCHAPv2 response captured; asleap cracks offline; largely deprecated but still found; WPA3 transition mode attacks: if both WPA2 and WPA3 advertised; dragonblood attacks against WPA3 SAE (CVE-2019-9494); side-channel timing and cache attacks; force client back to WPA2 through denial of WPA3 frames. Post-exploitation: once connected to network: ARP scan internal range; Responder (capture SMB/HTTP/LDAP credentials); network pivot to corporate resources; treat as internal network foothold.
What is a buffer over-read vulnerability?

Buffer over-read: read data beyond intended buffer boundary; expose adjacent memory contents; different from overflow (write, leads to RCE) though often leads to info disclosure or crash. How it works: application reads fixed number of bytes from user-controlled length field; if length claims more bytes than actually in buffer: reader accesses memory beyond buffer; returns adjacent memory contents to attacker. Heartbleed (CVE-2014-0160): most famous buffer over-read; OpenSSL TLS heartbeat extension; client sends: type=heartbeat, length=64, payload=hello; server responds with same payload using client-specified length; vulnerable code: memcpy(bp, pl, payload); where payload = client-specified length; client sends length=65535 but sends only 5 bytes; server reads 65535 bytes from memory; returns adjacent memory including: private keys, session cookies, passwords, other session data; no authentication required; any TLS connection to vulnerable server exploitable; millions of servers affected 2014; 60% of internet HTTPS servers at time. Other over-reads: format string vulnerabilities: printf(user_input) without format string; %x reads from stack; %s follows pointer; attacker reads stack memory with %x.%x.%x.%x; bounds checking failure: reading array element without checking array length; atoi() on user input used as array index; off-by-one: loop reads one byte past end; exposes one byte of adjacent memory; usually less impactful. Exploitation: extract: private keys (Heartbleed extracted private keys in practice); session tokens (replayed to hijack sessions); cleartext credentials; encryption keys; other cryptographic material in memory. Detection: server logs: heartbeat requests not normally logged; monitor for unusual heartbeat request sizes; certificate reissuance spike (Heartbleed response required reissuing all certificates); scanner: testssl.sh checks for Heartbleed; Nessus Heartbleed check. Mitigation: bounds checking: verify length <= buffer size before reading; use safe library functions; code review for length field usage; compiler flags: AddressSanitizer detects out-of-bounds reads; memory-safe languages (Rust, Go): bounds checking enforced by language; avoid C/C++ where possible for security-critical parsing.
What is cryptographic key management?

Cryptographic key management: generation, storage, distribution, rotation, and destruction of encryption keys; security depends entirely on key protection. Key generation: use CSPRNG (Cryptographically Secure Pseudo-Random Number Generator): os.urandom() (Python), SecureRandom (Java), /dev/urandom or getrandom() (Linux); never use weak RNG (rand(), Math.random(), time-seeded PRNG); key size: AES 256-bit; RSA 2048 or 3072-bit (4096 for 20+ year secrets); ECDSA P-256 or P-384; ChaCha20 256-bit. Key storage: HSM (Hardware Security Module): physical device; keys never leave HSM in plaintext; hardware-enforced access control; FIPS 140-2 Level 3 certified for highest security; cloud HSM: AWS CloudHSM, Azure Dedicated HSM; secrets manager: AWS Secrets Manager, HashiCorp Vault, Azure Key Vault; stores keys encrypted; access controlled by IAM; audit trail; automatic rotation; environment variables (last resort): not encrypted; visible in process listing; logged in CI/CD; do not store long-lived secrets in env vars; code storage (worst): hardcoded keys found by secret scanners; never. Key distribution: asymmetric key exchange (ECDH): derive shared secret without transmitting key; TLS does this; key wrapping: encrypt key with another key (KEK -- Key Encryption Key); transport wrapped key; only receiver with KEK can unwrap. Key rotation: mandatory for compliance (PCI DSS: rotate encryption keys at least annually); automatic rotation: AWS Secrets Manager automatic rotation Lambda; HashiCorp Vault dynamic secrets (short-lived credentials generated on demand); KMS automatic rotation (AWS: annual key material rotation); reasons to rotate: suspected compromise, personnel departure, scheduled policy, algorithm deprecation. Key destruction: securely overwrite key material; HSM: zeroize command; software: overwrite with zeros then free (zeroise before free in C); document destruction for compliance. Key hierarchy: KEK (Key Encryption Key): encrypts DEKs; stored in HSM; DEK (Data Encryption Key): encrypts actual data; wrapped by KEK; rotated frequently; shorter lifetime; separation: different keys for encryption and signing; different keys per data category (payment data vs PII vs logs).
What is penetration testing methodology for APIs?

API penetration testing methodology: structured assessment of web APIs for security vulnerabilities. Preparation: gather API documentation (OpenAPI/Swagger spec, Postman collection, WADL, RAML); import into testing tool (Postman, Burp Suite, Insomnia); understand: authentication mechanism (API key, JWT, OAuth), rate limiting (is it stated?), versioning, business context (what operations exist and what should they do?); create test accounts: at minimum two accounts at lowest privilege level; one admin/elevated account if possible; obtain valid tokens for each. Authentication testing: no auth: remove Authorization header; expect 401; wrong token: send invalid or expired token; expect 401; token expiry: JWTs have exp claim; wait for expiry; re-test with expired token; cross-user token: use user A token to access user B resources; expect 403; brute force: API key space small enough to brute force?
