Rate limit on auth failures? Token in query string: if API key in URL parameter: logged by server, proxies, CDNs; report as information disclosure. Authorisation testing: BOLA/IDOR: for every endpoint returning a resource with ID: change ID to another user resource; check if returned; test all HTTP methods; GET protected but POST to same endpoint not? Horizontal: user A accessing user B data; vertical: regular user accessing admin endpoints; test every admin endpoint with regular user token. Input testing: test all parameters with injection payloads: single quote (SQL injection probe), SSTI payloads ({{7*7}}), path traversal (../../etc/passwd), SSRF (http://169.254.169.254/), XSS (if reflected), command injection (;id;); send malformed input: wrong type (string for integer field), missing required field, extremely long input, special characters, null bytes. Mass assignment: send additional fields not in documentation; {role: admin, isAdmin: true, balance: 1000000}; does any extra field update in DB? Rate limiting: send 100 requests rapidly; measure throttling; automation-heavy endpoints (search, verify code, password reset): targeted rate limit testing; business flow abuse: buy 100 of limited stock item in parallel requests. API-specific testing: GraphQL: introspection query (reveals full schema); deeply nested queries (DoS via complexity); batch queries (rate limit bypass); SOAP/XML: XXE injection in SOAP body; gRPC: protobuf tampering; REST: HTTP method override headers (X-HTTP-Method-Override); content-type confusion (send JSON as XML or vice versa). Report format: each finding: endpoint, method, parameter, payload, expected vs actual response, impact, remediation.
What is the OWASP Application Security Verification Standard (ASVS)?

ASVS (Application Security Verification Standard): framework for testing and verifying web application security; defines security requirements at three levels. Purpose: provides testable security requirements (not just recommendations); can be used as: application security assessment standard, guidance for developers, requirements in procurement. Three verification levels: Level 1 (Opportunistic): minimum baseline; DAST and automated scanning can mostly verify; suitable for low-risk applications; tests obvious security flaws; ~50 requirements. Level 2 (Standard): recommended for most applications; DAST + SAST + manual testing; handles most application risks; ~130 requirements. Level 3 (Advanced): for highest security requirements (banking, healthcare, critical infrastructure); requires thorough manual testing, threat modelling, code review, architecture review; all 286 requirements. Chapters: V1 Architecture, Design, and Threat Modelling; V2 Authentication; V3 Session Management; V4 Access Control; V5 Validation, Sanitization, and Encoding; V6 Stored Cryptography; V7 Error Handling and Logging; V8 Data Protection; V9 Communication (TLS); V10 Malicious Code; V11 Business Logic; V12 Files and Resources; V13 API and Web Service; V14 Configuration. Example requirements: 2.1.1: Verify user passwords are at least 12 characters (after removing whitespace); 2.2.1: Verify anti-automation controls are effective (no brute force without rate limit); 3.2.1: Verify session tokens are generated using approved cryptographic RNG; 4.1.1: Verify access control enforced server-side; 5.2.3: Verify all SQL queries use parameterised queries or stored procedures; 6.2.1: Verify cryptographic modules fail securely (no fallback to weaker crypto); 7.1.1: Verify log no credentials or session tokens; 9.1.1: Verify TLS required for all connections. How to use: select level appropriate for application risk; map each requirement to: test case, control in place, status (pass/fail); identify gaps; prioritise remediation; use as pentest scope: ASVS Level 2 assessment for contract scoping; maps well to OWASP Top 10 and NIST 800-53.
How do you test for clickjacking?

Clickjacking: trick user into clicking on invisible or disguised UI element; attacker frames target site in iframe; overlays transparent layer; user clicks what appears to be attacker content but actually clicks on target site. How it works: attacker site includes target site in transparent iframe (opacity: 0) positioned over visible decoy content; user clicks attacker button (Download Free Game); actually clicks button on framed target site (Transfer Money, Like Page, Enable Camera); site context: must be logged in to target; cookie sent with iframe request; authenticated action performed without knowledge. Classic example: Like button hijacking (Likejacking 2009); camera/microphone enable click; transfer money button; purchase confirmation; email subscription. Prerequisites: target site does not prevent framing; user logged in to target (framing uses their session); target has clickable UI elements with significant actions. Testing: check X-Frame-Options header: DENY (cannot be framed), SAMEORIGIN (only same origin can frame), missing or ALLOW-FROM (potentially vulnerable); check Content-Security-Policy frame-ancestors directive: frame-ancestors none (cannot be framed), frame-ancestors self (only same-origin), frame-ancestors https://parent.com (specific origin); if neither header: potentially vulnerable; PoC: create HTML page framing target with iframe; style iframe: opacity:0.1; position:absolute; top:0; left:0; width:100%; height:100%; click target area; observe if target responds. Partial framing: even with X-Frame-Options SAMEORIGIN: vulnerable to framing from same origin (XSS could inject iframe); clickjacking possible via XSS even with framebusting. JavaScript framebusting (unreliable): some sites use JS to detect framing: if (window.self !== window.top) { window.top.location = window.self.location; }; bypass: sandbox attribute on iframe: sandbox=allow-forms allows form submission but disables JavaScript; framebusting JS cannot run; mitigation: do not rely on framebusting JS; use headers. Mitigation: X-Frame-Options: DENY (simplest); CSP frame-ancestors: none (modern; preferred over X-Frame-Options); frame-ancestors can specify allowed origins granularly; double-submit pattern for critical actions (require user to re-enter token); UI design: make critical actions require deliberate drag-and-drop (harder to clickjack) or typing (cannot automate via invisible click).
What is network flow analysis for security?

Network flow analysis: analyse connection-level metadata (NetFlow, IPFIX, sFlow) for security; no packet content; high-level traffic patterns. Flow record contents: source IP, destination IP, source port, destination port, protocol, byte count, packet count, start time, end time, TCP flags; generated by: network switches and routers (Cisco NetFlow, Juniper J-Flow), dedicated probes (Kentik, Plixer), cloud: AWS VPC Flow Logs, Azure NSG Flow Logs, GCP VPC Flow Logs. Why flows without packet content: privacy: no payload inspection; compliance: some regulated environments prohibit deep packet inspection; scale: full PCAP unsustainable at network core; cost: flow records 1/1000 the size of PCAP. Security use cases: detect beaconing (C2): regular interval connections from internal host to external IP; periodic pattern even without full packet content; RITA (Real Intelligence Threat Analytics): open-source beaconing detection algorithm; calculates beacon score based on: regularity of connection intervals, connection duration, byte size consistency; detect data exfiltration: large outbound transfer to unusual destination; sustained high-byte-count flow to cloud storage at unusual hours; internal reconnaissanc and lateral movement: internal IP scanning many other IPs (many short flows to different destinations with same source); workstation making many unique internal destination connections (lateral movement pattern); detect DDoS: many sources sending to single destination in short window; or single internal host sending many packets (participating in outbound DDoS). Tools: Ntopng: flow analysis and visualisation; IPFIX/NetFlow collector + Grafana; Elastic + Logstash flow input; Scrutinizer (Plixer): flow analysis; Stealthwatch (Cisco): ML-based anomaly detection on flow data; ELK + Flow input: scale analytics; Zeek: generates conn.log (similar to flow data but from PCAP); RITA: specifically for C2 beaconing detection from Zeek conn.log. AWS VPC Flow Logs analysis: Athena SQL: SELECT source_ip, dst_ip, dst_port, SUM(bytes) as total_bytes FROM vpcflowlogs WHERE dst_port = 443 GROUP BY source_ip, dst_ip, dst_port ORDER BY total_bytes DESC; find top talkers; correlate with threat intel.
What is social engineering via pretexting?

Pretexting: create fabricated scenario (pretext) to manipulate target into divulging information or taking action; builds false context of trust. Classic pretexts: IT support impersonation: call employee; claim to be IT helpdesk; We have detected unusual activity on your account. I need to verify your credentials and reset your access; can I confirm your username and password?; vendor or supplier: I am calling from your payroll software vendor regarding your account; request access credentials or banking details update; auditor or regulator: I am from the IRS / HMRC / financial regulator conducting a routine audit; need immediate access to financial records; executive impersonation (BEC context): email from CFO name: Urgent wire transfer needed for acquisition, confidential, do not go through normal channels; physical pretexts: maintenance engineer: enter building claiming to be HVAC/electrical/fire alarm technician; access server rooms; new employee: claim to be a new hire; ask colleagues for help getting set up; delivery person: enter secure area to deliver package. Why pretexting works: authority: claim to be from authority figure (executive, IT, auditor, police); urgency: create time pressure (must fix within the hour, legal consequences if not); social proof: everyone else has already done this; liking: build rapport before request; reciprocity: offer help before asking for something. Defence: verification procedures: never act on verbal request alone for sensitive actions; call back using number from corporate directory (not provided by caller); confirm with manager via separate channel; security awareness training: employees practice recognising pretexts; specific training on most common scenarios (IT helpdesk calls, executive wire transfer requests); call verification protocol: all IT helpdesk calls: ticket number required; employees verify ticket exists in system; out-of-band verification: confirm wire transfer request via phone call to known executive number; clear escalation path: if suspicious: hang up, verify through proper channel, report to security team. Testing: authorised social engineering test: call employees with pretext; measure success rate; identify departments most susceptible; provide targeted training; measure improvement over time.
What is software composition analysis (SCA) and dependency security?

SCA (Software Composition Analysis): identify open-source and third-party components in software; detect known vulnerabilities and licensing issues; essential for supply chain security. Why SCA critical: modern applications 70-90% open-source components; developers pull packages from npm, PyPI, Maven, etc.; package may have known CVE; developer unaware; SolarWinds and Log4Shell demonstrated supply chain vulnerability impact; SBOM (Software Bill of Materials): inventory of all components; required by some regulations and customers. SCA tools: Snyk: developer-friendly; integrates IDE, GitHub, CI/CD; auto PR for dependency updates; licence compliance; free tier; npm audit: built into npm; checks package-lock.json against npm advisories; pip-audit: Python equivalent; mvn dependency-check (OWASP Dependency Check): Java; CVE database; well-established; GitHub Dependabot: free; monitors repos; auto PRs for vulnerable dependency updates; alerts in security tab; WhiteSource/Mend: enterprise; comprehensive; Black Duck (Synopsys): enterprise; strong licence compliance; JFrog Xray: integrates with JFrog Artifactory; scans all artifacts in binary repository. How SCA works: parse package manifest (package.json, requirements.txt, pom.xml, go.sum, Cargo.toml, Gemfile.lock, gradle files, nuget packages); build dependency tree (direct + transitive dependencies); match each component to vulnerability database (NVD/CVE, GitHub Security Advisories, Snyk database, OSS Index); report findings by severity; suggest remediation (update to patched version). Transitive vulnerabilities: Log4Shell: most affected organisations used Log4j indirectly (transitive dependency through Java frameworks); not in direct dependencies; SCA must analyse full transitive tree. Fix options: update to patched version: most common; feasible if no breaking changes; virtual patch: WAF rule blocking exploitation while patch tested; accept risk: if not exploitable in your context (library included but vulnerable function not called); code analysis tools: Reachability analysis: is the vulnerable code actually called? (Snyk, Semgrep, Contrast Security); reduces noise significantly. CI/CD gating: fail build if: Critical or High CVE with no fix AND actively exploited; warn if: Critical or High CVE with fix available; accept policy: security team approval for exceptions; track technical debt of accepted risk.
What is SQL injection detection and automated scanning?

SQL injection detection: identify SQLi vulnerabilities through automated and manual techniques. Automated tools: sqlmap: most powerful SQL injection tool; automated detection and exploitation; usage: sqlmap -u http://target.com/page?id=1 --dbs (find databases); --technique flag: B (boolean-based blind), T (time-based blind), E (error-based), U (UNION-based), S (stacked queries); --level (1-5) and --risk (1-3): increase aggression; --data: POST body data (sqlmap -u URL --data param=value); --cookie: include session cookie; --headers: custom headers; --dbms: specify target DBMS (mysql, mssql, oracle, postgresql); --os-shell: attempt OS shell if DBMS has file privileges. Burp Suite Scanner: active scan all requests through proxy; detect SQL injection patterns in responses; error messages, timing differences, boolean response differences. OWASP ZAP: automated SQL injection scanner; active scan; API mode for CI integration. NoSQLMap: MongoDB and other NoSQL injection. Manual detection: inject into each parameter: single quote: param=test (observe error or behaviour change); boolean test: param=1 AND 1=1 (normal response) vs param=1 AND 1=2 (different response = blind SQLi); time delay: param=1; WAITFOR DELAY 0:0:5-- (MSSQL) or param=1 AND SLEEP(5)-- (MySQL); UNION test: param=1 UNION SELECT NULL-- (count columns: add NULLs until no error). Response analysis: database error messages (MySQL: You have an error in your SQL syntax; MSSQL: Unclosed quotation mark after the character string; Oracle: ORA-01756; PostgreSQL: unterminated quoted string at or near); different response length or content for true vs false boolean conditions; response time delay for time-based blind. Non-traditional injection points: HTTP headers: X-Forwarded-For: 1 OR 1=1, User-Agent, Referer; Cookie values; JSON body: {id: 1 OR 1=1}; XML body (with potential XXE); GraphQL variables; second-order (stored in DB, injected later); WAF bypass (if testing WAF-protected target): encoding, comments, whitespace alternatives. Differential analysis for blind: parameterised baseline request (clean); injection request 1: TRUE condition (1=1); injection request 2: FALSE condition (1=2); if request 1 response differs from request 2 response and matches baseline: blind SQLi confirmed; automate with binary search: extract data character by character using ASCII comparisons: AND ASCII(SUBSTRING(username,1,1)) > 64.
What is RBAC vs ABAC in access control?

RBAC vs ABAC: two dominant access control models; different granularity and complexity. RBAC (Role-Based Access Control): permissions assigned to roles; users assigned to roles; simple to manage; permissions flow through roles; example: Role Editor has permissions: post:create, post:edit, post:read; Role Admin has permissions: user:manage, post:delete, settings:write; user Alice assigned Editor role: Alice can create and edit posts but not delete or manage users. RBAC types: flat RBAC (most common): no hierarchy; roles independent; user may have multiple roles; hierarchical RBAC: roles inherit from parent roles (Manager inherits Employee permissions); Senior Editor inherits Editor permissions plus approvals; constrained RBAC: separation of duty (same user cannot hold two conflicting roles: Accountant and Auditor); RBAC strengths: simple to understand and implement; easy to audit (what can Editor do? What can Bob do?); easy to add new user (assign role); easy to update permissions (modify role); well-supported in frameworks. RBAC weaknesses: role explosion: many specific roles needed for complex systems (Admin for Region A, Admin for Region B); inflexible: same role grants same permissions everywhere regardless of context; cannot express: Manager can read reports ONLY for their department; time-based or location-based access difficult. ABAC (Attribute-Based Access Control): access decisions based on policies evaluating attributes; Subject attributes (user department, clearance level, location, manager); Resource attributes (data classification, owner, project, sensitivity); Environment attributes (time of day, IP address, authentication method); Action (read, write, delete, approve); policy engine evaluates: ALLOW IF user.department == resource.department AND user.clearance >= resource.classification AND environment.time BETWEEN 09:00 AND 18:00; ABAC strengths: fine-grained control; context-aware; no role explosion; powerful for complex requirements. ABAC weaknesses: complex to implement; difficult to audit (what can Alice do in every context?); performance: policy evaluation per request; policy management requires expertise. Implementation: OPA (Open Policy Agent): ABAC policy engine; Rego language; integrates with any service; policies as code; XACML: XML-based ABAC standard; heavy; enterprise; AWS IAM Conditions: ABAC-like conditions in IAM policies (if request from VPC endpoint, allow; else deny). In practice: most systems use RBAC for primary access control; add ABAC-style conditions for specific context requirements (time, location, MFA required); hybrid approaches most common.
What is application rate limiting and how do you implement it?

Rate limiting: restrict number of requests a user or IP can make in given time window; prevent brute force, DoS, resource exhaustion, and API abuse. Why rate limit: brute force prevention: without rate limiting, password brute force makes unlimited attempts; credential stuffing: automated tools test millions of credentials; API abuse: scraping, competitive intelligence gathering, DoS; resource protection: expensive operations (search, report, export) unbounded. Rate limiting strategies: fixed window: count requests in fixed time window (1 minute); reset count at window start; problem: burst at window boundary (50 requests in last second of window + 50 in first second of next = 100 in 2 seconds); sliding window: count requests in rolling time window relative to current time; more accurate; prevents boundary burst; more complex to implement; token bucket: bucket holds N tokens; each request consumes one token; tokens added at fixed rate; burst allowed up to bucket size; common algorithm; leaky bucket: requests added to queue; processed at fixed rate; queue overflow dropped; smooths traffic. Rate limit targets: per IP address: limit requests from single IP; shared hosting false positives; proxy bypass (attacker uses many IPs: rate limit per IP bypassed with botnet); per user: rate limit authenticated user; requires authentication before rate limiting; harder to bypass (must have many accounts); per endpoint: different limits for different endpoints; login: 10 attempts per minute; API: 1000/minute; resource-intensive: 10/minute; per API key: for API products; each customer has quota; Response: 429 Too Many Requests (correct status code); Retry-After: 60 header (seconds until can retry); or: 503 Service Unavailable (less informative but used); do not silently drop requests (client must know to retry). Implementation: Redis-based: INCR key; EXPIRE key; atomic operations; works across multiple server instances; Nginx: limit_req_zone $binary_remote_addr zone=one:10m rate=1r/s; limit_req zone=one burst=5 nodelay; application layer: Flask-Limiter (Python), express-rate-limit (Node.js), Spring Boot RateLimiter (Java), ASP.NET Core rate limiting middleware; API gateway: Kong, Apigee, AWS API Gateway -- built-in rate limiting; WAF: Cloudflare rate limiting rules. Advanced: per-user + per-IP: both limits apply; account lockout: after N failures: lock account for M minutes; exponential backoff: response time increases with repeated failures; CAPTCHA: challenge after N failures; alert: high rate of 429s from endpoint = possible brute force or DDoS in progress.
What is identity and access management (IAM) in cloud environments?

Cloud IAM (Identity and Access Management): control who can perform what actions on which cloud resources; most important security control in cloud. AWS IAM components: IAM user: long-term identity; username/password + access keys; not recommended for workloads (use roles instead); for humans: use SSO federation to roles; IAM group: collection of IAM users; attach policies to group; all group members inherit policies; IAM role: identity assumed by workloads or humans; no permanent credentials; temporary credentials issued by STS (Security Token Service); assumed by: EC2 instance, Lambda function, ECS task, cross-account access, IAM user (via sts:AssumeRole); IAM policy: JSON document defining permissions; attached to user, group, or role; identity-based policies (what can this identity do?); resource-based policies (who can access this resource?); AWS managed vs customer managed policies. Policy structure: Effect (Allow/Deny), Action (s3:GetObject, ec2:RunInstances, sts:AssumeRole), Resource (ARN or *), Condition (context-based restrictions). Policy evaluation order: explicit Deny always wins; explicit Allow after no Deny; implicit Deny (default). Least privilege principles: start with minimum; add permissions as needed; use AWS IAM Access Analyzer: analyses permissions; finds unused permissions; generates least-privilege policies from CloudTrail activity. IAM best practices: no root account access keys: secure root; use MFA; only for billing and account recovery; no IAM user access keys for applications: use IAM roles; temporary credentials rotate automatically; MFA everywhere: virtual MFA for IAM users; hardware MFA for root and privileged users; require MFA for sensitive API calls via Condition key: aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent: true; cross-account: explicit role assumption with minimum permissions; external ID for third-party access (confused deputy protection); Service Control Policies (SCP) in Organizations: guardrails even if IAM policy grants broader access; Deny regions not approved, Deny EC2 instance types too large, Deny disabling CloudTrail. Azure: Entra ID (Azure AD) for identity; RBAC (built-in roles: Owner, Contributor, Reader, custom); service principals for applications; managed identities (no credential management). GCP: IAM with resource hierarchy; service accounts for workloads; Workload Identity Federation for CI/CD.
How do you implement security in serverless architectures?

Serverless security: unique security considerations for functions-as-a-service (AWS Lambda, Azure Functions, GCP Cloud Functions); shared responsibility shifts but does not disappear. Attack surface: function code (SAST, dependency scanning); event inputs (all sources trigger Lambda: API Gateway, S3, SQS, SNS, EventBridge, Kinesis, DynamoDB streams -- each is potential injection point); function permissions (IAM role); environment variables (secrets); execution environment (container reuse between invocations). Code security: treat Lambda like any application code: input validation, output encoding, parameterised queries; injection: event input from SQS message or API Gateway can contain injection payloads; validate all inputs regardless of source; SAST: same as regular application code (Semgrep, CodeQL); dependencies: Lambda packages all dependencies; SCA (Snyk) on dependencies. IAM permissions: function execution role: minimum permissions; only specific actions on specific resources: s3:GetObject on specific bucket ARN, not s3:* on *; over-permissive Lambda role = attacker executes function = access to all permitted resources; resource policy: who can invoke function; restrict to specific services, accounts, conditions. Secrets management: never store secrets in environment variables (visible in Lambda console, stored in config, may be logged): use AWS Secrets Manager or SSM Parameter Store (SecureString); fetch at runtime: AWS SDK call to Secrets Manager; cache with TTL (avoid throttling); rotate automatically. Event injection: API Gateway payload injection: same as web app (SQLi, XSS, command injection, SSRF); validate all API Gateway event fields; SQS message injection: malicious messages crafted by attacker with SQS write access; validate all message content server-side; S3 event: filename injection (path traversal in key name); validate S3 key names. Cold start timing attacks: first invocation slower (cold start); timing oracle possible in some authentication scenarios; mitigate with provisioned concurrency (no cold start) or accept and design against timing attacks in auth logic. Logging and monitoring: CloudWatch Logs: Lambda automatically logs to CloudWatch; ensure: no secrets in log output; log sufficient context for incident investigation; X-Ray: distributed tracing; correlate across Lambda functions; GuardDuty Lambda Protection (2023): monitors Lambda execution for anomalies (unexpected DNS lookups, unusual API calls from Lambda).
What is the cybersecurity maturity model certification (CMMC)?

CMMC (Cybersecurity Maturity Model Certification): US Department of Defense requirement for defence contractors; verify adequate cybersecurity practices to protect Federal Contract Information (FCI) and Controlled Unclassified Information (CUI). Background: DoD supply chain vulnerabilities; contractors handling sensitive defence information; CMMC 2.0 (current): simplified from CMMC 1.0; aligned with NIST SP 800-171 (primary standard for CUI protection) and NIST SP 800-172 (enhanced). CMMC 2.0 levels: Level 1 (Foundational): 17 practices from FAR 52.204-21; basic cyber hygiene; self-assessment; applies to contracts with FCI only; practices: limit system access, identify users, screen personnel, limit physical access, maintain incident capability, assess risk. Level 2 (Advanced): 110 practices from NIST SP 800-171; equivalent to CMMC 1.0 Level 3; third-party assessment required for most contracts (C3PAO -- CMMC Third-Party Assessment Organization); annual self-assessment option for some contracts; required for contracts with CUI. Level 3 (Expert): 110 NIST 800-171 practices + 24 from NIST 800-172; government-led assessment (Defense Industrial Base Cybersecurity Assessment Center -- DIBCAC); for most critical programmes; protecting highly sensitive CUI. Assessment process: Level 2 (third-party): C3PAO conducts assessment; reviews policies, procedures, evidence; interviews personnel; tests controls; issues certificate (valid 3 years); CMMC 2.0 final rule (December 2024): phased into contracts; contractors must be certified before contract award. Key NIST 800-171 domains: Access Control (AC), Awareness and Training (AT), Audit and Accountability (AU), Configuration Management (CM), Identification and Authentication (IA), Incident Response (IR), Maintenance (MA), Media Protection (MP), Personnel Security (PS), Physical Protection (PE), Risk Assessment (RA), Security Assessment (CA), System and Communications Protection (SC), System and Information Integrity (SI). Gap assessment: NIST 800-171 self-assessment using DoD scoring methodology; 110 requirements; points-based (perfect = 110); -5 points per not met; 0 per partial; POAM (Plan of Action and Milestones): document gaps and remediation timeline; submit score to SPRS (Supplier Performance Risk System).
What is a Denial of Service (DoS) versus Distributed DoS (DDoS)?

DoS vs DDoS: attacks aimed at making service unavailable; differ in scale and source. DoS (Denial of Service): single attack source; one attacker machine sends traffic; easier to detect (single source IP); easier to mitigate (block source IP); less powerful (limited by single machine bandwidth and compute); historical: early DoS used simple tools (ping flood); modern attacks rarely single-source (immediately blocked). DDoS (Distributed Denial of Service): many attack sources (botnet: 10,000 to 1,000,000 compromised devices); attacker controls botnet C2; issues attack command; all bots send traffic simultaneously; massive scale possible (Terabit-level attacks); difficult to mitigate: cannot block all sources; legitimate IP addresses used (compromised homes, enterprises). Botnet types: IoT botnets: Mirai (2016): 620 Gbps Krebs, 1.1 Tbps OVH; comprised of cameras, DVRs, routers with default credentials; still active variants; PC botnets: TrickBot, Emotet (before disruption): banking trojans also participate in DDoS-for-hire; cloud botnets: compromised cloud instances (high bandwidth); DNS reflection/amplification using third-party resolvers (not attacker-owned but leveraged). Attack types: volumetric: flood bandwidth; SYN flood; UDP/ICMP flood; amplification (DNS, NTP, Memcached); protocol: exhaust connection state tables (SYN flood, fragmented packets); application layer: HTTP flood; slow attacks (Slowloris: hold connections open with slow send rate); most damaging because hard to distinguish from legitimate traffic; resource exhaustion: expensive DB queries; search with no index. DDoS mitigation: upstream scrubbing: cloud scrubbing centres (Cloudflare, Akamai Prolexic, Radware); anycast routing distributes attack across global PoPs; BGP blackholing: null-route attack traffic at ISP level; CDN: absorb HTTP layer attacks at edge; SYN cookies: no state for SYN flood; rate limiting; WAF for L7 attacks; service scaling: auto-scale during attack (AWS: Lambda + CloudFront absorbs without saturation); cost consideration: DDoS-for-hire services available for $5-50/hour; large enterprise attacks cost attacker more than defender with adequate cloud mitigation.
What is key rotation and why is it necessary?

Key rotation: replace old cryptographic key with new one; critical security practice; limits exposure window if key compromised. Why rotate keys: key compromise: if private key leaked (breach, insider, physical extraction): attacker can decrypt all data encrypted with it; decrypt past TLS sessions (if no PFS); forge signatures; rotation limits blast radius to data encrypted after compromise; regulatory requirement: PCI DSS: encryption key rotation at least annually; NIST guidelines recommend rotation periods based on key type and usage volume; forward secrecy: TLS with ECDHE: new ephemeral key per session; even if long-term key compromised: past sessions protected; key exposure duration reduction: shorter key lifetime = shorter exposure window if compromised; cryptographic period: amount of data or time key is used; high volume usage shortens recommended period. Types of rotation: symmetric keys (AES): data encryption keys (DEKs): rotate when: suspected compromise, scheduled period, employee with access leaves; key encryption keys (KEKs): rotate when: process that manages KEK changes, scheduled period; asymmetric keys: TLS certificates: 1-2 year validity; replaced before expiry; CA/Browser Forum: maximum 398 days validity; private key: generate new key pair; get new certificate; rotate at certificate renewal; SSH keys: employee SSH keys: rotate when employee leaves or periodically; service SSH keys: automated rotation; API keys and secrets: short-lived preferred (15 minutes to 24 hours); AWS STS temporary credentials auto-expire; Vault dynamic secrets: generated on-demand, short TTL, auto-expire; long-lived API keys: rotate at least annually; automate rotation. Implementation: AWS Secrets Manager: automatic rotation Lambda functions; built-in rotation for RDS, Redshift, DocumentDB, Amazon Aurora; custom Lambda for other secrets; HashiCorp Vault: dynamic secrets (database credentials generated per request, short TTL, revoked after); lease renewal; CertManager (Kubernetes): automatic TLS certificate rotation via Let's Encrypt; rotation without downtime: dual support period: both old and new key accepted simultaneously during transition; rotate consumers first; then retire old key; data re-encryption: if rotating at-rest encryption key: need to re-encrypt all data with new key; performance impact; plan for large datasets.
What is insider threat detection using UEBA?

UEBA (User and Entity Behaviour Analytics): ML-based detection of anomalous user and system behaviour; particularly effective for insider threats. How UEBA works: establish baseline: collect 30-90 days of normal user activity; activities: login times, locations, file access patterns, email recipients, data volumes, application usage, web browsing, printing; build statistical model per user and peer group; peer group: same department, same role, same geography; detect deviations: score each activity against baseline and peer group; cumulative risk score per user; alert when score exceeds threshold. Insider threat indicators UEBA detects: data theft before departure: spike in file downloads in week before resignation; mass email forwarding to personal account; unusual USB device activity; large print jobs of sensitive documents; accessing data outside normal role: finance user suddenly accessing R&D files; project manager accessing payroll data; no business justification; credential misuse: logging in from unusual location while supposedly in office (impossible travel or account sharing); logging in outside business hours for first time; logging in from anonymising service (Tor, VPN); privilege abuse: admin user accessing more systems than usual baseline; performing sensitive operations not done before; data exfiltration patterns: large file upload to cloud storage; large email attachment to external recipient; copying to removable media; creating archive files (zip, 7z) of many documents; reconnaissance behaviour: searching for sensitive documents outside normal scope; accessing HR or financial data; reading security policies or network documentation (possible planning). UEBA products: Exabeam: timeline-based; Smart Timelines show complete user activity session; easy incident review; Splunk UEBA: native SPLUNK integration; Microsoft Sentinel UEBA: integrates Azure AD, endpoint, cloud; Securonix: strong insider threat use cases; Varonis: data-access focused UEBA. Integration with HR: joiner/mover/leaver process: flag departing employees for enhanced monitoring; flag recent disciplinary actions; flag employees under PIP (Performance Improvement Plan); integrate HRIS with UEBA; response workflow: UEBA alert -> case creation -> manager notification -> interview -> HR and Legal involvement if confirmed; investigation must be proportionate and comply with employment law; document chain of custody for potential legal action.
What is vulnerability management programme maturity?

Vulnerability management maturity: how effectively an organisation identifies, prioritises, and remediates vulnerabilities. Maturity levels: Level 1 -- Reactive: only scan when auditor requests; scan results filed and ignored; no remediation SLA; patches applied ad-hoc; no tracking. Level 2 -- Repeatable: regular scanning schedule (monthly); results reviewed; patch tickets created; ad-hoc prioritisation; some SLAs defined; not consistently met. Level 3 -- Defined: risk-based prioritisation; CVSS + asset criticality + exploitability; defined SLAs (critical 7 days, high 30 days); SLA compliance tracked; exception process defined; executive dashboard. Level 4 -- Managed: continuous scanning (agent-based + authenticated network); threat intelligence integrated (EPSS, CISA KEV); SLA compliance > 90%; automated remediation for some vulnerability types (OS patching automation); false positive rate tracked; metrics-driven. Level 5 -- Optimised: real-time vulnerability exposure measurement; BAS (Breach and Attack Simulation) validates fixes; developer self-service (developers scan their own code/containers); predictive analytics (identify likely future exploits); VM programme continuously improved based on metrics; external assessment validates programme effectiveness. Key metrics: CVE-to-patch time (how long from CVE publication to patch deployment); patch SLA compliance rate; mean time to remediate by severity; vulnerability debt trend (growing or shrinking total open vulnerability count); CISA KEV coverage (what % of KEV vulnerabilities remediated within advisory timeline); re-open rate (vulnerabilities marked remediated that reappear = improper fix or regression). Programme components: asset inventory: cannot scan what you do not know; CMDB integration; authenticated scanning: agent-based (most complete); credentialed network scan; unauthenticated (external attacker view); risk scoring: CVSS + environment + threat intel + asset criticality = VPR or similar; remediation workflow: ticketing system (Jira, ServiceNow) integration; automated ticket creation and assignment; SLA tracking; exceptions: formal exception process; risk acceptance; compensating controls documented; compensating control review; cloud VM: CSPM + CWPP integration; cloud native tools (AWS Inspector, Azure Defender for Servers).
What is a hash and when do collisions matter?

Cryptographic hash functions: one-way function producing fixed-length digest; any input maps to unique output; small change in input produces completely different output (avalanche effect). Properties required: preimage resistance: given hash H, infeasible to find input M where hash(M)=H; second preimage resistance: given M, infeasible to find M2 where hash(M2)=hash(M); collision resistance: infeasible to find any M1, M2 where hash(M1)=hash(M2). Common hash functions: MD5: 128-bit; broken (collision attacks practical since 2005); Wang and Yu 2004 paper; never use for security; still common for checksums (integrity not security); SHA-1: 160-bit; broken; collision demonstrated by Google 2017 (SHAttered -- two different PDFs same SHA-1); deprecated by CA/Browser Forum for TLS certificates; SHA-256 (SHA-2 family): 256-bit; secure; no known practical attacks; widely used; SHA-3 (Keccak): different design from SHA-2; sponge construction; provides alternative if SHA-2 weaknesses found; BLAKE2, BLAKE3: modern; faster than SHA-2 in software; secure; used in many modern applications. When collisions matter: digital signatures: sign hash of document; if attacker can craft malicious document with same hash: forged signature valid; MD5 and SHA-1 certificate collisions allowed fraudulent CA certificates; code signing: signed binary verification; collision allows malicious binary with same hash as legitimate; version control: Git uses SHA-1 for commit IDs; SHAttered attack demonstrated malicious repo manipulation (mitigated by Git hardening). When collisions rarely matter: non-security checksums: verify file not corrupted in transit (not tampered by adversary); MD5 sufficient; HMAC: keyed hash; security of HMAC-MD5 better than raw MD5 (attacker needs key to compute valid HMAC); still deprecated in favour of HMAC-SHA256. Password storage: bcrypt, scrypt, Argon2 are not general hash functions; specifically designed for password hashing; intentionally slow; memory-hard; collision resistance not primary concern (preimage resistance matters); NEVER use raw MD5 or SHA for passwords (trivially reversed with rainbow tables or GPU cracking).
What is a zero-trust architecture?

Zero trust architecture: security model eliminating implicit trust; verify every user, device, and network flow regardless of location; never trust, always verify. Traditional perimeter security failure: inside network = trusted; outside = untrusted; VPN breach = full internal access; mobile workforce, cloud, BYOD erased perimeter; modern attacks breach perimeter then move laterally freely. Zero trust principles: verify explicitly: authenticate and authorise every request using all available data points (identity, location, device health, service/workload, data classification, anomalies); use least privilege access: limit user access with just-in-time and just-enough-access; segment access by network, user, devices, and application awareness; assume breach: minimise blast radius; segment access; verify end-to-end encryption; use analytics to get visibility, drive threat detection, and improve defences. Pillars of zero trust: Identity: strong authentication (MFA); identity as control plane; continuous validation; privileged identity management; Devices: device health verified before granting access; MDM compliance checked; device trusted if managed and compliant; Applications: application access controlled by policy; no network-level access; application-level access only; Data: classify data; protect data at all stages; enforce access based on classification; Infrastructure: telemetry from infrastructure; anomaly detection; JIT access to infrastructure; Networks: micro-segmentation; encrypt all traffic; minimise trust zones. Implementation: Microsoft Zero Trust model: six pillars with maturity stages (traditional, advanced, optimal); NIST SP 800-207: Zero Trust Architecture; DoD Zero Trust Strategy. Practical steps: MFA everywhere (highest impact, first priority); device compliance (MDM, endpoint health); ZTNA replacing VPN (application-level access); identity-based network segmentation (replace IP-based); data classification and DLP; continuous monitoring and analytics. Common misconception: zero trust is not a product; it is an architecture and strategy; many products claim to enable zero trust; no single product achieves it; requires: identity infrastructure (Azure AD, Okta), device management (Intune, Jamf), network control (ZTNA, SD-WAN, NSX), monitoring (SIEM, UEBA); multi-year programme for most enterprises.
What is red team threat emulation based on threat intelligence?

Threat emulation (intelligence-driven red teaming): simulate specific real-world threat actors targeting your organisation; more realistic than generic penetration testing. Why threat intelligence-driven: generic pentest tests all vulnerabilities; threat emulation tests what actual threats targeting your sector actually do; prioritises: detection and response against your most likely adversaries; gap analysis: can you detect APT29 TTP that successfully targeted 3 peer organisations last month? Framework: MITRE ATT&CK: catalog of real threat actor TTPs; CTID (Center for Threat-Informed Defense): advanced threat emulation planning; TIBER-EU: European framework for threat intelligence-based ethical red teaming; financial sector; adversary emulation plan steps: (1) threat intelligence: identify top 3 threat actors for your sector and region; gather TTPs: MITRE ATT&CK Groups page (APT29, Lazarus, TA505 etc.); vendor reports (Mandiant, CrowdStrike, Recorded Future); government advisories; (2) build emulation plan: select subset of TTPs relevant to your environment; create step-by-step playbook mimicking threat actor; realistic initial access vector (spearphishing, supply chain, exploiting specific CVE they use); (3) execute: red team executes exactly as documented threat actor would; use same tools when possible (or equivalent); maintain OPSEC level the actor uses; (4) measure: did blue team detect each TTP? At what stage? Dwell time before detection; (5) report: gaps in detection coverage vs this specific threat actor; prioritised recommendations. Example: APT29 (Cozy Bear) emulation: initial access: spearphishing with HTML smuggling or ISO file; tools: SUNBURST-like backdoor, CobaltStrike; techniques: credential dumping, lateral movement via RDWEB, Azure AD abuse, token theft; emulation plan: craft phishing matching APT29 style; deploy CS beacon with APT29 profile; attempt Azure AD token abuse; report detection gap. Tools: CALDERA (MITRE): automated ATT&CK emulation; Atomic Red Team: atomic tests per ATT&CK technique; Prelude Operator; Vectr: track emulation exercises; TRAM (Threat Report ATT&CK Mapper): extract TTPs from threat reports automatically.
What is supply chain security for software development?

Software supply chain security: secure all components, dependencies, tools, and processes that create and deliver software. Attack surfaces: source code: developer machine compromise; poisoned IDE plugins; CI/CD system: attacker accesses CI/CD (SolarWinds: Orion build system); injects malicious code during build; dependencies: malicious npm/PyPI packages; dependency confusion; typosquatting; binary artifacts: tampered build output; compromised artifact repository; deployment: infrastructure compromise during deployment; runtime: compromised Docker base images; malicious SBOM (Software Bill of Materials): SBOM = inventory of all components; NTIA minimum elements: supplier name, component name, component version, component hash, unique identifiers, dependency relationship, SBOM author, timestamp; SPDX and CycloneDX formats; SBOM required for US federal software procurement (Executive Order 14028). Securing each stage: development environment: developer workstation security (EDR, disk encryption, patching); code signing: sign all commits (git commit -S; GPG key); verified by repository (GitHub: require signed commits); code review: security-focused review for all code changes; no direct push to main; branch protection; PR review requirement. Source control: MFA for all accounts; minimal permissions (developers commit to feature branch only); branch protection; signed commits required; secret scanning (GitGuardian, GitHub secret scanning): detect credentials before commit or on push; automatic alert and revoke. CI/CD security: principle of least privilege: CI system has minimum permissions needed to build and test; secrets: use CI secrets vault (not in code); rotate CI credentials; SAST and SCA in pipeline: block builds with critical findings; ephemeral build environments: fresh container per build; no state from previous builds; build provenance: SLSA (Supply chain Levels for Software Artifacts): framework for build provenance; attestations signed by build system; consumers verify provenance. Artifact integrity: sign artifacts: Docker image signing (Cosign + Sigstore); package signing (npm provenance, pip TUF); verify signatures before deployment; SBOM generation and attestation: generate SBOM per release; sign SBOM; consumers verify SBOM matches deployed software. Runtime: verify image signatures before deployment (Connaisseur, Kyverno ImagePolicy Validator, OPA Gatekeeper); SBOM stored in OCI registry alongside image; automated vulnerability scanning in registry (Trivy, Grype).
What are common cryptographic mistakes in applications?

Common cryptographic mistakes: using crypto incorrectly despite using strong algorithms. Using MD5 or SHA1 for passwords: MD5/SHA1 are fast; GPU can compute 10 billion MD5/second; rainbow table or brute force trivial for common passwords; correct: bcrypt, Argon2id, scrypt (memory-hard, slow by design); bcrypt: $2a$12$ prefix indicates 4096 rounds of blowfish; adjust cost factor for ~100ms compute time. Using ECB mode (Electronic Codebook): CBC, GCM, CTR replace ECB; ECB: same plaintext block always produces same ciphertext block; pattern analysis reveals plaintext structure; famous ECB penguin (encrypted image still shows penguin shape); correct: AES-GCM (authenticated encryption) or AES-CBC with proper IV + HMAC. Static or predictable IV: CBC mode: if same IV reused with same key: identical plaintext blocks produce identical ciphertext; IV must be random and unique per encryption; GCM nonce: must NEVER repeat with same key; nonce reuse in GCM catastrophic (reveals authentication key); correct: generate random IV per encryption; use 96-bit nonce for GCM; never reuse nonce. Using symmetric encryption without authentication: confidentiality without integrity; attacker modifies ciphertext; padding oracle attacks (CBC); correct: AES-GCM (authenticated encryption; authentication built in) or AES-CBC + HMAC-SHA256 (encrypt-then-MAC). Weak or hardcoded key: key in source code; all deployments use same key; breach of one instance compromises all; key recovery from decompiled code; correct: generate unique key per deployment; store in KMS or secrets manager. Using custom cryptography: designing custom cipher or protocol; cryptographic design is extremely hard; custom crypto almost always broken; correct: use established algorithms (AES, RSA, ECDSA, ChaCha20); use established protocols (TLS 1.3, Signal Protocol). Insufficient randomness: using Math.random() or rand() for tokens, passwords, keys, nonces; predictable sequence; correct: use CSPRNG: os.urandom(), SecureRandom, crypto.randomBytes(). Not validating TLS certificates: ignore certificate errors in code (TrustAllCerts, HostnameVerifier returning true always); disables MITM protection; often done during development; never in production; correct: proper certificate validation; pin expected certificate for high-security applications. Timing attacks: password comparison using == (stops at first mismatch; timing reveals prefix match); correct: use constant-time comparison (hmac.compare_digest in Python, MessageDigest.isEqual in Java).
What are common Android application security vulnerabilities?

Android application security vulnerabilities: specific to Android platform and development patterns. Insecure data storage: SharedPreferences: stored as plaintext XML in app private directory; accessible if device rooted or ADB backup enabled; avoid storing sensitive data in SharedPreferences; SQLite databases: world-readable in some configurations; store sensitive data encrypted (SQLCipher); external storage (/sdcard): world-readable; any app with STORAGE permission can read; never store sensitive data on external storage; log leakage: Log.d() and Log.v() visible to any app with READ_LOGS permission; contains credentials, API keys, session tokens; remove logging in production builds (ProGuard/R8 can strip). Exported components: Activity, Service, BroadcastReceiver, ContentProvider with android:exported=true and no permission requirement; any app can launch Activity, bind Service, send Broadcast, query ContentProvider; deep link confusion: Activity handles intent URLs (myapp://action); exported without validation; arbitrary parameter injection; fix: set exported=false unless required; define permission; validate Intent input. Traffic interception: custom WebViews that trust all SSL certificates; network_security_config.xml cleartext traffic allowed; HTTP API endpoints; certificate validation disabled in code (custom TrustManager); fix: network_security_config.xml: cleartextTrafficPermitted=false; proper SSL validation. WebView vulnerabilities: addJavascriptInterface: exposes Java methods to JavaScript in WebView; if WebView loads untrusted content: attacker JavaScript calls Java methods with REFLECT annotation; pre-Android 17: any method accessible via JS; setJavaScriptEnabled(true): enable JS only when required; loadUrl with user-controlled URL: open redirect to malicious content; JavascriptInterface injection. Root detection and emulator detection bypass: some apps check for root to prevent running on rooted devices; Frida bypass: hook detection functions; SafetyNet / Play Integrity API: Google attestation; rooted device fails; harder to bypass. Insufficient cryptography: AES/ECB usage; hardcoded key in APK (decompile with jadx and search); encryption key derived from device ID (predictable); random number generation issues. Broadcast receivers: implicit broadcasts received by all apps; sensitive data in broadcast extras; fix: use local broadcasts or explicit intents with target package; or permissioned broadcast. Tools: MobSF (automated); apktool + jadx (static); Frida + objection (dynamic); adb logcat (log analysis).
What is exploit mitigation in modern operating systems?

Modern exploit mitigations: OS and compiler features that make exploitation harder; do not prevent vulnerabilities but raise exploitation cost. ASLR (Address Space Layout Randomisation): randomises memory layout (stack, heap, libraries, executable if PIE); attacker cannot hardcode addresses; bypass: info leak vulnerability reveals address; brute force (32-bit ASLR: small entropy, 1 in 256 chance); partial overwrite (only low bytes need accurate). NX/DEP (No-Execute / Data Execution Prevention): memory pages marked executable or writable but not both; stack and heap not executable; shellcode injected into data page cannot execute; bypass: ROP (Return-Oriented Programming): execute code in existing executable pages. Stack canary: random value placed before saved return address; verified before function return; if canary modified (stack overflow overwrite): abort; bypass: info leak reading canary; brute force (fork servers); overwrite without touching canary (heap overflow). Control Flow Integrity (CFI): restrict indirect call and jump targets; only valid targets allowed; Apple PAC (Pointer Authentication Code on ARM): sign pointers; validate before use; hardware-enforced; effective against JOP/ROP; LLVM CFI: compiler generates allowlist of valid indirect call targets. Safe Stack (LLVM): separates sensitive stack data (return addresses) into separate stack; inaccessible from normal stack overflow; Stack Clash mitigated. Secure Boot: verify boot loader signature before executing; prevent bootkit; measured boot with TPM. SMEP (Supervisor Mode Execution Prevention): CPU prevents kernel from executing code in user pages; prevents ret2user attacks. SMAP (Supervisor Mode Access Prevention): CPU prevents kernel from reading/writing user memory without explicit permission; requires kernel to explicitly enable user-space access; prevents kernel reading/writing attacker-controlled user data. PIE (Position Independent Executable): code randomised by ASLR (requires PIE; non-PIE executable loaded at fixed address even with ASLR); hardened compilers enable PIE by default. Fortified source (_FORTIFY_SOURCE): adds bounds checking to vulnerable C functions (strcpy, sprintf, memcpy) when buffer size known at compile time; detects some overflows at compile time. Sandbox: limit what process can do even if exploited; Chrome: multi-process with strict sandbox (no file access except designated); iOS/Android: app sandbox; seccomp (Linux): filter allowed system calls; AppArmor/SELinux (Linux): mandatory access control.
What is network access control list (ACL) versus firewall?

ACL vs Firewall: both control network traffic; different sophistication and deployment context. ACL (Access Control List): stateless packet filtering; evaluates each packet independently; does not track connection state; rules based on: source IP, destination IP, source port, destination port, protocol; permit or deny each packet; applied on router interface (inbound or outbound); Cisco extended ACL example: permit tcp 192.168.1.0/24 any eq 443 (allow HTTPS from internal); deny ip any any (implicit deny all); stateless limitation: must allow both directions explicitly; return traffic rule needed (permit tcp any 192.168.1.0/24 established for return packets -- using established keyword for TCP state approximation); UDP: no concept of established; must explicitly allow return traffic based on port; cannot handle FTP active mode (dynamic port negotiation). Stateful Firewall: tracks connection state (TCP three-way handshake, UDP pseudo-state, ICMP); once connection allowed outbound: return traffic automatically permitted; does not require explicit return rule; understands: SYN (new connection), ESTABLISHED (ongoing), RELATED (related connection like FTP data channel); more complex rule set but easier to manage; policies: instead of permit/deny per packet: allow initiated from inside, deny initiated from outside; commonly implemented: zone-based (inside, outside, DMZ zones; rules between zones). Next-Generation Firewall (NGFW): layer 7 inspection; application identification (not just port 80 = HTTP; identify Facebook, YouTube, Zoom by signature regardless of port); SSL inspection (decrypt HTTPS; inspect contents; re-encrypt); URL filtering; user identity integration (AD lookup -- firewall rule by user or group not just IP); IPS integration (inline intrusion prevention); sandboxing (send unknown files to sandbox for analysis); products: Palo Alto, Checkpoint, Fortinet, Cisco Firepower. WAF vs NGFW: WAF: application layer; HTTP/HTTPS specifically; understands HTTP semantics; OWASP Top 10 protection; NGFW: network layer; all protocols; application identification; URL filtering; IPS; WAF needed alongside NGFW for web application protection.
What is a penetration testing engagement kickoff?

Penetration testing kickoff: establish foundation for successful engagement; prevent misunderstandings and legal issues. Pre-kickoff (before meeting): review scope document; research target organisation (public information: website, LinkedIn, technology stack, recent news); identify any scope questions or concerns; prepare logistics (lab environment, VPN access, required tools). Kickoff meeting agenda: introductions: client and penetration testing team members; roles and responsibilities (client emergency contact, testing team members); scope review: confirm exact scope (IP ranges, domains, applications, system types); confirm exclusions (out-of-scope systems, prohibited techniques); timeline: testing windows (business hours only vs 24/7; specific maintenance windows for disruptive tests); kickoff date, daily check-ins, reporting deadline, debrief date; emergency procedures: if tester causes unintended outage: immediate notification protocol; if tester discovers active breach: what to do?; reporting: report format, distribution list, classification of report; communication: preferred communication channel (email, Slack, Teams, phone); frequency of updates; daily check-in calls if requested; safe harbour: confirm written authorisation; tester carries copy; sensitive systems: identify any particularly sensitive systems requiring extra care (production databases with PII, systems supporting critical processes); credential access: confirm method for providing access credentials if grey-box or white-box testing. During kickoff: ask open questions: Are there any systems that should not be disrupted? Any recent changes we should know about? Any ongoing incidents or maintenance windows?; confirm testing is not blackout period (financial quarter close, product launch, major audit); establish daily check-in schedule; exchange emergency contact information (24/7 phone numbers). After kickoff: confirm scope document in writing (email summary); document decisions made verbally; begin testing on confirmed start date. Common kickoff issues: scope creep (client adds systems after engagement started -- require written approval); delayed credential access (blocks internal testing); unresponsive emergency contact (document and proceed per plan); scope confusion (different understanding between client and tester -- resolve in writing immediately).
What is an intrusion detection system (IDS) and intrusion prevention system (IPS)?

IDS/IPS: detect and optionally block malicious network activity or host behaviour. IDS (Intrusion Detection System): monitors traffic; generates alerts; does not block; passive; advantages: no false positive impact (wrong block breaks legitimate traffic); disadvantages: human must act on alerts; attacker has execution time before response. IPS (Intrusion Prevention System): inline; actively blocks detected attacks; advantages: immediate blocking; disadvantages: false positives break legitimate traffic; must tune carefully. Types: Network IDS/IPS (NIDS/NIPS): tap or inline on network segment; analyse all network traffic; signature-based: match known attack patterns (SQL injection, exploit strings, malware C2 protocols); anomaly-based: detect deviations from baseline; products: Snort (open-source), Suricata (open-source, multi-threaded), Zeek (network analysis framework), Cisco Firepower, Palo Alto IPS, Darktrace. Host IDS/HIDS: agent on endpoint; monitor host activity: file changes (AIDE, Tripwire), log analysis, system call monitoring, rootkit detection; OSSEC (open-source HIDS): log analysis, file integrity, rootkit detection, active response; Wazuh: OSSEC fork; modern; SIEM integration. Detection methods: signature: match against database of known attack patterns; fast; reliable; cannot detect unknown (zero-day) attacks; Snort rules: alert tcp any any -> $HOME_NET 80 (flags:S; content:GET /admin HTTP/1.1; msg:HTTP admin access attempt); anomaly: machine learning baseline; detect deviations; higher false positive rate initially; detects zero-days. Snort vs Suricata: Snort: older; single-threaded; most widely deployed; huge community ruleset; Suricata: multi-threaded; higher performance; YAML rules; protocol detection (detects protocols on non-standard ports); TLS metadata extraction; integrated with Zeek/Bro for network forensics. Tuning: most IDS/IPS require significant tuning to reduce false positives: disable irrelevant rules (vulnerability scanner traffic); adjust thresholds; whitelist known-good sources; tuning period: 2-4 weeks before alert quality acceptable. Deployment: out-of-band (span port): monitors copy of traffic; IDS mode only; inline: traffic passes through device; IPS possible; single point of failure; HA required.
What is the difference between SaaS, PaaS, and IaaS security?

Cloud service models and security responsibilities: shared responsibility model; what customer must secure varies by service type. IaaS (Infrastructure as a Service): provider manages: physical hardware, hypervisor, facilities, network infrastructure; customer manages: operating system, middleware, runtime, applications, data, network configuration (security groups, VPCs), IAM, storage encryption, backups; examples: AWS EC2, Azure VMs, GCP Compute Engine; maximum control; maximum responsibility; customer must: patch OS, configure firewall, manage software stack, implement monitoring. PaaS (Platform as a Service): provider manages: physical, hypervisor, OS, runtime, middleware, autoscaling; customer manages: application code, data, application security (auth, authorisation, injection prevention), API security, environment configuration, access control to platform; examples: AWS Elastic Beanstalk, Google App Engine, Heroku, Azure App Service, AWS Lambda (serverless PaaS); customer does not manage OS patching; provider responsibility for platform components; customer focuses on application security. SaaS (Software as a Service): provider manages: everything except customer data and access management; customer manages: who has access and what level, data entered into system, integration security, data classification compliance, API key security; examples: Salesforce, Slack, Office 365, Google Workspace, ServiceNow; least control; fewest security responsibilities for customer; but: data risk (provider has your data), compliance obligations remain (GDPR -- you are data controller regardless of SaaS use), configuration security (public S3 buckets configured by customer remain customer responsibility in S3 -- IaaS). Shared responsibility breakdown: Physical security: always provider; Hypervisor: always provider (except colocation); OS: customer for IaaS, provider for PaaS and SaaS; Application: customer for IaaS and PaaS, provider for SaaS (but customer still responsible for application configuration and access); Data: always customer responsibility (encrypt, classify, access control); IAM: always customer responsibility (who has access to the service); Network controls: customer for IaaS VPC, partially shared for PaaS, provider for SaaS. Common misunderstandings: SaaS does not mean no customer security responsibility; customer still owns their data; GDPR obligations do not transfer to SaaS vendor; review vendor's DPA (Data Processing Agreement) and SCC (Standard Contractual Clauses); vendor security certifications (SOC 2, ISO 27001) reduce but do not eliminate customer diligence obligations.
What is threat hunting for lateral movement?

Lateral movement threat hunting: proactively search for signs of attacker traversal between systems; hunt before detection rule fires. Hunting hypotheses: (1) Attacker performed credential dumping from LSASS then used credentials to access other systems; (2) Attacker used WMI or PSExec for remote code execution on multiple hosts; (3) Attacker moved via Kerberoasted service account credentials. Data sources: Windows Security Event Logs (4624, 4648, 4672, 4776); Sysmon (process creation, network connections, remote thread); EDR telemetry (process tree, network connections, file access); NetFlow or VPC flow logs (connection metadata). Hunt 1 -- Impossible logon velocity: query: find accounts that authenticated to more than N distinct hosts within short time window (60 minutes); unusual for regular user to authenticate to >5 different servers in 60 minutes (could be IT doing work -- filter known admin accounts); alert threshold: 5+ unique hosts in 60 minutes from same account; Splunk: index=winevt EventCode=4624 LogonType=3 | bin _time span=1h | stats dc(ComputerName) as host_count by AccountName _time | where host_count > 5. Hunt 2 -- Lateral tool use: search for execution of known lateral movement tools: Event 4688 or Sysmon Event 1 with process name: psexec.exe, psexesvc.exe, wmiexec.py, smbexec.py, wmic.exe with /node: switch; or: powershell.exe with Invoke-Command -ComputerName or Enter-PSSession parameters; Sysmon: process parent is services.exe AND process name is cmd.exe or powershell.exe (PSExec pattern). Hunt 3 -- First-seen host pairs: baseline: build history of all source-destination authentication pairs; alert on: new source host authenticating to destination host never seen before; reduce: filter known IT admin pairs; expected new system onboarding pairs; results: unusual new connections = potential lateral movement. Hunt 4 -- Kerberos TGS spike: EDR or DC event logs: spike in TGS requests (4769) from single host; many different SPN targets; RC4 encryption requests; potential Kerberoasting scan or pass-the-ticket. Response to lateral movement findings: scope assessment (how many systems touched?); timeline (when did movement start?); contain (isolate compromised systems); eradicate (remove implants, revoke compromised credentials, patch exploitation path); recover.
What is secure software release management?

Secure release management: integrate security validation into software release process; ensure only secure, approved software reaches production. Release gating: before any code reaches production: required gates: security scan results (SAST, DAST, SCA, container scan); all Critical/High findings resolved or formally risk-accepted; vulnerability assessment of new dependencies; approval: security sign-off on major releases; automated gating in CI/CD: deployment blocked if security gates not passed; separate production credentials: production environment uses different credentials from development and staging; rotation on any suspected compromise; change management: all production changes: documented change request; security impact assessment; rollback plan; approval (CAB -- Change Advisory Board or automated for low-risk changes). Code signing: sign release artifacts (binaries, container images, packages); customer or deployment system verifies signature; prevent tampering between build and deployment; Sigstore/Cosign: keyless signing for container images; Notary v2: artifact signing for OCI registries; GPG signing for packages (Debian, RPM, npm). Release notes security content: document security-relevant changes; CVEs fixed in release; new security features; breaking changes in security controls; known issues. Rollback plan: every release has tested rollback procedure; if production incident caused by release: immediate rollback within SLA; blue-green deployment: run old and new version simultaneously; switch traffic; roll back by switching traffic back; blue-green eliminates downtime from rollback. Release environment isolation: production access segregated from developer access; separate credentials; audit logging of all production changes; JIT (Just-in-Time) production access via PAM; emergency access procedure documented and tested. Post-release monitoring: enhanced monitoring for 24-48 hours after release; alert on: new error rates, performance degradation, security-related log events; canary release: release to small percentage of users first; monitor for issues before full rollout; automated rollback trigger: if error rate exceeds threshold after release: automatically roll back. Security regression testing: ensure security fixes stay fixed; automated test for each previously reported vulnerability; security regression suite runs on every release; prevents reintroduction of known vulnerabilities.
What are common web server security misconfigurations?

Web server security misconfigurations: common issues in Apache, Nginx, IIS, and CDN configurations that create security risks. Directory listing: Apache: Options +Indexes enables directory listing; if no index.html: shows all files in directory; attackers find backup files, credentials, source code; fix: Options -Indexes or create index.html; Nginx: autoindex on; same issue. Verbose error messages: stack traces, file paths, internal IPs, library versions in error responses; fix: custom error pages; disable detailed errors in production; log internally but return generic error to user. Server version disclosure: Server: Apache/2.4.51 header; reveals version; attacker knows CVEs affecting that version; fix: ServerTokens Prod (Apache); server_tokens off (Nginx); suppress IIS header via URLRewrite or ARR. Default pages and files: Apache test page (/var/www/html/index.html default); phpinfo.php files left in web root (reveals PHP configuration, server details, loaded modules);.git folder accessible (curl https://target.com/.git/config reveals repository details; git-dumper tool can extract entire repo); fix: remove default pages; remove phpinfo(); block access to.git,.svn,.DS_Store; unnecessary HTTP methods: TRACE method: cross-site tracing (XST); combine with CSRF and XSS to steal cookies even with HttpOnly; fix: disable TRACE; allow only GET, POST, HEAD, OPTIONS; PUT/DELETE if required for API (with authentication);.htaccess exposure:.htaccess readable; reveals security rules; fix: block access to. files; Nginx: location ~ /\. { deny all; }. Missing security headers: X-Frame-Options, X-Content-Type-Options, Strict-Transport-Security, Content-Security-Policy, Referrer-Policy; fix: add security headers in server config. SSL/TLS misconfiguration: old protocol versions (SSLv3, TLS 1.0, TLS 1.1); weak cipher suites; self-signed certificates on public services; missing certificate renewal (expired cert); fix: TLS 1.2 and 1.3 only; strong cipher suites; automated cert renewal (Let's Encrypt + Certbot); Mozilla SSL Configuration Generator: recommended TLS configs. Upload directory: PHP execution in upload directory; attacker uploads shell.php; server executes; fix: PHP execution disabled in upload directory: Apache: php_admin_flag engine off; Nginx: location /uploads { include fastcgi.conf; deny all; } or: serve from separate domain without PHP; file permissions: web server user has write access to web root or config files; fix: web server: read-only access to web root; separate user for deployments.
What is security awareness training?

Security awareness training: educate employees about cybersecurity threats, policies, and safe behaviours; reduce human risk. Why training matters: phishing is the most common initial access vector; 95% of cybersecurity incidents involve human error (IBM Cost of Data Breach Report); technical controls cannot compensate for human behaviour completely; regulatory requirement: HIPAA, PCI DSS, ISO 27001 all require security awareness. Training programme components: (1) annual mandatory training: all employees complete annually; covers: phishing recognition, password security, acceptable use, data handling, incident reporting, social engineering, physical security; compliance record kept for audit; (2) role-based training: additional training for roles with elevated risk: finance: BEC (Business Email Compromise), wire transfer fraud; IT admins: privileged access, system hardening; developers: secure coding; HR: social engineering targeting employee data; customer service: social engineering over phone; (3) phishing simulations: send simulated phishing emails to all employees; track: open rate, click rate, credential entry rate, report rate; use click-throughs for immediate teachable moment (redirect to training page); measure improvement over time; report to management; NIST benchmark: <10% click rate as target; (4) security newsletters and communications: monthly security tips; relevant current threat news; celebrate security wins; create security culture. Delivery methods: eLearning modules: self-paced; tracked completion; gamification; vendors: KnowBe4, Proofpoint Security Awareness, Cofense, Infosec IQ; in-person training: workshops, tabletop exercises; video content: short engaging videos; microlearning: 2-5 minute modules; more effective than 1-hour annual module; posters and reminders: physical workspace reinforcement; QR codes to quick tips. Metrics: phishing simulation click rate trend; training completion rate; security incident count from human error; reporting rate (employees reporting suspicious emails); post-training knowledge assessment scores; executive dashboard: quarterly security metrics. Culture: security champions: employee advocates in each team; promote security culture; answer colleagues questions; security first: not security vs productivity; frame security as enabling work safely; psychological safety: encourage reporting mistakes without punishment; blame-free incident reporting.
What is ARP spoofing and how do you defend against it?

ARP spoofing (ARP poisoning): send fake ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) replies to associate attacker MAC address with victim IP; intercept traffic; MITM on local network. How ARP works: host wants to communicate with IP 192.168.1.1; broadcasts ARP request: who has 192.168.1.1? Tell 192.168.1.100; 192.168.1.1 replies: 192.168.1.1 is at MAC AA:BB:CC:DD:EE:FF; ARP cache updated: 192.168.1.1 -> AA:BB:CC:DD:EE:FF. ARP spoofing: ARP has no authentication; any host can send ARP reply; attacker sends gratuitous ARP: 192.168.1.1 is at MAC attacker:mac (to victim) and 192.168.1.100 is at MAC attacker:mac (to router); both victim and router send traffic to attacker; attacker forwards (MITM) or drops (DoS). Attack tools: arpspoof (dsniff package); Ettercap: comprehensive MITM framework; Bettercap: modern; web UI; Scapy: craft custom ARP packets. What attacker can do with MITM: sniff HTTP (plaintext) traffic; credentials, session cookies; SSL stripping (downgrade HTTPS to HTTP): attacker between victim and router; receives HTTPS from server; serves HTTP to victim; steal credentials from HTTP; inject malicious content; DNS spoofing (modify DNS responses); session hijacking (copy session cookie; use in attacker browser). Detection: ARP watch: arpwatch tool monitors ARP traffic; alert on IP-to-MAC mapping changes; XArp: ARP monitoring with anomaly detection; IDS rules for gratuitous ARP floods; endpoint: periodic ARP table inspection. Prevention: dynamic ARP inspection (DAI): switch feature; validates ARP packets against DHCP snooping binding table (IP-MAC-port-VLAN bindings); drops ARP packets with incorrect IP-to-MAC mapping; requires DHCP snooping enabled; most enterprise switches support; static ARP entries: manually configure correct MAC-IP mappings on critical systems (router, servers); cannot be overwritten by spoofed ARP; impractical for large networks; 802.1X: authenticate all devices before network access; limit which devices on network segment; encrypted protocols: TLS/HTTPS: ARP spoofing cannot decrypt TLS (attacker does MITM but cannot break TLS without certificate); HSTS: enforces HTTPS; prevents SSL strip; VPN: all traffic encrypted; ARP spoofing exposes only encrypted traffic; IPv6: NDP (Neighbour Discovery Protocol) replaces ARP; SEND (Secure Neighbour Discovery) uses cryptographic signatures; not widely deployed but more secure.
What is security information and event management (SIEM) tuning?

SIEM tuning: optimise detection rules and data collection to reduce false positives and improve true positive quality; ongoing process. Why tuning critical: new SIEM: thousands of alerts per day; mostly false positives; analysts overwhelmed; alert fatigue; ignore all alerts; miss real attacks; goal: SOC receives 50-100 high-quality alerts per day; >80% true positive rate; analysts have time to investigate each. Tuning process: (1) measure current state: how many alerts per day? How many true positives? Which rules generate most noise?; (2) identify high-noise rules: sort by alert count; top 10 noisy rules; investigate each FP; (3) tune rule or suppress: adjust threshold (raise from 5 events to 10 events before alert); add exception (known vulnerability scanner IP in allowlist; admin account excluded from certain rules); improve specificity (add condition: only alert if user is not in maintenance_accounts group); (4) validate: monitor rule for 1-2 weeks after change; confirm FP rate reduced, TP rate maintained; (5) repeat: continuous tuning cycle. False positive sources: scheduled tasks or scripts that match alert pattern (backup process triggers process injection rule); IT admin tools (vulnerability scanner triggers brute force rule); known external partners (partner IP triggers suspicious external connection rule); internal development practices (developers run security tests that trigger alerts). Suppression vs tuning: suppression: completely silence alerts matching specific criteria (never alert when source IP = vuln scanner); dangerous if overused; risk of suppressing real attack from same source; tuning: refine rule logic to better distinguish real from false; better approach; review suppressions periodically; expire suppressions when no longer needed. Use case prioritisation: identify highest-value detections for your threat model; tune these to perfection before worrying about lower-priority rules; quality > quantity; better to have 20 well-tuned critical rules than 200 noisy rules. Documentation: every tuning change documented: rule name, original logic, change made, reason for change, date, analyst; ensures changes reviewable; enables rollback if change introduces blind spot; audit trail for compliance.
How does SQL injection work in stored procedures?

SQL injection in stored procedures: stored procedures partially mitigate SQLi but do not eliminate it if implemented incorrectly.
