OAuth 2.0 flows: authorization code: most secure; used for web and mobile apps; code exchanged server-side for token; PKCE recommended; implicit (deprecated): token returned directly to browser; no code exchange; not recommended (token in URL); client credentials: machine-to-machine; no user interaction; use for service authentication; device code: limited input devices (TV, CLI); user authenticates on separate device. Common attacks: CSRF on authorization endpoint: state parameter missing or not validated; attacker initiates authorization; tricks user into completing (login CSRF); state binds authorization request to user session; must be random and validated. Open redirect in redirect_uri: attacker registers redirect_uri matching open redirect on legitimate site: https://legitimate.com/redirect?url=https://attacker.com; authorization code sent to attacker via redirect; RFC 6749 requires exact redirect_uri match (not prefix); many implementations too permissive. Authorization code injection: attacker obtains authorization code from other source; injects into victim authorization flow; PKCE prevents (attacker cannot exchange code without code_verifier). Token leakage: access token in URL (Referer header leaks to third parties, server logs, browser history); access tokens should be in Authorization header or POST body; never in URL. Mix-up attack: multiple authorization servers; client confuses responses between servers; bind token response to specific server. Insufficient scope validation: access token granted for limited scope; server does not validate scope on every request; token with user:read scope can access user:admin endpoints. Token storage (mobile/SPA): store tokens in memory (not localStorage or sessionStorage); XSS can steal localStorage tokens; in-memory tokens lost on page refresh (use refresh token pattern); service workers for token management. OAuth for authentication (OpenID Connect): OAuth 2.0 is authorization (not authentication); if used for authentication without proper nonce: attacker replays ID token; OpenID Connect adds: ID token (JWT with user identity), nonce (ties token to specific request), UserInfo endpoint; use OpenID Connect for authentication; validate: nonce, aud (audience), iss (issuer), exp (expiry), signature. Implementation: use well-maintained OAuth2 library; do not implement OAuth2 from scratch; verify all flows against OWASP OAuth Cheat Sheet; penetration test OAuth implementation specifically.
What is security in the Kubernetes ecosystem?

Kubernetes security: secure container orchestration platform covering cluster components, workloads, and configuration. Cluster component security: API server: all cluster communication through API server; authentication: certificates, OIDC (OpenID Connect), service account tokens; authorisation: RBAC (Role-Based Access Control); audit logging: all API calls logged; disable anonymous authentication (--anonymous-auth=false); enable audit logging (--audit-log-path); etcd: stores all cluster state including secrets; encrypt at rest (--encryption-provider-config); restrict access to etcd (firewall; only API server); kubelet: runs on each node; authentication: certificates; authorisation: RBAC or Node authoriser; disable read-only port (--read-only-port=0); kube-scheduler, kube-controller-manager: run with minimal permissions. RBAC (Role-Based Access Control): Roles and ClusterRoles: define permissions (API groups, resources, verbs); RoleBindings and ClusterRoleBindings: bind roles to users or service accounts; least privilege: minimum required permissions; avoid: cluster-admin binding for regular workloads, wildcard permissions (* on * resources); service account: each pod has service account; automountServiceAccountToken: false if pod does not need API access; avoid default service account; use dedicated service account per workload. Network policies: default: all pods communicate freely; NetworkPolicy restricts pod communication; ingress and egress policies; example: allow frontend pods to reach backend on 8080 only; deny all other traffic; requires CNI supporting NetworkPolicy: Calico, Cilium, Weave Net. Pod security: Pod Security Standards (PSS): replaces deprecated PodSecurityPolicy; three levels: Privileged (no restrictions), Baseline (minimal restrictions, prevents known privilege escalations), Restricted (hardened); enforce via Pod Security Admission controller; admission controllers: OPA Gatekeeper, Kyverno: policy-as-code; enforce: no privileged containers, no root user, read-only filesystem, resource limits, no hostPath mounts, required labels. Secret management: Kubernetes secrets: base64 encoded (not encrypted by default); encrypt at rest with KMS (AWS KMS, GCP KMS, Azure Key Vault); External secrets management: External Secrets Operator (Kubernetes operator syncing from AWS Secrets Manager, HashiCorp Vault, etc.); Sealed Secrets: encrypt secret before storing in Git; Vault Agent Injector: inject secrets from Vault into pods. Workload security: image security: sign images (Cosign); verify signatures before admission; scan images in registry and at admission; runtime security: Falco: detect runtime anomalies (unexpected exec in container, sensitive file read, privilege escalation attempt); Falco rules: alert on container shell (exec into container), sudo in container, write to /etc; supply chain: image from trusted registry only; distroless or minimal base images; no root user in Dockerfile (USER nonroot); read-only root filesystem.
What is content security policy (CSP) and how does it prevent XSS?

CSP (Content Security Policy): HTTP response header instructing browser what resources are permitted to load; prevents XSS by restricting script execution. How CSP prevents XSS: without CSP: browser executes any JavaScript in page (inline or from any source); XSS: inject <script>malicious code</script>; browser executes; with CSP: browser only executes scripts from allowed sources; inline scripts blocked unless explicitly allowed (unsafe-inline -- defeats purpose for XSS protection); attacker-injected script from external source: blocked if source not in allowlist. CSP directives: default-src: fallback for all resource types; script-src: JavaScript sources; style-src: CSS sources; img-src: image sources; connect-src: XMLHttpRequest, fetch, WebSocket destinations; font-src: web fonts; media-src: audio and video; object-src: plugins; frame-src: iframe sources; base-uri: restrict base element (prevents base tag injection); form-action: restrict form submission targets; upgrade-insecure-requests: auto-upgrade HTTP to HTTPS; block-all-mixed-content: block HTTP resources on HTTPS page. Restrictive CSP example: Content-Security-Policy: default-src none; script-src self; style-src self; img-src self data:; font-src self; connect-src self; frame-ancestors none; base-uri self; form-action self; prevents: loading scripts from CDN or external sources, inline event handlers (onclick=), javascript: URLs, framing (clickjacking), form submission to external sites. Nonce-based CSP: Content-Security-Policy: script-src nonce-RANDOM_VALUE; server generates cryptographic nonce per request; legitimate scripts: <script nonce=RANDOM_VALUE>; browser executes only scripts with matching nonce; attacker-injected scripts: no nonce; blocked; nonce must be unique per request (not reused); 128+ bit random value. Hash-based CSP: Content-Security-Policy: script-src sha256-BASE64_HASH; hash of exact script content; browser executes only scripts matching hash; inline scripts can be allowed by hash without unsafe-inline; content must be exact (any change = different hash). Reporting: Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only: test without blocking; Content-Security-Policy: default-src self; report-uri https://csp.example.com/report; browser sends violation reports; analyse before switching to enforcement mode. Common pitfalls: unsafe-inline: allows all inline scripts; defeats XSS protection; necessary for legacy apps; migrate away; unsafe-eval: allows eval(), setTimeout with string; required for some frameworks; avoid; wildcard: script-src *; allows any source; defeats purpose; CDN hosting: script-src cdn.example.com; fine for CDN but if CDN compromised: XSS possible; third-party widgets: adding Google Analytics, Hotjar, etc. requires adding their domains to script-src; each addition reduces protection; CSP bypass: JSONP endpoints on allowlisted domains; Angular, jQuery CDN with browser exploitation; open redirect to data: URI; base tag injection if base-uri not set; testing: CSP Evaluator (csp-evaluator.withgoogle.com): assess CSP strength.
What is endpoint privilege management?

Endpoint privilege management (EPM): control and monitor privileged access on endpoint devices; eliminate unnecessary admin privileges; reduce attack surface. The admin problem: 70-80% of enterprise attacks require admin privileges to succeed; malware gains admin privileges from logged-in admin user; reducing admin privileges significantly reduces attack surface; most users never need local admin: need admin for: installing software, changing system settings; do not need admin for: email, web browsing, office apps, business applications. Least privilege user (standard user): remove local admin from all user accounts; standard user account: cannot install software (without approval), cannot modify system files or registry, cannot disable security software, malware running as standard user: limited impact; challenge: some legitimate applications require admin (poorly designed software); address via application elevation (EPM tools). Application elevation: allow specific applications to run with elevated privileges without giving user admin; user right-clicks > run with elevated rights; EPM tool: validates application against allowlist; elevates only approved applications; no persistent admin rights; audit log every elevation; users never know admin password; just-in-time (JIT) elevation: request elevation for specific task with justification; approved by manager or auto-approved with business justification; time-limited elevation (1 hour); expires automatically; session recording: record all elevated sessions; screenshot, keystroke logging; evidence for audit and forensics. EPM products: CyberArk Endpoint Privilege Manager: most comprehensive; application control + privilege management; BeyondTrust Endpoint Privilege Management: Windows and Mac; strong application control; Thycotic (Delinea) Privilege Manager: mid-market; good value; PEDM (Privileged Endpoint Device Management) in PAM suites: CyberArk, BeyondTrust; ManageEngine PAM360; Microsoft LAPS (Local Administrator Password Solution): randomise local administrator password on each Windows device; stores in AD; prevent lateral movement via shared local admin password (if same local admin password on all workstations: pass-the-hash compromises all). Benefits measured: reduction in malware impact (malware without admin cannot modify system); reduced attack surface; audit trail of all privileged actions; compliance (PCI DSS requires no unnecessary admin rights on endpoints); reduced help desk calls (users cannot break systems without admin).
What is mobile device management (MDM) security?

MDM (Mobile Device Management): manage and enforce security policies on mobile devices; BYOD and corporate-owned; essential for remote workforce. MDM capabilities: enrolment: device enrolment in MDM (corporate: DEP/Apple Business Manager/Google Zero-Touch; BYOD: user enrolment); policy enforcement: screen lock (PIN, biometric), encryption mandatory, passcode complexity, OS version minimum, jailbreak/root detection; application management: deploy corporate apps; force-install security apps; block non-approved apps; remote actions: remote lock (if lost), remote wipe (if stolen or employee leaves), locate device; certificate management: deploy certificates for VPN, Wi-Fi, email; compliance enforcement: non-compliant device: conditional access blocks corporate resources until compliant; report compliance status. Corporate-owned device (COPE or COBO): full MDM control over entire device; can: read all installed apps, enforce any policy, remotely wipe entire device, view device location; acceptable use policies clearly communicated to employees; COPE (Corporate Owned Personally Enabled): corporate device; personal use permitted; clear privacy notice about monitoring. BYOD (Bring Your Own Device): employee-owned device; more restricted MDM profile; user enrolment (Apple) or work profile (Android): separates corporate and personal data; corporate data in managed container; MDM cannot see personal apps or data; remote wipe only corporate container (not entire device); employee privacy: MDM should not monitor personal apps or browsing; privacy policy communicated. Conditional access: Microsoft Intune + Azure Conditional Access: if device not enrolled in Intune: cannot access Office 365; if device not compliant (missing patch, no encryption): access blocked until remediated; Jamf + Azure AD: Apple devices; zero trust posture assessment before access. Zero-touch enrolment: Apple Business Manager + MDM: device ships directly to user; first boot: automatically enrols in MDM; corporate profile applied; no IT hands-on; Google Zero-Touch: Android equivalent; simplifies large-scale deployment. MDM bypass awareness: jailbreaking (iOS) and rooting (Android): bypass many MDM controls; MDM detects most jailbreak/root methods (but detection can be bypassed); jailbroken device policy: deny access to corporate resources; EDR on mobile: Zimperium zIPS, Lookout, Microsoft Defender for Endpoint on mobile: threat detection on devices; complement MDM (MDM = device management; EDR = threat detection). UEM (Unified Endpoint Management): manages both mobile and desktop; single console; Microsoft Intune, VMware Workspace ONE, IBM MaaS360: manage Windows, macOS, iOS, Android from one platform.
What is cyber threat modelling for cloud applications?

Cloud application threat modelling: systematically identify threats specific to cloud-native architectures; adapt traditional threat modelling for cloud context. Cloud-specific threats beyond traditional: multi-tenancy: shared compute and storage; side-channel attacks between tenants; hypervisor escape (uncommon but possible); cloud provider trust: cloud provider has physical and privileged access; cloud provider breach or insider; supply chain of cloud provider services; IAM complexity: overpermissive roles and policies; cross-account access; confused deputy; privilege escalation via IAM; credential exposure: IAM credentials, service account keys, API keys in code, containers, S3; snapshot and backup exposure: AMI, RDS snapshot shared publicly; backup accessible to unintended parties; data residency: data stored in unexpected region; cross-region replication; cost-based DoS: unlimited auto-scaling without budget alerts; attacker triggers auto-scale event; massive cloud bill (denial-of-wallet attack). STRIDE for cloud: Spoofing: steal IAM credentials; assume role; instance impersonation; Tampering: modify data in S3; modify Lambda function code; modify Container image in ECR; alter infrastructure (Terraform state manipulation); Repudiation: disable CloudTrail; delete logs before investigation; Information Disclosure: public S3 bucket; snapshot shared publicly; credentials in environment variables; over-permissive IAM; Denial of Service: terminate EC2 instances; delete RDS; deny access to critical resources; Elevation of Privilege: IAM privilege escalation (assume more permissive role); container escape to host; Lambda escape via SSRF to IMDS. Cloud data flow diagram elements: external actors: users (browser, mobile app), partner systems; services: Lambda, EC2, ECS, EKS, API Gateway, CloudFront; data stores: S3, RDS, DynamoDB, ElastiCache; trust boundaries: VPC boundary, IAM boundary, account boundary, internet boundary. Threat mitigation mapping: threat: credentials in code; mitigation: secrets management (Secrets Manager), SAST secret scanning; threat: public S3 bucket; mitigation: S3 Block Public Access, bucket policy, Macie; threat: IAM privilege escalation; mitigation: CIEM tool, access reviews, IAM Access Analyzer; threat: CloudTrail disabled; mitigation: CloudTrail with integrity validation, SCPs preventing CloudTrail disable; threat: SSRF to IMDS; mitigation: IMDSv2, WAF SSRF protection, input validation. Automating cloud threat modelling: Wiz: automatically maps cloud architecture graph; identifies attack paths; ThreatMapper (Deepfence): open-source cloud native threat mapping; identify internet-to-datastore attack paths automatically; runbooks: update threat model when architecture changes; include cloud security architect in design review.
What is a cyber security operations centre (SOC)?

SOC (Security Operations Centre): centralised team monitoring and responding to security threats; 24/7 coverage for enterprise security. SOC functions: continuous monitoring: SIEM alert monitoring; EDR alert triage; threat hunting; detection engineering (writing and tuning detection rules); incident response: triage alerts; investigate incidents; contain and eradicate threats; coordinate with IR team; threat intelligence: consume threat feeds; apply to detections; share intelligence; vulnerability management: track and report on vulnerability remediation; not remediate (that is IT operations); reporting: metrics and KPIs for management; compliance reporting; SOC maturity: Tier 1: basic monitoring; alert triage; escalation; Tier 2: deeper investigation; threat hunting; Tier 3: advanced hunting; malware RE; threat intelligence; detection engineering. Staffing: analyst tiers: L1 (triage), L2 (investigation), L3 (advanced), SOC Manager, Detection Engineer, Threat Intelligence Analyst; shift coverage: 24/7 requires 4-5 analysts per slot for coverage; in-house SOC: full control; institutional knowledge; expensive; MSSP/MDR: outsourced; faster time-to-operational; less institutional knowledge; hybrid: in-house management + MSSP for after-hours. Tools: SIEM (Splunk, Microsoft Sentinel, IBM QRadar, Chronicle, Elastic SIEM): log aggregation, correlation, alerting; EDR (CrowdStrike, SentinelOne, MDE): endpoint telemetry; SOAR (Splunk SOAR, Palo Alto XSOAR): automation and playbooks; threat intelligence: Recorded Future, Mandiant, MISP; vulnerability management: Tenable, Qualys; case management: ServiceNow Security Incident Response, Jira. SOC metrics: MTTD (Mean Time to Detect): average time from attack to detection; MTTR (Mean Time to Respond/Remediate): average time to contain; alert volume: total alerts per day; false positive rate: what % of alerts are FP; SLA compliance: what % of critical alerts responded to within SLA; escalation rate: what % of L1 alerts escalated to L2; analyst-to-alert ratio: sustainable workload measurement. MDR (Managed Detection and Response): premium MSSP model; vendor-managed EDR + SIEM; 24/7 human analysts; threat hunting; active response (quarantine, isolate on customer approval); retainer-based; suitable for organisations without 24/7 SOC capability.
What is SSLTLS certificate management?

TLS certificate management: lifecycle management of X.509 certificates; prevent expiry, enable automation, maintain trust. Certificate lifecycle: issuance: request certificate from CA; provide domain validation (DV), organisation validation (OV), or extended validation (EV); deployment: install certificate and private key on server; TLS termination; monitoring: track expiry dates; alert before expiry; renewal: renew before expiry (typically 30-90 days before); automation preferred; revocation: revoke compromised certificates; OCSP or CRL. Certificate types: DV (Domain Validated): CA verifies domain control only (DNS challenge, HTTP challenge); fastest (minutes); no organisation information; suitable for most web apps; OV (Organisation Validated): CA verifies domain + organisation identity; shows organisation in certificate details; browser shows padlock but no green bar; EV (Extended Validated): deprecated green bar; rigorous organisation verification; similar browser display to OV in modern browsers; less recommended now; Wildcard: *.example.com covers all first-level subdomains; one cert for all subdomains; risk: single compromise exposes all subdomains; Private/Internal CA: issue certificates for internal services; no public trust; employees must trust internal CA. Certificate Authorities: public trusted CAs: Let's Encrypt (free, DV only, automated); DigiCert, Sectigo, GlobalSign, Comodo (paid, DV/OV/EV); CA/Browser Forum: industry body; sets CA rules; Certificate Transparency (all public CAs must log certs). Let's Encrypt automation: ACME protocol: Automatic Certificate Management Environment; Certbot: most common ACME client; automates issuance and renewal; cron job for renewal; nginx, Apache plugins automatically reload; Caddy web server: automatic HTTPS (ACME built in); cert-manager (Kubernetes): automatically issue and renew TLS certificates in Kubernetes via Let's Encrypt or internal CA. Internal PKI: Microsoft Active Directory Certificate Services (AD CS): PKI for enterprise; issues certificates to domain members; AWS Private CA: managed private CA; issue private certificates; integrates with ACM; HashiCorp Vault PKI: secrets engine; issue and renew certificates; short-lived certificates. Certificate monitoring: alert 30-60 days before expiry: SIEM rule on certificate monitoring tool; Datadog, Nagios, Prometheus blackbox exporter monitor TLS expiry; Certificate Transparency monitoring: detect unexpected certificates issued for your domain. Common mistakes: expired certificate (user-visible; breaks HTTPS; prevented by automation); wrong domain (CN mismatch; subject alternative names missing); insecure key: RSA 1024-bit (too weak; use 2048 or 4096); weak cipher suite negotiated despite strong certificate; private key compromised (revoke and reissue immediately); wildcard overuse (one breach = all subdomains); certificate pinning without backup pin (rotation breaks app).
What is cybersecurity risk quantification?

Risk quantification: express cyber risk in financial terms; enable executive decision-making; prioritise investment. Why quantify: traditional: red/amber/green heat maps (qualitative); executives cannot compare: critical risk in IT vs operational risk; cannot calculate ROI of security control investment; financial quantification: compare security investment to risk reduction in dollars; justify security budget; prioritise controls by cost-effectiveness. FAIR (Factor Analysis of Information Risk): most widely adopted quantitative framework; decomposes risk into: Loss Event Frequency (how often does threat event occur?): Threat Event Frequency (how many times does threat agent attempt?), Vulnerability (% of attempts resulting in loss event); Loss Magnitude (how much does each event cost?): Primary Loss (direct cost: recovery, notification, fines), Secondary Loss (indirect: reputation, legal, regulatory); outputs: probability distribution of annual loss; 80th percentile loss exceedance curve; FAIR analysis: structured exercise; gather data: threat intelligence, vulnerability data, control effectiveness, historical incidents; quantify each component; Monte Carlo simulation: run thousands of scenarios; produce probability distribution. Example output: ransomware risk on corporate network: 90% confidence annual loss < $2.4M; mean annual loss $800K; 10% chance of loss > $5M per year. Using quantification for decisions: control ROI: current risk $800K annual loss; MFA investment $50K; MFA reduces risk by 60% ($480K reduction); ROI = ($480K - $50K) / $50K = 860% in year 1; cyber insurance: use FAIR output to size cyber insurance policy appropriately; risk appetite: executive sets threshold: accept risks under $100K annually; mitigate risks over $1M; risk transfer above threshold. Tools: RiskLens (SaaS, FAIR-based); SAFE Security (ML-based); Axio360; spreadsheet models; Cyentia Institute (research data on breach costs). Challenges: data quality: incident data scarce; threat event frequency estimates uncertain; model is estimate not truth; ranges more honest than point estimates; starting with qualitative then quantifying top risks is pragmatic approach; common criticism: garbage in garbage out; but even rough quantification better than qualitative; forces explicit assumption documentation.
What is asymmetric encryption and how is it used in security?

Asymmetric encryption (public-key cryptography): two mathematically related keys; public key encrypts or verifies; private key decrypts or signs; private key never shared. How it works: key pair: generate mathematically related pair: public key (share freely) and private key (keep secret); encryption: sender encrypts with recipient public key; only recipient private key can decrypt; signature: signer signs with private key; anyone with public key can verify signature; key exchange: Diffie-Hellman: exchange public values; derive shared secret without transmitting it; algorithms: RSA: most common; based on factoring large integers; RSA-2048 minimum (RSA-4096 for 20+ year security); ECDSA (Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm): signatures; smaller keys for equivalent security; P-256, P-384, Ed25519; ECDH (Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman): key exchange; TLS 1.3 uses X25519 (Curve25519 ECDH). Use cases: TLS certificate and key exchange: server has RSA or ECDSA certificate (public key); TLS handshake: ECDHE for key exchange (ephemeral asymmetric key pair derives symmetric session key); certificate verifies server identity (signature by CA); SSH: server has RSA/ECDSA/Ed25519 host key; client stores public key fingerprint; prevents MITM; client authentication: client has private key; server has authorised_keys; public key authentication; code signing: binary signed with developer private key; user verifies with developer public key; ensures binary not tampered; PGP email: recipient public key encrypts; sender private key signs; GPG implements PGP; digital certificates (X.509): certificate = public key + identity + CA signature; CA signs certificate with CA private key; browsers trust CA public keys (root store); blockchain: cryptocurrency wallets are ECDSA key pairs; transaction signed with private key; network verifies with public key. Performance: asymmetric operations much slower than symmetric; RSA-2048 sign: ~1ms; AES-256 encrypt 1MB: microseconds; hybrid encryption: encrypt data with symmetric key (AES-256, fast); encrypt symmetric key with asymmetric (RSA/ECDH); recipient decrypts asymmetric wrapper; uses symmetric key to decrypt data; TLS does this: ECDHE derives symmetric session key; AES-GCM encrypts data with session key.
What is a cybersecurity operations program maturity model?

Cybersecurity programme maturity model: assess and improve overall security programme; not just individual controls. Common frameworks: NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF): not strictly a maturity model but Tiers 1-4 approximate maturity; Tier 1 (Partial): ad hoc, reactive; Tier 2 (Risk Informed): risk management practices approved but not consistently implemented; Tier 3 (Repeatable): formal policies, repeatable processes; Tier 4 (Adaptive): actively adapting; threat and technology changes incorporated. C2M2 (Cybersecurity Capability Maturity Model): US DoE; 10 domains; 4 maturity indicator levels (MIL0-MIL3); initially oil and gas sector; broader adoption. CMMI for Security: adapts CMMI software process improvement; 5 levels: Initial (ad hoc), Managed (project-level), Defined (organisation-level), Quantitatively Managed (measured), Optimising (continuous improvement). Custom programme maturity assessment: domain-based: Identity and Access Management, Vulnerability Management, Incident Response, Security Architecture, Data Protection, Governance and Risk, Third-Party Risk, Security Operations, Application Security, Physical Security; each domain: define maturity criteria per level (1-5); assess against criteria; score each domain; create spider/radar chart; identify lowest-scoring domains; prioritise improvement roadmap. Maturity assessment process: self-assessment vs external assessment; structured interview + evidence review; scoring against criteria; gap analysis; prioritised roadmap with resource requirements; executive report with business context; common maturity levels described: Level 1 (Initial/Reactive): no documented processes; reactive to incidents; no formal programme; Level 2 (Developing): basic policies exist; some processes defined; inconsistently followed; Level 3 (Defined): documented processes; consistently followed; organisation-wide; Level 4 (Managed): metrics collected; performance tracked; data-driven decisions; Level 5 (Optimising): continuous improvement; benchmarking; adaptive to new threats. Roadmap development: prioritise domains with highest risk and lowest maturity; balance quick wins (raise awareness, get executive buy-in) with strategic improvements (programme-level changes); resource requirements: headcount, tools, training, external services; timeline: 12-24 months to next maturity level typically; board reporting: maturity progress as security KPI; link to risk reduction; justify ongoing investment.
How does a web application penetration test scope affect methodology?

Pentest scope and methodology: scope definition determines testing approach, depth, and deliverables. Black-box testing: no prior knowledge of application; simulate external attacker with no insider knowledge; methodology: discovery first (find all endpoints, technology, functionality); automated scanning (Burp, ZAP); manual exploitation; longer reconnaissance phase; misses: internal-only vulnerabilities, server-side code issues without source access; appropriate for: external adversary simulation, testing defensive visibility, initial assessment. Grey-box testing: partial knowledge provided: user credentials (one or more roles), partial documentation, technology stack; methodology: authentication testing from provided credential points; access control testing (use provided credentials); reduced reconnaissance; more time for exploitation; most common pentest engagement type; appropriate for: authenticated user abuse scenarios, majority of web application assessments; balances realism with efficiency. White-box testing: full knowledge: source code, architecture diagrams, network diagrams, credential for all roles, documentation; methodology: code review + dynamic testing; SAST on provided source code; comprehensive authentication and authorisation testing; business logic analysis with full context; most thorough; most expensive; appropriate for: critical applications, high-security environments, pre-launch assessments, finding maximum vulnerabilities. Scope elements: in-scope: specific domains (app.example.com, api.example.com), IP ranges, mobile applications, specific functionality; out-of-scope: production customer data, specific third-party components, social engineering, physical, denial of service (must be explicit); testing environment: production vs staging; if production: extra care required; data handling: discovered credentials and PII handling procedure; exclusions: security monitoring (do you notify SOC to expect test traffic?; or test SOC detection capability without notification?). Time-based scope: fixed time engagements: 5-10 days typical for web app pentest; time allocation: reconnaissance 10-15%, automated scanning 15-20%, manual testing 50-60%, reporting 15-20%; impact: grey-box assessment more efficient (less recon time); white-box most efficient (direct to code analysis); depth vs breadth: time-limited must choose: broad shallow assessment (find common vulns across all functionality) vs narrow deep assessment (thoroughly test payment functionality); discuss with client; match business risk. Engagement letter components: scope (exact), timeline, point of contact, emergency procedure, safe harbour, deliverables, payment.
What is a cyber resilience strategy?

Cyber resilience: ability to withstand cyberattacks, continue operations during incidents, and recover quickly; broader than cybersecurity (which focuses on prevention). Prevention vs resilience: pure prevention focus: invest only in stopping attacks; inevitable breach eventually (no 100% prevention); no recovery capability; long disruption when breach occurs; resilience approach: accept that some attacks will succeed; invest in: detection (find attacks quickly), containment (limit blast radius), recovery (restore operations fast), continuity (keep critical operations running during incident). Business continuity planning (BCP): identify critical business processes: revenue-generating, customer-facing, required; rank by Maximum Tolerable Downtime (MTD): how long can this process be down before irreversible harm?; for each critical process: identify supporting IT systems; develop continuity plan; test annually. Disaster Recovery (DR): RTO (Recovery Time Objective): maximum acceptable downtime; RTO drives recovery architecture choices; RPO (Recovery Point Objective): maximum acceptable data loss (how old can restored data be?); DR strategies by RTO: backup and restore (RTO hours-days), warm standby (RTO minutes-hours), pilot light (RTO minutes), multi-site active-active (RTO seconds); backup testing: regular test restores; backup value only proven if restore works; 3-2-1 rule: 3 copies, 2 different media types, 1 offsite. Incident response capability: IR plan: documented and tested; IR retainer: pre-contracted IR firm; accelerates incident response; tabletop exercises: practise responses; cyber insurance: financial resilience; covers: IR costs, legal fees, notification costs, ransom (if decided to pay), business interruption. Resilience by design: immutable infrastructure: deploy from code; if compromised: destroy and redeploy; no manual intervention; segmentation: limit blast radius; critical systems segment isolated from general network; defence in depth: multiple controls; single control failure does not cascade; chaos engineering (Netflix approach): intentionally test failure scenarios; inject failures in production; verify system handles; identify weak resilience points. Cyber resilience metrics: MTTD (Mean Time to Detect); MTTR (Mean Time to Recover from incident); backup restore test success rate; RTO/RPO achieved in DR tests; number of incidents that degraded but did not break operations vs those that caused full outage; target: 100% of incidents managed without customer impact long-term.
What is a cybersecurity career path and key skills?

Cybersecurity career paths: multiple specialisations; technical and non-technical roles. Entry paths: IT support and system administration: strong foundation; understand what normal looks like; software development: developer to application security; understand code; network engineering: network to network security; know the protocols; military or law enforcement: intelligence, digital forensics. Early certifications: CompTIA Security+: broad foundation; widely accepted for entry level; vendor-neutral; CompTIA Network+: networking foundation before Security+; CompTIA CySA+ (Cybersecurity Analyst): blue team focus; CEH (Certified hacker): red team basics; eJPT (eLearnSecurity Junior Penetration Tester): practical beginner pentest. Technical specialisations: penetration tester / red team: OSCP (Offensive Security Certified Professional): gold standard practical pentest cert; eWPT, eWPTX: web app pentest; GPEN, GWAPT (GIAC); advanced: OSED, OSEP, OSWE (Offensive Security advanced); bug bounty hunter: HackerOne, Bugcrowd; SOC analyst / blue team: GCIA (Intrusion Analyst), GCIH (Incident Handler); Microsoft SC-200 (Security Operations Analyst); threat hunter: requires EDR + SIEM expertise; ATT&CK knowledge; digital forensics and incident response (DFIR): GCFE (Forensic Examiner), GCFA (Forensic Analyst), GCFE; EnCE; cloud security: AWS Security Specialty, Azure AZ-500, GCP Professional Cloud Security Engineer; CCSP (Certified Cloud Security Professional); application security: GWEB, GWPT; CSSLP (Certified Secure Software Lifecycle Professional); OSWE; GRC (Governance Risk Compliance): CISSP (Certified Information Systems Security Professional): managerial; widely required for senior roles; CISM (Certified Information Security Manager): management focus; CRISC (Certified in Risk and Information Systems Control). Career progression: analyst -> senior analyst -> lead -> manager -> director -> CISO; technical individual contributor path: junior -> mid -> senior -> principal -> staff; management vs technical: many stay technical (principal/staff security engineer); others move to management; both valuable. Skills valued: hands-on lab practice: TryHackMe, HackTheBox, Hack The Box Pro Labs, OffSec Proving Grounds; CTF (Capture The Flag) competitions; open-source contributions (Metasploit modules, Burp extensions, YARA rules, Sigma rules); blog writing and conference talks: demonstrates expertise; builds reputation; soft skills: communication (explain technical risk to business), report writing, stakeholder management, project management.
What is purple team versus red team versus blue team?

Team colours in cybersecurity: specialised roles in security testing and operations. Red team: offensive; simulate real-world attackers; find vulnerabilities before adversaries do; methodologies: adversary simulation (mimic specific threat actors), goal-oriented (reach objective: domain admin, steal specific data), full-scope (physical, social engineering, digital); distinct from pentest: longer engagements, stealthier, realistic TTPs, test detection and response not just vulnerabilities; deliverable: comprehensive report on attack path, dwell time, detection gaps; personnel: hacker, former offensive security researchers; tools: Cobalt Strike, Metasploit, custom implants, physical access tools. Blue team: defensive; monitor, detect, and respond to threats; functions: SIEM monitoring, alert triage, incident response, threat hunting, detection engineering, vulnerability management, security architecture; 24/7 operations; persona: defenders, SOC analysts, incident responders, detection engineers; deliverable: operational security; metrics (MTTD, MTTR, false positive rate, coverage); tools: SIEM, EDR, SOAR, vulnerability scanner, network monitoring. Purple team: collaboration between red and blue; red team executes techniques; blue team checks detection immediately; real-time feedback loop; goal: improve detection coverage against specific TTPs; not just simulation but direct improvement; adversary emulation plans (ATT&CK-based); each technique tested and detection improved on the spot; deliverable: improved detection rules, data source gaps identified, coverage heat map. Yellow team (software security): developers and security engineers; build security in; secure code, security architecture, SAST, SCA, developer security training; combines software development (yellow) with security; DevSecOps is the yellow team approach. Green team (integration): some organisations use green for security automation and SOAR engineers who bridge red (attack knowledge) and blue (defensive response) through automation; less standardised term. Practical structure: small organisations: security generalists play all roles; medium: separate red team function (or external engagement), SOC/blue team; large enterprise: dedicated red team, SOC with L1/L2/L3, detection engineering team, threat intel team, purple team exercises quarterly; very large (FAANG, financial): all teams plus dedicated adversary simulation teams, AI/ML security research, offensive security research.
What is a responsible disclosure and vulnerability disclosure programme?

Process: researcher discovers vulnerability; contacts vendor: security@company.com, HackerOne, dedicated disclosure form; shares: vulnerability details, proof of concept, affected versions, CVSS assessment; vendor acknowledges within agreed SLA (typically 3-7 days); vendor investigates; confirms validity and severity; vendor develops patch: timeline agreed (typically 90 days; Google Project Zero standard); CVE requested and reserved; patch released; coordinated public disclosure: CVE published, vendor advisory, researcher credit; credit: researcher credited in advisory and CVE; sometimes cash bounty if bug bounty programme exists. Timelines: 90 days standard (Google Project Zero): vendor has 90 days to patch; if not patched: Project Zero publishes regardless; rationale: after 90 days vendor unlikely to patch without public pressure; CERT/CC: 45 days historically; NCSC (UK): flexible; negotiation: critical infrastructure, national security implications: extended timeline negotiable; active exploitation: shorter timeline. Legal protections: safe harbour: responsible vendor explicitly states will not pursue legal action for good-faith disclosure; Computer Fraud and Abuse Act (CFAA) concerns: US law; security researchers have been prosecuted; safe harbour reduces risk; EU Directive on attacks against information systems: similar concerns; disclosure agreement: some vendors require NDA; researchers should be cautious about broad NDAs. CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures): unique identifier for each vulnerability; CVE-2024-12345; CVE Numbering Authority (CNA): vendor or organisation authorised to assign CVEs; MITRE: top-level CNA; NIST NVD: enriches CVEs with CVSS scores and additional metadata; researchers can request CVE before disclosure (pre-allocation).
What is security for IoT devices?

IoT security: secure Internet of Things devices; cameras, sensors, industrial equipment, medical devices, home automation. IoT security challenges: resource constraints: limited CPU, memory, battery; cannot run full OS or AV; long lifecycle: deployed 10-20 years; vendor stops supporting; no patches; poor defaults: default username/password (admin/admin); default accounts not required to change; broad attack surface: many IoT protocols (MQTT, CoAP, Zigbee, Z-Wave, BLE, LoRaWAN); lack of visibility: traditional security tools do not inventory IoT; no EDR agent; heterogeneous: thousands of device types; no standard security approach. Common IoT vulnerabilities: default credentials: Mirai botnet exploited default credentials on cameras/DVRs at massive scale; unencrypted communication: cleartext HTTP, telnet, unencrypted MQTT; no authentication between IoT device and hub; outdated firmware: no update mechanism; no patch applied for years; insecure APIs: mobile app or web interface controlling device has injection, auth bypass; physical attacks: JTAG, UART debug interfaces accessible; extract firmware; reverse engineer; modify; unencrypted firmware: extract firmware; find credentials, encryption keys, proprietary algorithms. Security controls: secure defaults: unique per-device credentials (not factory default); require password change on first use; disable unused interfaces; encryption: TLS for all communication; WPA2/WPA3 for Wi-Fi IoT; BLE with proper pairing; authentication: device authentication with certificates; mutual TLS; network segmentation: IoT devices on dedicated VLAN; no communication between IoT and corporate network; restrict internet access; firmware updates: secure update mechanism (signed firmware); automated update push; discovery and inventory: passive network scanning (fingerprinting by network behaviour); Claroty, Armis, Ordr, Nozomi (OT/IoT visibility platforms). Medical devices: FDA cybersecurity guidance: pre-market and post-market; SBOM required; coordinated vulnerability disclosure; security patching; HIPAA PHI protection. OT/ICS (overlap with IoT): Purdue model network segmentation; air-gap critical control systems; out-of-band monitoring; IEC 62443 standard. Standards: NIST SP 800-213 (IoT Cybersecurity); ETSI EN 303 645 (European IoT security standard); ENISA IoT guidelines; PSA Certified: hardware security architecture.
What are common vulnerabilities in GraphQL APIs?

GraphQL security vulnerabilities: query language for APIs with unique attack surface beyond REST API issues. GraphQL basics: single endpoint (/graphql); client defines exact data shape; queries (read) and mutations (write); subscriptions (real-time); schema defines types, fields, queries, mutations. Introspection: GraphQL introspection: query the schema itself; discover all types, fields, queries, mutations; query: {__schema {types {name fields {name type {name}}}}}; in development: reveals full API surface; in production: should be disabled for external consumers; disable: graphql(schema, {introspection: false}); development tool exception: graphiql playground often left enabled in production. Denial of service -- query complexity: deeply nested queries: user { friends { friends { friends {... (20 levels deep) }}}}; N+1 queries: each friend requires separate DB query; amplification attack; protection: query depth limit (reject queries > N levels deep); query complexity limit (each field has cost; reject if total cost exceeds threshold); query timeout; rate limiting per query; persisted queries (allowlist of pre-approved queries; reject ad hoc queries). Authorization: field-level authorization missing: query user(id: 2) {adminNotes} (regular user accessing admin field); object-level: IDOR in GraphQL (change ID argument); mutation authorization: can regular user call admin mutations?; test all queries and mutations with insufficient privileges; batch mutations: GraphQL allows multiple mutations in one request; rate limiting per HTTP request insufficient; must rate limit per mutation. Injection via arguments: SQL injection in resolver arguments: getUser(name: test OR 1=1); NoSQL injection in MongoDB resolver: $where operator injection; SSRF via URL arguments: fetchURL(url: http://169.254.169.254/); inject in all string arguments; Test: GraphQL-specific tools: InQL (Burp Suite extension): introspection, query generation; GraphiQL: developer IDE for GraphQL; Altair: GraphQL client; Clairvoyance: introspection bypass (guess fields even when introspection disabled). Sensitive data in errors: GraphQL errors often verbose; reveal schema information even with introspection disabled; reveal field names from error messages; disable detailed errors in production; return generic error messages; log detailed errors server-side. Field suggestions: GraphQL returns Did you mean X? Suggestions for invalid field names; reveals valid field names even without introspection; disable suggestions in production (most frameworks have option). Batching attacks: GraphQL supports query batching (array of queries); rate limit bypass: 100 login mutations in one HTTP request = 100 password attempts; implement per-operation rate limiting not just per-HTTP request.
What is port scanning and service enumeration?

Port scanning: discover open network ports and services on target; foundation of network reconnaissance. TCP scanning: SYN scan (half-open, stealth): nmap -sS TARGET; send SYN; receive SYN-ACK = open, RST = closed, no response = filtered; no full connection; less likely logged than connect scan; requires root; Connect scan: full TCP three-way handshake; no root required; more reliably detected; UDP scan: nmap -sU TARGET; UDP ports (DNS 53, SNMP 161, DHCP 67/68, NTP 123, TFTP 69, NetBIOS 137, RADIUS 1812); slower (no handshake; timeout-based); service enumeration: version detection: nmap -sV TARGET (probe open ports; identify service and version); banner grabbing: nc -nv TARGET 22 (connect; read service banner; reveals: OpenSSH 8.2p1 Ubuntu). Nmap command examples: nmap -sV -p- --min-rate 5000 TARGET (all 65535 ports, fast, version detection); nmap -A TARGET (aggressive: OS detection, version, script scan, traceroute); nmap -sC TARGET (default script scan); nmap -p 80,443,8080,8443 TARGET (specific ports); nmap -iL targets.txt (scan list from file); nmap -oA output TARGET (save results in all formats:.nmap,.xml,.gnmap). NSE (Nmap Scripting Engine): nmap --script vuln TARGET (vulnerability scanning); nmap --script http-enum TARGET (web directory enumeration); nmap --script smb-enum-shares TARGET (enumerate SMB shares); nmap --script banner TARGET (grab banners from all open ports). Masscan: fastest port scanner; 10M packets/second; masscan -p0-65535 TARGET --rate=100000; use for quick discovery before detailed nmap; combine: masscan to find open ports, nmap for version and scripts. Service-specific enumeration: FTP (21): anonymous login (ftp TARGET; anonymous); list files; SMTP (25): VRFY/EXPN (user enumeration on some mail servers); telnet TARGET 25; VRFY admin; SMB (445): nmap --script smb-enum-shares,smb-enum-users TARGET; smbclient -L //TARGET -N (null session); HTTP (80/443): web application; gobuster for directories; detect CMS; SNMP (161): snmpwalk -v 2c -c public TARGET (community string enumeration); reveals: system info, network interfaces, running processes, installed software; common community string: public, private, community; LDAP (389/636): ldapsearch -x -H ldap://TARGET -s base namingContexts (anonymous LDAP query). Evasion: slow scanning: nmap -T1 or -T2; decoys: nmap -D RND:5 TARGET; fragment packets: nmap -f TARGET; randomise port order: nmap --randomize-hosts TARGET.
What is XSS via file uploads?

XSS via file uploads: inject malicious JavaScript through file upload functionality; bypass normal XSS input filtering; achieve stored XSS or client-side execution. Attack types: SVG XSS: SVG files are XML; can contain JavaScript; upload SVG file with embedded script: <?xml version=1.0 standalone=no?><!DOCTYPE svg PUBLIC -//W3C//DTD SVG 1.1//EN http://www.w3.org/Graphics/SVG/1.1/DTD/svg11.dtd><svg xmlns=http://www.w3.org/2000/svg width=200 height=200><script type=text/javascript>alert(XSS)</script></svg>; if server serves uploaded SVG with Content-Type: image/svg+xml: browser renders as SVG and executes JavaScript; impact: if served from same origin: full XSS; access cookies, localStorage, DOM; HTML file upload: upload.html file with XSS payload; if served from same origin: full XSS; EXIF metadata XSS: metadata in JPEG files; if application displays EXIF data without sanitisation: XSS possible (limited; requires EXIF display); polyglot files: file that is valid as multiple formats; JPEG+JavaScript: file starts with JPEG magic bytes (FFD8FF); also valid JavaScript (content after JPEG header); serve as Content-Type: text/javascript; script src to polyglot file; PDF XSS: PDF files can contain JavaScript (PDF JavaScript); if displayed in browser PDF renderer: executes; older browsers more susceptible; modern browsers sandboxed. Why file upload XSS bypasses filters: normal XSS filtering focuses on HTML form inputs; file upload less scrutinised; server may not inspect file content for scripts; file type validation may pass SVG as image; Content-Type from upload may be trusted without verification. Exploitation: upload SVG; share link; victim clicks link; browser renders SVG; JavaScript executes in origin context; cookie theft: document.cookie; localStorage theft: localStorage.getItem(token); CSRF token theft; key logging. Mitigation: serve uploaded files from separate domain (uploads.cdn.example.com): XSS limited to CDN domain, cannot access main app cookies or localStorage; Content-Type validation: serve uploaded files with correct content type (image/jpeg, image/png) regardless of file content; never serve as text/html; SVG: if SVG upload allowed: sanitise SVG (remove script tags and event handlers) -- DOMPurify sanitises SVG; or serve as Content-Disposition: attachment (download instead of display); CSP: frame-src restrictions limit where content can be embedded; File validation: reject SVG if not needed; magic bytes check; re-encode images (strips SVG/JavaScript from JPEG by re-encoding through image library).
What is Active Directory certificate services (AD CS) and its security risks?

AD CS (Active Directory Certificate Services): Microsoft PKI implementation; issues certificates for users, computers, and services; significant attack surface in many environments. AD CS components: Certificate Authority (CA): root CA or subordinate CA; issues certificates; Windows Certificate Authority; Certificate Templates: define what certificates CA will issue; what attributes; who can request; Web Enrollment (certsrv): IIS-based certificate request interface; OCSP Responder: certificate revocation status; Network Device Enrollment Service (NDES): SCEP for network devices. Security vulnerabilities (ESC classes from SpecterOps research): ESC1 -- Misconfigured certificate templates: template allows requestor to specify arbitrary Subject Alternative Name (SAN); SAN can be domain admin UPN or email; request certificate for admin@corp.com; authenticate as domain admin with issued cert; ESC2 -- Misconfigured certificate templates (Any Purpose EKU or no EKU): certificate can be used for any purpose; includes client authentication; request cert; use for domain auth; ESC3 -- Misconfigured enrollment agent templates: enrollment agent cert allows requesting certs on behalf of any user; chain to admin auth; ESC4 -- Vulnerable certificate template access control: low-privileged user can modify template settings; modify to ESC1; ESC5 -- Vulnerable PKI object access control: DACL on CA object, CA server, RPC/DCOM interface; ESC6 -- EDITF_ATTRIBUTESUBJECTALTNAME2 flag: CA configured to include SAN from certificate request even if not specified in template; any template request can specify SAN; ESC7 -- Vulnerable CA access control: user has ManageCA or ManageCertificates; can issue pending/failed certificates; ESC8 -- NTLM relay to AD CS HTTP endpoints: web enrollment does not require authentication; NTLM relay to certsrv; obtain certificate for relayed machine account; authenticate as domain controller; NTLM relay attack: PetitPotam coerces DC to authenticate to attacker; attacker relays to certsrv; gets DC certificate; DCSync. Tools: Certify (SharpCollection): enumerate misconfigured templates; request certificates; Certipy (Python): enumerate and exploit ESC attacks; BloodHound: 5.0+ includes AD CS nodes and edges; shows certificate-based attack paths. Remediation: audit certificate templates: restrict who can request; disable SANs unless required; remove write access from non-admins; PKINIT restrictions; Require CA manager approval for sensitive templates; NTLM relay: enforce HTTPS + EPA (Extended Protection for Authentication) on AD CS web enrollment; disable HTTP enrollment if not needed.
How do you perform cloud penetration testing on AWS?

AWS penetration testing: assess Amazon Web Services environment; identity, configuration, services, and data security. Permission to test: AWS Acceptable Use Policy: no need to request permission for penetration testing of own account; prohibited without permission: DDoS attacks on AWS infrastructure, port flooding, protocol flooding; rules of engagement: document scope; test only authorised accounts; no attacking AWS shared infrastructure. Reconnaissance: credential discovery: AWS credentials in source code, S3 public buckets, instance metadata, EC2 user data; tools: truffleHog, git-secrets, detect-secrets; S3 public bucket enumeration: aws s3 ls --no-sign-request s3://bucket-name (anonymous access); bucket name guessing: company-name, company-name-backup, company-name-logs; cloud_enum (automated bucket/storage enumeration); network discovery: nmap scanning of EC2 instances; AWS metadata for instance topology; account enumeration: error message differences for valid vs invalid account IDs (some services reveal account ID); IAM enumeration: if credentials obtained; Principal Mapper (PMapper): IAM permission analysis; identify privilege escalation paths; aws iam list-users, list-roles, list-policies; Pacu: AWS exploitation framework; modular; reconnaissance and exploitation. IAM privilege escalation: if initial access with limited IAM credentials; PMapper: automatically identifies escalation paths; common paths: CreateRole + AttachRolePolicy (create role with admin; assume it); PassRole + CreateFunction (pass privileged role to Lambda function; invoke function); CloudFormation stack with role; AttachUserPolicy; CreateLoginProfile; SetDefaultPolicyVersion; UpdateAssumeRolePolicy; Exploit: create admin role and assume it; PMapper: python3 -m principalmapper --profile TARGET graph create; python3 -m principalmapper --profile TARGET analysis --privesc. Service exploitation: SSRF to IMDS: EC2 applications with SSRF can reach 169.254.169.254; retrieve instance role credentials; exploit S3: misconfigured bucket policies; public objects; bucket ACLs; lambda exploitation: environment variable secrets; injection via event sources; RDS: public accessibility; default credentials; ECS/EKS: container escape; overprivileged task roles; API Gateway: authentication bypass; injection. Post-exploitation in AWS: CloudTrail evasion (delete events if permissions allow); persistence (IAM user, access key, role backdoor); data exfiltration (S3 sync); privilege escalation to OrganizationAccountAccessRole (cross-account admin). Tools: Pacu (AWS exploitation); ScoutSuite (multi-cloud security audit); CloudMapper (AWS account visualisation); cloudsplaining (IAM policy analysis); Prowler (security assessment); ROADtools (Entra ID equivalent); CloudFox (privilege escalation paths).
What is broken authentication in web applications?

Broken authentication: weaknesses in authentication implementation; allow attackers to compromise credentials, session tokens, or bypass authentication. Common broken authentication vulnerabilities: weak passwords accepted: no minimum length, no complexity, common passwords allowed (admin, password123); no protection against credential stuffing (list of breached username/password combos tested against site); account enumeration: login error reveals different message for valid vs invalid username: username not found (reveals username does not exist) vs incorrect password (reveals username exists); test: different response time, response body, status code between valid and invalid username; fix: identical error for both (invalid credentials); brute force: no rate limiting on login endpoint; lockout not implemented; CAPTCHA absent; credential stuffing: billions of breached credentials available; attackers test against new site; requires: rate limiting, MFA, anomaly detection (many different source IPs). Insecure forgot password: reset token in URL (logged by proxies and browsers); token not expired after use; token not time-limited (valid for days); token predictable (sequential, time-based); token sent over insecure channel; user enumeration via forgot password (reveals if email registered); exploit: request reset for victim; intercept token from URL or predict; reset password; gain access. Default credentials: admin/admin, admin/password, guest/guest; devices, applications, cloud services with default credentials; test: admin panels, development ports, API test interfaces; tools: SecLists default credentials list; DefaultCreds-Cheat-Sheet. Session fixation: attacker sets victim session ID (via URL or cookie injection); victim logs in; session ID elevated to authenticated; attacker uses same ID; fix: generate new session ID on login. Weak session tokens: sequential (predict next token); base64 encoded user ID (decode and modify); short (brute forceable); time-based (predictable); test: intercept session token; decode (base64, JWT without validation, URL decode); try to predict or manipulate; tools: Burp Sequencer: analyse session token randomness; statistical test; Hackvertor (Burp extension): decode and modify tokens. Broken logout: logout does not invalidate server-side session; cookie cleared client-side but session still valid on server; exploit: capture session token before logout; reuse after logout; fix: delete server-side session on logout; for JWTs: token blocklist or short expiry.
What is the PTES (Penetration Testing Execution Standard)?

PTES (Penetration Testing Execution Standard): comprehensive methodology defining phases, tools, and deliverables for penetration tests; industry reference. Seven phases: (1) Pre-engagement Interactions: scope definition; rules of engagement; emergency contact procedures; legal authorisation; NDA; payment terms; timeline; deliverable format; goals and success criteria. (2) Intelligence Gathering: OSINT; technical, organisation, and people reconnaissance; passive and active methods; tools: theHarvester, Maltego, Recon-ng, Shodan; deliverable: target profile; attack surface map. (3) Threat Modelling: identify highest-priority targets; threat actors relevant to organisation; attack vectors most likely to be exploited; map to scope and intelligence gathered; create attack plan focusing on highest-risk areas. (4) Vulnerability Analysis: active scanning: Nessus, OpenVAS; web scanning: Burp Suite, Nikto, OWASP ZAP; manual analysis; network scanning: nmap; service enumeration; identify vulnerabilities in discovered services and applications. (5) Exploitation: exploit identified vulnerabilities; gain access; demonstrate impact; evidence collection; tools: Metasploit, Burp Suite, custom exploits, Impacket, CME; escalate privileges; document each step. (6) Post Exploitation: maintain access; explore network; privilege escalation; lateral movement; data collection (evidence of what could be reached); assess business impact; cleanup (remove tools, artefacts -- restore to pre-test state except as agreed). (7) Reporting: executive summary; technical findings; attack narrative; evidence (screenshots, command output); risk ratings; remediation recommendations; retesting suggestions; appendices (tool output, references). PTES vs OWASP Testing Guide: PTES: general penetration testing (network, application, social engineering); OWASP Testing Guide: web application specific; very detailed web vulnerability testing methodology; complement each other; use OWASP Testing Guide for web portion of PTES. Why PTES matters: provides client expectations framework; testers follow consistent methodology; comparable engagements; reduces scope ambiguity; quality assurance. Scope document based on PTES: both tester and client sign; explicitly lists: in-scope, out-of-scope, permitted techniques, prohibited techniques, timeline, contacts, reporting requirements.
What is security validation and breach attack simulation?

BAS (Breach and Attack Simulation): continuously simulate attacks against real production environment; validate controls work as expected; find gaps before real attackers. Why BAS: security teams assume controls work; BAS proves they do (or do not); changes happen constantly (new firewall rules, WAF rule changes, SIEM tuning); controls may drift from known-good state; BAS detects drift; frequency: automated BAS runs 24/7 or daily; penetration test: annual or quarterly; gap between tests is risk window. How BAS works: BAS platform: agents deployed in production environment; agent simulates attack behaviours safely (no actual damage); traffic generated matches real attack patterns; results: which attacks were blocked, detected, or missed; coverage: antivirus bypass simulation (known malware samples; check EDR/AV blocks), email simulation (phishing email delivery; check email gateway blocks), web attack simulation (attack agent sending HTTP attacks to WAF; check WAF blocks), network simulation (lateral movement simulation; check network controls), exfiltration simulation (data exfiltration attempts; check DLP and egress controls). BAS vs penetration testing: penetration testing: human-driven; creative; finds unknown vulnerabilities; quarterly or annual; BAS: automated; known attack library; validates controls against known attacks; continuous; complement not replace each other. Specific validation capabilities: EDR validation: run known malware sample; verify EDR quarantines; MITRE ATT&CK technique execution: execute atomic tests; verify SIEM alerts; email gateway: send phishing simulation; verify gateway catches; WAF: send OWASP Top 10 payloads; verify WAF blocks; lateral movement: simulate PsExec, WMI movement; verify network detection. Products: SafeBreach: comprehensive; 10,000+ attack playbooks; Cymulate: enterprise BAS; MITRE ATT&CK mapped; AttackIQ: ATT&CK-aligned; purple team integration; Picus Security: threat exposure management; CISA recommended BAS practices; open-source: Atomic Red Team (manual BAS); Caldera (MITRE, automated ATT&CK emulation). Reporting: control effectiveness score (% of attacks blocked + detected); comparison to previous period (is coverage improving?); ATT&CK coverage heat map; prioritised gaps for remediation; compare to industry benchmark.
What are common application layer DDoS attack patterns?

Application layer DDoS (Layer 7 DDoS): target application resources not bandwidth; more sophisticated; harder to distinguish from legitimate traffic. Why layer 7 effective: small volume can exhaust application resources; each request: DB query, compute, API call; attacker sends slow/moderate request volume; each request expensive server-side; 10,000 legitimate req/sec sustainable; 1,000 crafted req/sec to expensive endpoint: server exhaustion. Attack types: HTTP flood: high volume HTTP GET or POST requests; volumetric but targeting application (not just network bandwidth); simple mitigation: rate limit per IP; sophisticated: distributed botnet with many IPs; rate limit per session or browser fingerprint; slow HTTP attacks: Slowloris: open many HTTP connections; send headers extremely slowly; server waiting for complete request; consumes connection slots; servers have limited concurrent connections; mitigation: connection timeout; limit connections per IP; RUDY (R-U-Dead-Yet): POST request with huge Content-Length; send body one byte per minute; server waits for complete body; HTTP range attack: Range: bytes=0-1 requests; server processes many overlapping ranges; expensive server-side computation; Cache busting: add random query parameter (search?q=keyword&rand=12345); CDN cache miss every request; all requests reach origin; overwhelm origin server behind CDN; login endpoint targeting: authentication endpoints computationally expensive (bcrypt); focus flood on login; server cannot process other requests; search endpoint targeting: complex database queries; attacker triggers expensive searches. Mitigation: rate limiting per IP and per session; JS challenge (client-side JavaScript execution proves legitimate browser vs bot); CAPTCHA for suspicious traffic; device fingerprinting (TLS fingerprint, HTTP/2 fingerprint, browser characteristics); geographic blocking (if attack concentrated in specific region); CDN / DDoS scrubbing (Cloudflare, Akamai, Radware, AWS Shield Advanced): absorb L7 attacks at edge; detect and mitigate application layer attacks; autoscaling: additional capacity during attack (buy time; not solution since cost may be unsustainable); IP reputation: block known bad actor IPs; challenge unknown IPs; WAF rules targeting specific attack patterns; circuit breaker: application-level: if error rate exceeds threshold: return cached or simplified response; shed load gracefully. Cloudflare application layer DDoS: 40M+ requests/second blocked during largest documented L7 attack (2022).
What is security control assurance?

Security control assurance: verify controls work as intended; not just that they exist. Why assurance matters: compliance checkbox: control documented as present; actual effectiveness not verified; example: SIEM alerting rule exists on paper; never tested; attacker uses technique covered by rule; alert never fires; assurance: control exists AND works as intended. Assurance methods: technical testing: penetration testing validates controls prevent/detect attacks; red team exercises test detection and response controls; BAS (Breach and Attack Simulation): continuous automated control validation; vulnerability scanning: confirms patches applied; configuration review: confirms hardening settings applied; Control effectiveness testing: SIEM alert test: generate test event matching alert rule; confirm alert fires within expected time; EDR test: run known malicious sample; confirm quarantine action occurs; backup restore test: restore from backup; verify data integrity and completeness; MFA test: attempt login without second factor; confirm blocked; firewall rule test: attempt to make connection blocked by policy; confirm blocked; log completeness test: generate specific events; verify all appear in SIEM; alert timing test: measure how long from event to alert (MTTD from control perspective). Continuous control monitoring: automated tools check control status continuously; GRC platform (ServiceNow GRC, RSA Archer, MetricStream) with automated evidence collection; security ratings (SecurityScorecard, BitSight): external view of control effectiveness; Tenable.sc / Qualys: continuous vulnerability assessment (patch control); CSPM: continuous cloud configuration compliance check; SOAR playbooks trigger control tests on schedule. Assurance reporting: control health dashboard: all controls with current status; passing (green), failing (red), degraded (amber); trend: is control health improving?; exceptions: controls that have failed assurance; risk acceptance or remediation plan; audit evidence: control test results stored; available for auditors; third-party assurance: SOC 2 Type II: auditor tests controls over 6-12 month period; not just point-in-time; ISO 27001 surveillance audit: annual check controls still operating; penetration test report: independent evidence of control effectiveness (or failure). NIST SP 800-53A: assessment procedures for each control in NIST 800-53; defines how to assess each control (examine, interview, test); provides structured assessment methodology.
What is Kerberos constrained delegation abuse?

Constrained delegation: allows service account to impersonate users but only to specific services (SPNs); intended as safer alternative to unconstrained delegation; still exploitable if misconfigured. How constrained delegation works: configured on service account A (not on target service); A can request Kerberos service ticket on behalf of any user for specific SPNs (e.g. cifs/fileserver.corp.com); requires S4U2Self (Service for User to Self) and S4U2Proxy (Service for User to Proxy) Kerberos extensions. Exploitation: if attacker compromises service account or computer account with constrained delegation configured: enumerate delegation: Get-ADUser -Filter {TrustedToAuthForDelegation -eq $True} (Protocol Transition delegation: S4U2Self can be used for any user including not authenticated to service, very powerful); PowerView: Get-DomainUser -TrustedToAuth; Get-DomainComputer -TrustedToAuth; use Rubeus: Rubeus.exe s4u /user:serviceAccount /aes256:HASH /impersonateuser:Administrator /msdsspn:cifs/server.corp.com /ptt; impersonates domain admin to the target SPN; access target service as domain admin; protocol transition (unconstrained S4U2Self): service account with TrustedToAuthForDelegation flag; can request Kerberos ticket for ANY user to itself without that user authenticating; then use S4U2Proxy to get ticket for target SPN; domain escalation if constrained delegation points to DC SPN. Resource-based constrained delegation (RBCD): configured on back-end resource (not on requesting service account); resource trusts specific accounts to delegate; RBCD abuse: if attacker has GenericWrite on computer account: set msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity attribute; create computer account or use attacker-controlled account; computer account can now delegate to target; attacker impersonates admin to target; Rubeus.exe s4u /user:ATTACKER_COMPUTER$ /rc4:HASH /impersonateuser:Administrator /msdsspn:cifs/TARGET.corp.com /ptt. Detection: Event 4769 with Kerberos ticket for unexpected SPN; S4U2Proxy events in DC logs; anomalous service ticket requests where requesting service does not typically need that target service; Microsoft Defender for Identity: detects constrained delegation abuse patterns. Prevention: review all delegation settings; remove unnecessary delegation; use Protected Users group (prevents delegation of user credentials); mark sensitive accounts as Account is sensitive and cannot be delegated; prefer RBCD over legacy constrained delegation; audit delegation settings quarterly.
What is API rate limiting bypass?

API rate limiting bypass: circumvent API request throttling controls; send more requests than intended; brute force, data scraping, DDoS. Rate limiting mechanisms and bypasses: IP-based rate limiting: limit per source IP; bypass: rotate IPs (VPN, proxy, botnet); if rate limit is per IP with no other factor: 100 IPs = 100x normal limit; X-Forwarded-For header: some APIs trust XFF header for IP determination; attacker sends X-Forwarded-For: 1.2.3.4 with each request; if API trusts this header: each unique XFF value = different IP for rate limiting; brute force by rotating XFF values; User-Agent rotation: if rate limited per User-Agent; rotate user agents; less effective if combined with IP. Account-based bypass: multiple accounts: create 100 accounts; each has own rate limit; total throughput 100x; sub-account or API key proliferation. Endpoint bypass: rate limit on /api/v1/login; same functionality at /api/v2/login, /api/v1/authenticate; different endpoint counts separately; test: enumerate all equivalent endpoints. Time-based bypass: sliding window vs fixed window: fixed window: 100 requests per minute window resets at :00; send 100 at :59 and 100 at :01 = 200 in 2 seconds; if sliding window: less exploitable; race conditions: concurrent requests sent simultaneously before rate limit increments; 50 concurrent requests: rate limit may only count first before blocking others. HTTP method bypass: rate limit on GET /resource; POST /resource same data but different method; separate counters per method. Response manipulation: 429 Too Many Requests response: client backs off; but: some clients respect Retry-After header; if Retry-After: 0 or small: send again immediately; Retry-After manipulation: some implementations vulnerable to forged response headers. Detection: unusual request patterns from single source (even across IPs if correlated by fingerprint); JA3/JA3S TLS fingerprint correlation; browser fingerprinting (consistent non-browser fingerprint across rotating IPs); request timing analysis (perfectly regular timing = automation); prevent: JWT or session-based rate limiting (harder to rotate than IP); multi-factor rate limiting (IP + user + endpoint + method); challenge suspected bots (CAPTCHA, JS challenge); monitor 429 error rate (spike = bypass attempt or misconfigured client); consistent request signature correlation across IPs.
What is a cybersecurity tabletop exercise design?

Tabletop exercise design: structured simulation of security scenario; guide participants through decision-making; identify gaps in plans and processes. Design principles: realistic but safe: scenario plausible and relevant to organisation; no actual systems affected; appropriate complexity: enough detail to be realistic; not so complex participants lost; escalating severity: start manageable; add complications; increase pressure; decision points: force participants to make real decisions; reveal process gaps; multi-team involvement: technical, management, legal, communications, finance; all roles exercise their functions. Scenario selection: choose based on: current threat landscape (ransomware most common); organisation sector (healthcare: PHI breach; finance: BEC fraud); recent incidents in industry peers; threat intelligence current advisories; risk assessment top risks; tabletop types: ransomware attack; BEC and wire transfer fraud; insider threat data exfiltration; third-party vendor breach; DDoS during critical period; physical security + cyber combined; nation-state targeted attack. Exercise structure (2-4 hours): (0:00-0:10) Introduction: objectives, ground rules, participants, facilitator, observer role, no phones/laptops (focus); (0:10-0:30) Scenario presentation: initial situation; inject 1: first indication of problem; what does team do?; discussion: actions, responsibilities, communications, escalation; (0:30-1:00) Complication: inject 2: scope worsens; attacker persistence found; data exfiltration discovered; press enquiry; customer complaint; discussion: revised actions; containment strategy; communications; (1:00-1:30) Crisis: inject 3: senior executive unavailable; third-party impacted; regulatory question; board notification needed; test: crisis communications; chain of command; external notifications; (1:30-2:00) Resolution and debrief: facilitate lessons learned; what went well?; what gaps found?; action items; who is responsible?; timeline? Facilitator role: guide not answer questions; inject additional complications when discussion stalls; probe: who makes this decision? What is the approval process? Who has authority to spend $X on IR retainer?; capture findings: scribe records key decisions, gaps, action items. Follow-up: written exercise report: scenario, participants, key decisions, gaps identified, action items; owners and deadlines; update IR plan based on gaps; retest updated plan in next exercise; schedule recurring exercises (quarterly for high-maturity; annual minimum).
How do you implement multi-factor authentication?

MFA implementation: add second factor to authentication; dramatically reduces account takeover risk; most impactful single security control. MFA types by security level (least to most secure): SMS OTP (one-time password): verification code sent via text message; weakest MFA; vulnerabilities: SIM swap attack (attacker ports number to their SIM), SS7 interception (telecom protocol vulnerability), real-time phishing (attacker forwards code in real time), malware on phone; still much better than no MFA; do not use for high-security applications; TOTP (Time-based OTP): Google Authenticator, Microsoft Authenticator, Authy; RFC 6238 standard; generates 6-digit code based on shared secret + time; valid for 30 seconds; phishable (real-time phishing: AiTM proxy captures code and uses immediately); more secure than SMS (no carrier dependency); push notification: Duo, Microsoft Authenticator push; user approves notification on phone; MFA fatigue: attacker sends many push requests; user accidentally approves; Duo with number matching: push shows number; user must enter same number in app; prevents accidental approval; number matching recommended; FIDO2/WebAuthn passkeys: hardware security key (YubiKey, Google Titan) or device biometric (Touch ID, Face ID, Windows Hello); phishing-resistant: bound to origin (domain); cannot be used on phishing site; strongest available; replaces password + second factor; no shared secret to steal. Implementation -- web application: TOTP setup: server generates secret; QR code or manual entry for authenticator app; store hashed secret server-side; on login: prompt for code; validate against current and previous window (account for time skew); backup codes: generate 10+ one-time backup codes; user stores securely; used if primary MFA device unavailable; FIDO2/WebAuthn (phishing-resistant): navigator.credentials.create() API call; device performs local verification; signed assertion sent to server; server verifies against stored credential; no secret transmitted; origin binding prevents phishing.
