Foundational books: The Web Application Hacker Handbook (Stuttard, Pinto): comprehensive web security reference; covers all web vulnerability classes with exploitation and defence; The Hacker Playbook series (Peter Kim): practical penetration testing; red team tactics; Social Engineering: The Science of Human Hacking (Christopher Hadnagy): social engineering techniques and defence; Penetration Testing (Georgia Weidman): beginner to intermediate pentesting; The Art of Intrusion (Mitnick): real-world attack stories; educational; Security Engineering (Ross Anderson): comprehensive security engineering from first principles; especially chapter on psychology of security; Silence on the Wire (Michal Zalewski): network security and passive reconnaissance. Advanced offensive: The Shellcoder Handbook (Anley et al.): binary exploitation deep dive; Hacking: The Art of Exploitation (Erickson): assembly, shellcode, exploits; A Guide to Kernel Exploitation (Perla, Oldani): kernel attack techniques; The Art of Memory Forensics (Ligh et al.): memory analysis and forensics; Rootkits and Bootkits (Matrosov): advanced persistent malware. Defensive: The Practice of Network Security Monitoring (Bejtlich): network security monitoring and analysis; Blue Team Handbook (Don Murdoch): defender reference; Applied Incident Response (Steve Anson): IR methodology; Red Team Development and Operations (Joe Vest): red team programme building. Standards and frameworks: NIST Special Publications (free): SP 800-53, SP 800-61, SP 800-115, SP 800-207; OWASP (free): Web Security Testing Guide (WSTG), Mobile Security Testing Guide (MSTG), Application Security Verification Standard (ASVS); MITRE ATT&CK (free): adversary tactics and techniques; CIS Controls (free with registration): prioritised security controls; SANS Reading Room (free): thousands of security papers on specific topics. Continuous learning: Krebs on Security (krebsonsecurity.com): investigative journalism on cybersecurity; Schneier on Security: expert commentary; threat intelligence blogs: CrowdStrike Intel, Mandiant, Palo Alto Unit 42, Recorded Future, Dragos; SANS Internet Stormcast (daily podcast: 5 minutes); Darknet Diaries (podcast): real attack stories; Black Hat and DEF CON talks: YouTube archives; key conferences: RSA, Black Hat, DEF CON, SANS CTI Summit, BSides (local), OffensiveCon; CTF (Capture The Flag): competitive hacking; learn by doing; platforms: PicoCTF, HackTheBox, TryHackMe, CTFtime.org; certifications roadmap: Security+ -> OSCP/GPEN -> (specialisation) cloud/DFIR/appsec.
What is active directory reconnaissance with BloodHound?

BloodHound: visualise Active Directory attack paths; graph-based analysis; find shortest path to Domain Admins; used by red teams and defenders. How it works: SharpHound (collector): run on domain-joined machine; collects AD data: users, groups, computers, GPOs, trusts, sessions (who is logged where), local admin rights; outputs JSON files; BloodHound (GUI): Neo4j graph database backend; import JSON; visualise AD as graph; nodes: users, computers, groups, domains, GPOs; edges: relationships (MemberOf, AdminTo, HasSession, CanRCE, WriteDACL, etc.); find attack paths: shortest path to Domain Admins from unprivileged user; attack path visualisation: click: Find Shortest Path to Domain Admins; BloodHound shows step-by-step: User A -> has session on Computer B -> local admin Computer C -> has ACL rights on Service Account D -> Service Account D MemberOf Domain Admins. Data collection with SharpHound: run as any domain user; SharpHound.exe --CollectionMethods All --OutputDirectory C:\temp; collection methods: Default (fast; sessions may miss), All (everything; longer), Session (user sessions), ACL (permissions), Trusts (domain trusts), LocalAdmin (local admin rights); Invoke-BloodHound (PowerShell); BloodHound.py (Linux; remote collection via LDAP and SMB): bloodhound-py -u user -p password -d corp.com -c all -dc DC.corp.com. Built-in queries: Find All Domain Admins; Find Shortest Paths to Domain Admins; Find Principals with DCSync Rights; Find Computers Where Domain Users Are Local Admin; Find AS-REP Roastable Users; Find Kerberoastable High Value Targets; Find Computers With Unsupported Operating Systems; Shortest Paths from Kerberoastable Users; custom Cypher queries: MATCH (u:User)-[:AdminTo]->(c:Computer) WHERE u.enabled=true RETURN u,c (find users with local admin rights); MATCH (u:User)-[r:GenericAll|GenericWrite|WriteDACL|WriteOwner|ForceChangePassword|AllExtendedRights]->(n) WHERE NOT u.admincount RETURN u,r,n (ACL misconfigurations). Defensive use: run BloodHound internally (BloodHound Enterprise or free version); find and fix: tier-0 exposure (paths from unprivileged to Domain Admins), high-value target exposure, overprivileged accounts; BloodHound Enterprise (SpecterOps): continuous monitoring; alert when new path appears; compare snapshots; metrics: attack path exposure score. Defensive remediation based on BloodHound: break attack paths: remove unnecessary local admin rights, reduce ACL permissions, implement tiered access model, enable Protected Users group, reduce session exposure (privileged users log in to privileged workstations only).
What is open redirect and how do you exploit it?

Open redirect: web application redirects user to URL supplied in parameter without validation; attacker uses trusted domain to redirect to malicious site. How it works: application: GET /redirect?url=https://trusted.com/dashboard (redirect after login); legitimate use: redirect user to intended page after authentication; attack: /redirect?url=https://attacker.com; user clicks link from trusted domain; browser follows redirect to attacker site; victim sees trusted domain in original link; trusts it. Why it matters: phishing: send link to victim: https://trusted-bank.com/redirect?url=https://evil-bank.com; email gateway sees trusted-bank.com; passes through; victim clicks; lands on phishing page; OAuth credential theft: OAuth callback URL; if vulnerable: attacker crafts: https://legitimate.com/redirect?url=https://attacker.com; send as OAuth redirect_uri; tokens redirected to attacker (if server does not validate redirect_uri strictly); SSRF: in some server-side fetching contexts open redirect chained to SSRF; bypass URL whitelist in SSRF protection. Bypass techniques: filter: /redirect?url=https://evil.com (blocked if filter checks); bypass: URL encoding: url=https%3A%2F%2Fevil.com; double encoding: url=https%253A%252F%252Fevil.com; backslash: url=https:\\evil.com; browser normalises; whitelisted domain bypass: url=https://trusted.com@evil.com (@ is userinfo; host is evil.com); url=https://trusted.com.evil.com; url=https://evil.com/trusted.com; javascript: url=javascript:alert(1) (in some contexts leads to XSS); null byte: url=https://evil.com%00.trusted.com. Finding open redirects: search for parameters: next, redirect, return, url, return_url, returnTo, goto, forward, destination, redirect_uri, next_url; common in: OAuth flows, login redirects, logout redirects; test: replace value with https://burpcollaborator.net; confirm redirect; tools: OpenRedirectBuster, ParamSpider + ffuf; Burp passive scanner catches many. Prevention: avoid user-controlled redirects: redirect to relative paths only; whitelist approach: maintain allowlist of permitted redirect URLs; validate against exact list; do not prefix-match (attacker uses trusted.com.attacker.com); relative URL only: redirect to path (/dashboard) not absolute URL; if absolute required: validate scheme (https only), hostname (must match own domain), no @; warn user: if must redirect externally: interstitial warning page You are being redirected to: [URL] with confirm button; URL parameterisation: encode destination as opaque token in DB; user cannot control actual URL.
What is buffer overflow and stack smashing?

Buffer overflow: write beyond allocated buffer boundary; corrupt adjacent memory; classic vulnerability leading to arbitrary code execution. How stack works: stack: LIFO memory region; grows downward; stack frame per function call: local variables, saved base pointer (SBP), return address, function arguments; buffer: fixed-size allocation for string or data; C functions: gets(), strcpy(), sprintf() do not check length. Stack buffer overflow: C code: char buffer[256]; gets(buffer); attacker input: 300 bytes + shellcode + return address pointing to shellcode; memory layout: buffer[256] then SBP then RIP (return address); overflow: write 256 bytes (fill buffer) + 8 bytes (overwrite SBP) + 8 bytes (overwrite RIP); attacker controls RIP; function returns; CPU jumps to attacker-controlled address; if attacker puts shellcode in buffer: jumps to shellcode; RCE; NOP sled: prepend NOP instructions before shellcode; return address into NOP sled; execution slides to shellcode; increases reliability. Protections and bypasses: stack canary: random value placed between buffer and return address; before function returns: check canary; if modified (overflow occurred): crash; bypass: information leak reveals canary value; overwrite with correct canary; format string vulnerability leaks canary; ASLR (Address Space Layout Randomisation): randomise base addresses of stack, heap, libraries; stack address unknown; bypass: info leak reveals stack address; brute force (32-bit ASLR: 16 bits entropy; feasible); partial overwrite (only last bytes of address); NX/DEP (No-Execute): stack and heap marked non-executable; cannot execute shellcode on stack; bypass: Return-Oriented Programming (ROP); instead of shellcode: chain existing code gadgets (sequences ending in RET); each gadget does small operation; chain achieves arbitrary computation without new code; ROP: find gadgets: ROPgadget, ropper, pwntools rop; chain: pop rdi; ret (set argument); system() address (execute /bin/sh); no executable shellcode needed; bypass ASLR + NX combined: need leak for ASLR; then ROP; ret2libc: return to system() in libc; pass /bin/sh string; classic NX bypass; RELRO: relocations read-only; prevents GOT (Global Offset Table) overwrite; Full RELRO: complete GOT protection. Practice environments: protostar (Exploit Education), pwn.college, pwnable.kr, pwnable.tw, CTF challenges; tools: pwntools (Python), gdb-peda/pwndbg/GEF, checksec (check binary protections).
What is threat intelligence sharing and formats?

Threat intelligence sharing: share indicators and threat knowledge between organisations; collective defence; faster response to campaigns. Why sharing: attackers reuse infrastructure (IPs, domains, malware) across victims; if one org detects and shares: others can block before attacked; defenders share; attackers already share tools and techniques; information sharing reduces asymmetry. Sharing formats: STIX (Structured Threat Information eXpression): XML/JSON format; standard for threat intel; STIX 2.1: current; objects: Indicator (IP, hash, pattern), Malware, Threat Actor, Campaign, Attack Pattern (ATT&CK techniques), Course of Action, Observed Data, Relationship; example: Indicator with pattern: [file:hashes.MD5 = abc123]; TAXII (Trusted Automated eXchange of Intelligence Information): protocol for sharing STIX over HTTPS; API: collections (groups of STIX objects), push and pull; MISP (Malware Information Sharing Platform): open-source; database and API for sharing indicators; widely used by ISACs and CERTs; event-based sharing; correlation engine; OpenIOC: Mandiant format; XML; indicator of compromise format; older; less widely used now; YARA: malware detection rules; shareable; community rules on GitHub (YARA-Rules project); Sigma: detection rules; shareable; converted to SIEM queries. Sharing communities: ISACs (Information Sharing and Analysis Centers): sector-specific; FS-ISAC (financial), H-ISAC (health), E-ISAC (energy), IT-ISAC; membership required; vetted members; high-quality sharing; CERTs (Computer Emergency Response Teams): national CERTs; US-CERT (CISA), NCSC (UK), BSI (Germany), ANSSI (France); share with critical infrastructure; FIRST (Forum of Incident Response and Security Teams): global CERT coordination; Traffic Light Protocol (TLP): colour-based sharing classification; TLP:RED (not for sharing beyond recipient), TLP:AMBER (limited disclosure to own organisation), TLP:AMBER+STRICT (limited to organisation and need-to-know), TLP:GREEN (community sharing), TLP:CLEAR (public); STIX objects include TLP marking. Technical sharing platforms: MISP: most widely deployed; OpenTAXII server; Anomali STAXX (free TAXII client); Recorded Future, Mandiant Advantage, Crowdstrike Intel: commercial with STIX/TAXII output; OpenCTI: open-source threat intelligence platform; graph-based; STIX 2.1; integrations with MISP, VirusTotal, MITRE ATT&CK. Challenges: trust: do not want to share vulnerability details with potential competitor; legal: GDPR (IP addresses = personal data?); classification: know what to share (indicators OK, internal network details not); indicator quality: stale indicators waste defender time; expiration timestamps on STIX objects; automation: consuming intel manually = too slow; SOAR integration: auto-block IPs from threat feeds; EDR integration: auto-add hashes to blocklist.
What is serverless security?

Serverless security: security challenges and controls for AWS Lambda, Azure Functions, Google Cloud Functions, and similar platforms. Serverless attack surface: function code vulnerabilities: injection in event processing, insecure dependencies, secrets in environment variables or code; misconfigured triggers: function triggered by unauthenticated source; over-permissive IAM role: function has broader AWS permissions than needed; SSRF from within function: function can reach IMDS (instance metadata service) in some runtimes; dependency vulnerabilities: same SCA risks as regular apps; cold start security: function initialisation; shared execution environment between invocations (but not between tenants); event injection: function processes untrusted data from SQS, SNS, API Gateway, S3 events; injection possible if data not validated. Common attack patterns: function takeover: exploit vulnerability in function code; execute code in function context; access function IAM role; escalate via over-permissive role; event injection: Lambda processes SQS message containing SQL injection or command injection; function queries database or executes system call with injected content; dependency confusion: function uses npm/pip packages; dependency confusion attack; CI/CD compromise: deploy malicious function code through compromised pipeline; secrets exposure: environment variables visible to anyone with Lambda GetFunctionConfiguration permission; secrets in code (hardcoded). Security controls: least privilege IAM: Lambda execution role only needs permissions for specific S3 bucket or DynamoDB table; not wildcard permissions; review with IAM Access Analyzer; function-level policies: resource-based policy restricts who can invoke function; limit to specific services or accounts; input validation: validate and sanitise all event data before processing; treat all event data as untrusted; secrets management: use AWS Secrets Manager or Parameter Store (SecureString); retrieve at runtime; not environment variables; dependency management: pin versions; scan with SCA tools (Snyk, npm audit, pip-audit); SBOM; timeout and concurrency limits: prevent runaway costs; protect from abuse; logging and monitoring: CloudWatch Logs for function output; X-Ray for tracing; CloudTrail for API calls (including invoke calls); GuardDuty for Lambda protection (2022): detect: unusual function activity, crypto mining in Lambda, data exfiltration from Lambda; Falco Serverless (experimental): detect anomalous syscalls in Lambda. Ephemeral security: Lambda execution environment shared across invocations (same function); residual data in /tmp (max 512MB): cleared between function environments but not between same warm instance invocations; do not store sensitive data in /tmp; clear sensitive variables after use; RASP equivalent: protego (now part of Datadog): function-level protection agent for Lambda.
What is digital forensics evidence handling?

Digital forensics evidence handling: collect, preserve, and analyse evidence maintaining chain of custody; admissibility in legal proceedings. Evidence types: disk images: full sector-by-sector copy; memory dumps: volatile RAM; network captures: PCAP; log files; mobile device images; cloud data. Chain of custody: document every hand that touches evidence; from collection to court; form: who collected, when, where, how; who received, when; who had access; break in chain: evidence potentially inadmissible; label every evidence item: unique ID, date, time, collector name. Evidence acquisition: first principle: do not alter original evidence; write blocker: hardware or software; prevents any write to evidence disk during imaging; verify original not modified; disk imaging: dd: dd if=/dev/sda of=image.dd bs=4M; dc3dd: dd with hashing; FTK Imager: GUI; cross-platform; EWF format (Expert Witness Format):.E01; includes metadata; widely supported; imaging order: most volatile first (RAM, then disk); RAM: most volatile; power off = gone; capture first; tools: WinPmem, DumpIt, Belkasoft RAM Capturer (Windows); AVML, LiME (Linux kernel module); cloud: API-based collection (AWS: EC2 snapshot, CloudTrail export, S3 access logs); Azure: disk snapshot, activity log export; mobile: logical (contacts, messages, app data) vs physical (full chip-off image); Cellebrite UFED, Oxygen Detective, Grayshift GrayKey (iOS). Hashing: MD5 and SHA-256 hash immediately after acquisition; hash of evidence file; hash must match throughout case; any change detected; forensic image integrity: hash acquired image; periodically re-verify hash; report: document hash values. Analysis environment: work on forensic copy (not original); mount image read-only: mount -o ro,loop image.dd /mnt/evidence; analyse copy; never execute code from evidence image on forensic workstation. Tools: Autopsy (open-source): GUI forensic platform; timeline, keyword search, hash analysis; Sleuth Kit: CLI forensic toolkit; file system analysis; Volatility: memory forensics; process analysis, network connections, artefacts from memory; EnCase (OpenText): commercial; widely accepted in courts; FTK (Forensic Toolkit, AccessData): commercial; database-backend for large cases; AXIOM (Magnet Forensics): user activity analysis; cloud evidence; Plaso: super timeline generator (log2timeline); correlate artefacts from many sources. Reporting: accurate, objective, reproducible; methodology documented; findings supported by evidence; screenshots and hash values; expert can be cross-examined; limitations stated clearly (what was not analysed, what was unknown).
What is a capture the flag (CTF) competition methodology?

CTF (Capture The Flag): cybersecurity competition; solve security challenges to get flags; learn skills; categories and methodology. CTF formats: Jeopardy: solve challenges across categories; each challenge has flag (string); earn points for each; Attack-Defense: each team has vulnerable server; attack others; defend own; King of the Hill: control server; maintain access; prevent others from taking over. Categories: web: XSS, SQL injection, SSRF, SSTI, XXE, deserialization, OAuth bypass, GraphQL; binary exploitation (pwn): buffer overflow, ROP chains, heap exploitation, format strings; reverse engineering (RE): decompile binary; understand algorithm; reproduce output; cryptography: decrypt ciphertext; find key; exploit weak crypto (timing attacks, mathematical flaws); forensics: analyse PCAP, disk image, memory dump; recover hidden data; steganography: data hidden in image, audio, video; OSINT: find information from public sources; miscellaneous. Web methodology: browse application; view source; check robots.txt, sitemap.xml; cookies and headers; try obvious: /admin, /flag, /backup; identify technology (Wappalyzer); Burp Suite: intercept; try injections in all fields; SQL: sqlmap or manual; LFI: path traversal; command injection; source code: if provided: read carefully; find injection points; logic flaws. Binary exploitation (pwn) methodology: checksec: identify protections (stack canary, ASLR, NX, RELRO, PIE); file: 32 or 64 bit? ELF, PE? strings: any useful strings, flags in binary?; disassemble: Ghidra or radare2; identify vulnerability: buffer overflow (gets, strcpy), format string (printf(user_input)), use-after-free; exploit: write exploit with pwntools; debug with gdb/pwndbg. Reverse engineering methodology: strings: any obvious flags or interesting strings; detect packing (UPX: unpack before analysis); Ghidra or IDA: decompile; find main; understand program logic; identify check (if input equals expected: print flag); recreate check in reverse; angr: binary analysis with symbolic execution; solve constraints automatically for correct input. Cryptography methodology: identify algorithm: cipher type, key size; known plaintext: if example input/output given; frequency analysis for substitution ciphers; CyberChef: try many decodings; factor RSA modulus if small (factordb.com); padding oracle; timing oracle; SageMath for math-heavy challenges. Tools: pwntools (Python exploit development), PwnDbg (GDB), Ghidra, angr, CyberChef, Burp Suite, Wireshark, Volatility, Autopsy. Resources: CTFtime.org: upcoming CTF list and past challenges; HackTheBox, TryHackMe: practice; picoCTF: beginner-friendly; past challenge writeups: learn from others.
What is application security programme for software development teams?

Application security programme: systematic approach to building secure software; integrate security throughout SDLC; developer-centric. Programme components: security requirements: define security requirements at project start; not as afterthought; ASVS (OWASP Application Security Verification Standard): comprehensive security requirements by level (L1 basic, L2 standard, L3 advanced); ASVS mapped to OWASP Top 10 and compliance requirements; NIST SP 800-64: security considerations in SDLC; requirement categories: authentication, session management, access control, cryptography, data protection, error handling, logging. Threat modelling in design: architecture review: security architect reviews design; threat model per service or significant feature; STRIDE per component; output: security requirements for implementation; prioritised risks; developer security training: language-specific: Secure Java, Secure Python, Secure JavaScript; OWASP Top 10 awareness; developers fix their own vulnerabilities (shift left culture); training platforms: Secure Code Warrior, Checkmarx Codeblossom, Kontra Application Security Training; annual minimum; role-specific: developers, QA, architects. Code review security: security review gate: high-risk changes reviewed by security team or security champion; automated: SAST runs on all PRs; manual: security checklist for sensitive code (authentication, authorisation, crypto, data handling); security champions: developer in each team with security focus; first point of contact; bridge between security team and developers; trained by security team; handle first-level code review. Vulnerability management: discovered vulnerabilities tracked in issue tracker; severity-based SLA: critical 24 hours, high 7 days, medium 30 days, low 90 days; secure design principles reference: fail securely (on error: deny rather than allow), defence in depth, principle of least privilege, complete mediation (check access every time, not once), separation of duties, minimise attack surface, do not trust services (validate third-party data), open design (security through obscurity not a control); pre-production security testing: SAST, DAST, SCA before release; penetration test for major features; third-party dependencies: SCA (Software Composition Analysis): Snyk, Dependabot, OWASP Dependency-Check; auto-PR for dependency updates; SBOM generated per release; metrics: vulnerabilities found per KLOC (thousand lines of code); SAST false positive rate; time to remediate by severity; % of features with threat model; % of high-risk changes with security review; developer security training completion rate; DAST coverage (% of API endpoints tested); penetration test finding count trend.
What is the difference between vulnerability, threat, and risk in cybersecurity?

Vulnerability, threat, and risk: foundational risk concepts; often confused; precise language matters for communication. Definitions: vulnerability: weakness in system, application, process, or control; exists regardless of attacker; examples: unpatched CVE in Apache, weak password policy, no MFA on VPN, unlocked server room door, misconfigured S3 bucket; threat: actor or event that could exploit a vulnerability; has capability and intent; types: threat actor (nation-state, cybercriminal, insider, hacktivist), threat event (phishing, ransomware, DDoS, insider data theft), natural (hurricane destroying data centre), accidental (employee mistake); risk: probability of threat exploiting vulnerability combined with impact if it does; risk = f(threat, vulnerability, impact); risk is not just vulnerability (vulnerability without threat = no risk); risk is not just threat (threat without vulnerability = no risk). Example illustration: vulnerability: web application has SQL injection; threat: financially-motivated cybercriminal group; impact: exposure of 1 million customer records; risk: $5M expected loss at 30% probability = $1.5M annual loss expectancy; same vulnerability, different risk context: vulnerability: SQL injection in internal HR tool; threat: limited; only internal employees; access controlled; impact: fewer records, less sensitive; risk: lower than internet-facing app with same vulnerability. Risk formula: qualitative: risk = likelihood x impact; 5x5 matrix (likelihood 1-5, impact 1-5); result: 1-25 risk score; map to Low/Medium/High/Critical; quantitative: FAIR model; annual loss expectancy (ALE) = SLE x ARO; Single Loss Expectancy (SLE): loss if single incident occurs; Annualised Rate of Occurrence (ARO): probability per year. Control reduces risk by: reducing likelihood: MFA (threat less likely to succeed), patching (vulnerability removed), monitoring (faster detection = less impact); reducing impact: backups (faster recovery), encryption (breach has less impact), segmentation (blast radius limited); residual risk: risk after controls applied; some risk always remains; must be accepted or transferred (cyber insurance). Risk management decisions: avoid: do not do the risky activity; accept: risk within appetite; mitigate: apply controls; transfer: cyber insurance, contract liability; risk appetite: executive-set threshold; risks above appetite must be mitigated or escalated for acceptance; risk register: track all identified risks; owner, rating, mitigations, residual risk, review date.
How do you scope a penetration test engagement?

Scoping defines what will and will not be tested; prevents legal issues and sets expectations. Scope components: (1) In-scope assets: IP ranges, domains, applications, API endpoints, network segments, physical locations; specify explicitly (10.0.0.0/24, app.company.com, mobile app v2.3). (2) Out-of-scope assets: systems too fragile to test (medical devices, OT/SCADA); third-party services not owned by client (AWS infrastructure itself, Cloudflare); shared hosting environments; explicitly list exclusions. (3) Testing types: external perimeter (from internet); internal network (from inside office or VPN); web application; social engineering; physical; cloud; explicitly agree which phases. (4) Testing methods: black-box (no prior knowledge); grey-box (credentials or network access provided); white-box (full documentation, source code, admin access). (5) Authorized testing windows: business hours vs off-hours; change freeze periods; holidays; some tests scheduled during maintenance windows. (6) Rules of Engagement (RoE): emergency contacts (24/7 phone if test causes outage); what to do on finding critical vuln (stop and call? continue?); tools allowed (no DoS tools against production?); geographic restrictions; data handling (no copying customer data). (7) Legal: signed Master Services Agreement (MSA) and Statement of Work (SoW); get-out-of-jail letter listing authorized tester names, test window, and scope; essential for external testers. Deliverables: report format, executive summary, technical findings with CVSS scores, remediation guidance, retest included?
How do you write a penetration test report?

Penetration test report structure: Executive Summary: 1-2 pages; non-technical language; business impact; overall risk rating; key findings summary; remediation priorities; suitable for C-suite and board. Scope and Methodology: what was tested (dates, systems, testing types); what was not tested; testing approach (black/grey/white box, tools used); team composition; any limitations encountered. Risk Rating: overall risk: Critical/High/Medium/Low/Informational; color-coded; methodology for rating (CVSS, DREAD, or custom); summary statistics (X Critical, Y High findings). Findings: for each vulnerability: unique finding ID; title; risk rating with CVSS score; affected systems; description (what is it?); evidence (screenshots, request/response, command output); business impact (what could attacker do?); remediation recommendation (specific, actionable); references (CVE, CWE, OWASP). Remediation roadmap: prioritised list; suggested SLAs (Critical: 7 days; High: 30 days; Medium: 90 days). Appendices: raw scan output; full request/response for web findings; tool commands used; network diagrams. Writing quality: findings must be reproducible from description alone; screenshots should include timestamps and domain; avoid jargon in executive sections; be specific about impact (not just possible data breach -- specify what data, how accessed, regulatory implications). Retest: after remediation, retest to verify fixes; document in addendum or separate retest report.
How do you approach privilege escalation on Linux?

Linux privilege escalation methodology: Enumeration: id (current user and groups); sudo -l (what can current user run as sudo); find / -perm -4000 2>/dev/null (SUID binaries -- run as owner, often root); cat /etc/passwd; cat /etc/shadow (if readable); ls -la /etc/cron* (cron jobs); env (environment variables -- PATH, LD_PRELOAD); cat /proc/1/environ (process 0 environment). SUID exploitation: if SUID binary allows arbitrary code execution or file read: /usr/bin/find -perm /u=s -exec /bin/sh -p ; or GTFOBins (gtfobins.github.io) has SUID exploit one-liners for common binaries (find, vim, nmap, cp, python, perl). Sudo exploitation: sudo -l shows (ALL) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/vim; use GTFObins sudo vim -c :!/bin/bash to get root shell. Cron jobs: world-writable script called by root cron: replace script with reverse shell; or PATH hijacking in cron -- if cron script calls ls without full path and attacker controls PATH. Writable /etc/passwd: if writable, add new root user: echo hackerx::0:0::/root:/bin/bash >> /etc/passwd; login as hackerx with no password. Weak file permissions: /etc/shadow readable by www-data; crack hashes; writable cron scripts. Kernel exploits: uname -r for kernel version; searchsploit local privilege escalation; DirtyCow (CVE-2016-5195) for older kernels; overlayfs CVE-2023-0386. LD_PRELOAD exploitation: if sudo preserves LD_PRELOAD: compile shared library that spawns shell; sudo LD_PRELOAD=/tmp/evil.so find. Tools: LinPEAS (LinPEAS.sh -- comprehensive auto-enumeration); linux-exploit-suggester (suggest kernel exploits based on version).
How do you approach privilege escalation on Windows?

Windows privilege escalation methodology: Enumeration: whoami /all (user, groups, privileges); systeminfo (OS version, patch level); wmic qfe list brief (installed patches -- find missing); net localgroup administrators (local admin members); wmic product get name,version (installed software with versions). Service exploitation: sc qc SERVICE_NAME (service config including binary path); if binary path writable: replace with malicious executable; or unquoted service path (C:\Program Files\My App\app.exe -- Windows tries C:\Program.exe, C:\Program Files\My.exe first; place executable in those paths). Weak permissions: icacls C:\path\to\service.exe (check if writable by current user); PowerUp: Invoke-AllChecks (PowerSploit -- comprehensive Windows privesc checker). Scheduled tasks: schtasks /query /fo LIST /v | find /i PATH (tasks running as SYSTEM with writable scripts). Token exploitation: if SeImpersonatePrivilege or SeAssignPrimaryTokenPrivilege (common for service accounts like IIS, SQL Server): use PrintSpoofer, RoguePotato, SweetPotato, or JuicyPotato to impersonate SYSTEM token. AlwaysInstallElevated: if policy set, MSI packages install with SYSTEM; msfvenom -p windows/x64/shell_reverse_tcp... -f msi -o evil.msi; msiexec /quiet /qn /i evil.msi. DLL hijacking: Windows searches PATH for DLLs; if directory in search path writable: place malicious DLL with expected name; application loads malicious DLL. UAC bypass: fodhelper.exe registry hijack; CMSTPLUA COM object; eventvwr.exe; rundll32 ShellExec_RunDLL; auto-elevating binaries that read from user-writable locations. Tools: WinPEAS.exe; PowerUp.ps1; SharpUp.exe; Seatbelt.exe.
How do you use sqlmap for automated SQL injection testing?

SQLmap: automated SQL injection detection and exploitation tool. Basic usage: sqlmap -u http://target.com/page?id=1 (test GET parameter); sqlmap -u http://target.com/page --data=id=1 (POST parameter); sqlmap -r request.txt (Burp-exported raw request -- handles any HTTP method and complex requests). Detection: sqlmap tests boolean-based, error-based, UNION-based, time-based blind, and stacked query injection; --level=5 --risk=3 (maximum coverage, more aggressive payloads); --dbms=mysql (hint database type to reduce payloads). Authenticated testing: --cookie=PHPSESSID=abc123 (session cookie); or --headers=Authorization: Bearer TOKEN. Database enumeration: --dbs (list all databases); --tables -D database_name (list tables); --columns -D db -T table (list columns); --dump -D db -T users (dump table); --dump-all (dump everything -- careful on production). OS and file operations (if DBA privileges): --os-shell (interactive OS shell via SQL injection -- requires FILE privilege); --file-read=/etc/passwd (read file via SQL); --file-write=shell.php --file-dest=/var/www/html/shell.php (write webshell). WAF bypass: --tamper=space2comment (replace spaces with SQL comments); --tamper=between (replace > with BETWEEN); --random-agent (random User-Agent); --delay=1 (slow down to avoid rate limiting); --tor (route through Tor). HTTPS and cookies: --ignore-proxy for direct connections; specify SSL cert if needed. Dumping hashes: if users table contains hashes, sqlmap --dump -D app -T users and --passwords will attempt to crack hashes automatically.
Explain the concept of threat modeling and how to perform it.

Threat modeling: structured process to identify security threats, prioritise them, and determine mitigations. Why: catching security issues at design phase is 10-100x cheaper than post-deployment. STRIDE model (Microsoft): Spoofing (impersonating another user or component); Tampering (modifying data in transit or at rest); Repudiation (denying having performed an action); Information Disclosure (exposure of sensitive data); Denial of Service (making system unavailable); Elevation of Privilege (gaining higher permissions). Process: (1) Define scope: what system? What are we protecting? What are the valuable assets and entry points? (2) Create data flow diagram (DFD): model how data flows through system; external entities (users, external services); processes; data stores; trust boundaries (dotted lines where privilege changes -- internet to DMZ, DMZ to internal). (3) Identify threats: for each element and trust boundary, apply STRIDE; brainstorm threats; PASTA (Process for Attack Simulation and Threat Analysis) alternative. (4) Rate and prioritise threats: DREAD (Damage, Reproducibility, Exploitability, Affected users, Discoverability) -- 1-10 scale; or CVSS-like scoring; prioritise high-risk threats. (5) Mitigations: for each threat, design control: authentication (spoofing), integrity checks/signing (tampering), audit logging (repudiation), encryption (disclosure), rate limiting/availability architecture (DoS), least privilege (EoP). (6) Validate: were mitigations implemented? Retest in next iteration. Tools: Microsoft Threat Modeling Tool (auto-generates STRIDE threats from DFD); OWASP Threat Dragon; draw.io for DFDs.
How do you test a thick client application?

Thick client (desktop application) security testing: architecture types: two-tier (client connects directly to database); three-tier (client connects to application server, which connects to database). Traffic interception: identify protocols used (HTTP/S, proprietary TCP, named pipes, COM, WCF); HTTP: configure Burp proxy; non-HTTP: use Echo Mirage or Wireshark to capture; Java RMI: intercept RMI traffic;.NET remoting or WCF: intercept with Wireshark or WireShark + SSL decryption. Memory analysis: Process Hacker (view process memory strings); attach to process with OllyDbg or x64dbg; strings in memory may reveal credentials, keys, business logic. Binary analysis: string extraction (strings.exe or PEStudio on Windows); decompilation:.NET binaries: dotPeek, dnSpy, JetBrains dotPeek -- view almost original C# source; Java: JAD, Procyon, Recaf; obfuscated binaries: Ghidra, IDA Pro, Binary Ninja for reverse engineering. Local storage: files created by application (AppData, ProgramData, temp); registry keys (HKCU, HKLM); SQLite databases; credential storage (DPAPI protected files, Credential Manager). Functionality testing: input validation (same attacks as web: SQLi, XSS in rendered HTML, command injection); business logic (can user access another user data?); authentication (remember-me tokens stored securely?); update mechanism (is update signed? MITM possible to inject malicious update?). DLL hijacking: identify DLLs loaded by application; check if writable path in DLL search order; plant malicious DLL for privilege escalation. Automation tools: MITM Proxy for HTTP; API Scanner for REST APIs; Wireshark + ssldump for TLS inspection.
How do you secure an API and what vulnerabilities to test for?

API security testing checklist: (1) Authentication: is authentication required for all sensitive endpoints? Test removing Authorization header; test with invalid/expired tokens; JWT vulnerabilities (alg:none, weak secret, jku injection). (2) Authorisation: IDOR -- change object IDs to other user IDs; test object-level (BOLA) and function-level (BFLA) access control; tenant isolation in multi-tenant APIs. (3) Rate limiting: brute-force login endpoint; send 1000 requests rapidly; should get 429; test distributed rate limiting (same request from different IPs). (4) Input validation: inject SQLi, XSS, command injection in all parameters; test with special characters in strings; integer overflow for numeric fields; nested JSON/XML for injection. (5) Excessive data exposure: does API return more fields than needed? Filter on client-side vs server-side; look for hidden fields in response (internal IDs, system fields, other user data). (6) Mass assignment: send extra fields in POST/PUT body that should not be user-settable; role=admin, verified=true, balance=9999. (7) Security headers: CORS misconfiguration (Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * with credentials); X-Content-Type-Options; Content-Security-Policy for APIs returning HTML. (8) Sensitive data in transport: PII in query string (gets logged); tokens in URL; check all responses for secrets. (9) API versioning: test old API versions (v1 may lack security controls added in v2); deprecated endpoints. (10) GraphQL specific: introspection enabled; batching attacks; depth limiting; SSRF via queries. Tools: Burp Suite; Postman for functional + security; OWASP ZAP; Arjun (hidden parameter discovery); Swagger UI + API fuzzing with Restler or CATS.
How do you test mobile deep links and URL scheme vulnerabilities?

Deep link security testing: deep links and URL schemes allow external apps and web pages to open specific app screens. Android Intent filters: defined in AndroidManifest.xml: <intent-filter><action android:name='android.intent.action.VIEW'/><data android:scheme='myapp' android:host='open'/></intent-filter>; accessible from any app on device or via web page. Testing: enumerate all URL schemes and deep links in AndroidManifest.xml or iOS Info.plist; test each with ADB: adb shell am start -W -a android.intent.action.VIEW -d 'myapp://open?redirect=https://attacker.com' com.target.app; check if deep link parameters are validated. Vulnerabilities: (1) Unvalidated redirect: myapp://login?redirect=https://attacker.com; after auth, redirects externally; open redirect via deep link. (2) XSS via deep link: myapp://webview?url=javascript:alert(1); if WebView loads URL from deep link parameter. (3) Fragment injection: myapp://settings?fragment=../admin; if app loads Fragment based on parameter, can access any Fragment regardless of auth. (4) Deeplink parameter injection into WebView: myapp://page?param=<script>; if param is directly rendered in WebView HTML. (5) Task hijacking: Android intent task affinity attack; malicious app with same task affinity intercepts deep link handling; allowTaskReparenting exploit. (6) iOS Universal Links (HTTPS-based): more secure; require server-side apple-app-site-association JSON file verification; fallback to web page if app not installed. Testing tools: Frida hooks to intercept deep link handling; logcat for debug output; Android Activity Inspector; iOS URL Scheme Fuzzer.
What is BGP hijacking and how does it work?

BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) is the routing protocol of the internet; connects Autonomous Systems (AS); based on trust -- ASes announce which IP prefixes they own; no cryptographic validation in original BGP. BGP hijacking: attacker announces IP prefix belonging to someone else; routers accept most specific or shortest AS path advertisement; traffic destined for victim IP routed to attacker instead. Types: (1) Prefix hijacking: attacker AS announces entire prefix owned by victim (e.g., announces 8.8.8.0/24 -- Google DNS); may receive some traffic depending on routing topology. (2) More specific prefix: announce more specific prefix (8.8.8.0/25 covers half of 8.8.8.0/24); routers prefer more specific routes; attacker captures all traffic to that half. (3) AS path manipulation: insert victim AS in path to create shorter apparent path; routers may prefer. Impact: intercept email (Amazon Route 53 BGP hijack 2018 -- attackers rerouted MyEtherWallet DNS traffic); denial of service; traffic analysis and decryption. Real incidents: Pakistan Telecom (2008) accidentally hijacked YouTube; China Telecom (2010, 2019) controversially rerouted US traffic through China; KrebsOnSecurity DDoS mitigation (attacker withdrew Prolexic routes). Detection: BGPmon; RIPE NCC BGP route monitoring; IRR (Internet Routing Registry) inconsistency alerts; RTBH (Remotely Triggered Black Hole) filtering. RPKI (Resource Public Key Infrastructure): cryptographic certificates attest which AS is authorised to announce each prefix; Route Origin Authorisation (ROA) signed by prefix owner; BGP routers with RPKI validation reject invalid announcements; adoption increasing but not universal; fully deployed RPKI would prevent most hijacks.
How do you attack Bluetooth devices?

Bluetooth attack surface: classic Bluetooth (BR/EDR for audio, file transfer) and BLE (Bluetooth Low Energy for IoT, fitness, proximity). Reconnaissance: hcitool scan (classic BT device discovery); hcitool lescan (BLE discovery); btlejack (BLE sniffing without prior knowledge of device); bluehydra (passive BT device discovery via monitoring). RFCOMM attacks: rfcomm connect TARGET_MAC CHANNEL (connect to SPP serial port profile; may not require pairing depending on device). SDP enumeration: sdptool browse TARGET_MAC (list supported Bluetooth profiles -- headsets, file transfer, serial port). Classic BT vulnerabilities: Blueborne (2017, CVE-2017-0781): remote code execution via BlueBorne vulnerabilities in Bluetooth stack of Android, Linux, iOS, Windows; no pairing required; worm-capable; most patched. KNOB (Key Negotiation of Bluetooth, CVE-2019-9506): downgrade encryption key entropy to 1 byte; brute-forceable; affects all BR/EDR devices; patch requires minimum key length. BLE vulnerabilities: GATT (Generic Attribute Profile) services often lack authentication; read/write characteristics without pairing; PoCs exist for popular IoT devices. Sweyntooth (2020): 11 BLE stack vulnerabilities in SoC vendors; deadlock, crash, or bypass pairing; affected pacemakers, blood glucose monitors, smart locks. Wiretapping: btsniffer; Wireshark with BTSnoop log; capture unencrypted BLE advertising and data packets; some BLE devices transmit medical data unencrypted. Tools: GATTacker (BLE MITM); Bettercap (BLE enumeration and exploitation); scapy with bluetooth module; Ubertooth One (hardware for promiscuous BT sniffing).
How do you perform network traffic analysis to find anomalies?

Network traffic analysis (NTA) for security: Capture sources: NetFlow/IPFIX (5-tuple metadata from routers/switches -- efficient, long retention, no payload); Zeek (open-source network analysis framework -- creates structured logs from PCAP: conn.log, dns.log, http.log, ssl.log, files.log, x509.log); PCAP (full packet capture -- high storage, complete analysis). Key Zeek logs: conn.log: source/dest IP, port, protocol, bytes, duration, connection state; dns.log: all DNS queries and responses -- detect C2, DGA, tunneling; http.log: HTTP requests with URIs, host, user-agent, response codes; ssl.log: TLS connections with server name (SNI), certificate, JA3 hash; files.log: file transfers with MD5/SHA1 hashes -- detect malware downloads; weird.log: protocol anomalies. JA3/JA3S fingerprinting: hash of TLS ClientHello/ServerHello fields; same TLS client produces same JA3 regardless of server; known malware JA3 hashes in threat intel; detect Cobalt Strike (JA3: 72a7c13d8cc8cbc4e69a1f1e14d9ae9f), Metasploit, custom RATs. Beaconing detection: RITA (Real Intelligence Threat Analytics): analyses Zeek conn.log; scores connections by beacon regularity, skew, duration, byte consistency; identifies C2 communication. Anomaly detection: DNS queries to high-entropy domains (DGA detection); large DNS responses (tunneling); unusual protocol on standard port (SSH over port 443 vs legitimate HTTPS); certificate anomalies (self-signed, expired, suspicious CN); high-volume connections to single destination (data exfiltration). Tools: Security Onion (all-in-one platform: Zeek, Suricata, Elastic/Kibana, Rita); Elastic Stack with Zeek beats; Splunk stream for network data.
Explain wireless intrusion detection and prevention systems.

Wireless IDS/IPS (WIDS/WIPS): detect and prevent unauthorized wireless activity. What to detect: rogue access points (unauthorized APs on corporate property using corporate network name or mimicking infrastructure); evil twin attacks (attacker AP with same SSID as legitimate); ad-hoc networks (peer-to-peer connections bypassing network controls); deauthentication floods (DoS -- attacker sends disassociation frames to disconnect clients); client anomalies (clients associating with unknown APs; clients probing for non-corporate SSIDs revealing home/travel network names). Detection methods: active scanning: WIDS sensor uses a radio to continuously scan all channels; detects APs and clients; compares against whitelist of known infrastructure; flags unknown APs. Passive monitoring: dedicated monitor mode interface; captures all 802.11 frames; detects management frame anomalies; correlates beacon, probe, association frames. Fingerprinting: identify AP and client by MAC OUI, supported rates, probe SSIDs, frame sequences; difficult to spoof perfectly. WIPS response: automatic deauthentication of rogue clients (controversial -- may interfere with legitimate networks); alert to security team; port-level shutdown if rogue AP plugged into wired network. 802.11w (Management Frame Protection, MFP): cryptographically signs management frames (deauth, disassociation); prevents deauth attacks; supported in WPA3 (mandatory) and WPA2 (optional). Products: Cisco Wireless (integrated WIPS with controller-based architecture); Cisco Meraki; Extreme Networks; Zebra/Motorola AirDefense; open-source: Kismet (passive WIDS). Zero-trust wireless: assume wireless is hostile; require VPN even on corporate WiFi; authenticate at application layer; segment wireless clients from internal network.
How does TLS 1.3 improve security over TLS 1.2?

TLS 1.3 (RFC 8446, 2018) improvements over TLS 1.2: (1) Removed weak cipher suites: eliminated all CBC cipher suites (BEAST, POODLE vulnerable); removed RC4, 3DES, DES, MD5; only AEAD ciphers allowed: AES-128-GCM, AES-256-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305; removed RSA key exchange (no PFS); removed DHE (only ECDHE). (2) Mandatory Forward Secrecy: only ECDHE key exchange; every session has fresh ephemeral keys; past sessions cannot be decrypted even with private key compromise. (3) Faster handshake: TLS 1.2: 2 round trips before application data; TLS 1.3: 1 round trip (1-RTT); 0-RTT resumption (send data in first message using session ticket -- but replay attacks possible; use only for idempotent requests). (4) Removed vulnerable features: no renegotiation (TLS renegotiation attacks); no compression (CRIME attack); no export-grade cryptography; no RSA PKCS#1 v1.5 (ROBOT attack). (5) Improved certificate handling: OCSP stapling required; reduced reliance on client certificate verification round-trips. (6) Encrypted handshake: certificate and extensions encrypted earlier in handshake than TLS 1.2; less metadata visible to passive observer. Challenges: middlebox compatibility: corporate TLS inspection proxies often break TLS 1.3 (cannot decrypt due to PFS); many enterprises still filter HTTPS by downgrading to TLS 1.2; ECH (Encrypted Client Hello) further hides SNI from network observers. Enabling TLS 1.3: Nginx: ssl_protocols TLSv1.2 TLSv1.3; OpenSSL 1.1.1+ required; Apache: SSLProtocol all -SSLv3 -TLSv1 -TLSv1.1.
What is DNSSEC and how does it work?

DNSSEC (DNS Security Extensions): adds cryptographic signatures to DNS records to ensure authenticity and integrity. Problem it solves: DNS responses can be spoofed (cache poisoning, BGP hijacking); no way to verify response came from authoritative server and was not tampered with. How it works: each DNS zone has a key pair; Zone Signing Key (ZSK) signs all resource records (A, MX, CNAME, etc.); Key Signing Key (KSK) signs the ZSK; creates chain of trust from root zone downward. Record types: DNSKEY: contains public key(s) for zone; RRSIG: cryptographic signature over a set of resource records (signed with ZSK); DS (Delegation Signer): hash of child zone DNSKEY; stored in parent zone; links trust from parent to child; NSEC/NSEC3: authenticated denial of existence (proves a name does not exist). Validation chain: resolver starts at root zone (implicitly trusted -- 13 root key operators); root DS points to.com ZSK;.com DS points to example.com ZSK; resolver validates RRSIG on every DNS response using DNSKEY. DNSSEC deployment: root zone signed since 2010; most TLDs signed; major ISP resolvers validate DNSSEC; enables DANE (DNS-based Authentication of Named Entities) for certificate pinning via TLSA records; DoH (DNS-over-HTTPS) encrypts DNS queries but DNSSEC validates authenticity; complementary. Limitations: does not encrypt DNS queries (only authenticates); complex to manage zone signing; key rollovers require careful coordination; zone enumeration with NSEC (NSEC3 with opt-out mitigates); software complexity introduced bugs (BIND vulnerabilities in DNSSEC validation).
Explain common attack techniques against VPNs.

VPN attack surface and exploitation techniques: (1) Authentication attacks: IPsec/IKEv1 aggressive mode: pre-shared key hash exposed without authentication; crack hash offline (ike-scan, psk-crack); eliminate by requiring certificates or IKEv2. SSL VPN login brute force: if no lockout or rate limiting on portal login; Hydra, Burp Intruder. Password spraying against ActiveDirectory-integrated VPN: one attempt per user per lockout period. (2) Vulnerability exploitation: Pulse Secure (CVE-2019-11510): unauthenticated arbitrary file read; read /etc/passwd and VPN session files; extract user passwords; widely exploited by APT groups. Citrix ADC (CVE-2019-19781): directory traversal RCE; no authentication required; Shodan showed 80,000 vulnerable systems. Fortinet FortiOS (CVE-2018-13379): unauthenticated SSL VPN path traversal; read sslvpn_websession files containing cleartext credentials. Palo Alto GlobalProtect (CVE-2024-3400): unauthenticated OS command injection; CVSS 10.0; exploited in the wild as zero-day. (3) Split tunneling exploitation: if VPN uses split tunneling (only certain traffic through VPN), attacker on same network segment as VPN client can access client via non-VPN interface; reach internal resources the VPN client can access. (4) Post-compromise: once VPN gateway compromised: dump active session database (usernames, auth tokens); move laterally to internal network; install persistent backdoor. (5) Certificate validation: if VPN client does not validate server certificate: fake VPN server, capture credentials. Defense: MFA on VPN; certificate-based auth; patch immediately (VPN vulns are high-value targets); monitor for unusual connection volumes; ZTNA replacing traditional VPN.
Explain the APT28 (Fancy Bear) threat actor group.

APT28 (Fancy Bear, Sofacy, Pawn Storm, Sednit, Strontium): Russian GRU (military intelligence) Unit 26165 and 74455 sponsored threat actor. Active since at least 2004; one of most sophisticated and prolific APT groups. Notable operations: 2016 US Presidential Election: spearphishing attacks on DNC, DCCC, Clinton campaign staff; compromised John Podesta Gmail (spearphishing via Google Docs link); Guccifer 2.0 front released stolen documents; Mueller indictment named 12 GRU officers. 2014-2017 Ukraine: BlackEnergy/Industroyer attacks on Ukrainian power grid (2015, 2016 blackouts); Olympic Destroyer (2018 Pyeongchang) false flag. German Bundestag (2015): compromised parliamentary networks; exfiltrated data. MH17 disinformation: hacked Bellingcat researchers. TTPs: initial access via spearphishing (Fancy Bear favors credential harvesting pages mimicking Google, Microsoft login); zero-day exploits; custom malware: X-Agent (cross-platform implant for Windows, macOS, Linux, iOS, Android), X-Tunnel, Sofacy/GAMEFISH, LoJax (UEFI rootkit -- first in wild); living-off-the-land (PowerShell, WMI); Tor for C2; credential harvesting via MiMiKatz; lateral movement via PtH. Industry tracking: APT28 by Mandiant; Fancy Bear by CrowdStrike; Sofacy by Kaspersky/ESET; Strontium by Microsoft; Pawn Storm by Trend Micro -- same group. Detection: X-Agent indicators (specific registry keys, mutex names); GAMEFISH network signatures; UEFI scanning for LoJax; spearphishing domain patterns.
What is the Lazarus Group and what are their notable attacks?

Lazarus Group: North Korean state-sponsored threat actor attributed to DPRK Reconnaissance General Bureau; financially motivated (cryptocurrency theft to fund DPRK programs) and espionage/sabotage. Notable attacks: Sony Pictures (2014): destroyed infrastructure (Shamoon-like wiper malware), leaked films, emails; damage $35M+; retaliation for film mocking Kim Jong-un. Bangladesh Bank Heist (2016): compromised Bangladesh Bank SWIFT network; submitted fraudulent $951M transfer requests; $81M stolen before detected. WannaCry (2017): global ransomware outbreak; 200,000+ systems in 150 countries; NHS UK severely impacted; exploited EternalBlue (NSA-developed SMB exploit); blamed on Lazarus by US, UK, Australia. Crypto exchange thefts ($2B+ total): AppleJeus supply chain attack (fake trading app); Axie Infinity Ronin bridge hack ($625M, 2022); Harmony bridge hack ($100M, 2022). Sub-groups: Bluenoroff (financial theft, SWIFT attacks); Andariel (espionage, destructive attacks on South Korea); Hidden Cobra (US government name). TTPs: spearphishing with malicious documents (macro-laden Word docs); LinkedIn fake job offer social engineering; custom malware (FALLCHILL, HARDRAIN, BADCALL, AppleJeus); watering hole attacks; SWIFT manipulation via custom malware injected into legitimate SWIFT Alliance software; cryptocurrency mixing for money laundering (Tornado Cash, ChipMixer). Detection: unique malware families; DPRK-specific network infrastructure; fake crypto/DeFi applications targeting financial professionals.
Explain the FIN7 cybercrime group and their operations.

FIN7 (also Navigator, Carbanak, Carbon Spider): sophisticated financially motivated cybercrime group; responsible for $1B+ in theft from financial institutions and retail. Operations: targeted banks and payment card processors globally with Carbanak malware (2013-2018): compromised bank employee workstations, recorded screen activity at ATMs, manipulated SWIFT transfers, instructed ATMs to dispense cash on demand; ~100 financial institutions in 30 countries; $900M+ stolen. Retail targeting: restaurant chains, hotel chains (Applebee's, Chili's, Arby's, Saks Fifth Avenue, Jason's Deli, Noodles & Company, Red Robin); compromised POS (Point of Sale) systems; exfiltrated payment card data; created payment card shop to monetise; millions of cards stolen. TTPs: initial access: highly targeted spearphishing to restaurant/hotel managers; subject lines: complaint about food, job application, catering inquiry; malicious attachments (macro Word docs,.LNK files with obfuscated commands); custom tools: CARBANAK/ANUNAK backdoor (sophisticated, persistent, screen capture, video recording); BATELEUR (JavaScript backdoor); GRIFFON (lightweight JavaScript RAT); Cobalt Strike for post-exploitation; very patient -- months of reconnaissance before monetisation; clear escalation path from initial access to domain admin. Law enforcement: 2018 three Ukrainian nationals arrested; 2020 two more arrested; one extradited to US; multiple members still operating. Defense lessons: anomalous RDP connections from server; ATM software changes; unusual outbound connections from payment processing systems; phishing simulation training.
How do you identify and attribute a threat actor?

Threat actor attribution: process of identifying who is responsible for a cyber attack. Levels: tactical (who is currently attacking?), operational (same actor as previous campaign?), strategic (nation-state or criminal? what is their goal?). Attribution evidence: Technical indicators: unique malware code reuse across campaigns (code similarities, shared libraries, same obfuscation technique, mutex names); infrastructure overlaps (same IP, domain, ASN used in multiple campaigns); TTPs (specific attack chain, tooling, exploits preferred by actor); timing patterns (working hours, holidays consistent with a timezone or specific country). Linguistic analysis: error messages, comments in code, keyboard layout artifacts (Cyrillic key slip), compilation metadata. Operational security mistakes: developers log into personal accounts from malware C2 infrastructure; use of personal email in domain registration; metadata in documents (author name, organisation); geolocation of login activity. Diamond Model: adversary (who) + capability (what tools) + infrastructure (where) + victim (who targeted) = complete picture for attribution. Challenges: false flags (attackers plant evidence pointing to other actors; Olympic Destroyer used North Korean-looking code but attributed to Russia); shared tools (criminal and state actors use same commercial tools -- Cobalt Strike, Metasploit; undermines tool-based attribution); proxy infrastructure (VPNs, Tor, hacked third-party servers); intelligence gaps (classified human intelligence often drives government attribution). Standards: STIX 2.1 Intrusion Set for expressing attribution; MITRE ATT&CK groups for public attribution; Mandiant, CrowdStrike, and government agencies publish attribution reports with varying evidence levels. Legal standard vs intelligence standard: beyond reasonable doubt (criminal prosecution) vs more likely than not (intelligence assessment).
How do you configure and use Splunk for security monitoring?

Splunk SIEM configuration for security operations: Data ingestion: universal forwarder installed on every endpoint; syslog for network devices and Linux; Heavy forwarder for high-volume sources; Splunk Connect for Kubernetes; Windows Event Logs: Security, System, Application, PowerShell; Sysmon: detailed process, network, registry events; add-ons (TAs) normalize data to Common Information Model (CIM). Search Processing Language (SPL): index=windows EventCode=4624 Logon_Type=3 | stats count by src_ip dest_ip Account_Name | sort -count; rex for regex extraction; eval for computed fields; rex field=message "Audit (?P<action>\w+)"; tstats for accelerated search on large datasets; join, append for combining datasets. Alerts: savedsearches.conf or GUI; scheduled search + threshold trigger (count > 10 in 5 min); real-time alerts; action: email, webhook (PagerDuty, Jira), run script (automated response). Notable alerts: Splunk Enterprise Security (ES) creates Notable Events in Incident Review; analyst reviews, assigns, investigates; risk scoring accumulates risk per user or system. Key security searches: 4625 (failed logon) by user: failed logons by user -- find password spray (many users same source); 4724 (password reset) spike; 7045 (service install) -- new services (malware persistence); DNS to high-entropy domain: index=dns | eval domain_len=len(query) | where domain_len > 50; baseline deviation: sourcetype=WinEventLog:Security EventCode=4624 | timechart span=1h count | anomalydetection. Dashboards: SOC dashboard with key metrics; per-analyst incident queue; threat hunting dashboard. Common add-ons: Splunk ES; Splunk ITSI; TA-Windows; TA-Sysmon; TA-CrowdStrike; TA-Palo Alto.
Explain how to use the MITRE ATT&CK framework for detection engineering.

Detection engineering using MITRE ATT&CK: for each ATT&CK technique relevant to your threat model, build detection rules. Process: (1) Prioritise techniques: identify threat actors targeting your sector; pull their ATT&CK techniques from ATT&CK Groups page; focus detection on most likely techniques (not all 700+). (2) Research data sources: ATT&CK technique page lists data sources required for detection (Process Creation for T1059 Command and Scripting Interpreter; Network Traffic for T1071 C2); ensure those sources are collected. (3) Write detection rule: test-driven approach: set up lab; execute technique; observe artifacts; write rule to catch those artifacts; verify rule fires; test against clean baseline to check FP rate. (4) Validate: run test tool like Atomic Red Team (atomicredteam.io) which has test scripts for each ATT&CK technique; run atomic test; confirm detection fires. Example detection for T1003.001 (LSASS Memory): Sysmon Event 10 (ProcessAccess) where TargetImage contains lsass.exe and GrantedAccess = 0x1010 or 0x1038 (read process memory); Sigma rule: logsource -- category: process_access windows; detection -- selection: TargetImage: '*\lsass.exe'; GrantedAccess: '0x1010|0x1038'; filter: SourceImage: 'C:\Windows\*'; condition: selection and not filter. Sigma: vendor-agnostic detection rule language; write once, convert to Splunk SPL, Elastic KQL, QRadar AQL, Microsoft Sentinel KQL; Sigma HQ GitHub has thousands of community rules. ATT&CK Navigator coverage: import rules into Navigator; colour-code by detection confidence; identify gaps; visualise coverage vs threat actor techniques. Continuous improvement: threat hunt finds new TTP; new rule written; added to detection library; coverage increases.
What is SOAR (Security Orchestration, Automation, and Response)?

SOAR: platforms that automate security operations workflows, integrate security tools, and orchestrate response actions. Components: (1) Orchestration: connect disparate security tools via APIs; Splunk SOAR (formerly Phantom), Palo Alto XSOAR, Microsoft Sentinel SOAR, Swimlane, IBM Resilient; pre-built integration apps for 300+ tools (VirusTotal, SentinelOne, CrowdStrike, ServiceNow, Jira). (2) Automation: run automated actions without human intervention; trigger on SIEM alert; run enrichment, containment, notification automatically; reduce MTTR (mean time to respond) from hours to minutes. (3) Case Management: centralise incident data; investigation notes; evidence; analyst assignment; SLA tracking. Playbooks: defined workflows for specific alert types; common SOAR playbooks: Phishing response: alert received -> extract URLs/attachments -> check VirusTotal -> if malicious: block URL on proxy, isolate endpoint, notify user, create ticket, notify manager; Malware alert: alert -> get process info from EDR -> check hash -> if known malicious: isolate host, dump memory, create P1 incident ticket, page on-call analyst; Brute force: alert -> get source IP -> check reputation -> if external: block IP on firewall, add to watchlist -> check if any account successfully authenticated during spray -> if yes: disable account, force password reset. Automation value: eliminate repetitive analyst tasks; L1 spends 40% of time on alert triage that can be automated; reduce analyst burnout; increase alert handling capacity; ensure consistent response (humans skip steps under pressure, playbooks do not). Metrics: alerts handled per analyst per day (before/after SOAR); MTTD/MTTR improvement; automation rate (% of alerts fully automated without human action).
How do you implement a data loss prevention (DLP) program?

DLP (Data Loss Prevention): tools and processes to prevent sensitive data from leaving the organisation without authorisation. Data classification: first, classify data by sensitivity (Public, Internal, Confidential, Restricted/Secret); tag documents with metadata; DLP policies enforce rules based on classification. Content inspection techniques: regular expressions (regex): credit card patterns (16 digits, Luhn algorithm valid), SSN (XXX-XX-XXXX), passport numbers; keyword matching (secret, classified, confidential); fingerprinting (hash of sensitive document; detect copies even if reformatted); machine learning classification. DLP deployment points: Network DLP: inline on email gateway, web proxy, upload traffic; inspect outbound for sensitive content; block or quarantine; alert analyst; endpoint DLP: agent on laptop; monitor file copy to USB, upload to cloud storage (Google Drive personal, Dropbox), print, screen capture; Cloud DLP (CASB -- Cloud Access Security Broker): API integration with cloud services (Microsoft 365, Google Workspace, Box); monitor and control data in cloud; also intercept cloud access from browser. Common DLP use cases: PCI DSS (prevent cardholder data exfiltration); HIPAA (PHI protection); IP protection (source code, formulas, strategic plans); GDPR (EU personal data). Email DLP: inspect outbound email body and attachments; prevent sending PII to personal email; detect accidental or malicious data egress; Microsoft Purview Information Protection, Proofpoint DLP, Mimecast. Challenges: false positives (financial reports legitimately contain credit card patterns); encryption (DLP cannot inspect encrypted content it does not control -- endpoint agent required); encryption-in-transit (need SSL inspection for HTTPS traffic); user experience impact (quarantine delays legitimate email). Incident handling: DLP alert -> review content -> determine intent (accidental vs malicious) -> escalate if malicious -> coordinate with HR/legal.
Explain memory-safe languages and why they matter for security.

Memory safety: programs written in C and C++ are vulnerable to memory corruption bugs (buffer overflows, use-after-free, double free, null dereference) because they give programmers direct memory control without automatic bounds checking. Security impact of memory unsafety: ~70% of vulnerabilities in Microsoft products, Google Chrome, and Android are memory safety bugs; exploited for RCE, privilege escalation, information disclosure; entire exploit categories (stack/heap overflow, ROP chains) exist because of memory unsafety. Memory-safe languages: Rust: systems programming language with compile-time memory safety guarantees via ownership, borrowing, and lifetimes; no garbage collector (zero-cost abstraction); unsafe blocks allowed when needed; increasingly adopted for OS kernels (Linux 6.1 added Rust), browsers (Firefox components), embedded systems; AWS, Google, Microsoft, Cloudflare using Rust for security-critical code. Go: garbage-collected; bounds checking; no pointer arithmetic; null-safe type system (no null pointers, uses zero values); simpler than Rust; Kubernetes, Docker, many cloud-native tools. Java, Python, C#: garbage-collected; bounds-checked arrays; no raw pointer manipulation; historically safe from memory bugs but have other vulnerability classes (injection, deserialization). Memory safety enforcement options for C/C++: Address Sanitizer (ASan): compile-time instrumentation detecting buffer overflows, use-after-free at runtime; used in testing but too slow for production. Control Flow Integrity (CFI): limits valid call targets; reduces ROP gadget exploitation. GCC/Clang -fstack-protector: stack canary detects stack buffer overflows. US CISA and NSA recommend memory-safe languages for new code; Biden Executive Order 14028 promotes secure software development.
What is fuzzing and how is it used for vulnerability research?

Fuzzing (fuzz testing): automated technique sending random, malformed, or unexpected input to a program to find crashes, hangs, or unexpected behavior indicating vulnerabilities. Types: (1) Black-box fuzzing (dumb fuzzing): send completely random data to target; simple; low coverage; find obvious bugs. (2) Mutation-based: start with valid inputs; mutate them (flip bits, change values, insert bytes); more targeted than random; common for file format fuzzing. (3) Generation-based: generate inputs from specification/grammar; valid structure but with invalid values; better for complex protocols. (4) Coverage-guided (grey-box): instrument program to track which code paths executed; guide fuzzer to explore new paths; most effective; foundation of modern fuzzing. Coverage-guided tools: AFL++ (American Fuzzy Lop++): state of the art; instruments binary or source; genetic algorithm to evolve inputs; find memory corruption bugs; used to find thousands of CVEs. LibFuzzer: in-process fuzzer; part of LLVM; target function receives random bytes; fast (no process spawn per test case); used by Chromium, OpenSSL, many projects. Honggfuzz: supports hardware-based coverage; works with closed-source binaries. OSS-Fuzz: Google continuous fuzzing for critical open-source; fuzzes 1000+ projects; found 10,000+ vulnerabilities. Targets: file parsers (images, documents, PDF, audio -- high attack surface, complex parsing); network protocol implementations; compression libraries; cryptographic libraries; operating system kernels. Sanitizers: compile with ASan (detect buffer overflows), UBSan (undefined behavior), MemorySanitizer (uninitialised reads); without sanitizers, many bugs cause silent misbehavior rather than crash. Crash triage: deduplicate crashes (address-based or stacktrace-based); asan output shows allocation/free stack for UAF; root cause analysis for exploit development.
How do you exploit UEFI firmware vulnerabilities?

UEFI (Unified Extensible Firmware Interface): modern firmware replacing BIOS; more powerful, complex, and attackable. Attack surface: (1) SPI flash: UEFI firmware stored in SPI flash chip; if SPI write protection misconfigured (chipset registers), attacker with kernel access can overwrite firmware. (2) Secure Boot bypass: Secure Boot verifies bootloader and OS kernel signatures; bypasses: revoked but still accepted EFI binaries (BlackLotus exploits CVE-2023-24932 -- Windows Secure Boot bypass); BootHole (CVE-2020-10713) buffer overflow in GRUB2 bootloader; vendor-specific vulnerabilities in Secure Boot implementation; MOK (Machine Owner Key) enrollment abuse. (3) SMM (System Management Mode) vulnerabilities: CPU enters SMM on SMI (System Management Interrupt); executes firmware code at highest privilege (ring -2); if SMM code has vulnerabilities (buffer overflows in SMM handlers), attacker from ring 0 (OS kernel) can execute code in SMM; SMM code can modify UEFI and bypass all OS-level security. Notable UEFI malware: LoJax (2018, APT28): first in-wild UEFI rootkit; persistence survives OS reinstall and disk replacement; modified legitimate Lojack (anti-theft) firmware; replaces SPI flash. BlackLotus (2023): first in-wild Secure Boot bypass; runs on fully-patched Windows 11; disables Bitlocker, Defender, Hypervisor-Protected Code Integrity; sold on dark web as crimeware kit. MoonBounce (2022, APT41): UEFI implant in SPI flash firmware. Detection: fwupd/LVFS firmware version tracking; chipsec security checker for UEFI vulnerabilities; BIOS Integrity Measurement (BIM); EDR agent reports UEFI hash changes. Defense: enable Secure Boot with UEFI Secure Boot; keep firmware updated; enable SMM_BWP (BIOS Write Protect); Intel Boot Guard fuses (one-time programmable root of trust).
Explain kernel exploitation techniques.

Kernel exploitation: compromising the operating system kernel to achieve ring 0 privilege from user space. Why valuable: kernel compromise = full system control; disable security software; load rootkit; read any process memory; persist through reboots. Linux kernel vulnerabilities: race conditions (TOCTOU -- time-of-check-time-of-use in system calls); use-after-free in kernel objects (slab allocator exploitation); integer overflows in privilege checks; type confusion in ioctl handlers; null pointer dereference (mmap NULL page was exploitable pre-mmap_min_addr). CVE examples: Dirty Cow (CVE-2016-5195): race condition in copy-on-write; write to read-only memory mapped file; root from any user; very reliable; widespread exploitation. Dirty Pipe (CVE-2022-0847): Linux kernel 5.8-5.16; write to arbitrary files including /etc/passwd and SUID binaries; root privesc; fast and reliable. Overlayfs (CVE-2023-0386): local privilege escalation; widespread in Ubuntu, container environments. Windows kernel exploitation: KASLR (Kernel Address Space Layout Randomization): kernel base address randomised; must leak kernel address (e.g., via NtQuerySystemInformation, user-to-kernel memory disclosure); Pool corruption: non-paged pool and paged pool; overflow pool header corrupts adjacent allocations; Windows 10+ pool hardening made more difficult; Exploited in wild: CVE-2021-34527 PrintNightmare, CVE-2022-21882 Win32k EoP. Kernel protections: SMEP (Supervisor Mode Execution Prevention): kernel cannot execute user-space code; ROP required; SMAP (Supervisor Mode Access Prevention): kernel cannot read/write user-space without explicit permission; KPTI (Kernel Page Table Isolation): meltdown mitigation; kernel and user page tables separated; KASLR + kASLR bypass via leaks. Mitigations making exploitation harder: lockdown LSM (Linux 5.4+); seccomp; kernel CFI (Clang-based Control Flow Integrity in Android kernel).
What are the security considerations for embedded systems and IoT?

Embedded/IoT security challenges: resource constraints (limited CPU, RAM, no MMU on some); long lifecycle (10-20 years, infrequent updates); physical access; network connectivity (attack surface without traditional security tooling). Common vulnerabilities: (1) Default credentials: admin/admin, admin/password, root/root, empty password; botnets (Mirai) compromised 600,000 routers/cameras with default credentials; enumerate via Shodan; test with Hydra. (2) Outdated firmware: vendor stops supporting product; known CVEs never patched; check firmware version against CVE database. (3) Unencrypted update channels: firmware downloaded over HTTP; MITM injects malicious firmware; verify signature before installing. (4) Hardcoded backdoors: vendor leaves debug accounts (user: admin, password: Sup3r5ecret123) for manufacturing; often found via firmware reverse engineering. (5) Exposed debugging interfaces: JTAG, UART serial port exposed on PCB; physical access yields root shell; common on routers, IP cameras. (6) Insecure protocols: Telnet instead of SSH; FTP instead of SFTP; HTTP instead of HTTPS; no TLS on MQTT. (7) Memory corruption: C/C++ firmware without protections; buffer overflows in parsing HTTP headers, UPnP, SNMP. Firmware analysis: download from vendor website; binwalk -e firmware.bin (extract filesystems); Squashfs/JFFS2 extraction; strings for hardcoded credentials and URLs; Ghidra for reverse engineering custom code; EMBA (embedded analyzer tool) automated. Attack tools: routersploit (exploit framework for embedded devices); Shodan for discovery; nmap for port scanning. Secure design: secure boot (verify firmware signature); encrypted storage; secure OTA update channel; ASLR/NX if architecture supports; principle of least functionality.
Explain how modern antivirus and EDR solutions detect malware.

AV/EDR detection layers: (1) Static analysis: file hash matching against known malware database; fast but misses polymorphic/metamorphic malware; vendor updates signatures continuously. YARA rules: pattern matching on byte sequences and strings; detect malware families by characteristic patterns even in modified samples. Machine learning on PE headers: entropy, import table, section names, size anomalies; detect packed malware (high entropy sections) and unusual imports. (2) Dynamic/Behavioral analysis: sandbox execution: detonate sample in isolated VM; observe behavior: file creation, registry changes, network connections, process injection; Cuckoo Sandbox, Joe Sandbox, Any.run, Hybrid Analysis; sandboxes subject to evasion (check for VM artifacts). Behavior monitoring (EDR): hook system calls at kernel level; monitor process creation, file operations, registry, network, memory allocation; alert on suspicious patterns: word.exe spawning cmd.exe; powershell.exe with encoded commands; process injection (WriteProcessMemory + CreateRemoteThread); mass file rename (ransomware). (3) Memory scanning: scan running process memory for known malware signatures or suspicious patterns; detect fileless malware that never touches disk; Malfind (Volatility): MZ header in unexpected memory regions with execute bit. (4) Network detection: C2 traffic signatures in IDS/IPS; JA3 TLS fingerprints; DNS request patterns; anomalous outbound connections. (5) AMSI (Antimalware Scan Interface): OS hook for PowerShell, VBScript, JScript; script content scanned before execution; catches obfuscated malicious scripts; attackers attempt AMSI bypass. (6) ML-based anomaly: baseline normal behavior; alert on deviations; reduces reliance on signatures; catches unknown threats.
What is Living Off the Land (LOLBAS) and how do attackers use it?

LOLBAS (Living Off the Land Binaries And Scripts): attackers use legitimate OS binaries and scripts to execute malicious actions; evades detection because legitimate tools are whitelisted.
